shelves.title: Albuminuria thresholds & progression to CKD stage 3 Deposit #2 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Where does albuminuria risk actually begin — and what drives progression?
shelves.balance: Risk begins well inside the “normal” range — progression risk roughly doubles above a urine albumin of ~ 8.4 mg/g in type 2 diabetes, far below the standard 30 mg/g boundary, which is a consensus classification line rather than a risk inflection. Over decades, blood pressure drives albuminuria up, while blood pressure, smoking, and cholesterol drive kidney function down — and falling kidney function mechanically raises measured albuminuria on its own.

cards.headline: Where albuminuria risk actually begins in type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: UACR cut-point 8.44 mg/g ; above it, CKD progression HR 1.88 (1.65–2.14) ; men 10.59 (HR 2.35), women 8.15 (HR 1.46) — 4,821 normoalbuminuric T2D outpatients, Taiwan.
cards.people: 4,821 normoalbuminuric T2D outpatients, Taiwan
cards.result: UACR cut-point 8.44 mg/g ; above it, CKD progression HR 1.88 (1.65–2.14) ; men 10.59 mg/g (HR 2.35 ), women 8.15 mg/g (HR 1.46 )
cards.watchOut: The paper’s abstract prints the male cut-point as >10.9 mg/g; the body text gives 10.59, used here. An impossible AUC interval in the paper was omitted.
cards.source: Tang et al., Front Endocrinol 2022
cards.search: albuminuria risk begins type 2 diabetes tang frontiers endocrinology 2022 uacr cut-point 8.44 taiwan normoalbuminuric ckd progression hazard ratio men women

cards.headline: What actually drives albuminuria and GFR loss over 24 years
cards.summary: ACR progression driven only by blood pressure (systolic β 0.36 ; diastolic β 0.40 ); eGFR decline by systolic BP ( β −0.12 ), smoking ( β −2.05 ), cholesterol ( β +0.86 , protective direction) — 718 T2D patients, Salford UK.
cards.people: 718 T2D patients, Salford UK
cards.result: ACR progression driven only by blood pressure (systolic β 0.36 ; diastolic β 0.40 ); eGFR decline by systolic BP ( β −0.12 ), smoking ( β −2.05 ), cholesterol ( β +0.86 , protective direction); eGFR fell 1.02 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr ; 10-yr mortality 6.6% / 14.5% / 26.6% by kidney status
cards.watchOut: Two corrupted estimates in the published abstract (a confidence interval not containing its estimate; a reversed interval) were omitted rather than guessed.
cards.source: Matheou et al., Diabetic Medicine 2026
cards.search: matheou 2026 albuminuria gfr loss 24 years salford type 2 diabetes blood pressure smoking cholesterol diabetic medicine prospective cohort beta egfr decline mortality

cards.headline: Why losing nephrons raises albuminuria by itself
cards.summary: After kidney donation, albumin permeability +31% (p<0.001); at 50% GFR loss, leak per remaining GFR 1.8× / 2.1× / 1.6× ; at 70% loss, 3.1× / 4.4× / 2.6× — donor + 3 CKD cohorts.
cards.type: Observational analysis of donor + 3 CKD cohorts (ALTOLD, MDRD, AASK, CRIC), Am J Nephrol 2019
cards.people: Living kidney donors (ALTOLD) and CKD participants from MDRD, AASK and CRIC
cards.result: After kidney donation, albumin permeability +31% (p<0.001); at 50% GFR loss, leak per remaining GFR 1.8× / 2.1× / 1.6× ; at 70% loss, 3.1× / 4.4× / 2.6×
cards.watchOut: Secondary analysis of cohorts assembled for other purposes, so the comparison across them is observational rather than designed
cards.source: Willows et al., Am J Nephrol 2019

cards.headline: The thresholds the field currently uses (KDIGO)
cards.summary: A1 under 30 mg/g ; A2 30–300 ; A3 over 300 ; nephrotic range above 2,220 mg/g — boundaries are consensus classification lines, not empirical risk inflections.
cards.people: Not applicable — a guideline, not a study
cards.result: A1 under 30 mg/g ; A2 30–300 mg/g ; A3 over 300 mg/g ; nephrotic range above 2,220 mg/g ; boundaries are consensus classification lines, not empirical risk inflections
cards.watchOut: Consensus thresholds set for classification and communication — a different job from identifying the level at which risk actually begins to rise
cards.source: KDIGO CKD Guideline, Kidney Int Suppl 2013

cards.headline: The two famous kidney genes didn’t replicate — but a new one, hemicentin 1, showed up.
cards.summary: No significant P values in CNDP1 or ELMO1 ; one SNP pair in hemicentin 1 ( HMCN1 ), unadjusted P = 6.1×10⁻⁵ — 455 Mexican-American patients with diabetic nephropathy vs 437 controls, 670 SNPs.
cards.people: 455 Mexican-American patients with diabetic nephropathy vs 437 controls with long-term diabetes but no nephropathy; 3 centers. 670 SNPs: 42 in CNDP1, 227 in ELMO1, 401 in 8 other genes.
cards.result: No region in CNDP1 or ELMO1 showed significant P values — the two genes previously associated with diabetic nephropathy in other ethnic groups did not replicate. One association was found: a SNP pair (rs2146098 and rs6659783) in hemicentin 1 (HMCN1), unadjusted P = 6.1×10⁻⁵; a rare haplotype in the region was subsequently identified.
cards.watchOut: The HMCN1 P value is unadjusted, with 670 SNPs tested — a multiple-testing caveat the abstract does not resolve, and there is no replication cohort. This is a mostly-negative study with one unadjusted signal, not a confirmed gene.
cards.source: Kim S et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2010;5(6):1072–1078. PMID 20299368. PMCID PMC2879299. DOI 10.2215/CJN.06550909.

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors and kidney protection
shelves.question: Do SGLT2 inhibitors slow chronic kidney disease progression — in people with and without diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Humans
shelves.balance: Three dedicated kidney trials, three positive primary outcomes — the most consistent story in this drug class, and it holds in people without diabetes.

cards.headline: In diabetic kidney disease, canagliflozin slowed progression to kidney failure by 30%.
cards.summary: CREDENCE — primary composite 43.2 vs 61.2 events per 1,000 patient-years (HR 0.70); renal-specific composite HR 0.66; heart-failure hospitalization HR 0.61 — 4,401 patients, stopped early for efficacy.
cards.people: 4,401 patients with type 2 diabetes, eGFR 30 to <90, and albuminuria (ACR >300 to 5,000 mg/g), all on renin–angiotensin blockade; median follow-up 2.62 years; stopped early for efficacy
cards.result: Primary composite (end-stage kidney disease, doubling of creatinine, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes) 43.2 vs 61.2 events per 1,000 patient-years (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.59–0.82); renal-specific composite HR 0.66; end-stage kidney disease HR 0.68; cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke HR 0.80; heart-failure hospitalization HR 0.61. No difference in amputation or fracture
cards.watchOut: Everyone in this trial had albuminuric diabetic kidney disease on RAS blockade — it does not speak to kidney disease without heavy albuminuria
cards.source: Perkovic V, et al.; CREDENCE Trial Investigators. Canagliflozin and Renal Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes and Nephropathy. N Engl J Med. 2019;380:2295–2306. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1811744. PMID 30990260 · NCT02065791.

cards.headline: Dapagliflozin cut kidney failure and death in chronic kidney disease — with or without diabetes.
cards.summary: DAPA-CKD — primary composite 9.2% vs 14.5% (HR 0.61; NNT 19); death from any cause 4.7% vs 6.8% (HR 0.69) — 4,304 patients, 32.5% without type 2 diabetes.
cards.people: 4,304 patients with CKD (eGFR 25–75, ACR 200–5,000 mg/g); 32.5% did not have type 2 diabetes; median follow-up 2.4 years; stopped early for efficacy
cards.result: Primary composite (sustained ≥50% eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes) 9.2% vs 14.5% (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51–0.72; NNT 19); kidney-specific composite HR 0.56; death from any cause 4.7% vs 6.8% (HR 0.69)
cards.watchOut: Stopped early, which can exaggerate effects; the population had albuminuric CKD, so non-albuminuric disease is less covered
cards.source: Heerspink HJL, et al.; DAPA-CKD Trial Committees and Investigators. Dapagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:1436–1446. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2024816. PMID 32970396 · NCT03036150.

cards.headline: Empagliflozin slowed kidney disease progression across the broadest CKD population yet tested.
cards.summary: EMPA-KIDNEY — primary composite 13.1% vs 16.9% (HR 0.72); hospitalization for any cause HR 0.86; no significant effect on cardiovascular death or death from any cause — 6,609 patients, 54% without diabetes.
cards.people: 6,609 patients with CKD at risk of progression (eGFR ≥20 to <45, or ≥45 to <90 with ACR ≥200 mg/g); 54% did not have diabetes; median follow-up 2.0 years
cards.result: Primary composite (kidney disease progression or cardiovascular death) 13.1% vs 16.9% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.64–0.82); hospitalization for any cause HR 0.86. No significant effect on heart-failure hospitalization or cardiovascular death (4.0% vs 4.6%) or on death from any cause (4.5% vs 5.1%)
cards.watchOut: The win is kidney progression — this trial did not show a mortality or heart-failure benefit, and serious adverse events were similar in both groups
cards.source: The EMPA-KIDNEY Collaborative Group. Empagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:117–127. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2204233. PMID 36331190 · NCT03594110.

shelves.title: Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) in diabetic kidney disease
shelves.question: Does finerenone — a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist — slow diabetic kidney disease and prevent cardiovascular events, on top of RAS blockade?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Naphthyridines · Albuminuria · Humans
shelves.balance: Two trials, one drug, complementary halves: in advanced diabetic kidney disease the kidney win leads (HR 0.82); in earlier disease the cardiovascular win leads (HR 0.87) and the kidney signal does not reach significance. Hyperkalemia is the recurring price in both — roughly double the placebo rate, though few patients had to stop.

cards.headline: In advanced diabetic kidney disease, finerenone slowed progression — kidney failure, big GFR loss, or renal death in 17.8% vs 21.1%.
cards.summary: FIDELIO-DKD — primary kidney composite 17.8% vs 21.1% (HR 0.82); cardiovascular composite HR 0.86; UACR −31% at month 4; hyperkalemia 18.3% vs 9.0% — 5,734 patients, median 2.6 years.
cards.people: 5,734 patients with type 2 diabetes and advanced CKD (mean eGFR 44 ml/min/1.73 m², median UACR 852 mg/g), all on maximally tolerated RAS blockade; median follow-up 2.6 years
cards.result: Primary kidney composite (kidney failure, sustained ≥40% eGFR decline, or death from renal causes) 17.8% vs 21.1% (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.93) — NNT 29 at 3 years; key secondary cardiovascular composite 13.0% vs 14.8% (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.99); UACR −31% vs placebo at month 4. Hyperkalemia 18.3% vs 9.0% , and hyperkalemia led to discontinuation in 2.3% vs 0.9%
cards.source: Bakris GL, et al.; FIDELIO-DKD Investigators. Effect of Finerenone on Chronic Kidney Disease Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:2219–2229. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2025845. PMID 33264825 · NCT02540993.
cards.search: finerenone fidelio-dkd diabetic kidney disease bakris new england journal 2020 nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist kidney failure hyperkalemia pmid 33264825 aged albuminuria creatinine diabetes mellitus, type 2 diabetic nephropathies double-blind method female glomerular filtration rate humans hyperkalemia male naphthyridines renal insufficiency, chronic treatment outcome nct02540993 e11.22 5a11 gb61.z rxcui 2562811 finerenone

cards.headline: In earlier diabetic kidney disease, finerenone’s win was cardiovascular — 12.4% vs 14.2% — driven by fewer heart-failure hospitalizations.
cards.summary: FIGARO-DKD — primary cardiovascular composite 12.4% vs 14.2% (HR 0.87), driven by heart-failure hospitalization (HR 0.71); the kidney composite (HR 0.87) was not significant — 7,437 patients, median 3.4 years.
cards.people: 7,437 patients randomized (7,352 in the primary analysis) with type 2 diabetes and earlier-stage CKD (mean eGFR 68 ml/min/1.73 m²), on RAS blockade; median follow-up 3.4 years
cards.result: Primary cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or heart-failure hospitalization) 12.4% vs 14.2% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76–0.98), driven by heart-failure hospitalization (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.90); the secondary kidney composite occurred in 9.5% vs 10.8% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76–1.01) — not significant. Hyperkalemia led to discontinuation in 1.2% vs 0.4%
cards.source: Pitt B, et al.; FIGARO-DKD Investigators. Cardiovascular Events with Finerenone in Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2021;385:2252–2263. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2110956. PMID 34449181 · NCT02545049.

shelves.title: Spironolactone (steroidal MRA) and albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease
shelves.question: Does adding spironolactone to maximal ACE inhibitor / ARB therapy lower albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease — and has that ever been shown to change outcomes?
shelves.balance: The albuminuria effect is real and reproducible — about a third lower, on top of maximal RAS blockade, within weeks, and not explained by blood pressure. But every positive trial is small, short, and surrogate-only; the one large hard-outcome trial, in mostly non-albuminuric stage 3b CKD, found no cardiovascular benefit and two of three patients stopped the drug inside six months. A marker that moves, at a tolerability price.

cards.headline: Adding spironolactone to maximal ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy cut albuminuria by a third in 8 weeks.
cards.summary: Rossing 2005 crossover trial — albuminuria −33% (95% CI 25–41) on spironolactone 25 mg; 24-hour BP −6/−4 mmHg — 21 patients, 8 weeks per period.
cards.people: 21 patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy, already on maximally recommended ACE inhibitor/ARB doses; spironolactone 25 mg/day vs placebo, 8 weeks each
cards.result: Albuminuria −33% (95% CI 25–41) on spironolactone; fractional albumin clearance −40%; 24-hour blood pressure −6/−4 mmHg; the albuminuria change did not correlate with the blood-pressure change. One patient was excluded for hyperkalemia; GFR dipped reversibly by 3 ml/min/1.73 m²
cards.source: Rossing K, Schjoedt KJ, Smidt UM, Boomsma F, Parving HH. Beneficial effects of adding spironolactone to recommended antihypertensive treatment in diabetic nephropathy: a randomized, double-masked, cross-over study. Diabetes Care. 2005;28(9):2106–2112. DOI 10.2337/diacare.28.9.2106. PMID 16123474.
cards.search: spironolactone rossing 2005 diabetic nephropathy albuminuria crossover diabetes care ace inhibitor arb pmid 16123474

cards.headline: On top of maximal ACE inhibition, spironolactone cut albuminuria 34% — adding an ARB did not.
cards.summary: Mehdi 2009 — UACR change vs placebo: spironolactone −34.0% (P = 0.007); losartan add-on −16.8%, not significant — 81 patients, all on lisinopril 80 mg/day, 48 weeks.
cards.people: 81 patients with diabetes, hypertension, and UACR ≥300 mg/g, all on lisinopril 80 mg/day; add-on spironolactone 25 mg, losartan 100 mg, or placebo for 48 weeks
cards.result: UACR vs placebo: spironolactone −34.0% (95% CI −51.0 to −11.2; P = 0.007); losartan add-on −16.8% , not significant. Blood pressure did not differ between groups; serum potassium was higher in both add-on arms
cards.source: Mehdi UF, Adams-Huet B, Raskin P, Vega GL, Toto RD. Addition of angiotensin receptor blockade or mineralocorticoid antagonism to maximal angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition in diabetic nephropathy. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2009;20(12):2641–2650. DOI 10.1681/ASN.2009070737. PMID 19926893.
cards.search: spironolactone mehdi 2009 diabetic nephropathy lisinopril losartan albuminuria journal american society nephrology pmid 19926893

cards.headline: A multicenter trial repeated the result: albuminuria down 33% in 8 weeks.
cards.summary: Kato 2015 multicenter RCT — albuminuria −33% (P = 0.0002) with add-on spironolactone 25 mg, significant after adjustment for systolic BP and eGFR — 52 Japanese patients, 8 weeks.
cards.people: 52 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetic nephropathy on RAS blockade; add-on spironolactone 25 mg/day for 8 weeks
cards.result: Albuminuria −33% (P = 0.0002), remaining significant after adjustment for systolic blood pressure and eGFR; eGFR fell significantly on spironolactone; no patients were excluded for hyperkalemia
cards.source: Kato S, Maruyama S, Makino H, et al. Anti-albuminuric effects of spironolactone in patients with type 2 diabetic nephropathy: a multicenter, randomized clinical trial. Clin Exp Nephrol. 2015;19(6):1098–1106. DOI 10.1007/s10157-015-1106-2. PMID 25795029.
cards.search: spironolactone kato 2015 anti-albuminuric type 2 diabetic nephropathy multicenter randomized clinical experimental nephrology japan pmid 25795029

cards.headline: The one large outcome trial found nothing: cardiovascular events 16.7% vs 16.0%, HR 1.05 — and two of three patients stopped the drug.
cards.summary: BARACK-D — primary cardiovascular composite 16.7% vs 16.0% (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.81–1.37); two-thirds of the spironolactone arm stopped within 6 months — 1,434 patients with stage 3b CKD, 3 years.
cards.type: Prospective randomized open blinded-endpoint (PROBE) outcome trial (BARACK-D)
cards.people: 1,434 patients randomized (1,372 in the primary analysis) with stage 3b CKD in English primary care, mean age 74.8 years, mostly non-albuminuric (median ACR 1.5 mg/mmol); spironolactone 25 mg/day plus usual care vs usual care, 3 years
cards.result: Primary cardiovascular composite 16.7% vs 16.0% (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.81–1.37) — no benefit. Two-thirds of the spironolactone arm stopped treatment within 6 months, mostly for prespecified safety stops: eGFR decline 35.4%, side effects 18.9%, hyperkalemia 8.0%. The authors conclude spironolactone should not be used in stage 3b CKD without another specific indication
cards.source: Hobbs FDR, et al.; BARACK-D Investigators. Low-dose spironolactone and cardiovascular outcomes in moderate stage chronic kidney disease: a randomized controlled trial. Nat Med. 2024. DOI 10.1038/s41591-024-03263-5. PMID 39349629.
cards.search: spironolactone barack-d cardiovascular outcomes stage 3b chronic kidney disease nature medicine 2024 hobbs null discontinuation pmid 39349629

shelves.title: Blocking the renin-angiotensin system in diabetic kidney disease: the anchor trials
shelves.question: In diabetic kidney disease, does blocking the renin–angiotensin system protect the kidney beyond blood-pressure lowering — and is blocking it twice, with an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, better than blocking it once?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Antihypertensive Agents · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Three decades, one axis: captopril halved renal failure in type 1 nephropathy (Lewis), losartan and irbesartan repeated it in type 2 (RENAAL, IDNT — with amlodipine proving it was never just blood pressure), and ONTARGET drew the ceiling — doubling the blockade adds harm, not protection. Every proteinuria shelf that followed (#69 SGLT2, #73 finerenone, #74 spironolactone, #75 GLP-1, #76 pioglitazone) is measured against patients already standing on this foundation. (Panel position: ADA Standards of Care — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Lewis 1993: captopril halved the kidney’s decline in type 1 diabetes — doubling of creatinine in 25 vs 43 patients — at comparable blood pressure.
cards.summary: The Lewis captopril trial 1993 — doubling of the serum creatinine concentration occurred in 25 patients on captopril vs 43 on placebo, a 48% risk reduction (P=0.007); the combined endpoint of death, dialysis, or transplantation was reduced by about 50% ; blood pressure was otherwise controlled in both arms, so the protection was not a pressure effect — 409 patients with type 1 diabetes and overt nephropathy; median follow-up about three years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 1993
cards.people: 409 patients with insulin-dependent (type 1) diabetes and diabetic nephropathy — urinary protein excretion of 500 mg or more per day and a serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL or less, most with diabetic retinopathy. Captopril 25 mg three times daily (207 patients) vs placebo (202), with other antihypertensive drugs used in both arms, as needed, to reach the same blood-pressure goals; median follow-up about three years
cards.result: Doubling of the serum creatinine concentration occurred in 25 patients in the captopril group vs 43 in the placebo group — a 48% reduction in risk (P=0.007) — and the combined endpoint of death, dialysis, or renal transplantation was reduced by approximately 50% . The protection persisted after adjustment for blood pressure and was greatest in patients entering with the highest creatinine concentrations: captopril’s benefit was specific to the drug’s action, not a by-product of pressure control
cards.watchOut: Type 1 diabetes with established, overt nephropathy, in the pre-statin, pre-SGLT2 era: the absolute progression rates belong to 1993, not to a modern clinic, though the relative protection is the finding the whole cluster stands on. Captopril three times daily was the regimen; the once-daily ARB trials that followed (Cards 2 and 3) carried the class into type 2 disease. At 409 patients the trial is small by modern standards — but blinded, and its effect was large
cards.source: Lewis EJ, Hunsicker LG, Bain RP, Rohde RD; The Collaborative Study Group. The effect of angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibition on diabetic nephropathy. N Engl J Med. 1993;329(20):1456–1462. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199311113292004. PMID 8413456.
cards.search: lewis 1993 captopril diabetic nephropathy type 1 diabetes ace inhibition nejm doubling creatinine pmid 8413456 adult captopril creatinine diabetic nephropathies double-blind method female follow-up studies humans kidney male middle aged patient compliance prospective studies e11.22 5a11 gb61.z rxcui 1998 captopril

cards.headline: RENAAL 2001: losartan cut the renal composite by 16% in type 2 nephropathy — ESRD by 28%, proteinuria by 35%; death did not move.
cards.summary: RENAAL 2001 — the primary composite (doubling of creatinine, end-stage renal disease, or death) was reached by 327 patients on losartan vs 359 on placebo, a 16% risk reduction (P=0.02); doubling of creatinine fell 25% (P=0.006); end-stage renal disease fell 28% (P=0.002); proteinuria fell 35% (P<0.001); there was no effect on mortality — 1,513 patients with type 2 diabetes and nephropathy; mean follow-up 3.4 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 2001
cards.people: 1,513 patients with type 2 diabetes and nephropathy — urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 300 or more (or heavy proteinuria) with a serum creatinine of 1.3–3.0 mg/dL — at 250 centers in 28 countries. Losartan 50 mg daily, titrated to 100 mg (751 patients), vs placebo (762), both added to conventional therapy that excluded ACE inhibitors and other ARBs; mean follow-up 3.4 years
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 327 patients (43.5%) in the losartan group and 359 (47.1%) in the placebo group — a 16% risk reduction (P=0.02) . Doubling of creatinine was reduced by 25% (P=0.006) and end-stage renal disease by 28% (P=0.002) — losartan delayed dialysis. Proteinuria fell by 35% (P<0.001) . There was no significant effect on mortality — stated plainly, because the composite contains death; the renal components carried the result. A secondary gain: first hospitalization for heart failure fell 32% (P=0.005)
cards.watchOut: Losartan’s victory here is renal, and this card does not inflate it into a survival claim. The blood-pressure differences between the arms were small, supporting a kidney-specific effect, but the trial cannot fully exclude a pressure contribution. ARB monitoring — creatinine and potassium after initiation — was built into the protocol, and the protection applies to patients with established nephropathy, not to prevention in normoalbuminuric diabetes
cards.source: Brenner BM, Cooper ME, de Zeeuw D, et al; RENAAL Study Investigators. Effects of losartan on renal and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and nephropathy. N Engl J Med. 2001;345(12):861–869. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa011161. PMID 11565518.
cards.search: renaal brenner losartan type 2 diabetes nephropathy nejm 2001 end-stage renal disease proteinuria pmid 11565518 adult aged angiotensin receptor antagonists antihypertensive agents cardiovascular diseases creatine creatinine diabetes mellitus, type 2 diabetic nephropathies disease progression double-blind method female humans hypertension kidney failure, chronic losartan male middle aged proteinuria e11.22 5a11 gb61.z rxcui 52175 losartan

cards.headline: IDNT 2001: irbesartan beat placebo by 20% and amlodipine by 23% — the comparison arm that proves it was never just blood pressure.
cards.summary: IDNT 2001 — the primary composite (doubling of creatinine, end-stage renal disease, or death from any cause) occurred in 32.6% on irbesartan vs 39.0% on placebo ( 20% lower , P=0.02) and 41.1% on amlodipine ( 23% lower , P=0.006), at essentially the same achieved blood pressures in the two active arms; proteinuria fell 33% on irbesartan vs 10% on placebo and 6% on amlodipine — 1,715 hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetic nephropathy; mean follow-up 2.6 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, three-arm trial, N Engl J Med 2001
cards.people: 1,715 hypertensive patients with nephropathy due to type 2 diabetes — proteinuria of 900 mg or more per day and a serum creatinine of 1.0–3.0 mg/dL in women or 1.2–3.0 mg/dL in men. Irbesartan 300 mg daily (579 patients), amlodipine 10 mg daily (567), or placebo (569), each with conventional therapy added to a target blood pressure of 135/85 mm Hg or less; mean follow-up 2.6 years
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint occurred in 189 patients ( 32.6% ) in the irbesartan group, 222 ( 39.0% ) in the placebo group, and 233 ( 41.1% ) in the amlodipine group: irbesartan’s risk was 20% lower than placebo (P=0.02) and 23% lower than amlodipine (P=0.006) — while achieved blood pressure was essentially identical in the two active arms. Doubling of creatinine: 33% lower than placebo (P=0.003) and 37% lower than amlodipine (P<0.001). End-stage renal disease trended 23% lower against both comparisons (P=0.07 — not significant, stated plainly). Proteinuria fell 33% on irbesartan, vs 10% on placebo and 6% on amlodipine. There were no significant differences in mortality or the cardiovascular composite
cards.watchOut: The amlodipine arm is the experiment inside the experiment — and a standing warning that a drug can lower blood pressure by the same amount and protect the kidney less. Baseline proteinuria was heavy (about 2.9 g/day), so the result speaks to overt nephropathy, not to early or normoalbuminuric disease. Serum potassium ran higher on irbesartan — the monitoring obligation that travels with every RAS prescription

cards.headline: ONTARGET 2008: telmisartan matched ramipril — and combining the two added harm, not protection. The ceiling of the axis.
cards.summary: ONTARGET 2008 — the primary outcome (death from cardiovascular causes, myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure) occurred in 16.7% on telmisartan vs 16.5% on ramipril (RR 1.01 — telmisartan noninferior); the combination produced 16.3% — no additional benefit — with more hypotension, syncope, and renal dysfunction ( 13.5% vs 10.2% , P<0.001) — 25,620 patients with vascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage; median follow-up 56 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2008
cards.people: 25,620 patients with coronary, peripheral, or cerebrovascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, without heart failure (mean age 66.4 years; 27% women). Ramipril 10 mg daily (8,576), telmisartan 80 mg daily (8,542), or the combination of both (8,502); every participant first tolerated a run-in period taking both drugs; median follow-up 56 months
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 1,412 patients ( 16.5% ) in the ramipril group and 1,423 ( 16.7% ) in the telmisartan group — relative risk 1.01 (97.5% CI 0.93–1.10) , meeting the prespecified criterion for noninferiority; telmisartan caused less cough and angioedema. The combination group’s event rate (1,386 patients; 16.3% ) was no better, and its harms were worse: more hypotensive symptoms and syncope, and more renal dysfunction — 13.5% vs 10.2% on ramipril (P<0.001) — with more hyperkalemia and a greater decline in kidney function. Dual blockade bought adverse events, not protection
cards.watchOut: Participants entered only after tolerating both drugs in a run-in, so real-world intolerance — cough, angioedema, creatinine rises — is higher than this trial’s rates suggest. ONTARGET was not a nephropathy trial: most participants had vascular disease without heavy proteinuria, and even so the combination injured kidneys more often; a secondary renal analysis (dialysis, doubling of creatinine, or death) was significantly worse with dual therapy. The finding ended routine ACE-inhibitor-plus-ARB prescribing

shelves.title: Hyponatremia: how fast is too fast — and who says so?
shelves.question: The emergency treatment of low sodium turns on two numbers everyone quotes and almost nobody can source: the bolus, and the ceiling.
shelves.mesh: Hyponatremia · Saline Solution, Hypertonic · Infusions, Intravenous · Inappropriate ADH Syndrome · Sodium Chloride · Hospital Mortality · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: The ceilings are real practice and the injury they guard against is real — but they were set by expert panels grading their own evidence D, and no randomized trial of correction speed has ever been run. The one trial we have says bolus and infusion are equally safe ways to give hypertonic saline. And across nearly 12,000 patients in the modern cohorts, the association runs against the fear: correcting slowly tracked with more deaths — about 32 extra per thousand versus rapid correction — while demyelination stayed rare at every speed. Treat the ceiling as a guardrail, not a cliff edge: below it, the documented danger is leaving a seizing, encephalopathic patient hyponatremic — and in concentrated-urine states, normal saline itself can push the sodium further down (Reference 5).

cards.headline: SALSA: the only randomized trial — and it tested the delivery, not the speed (2021)
cards.result: Baek SH et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92 (PMID 33104189 · NCT02887469). In three Korean hospitals, 178 patients with symptomatic severe hyponatremia (sodium 125 or below, mean 118) were randomized to rapid intermittent bolus or slow continuous infusion of 3% saline. Overcorrection — the trial's primary outcome — occurred in 17.2% on bolus vs 24.2% on infusion (difference −6.9 percentage points; P=0.26): no significant difference. The bolus arm reached its one-hour sodium target more often and needed therapeutic relowering less often, and there was no osmotic demyelination in either arm. SALSA is the best randomized evidence in this field, and its limit is the lesson: it randomized how hypertonic saline is given, in one modestly sized trial, with a laboratory endpoint. The question emergency physicians actually argue about — how fast may the sodium rise — has never been randomized at all.

cards.headline: Ayus 2024: across 11,811 patients, slow correction tracked with more deaths
cards.result: Ayus JC et al., JAMA Intern Med 2025;185 (published online November 18, 2024; PMID 39556338). A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies covering 11,811 hospitalized adults with severe hyponatremia (sodium below 120, or below 125 with severe symptoms) compared rapid correction (at least 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours) against slow and very slow correction. Rapid correction was associated with 32 fewer in-hospital deaths per 1,000 patients than slow correction (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.55–0.82; moderate-certainty evidence) and 221 fewer per 1,000 than very slow correction; at 30 days the differences were 61 and 134 fewer deaths per 1,000 (low certainty). Hospital stays were shorter by 1.2 to 3.1 days. Critically, rapid correction was NOT associated with more osmotic demyelination. These are cohorts, not trials — patients corrected slowly may simply have been sicker — but the paper states the field's position plainly: safe limits are uncertain 'as randomized clinical trials have not been conducted.'

cards.headline: The ceilings themselves: 10–12 a day, graded 1D
cards.result: The numbers on the wall come from two documents. The US Expert Panel (Verbalis et al., 2013; PMID 24074529) set the limit at 10–12 mmol/L in any 24 hours and 18 in any 48, tightened to 8 per 24 hours for patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination. The European Clinical Practice Guideline (Spasovski et al., 2014; PMID 24569125) set 10 in the first 24 hours and 8 per day thereafter. Both are honest about their foundations: the European guideline grades its hypertonic-saline bolus recommendation 1D — a strong recommendation resting on very-low-quality evidence — and the US panel's corresponding advice is expert opinion. The harm the ceilings guard against is real and devastating: osmotic demyelination, concentrated in patients with sodium at or below 105, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and advanced liver disease. But no study has ever located the cliff edge the ceilings imply — demyelination is documented across a wide range of correction rates, and its absence at high rates is documented too. The ceilings are a consensus safety margin, not a measured threshold.

cards.headline: Reading the hyponatremia evidence together: what the emergency physician actually faces
cards.result: At 3 a.m. the decisions are two. First, the symptomatic patient — seizing, comatose, encephalopathic: give hypertonic saline in boluses and raise the sodium 4–6 mmol/L promptly to stop the brain emergency; SALSA says the bolus route is at least as safe as an infusion and faster to target, and no guideline dissents. Second, the ceiling for the following hours: the panels say 8–12 in 24 hours depending on risk, graded at the lowest level of evidence, while the largest pooled dataset associates staying far under the ceiling with more deaths and no fewer demyelinations. The disciplined practice the evidence supports: treat symptoms aggressively, respect the ceiling as a guardrail rather than a law of physiology, monitor relentlessly, and know that the risk runs in both directions — a point the guidelines, written when only one direction had case reports, could not yet make.

cards.headline: The harm in the other direction: the wrong fluid can push sodium down
cards.result: In severe symptomatic hyponatremia — sodium below 120, the conservative line — the choice of fluid is not a detail. In a patient whose urine is highly concentrated — SIADH physiology, urine osmolality above ~500 mOsm/kg — a liter of normal saline does not raise the sodium; it can lower it. The liter carries 308 mOsm of salt, excreted in roughly 600 mL of concentrated urine, leaving ~400 mL of free water behind — the 'desalination' the European guideline warns of (Spasovski 2014, PMID 24569125). The clinical record of the untreated direction is case evidence, and it is grim: in the endometrial-ablation series (Arieff & Ayus, JAMA 1993, PMID 8355387), three women with hyponatremic encephalopathy treated promptly with hypertonic saline recovered completely; the fourth, whose treatment came only after seizures and respiratory arrest, died — autopsy showed cerebral edema with tonsillar herniation. In the larger postoperative series (Ayus 1992, PMID 1443949), 38 of 65 encephalopathy patients had already arrested before the diagnosis was made. No randomized trial of withholding hypertonic saline exists or could; this card rests on mechanism and consistent case evidence, and says so.

shelves.title: Hypernatremia: the speed limit that was never measured
shelves.question: Every trainee learns the speed limit for bringing high sodium down. Almost none learn that in adults, it was never measured.
shelves.mesh: Hypernatremia · Sodium · Cohort Studies · Retrospective Studies · Critical Illness · Hospital Mortality · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: For high sodium, the famous limit — no faster than about ten points a day, lest the brain swell — has never been tested in an adult trial. It was borrowed from neonatal cases and expert opinion. In the two large modern adult cohorts, rapid correction produced not one attributed case of cerebral edema, while slow correction carried roughly double the adjusted odds of death. That gap is confounded — the sickest patients correct slowest — but the asymmetry is the finding: one side of the argument has more than 4,700 patients behind it; the other has a tradition.

cards.headline: Feigin 2023: in 4,265 adults, slow correction doubled the adjusted odds of death
cards.result: Feigin E et al., JAMA Network Open 2023;6:e2335415 (PMID 37768662). Every adult with severe hypernatremia (sodium 155 or above) at Tel Aviv Medical Center from 2007 to 2021: 4,265 patients, median age 78. Only 343 (8%) were corrected fast — faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour, the customary ceiling. Thirty-day mortality was 31.8% in the fast group vs 50.7% in the slow (adjusted odds ratio for slow correction 2.02, 95% CI 1.55–2.62), and the association held separately for hypernatremia present on admission (aOR 1.64) and acquired in hospital (aOR 2.19). The fast group also left hospital sooner (median 5.0 vs 7.2 days). Most important for this shelf: the investigators chart-reviewed every flagged case of cerebral edema, seizure, or altered consciousness, and not one neurological complication was attributed to rapid correction. Retrospective and confounded — patients who correct slowly are usually sicker — but the feared harm is simply not in the data.

cards.headline: Chauhan 2019: a third of ICU patients corrected 'too fast' — with zero cerebral edema
cards.result: Chauhan K et al., Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2019;14:656–663 (PMID 30948456). In 449 critically ill adults with hypernatremia (122 present on admission, 327 hospital-acquired), rapid correction — faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour, including 78 patients corrected by more than 12 mmol/L in a day — occurred in about a third of patients. It was not associated with in-hospital mortality in either group (admission: 25% rapid vs 28% slow; hospital-acquired: 44% vs 40%; adjusted odds ratios 1.3 with wide confidence intervals in both). And there were no cases of cerebral edema in the 78 patients corrected fastest, nor any attributable case in the entire cohort on chart review. The authors' own summary of the customary speed limit deserves quoting in spirit: the target rate in universal use is supported by negligible data. Two independent cohorts, two health systems, the same null result for the feared complication.

cards.headline: Where the speed limit came from: neonatal cases and expert opinion
cards.result: The rule — correct chronic hypernatremia no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour, roughly 10 mmol/L per day — entered adult practice by borrowing. As Feigin and colleagues note in their introduction, the cerebral edema that rapid correction is feared to cause was documented mainly in neonates, whose brains, skulls, and water handling differ from adults'; the adult limit itself rests on expert opinion, and clinical data supporting the safety or benefit of slow correction in adults are scarce. The borrowing had a second source: hyponatremia, where rapid correction genuinely can injure the brain (osmotic demyelination) — and the two disorders were treated as mirror images, although the brain's adaptation to high sodium (accumulating organic osmolytes) and to low sodium are not symmetric problems. No randomized trial of hypernatremia correction rate exists in any age group of adults. The speed limit is a custom with a citation history, not a measured toxicity threshold — and customs deserve shelves too, labeled as customs.

cards.headline: Reading the hypernatremia evidence together: fear the sodium, not the slope
cards.result: Hold the two facts side by side. Fact one: hypernatremia itself is dangerous company — it is associated with higher mortality than any other electrolyte abnormality, largely because it strikes patients who cannot ask for water: the very old, the critically ill, the neurologically impaired. Fact two: across more than 4,700 adults in the modern cohorts, nobody has produced the cerebral edema that the speed limit exists to prevent, while patients left hypernatremic longer died more — an association soaked in confounding, since dying patients are hard to correct, but consistent in direction. The practice this evidence supports is not recklessness: correct the water deficit, find and treat the cause (access to water, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis), and monitor. It is a refusal to let fear of an unmeasured slope strand a patient at a sodium of 160 for days. If a future trial ever randomizes correction speed in adults, this shelf will be rewritten; until then, the honest label for the 10-a-day rule is: traditional, plausible, unproven.

shelves.title: Sodium bicarbonate in CKD: the open-label win and the blinded null
shelves.question: Does treating metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate slow kidney failure in chronic kidney disease?
shelves.mesh: Acid-Base Equilibrium · Acidosis · Administration, Oral · Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Bicarbonates · Biomarkers · Blood Proteins · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Creatinine · Diet · Dietary Proteins · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fruit · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypertension · Italy · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Status · Potassium · Quality of Life · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Serum Albumin · Sodium Bicarbonate · Survival Rate · Texas · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vegetables
shelves.balance: The two trials split exactly the way the library's evidence hierarchy predicts. UBI — open-label, no placebo — reported large wins on hard endpoints: less progression, less dialysis, fewer deaths. BiCARB — double-blind, placebo-controlled, in older patients with milder acidosis — found nothing: no functional benefit, no GFR benefit, higher costs, and slightly worse quality of life. And the mechanism is acid retention itself — retained acid drives compensatory ammonia production and endothelin-1 that injure the tubulointerstitium — which is why a diet can do what the pill does, and why the open-label/blinded split here is about proof, not plausibility. Correcting a low bicarbonate is cheap and reasonable; believing the mortality claim requires the blinded trial that hasn't confirmed it.

cards.headline: UBI 2019: bicarbonate cut the progression endpoint (6.6% vs 17.0%), dialysis starts, and deaths — in an open-label trial.
cards.summary: Over ~30 months, the primary endpoint (doubling of creatinine / progression composite) occurred in 6.6% on bicarbonate vs 17.0% on standard care (P<0.001). Dialysis started in 6.9% vs 12.3% (P=0.016); death in 3.1% vs 6.8% (P=0.004). No significant effects on blood pressure, weight, or hospitalizations.
cards.people: 740 patients with CKD stages 3–5 and metabolic acidosis (376 bicarbonate, 364 standard care); mean age 67.8, creatinine clearance ~30 mL/min, serum bicarbonate ~21.5 mmol/L
cards.result: Over ~30 months, the primary endpoint (doubling of creatinine / progression composite) occurred in 6.6% on bicarbonate vs 17.0% on standard care (P<0.001). Dialysis started in 6.9% vs 12.3% (P=0.016); death in 3.1% vs 6.8% (P=0.004). No significant effects on blood pressure, weight, or hospitalizations.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo — patients and clinicians knew, and endpoints like 'start dialysis' are clinician decisions, exactly the kind unblinding bends. The effect sizes are large enough to demand blinded confirmation.
cards.source: Di Iorio BR et al., J Nephrol 2019 (PMID 31598912 · NCT01640119)

cards.headline: BiCARB 2020: blinded and placebo-controlled, bicarbonate improved nothing — and cost more.
cards.summary: At 12 months, physical function (Short Physical Performance Battery) was 8.3 points on bicarbonate vs 8.8 on placebo (adjusted effect −0.4, 95% CI −0.9 to 0.1; P=0.15), and the GFR treatment effect was 0.6 mL/min/1.73m² (−0.8 to 2.0; P=0.39) — both null. Bicarbonate cost more (£564 over a year), scored lower on quality of life, and had more adverse events (457 vs 400).

shelves.title: Lowering urate to protect the kidney: three trials, no protection
shelves.question: Does lowering serum urate with allopurinol slow the progression of chronic kidney disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Allopurinol · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Gout Suppressants · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Renin-Angiotensin System · Treatment Failure · Uric Acid · Xanthine Oxidase · Febuxostat · Hyperuricemia
shelves.balance: A beautiful epidemiologic association — high urate, faster decline — taken to trial twice in the same journal issue, and both times the kidney slopes came out identical. CKD-FIX (advanced CKD, mean eGFR 32): −3.33 vs −3.23 ml/min/yr. PERL (type 1 diabetes, measured iohexol GFR): a between-group difference of 0.001 after washout — as null as null gets, with the urate separation fully achieved (6.1 → 3.9 mg/dL). Urate is a marker of kidney disease, not a driver of it. FEATHER (Reference 3) makes three: febuxostat in stage 3 CKD with asymptomatic hyperuricemia, eGFR slope difference 0.70 (−0.21 to 1.62), P=0.1 — the drug prevented gout (0.91% vs 5.86%) and did not protect the kidney. Closing line: the ACR 2020 guideline and KDIGO 2024 both advise against treating asymptomatic hyperuricemia to protect the kidney.

cards.headline: CKD-FIX 2020: allopurinol in stage 3–4 CKD — eGFR declined 3.33/yr on drug vs 3.23/yr on placebo (difference −0.10; P=0.85).

cards.headline: FEATHER: febuxostat did not slow eGFR decline in stage 3 CKD (slope difference 0.70, P=0.1) — but prevented gout
cards.summary: Mean eGFR slope: +0.23 ml/min/1.73 m²/year on febuxostat vs −0.47 on placebo (difference 0.70 , −0.21 to 1.62; P=0.1 — not significant ); gouty arthritis 0.91% vs 5.86% (P=0.007) — 441 patients analyzed.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (FEATHER), Am J Kidney Dis 2018
cards.people: 467 patients with stage 3 CKD and asymptomatic hyperuricemia at 55 medical institutions in Japan; 443 randomized, and 441 (219 febuxostat, 222 placebo) included in the analysis; treatment for 108 weeks. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mean eGFR slope between febuxostat (0.23±5.26 ml/min/1.73 m² per year) and placebo (−0.47±4.48) groups (difference 0.70, 95% CI −0.21 to 1.62; P=0.1). The incidence of gouty arthritis was significantly lower on febuxostat (0.91%) than on placebo (5.86%) (P=0.007). No adverse events specific to febuxostat were observed. The trial’s closing position matches this shelf’s other two cards: febuxostat did not mitigate the decline in kidney function in stage 3 CKD with asymptomatic hyperuricemia. ACR 2020 and KDIGO 2024 both advise against treating asymptomatic hyperuricemia to protect the kidney.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup findings (benefit in patients without proteinuria, P=0.005, and in those with creatinine below the median, P=0.009) are the usual pattern that follows a null primary endpoint and are not carded as findings. GFR was estimated rather than measured, and patients with stage 4 or 5 CKD were excluded. Funded by Teijin Pharma Limited, febuxostat’s maker.

shelves.title: Chasing hemoglobin with ESAs in kidney disease: the target was the harm.
shelves.question: In CKD patients not on dialysis, does using an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent to push hemoglobin to normal (13 g/dL or above) improve cardiovascular outcomes versus partial correction?
shelves.mesh: Anemia · Darbepoetin alfa · Epoetin Alfa · Erythropoietin · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic
shelves.balance: CHOIR (targets 13.5 vs 11.3) — the high target caused MORE of the composite, 17.5% vs 13.5%, HR 1.34, and the trial stopped early. CREATE (13–15 vs 10.5–11.5) — no cardiovascular benefit, and more patients in the high group reached dialysis (127 vs 111). TREAT, the only placebo-controlled trial — no benefit on either primary composite, and stroke nearly doubled, 5.0% vs 2.6%, HR 1.92. What the drugs did deliver: fewer transfusions (TREAT 297 vs 496 patients) and modest quality-of-life gains (CREATE).

cards.headline: CHOIR 2006: targeting hemoglobin 13.5 brought more death, MI, heart-failure admissions and stroke than 11.3 — HR 1.34, stopped early.
cards.summary: Primary composite (death, MI, hospitalization for heart failure, stroke): 125 events (17.5%) vs 97 (13.5%), HR 1.34 (1.03–1.74), P=0.03. Quality of life was similar; more serious adverse events in the high-target group.
cards.people: 1,432 patients with CKD and anemia; 715 assigned to a hemoglobin target of 13.5 g/dL vs 717 to 11.3 g/dL (epoetin alfa); median follow-up 16 months; stopped early
cards.result: Primary composite (death, MI, hospitalization for heart failure, stroke): 125 events (17.5%) vs 97 (13.5%), HR 1.34 (1.03–1.74), P=0.03. Quality of life was similar; more serious adverse events in the high-target group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with an early stop can exaggerate an effect — but CREATE and TREAT point the same way. The post-hoc idea that high doses in non-responders explain the harm is a hypothesis, not the trial’s primary claim.
cards.source: Singh AK et al., N Engl J Med 2006 (PMID 17108343 · NCT00211120)

cards.headline: CREATE 2006: full correction to 13–15 gave no cardiovascular benefit and more dialysis (127 vs 111) — quality of life was the one gain.
cards.summary: First cardiovascular event 58 vs 47, HR 0.78 (0.53–1.14), P=0.20 — not significant. Dialysis 127 vs 111 (P=0.03). GFR decline was equal. General health and physical function improved more with full correction (P=0.003 and P<0.001); more hypertension episodes and headaches in that group.
cards.people: 603 patients, eGFR 15–35 ml/min, hemoglobin 11.0–12.5 g/dL; 301 assigned to a normal-range target of 13–15 g/dL vs 302 to a subnormal 10.5–11.5 g/dL (epoetin beta started only if hemoglobin fell below 10.5)
cards.result: First cardiovascular event 58 vs 47, HR 0.78 (0.53–1.14), P=0.20 — not significant. Dialysis 127 vs 111 (P=0.03). GFR decline was equal. cards.watchOut: The shelf’s one genuine benefit signal — quality of life — comes from an open-label trial, where expectation can inflate it. The hard outcomes point the other way or nowhere.

cards.headline: TREAT 2009: the placebo-controlled test — no benefit on either primary composite, and stroke nearly doubled, 5.0% vs 2.6% (HR 1.92).
cards.summary: Death or a cardiovascular event 632 vs 602, HR 1.05 (0.94–1.17), P=0.41. Death or end-stage renal disease 652 vs 618, HR 1.06 (0.95–1.19), P=0.29. Fatal or nonfatal stroke 101 (5.0%) vs 53 (2.6%), HR 1.92 (1.38–2.68), P<0.001. Red-cell transfusions 297 vs 496 patients (P<0.001); fatigue improved modestly. Achieved median hemoglobin 12.5 vs 10.6 g/dL.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the placebo arm received rescue darbepoetin if hemoglobin fell below 9.0 g/dL)
cards.people: 4,038 patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD (eGFR 20–60) and hemoglobin ≤11 g/dL; 2,012 darbepoetin alfa targeting ~13 g/dL vs 2,026 placebo
cards.result: Death or a cardiovascular event 632 vs 602, HR 1.05 (0.94–1.17), P=0.41. Death or end-stage renal disease 652 vs 618, HR 1.06 (0.95–1.19), P=0.29. Fatal or nonfatal stroke 101 (5.0%) vs 53 (2.6%), HR 1.92 (1.38–2.68), P<0.001. Red-cell transfusions 297 vs 496 patients (P<0.001); fatigue improved modestly. Achieved median hemoglobin 12.5 vs 10.6 g/dL.

shelves.title: Early vs late dialysis start: starting sooner did not help patients live longer
shelves.question: In adults with progressive stage 5 chronic kidney disease, does planning to start dialysis early (at eGFR 10–14) improve survival compared with waiting until eGFR falls to 5–7 or symptoms demand it?
shelves.mesh: Kidney Failure, Chronic · Renal Dialysis · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Time Factors · Uremia · Humans
shelves.balance: One trial is the whole shelf, and it is a good one: 828 patients randomized to start dialysis at eGFR 10–14 or to wait for 5–7. Starting early bought about 5.6 extra months on dialysis and no survival benefit (HR 1.04) — and three-quarters of the “late” group still started above their target eGFR when symptoms demanded it, which is the real-world lesson: start when the patient needs it, not when a number says so. No second randomized trial of dialysis timing exists. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: IDEAL: planned early dialysis start did not improve survival (HR 1.04)
cards.summary: Deaths: 37.6% with planned early start vs 36.6% with planned late start over a median 3.59 years (hazard ratio 1.04 , 0.83–1.30; P=0.75); median time to dialysis 1.80 vs 7.40 months — 828 patients.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (IDEAL), N Engl J Med 2010 — the only randomized trial of dialysis timing ever completed; this shelf is a single-trial shelf, flagged as such
cards.people: 828 adults at 32 centres in Australia and New Zealand; mean age 60.4 years; 542 men and 286 women; 355 with diabetes. Median time to dialysis initiation 1.80 months (early) vs 7.40 months (late).
cards.result: Death from any cause: 152 of 404 patients (37.6%) in the early-start group vs 155 of 424 (36.6%) in the late-start group (hazard ratio with early initiation 1.04, 95% CI 0.83–1.30; P=0.75), over a median follow-up of 3.59 years. There was no significant difference in cardiovascular events, infections, or complications of dialysis; the trial’s secondary analyses agreed (composite cardiovascular events HR 1.23, 0.97–1.56; infectious events HR 0.87, 0.70–1.08). In the late-start group, 75.9% of patients ultimately began dialysis at an eGFR above the 7.0 target, because symptoms developed.
cards.watchOut: A planned-start trial, not a deferral-forever trial: it answers “should we start by the numbers?” (no survival gain) rather than “can dialysis be postponed indefinitely?” (not tested — symptoms overruled the protocol in most late-start patients). Funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and others.
cards.source: Cooper BA et al. A randomized, controlled trial of early versus late initiation of dialysis. N Engl J Med. 2010;363:609-19. PMID 20581422 · ACTRN12609000266268.

shelves.title: Frequent hemodialysis: better intermediate outcomes, a mortality warning in follow-up
shelves.question: In patients on maintenance hemodialysis, does dialyzing six times a week instead of three improve outcomes — and what does the only long-term mortality follow-up show?
shelves.mesh: Kidney Failure, Chronic · Renal Dialysis · Hemodialysis, Home · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular · Hypertension · Hyperphosphatemia · Humans
shelves.balance: Dialyzing six times a week instead of three clearly changes physiology — better blood-pressure and phosphate control in both FHN trials — and in the in-center Daily trial it improved composites of death-or-left-ventricular-mass and death-or-physical-health-score, in relative terms. The smaller Nocturnal trial found neither, and its extended follow-up produced the shelf’s warning: a mortality hazard ratio of 3.88 in the nocturnal arm, from tiny numbers with an implausibly healthy control group — carded as cautionary observational context, not proof of harm. More frequent dialysis also meant more vascular-access interventions. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: FHN Daily: six-times-weekly in-center dialysis improved both coprimary composites
cards.summary: Death or increase in left ventricular mass: hazard ratio 0.61 (0.46–0.82); death or decrease in physical-health composite score: hazard ratio 0.70 (0.53–0.92) — both in relative terms; vascular-access interventions hazard ratio 1.71 (1.08–2.73) — 245 patients.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (Frequent Hemodialysis Network Daily Trial), N Engl J Med 2010
cards.people: 245 patients randomized to hemodialysis six times per week (n=125) or three times per week (n=120) for 12 months; the frequent group averaged 5.2 sessions per week, with weekly standard Kt/V 3.54±0.56 vs 2.49±0.27. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Frequent hemodialysis was associated with significant benefits on both coprimary composites: hazard ratio for death or increase in left ventricular mass, 0.61 (95% CI 0.46–0.82); hazard ratio for death or a decrease in the physical-health composite score, 0.70 (0.53–0.92) — both relative measures. Hypertension and hyperphosphatemia control improved. There were no significant effects on cognitive performance, self-reported depression, serum albumin, or erythropoiesis-stimulating-agent use. Patients on frequent dialysis underwent more interventions related to vascular access (hazard ratio 1.71, 1.08–2.73).
cards.watchOut: The composites pair death with a surrogate (MRI left-ventricular mass; a questionnaire score), and deaths were few — the composites are carried mainly by their surrogate components. Funded by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and others.
cards.source: FHN Trial Group; Chertow GM et al. In-center hemodialysis six times per week versus three times per week. N Engl J Med. 2010;363:2287-300. PMID 21091062 · NCT00264758.

cards.headline: FHN Nocturnal: six-times-weekly home nocturnal dialysis — both coprimary outcomes null, trial underpowered
cards.summary: Death or left-ventricular-mass change: hazard ratio 0.68 ; death or physical-health-composite change: hazard ratio 0.91 — neither significant; phosphate and blood-pressure control improved; a trend to more vascular-access events — 87 patients.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (Frequent Hemodialysis Network Nocturnal Trial), Kidney Int 2011
cards.people: 87 patients randomized to nocturnal hemodialysis six times per week at home (n=45) or conventional hemodialysis three times per week (n=42), all with single-use high-flux dialyzers; the nocturnal arm achieved a 1.82-fold higher weekly standard Kt/V and 2.45-fold higher weekly treatment time. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: No significant effect of nocturnal hemodialysis on either coprimary outcome: hazard ratio 0.68 for death or left ventricular mass (MRI), and 0.91 for death or RAND Physical Health Composite. Control of hyperphosphatemia and hypertension improved in the nocturnal arm; no significant benefit on cognitive performance, depression, nutrition or anemia markers, or hospitalization; a trend toward increased vascular access events in the nocturnal arm.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment stopped far short of the planned sample (~250), so the null may be a power failure rather than proof of no effect — the left-ventricular-mass hazard ratio (0.68) points the same way as the Daily trial’s without the numbers to confirm it. Possible explanations named by the authors: limited sample size and patient characteristics.

cards.headline: FHN Nocturnal extended follow-up: mortality hazard ratio 3.88 in the nocturnal arm — a cautionary observational signal
cards.summary: In post-trial follow-up (median total 3.7 years), deaths numbered 14 in the nocturnal arm vs 5 in the conventional arm; overall mortality hazard ratio 3.88 (1.27–11.79; P=0.01) — carded here as cautionary observational context only, with the authors’ own warnings attached.
cards.type: Post-trial observational extended follow-up of a randomized cohort, Am J Kidney Dis 2015
cards.people: The 87 FHN Nocturnal Trial participants who consented to extended follow-up; deaths ascertained through July 2011 by linkage to the US Renal Data System and study-centre queries; median follow-up for the trial plus post-trial period 3.7 years. After the trial year, participants could freely change their dialysis prescription.
cards.result: Deaths: 2 during the trial year and 12 more during extended follow-up in the nocturnal arm, vs 1 and 4 in the conventional arm. Overall mortality hazard ratio for the nocturnal group 3.88 (95% CI 1.27–11.79; P=0.01). An as-treated analysis with a 12-month running treatment average gave HR 3.06 (1.11–8.43; P=0.03); with a 6-month running average, HR 1.12 (0.44–3.22; P=0.7).
cards.watchOut: The authors’ own cautions, printed with the number: the conventional arm’s mortality (0.03 deaths per patient-year) was surprisingly — implausibly — low; the sample is tiny, so statistical power for mortality is minimal; and post-trial prescription changes were frequent. This card records a warning to investigate, not a finding of harm.
cards.source: Rocco MV et al. Long-term Effects of Frequent Nocturnal Hemodialysis on Mortality: The Frequent Hemodialysis Network (FHN) Nocturnal Trial. Am J Kidney Dis. 2015;66:459-68. PMID 25863828 · parent trial NCT00271999.

shelves.title: Intravenous iron in kidney disease: dose and target matter
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and iron-deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron — given proactively at higher doses, or targeting a higher ferritin — improve outcomes compared with reactive low-dose or oral iron?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Ferric Compounds · Ferric Oxide, Saccharated · Ferritins · Renal Dialysis · Humans
shelves.balance: In dialysis patients, giving iron proactively at high dose (PIVOTAL) beat waiting for deficiency: fewer first cardiovascular events or deaths (HR 0.85), fewer recurrent events (rate ratio 0.77), and less erythropoiesis-stimulating agent needed — with death alone not significantly different (HR 0.84, P=0.054) and identical infection rates. Before dialysis (FIND-CKD), IV iron beat oral iron only when it targeted a high ferritin (400–600 µg/L); the low target was indistinguishable from pills. Dose and target, not the IV route alone, are the active ingredients. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: PIVOTAL: proactive high-dose IV iron beat reactive low-dose on the cardiovascular composite (HR 0.85); death alone not significant
cards.summary: Primary composite (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, heart-failure hospitalization, or death): 29.3% on proactive high-dose iron vs 32.3% on reactive low-dose (hazard ratio 0.85 , 0.73–1.00; P=0.04 for superiority); recurrent events rate ratio 0.77 (0.66–0.92); infection rates identical — 2,141 patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label randomized trial with blinded endpoint evaluation (PIVOTAL), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 2,141 adults on maintenance hemodialysis, randomized to high-dose proactive iron sucrose (n=1,093) or low-dose reactive iron sucrose (n=1,048); median follow-up 2.1 years. (Mean age and sex mix are not printed in the abstract and are carried as a gate item.)
cards.result: Primary endpoint events: 320 patients (29.3%) in the high-dose group vs 338 (32.3%) in the low-dose group (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–1.00; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.04 for superiority). Recurrent events: 429 vs 507 (rate ratio 0.77, 0.66–0.92). Death alone was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.84, 0.71–1.00; P=0.054) — the composite win is not a proven mortality win. Median monthly iron dose 264 mg vs 145 mg; median monthly erythropoiesis-stimulating-agent dose 29,757 vs 38,805 IU (median difference −7,539 IU). Infection rates were the same in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The superiority P value (0.04) rests on a confidence interval that touches 1.00, in an open-label trial (endpoints were adjudicated blind). Population: incident dialysis patients in UK centres. Funded by Kidney Research UK.
cards.source: Macdougall IC et al. Intravenous Iron in Patients Undergoing Maintenance Hemodialysis. N Engl J Med. 2019;380:447-458. PMID 30365356 · EudraCT 2013-002267-25 (no NCT in the trial record).

cards.headline: FIND-CKD: IV iron to a high ferritin target delayed other anemia therapy vs oral iron (HR 0.65); the low target did not
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (needing other anemia management, or a hemoglobin trigger): 23.5% with IV ferric carboxymaltose targeting ferritin 400–600 µg/L vs 31.8% on oral iron (hazard ratio 0.65 , 0.44–0.95); low-target IV iron (100–200) was 32.2% — no better than pills — 626 patients.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, multicentre trial (FIND-CKD), Nephrol Dial Transplant 2014
cards.people: 626 patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD, anemia, and iron deficiency, randomized (1:1:2) to IV ferric carboxymaltose at a high or low ferritin target, or oral iron, for 56 weeks. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Primary endpoint occurred in 36 patients (23.5%) in the high-ferritin IV group, 49 (32.2%) in the low-ferritin IV group, and 98 (31.8%) in the oral iron group (hazard ratio for high-ferritin IV vs oral iron 0.65, 95% CI 0.44–0.95; P=0.026). Hemoglobin rise was greater with high-ferritin IV iron (P=0.014), and more patients achieved a hemoglobin increase ≥1 g/dL (hazard ratio 2.04, 1.52–2.72; P<0.001). Adverse and serious adverse event rates were similar across groups; no renal toxicity signal, and no difference in cardiovascular or infectious events.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a process outcome — needing an ESA, other iron, or transfusion, or hitting a hemoglobin trigger — not death or cardiovascular events, which did not differ. The lesson is the target, not the route: low-target IV iron matched oral iron.

shelves.title: Phosphate binders: calcium-free vs calcium-based — no proven outcome difference
shelves.question: In patients on dialysis with hyperphosphatemia, do non-calcium-based phosphate binders (sevelamer, lanthanum) reduce death or cardiovascular events compared with calcium-based binders?
shelves.mesh: Hyperphosphatemia · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Chelating Agents · Sevelamer · Lanthanum · Calcium Carbonate · Humans
shelves.balance: The binder wars end in a draw on outcomes. DCOR (sevelamer vs calcium-based binders, 2,103 patients) found no significant overall mortality difference; LANDMARK (lanthanum vs calcium carbonate, 2,309 randomized) found no difference in cardiovascular events and a higher cardiovascular-death rate on the non-calcium binder. The older meta-analytic claim of a 22% relative mortality advantage for non-calcium binders (Reference 3) is carded MAYBE (weak evidence): it predates LANDMARK and pools trials whose individual binder classes were each non-significant. Choose a binder on phosphate control, calcium load, pill burden, tolerance, and cost — not on a promised survival benefit. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: DCOR: sevelamer vs calcium-based binders — mortality not significantly different overall
cards.summary: All-cause and cause-specific mortality rates were not significantly different between sevelamer and calcium-based binders in 2,103 hemodialysis patients; the only significant signal was an age interaction — a mortality benefit confined to patients over 65 .
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, open-label, parallel-design trial (DCOR), Kidney Int 2007
cards.people: 2,103 prevalent hemodialysis patients randomized to sevelamer or calcium-based binders; 1,068 patients completed the study. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: All-cause mortality rates and cause-specific mortality rates (cardiovascular, infection, other) were not significantly different between sevelamer and calcium-based binders (adjusted relative risk 0.92, not significant). There was a significant interaction between age and treatment effect: only in patients over 65 years was there a significant mortality lowering with sevelamer (subgroup relative risk 0.77), and that suggestion was of lower overall — not cardiovascular-linked — mortality.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and sponsor-run (Genzyme, sevelamer’s maker), with only about half of randomized patients completing the study — attrition that weakens every estimate. The over-65 subgroup result is hypothesis-grade. No registry ID appears in this 2007 trial’s record (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Suki WN et al. Effects of sevelamer and calcium-based phosphate binders on mortality in hemodialysis patients. Kidney Int. 2007;72:1130-7. PMID 17728707.

cards.headline: LANDMARK: lanthanum vs calcium carbonate — cardiovascular events not different (HR 1.11); cardiovascular death higher on lanthanum
cards.summary: Composite cardiovascular events: 4.80 vs 4.30 per 100 person-years on lanthanum vs calcium carbonate (hazard ratio 1.11 , 0.88–1.41; P=0.37); all-cause death hazard ratio 1.10 (0.88–1.37); cardiovascular death hazard ratio 1.51 (1.01–2.27) against lanthanum — 2,309 randomized patients.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, parallel-group trial with blinded endpoint adjudication (LANDMARK), JAMA 2021
cards.people: 2,374 patients enrolled at 273 hemodialysis facilities in Japan; 2,309 randomized (median age 69 years; 40.5% women) to lanthanum carbonate (n=1,154) or calcium carbonate (n=1,155), titrated to serum phosphate 3.5–6.0 mg/dL; median follow-up 3.16 years; 1,851 (80.2%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Primary composite cardiovascular events occurred in 147 of 1,063 patients in the lanthanum group and 134 of 1,072 in the calcium carbonate group (incidence 4.80 vs 4.30 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.88–1.41; P=0.37). No significant differences in all-cause death (HR 1.10, 0.88–1.37; P=0.42) or hip fracture (HR 1.21, 0.62–2.35). The lanthanum group had a higher risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.51, 1.01–2.27; P=0.045) and of secondary hyperparathyroidism (HR 1.62, 1.19–2.20). Adverse events: 25.7% vs 23.4%.
cards.watchOut: Japanese patients selected for calcification risk, in an open-label trial with low event rates — the authors note findings may not apply to higher-risk patients. The cardiovascular-death signal is one secondary component among many: a warning against assuming non-calcium binders are safer, not proof that lanthanum kills.
cards.source: Ogata H et al. Effect of Treating Hyperphosphatemia With Lanthanum Carbonate vs Calcium Carbonate on Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease Undergoing Hemodialysis: The LANDMARK Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;325:1946-1954. PMID 34003226 · NCT01578200 · UMIN000006815.

cards.headline: Jamal 2013 meta-analysis: 22% relative mortality reduction with non-calcium binders — carded MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Across 11 randomized trials (4,622 patients), non-calcium-based binders were associated with a 22% relative reduction in all-cause mortality vs calcium-based binders (risk ratio 0.78 , 0.61–0.98) — carded MAYBE (weak evidence) : see the Watch out before quoting it.
cards.type: Systematic review and updated meta-analysis of randomized trials, Lancet 2013 — carded at MAYBE (weak evidence) inside this POSSIBLE shelf
cards.people: 11 randomized trials reporting mortality, 4,622 patients with chronic kidney disease, pooling trials published up to October 2012 (an update adding 5 new randomized trials to a previous meta-analysis).
cards.result: Patients assigned to non-calcium-based binders had a 22% relative reduction in all-cause mortality compared with those assigned to calcium-based phosphate binders (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.61–0.98), in a DerSimonian-and-Laird random-effects pooling of the randomized trials.
cards.watchOut: Why this card is graded MAYBE (weak evidence): the pooled estimate predates LANDMARK (Reference 2), the largest trial, which found no benefit for a non-calcium binder and a higher cardiovascular-death rate; within the meta-analysis, no individual binder class carried the effect on its own; and the underlying trials were mostly short with high dropout (DCOR, Card 1, lost about half its patients). The claim is printed at full size with its grade attached — it does not carry this shelf.
cards.source: Jamal SA et al. Effect of calcium-based versus non-calcium-based phosphate binders on mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. 2013;382:1268-77. PMID 23870817.

shelves.title: Cinacalcet in dialysis (EVOLVE): the primary outcome was null
shelves.question: In patients on hemodialysis with moderate-to-severe secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the calcimimetic cinacalcet reduce death or major cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary · Cinacalcet · Cardiovascular Diseases · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Parathyroid Hormone · Renal Dialysis · Humans
shelves.balance: EVOLVE asked whether lowering parathyroid hormone with cinacalcet would prevent death and cardiovascular events in dialysis patients, and its primary answer was no: HR 0.93 (0.85–1.02), P=0.11 — printed first on the card, because everything favorable on this shelf (the adjusted HR 0.88, the lag-censored HR 0.85, the older-patient subgroup HR 0.74) was computed after that null, in a trial where about two-thirds of patients stopped their assigned drug. What cinacalcet demonstrably did was lower PTH and reduce parathyroidectomy (HR 0.44). For cardiovascular or mortality benefit, the verdict is MAYBE (weak evidence). Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: EVOLVE: cinacalcet did not significantly reduce death or major cardiovascular events (HR 0.93, P=0.11) — primary outcome null, printed first
cards.summary: Primary outcome null: the composite of death, myocardial infarction, hospitalization for unstable angina, heart failure, or a peripheral vascular event occurred in 48.2% on cinacalcet vs 49.2% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93 , 0.85–1.02; P=0.11 — not significant ) — 3,883 patients. Hypocalcemia and gastrointestinal adverse events were significantly more frequent on cinacalcet.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial (EVOLVE), N Engl J Med 2012
cards.people: 3,883 patients with moderate-to-severe secondary hyperparathyroidism (median intact PTH 693 pg/mL, 10th–90th percentile 363–1694) on hemodialysis, randomized to cinacalcet (n=1,948) or placebo (n=1,935); followed for up to 64 months; median study-drug exposure 21.2 vs 17.5 months. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint was reached by 938 of 1,948 patients (48.2%) in the cinacalcet group and 952 of 1,935 (49.2%) in the placebo group: relative hazard 0.93 (95% CI 0.85–1.02), P=0.11 — not significant in the unadjusted intention-to-treat primary analysis. Hypocalcemia and gastrointestinal adverse events were significantly more frequent with cinacalcet.
cards.watchOut: Everything after the primary result is rescue analysis: covariate-adjusted HR 0.88 (0.79–0.97); lag-censoring 6 months after stopping drug, HR 0.85; parathyroidectomy HR 0.44 — the one decisive benefit; and a prespecified age split (≥65 years HR 0.74 vs <65 HR 0.99; interaction P=0.01) that Australia’s PBAC declined to turn into an age-based restriction. About two-thirds of patients stopped study drug, and some placebo patients crossed to commercial cinacalcet, diluting the intention-to-treat contrast. Funded by Amgen, cinacalcet’s maker.
cards.source: EVOLVE Trial Investigators; Chertow GM et al. Effect of cinacalcet on cardiovascular disease in patients undergoing dialysis. N Engl J Med. 2012;367:2482-94. PMID 23121374 · NCT00345839.

shelves.title: Tolvaptan in ADPKD: slower kidney growth, slower decline, a liver to watch
shelves.question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does the vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist tolvaptan slow kidney growth and the loss of kidney function — in early and in later-stage disease?
shelves.mesh: Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant · Tolvaptan · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Benzazepines · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Kidney · Humans
shelves.balance: Tolvaptan is the first drug shown to slow ADPKD itself: kidney growth roughly halved over 3 years in early disease (TEMPO 3:4), and eGFR decline slowed by about 1.27 ml/min/1.73 m² per year in later disease (REPRISE) — in a trial that randomized only patients who had already tolerated the drug in a run-in. The benefits are slopes, not prevented kidney failure, and they are bought with aquaretic side effects (thirst, polyuria), a 23% discontinuation rate in TEMPO, and a liver-enzyme signal that requires regular monitoring. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: TEMPO 3:4: tolvaptan halved kidney growth (2.8% vs 5.5% per year) over 3 years
cards.summary: Total kidney volume grew 2.8% per year on tolvaptan vs 5.5% per year on placebo (P<0.001); the clinical-progression composite favored tolvaptan ( 44 vs 50 events per 100 follow-up-years); discontinuation 23% vs 14% — 1,445 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (TEMPO 3:4), N Engl J Med 2012
cards.people: 1,445 patients with ADPKD randomized 2:1 to tolvaptan (highest tolerated of three twice-daily split-dose regimens) or placebo for 3 years; mean age 39 years (per the trial report). (Sex mix is not printed in the abstract and is carried as a gate item.)
cards.result: Increase in total kidney volume: 2.8% per year (95% CI 2.5–3.1) on tolvaptan vs 5.5% per year (5.1–6.0) on placebo (P<0.001). The composite of clinical progression favored tolvaptan (44 vs 50 events per 100 follow-up-years, P=0.01; composite hazard ratio 0.87), with lower rates of worsening kidney function (2 vs 5 events per 100 person-years, P<0.001) and kidney pain (5 vs 7, P=0.007). Kidney function declined more slowly on tolvaptan (reciprocal serum creatinine slope −2.61 vs −3.81 per year, P<0.001; eGFR slope −2.78 vs −3.70 ml/min/1.73 m² per year). Fewer ADPKD-related adverse events but more aquaresis-related and hepatic adverse events on tolvaptan, contributing to a higher discontinuation rate (23% vs 14%).
cards.watchOut: Aquaresis is the daily price of this drug — thirst and polyuria — and the hepatic adverse events seen here are why liver monitoring is mandatory with tolvaptan. Kidney volume is a surrogate; the kidney-function components of the composite point the same way. Funded by Otsuka, tolvaptan’s maker.
cards.source: Torres VE et al. Tolvaptan in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. N Engl J Med. 2012;367:2407-18. PMID 23121377 · NCT00428948.
