cards.headline: REPRISE: in later-stage ADPKD, tolvaptan slowed eGFR decline by 1.27 ml/min/1.73 m² over 1 year
cards.summary: Change in eGFR over 1 year: −2.34 on tolvaptan vs −3.61 ml/min/1.73 m² on placebo (difference 1.27 , 0.86–1.68; P<0.001); ALT elevations >3× the upper limit of normal in 5.6% vs 1.2% , reversible on stopping — 1,370 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomized-withdrawal, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (REPRISE), N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 1,370 patients with ADPKD (aged 18–55 with eGFR 25–65, or 56–65 with eGFR 25–44 ml/min/1.73 m²) randomized 1:1 after an 8-week prerandomization period with sequential placebo and tolvaptan run-in phases that tested each patient’s ability to take tolvaptan without dose-limiting side effects (126 of 1,496 run-in patients did not proceed to randomization). (Mean age and sex mix are not printed in the abstract.)
cards.result: Change in eGFR from baseline to follow-up (interpolated to 1 year): −2.34 ml/min/1.73 m² (95% CI −2.81 to −1.87) on tolvaptan vs −3.61 (−4.08 to −3.14) on placebo (difference 1.27, 0.86–1.68; P<0.001). Alanine aminotransferase elevations to more than 3 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 38 of 681 patients (5.6%) on tolvaptan vs 8 of 685 (1.2%) on placebo; elevations were reversible after stopping tolvaptan, and no bilirubin elevation above twice the upper limit was detected.
cards.watchOut: The run-in flatters the drug: everyone randomized had already proved they could tolerate tolvaptan, so both the benefit’s cleanliness and the harm rates understate what an unselected clinic population starting fresh would see. Monthly liver monitoring was built into the trial. Funded by Otsuka.
cards.source: Torres VE et al. Tolvaptan in Later-Stage Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease. N Engl J Med. 2017;377:1930-1942. PMID 29105594 · NCT02160145.

shelves.title: Immunosuppression in IgA nephropathy: steroids work and harm; targeted budesonide and sparsentan
shelves.question: In patients with IgA nephropathy at high risk of progression despite optimized supportive care, does immunosuppression — systemic steroids, targeted-release budesonide, or the dual endothelin–angiotensin antagonist sparsentan — slow the loss of kidney function, and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Glomerulonephritis, IGA · Methylprednisolone · Glucocorticoids · Budesonide · Proteinuria · Immunosuppression Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: High-risk IgA nephropathy is treatable, and every effective option charges for its benefit. Methylprednisolone cut the composite of kidney-function decline, kidney failure, or kidney death nearly in half in relative terms (TESTING, HR 0.53) while roughly quadrupling serious adverse events, concentrated in the abandoned full-dose era. STOP-IgAN’s null on eGFR loss — printed on its card — is the fence: older combination immunosuppression added to optimized supportive care did not slow decline, and about a third of its run-in patients remitted on supportive care alone. Targeted-release budesonide (NefIgArd) and the non-immunosuppressive sparsentan (PROTECT) preserved eGFR slope and cut proteinuria with gentler, though real, side-effect ledgers. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: TESTING: methylprednisolone cut kidney progression (HR 0.53) — with more serious infections, concentrated at full dose
cards.summary: Primary composite (40% eGFR decline, kidney failure, or death from kidney disease): 28.8% on methylprednisolone vs 43.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.53 , 0.39–0.72); kidney failure alone hazard ratio 0.59 (0.40–0.87); serious adverse events 10.9% vs 2.8% — 503 patients.
cards.type: International, multicentre, double-blind, randomized clinical trial (TESTING), JAMA 2022
cards.people: 503 participants at 67 centres in Australia, Canada, China, India, and Malaysia; mean age 38 years; 198 (39%) women; mean eGFR 61.5 ml/min/1.73 m²; mean proteinuria 2.46 g/day; mean follow-up 4.2 years; 493 (98%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 74 participants (28.8%) on methylprednisolone vs 106 (43.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.39–0.72; P<.001; absolute annual event-rate difference −4.8% per year). Kidney failure: 50 (19.5%) vs 67 (27.2%) (HR 0.59, 0.40–0.87; P=.008); 9 of 11 prespecified secondary outcomes favored methylprednisolone. Effect seen in both dose eras (full-dose HR 0.58; reduced-dose HR 0.27; heterogeneity P=.11). Serious adverse events: 28 patients (10.9%) vs 7 (2.8%), concentrated in the full-dose era (16.2% vs 3.2%), primarily serious infections; deaths numbered 6 vs 3.
cards.watchOut: The trial changed itself mid-course: after 262 participants were randomized, excess serious infections forced the methylprednisolone dose down (from 0.6–0.8 to 0.4 mg/kg/day) and pneumocystis prophylaxis in. The reduced-dose era’s larger efficacy estimate rests on smaller numbers. Benefit and harm are both real, and both are printed.
cards.source: Lv J et al. Effect of Oral Methylprednisolone on Decline in Kidney Function or Kidney Failure in Patients With IgA Nephropathy: The TESTING Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022;327:1888-1898. PMID 35579642 · NCT01560052.

cards.headline: STOP-IgAN: added immunosuppression raised remission but did not slow eGFR loss — the null, printed
cards.summary: Full clinical remission at 3 years: 17% with added immunosuppression vs 5% with supportive care alone (P=0.01) — but eGFR loss of ≥15 ml/min/1.73 m²: 26% vs 28% (P=0.75), and no difference in annual eGFR decline; more severe infections, impaired glucose tolerance, and weight gain on immunosuppression — 162 randomized patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomized controlled trial (STOP-IgAN), N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: 337 patients entered the supportive-care run-in; 309 completed it, and in 94 the proteinuria fell below 0.75 g/day on supportive care alone, so they were not randomized. 162 patients were randomized: 80 to supportive care alone, 82 to supportive care plus immunosuppression, for 3 years. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Full clinical remission: 14 patients (17%) in the immunosuppression group vs 4 (5%) in the supportive-care group (P=0.01). Decrease in eGFR of at least 15 ml/min/1.73 m²: 21 patients (26%) on immunosuppression vs 22 (28%) on supportive care (P=0.75). No significant difference in the annual decline in eGFR. More patients in the immunosuppression group had severe infections, impaired glucose tolerance, and weight gain of more than 5 kg in the first year; one patient in the immunosuppression group died of sepsis.
cards.watchOut: The remission win was a proteinuria endpoint; on the outcome that matters — losing kidney function — the groups were identical, and every listed harm sat in the immunosuppression arm. The run-in is the quiet lesson: roughly a third of screened patients reached the proteinuria target on supportive care alone and never needed the drugs.
cards.source: Rauen T et al. Intensive Supportive Care plus Immunosuppression in IgA Nephropathy. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:2225-36. PMID 26630142 · NCT00554502.

cards.headline: NefIgArd: targeted-release budesonide preserved eGFR over 2 years (benefit 5.05 ml/min/1.73 m²)
cards.summary: Time-weighted average eGFR over 2 years favored Nefecon by 5.05 ml/min/1.73 m² (3.24–7.38; P<0.0001) after a 9-month course: average change −2.47 vs −7.52 ml/min/1.73 m²; proteinuria reduction durable off-drug — 364 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial (NefIgArd), Lancet 2023
cards.people: 364 patients (182 per group) at 132 sites in 20 countries; 240 (66%) men and 124 (34%) women; 275 (76%) White; median age 43 years (per the trial report). Treatment 9 months, then 15 months of observational follow-up off study drug, supportive care continued throughout.
cards.result: Time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years showed a statistically significant treatment benefit for Nefecon vs placebo (difference 5.05 ml/min/1.73 m², 95% CI 3.24–7.38; P<0.0001), with time-weighted average changes of −2.47 ml/min/1.73 m² on Nefecon vs −7.52 on placebo. Proteinuria fell by about 31% vs 5% at 9 months and remained about 34% lower at 24 months. Most common treatment-emergent adverse events on Nefecon: peripheral oedema (17% vs 4% on placebo), hypertension (12% vs 3%), muscle spasms (12% vs 4%), acne (11% vs 1%), headache (10% vs 8%). No treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: A locally acting steroid still acts systemically in part — the oedema, hypertension, and acne ledger is milder than TESTING’s systemic-steroid ledger but is not empty. The endpoint is eGFR trajectory over 2 years, not kidney-failure events. Funded by Calliditas Therapeutics, Nefecon’s maker.

cards.headline: PROTECT: sparsentan vs irbesartan — proteinuria −42.8% vs −4.4% at 110 weeks, slower chronic eGFR decline
cards.summary: Proteinuria change at 110 weeks: −42.8% on sparsentan vs −4.4% on maximally titrated irbesartan (geometric mean ratio 0.60 , 0.50–0.72); chronic eGFR slope −2.7 vs −3.8 ml/min/1.73 m²/year (difference 1.1, 0.1–2.1; P=0.037); composite kidney-failure endpoint 9% vs 13% (relative risk 0.7, 0.4–1.2, not significant) — 404 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial (PROTECT), Lancet 2023
cards.people: 406 patients randomized at 134 sites in 18 countries (203 per group); 404 received study drug and form the analysis set; 282 (70%) male; mean age 46 years and mean eGFR 57 ml/min/1.73 m² (per the trial report). Sparsentan target dose 400 mg daily vs irbesartan 300 mg daily.
cards.result: Proteinuria reduction at the 36-week primary endpoint (−49.8% vs −15.1%) was maintained: at 110 weeks, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio changed by −42.8% on sparsentan vs −4.4% on irbesartan (geometric least-squares mean ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.50–0.72). eGFR chronic slope (weeks 6–110): −2.7 vs −3.8 ml/min/1.73 m²/year (difference 1.1, 0.1–2.1; P=0.037); total slope difference 1.0 (−0.03 to 1.94; P=0.058); absolute eGFR change −5.8 vs −9.5. The composite kidney-failure endpoint (confirmed 40% eGFR reduction, end-stage kidney disease, or death) occurred in 18 of 202 (9%) on sparsentan vs 26 of 202 (13%) on irbesartan (relative risk 0.7, 0.4–1.2). Treatment-emergent adverse events were well balanced, with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: Sparsentan is not immunosuppression — it blocks endothelin and angiotensin receptors in one molecule, and sits on this shelf as the non-immune comparator therapy. Its hard composite endpoint was not significant; the proven wins are proteinuria and slope, against full-dose irbesartan — an active comparator, not placebo. Funded by Travere Therapeutics, sparsentan’s maker.
cards.source: Rovin BH et al. Efficacy and safety of sparsentan versus irbesartan in patients with IgA nephropathy (PROTECT): 2-year results from a randomised, active-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2023;402:2077-2090. PMID 37931634 · NCT03762850.

shelves.title: Stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in advanced CKD: stopping did not slow the kidney decline
shelves.question: In patients with advanced, progressive chronic kidney disease (eGFR below 30), does stopping renin–angiotensin system inhibitors — ACE inhibitors and ARBs — slow the loss of kidney function, or is it safer to continue them?
shelves.mesh: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Renin-Angiotensin System · Humans
shelves.balance: The randomized answer is no: in STOP-ACEi, stopping RAS inhibitors in advanced CKD did not slow the eGFR decline at 3 years (difference −0.7 ml/min/1.73 m², P=0.42), and kidney failure or dialysis started somewhat more often in the stopping group (62% vs 56%; HR 1.28, confidence interval crossing 1). The observational counterpoint (Fu 2021) cuts the other way on the outcomes patients fear most — stopping was associated with higher 5-year risks of death and major cardiovascular events, though a lower risk of starting kidney replacement therapy — but it is observational, and people who stop these drugs differ from people who continue them. Read together: there is no kidney case for routinely stopping, and a possible safety case against it. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: STOP-ACEi: stopping RAS inhibitors did not slow eGFR decline (difference −0.7 at 3 years, P=0.42)
cards.summary: eGFR at 3 years: 12.6 in the discontinuation group vs 13.3 ml/min/1.73 m² in the continuation group (difference −0.7 , 95% CI −2.5 to 1.0; P=0.42); end-stage kidney disease or kidney replacement therapy 62% vs 56% (hazard ratio 1.28 , 0.99–1.65) — 411 patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomized trial (STOP-ACEi), N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 411 patients with advanced and progressive CKD (eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m²) enrolled at UK centres. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At 3 years, least-squares mean eGFR was 12.6±0.7 ml/min/1.73 m² in the discontinuation group and 13.3±0.6 in the continuation group (difference −0.7; 95% CI −2.5 to 1.0; P=0.42), a negative value favoring continuation. End-stage kidney disease or initiation of kidney replacement therapy occurred in 128 patients (62%) who stopped vs 115 (56%) who continued (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.65). Cardiovascular events numbered 108 vs 88 and deaths 20 vs 22. No heterogeneity across the prespecified subgroups (age, eGFR, diabetes type, blood pressure, proteinuria).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the trial was powered on eGFR, not on events: the kidney-replacement hazard ratio of 1.28 leans against stopping but its confidence interval crosses 1. What the trial settles is the kidney question — stopping bought no eGFR benefit. Funded by the UK National Institute for Health Research and the Medical Research Council.

cards.headline: Fu 2021 (observational counterpoint): stopping was associated with more death and cardiovascular events — and less kidney replacement therapy
cards.summary: 5-year absolute risks, stopping vs continuing: death 54.5% vs 40.9% (difference +13.6 per 100 patients); major cardiovascular events 59.5% vs 47.6% (+11.9); kidney replacement therapy 27.9% vs 36.1% (−8.3) — 10,254 patients, observational.
cards.type: Observational study using target-trial emulation (Swedish Renal Registry), J Am Soc Nephrol 2021 — labeled observational
cards.people: 10,254 prevalent RAS-inhibitor users who developed eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m² under nephrologist care, 2007–2017; median age 72 years; 36% women; median eGFR 23 ml/min/1.73 m²; 1,553 (15%) stopped within 6 months.
cards.result: Compared with continuing, stopping was associated with higher absolute 5-year risks of death (54.5% vs 40.9%; absolute difference +13.6 events per 100 patients) and major adverse cardiovascular events (59.5% vs 47.6%; +11.9 per 100), but a lower absolute risk of kidney replacement therapy (27.9% vs 36.1%; −8.3 per 100). Results were consistent across eGFR levels at stopping, subgroups, albuminuria and potassium adjustments, and a time-dependent marginal structural model.
cards.watchOut: Observational: patients who stop RAS inhibitors are usually stopping for a reason — illness, hypotension, a rising potassium — and emulation methods cannot fully remove that confounding by indication. The death and cardiovascular associations are printed as associations, and this shelf’s randomized card (STOP-ACEi, Card 1) remains the stronger design for the kidney question. The two agree on one point: stopping did not protect the kidney.
cards.source: Fu EL et al. Stopping Renin-Angiotensin System Inhibitors in Patients with Advanced CKD and Renal Outcomes. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2021;32:424-435. PMID 33372009. No registry ID (observational registry study).

shelves.title: Preventing contrast-associated kidney injury: neither bicarbonate nor acetylcysteine helped — and routine hydration went unproven
shelves.question: In patients at risk of kidney injury from iodinated contrast, do intravenous sodium bicarbonate, oral acetylcysteine, or routine prophylactic intravenous hydration prevent acute kidney injury and its consequences?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Contrast Media · Acetylcysteine · Sodium Bicarbonate · Angiography · Fluid Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: Two widely used rituals failed their trials. PRESERVE (5,177 high-risk patients) found no benefit of bicarbonate over saline, and none of acetylcysteine over placebo, for death, dialysis, or persistent kidney damage at 90 days — or for contrast-associated kidney injury itself. AMACING went one step further and asked whether the saline ritual is needed at all in patients with eGFR 30–59: kidney injury occurred in 2.6% with no prophylaxis vs 2.7% with hydration, noninferior and cost-saving, while 5.5% of hydrated patients had a hydration complication. The honest fence: AMACING excluded eGFR below 30 and emergency cases, so its answer does not extend to the highest-risk patients. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: PRESERVE: no benefit of bicarbonate over saline, or of acetylcysteine over placebo (primary outcome 4.4% vs 4.7% and 4.6% vs 4.5%)
cards.summary: Primary composite (death, dialysis, or persistent ≥50% creatinine rise at 90 days): bicarbonate 4.4% vs saline 4.7% (odds ratio 0.93 , 0.72–1.22; P=0.62); acetylcysteine 4.6% vs placebo 4.5% (odds ratio 1.02 , 0.78–1.33; P=0.88); no difference in contrast-associated kidney injury — 4,993 patients in the primary analysis.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, 2-by-2 factorial randomized trial (PRESERVE), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 5,177 patients at high risk for renal complications scheduled for angiography were randomized; 4,993 entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary end point occurred in 110 of 2,511 patients (4.4%) in the sodium bicarbonate group vs 116 of 2,482 (4.7%) in the sodium chloride group (odds ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.22; P=0.62), and in 114 of 2,495 (4.6%) in the acetylcysteine group vs 112 of 2,498 (4.5%) on placebo (odds ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.33; P=0.88). There was no interaction between the two interventions (P=0.33) and no significant between-group difference in contrast-associated acute kidney injury.
cards.watchOut: The sponsor stopped the trial after a prespecified interim analysis — a futility stop, which strengthens rather than weakens the null: neither intervention was close to working. Funded by the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia.
cards.source: Weisbord SD et al. Outcomes after Angiography with Sodium Bicarbonate and Acetylcysteine. N Engl J Med. 2018;378:603-614. PMID 29130810 · NCT01467466.

cards.headline: AMACING: no prophylaxis was noninferior to guideline hydration (kidney injury 2.6% vs 2.7%) — and cheaper
cards.summary: Contrast-induced nephropathy: 2.6% with no prophylaxis vs 2.7% with intravenous hydration (absolute difference −0.10% , one-sided 95% CI −2.25 to 2.06; noninferiority margin 2.1%); no dialysis or related deaths within 35 days; hydration complications in 5.5% of hydrated patients — 660 patients.
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, open-label, phase 3 noninferiority trial (AMACING), Lancet 2017
cards.people: 660 patients with eGFR 30–59 ml/min/1.73 m² undergoing elective contrast procedures at Maastricht University Medical Centre, the Netherlands; 332 assigned to no prophylaxis, 328 to intravenous 0.9% saline. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Contrast-induced nephropathy was recorded in 8 of 307 patients (2.6%) without prophylaxis and 8 of 296 (2.7%) with hydration — absolute difference −0.10% (one-sided 95% CI −2.25 to 2.06; P=0.4710 against the 2.1% noninferiority margin). No prophylaxis was cost-saving. No patient needed dialysis and no related deaths occurred within 35 days; 18 of 328 hydrated patients (5.5%) had complications associated with intravenous hydration.
cards.watchOut: The fence matters: AMACING excluded eGFR below 30, previous dialysis, and emergency presentations — the patients clinicians worry about most were not in this trial. Its answer covers elective procedures at eGFR 30–59, and no further. Single-centre and open-label (laboratory staff were masked).
cards.source: Nijssen EC et al. Prophylactic hydration to protect renal function from intravascular iodinated contrast material in patients at high risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (AMACING). Lancet. 2017;389:1312-1322. PMID 28233565 · NCT02106234.

shelves.title: Potassium binders to keep RAAS inhibitors going: enablement proven, outcomes not
shelves.question: In patients whose renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) are limited by high potassium, do the newer potassium binders — patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate — control potassium well enough to keep patients on the RAASi doses that help them?
shelves.mesh: Hyperkalemia · Polymers · Silicates · Renin-Angiotensin System · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Heart Failure · Humans
shelves.balance: The enablement claim is real. In OPAL-HK, patients who stayed on patiromer stayed on their RAAS inhibitors (94% vs 44% after withdrawal to placebo), and hyperkalemia recurred in 15% vs 60%. DIAMOND and REALIZE-K repeat the pattern in heart failure: fewer hyperkalemia events, fewer forced dose cuts. But the shelf’s framing is enablement, not outcomes — DIAMOND’s primary endpoint was switched during the trial from cardiovascular death or hospitalization to the change in serum potassium, so it cannot testify about outcomes at all; and REALIZE-K’s exploratory cardiovascular composite ran the wrong way (11% vs 3%), underpowered but printed here as a caution, not buried. Whether binder-enabled RAASi therapy saves lives remains untested. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: OPAL-HK: patiromer kept potassium down — and kept 94% of patients on their RAAS inhibitors vs 44% on placebo
cards.summary: Initial phase: potassium fell by −1.01 mmol/L and 76% reached target at week 4. Randomized withdrawal: hyperkalemia recurrence (≥5.5 mmol/L) 15% on patiromer vs 60% on placebo (P<0.001), and 94% vs 44% remained on RAAS inhibitor therapy (trial report) — 237 patients in the initial-phase analysis, 107 in the withdrawal phase.
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, single-blind initial phase with a randomized withdrawal phase (OPAL-HK), N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: Patients with CKD receiving RAAS inhibitors, with serum potassium 5.1 to <6.5 mmol/L: 237 patients in the initial treatment-phase analysis, of whom 107 with more severe baseline hyperkalemia entered the 8-week randomized withdrawal phase (55 patiromer, 52 placebo). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In the initial phase, the mean change in serum potassium was −1.01±0.03 mmol/L (P<0.001), and 76% (95% CI 70 to 81) of patients reached the target range (3.8 to <5.1 mmol/L) at week 4. In the withdrawal phase, hyperkalemia (potassium ≥5.5 mmol/L) recurred in 60% of the placebo group vs 15% of the patiromer group through week 8 (P<0.001); per the trial report, 94% of patients continuing patiromer remained on RAAS inhibitor therapy vs 44% of those switched to placebo. Mild-to-moderate constipation was the most common adverse event (11%); hypokalemia occurred in 3%.
cards.watchOut: A potassium trial, not an outcomes trial: the endpoints are the potassium level, its recurrence, and whether the RAAS inhibitor stayed on board. The 94% vs 44% continuation figure comes from the trial report rather than the abstract. Withdrawal designs also flatter the drug — everyone randomized had already responded to it. Funded by Relypsa, patiromer’s maker.
cards.source: Weir MR et al. Patiromer in Patients with Kidney Disease and Hyperkalemia Receiving RAAS Inhibitors. N Engl J Med. 2015;372:211-221. PMID 25415805 · NCT01810939.

cards.headline: DIAMOND: patiromer controlled potassium and cut hyperkalemia events — after the primary endpoint was switched from cardiovascular outcomes to potassium
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (after the switch): adjusted mean potassium change +0.03 mmol/L on patiromer vs +0.13 on placebo (difference −0.10 mmol/L; P<0.001); hyperkalemia >5.5 mmol/L hazard ratio 0.63 (0.45–0.87); MRA dose reductions hazard ratio 0.62 — 878 randomized patients.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, double-blind, randomized withdrawal trial (DIAMOND), Eur Heart J 2022
cards.people: 1,642 patients with HFrEF and current or historical RAASi-related hyperkalemia were screened; 1,195 entered the patiromer run-in with RAASi optimization; 878 (84.6% of run-in completers) achieved the specified RAASi target doses and were randomized (439 patiromer, 439 placebo); median follow-up 27 weeks. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The adjusted mean change in serum potassium was +0.03 mmol/L on patiromer vs +0.13 mmol/L on placebo (between-group difference −0.10 mmol/L; P<0.001). Hyperkalemia >5.5 mmol/L was less frequent on patiromer (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.87; P=0.006), as were MRA dose reductions (hazard ratio 0.62; 0.45 to 0.87) and total hyperkalemia events (77.7 vs 118.2 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.66; 0.53 to 0.81). Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint switch is printed plainly, because it defines what this trial can claim: DIAMOND was designed with a primary endpoint of time to first cardiovascular death or cardiovascular hospitalization, and — during the COVID-19 pandemic, before unblinding — that endpoint was revised to the change in serum potassium. DIAMOND therefore proves potassium control and RAASi enablement. It says nothing about whether the strategy improves outcomes.
cards.source: Butler J et al. Patiromer for the management of hyperkalemia in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: the DIAMOND trial. Eur Heart J. 2022;43:4362-4373. PMID 35900838 · NCT03888066.

cards.headline: REALIZE-K: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate kept spironolactone going (optimal response 71% vs 36%) — with a cardiovascular caution, 11% vs 3%
cards.summary: Optimal response (normokalemia on spironolactone ≥25 mg/day without rescue therapy): 71% on SZC vs 36% on placebo (odds ratio 4.45 , 2.89–6.86; P<0.001); on spironolactone ≥25 mg/day 81% vs 50% . Caution: the exploratory composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure occurred in 11% on SZC vs 3% on placebo (nominal P=0.034) — 203 randomized patients.
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, randomized withdrawal trial (REALIZE-K), J Am Coll Cardiol 2025
cards.people: 203 participants with symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%) on guideline therapy except MRA, with hyperkalemia before or during spironolactone titration, were randomized after an open-label run-in (102 SZC, 101 placebo). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: An optimal treatment response was achieved by 71% on SZC vs 36% on placebo (odds ratio 4.45; 95% CI 2.89 to 6.86; P<0.001). SZC also improved the first four hierarchical secondary endpoints: normokalemia on the randomization spironolactone dose without rescue (58% vs 23%; odds ratio 4.58), receiving spironolactone ≥25 mg/day (81% vs 50%; odds ratio 4.33), time to hyperkalemia (hazard ratio 0.51; 0.37 to 0.71), and time to spironolactone decrease or discontinuation for hyperkalemia (hazard ratio 0.37; 0.17 to 0.73). Quality-of-life scores did not differ at 6 months. Overall and serious adverse events were balanced (64% vs 63%; 23% vs 22%).
cards.watchOut: The caution is carded, not buried: the exploratory composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure occurred in 11 participants (11%) on SZC — one cardiovascular death and ten heart-failure events — vs 3 (3%) on placebo (one cardiovascular death, two heart-failure events; nominal P=0.034). The trial was not powered for clinical outcomes, so this may be chance — but it points the wrong way, and the authors say it should factor into clinical decisions. Like every card on this shelf, the proven benefit is enablement, not outcomes.
cards.source: Kosiborod MN et al. Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate for Management of Hyperkalemia During Spironolactone Optimization in Patients With Heart Failure. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2025;85:971-984. PMID 39566872 · NCT04676646.

shelves.title: Don’t treat asymptomatic bacteriuria: the bacteria are not the disease
shelves.question: Bacteria in the urine, no symptoms: treat, or leave alone?
shelves.mesh: Bacteriuria · Asymptomatic Infections · Urinary Tract Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antimicrobial Stewardship · Pregnancy · Humans
shelves.balance: Leave it alone. In diabetic women — the group most often treated — antibiotics cleared the urine and prevented nothing (symptomatic episodes 42% treated vs 40% untreated; Harding 2002). In young women with recurrent UTI, treating the quiet bacteriuria made things worse: recurrence 46.8% vs 13.1% untreated, an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.09, labeled observational on its card (Cai 2012). The IDSA exceptions are printed here because they are part of the rule: DO screen and treat in pregnancy, and before invasive urologic procedures. Everyone else’s positive culture without symptoms is colonization, not a diagnosis. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Harding 2002: treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in diabetic women prevented nothing — symptomatic episodes 42% treated vs 40% untreated
cards.summary: At least one symptomatic urinary episode over a mean 27 months: 42% of the antimicrobial-therapy group vs 40% of the placebo group; time to first symptomatic episode was similar — 105 women. Eradicating the bacteria (20% vs 78% still bacteriuric at 4 weeks) did not change the clinical outcome.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (initial 6 weeks) with up to 3 years of screening follow-up, N Engl J Med 2002. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists.
cards.people: 105 women over 16 years of age with diabetes, bacteriuria (≥10⁵ colony-forming units per milliliter in two consecutive specimens), and no urinary symptoms (50 placebo, 55 antimicrobial therapy). (The abstract does not print mean age.)
cards.result: Four weeks after the initial course, bacteriuria persisted in 78% of placebo recipients vs 20% of treated women (P<0.001) — the treatment cleared urine, as antibiotics do. But during a mean follow-up of 27 months, 20 of 50 women in the placebo group (40%) and 23 of 55 in the antimicrobial group (42%) had at least one symptomatic urinary episode, and the time to a first episode was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The trial is small and in diabetic women specifically — the population in whom treatment was most often recommended. Its lesson generalizes through the guideline card (Reference 3): clearing a laboratory finding is not the same as preventing a disease. Eradication also repeatedly failed — most treated women were bacteriuric again within months.
cards.source: Harding GK et al. Antimicrobial treatment in diabetic women with asymptomatic bacteriuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347:1576-83. PMID 12432044 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Cai 2012: treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in young women with recurrent UTI caused harm — recurrence 46.8% treated vs 13.1% untreated (HR 3.09, labeled)
cards.summary: Recurrent symptomatic UTI by final follow-up: 46.8% in the treated group vs 13.1% untreated (relative risk 3.17, 95% CI 2.55 to 3.90, in the paper’s crude analysis; the paper’s adjusted hazard ratio for subsequent symptomatic UTI was 3.09 , as labeled in the shelf brief) — 673 women, prospective but NOT randomized.
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Cai 2012) — treatment was not randomized; carded and labeled as observational.
cards.people: 673 consecutive asymptomatic young women with demonstrated bacteriuria and a history of recurrent UTI (312 not treated, 361 treated), followed at 3, 6, and 12 months. (The abstract does not print mean age.)
cards.result: At 6 months, recurrence was 7.6% in the untreated group vs 29.7% in the treated group; by the final follow-up, 41 of 312 untreated women (13.1%) and 169 of 361 treated women (46.8%) had recurred (relative risk 3.17; 95% CI 2.55–3.90; P<0.0001). The study’s adjusted estimate for treatment as a risk factor for subsequent symptomatic UTI was a hazard ratio of 3.09. The authors’ reading: the resident bacteriuria may protect against superinfection, and eradicating it invites a symptomatic strain in.
cards.watchOut: Observational and unblinded — women were not randomized to treatment, so confounding by indication is possible in principle. But the effect is large (beyond this library’s 2.0 floor for harm), dose-consistent across follow-ups, and mechanistically coherent with the randomized null on Card 1; it is carded as harm evidence, labeled observational. Quality of life was also measured and favored not treating.
cards.source: Cai T et al. The role of asymptomatic bacteriuria in young women with recurrent urinary tract infections: to treat or not to treat? Clin Infect Dis. 2012;55:771-7. PMID 22677710 · No registry number (observational study).

cards.headline: IDSA 2019 guideline (Nicolle): don’t screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria — except pregnancy and before invasive urologic procedures
cards.summary: The 2019 IDSA update recommends screening and treatment ONLY in pregnant women and in patients about to undergo invasive urologic procedures ; it recommends against treatment in healthy women, older adults, people with diabetes, catheterized patients, and spinal-cord-injury patients. A guideline card — the guideline itself is the subject, per this library’s Shelf #46 precedent.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline — 2019 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (Nicolle 2019). Guidelines carry no registry number.
cards.people: Applies across populations: healthy women and men, older adults, pregnancy, diabetes, indwelling catheters, spinal cord injury, transplant recipients, and neutropenia (the last two addressed for the first time in this update).
cards.result: The 2005 IDSA guideline recommended treatment only in pregnancy or before invasive urologic procedures; the 2019 update reaffirmed that boundary after reviewing the intervening trial evidence — including the diabetic-women trial on Card 1 — and extended explicit ‘do not treat’ recommendations to additional populations. It also names treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria as an important contributor to inappropriate antimicrobial use.
cards.watchOut: A guideline is a synthesis, not a trial — it is carded here because the shelf’s question is a practice rule, and the rule’s exceptions (pregnancy, urologic procedures) are part of the evidence’s shape. The trial evidence underneath it is Cards 1 and 2.
cards.source: Nicolle LE et al. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria: 2019 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis. 2019;68:e83-e110. PMID 30895288 · No registry number (guideline).

shelves.title: Seven versus fourteen days for UTI: a week is enough
shelves.question: For urinary tract infection — kidney infection in women, UTI in men, and the bacteremia that so often starts in the urinary tract — does the second week of antibiotics buy anything?
shelves.mesh: Pyelonephritis · Urinary Tract Infections · Ciprofloxacin · Bacteremia · Drug Administration Schedule · Duration of Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: Three noninferiority trials, three populations, one answer. Women with acute pyelonephritis: 7 days of ciprofloxacin cured 97%, 14 days 96% (Sandberg). Afebrile men with UTI: symptom resolution 93.1% on 7 days vs 90.2% on 14 (Drekonja). And BALANCE — 3,608 bloodstream infections, the urinary tract their commonest source — found 90-day mortality of 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14. The exclusions matter and are printed on the cards: febrile men, S. aureus bacteremia, deep foci, and severe immunosuppression were not in these trials. Within the studied ground, the second week is habit, not therapy. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Sandberg 2012: 7 days of ciprofloxacin tied 14 days for acute pyelonephritis in women — cure 97% vs 96%
cards.summary: Short-term clinical cure: 97% (71/73) on 7 days vs 96% (80/83) on 14 days (difference −0.9%; 90% CI −6.5 to 4.8; noninferior); long-term cumulative efficacy 93% in each group — 248 women randomized.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label first week / double-blind placebo-controlled second week, noninferiority trial, Lancet 2012
cards.people: 248 women aged 18 or older with presumptive community-acquired acute pyelonephritis at 21 Swedish centres (126 assigned 7 days, 122 assigned 14 days; 73 and 83 analyzed per protocol). (The abstract does not print mean age.)
cards.result: Short-term clinical cure occurred in 71 (97%) patients treated for 7 days and 80 (96%) treated for 14 days (difference −0.9%; 90% CI −6.5 to 4.8; P=0.004 for noninferiority). Cumulative efficacy at long-term follow-up was 93% in each group (68 of 73 vs 78 of 84). Both regimens were well tolerated; adverse events after the first week were reported by 5% (7-day) and 6% (14-day) of compliers.
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol analysis, as noninferiority trials of duration usually are — and a fluoroquinolone trial from before fluoroquinolone stewardship tightened; the duration answer travels to other agents better than the drug choice does. Registered with EudraCT (2005-004992-39) and as ISRCTN73338924, as printed in the abstract.
cards.source: Sandberg T et al. Ciprofloxacin for 7 days versus 14 days in women with acute pyelonephritis: a randomised, open-label and double-blind, placebo-controlled, non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2012;380:484-90. PMID 22726802 · EudraCT 2005-004992-39 · ISRCTN73338924.

cards.headline: Drekonja 2021: in afebrile men with UTI, 7 days tied 14 days — symptom resolution 93.1% vs 90.2%
cards.summary: Resolution of UTI symptoms 14 days after completing active treatment: 93.1% (122/131) on 7 days vs 90.2% (111/123) on 14 days (difference 2.9%; noninferiority met against a 10% margin) — 272 men randomized at 2 VA medical centers.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial, JAMA 2021
cards.people: 272 afebrile men with presumed symptomatic UTI at 2 US Veterans Affairs medical centers (136 per group); median age 69 years (interquartile range 62–73); 254 (93.4%) were in the primary as-treated analysis and all completed the trial.
cards.result: Symptom resolution occurred in 122 of 131 participants (93.1%) in the 7-day group vs 111 of 123 (90.2%) in the 14-day group (difference 2.9% [1-sided 97.5% CI, −5.2% to ∞]), meeting the noninferiority criterion; the as-randomized analysis agreed. Recurrence and adverse events within 28 days of stopping did not favor the longer course.
cards.watchOut: Afebrile men only — febrile men, in whom prostatitis and bacteremia enter the picture, were not studied, and the VA population skews older. The trial answers the common clinic case (afebrile male UTI), not every male UTI. (The abstract record does not print a registry number.)

cards.headline: BALANCE 2025: for bloodstream infection — much of it from the urinary tract — 7 days tied 14 days on 90-day mortality
cards.summary: Death by 90 days: 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14 days (difference −1.6 percentage points, 95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8; noninferiority margin 4 points) — 3,608 patients; the urinary tract was the commonest source (42.2%).
cards.type: Multicentre randomized noninferiority trial (BALANCE), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 3,608 hospitalized patients with bloodstream infection across 74 hospitals in seven countries (1,814 assigned 7 days, 1,794 assigned 14 days); 55.0% were in the ICU at enrollment. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.) Sources: urinary tract 42.2%, abdomen 18.8%, lung 13.0%, vascular catheters 6.3%, skin or soft tissue 5.2%.
cards.result: By 90 days, 261 patients (14.5%) assigned 7 days and 286 (16.1%) assigned 14 days had died (difference −1.6 percentage points [95.7% CI, −4.0 to 0.8]), showing noninferiority of the shorter course; the per-protocol analysis agreed (difference −2.0; 95% CI −4.5 to 0.6). Patients were treated longer than assigned in 23.1% of the 7-day group and 10.7% of the 14-day group.
cards.watchOut: BALANCE excluded severe immunosuppression, foci requiring prolonged treatment, and Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia — the 7-day answer does not extend there. It is carded on this shelf because the urinary tract was its largest source; its home question is bloodstream infection generally. (The abstract record does not print a registry number.)

shelves.title: Intravenous iron for iron-deficiency anemia in non-dialysis CKD: faster repletion and fewer escalations — no event benefit shown
shelves.question: In non-dialysis chronic kidney disease with iron-deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron beat oral iron on anything beyond the blood count?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Ferric Compounds · Ferritins · Hemoglobins · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans
shelves.balance: The honest claim for IV iron before dialysis is narrow, and this shelf states it narrowly: ferritin-targeted IV ferric carboxymaltose repletes faster and delays the day a patient needs an ESA, other iron, or a transfusion (FIND-CKD, Card 1 — re-carded from its home on Shelf #294 , the kidney-iron dose-and-target shelf) — a treatment-trigger endpoint, not an event endpoint. No trial here shows a mortality or cardiovascular benefit , and the one trial that asked a harder question, REVOKE (Reference 2), found no difference in kidney-function decline and was stopped early over more serious cardiovascular and infectious events on IV iron. The heart-failure iron literature is a different population and lives on Shelf #122 — linked, not merged. POSSIBLE is the stamp because the repletion claim is real but the outcome claims are absent and the safety record is mixed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: FIND-CKD (Macdougall 2014): IV iron to a HIGH ferritin target delayed other anemia management vs oral iron (HR 0.65); the low target did not [re-card — home Shelf #294]
cards.summary: 626 patients with non-dialysis CKD, anemia and iron deficiency, not on ESAs: IV ferric carboxymaltose targeting ferritin 400–600 vs 100–200 vs oral iron. The primary endpoint — needing other anemia management (ESA, other iron, transfusion) or hitting a hemoglobin trigger — occurred in 23.5% (high target) vs 32.2% (low target) vs 31.8% (oral) ; high target vs oral HR 0.65 [0.44–0.95], P=0.026 . The endpoint is about treatment triggers, not events — and the record states no difference in cardiovascular or infectious events . Re-card: this trial's home is Shelf #294 ; counted once, there.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (FIND-CKD), Nephrol Dial Transplant 2014 — 56-week, open-label. Re-card; home Shelf #294. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00994318.
cards.people: 626 patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD, anaemia and iron deficiency not receiving erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, randomized 1:1:2 to high-ferritin IV ferric carboxymaltose, low-ferritin IV ferric carboxymaltose, or oral iron. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The primary end point occurred in 36 patients (23.5%), 49 (32.2%) and 98 (31.8%) in the high-ferritin FCM, low-ferritin FCM and oral iron groups respectively (HR 0.65 [0.44–0.95]; P=0.026 for high-ferritin FCM vs oral iron). The increase in hemoglobin was greater with high-ferritin FCM vs oral iron (P=0.014), and more patients achieved an Hb increase ≥1 g/dL (HR 2.04 [1.52–2.72]; P<0.001). Rates of adverse events and serious adverse events were similar in all groups; within the trial's limitations there was no renal toxicity and no difference in cardiovascular or infectious events.
cards.watchOut: Read the endpoint before the hazard ratio: FIND-CKD's win is a delay in starting ESAs or other anemia therapy — a process outcome — achieved only by the high ferritin target; the low target was indistinguishable from oral iron (32.2% vs 31.8%). No trial on this shelf shows a mortality or cardiovascular-event benefit, and this card claims none.
cards.source: Macdougall IC et al. FIND-CKD: a randomized trial of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose versus oral iron in patients with chronic kidney disease and iron deficiency anaemia. cards.headline: REVOKE (Agarwal 2015): the kidney-function question was NULL — and the trial was stopped early over serious adverse events on IV iron
cards.summary: 136 patients with stage 3–4 CKD and iron-deficiency anemia, IV iron sucrose (1 g total) vs oral ferrous sulfate: measured-GFR decline over 2 years was the same — −4.0 vs −3.6 mL/min/1.73 m² (difference −0.35 [−2.9 to 2.3]). The safety board stopped the trial early: serious cardiovascular events numbered 55 events in 17 participants on IV iron vs 36 in 19 on oral iron (adjusted incidence rate ratio 2.51 [1.56–4.04]) , and hospitalizing infections were also more frequent (adjusted IRR 2.12 [1.24–3.64]). Event counts exceed participant counts — recurrent events in a small trial — and that fragility prints with the signal.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (REVOKE), Kidney Int 2015 — open-label, terminated early on the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 136 patients with stage 3 and 4 CKD and iron-deficiency anemia: 69 assigned to open-label oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily for 8 weeks, 67 to intravenous iron sucrose 200 mg every 2 weeks to a total of 1 g. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The trial was terminated early on the recommendation of an independent data and safety monitoring board, based on little chance of finding differences in mGFR slopes but a higher risk of serious adverse events in the intravenous iron group. mGFR declined similarly over two years (oral −3.6, intravenous −4.0 mL/min/1.73 m²; between-group difference −0.35 [−2.9 to 2.3]). There were 36 serious cardiovascular events among 19 participants on oral iron and 55 among 17 on intravenous iron (adjusted incidence rate ratio 2.51 [1.56–4.04]); infections resulting in hospitalization had an adjusted incidence rate ratio of 2.12 [1.24–3.64].
cards.watchOut: REVOKE is small, open-label, and was stopped early — three reasons its harm signal is a warning, not a verdict. But it is the only trial here that randomized the kidney-function question, its answer was null, and the signal runs opposite to FIND-CKD's reassurance (different iron, different dose, different design: 1 g of iron sucrose over 8 weeks vs ferritin-targeted carboxymaltose over a year). The shelf holds both without averaging them away.

shelves.title: Thiazides to prevent kidney stone recurrence: the one large modern trial was null
shelves.question: Do thiazide diuretics prevent recurrence of calcium kidney stones?
shelves.mesh: Kidney Calculi · Nephrolithiasis · Hydrochlorothiazide · Sodium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors · Thiazides · Recurrence · Calcium Oxalate · Secondary Prevention · Humans
shelves.balance: For decades thiazides were standard prevention on the strength of small old trials. The one large modern test removed the support: NOSTONE (416 patients with recurrent calcium stones, median follow-up 2.9 years) found recurrence in 59% on placebo, 59% on hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, 56% on 25 mg and 49% on 50 mg — rate ratios 1.33, 1.24 and 0.92, no dose relation (P=0.66), with more hypokalemia, gout, new diabetes, skin allergy and creatinine rises on the drug. The older record is genuinely positive but small and soft: Laerum & Larsen's 50-patient general-practice trial (probability of staying stone-free 75% thiazide vs 45% placebo) and Ettinger's chlorthalidone trial, whose own authors warned that even placebo arms beat historical predictions. The syntheses split by era and population: the 2013 ACP review found thiazides halved recurrence (RR 0.52) in multiple-stone formers, and a 2025 updated meta-analysis still pools to RR 0.63 — but restricted to hypercalciuric patients and built from those same small trials. The honest summary: unselected recurrence prevention at modern doses is a null; a hypercalciuria-selected benefit remains possible and untested at NOSTONE's scale. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY null for hydrochlorothiazide at 12.5–50 mg in unselected recurrent calcium stone formers (NOSTONE) / POSSIBLE benefit in hypercalciuric patients, where the older small trials were done — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: NOSTONE (Dhayat 2023, NEJM): hydrochlorothiazide did NOT prevent stone recurrence at any dose — 59% placebo vs 59%, 56%, 49% across 12.5/25/50 mg
cards.summary: 416 patients with recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones randomised double-blind to hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, 25 mg or 50 mg once daily or placebo; median follow-up 2.9 years. Primary endpoint (symptomatic or radiologic recurrence): 60/102 (59%) placebo, 62/105 (59%) on 12.5 mg (rate ratio 1.33 [95% CI 0.92–1.93]), 61/108 (56%) on 25 mg (rate ratio 1.24 [0.86–1.79]), 49/101 (49%) on 50 mg (rate ratio 0.92 [0.63–1.36]). No dose–response relation (P=0.66). Hypokalemia, gout, new-onset diabetes, skin allergy and creatinine >150% of baseline were all more common on hydrochlorothiazide.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (NOSTONE), N Engl J Med 2023. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03057431.
cards.people: 416 patients with recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones randomised across the four arms (102 placebo; 105, 108 and 101 on ascending doses); median follow-up 2.9 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Primary-endpoint events: placebo 60/102 (59%); hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg 62/105 (59%), rate ratio 1.33 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.93); 25 mg 61/108 (56%), rate ratio 1.24 (0.86 to 1.79); 50 mg 49/101 (49%), rate ratio 0.92 (0.63 to 1.36). No relation between dose and the primary endpoint (P=0.66).
cards.watchOut: Card the null as a null: at the doses actually prescribed, in unselected recurrent calcium stone formers, hydrochlorothiazide did not prevent recurrence — and its harms were not hypothetical. NOSTONE did not select for hypercalciuria, which is the fence the older positive trials hide behind (References 2–4).
cards.source: Dhayat NA et al. Hydrochlorothiazide and Prevention of Kidney-Stone Recurrence. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(9):781-791. PMID 36856614 · NCT03057431

cards.headline: Laerum & Larsen 1984: in 50 recurrent stone formers, thiazide kept 75% stone-free vs 45% on placebo — small, old, one-tailed
cards.summary: 50 recurrent stone formers in Norwegian general practice randomised double-blind to hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg twice daily or placebo, median 3 years. The number of patients forming new stones was significantly higher on placebo (P=0.05, one-tailed test); the probability of not forming a new stone during treatment was 45% on placebo and 75% on thiazide. The placebo group itself formed substantially fewer stones than expected — the authors' own warning about uncontrolled comparisons.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Acta Med Scand 1984. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 50 recurrent stone formers in general practice; median follow-up 3 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Probability of remaining free of new stones during treatment: 75% on hydrochlorothiazide vs 45% on placebo; new-stone formation significantly more frequent on placebo (P=0.05, one-tailed). Where a stone did form, thiazide prolonged the stone-free interval (P≤0.01). The thiazide effect seemed independent of urinary calcium but less beneficial with hyperuricosuria.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, a one-tailed P=0.05, and 1984 imaging and follow-up: this is the size of evidence NOSTONE was built to replace. It keeps a hypercalciuria-era hypothesis alive; it does not outweigh a 416-patient null.
cards.source: Laerum E, Larsen S. Thiazide prophylaxis of urolithiasis. A double-blind study in general practice. Acta Med Scand. 1984;215(4):383-9. PMID 6375276

cards.headline: Ettinger 1988: chlorthalidone cut calculous events 90.1% versus predicted rates — and placebo cut them 56.1%, the authors' own warning
cards.summary: Double-blind random-allocation trial of chlorthalidone 25 or 50 mg, magnesium hydroxide, or placebo for recurrent calcium oxalate calculi. All groups formed far fewer calculi than their pretreatment rates predicted: placebo 56.1% fewer (P<0.01), magnesium hydroxide 73.9% and 62.3% fewer, chlorthalidone 90.1% fewer — significantly better than placebo or magnesium (P<0.01), with both chlorthalidone doses similar.
cards.type: Double-blind, random-allocation controlled trial, J Urol 1988. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed. The record's abstract does not print the number randomised, and none is printed here.
cards.people: Patients with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney calculi assigned to chlorthalidone (25 or 50 mg), magnesium hydroxide (650 or 1,300 mg) or placebo. The record's abstract does not print the sample size, mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Calculous events versus predicted (pretreatment-rate) rates: chlorthalidone 90.1% fewer; placebo 56.1% fewer (P less than 0.01); magnesium hydroxide 73.9% and 62.3% fewer at the two doses. Chlorthalidone was significantly better than placebo or magnesium hydroxide (P less than 0.01).
cards.watchOut: The comparison that flatters chlorthalidone is against predicted rates, not purely against the concurrent placebo event rate — and the placebo arm's own 56.1% drop is the standing lesson of this literature: stone trials regress, which is why NOSTONE's concurrent-control null governs.

cards.headline: Porto 2025 updated meta-analysis: pooling the RCTs still favours thiazides (RR 0.63) — in hypercalciuric patients, from the pre-NOSTONE-sized trials
cards.summary: Systematic review, meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of RCTs comparing thiazides with placebo for stone recurrence in patients with hypercalciuria: 10 trials, 650 patients on thiazides and 672 on placebo. Recurrence RR 0.63 [95% CI 0.49–0.83], P=0.0007, I²=65%. Twenty-four-hour calciuria was lower on thiazides (mean difference −40.59 [−76.39 to −4.79]); citraturia did not differ. The 2013 ACP-guideline review (Fink) had likewise found thiazides reduced composite recurrence (RR 0.52 [0.39–0.69], moderate-strength evidence) in patients with multiple past calcium stones.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Minerva Urol Nephrol 2025. The record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 10 RCTs in patients with hypercalciuria: 650 assigned thiazides, 672 placebo. The record's abstract does not print a pooled mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Stone recurrence: RR 0.63 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P=0.0007; I²=65%) favouring thiazides. 24-hour calciuria lower on thiazides (mean difference −40.59, 95% CI −76.39 to −4.79; P=0.03); 24-hour citraturia no difference (mean difference −29.70, 95% CI −83.02 to 23.63).
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative benefit assembled from small, old, hypercalciuria-selected trials — with I²=65% heterogeneity — does not repeal NOSTONE's null in unselected patients; it defines the population in which a benefit remains possible and a modern confirmatory trial is still owed. Whether NOSTONE itself sits inside this pool is not stated in the record's abstract, and the card does not assume it.
cards.source: Porto BC et al. Thiazide diuretics for preventing calcium oxalate recurrent kidney stones: an updated systematic review, meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials. Minerva Urol Nephrol. 2025;77(3):298-307. PMID 40528770

cards.headline: Synthesis: prescribe from NOSTONE, hypothesise from the old trials — the hypercalciuria question is the one still open
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–4. The only large, modern, placebo-controlled test (NOSTONE, n=416) is null at every dose with real harms. The positive record is small (n=50), old (1984–2013 syntheses), partly built on predicted-rate comparisons, and concentrated in hypercalciuric or multiple-stone populations. Needed evidence: a NOSTONE-scale trial restricted to documented hypercalciuria, with symptomatic recurrence as the endpoint; until then the closing position is that routine thiazide prevention for unselected recurrent calcium stone formers is not supported, and no in-flight trial meeting that description was identified in the 2026-11-08 sweep.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–4 together and names the missing trial.
cards.people: 416 patients in the modern trial; 50 in the pivotal old trial; 1,322 patients across the 2025 meta-analysis pool.
cards.result: NOSTONE recurrence: 59% placebo vs 59%/56%/49% across ascending hydrochlorothiazide doses, no dose relation (P=0.66). Pooled older-trial recurrence: RR 0.52 (2013 ACP review, multiple-stone formers) and RR 0.63 (2025 update, hypercalciuric patients).
cards.watchOut: Do not average the eras into a single number: a pooled RR drawn from 1980s trials and a 2023 null at three doses describe different populations and different evidentiary weight.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 36856614, PMID 6375276, PMID 3280829, PMID 23546565 and PMID 40528770 on this shelf; no additional source.

shelves.title: Medical expulsive therapy for ureteral stones: the large trials were null overall; a larger-stone signal survives in one subgroup
shelves.question: Do alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) or calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine), given as medical expulsive therapy, increase spontaneous passage of ureteral stones?
shelves.mesh: Ureteral Calculi · Urinary Calculi · Tamsulosin · Nifedipine · Colic · Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Antagonists · Calcium Channel Blockers · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Male · Female
shelves.balance: Medical expulsive therapy was adopted on meta-analyses of small trials; the large trials then failed to confirm it. SUSPEND (1,167 patients, stones ≤10 mm, 24 UK hospitals) found no need for further intervention in 80% on placebo, 81% on tamsulosin and 80% on nifedipine — adjusted risk differences of 1.3 and 0.5 percentage points, both null, with no subgroup rescue by stone size or location in its full HTA analysis. The US STONE trial (512 emergency-department patients, stones <9 mm) found passage in 50% on tamsulosin vs 47% on placebo (RR 1.05, P=0.60). One signal survives, fenced where it belongs: in Furyk's distal-stone trial the overall result was null (87.0% vs 81.9%), but the prespecified subgroup with 5–10 mm stones passed in 83.3% on tamsulosin vs 61.0% on placebo (difference 22.4 percentage points, NNT 4.5) — a subgroup of 77 patients inside a null trial, hypothesis-grade, not a licence to treat every colic. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY no benefit for stones ≤5 mm or unselected ureteric colic / POSSIBLE for distal stones 5–10 mm — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: SUSPEND (Pickard 2015, Lancet): tamsulosin and nifedipine both null — 80% passed without intervention on placebo, 81% tamsulosin, 80% nifedipine
cards.summary: 1,167 adults (18–65) with a single ureteric stone ≤10 mm on CT, managed expectantly at 24 UK hospitals, randomised double-blind to tamsulosin 400 µg, nifedipine 30 mg or placebo daily for up to 4 weeks. Primary outcome (no further intervention needed for stone clearance within 4 weeks): 303/379 (80%) placebo, 307/378 (81%) tamsulosin (adjusted risk difference 1.3% [95% CI −5.7 to 8.3], P=0.73), 304/379 (80%) nifedipine (0.5% [−5.6 to 6.5], P=0.88). No difference for active treatment overall (P=0.78) or between the two drugs (P=0.77). Serious adverse events were few (three on nifedipine, one on placebo).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (SUSPEND), Lancet 2015. Registries verified against the record's own databank: EudraCT 2010-019469-26 · ISRCTN69423238.
cards.people: 1,167 participants randomised (391 tamsulosin, 387 nifedipine, 399 placebo per the trial's full HTA report); 1,136 (97%) in the primary analysis; adults 18–65 with CT-confirmed single ureteric stones ≤10 mm. The Lancet record's abstract does not print a mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: No further intervention needed by 4 weeks: placebo 303/379 (80%); tamsulosin 307/378 (81%), adjusted risk difference 1.3% (95% CI −5.7 to 8.3; P=0.73); nifedipine 304/379 (80%), adjusted risk difference 0.5% (−5.6 to 6.5; P=0.88). Overall active-versus-placebo comparison P=0.78.
cards.watchOut: The null is the headline and it is a strong one — wide inclusion, placebo control, 97% primary-outcome ascertainment. The trial's full HTA report (PMID 26244520, same trial, not separately carded) states the findings were unchanged in sensitivity analyses by sex, stone size and stone location: SUSPEND itself offers no subgroup rescue, and this card does not invent one.

cards.headline: STONE trial (Meltzer 2018, JAMA Intern Med): tamsulosin null again in US emergency departments — passage 50% vs 47% (RR 1.05, P=0.60)
cards.summary: 512 emergency-department patients with a symptomatic ureteral stone <9 mm on CT randomised double-blind to tamsulosin 0.4 mg or placebo daily for 28 days. Passage by day 28 (visualisation or capture): 50% tamsulosin vs 47% placebo (relative risk 1.05 [95.8% CI 0.87–1.27], P=0.60). No secondary outcome — crossover, time to passage, return to work, analgesia, hospitalisation, surgery, repeat ED visit — differed significantly.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, JAMA Intern Med 2018. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00382265.
cards.people: 512 participants randomised; 497 evaluated for the primary outcome. Mean age 40.6 years (range 18–74); 139 (27.1%) women; mean stone diameter 3.8 mm (SD 1.4).
cards.result: Stone passage by day 28: 50% on tamsulosin vs 47% on placebo (relative risk 1.05; 95.8% CI 0.87 to 1.27; P=0.60). No secondary outcome differed significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Mean stone size was only 3.8 mm — stones that mostly pass anyway; the trial's own conclusion is limited to stones smaller than 9 mm and it cannot test the 5–10 mm distal hypothesis raised by Furyk (Reference 3). Two nulls (this and SUSPEND) in different health systems are harder to explain away than one.
cards.source: Meltzer AC et al. Effect of Tamsulosin on Passage of Symptomatic Ureteral Stones: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(8):1051-1057. PMID 29913020 · NCT00382265

cards.headline: Furyk 2016: null overall for distal stones (87.0% vs 81.9%) — with a prespecified 5–10 mm subgroup signal (83.3% vs 61.0%, NNT 4.5) that stays fenced as a subgroup
cards.summary: 403 adults with distal ureteric stones ≤10 mm on CT randomised double-blind to tamsulosin 0.4 mg or placebo for 28 days; 316 had the 28-day CT. Passage: 140/161 (87.0%) tamsulosin vs 127/155 (81.9%) placebo — difference 5.0% [95% CI −3.0 to 13.0], not significant. In the prespecified subgroup with large stones (5–10 mm), passage was 30/36 (83.3%) on tamsulosin vs 25/41 (61.0%) on placebo — difference 22.4% [3.1 to 41.6], NNT 4.5. No differences in interventions, time to self-reported passage, pain or analgesia; adverse events mild and similar.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial, Ann Emerg Med 2016. Registry verified against the record's own databank: ACTRN12610000623099.
cards.people: 403 patients randomised; 81.4% men; median age 46 years; median stone size 4.0 mm (tamsulosin) and 3.7 mm (placebo); 316 received the 28-day CT and form the passage analysis.
cards.result: Overall passage on 28-day CT: 87.0% (140/161) tamsulosin vs 81.9% (127/155) placebo, difference 5.0% (95% CI −3.0 to 13.0). Prespecified 5–10 mm subgroup: 83.3% (30/36) vs 61.0% (25/41), difference 22.4% (95% CI 3.1 to 41.6), NNT 4.5.
cards.watchOut: SUBGROUP — fenced. The subgroup is 77 patients inside an overall-null trial whose primary analysis itself rests on the 316 of 403 who returned for CT. It is prespecified, which earns it a hearing, and it aligns with the pharmacology (larger distal stones have room to be helped); it is not a positive trial of 5–10 mm stones, and SUSPEND's size-stratified analyses did not reproduce it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stop offering expulsive therapy to every colic; the only live question is distal stones of 5–10 mm
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. Three placebo-controlled trials totalling over 2,000 randomised patients find no overall benefit for tamsulosin (or nifedipine) on stone passage or need for intervention. The single contrary signal is a 77-patient prespecified subgroup (Furyk, distal 5–10 mm). Needed evidence: an adequately powered trial restricted to distal stones 5–10 mm with CT-confirmed passage — no such trial appeared in the freshness sweep dated 2026-11-08; the shelf names it here as the closing gap rather than upgrading the subgroup.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–3 together and names the missing trial.
cards.people: 1,167 (SUSPEND) + 512 (STONE) + 403 (Furyk) randomised patients with ureteric stones ≤10 mm.
cards.result: Placebo-arm passage/no-intervention rates: 80% (SUSPEND), 47% by capture at day 28 (STONE, smaller stones, stricter outcome), 81.9% on CT (Furyk). Active-arm advantages: +1.3, +3 (RR 1.05) and +5.0 percentage points overall — all non-significant; +22.4 points in the one fenced subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Outcome definitions differ across the three trials (no-intervention, patient capture, CT passage), which is why the placebo rates differ; the within-trial comparisons are the evidence, not cross-trial rate shopping.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 25998582, PMID 29913020 and PMID 26194935 on this shelf; no additional source.

shelves.title: Antibiotic duration for UTI in men: 7 versus 14 days — afebrile men are settled; febrile men are not
shelves.question: In men with urinary tract infection, is 7 days of antibiotics enough compared with 14 days?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Tract Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Ciprofloxacin · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Duration of Therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Fever · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: The men's question splits on fever. For afebrile men, the one dedicated trial — Drekonja 2021, 272 VA patients on ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — found 7 days noninferior to 14 for symptom resolution (93.1% vs 90.2% in the as-treated analysis); that trial's home is Shelf #316, where it sits with the women's pyelonephritis and bloodstream-infection duration trials, and it is pointed to here rather than re-carded. For febrile UTI, the only randomised duration evidence including men points the other way at short-term follow-up: van Nieuwkoop 2017 (200 randomised, ciprofloxacin 7 vs 14 days) confirmed noninferiority in women but found 7 days inferior in men at the 10–18-day visit (clinical cure 86% vs 98%; difference −11.2 percentage points), even though by 70–84 days the men's long-term cure met noninferiority. So: a week for the afebrile man rests on one good trial; a week for the febrile man rests on a subgroup that failed its short-term test and recovered later. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: van Nieuwkoop 2017 (BMC Med): febrile UTI — 7 days was inferior to 14 in men at short-term follow-up (cure 86% vs 98%), noninferior by 70–84 days
cards.summary: Pragmatic randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial in 35 Dutch primary-care centres and 7 emergency departments: adults with febrile UTI assigned to ciprofloxacin for 7 days or 14 days (second week ciprofloxacin or placebo). Of 357 included, 200 were randomised (97 to 7 days, 103 to 14 days). Short-term clinical cure overall: 90% (7 days) vs 95% (14 days) — noninferiority not confirmed (difference −4.5% [90% CI −10.7 to 1.7], P for noninferiority 0.072). Prespecified sex subgroup: women 94% vs 93% (noninferiority confirmed); men 86% vs 98% (difference −11.2 points [90% CI −20.6 to −1.8]; inferiority confirmed at short term). Long-term clinical cure (70–84 days) met noninferiority overall and in both sex subgroups.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial, BMC Med 2017. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00809913 (also registered NTR1583, as printed in the record).
cards.people: 200 randomised adults with febrile urinary tract infection (97 assigned 7 days, 103 assigned 14 days), men and women aged ≥18, Netherlands. The record's abstract does not print the number of men randomised or a mean age, and none are printed here.
cards.result: Short-term clinical cure: 85 patients (90%) on 7 days vs 94 patients (95%) on 14 days, counts and percentages as printed in the record — difference −4.5% (90% CI −10.7 to 1.7), noninferiority not confirmed overall. Men: 86% vs 98% (difference −11.2; 90% CI −20.6 to −1.8; P superiority 0.025 — inferiority confirmed). Women: 94% vs 93% (difference 0.9; noninferiority confirmed). Bacteriologic cure 93% vs 97%; long-term clinical cure 92% vs 91%, noninferior overall and in both sex subgroups.

shelves.title: Remote ischaemic preconditioning to prevent injury from cardiac surgery
shelves.question: Does remote ischaemic preconditioning protect the kidney and heart during cardiac surgery?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, Intravenous · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Cardiopulmonary Bypass · Elective Surgical Procedures · Ischemia · Ischemic Preconditioning/methods · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large multicentre sham-controlled trials published back-to-back in 2015 found no benefit. RIPHeart (1,385 patients in the full analysis set) found the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or acute renal failure in 14.3% with preconditioning versus 14.6% with sham (P=0.89), and ERICCA (1,612 patients) found its 12-month composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, revascularisation or stroke in 26.5% versus 27.7% (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15; P=0.58). Acute kidney injury — the kidney component of this shelf's question — did not differ in either trial. Smaller earlier single-centre reports of kidney protection were not confirmed at scale.

cards.headline: RIPHeart: upper-limb preconditioning did not reduce death, infarction, stroke or acute renal failure after cardiac surgery
cards.summary: RIPHeart: the in-hospital composite (death, infarction, stroke or acute renal failure) occurred in 14.3% vs 14.6% (P=0.89) — preconditioning did nothing.
cards.people: 1,403 adults scheduled for elective cardiac surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass underwent randomisation; the full analysis set comprised 1,385 patients (692 preconditioning, 693 sham). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The composite primary end point (death, myocardial infarction, stroke or acute renal failure up to hospital discharge) occurred in 99 patients (14.3%) in the preconditioning group and 101 (14.6%) in the sham group (P=0.89). Individual components: death 1.3% versus 0.6% (P=0.21), myocardial infarction 6.8% versus 9.1% (P=0.12), stroke 2.0% versus 2.2% (P=0.79), acute renal failure 6.1% versus 5.1% (P=0.45). No treatment effect was found in any subgroup, and no preconditioning-related adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: All patients were under total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol, which the authors note as the trial context; the trial tests preconditioning under propofol, not under every anaesthetic regimen.
cards.source: Meybohm P et al. A Multicenter Trial of Remote Ischemic Preconditioning for Heart Surgery. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:1397-407. PMID: 26436208. Registry ID: NCT01067703 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank).

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large sham-controlled trials agree — no kidney or heart protection from preconditioning in cardiac surgery
cards.summary: Two large sham-controlled trials agree: no kidney or heart protection from preconditioning in cardiac surgery — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 1,385 patients analysed in RIPHeart and 1,612 patients in ERICCA.
cards.result: RIPHeart's in-hospital composite was 14.3% versus 14.6% (P=0.89) and ERICCA's 12-month composite was 26.5% versus 27.7% (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15); acute kidney injury/renal failure did not differ in either trial. This shelf is stamped LIKELY for the null: the two largest trials are concordant and sham-controlled, so remote ischaemic preconditioning should not be presented as kidney or heart protection during cardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: The stamp covers elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass as tested; it does not address preconditioning in other organs or emergency settings.

shelves.title: Belatacept vs ciclosporin after kidney transplantation
shelves.question: Does belatacept-based immunosuppression preserve kidney function better than ciclosporin, and at what rejection cost?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept · Cyclosporine/therapeutic use · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Immunoconjugates/therapeutic use · Immunosuppression Therapy · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Incidence
shelves.balance: SPLIT: LIKELY better renal function / POSSIBLE overall. In the twin phase-3 BENEFIT trials, belatacept gave similar patient/graft survival to ciclosporin at 12 months (BENEFIT: 95% more-intensive, 97% less-intensive, 93% ciclosporin; BENEFIT-EXT: 86%, 89%, 85%) with better measured GFR (BENEFIT: 65, 63 versus 50 mL/min) and fewer patients reaching the composite renal impairment end point. The cost was more early acute rejection in BENEFIT (22% and 17% versus 7%; similar rates in BENEFIT-EXT: 18%, 18%, 14%) and more posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder, concentrated in the central nervous system, on belatacept. Kidney function — a surrogate — favours belatacept; survival does not differ at 1 year, so the overall stamp cannot exceed POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: BENEFIT: belatacept preserved renal function better than ciclosporin, with more early acute rejection
cards.summary: BENEFIT: the renal-impairment composite was reached by 55%/54% on belatacept vs 78% on ciclosporin, with similar survival (95%/97% vs 93%) — and more early acute rejection.
cards.people: Adults receiving a kidney transplant from living or standard-criteria deceased donors, randomised to more-intensive belatacept, less-intensive belatacept or ciclosporin. The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, patient/graft survival was similar (95% more-intensive, 97% less-intensive, 93% ciclosporin). The composite renal impairment end point was reached by 55% (more-intensive) and 54% (less-intensive) versus 78% on ciclosporin (P≤0.001 for each belatacept regimen versus ciclosporin), and measured GFR was 65, 63 and 50 mL/min respectively (P≤0.001). Acute rejection was more frequent and higher grade on belatacept (22% and 17% versus 7%). Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder was more common in the belatacept groups.
cards.watchOut: Renal function at 12 months is a surrogate; patient/graft survival — the hard outcome — did not differ, and the rejection and lymphoproliferative-disorder excess runs against the renal gain.
cards.source: Vincenti F et al. A phase III study of belatacept-based immunosuppression regimens versus cyclosporine in renal transplant recipients (BENEFIT study). Am J Transplant. 2010;10:535-46. PMID: 20415897. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: BENEFIT-EXT: in extended-criteria donor kidneys, renal function again favoured belatacept; survival did not differ
cards.summary: BENEFIT-EXT (extended-criteria donors): renal impairment 71%/77% vs 85% ; survival again similar.
cards.people: Adult recipients of extended-criteria donor kidneys, randomised to more-intensive belatacept, less-intensive belatacept or ciclosporin. The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix.
