shelves.title: High fluid intake to prevent kidney-stone recurrence
shelves.question: Does drinking enough water to produce over 2 litres of urine a day prevent stone recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Calcium Oxalate/analysis · Drinking · Kidney Calculi/chemistry/physiopathology/prevention & control · Recurrence · Urine · Adherence Interventions · Fluid Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-flagship-trial ceiling. Borghi 1996, the one randomised trial of high water intake itself (199 first-episode idiopathic calcium stone formers, 5 years), found recurrence in 12 of 99 patients advised high water intake versus 27 of 100 with no treatment — 12.1% versus 27.0%, an absolute difference of about 15 percentage points. The 2026 PUSH trial (1,658 participants) tested something different — a behavioural programme to help people drink more, on top of guideline care advising high intake in both arms — and found symptomatic recurrence in 19% versus 20% (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20): the programme raised urine volume modestly but did not reduce events. So: drinking more water probably helps; programmes to make people drink more have not been shown to. Distinct from Shelf #483 (thiazides for stone recurrence, including the NOSTONE null — a drug question, not re-carded here).

cards.headline: Borghi 1996: high water intake halved 5-year stone recurrence — 12 of 99 versus 27 of 100
cards.summary: Borghi 1996: 5-year recurrence 12 of 99 vs 27 of 100 (12.1% vs 27.0%; P=0.008) on high water intake.
cards.people: 199 patients after a first episode of idiopathic calcium nephrolithiasis, randomised to high water intake with no dietetic change (group 1, n=99) or no treatment (group 2, n=100), followed prospectively for 5 years; 101 non-stone-forming controls were studied for baseline comparisons. Sex-specific baseline urine volumes are reported in the abstract; mean age is not stated.
cards.result: Recurrences within 5 years occurred in 12 of 99 patients in the high-intake group and 27 of 100 in the untreated group (P=0.008) — 12.1% versus 27.0%. The average interval to recurrence was 38.7 ± 13.2 months versus 25.1 ± 16.4 months (P=0.016). Relative supersaturations of calcium oxalate, brushite and uric acid fell sharply during follow-up only in the high-intake group. Baseline urine volume was lower in stone formers than controls (men 1,057 ± 238 versus 1,401 ± 562 mL/24 h, P<0.0001; women 990 ± 230 versus 1,239 ± 440 mL/24 h, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A single 1996 trial, unblinded by nature, in first-episode idiopathic calcium stone formers; patients with recurrences had higher baseline calcium excretion, and the authors advise adjuvant diet or drug therapy for hypercalciuria.
cards.source: Borghi L et al. Urinary volume, water and recurrences in idiopathic calcium nephrolithiasis: a 5-year randomized prospective study. J Urol. 1996;155:839-43. PMID: 8583588. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PUSH 2026: a behavioural programme to drink more raised urine volume but did not reduce stone recurrence
cards.summary: PUSH 2026: a behavioural programme raised urine volume but recurrence was 19% vs 20% (hazard ratio 0.96) — null.
cards.people: 1,658 participants aged 12 years and older with a history of urinary stone disease and low 24-hour urine volumes, at six US academic centres (826 intervention, 832 control); median age 44 years (IQR 29–59), 946 (57%) female; 66.6% were recurrent stone formers.
cards.result: At a median follow-up of 738 days, symptomatic stone recurrence (stone passage or procedural intervention) occurred in 154 participants (19%) in the intervention group and 165 (20%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20). Urine volume rose in both groups and was higher in the intervention group at months 6, 12, 18 and 24; there was no difference in stone growth of at least 2 mm, new stones, or the composite of recurrence, new formation or growth. No hyponatraemia requiring hospitalisation occurred; asymptomatic hyponatraemia occurred in 12 (1%) versus 2 (<1%).
cards.watchOut: PUSH does not test water versus no water: the control group received guideline-concordant care, which itself advises high fluid intake. Its null is about adherence programmes, not about urine volume.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 199 first-episode stone formers in Borghi 1996 and 1,658 stone formers in PUSH 2026.
cards.result: Borghi found 5-year recurrence of 12.1% with high water intake versus 27.0% untreated (P=0.008); PUSH found 2-year symptomatic recurrence of 19% versus 20% (hazard ratio 0.96) for a behavioural adherence programme over guideline care. shelves.title: Methenamine hippurate instead of prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent UTI
shelves.question: Is methenamine hippurate non-inferior to daily low-dose antibiotics for preventing recurrent UTI in women?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Hippurates/administration & dosage · Methenamine/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Recurrence · Urinary Tract Infections/microbiology/prevention & control · Urinary Tract Infections/prevention & control/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-head-to-head-trial ceiling, now with a placebo-controlled companion. ALTAR (2022), the one non-inferiority trial against daily antibiotics (205 women in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), found 1.38 antibiotic-treated UTI episodes per person-year on methenamine versus 0.89 on antibiotics — an absolute difference of 0.49 episodes (90% CI 0.15 to 0.84), inside the predefined 1-episode margin, so non-inferiority was met while antibiotics remained numerically better. The 2025 ImpresU trial (281 women aged 70 or older) found fewer antibiotic treatments for UTI on methenamine than placebo during 6 months of treatment (incidence rate ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.0; P=0.049) — a ratio inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so not solid evidence on its own — and a rebound after stopping (rate ratio 1.7 in the 6-month follow-up). Together: a reasonable non-antibiotic option, not a proven equal in every population.

cards.headline: ALTAR 2022: methenamine was non-inferior to daily antibiotics, but episodes were numerically more frequent
cards.summary: ALTAR 2022: UTI incidence 1.38 vs 0.89 episodes per person-year — non-inferiority met against a 1-episode margin, while daily antibiotics stayed numerically superior.
cards.people: 240 women aged 18 years or older with recurrent urinary tract infections requiring prophylactic treatment, randomised at eight UK centres to antibiotic prophylaxis (120) or methenamine hippurate (120) for 12 months; the modified intention-to-treat analysis comprised 205 participants (102 antibiotics, 103 methenamine). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The incidence of symptomatic, antibiotic-treated urinary tract infections during the 12-month treatment period was 0.89 episodes per person year (95% CI 0.65 to 1.12) in the antibiotics group and 1.38 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.72) in the methenamine group — an absolute difference of 0.49 episodes per person year (90% CI 0.15 to 0.84), within the predefined non-inferiority margin of one episode per person year. Adverse reactions were reported by 24% in the antibiotic group and 28% in the methenamine group, and most were mild.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial with crossover allowed; non-inferiority against a wide (1 episode per person-year) margin is not equality — antibiotics prevented about half an episode per person-year more.

cards.headline: ImpresU 2025: methenamine beat placebo during treatment in women 70+, with rebound after stopping
cards.summary: ImpresU 2025 (women 70+): on-treatment incidence rate ratio 0.75 [0.57 to 1.0] vs placebo — with rebound after stopping.
cards.people: 289 women aged 70 years or older with recurrent urinary tract infections recruited from general practice in four European countries; 281 (97%) were included in the main analysis (140 methenamine hippurate 1 g twice daily, 141 placebo), with a 6-month treatment period and 6-month follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age beyond the 70+ eligibility.
cards.result: During treatment, the methenamine group had a lower incidence of antibiotic treatments for urinary tract infections than placebo (incidence rate ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.0; P=0.049). During follow-up after treatment stopped, the ratio reversed: rate ratio 1.7 (95% CI 1.3 to 2.3; P<0.001). There were no important differences in symptom severity or duration, or in complications.
cards.watchOut: The treatment-period rate ratio of 0.75 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid evidence on its own, and its confidence interval reaches 1.0; the post-treatment rebound is part of the result, not a footnote.

cards.headline: Synthesis: methenamine is a credible non-antibiotic alternative — POSSIBLE, with a rebound warning
cards.summary: Methenamine is a credible non-antibiotic alternative — POSSIBLE, with the rebound warning on the card.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 205 women in the ALTAR modified intention-to-treat analysis and 281 women aged 70 or older in ImpresU.
cards.result: ALTAR met its non-inferiority margin versus daily antibiotics (difference 0.49 episodes per person-year, 90% CI 0.15 to 0.84, against a 1-episode margin) while antibiotics stayed numerically superior; ImpresU showed a modest on-treatment advantage over placebo (rate ratio 0.75) followed by rebound after stopping (rate ratio 1.7). Proposed stamp POSSIBLE: one head-to-head trial plus one placebo-controlled trial in older women support methenamine as an antibiotic-sparing option, with effect sizes too modest for a higher stamp.
cards.watchOut: Stopping methenamine after 6 months was followed by more infections in ImpresU; any recommendation to start it should carry a plan for duration.

shelves.title: Personalised cooler dialysate (MyTEMP)
shelves.question: Does dialysing at a personalised cooler temperature reduce cardiovascular death or hospitalisation in maintenance haemodialysis?
shelves.mesh: Dialysis Solutions/adverse effects · Renal Dialysis/methods · Cold Temperature/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): MyTEMP, a single but very large pragmatic cluster-randomised trial (84 centres, 15,413 patients, about 4.3 million haemodialysis treatments), found the primary composite of cardiovascular death or hospital admission with myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or congestive heart failure in 21.4% of patients on personalised cooler dialysate versus 22.4% on standard 36.5°C dialysate (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00, 96% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=0.93). The mean intradialytic systolic blood-pressure drop was also essentially identical (26.6 versus 27.1 mm Hg). The trial is null on its primary outcome and makes no benefit claim; its size earns the null a LIKELY stamp despite being a single trial.

cards.headline: MyTEMP: personalised cooler dialysate did not reduce cardiovascular death or hospitalisation — 21.4% versus 22.4%
cards.summary: MyTEMP (15,413 patients): the cardiovascular composite occurred in 21.4% vs 22.4% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00 [0.89 to 1.11]).
cards.people: 84 haemodialysis centres in Ontario, Canada (42 personalised cooler dialysate, 42 standard temperature), providing outpatient maintenance haemodialysis to 15,413 patients (8,000 cooler, 7,413 standard) over the 4-year trial period. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (cardiovascular-related death or hospital admission with myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or congestive heart failure) occurred in 1,711 patients (21.4%) in the cooler-dialysate group versus 1,658 (22.4%) in the standard-temperature group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00, 96% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=0.93). Mean dialysate temperature achieved was 35.8°C versus 36.4°C.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, centre-level policy intervention delivered pragmatically; the achieved temperature separation was 0.6°C, smaller than the protocol's per-patient target for some patients.
cards.source: MyTEMP Investigators. Personalised cooler dialysate for patients receiving maintenance haemodialysis (MyTEMP): a pragmatic, cluster-randomised trial. Lancet. 2022;400:1693-1703. PMID: 36343653. Registry ID: NCT02628366 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank).

cards.headline: MyTEMP (secondary): intradialytic blood-pressure drop was no smaller on cooler dialysate
cards.summary: MyTEMP, secondary: intradialytic systolic drop 26.6 vs 27.1 mm Hg — no haemodynamic advantage either.
cards.people: The same 15,413 patients and 84 centres as the primary-outcome card.
cards.result: The mean drop in intradialytic systolic blood pressure was 26.6 mm Hg in the cooler-dialysate group and 27.1 mm Hg in the standard-temperature group (mean difference −0.5 mm Hg, 99% CI −1.4 to 0.4; P=0.14) — no haemodynamic advantage accompanied the temperature policy.
cards.watchOut: A secondary outcome of the same single trial; it explains, but does not independently replicate, the primary null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one very large pragmatic trial, null on events and on blood pressure — LIKELY the null
cards.summary: One very large pragmatic trial, null on events and on blood pressure — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the single MyTEMP trial of 15,413 patients in 84 centres.
cards.result: Primary composite 21.4% versus 22.4% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00, 96% CI 0.89 to 1.11) and intradialytic systolic drop 26.6 versus 27.1 mm Hg. Proposed stamp LIKELY for the null: single-trial shelves usually cap lower, but 15,413 patients and 4.3 million treatments with a hazard ratio centred exactly on 1.00 make chance an unlikely explanation for the absence of benefit. The abstract's own conclusion — that the rising popularity of cooler dialysate is called into question — is the shelf's conclusion.
cards.watchOut: The stamp covers centre-wide personalised cooler dialysate as a policy in maintenance haemodialysis; it does not rule on individually targeted cooling for specific symptoms, which MyTEMP did not test as an end point.
cards.source: Synthesis of MyTEMP Investigators. Lancet. 2022;400:1693-1703. PMID: 36343653. Registry ID as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Hemodiafiltration versus high-flux hemodialysis
shelves.question: In maintenance dialysis, does high-dose hemodiafiltration reduce mortality versus conventional high-flux hemodialysis?
shelves.mesh: Hemodiafiltration/adverse effects,methods · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications,mortality,therapy · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects · Renal Insufficiency/etiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality,prevention & control · Hemodiafiltration/methods · Hospitalization
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary claim is all-cause mortality). Two randomised trials point the same way: CONVINCE (1,360 patients, median 30 months) found death from any cause in 17.3% on high-dose hemodiafiltration versus 21.9% on high-flux hemodialysis (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.93), and the earlier open-label ESHOL trial (906 patients) found a relative hazard of 0.70 (0.53 to 0.92) for all-cause mortality. Both headline ratios are relative measures sitting outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's centre but neither is a ≤0.5 effect; the stamp rests on two concordant randomised trials with absolute rates printed beside the relative figures, and it remains proposed until the developer rules.

cards.headline: CONVINCE 2023: high-dose hemodiafiltration lowered all-cause mortality versus high-flux hemodialysis — deaths 17.3% vs 21.9%, relative hazard 0.77
cards.summary: CONVINCE 2023: high-dose hemodiafiltration lowered all-cause mortality vs high-flux hemodialysis — deaths 17.3% vs 21.9% , relative hazard 0.77. (Tier C — mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 1,360 patients with kidney failure who had received high-flux hemodialysis for at least 3 months and were candidates for a convection volume of at least 23 litres per session, randomised to high-dose hemodiafiltration (683) or continuation of conventional high-flux hemodialysis (677); median follow-up 30 months (interquartile range 27 to 38). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause occurred in 118 patients (17.3%) in the hemodiafiltration group and 148 patients (21.9%) in the hemodialysis group (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.93 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). The mean convection volume during the trial in the hemodiafiltration group was 25.3 litres per session. Key secondary outcomes were cause-specific death, a composite of fatal or nonfatal cardiovascular events, kidney transplantation, and recurrent hospitalisations.
cards.watchOut: Pragmatic and unblinded by nature (a dialysis modality cannot be masked), and entry required candidacy for high convection volumes — the result applies to patients who can achieve high-dose hemodiafiltration, not to every dialysis patient.
cards.source: Blankestijn PJ et al. Effect of Hemodiafiltration or Hemodialysis on Mortality in Kidney Failure. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(8):700-709. PMID: 37326323. Registry ID: NTR7138 (Dutch Trial Register), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ESHOL 2013: switching to high-efficiency online hemodiafiltration carried a relative hazard of 0.70 for all-cause mortality
cards.summary: ESHOL 2013: switching to high-efficiency online hemodiafiltration carried a relative hazard of 0.70 for all-cause mortality.
cards.people: 906 chronic hemodialysis patients assigned to continue hemodialysis (450) or switch to high-efficiency postdilution online hemodiafiltration (456). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with continued hemodialysis, online hemodiafiltration was associated with a 30% relative lower risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.70, 95% confidence interval 0.53 to 0.92; P=0.01), a 33% relative lower risk of cardiovascular mortality (hazard ratio 0.67, 0.44 to 1.02; P=0.06 — not statistically significant), and a 55% relative lower risk of infection-related mortality (hazard ratio 0.45, 0.21 to 0.96; P=0.03). The authors' estimated number needed to treat suggested switching eight patients might prevent one annual death. Rates of dialysis sessions complicated by hypotension and of all-cause hospitalisation were lower with hemodiafiltration. The abstract reports relative hazards without the absolute mortality rates, so no absolute rates are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country-era trial run a decade before CONVINCE, and its cardiovascular-mortality component did not reach significance — the concordance with CONVINCE is on all-cause mortality, not on every cause-specific slice.
cards.source: Maduell F et al. High-efficiency postdilution online hemodiafiltration reduces all-cause mortality in hemodialysis patients. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2013;24(3):487-97. PMID: 23411788. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank registration entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised trials, one direction — high-dose hemodiafiltration lowered mortality in both, stamp proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: Two randomised trials, one direction — high-dose hemodiafiltration lowered mortality in both: LIKELY, proposed (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CONVINCE 2023 (1,360 patients) and ESHOL 2013 (906 patients).
cards.result: CONVINCE's absolute rates (17.3% vs 21.9% dead over a median 30 months; relative hazard 0.77) and ESHOL's relative hazard of 0.70 agree that high-dose, high-convection-volume hemodiafiltration beat conventional (high-flux) hemodialysis on all-cause mortality in patients able to receive it. This shelf is about dialysis MODALITY only: dialysis frequency lives on Shelf #293 and cooler dialysate on Shelf #597, and neither is re-carded here. Because the claim is a mortality claim, the LIKELY stamp is proposed only, pending the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Both trials required patients who could achieve high convection volumes; neither answers whether lower-dose hemodiafiltration, or hemodiafiltration in patients who cannot reach those volumes, shares the benefit.

shelves.title: Roxadustat and the HIF stabilizers for anaemia in chronic kidney disease
shelves.question: Do hypoxia-inducible-factor stabilizers raise haemoglobin as well as injected ESAs in non-dialysis and dialysis CKD — and what do the cardiovascular safety data show?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/chemically induced · Anemia/drug therapy,etiology · Cholesterol/blood · Glycine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Hematinics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hemoglobins/analysis · Hyperkalemia/chemically induced
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for haemoglobin efficacy; POSSIBLE for cardiovascular safety — the safety half is PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: it rests on a MACE composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction and stroke). Twin Chinese phase 3 trials showed roxadustat raising haemoglobin versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD (+1.9 vs −0.4 g/dL at weeks 7–9) and non-inferior to epoetin alfa on dialysis. The pooled non-dialysis analysis (4,277 patients) found no increased risk of MACE (hazard ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.27 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 band where ratios alone are not solid evidence) and noninferiority to placebo for MACE; that supports 'no large excess shown', not proof of cardiovascular safety, hence POSSIBLE on the safety half.

cards.headline: Chen 2019 (non-dialysis): roxadustat raised haemoglobin by 1.9 g/dL while placebo fell by 0.4 g/dL over weeks 7–9
cards.summary: Chen 2019 (non-dialysis): roxadustat raised haemoglobin by 1.9 g/dL while placebo fell by 0.4 g/dL over weeks 7–9.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (8-week randomised phase, then 18-week open-label roxadustat)
cards.people: 154 patients with chronic kidney disease not undergoing dialysis, at 29 sites in China, randomised 2:1 to roxadustat or placebo three times weekly; all had a baseline haemoglobin of 7.0 to 10.0 g per deciliter. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The mean (±SD) change from baseline in haemoglobin, averaged over weeks 7 through 9, was an increase of 1.9±1.2 g per deciliter with roxadustat and a decrease of 0.4±0.8 g per deciliter with placebo (P<0.001). Hepcidin fell more with roxadustat (mean reduction 56.14±63.40 vs 15.10±48.06 ng per milliliter), and total cholesterol fell by 40.6 vs 7.7 mg per deciliter. Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis occurred more frequently in the roxadustat group. Efficacy was maintained during the 18-week open-label period in which all patients received roxadustat.
cards.watchOut: Small (154 patients), single-country, and only 8 weeks of placebo-controlled treatment: it proves short-term haemoglobin correction, not durability or outcomes.
cards.source: Chen N et al. Roxadustat for Anemia in Patients with Kidney Disease Not Receiving Dialysis. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(11):1001-1010. PMID: 31340089. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02652819, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Chen 2019 (dialysis): roxadustat was non-inferior to epoetin alfa for haemoglobin change over weeks 23–27
cards.summary: Chen 2019 (dialysis): roxadustat was non-inferior to epoetin alfa for haemoglobin change over weeks 23–27.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase 3 trial (non-inferiority design)
cards.people: 305 patients in China who had been undergoing dialysis and epoetin alfa therapy for at least 6 weeks, randomised 2:1 to roxadustat (204) or epoetin alfa (101) three times weekly for 26 weeks; 256 patients completed the treatment period; mean baseline haemoglobin was 10.4 g per deciliter. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The mean (±SD) change in haemoglobin from baseline to weeks 23 through 27 was 0.7±1.1 g per deciliter with roxadustat and 0.5±1.0 with epoetin alfa; roxadustat was statistically noninferior (difference 0.2, 95% confidence interval −0.02 to 0.5; the non-inferiority margin was −1.0 g per deciliter). Roxadustat increased transferrin, maintained serum iron, lowered hepcidin more, and lowered total and LDL cholesterol more than epoetin alfa. Hyperkalemia and upper respiratory infection were more frequent with roxadustat; hypertension was more frequent with epoetin alfa.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on a haemoglobin surrogate against one ESA, in one country, over 26 weeks — it does not compare roxadustat with placebo on dialysis or speak to hard outcomes.
cards.source: Chen N et al. Roxadustat Treatment for Anemia in Patients Undergoing Long-Term Dialysis. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(11):1011-1022. PMID: 31340116. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02652806, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Provenzano 2021 (pooled, non-dialysis): haemoglobin rose 1.9 vs 0.2 g/dL and MACE was not increased versus placebo — relative hazard 1.10, inside the caution band
cards.summary: Provenzano 2021 (pooled, non-dialysis): haemoglobin rose 1.9 vs 0.2 g/dL and MACE was not increased vs placebo — relative hazard 1.10, inside the 0.5–2.0 band (printed on the card; no safety claim beyond it).
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials
cards.people: 4,277 patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD and CKD-related anaemia (roxadustat 2,391; placebo 1,886); mean (SD) baseline haemoglobin 9.1 (0.7) g/dl and mean eGFR 20 (12) ml/min per 1.73 m2. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean change in haemoglobin averaged over weeks 28–52 was 1.9 g/dl on roxadustat versus 0.2 g/dl on placebo (treatment difference 1.7, 95% confidence interval 1.7 to 1.8). Red-cell transfusion in the first 52 weeks was lower with roxadustat (6.1 vs 20.4 per 100 patient-exposure years; hazard ratio 0.26, 0.21 to 0.32 — a relative measure). There were no increased risks of MACE (hazard ratio 1.10, 0.96 to 1.27), MACE+ (1.07, 0.94 to 1.21), all-cause mortality (1.08, 0.93 to 1.26), or individual MACE+ components, and roxadustat was noninferior to placebo for MACE. MACE here is the composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction and stroke.

shelves.title: Membranous nephropathy: rituximab versus calcineurin inhibition
shelves.question: In primary membranous nephropathy, does rituximab beat cyclosporine for durable remission (MENTOR) — and a rituximab sequence versus cyclical steroids/cyclophosphamide (STARMEN)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Cyclosporine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Glomerulonephritis, Membranous/drug therapy · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials answer the two halves. MENTOR (130 patients) showed rituximab non-inferior to cyclosporine for remission at 12 months (60% vs 52%) and clearly superior at maintaining remission at 24 months (60% vs 20%; risk difference 40 percentage points). STARMEN (86 patients) then showed the older cyclical corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide regimen beating a sequential tacrolimus–rituximab regimen on the same 24-month remission outcome (83.7% vs 58.1%; relative risk 1.44 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates). Rituximab's win is over a calcineurin inhibitor's durability, not over the cyclical alkylating regimen.

cards.headline: MENTOR 2019: rituximab matched cyclosporine at 12 months (60% vs 52% in remission) and beat it at 24 months (60% vs 20%)
cards.summary: MENTOR 2019: rituximab matched cyclosporine at 12 months (60% vs 52% in remission) and beat it at 24 months ( 60% vs 20% ).
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, non-inferiority trial with 24-month follow-up
cards.people: 130 patients with membranous nephropathy, proteinuria of at least 5 g per 24 hours and creatinine clearance of at least 40 ml per minute per 1.73 m2, on angiotensin-system blockade for at least 3 months, randomised to intravenous rituximab (65) or oral cyclosporine for 12 months (65). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, 39 of 65 patients (60%) in the rituximab group and 34 of 65 (52%) in the cyclosporine group had a complete or partial remission of proteinuria (risk difference 8 percentage points, 95% confidence interval −9 to 25; P=0.004 for noninferiority). At 24 months, 39 patients (60%) on rituximab and 13 (20%) on cyclosporine remained in complete or partial remission (risk difference 40 percentage points, 25 to 55; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority). Anti-PLA2R antibodies fell faster and further on rituximab. Serious adverse events occurred in 11 patients (17%) on rituximab and 20 (31%) on cyclosporine (P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 24-month gap is largely cyclosporine remissions relapsing after the drug stopped at 12 months — the trial compares a durable B-cell strategy against a time-limited calcineurin course, as designed.
cards.source: Fervenza FC et al. Rituximab or Cyclosporine in the Treatment of Membranous Nephropathy. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(1):36-46. PMID: 31269364. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01180036, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: STARMEN 2021: cyclical steroids–cyclophosphamide beat sequential tacrolimus–rituximab — remission 83.7% vs 58.1% at 24 months
cards.summary: STARMEN 2021: cyclical steroids–cyclophosphamide beat sequential tacrolimus–rituximab — remission 83.7% vs 58.1% at 24 months.
cards.people: 86 patients with primary membranous nephropathy and persistent nephrotic syndrome after a six-month observation period, assigned 43 each to six-month cyclical corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide treatment or sequential tacrolimus (full dose six months, tapering three more) plus a single 1 g rituximab dose at month six. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — complete or partial remission of nephrotic syndrome at 24 months — occurred in 36 patients (83.7%) in the corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide group and 25 (58.1%) in the tacrolimus–rituximab group (relative risk 1.44, 95% confidence interval 1.08 to 1.92 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). Complete remission at 24 months occurred in 26 patients (60%) versus 11 (26%) (relative risk 2.36, 1.34 to 4.16). Immunological response (anti-PLA2R depletion) was faster with corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide. Relapses occurred in one versus three patients, and serious adverse events were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Small (86 patients), open-label, and the rituximab arm used a single 1 g dose after tacrolimus — a deliberately sequential design, not the MENTOR rituximab regimen; the two trials' rituximab arms are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Fernández-Juárez G et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: rituximab outlasts cyclosporine, but the cyclical steroid–cyclophosphamide regimen outlasted a tacrolimus–rituximab sequence
cards.summary: Rituximab outlasts cyclosporine, but the cyclical regimen outlasted a tacrolimus–rituximab sequence — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MENTOR 2019 (130 patients) and STARMEN 2021 (86 patients).
cards.result: Read together, the pair separates two claims that are often merged: rituximab is the more durable of the two MENTOR arms (60% vs 20% still in remission at 24 months), while in STARMEN the classic cyclical regimen achieved remission in 83.7% versus 58.1% for a tacrolimus-then-rituximab sequence. The shelf therefore supports rituximab over calcineurin inhibition for durability, and does not support ranking rituximab-based therapy above cyclical corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide on this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded and both are modest in size; remission of proteinuria is the outcome throughout — neither trial was powered for kidney failure or death.

shelves.title: Lupus nephritis induction: mycophenolate versus cyclophosphamide
shelves.question: For induction in proliferative lupus nephritis, is mycophenolate non-inferior to IV cyclophosphamide — full-dose (ALMS) or low-dose “Euro-Lupus” — and what does long-term follow-up show?
shelves.mesh: Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Ethnicity · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Injections, Intravenous · Lupus Nephritis/drug therapy,mortality,pathology · Mycophenolic Acid/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for comparability, not superiority): The international ALMS induction trial (370 patients, classes III–V) found nearly identical response rates for mycophenolate and IV cyclophosphamide (56.2% vs 53.0%) and explicitly did not meet its objective of showing mycophenolate superior. The Euro-Lupus trial (90 patients) separately showed a low-dose IV cyclophosphamide regimen (cumulative 3 g, followed by azathioprine) achieving results comparable to a high-dose regimen (treatment failure 16% vs 20%; renal remission 71% vs 54%, neither difference statistically significant). Two randomised trials thus support mycophenolate as a comparable induction option and low-dose cyclophosphamide as a comparable dose strategy — neither supports a superiority claim for any arm.

cards.headline: ALMS 2009: mycophenolate response 56.2% vs IV cyclophosphamide 53.0% — the trial did not show mycophenolate superior
cards.summary: ALMS 2009: mycophenolate response 56.2% vs IV cyclophosphamide 53.0% — the trial did not show mycophenolate superior.
cards.type: Multinational, randomised, open-label, two-phase (induction and maintenance) trial — 24-week induction report
cards.people: 370 patients with classes III through V lupus nephritis randomised to open-label mycophenolate mofetil (target 3 g/d; 185) or IV cyclophosphamide (0.5 to 1.0 g/m2 monthly pulses; 185), both with prednisone tapered from a maximum of 60 mg/d. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Response (a prespecified decrease in urine protein/creatinine ratio with stabilisation or improvement in serum creatinine) occurred in 104 (56.2%) of 185 patients on mycophenolate and 98 (53.0%) of 185 on IV cyclophosphamide — no significant difference. Secondary endpoints, including complete renal remission and systemic disease activity, were also similar. There were nine deaths in the mycophenolate group and five in the cyclophosphamide group, and no significant differences in adverse events, serious adverse events, or infections. The authors state the study did not meet its primary objective of showing mycophenolate was superior to IV cyclophosphamide.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and designed as a superiority trial that failed on its own terms: 'not significantly different' here supports comparability in practice, but the trial was not a formal non-inferiority design, and the death counts (9 vs 5) are small and not a powered safety comparison.
cards.source: Appel GB et al. Mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide for induction treatment of lupus nephritis. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2009;20(5):1103-12. PMID: 19369404. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank registration entry.

cards.headline: Euro-Lupus 2002: low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (3 g cumulative) matched high-dose — treatment failure 16% vs 20%, renal remission 71% vs 54%
cards.summary: Euro-Lupus 2002: low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (3 g cumulative) matched high-dose — treatment failure 16% vs 20%, renal remission 71% vs 54%.
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised trial (single-blind per the record's indexing)
cards.people: 90 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and proliferative glomerulonephritis randomised to high-dose IV cyclophosphamide (six monthly then two quarterly pulses) or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (six fortnightly fixed 500 mg pulses), each followed by azathioprine; median follow-up about 41 months in both groups. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 16% of the low-dose group and 20% of the high-dose group (not statistically significant). Serum creatinine, albumin, C3, 24-hour urinary protein and disease activity scores improved significantly in both groups during the first year. Renal remission was achieved in 71% of the low-dose group and 54% of the high-dose group (not statistically significant); renal flares occurred in 27% and 29%. Episodes of severe infection were more than twice as frequent in the high-dose group, though the difference was not statistically significant. The authors conclude the low-dose regimen followed by azathioprine achieves clinical results comparable to the high-dose regimen in European patients.
cards.watchOut: Only 90 patients, in a European population, from 2002: every comparison is underpowered, so 'comparable' means no difference was detected, within wide uncertainty — and the low-dose strategy is a cyclophosphamide-dose answer, not a mycophenolate comparison.
cards.source: Houssiau FA et al. Immunosuppressive therapy in lupus nephritis: the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial, a randomized trial of low-dose versus high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide. cards.headline: Synthesis: two ways to spare patients the heaviest regimen — mycophenolate instead of cyclophosphamide, or much less cyclophosphamide
cards.summary: Two ways to spare patients the heaviest regimen — LIKELY (comparability).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ALMS 2009 (370 patients) and the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial 2002 (90 patients).
cards.result: ALMS gives the drug-substitution answer: mycophenolate's response rate (56.2%) was essentially the IV cyclophosphamide rate (53.0%), with similar remission and safety profiles, in a trial that honestly reports failing to show superiority. Euro-Lupus gives the dose-reduction answer: a 3 g cumulative cyclophosphamide course followed by azathioprine produced failure, remission and flare rates statistically indistinguishable from a much larger cumulative dose over ~41 months. Maintenance-phase and add-on biologic questions in lupus live on Shelf #386 and are not re-carded here; this shelf is induction only.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate the modern add-on era (belimumab, voclosporin, obinutuzumab combinations), so the shelf compares the two backbone regimens, not today's combination strategies.

shelves.title: ANCA vasculitis with kidney failure: plasma exchange and steroid dose
shelves.question: In severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, does plasma exchange reduce death or end-stage kidney disease — and is a reduced-dose steroid regimen as safe (PEXIVAS; MEPEX as the earlier exchange trial)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis/complications,drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Cyclophosphamide/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite is death or end-stage kidney disease). LIKELY for the PEXIVAS null: in 704 patients followed up to 7 years, plasma exchange did not reduce death or ESKD (28.4% vs 31.0%; hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.13 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside it), a very large null that may carry LIKELY under the library's large-null rule; the same trial found a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen noninferior to standard dose on the same composite, with fewer serious infections. POSSIBLE for the older MEPEX signal: in 137 patients presenting with creatinine above 500 micromol/L, exchange beat IV methylprednisolone on dialysis independence at 3 months (69% vs 49%) — a smaller, earlier, severe-renal-only trial whose recovery endpoint PEXIVAS did not reproduce on death/ESKD.

cards.headline: PEXIVAS 2020: plasma exchange did not reduce death or ESKD — 28.4% vs 31.0%, relative hazard 0.86 — and reduced-dose steroids were noninferior
cards.summary: PEXIVAS 2020: plasma exchange did not reduce death or ESKD — 28.4% vs 31.0% , relative hazard 0.86 — and reduced-dose steroids were noninferior. (Tier C — death/ESKD composite; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design (plasma exchange vs none; reduced-dose vs standard-dose oral glucocorticoids)
cards.people: Patients with severe ANCA-associated vasculitis (eGFR below 50 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 or diffuse pulmonary haemorrhage): 352 assigned to plasma exchange and 352 to no plasma exchange; in the glucocorticoid comparison, 330 to reduced-dose and 325 to standard-dose regimens; follow-up up to 7 years for the primary composite of death from any cause or end-stage kidney disease. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause or ESKD occurred in 100 of 352 patients (28.4%) in the plasma-exchange group and 109 of 352 (31.0%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 1.13; P=0.27 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). For glucocorticoids, death or ESKD occurred in 92 of 330 patients (27.9%) on the reduced-dose regimen and 83 of 325 (25.5%) on standard dose (absolute risk difference 2.3 percentage points, 90% CI −3.4 to 8.0), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (margin 11 percentage points). Serious infections at 1 year were less common with reduced-dose glucocorticoids (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 0.52 to 0.93 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: The exchange comparison is open by nature and its interval (0.65 to 1.13) cannot exclude a modest benefit; the claim carded is 'did not reduce' as the trial concluded, at this size and follow-up — not proof of zero effect in every subgroup.
cards.source: Walsh M et al. Plasma Exchange and Glucocorticoids in Severe ANCA-Associated Vasculitis. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(7):622-631. PMID: 32053298. Registry IDs: ISRCTN07757494 and ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00987389, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: MEPEX 2007: in creatinine above 500 micromol/L, plasma exchange beat IV methylprednisolone on dialysis independence at 3 months — 69% vs 49%
cards.summary: MEPEX 2007: in creatinine above 500 µmol/L (≈5.66 mg/dL), plasma exchange beat IV methylprednisolone on dialysis independence at 3 months — 69% vs 49%.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of adjunctive therapy in severe renal vasculitis
cards.people: 137 patients with a new diagnosis of ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis confirmed by renal biopsy and serum creatinine above 500 micromol/L (5.8 mg/dl), randomised to seven plasma exchanges (70) or 3000 mg of intravenous methylprednisolone (67); both groups also received oral cyclophosphamide and oral prednisolone. cards.headline: Synthesis: the large modern trial is null on death/ESKD; the small severe-renal trial's recovery benefit survives only as a fenced POSSIBLE (Tier C, proposed)
cards.summary: The large modern trial is null on death/ESKD (LIKELY); the small severe-renal trial's recovery benefit survives only as a fenced POSSIBLE — Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PEXIVAS 2020 (704 patients in the exchange comparison) and MEPEX 2007 (137 patients).
cards.result: PEXIVAS answers the shelf's headline question at the largest scale: plasma exchange did not reduce the composite of death or end-stage kidney disease (28.4% vs 31.0%), while reduced-dose glucocorticoids were noninferior to standard dose on the same outcome with fewer serious infections (relative rate 0.69). MEPEX's dialysis-independence advantage (69% vs 49% at 3 months) came from patients presenting with creatinine above 500 micromol/L against a steroid-pulse comparator, and its 1-year survival was no better (73% vs 76%) — so the recovery signal is kept, fenced to that severe presentation, and never upgraded into a survival claim.
cards.watchOut: Quoting MEPEX without PEXIVAS reverses the evidence order: the later trial is five times larger, followed patients up to 7 years, and tested exchange against no exchange.
cards.source: Synthesis of Walsh M et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(7):622-631. PMID: 32053298; Jayne DR et al. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2007;18(7):2180-8. PMID: 17582159. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Preventing AV fistula failure: clopidogrel and fish oil
shelves.question: After new fistula creation, does clopidogrel prevent early thrombosis (DAC) or fish oil prevent failure (FAVOURED) — and do either improve usability for dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Arteriovenous Shunt, Surgical/adverse effects · Clopidogrel · Graft Occlusion, Vascular/prevention & control · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Renal Dialysis/methods · Thrombosis/etiology,prevention & control · Ticlopidine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for the null on the outcome that matters — usability/failure — and POSSIBLE for clopidogrel's isolated thrombosis effect. In DAC (877 patients), clopidogrel cut fistula thrombosis at 6 weeks (12.2% vs 19.5%; relative risk 0.63 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside it) but did not increase the proportion of fistulas becoming suitable for dialysis (61.8% vs 59.5% unsuitable-failure rates as reported; relative risk for failure 1.05). In FAVOURED (567 randomised), neither fish oil (failure 47% vs 47%; relative risk 1.03) nor aspirin in its factorial subset (45% vs 43%; relative risk 1.05) reduced fistula failure at 12 months. Preventing a clot is not the same as producing a usable fistula, and the stamps keep those apart.

cards.headline: DAC 2008: clopidogrel cut early fistula thrombosis (12.2% vs 19.5%) but fistulas became suitable for dialysis no more often
cards.summary: DAC 2008: clopidogrel cut early fistula thrombosis (12.2% vs 19.5%) but fistulas became suitable for dialysis no more often.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 9 US centres (enrolment stopped early on an efficacy stopping rule for thrombosis)
cards.people: 877 participants with end-stage renal disease or advanced chronic kidney disease, randomised within 1 day after fistula creation to clopidogrel (300 mg loading dose, then 75 mg daily; 441) or placebo (436) for 6 weeks, and followed until 150 to 180 days after fistula creation or 30 days after starting dialysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Fistula thrombosis at 6 weeks occurred in 53 (12.2%) participants on clopidogrel and 84 (19.5%) on placebo (relative risk 0.63, 95% confidence interval 0.46 to 0.97; P=0.018 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). Failure of the fistula to become suitable for dialysis did not differ: the reported failure proportions were 61.8% on clopidogrel and 59.5% on placebo (relative risk 1.05, 0.94 to 1.17; P=0.40). Suitability meant use at a dialysis blood pump rate of at least 300 mL/min during 8 of 12 dialysis sessions.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped early for the thrombosis endpoint, which can exaggerate that endpoint's apparent effect; and the thrombosis win is exactly the kind of intermediate outcome the library discounts when the patient-facing outcome (a usable fistula) does not move.
cards.source: Dember LM et al. Effect of clopidogrel on early failure of arteriovenous fistulas for hemodialysis: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2008;299(18):2164-71. PMID: 18477783. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00067119, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: FAVOURED 2017: fish oil did not reduce fistula failure (47% vs 47%), and neither did aspirin in the factorial subset (45% vs 43%)
cards.summary: FAVOURED 2017: fish oil did not reduce fistula failure (47% vs 47%), and neither did aspirin in the factorial subset (45% vs 43%).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, controlled trial with a 2-by-2 factorial element (fish oil vs placebo in all; aspirin vs placebo in a subset)
cards.people: 567 randomised participants with stage 4 or 5 chronic kidney disease, recruited 2008–2014 at 35 dialysis centres in Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, treated from 1 day before fistula-creation surgery for 12 weeks and observed for 12 months; 359 (63%) were male, 264 (47%) had diabetes, and mean (SD) age was 54.8 (14.3) years. The aspirin comparison randomised a subset of 406 participants.
cards.result: Fistula failure at 12 months (a composite of thrombosis, abandonment and/or cannulation failure) occurred in 128 of 270 patients (47%) on fish oil and 125 of 266 (47%) on placebo (relative risk adjusted for aspirin use 1.03, 95% confidence interval 0.86 to 1.23; P=0.78 — a relative measure). Fish oil also did not reduce thrombosis (22% vs 23%), abandonment (19% vs 22%) or cannulation failure (40% vs 39%). In the aspirin subset, failure occurred in 87 of 194 (45%) on aspirin and 83 of 194 (43%) on placebo (relative risk 1.05, 0.84 to 1.31; P=0.68). The authors conclude neither fish oil supplementation nor aspirin reduced failure of new arteriovenous fistulae within 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The aspirin comparison covers only the 406-patient factorial subset, so its interval is wider; and treatment lasted 12 weeks against a 12-month outcome — the trial tests peri-creation prophylaxis, not indefinite therapy. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Irish AB et al. Effect of Fish Oil Supplementation and Aspirin Use on Arteriovenous Fistula Failure in Patients Requiring Hemodialysis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2017;177(2):184-193. PMID: 28055065. Registry ID: ACTRN12607000569404, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an anti-thrombotic effect that never became a usable fistula — LIKELY the null on usability, POSSIBLE on thrombosis alone
cards.summary: An anti-thrombotic effect that never became a usable fistula — LIKELY the null on usability, POSSIBLE on thrombosis alone.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DAC 2008 (877 participants) and FAVOURED 2017 (567 randomised participants).
cards.result: The two trials agree on the outcome patients feel: no tested drug made more fistulas usable — DAC's suitability failure was 61.8% vs 59.5% despite fewer thromboses, and FAVOURED's failure rate was identical on fish oil (47% vs 47%) and no better on aspirin (45% vs 43%). DAC's thrombosis reduction (12.2% vs 19.5%, relative risk 0.63) is real on its own terms but is fenced as an intermediate endpoint that did not translate, which is why it carries only POSSIBLE beside the LIKELY null on usability.
cards.watchOut: Do not prescribe from the thrombosis figure alone: in DAC the fistulas that avoided clotting still failed to mature at the same rate.

shelves.title: Difelikefalin for dialysis itch
shelves.question: Does the kappa-opioid agonist difelikefalin reduce uraemic pruritus in hemodialysis patients versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications,therapy · Piperidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pruritus/drug therapy,etiology · Receptors, Opioid/agonists · Renal Dialysis · Uremia/complications
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A twin phase 3 programme with concordant results. KALM-1 (378 randomised) found a ≥3-point improvement in worst-itch score at week 12 in 51.9% on difelikefalin versus 30.9% on placebo on observed data (imputed 49.1% vs 27.9%; P<0.001), and the pooled KALM-1/KALM-2 analysis (851 participants) found the same endpoint in 51.1% versus 35.2% (P<0.001), with parallel gains on itch-related quality-of-life scales. The endpoint is a patient-reported symptom score — the outcome that matters for this question — over 12 weeks of treatment.

cards.headline: KALM-1 2020: difelikefalin beat placebo on itch — ≥3-point WI-NRS improvement in 51.9% vs 30.9% at week 12
cards.summary: KALM-1 2020: difelikefalin beat placebo on itch — ≥3-point WI-NRS improvement in 51.9% vs 30.9% at week 12.
cards.people: 378 patients undergoing hemodialysis who had moderate-to-severe pruritus, randomised to intravenous difelikefalin 0.5 μg per kilogram or placebo three times per week for 12 weeks; the primary-outcome analysis sets comprised 158 patients on difelikefalin and 165 on placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A decrease of at least 3 points in the weekly mean 24-hour Worst Itching Intensity Numerical Rating Scale (WI-NRS, 0 to 10) at week 12 occurred in 82 of 158 patients (51.9%) on difelikefalin versus 51 of 165 (30.9%) on placebo; with imputation, 49.1% versus 27.9% (P<0.001). The ≥4-point improvement also favoured difelikefalin (imputed 37.1% vs 17.9%; observed 64 of 158 vs 35 of 165; P<0.001), as did itch-related quality of life on the 5-D itch and Skindex-10 scales. Diarrhea, dizziness and vomiting were more common with difelikefalin.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, a symptom-score endpoint, and an analysis set smaller than the randomised total — the trial shows short-term itch relief on dialysis, not effects on sleep, mood outcomes beyond the itch scales, or longer horizons.
cards.source: Fishbane S et al. A Phase 3 Trial of Difelikefalin in Hemodialysis Patients with Pruritus. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(3):222-232. PMID: 31702883. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03422653, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: KALM-1/KALM-2 pooled 2022: 851 patients, ≥3-point itch improvement 51.1% vs 35.2%, with quality-of-life gains in parallel
cards.summary: KALM-1/KALM-2 pooled 2022: 851 patients, ≥3-point itch improvement 51.1% vs 35.2%, with quality-of-life gains in parallel.
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (KALM-1 and KALM-2), each with a 52-week open-label extension
cards.people: 851 participants randomised (difelikefalin 426; placebo 425): adults with moderate-to-severe chronic-kidney-disease-associated pruritus treated by hemodialysis in North America, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region, given intravenous difelikefalin 0.5 mcg/kg or placebo three times weekly for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Achievement of a ≥3-point WI-NRS reduction was significantly greater with difelikefalin (51.1%) than placebo (35.2%; P<0.001), as was a ≥4-point reduction (38.7% vs 23.4%; P<0.001), with efficacy appearing by week 1 and sustained. More participants on difelikefalin achieved clinically meaningful decreases of at least 15 points on Skindex-10 (55.5% vs 40.5%; P<0.001) and at least 5 points on the 5-D Itch scale (52.1% vs 42.3%; P=0.01), with 5-D Itch effects sustained up to 64 weeks in the extension. Results were consistent across the subgroups examined.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of the same programme, not an independent replication: KALM-1's patients are counted in both cards on this shelf, so the shelf's evidence is one twin-trial programme, counted once. The authors also note the itch scales are not used in routine dialysis care, so real-world effect sizes may differ.
cards.source: Topf J et al. Efficacy of Difelikefalin for the Treatment of Moderate to Severe Pruritus in Hemodialysis Patients: Pooled Analysis of KALM-1 and KALM-2 Phase 3 Studies. Kidney Med. 2022;4(8):100512. PMID: 36016762. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03422653 (KALM-1) and NCT03636269 (KALM-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one twin-trial programme, one consistent symptom benefit — LIKELY for 12-week itch relief on hemodialysis
cards.summary: One twin-trial programme, one consistent symptom benefit — LIKELY for 12-week itch relief on hemodialysis.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: KALM-1 (378 randomised) and the pooled KALM-1/KALM-2 analysis (851 participants).
cards.result: KALM-1's observed ≥3-point response gap (51.9% vs 30.9%) and the pooled programme's gap (51.1% vs 35.2%) are the same finding at two levels of the same evidence, supported by quality-of-life scales moving in the same direction (Skindex-10 meaningful improvement 55.5% vs 40.5%). Counted once as a programme, two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with concordant symptom results support LIKELY for short-term relief of moderate-to-severe dialysis itch.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses itch in non-dialysis CKD, other antipruritic drugs, or benefit beyond the 12-week randomised period; the 64-week figures come from an open-label extension.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fishbane S et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(3):222-232. PMID: 31702883; Topf J et al. Kidney Med. 2022;4(8):100512. PMID: 36016762. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Transplant immunosuppression: the low-dose tacrolimus standard
shelves.question: Which initial regimen after kidney transplant best balances rejection, graft function, and harm — the four-arm ELITE-Symphony comparison that set modern practice?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Calcineurin Inhibitors · Cyclosporine/administration & dosage · Daclizumab · Diabetes Mellitus/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single landmark four-arm randomised trial (1,645 recipients) found the low-dose tacrolimus regimen (with daclizumab induction, mycophenolate and corticosteroids) giving the highest mean calculated GFR at 12 months (65.4 ml per minute vs 56.7 to 59.4 in the other arms), the lowest biopsy-proven acute rejection rate (12.3% vs 25.8% standard-dose cyclosporine, 24.0% low-dose cyclosporine, 37.2% low-dose sirolimus), and the highest allograft survival (94.2% vs 89.3% to 93.1%). One trial, however large and practice-setting, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the single-trial rule; the regimen question has not been re-randomised at this scale. Belatacept-versus-ciclosporin is a different comparison and stays home on Shelf #590.

cards.headline: ELITE-Symphony 2007: low-dose tacrolimus led all four arms on graft function (GFR 65.4), rejection (12.3%) and graft survival (94.2%) at 12 months
cards.summary: ELITE-Symphony 2007: low-dose tacrolimus led all four arms on graft function (GFR 65.4), rejection (12.3%) and graft survival (94.2%) at 12 months.
cards.people: 1,645 renal-transplant recipients randomised to standard-dose cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids, or to daclizumab induction, mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids combined with low-dose cyclosporine, low-dose tacrolimus, or low-dose sirolimus. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The mean calculated GFR at 12 months was higher with low-dose tacrolimus (65.4 ml per minute) than in the other three groups (range 56.7 to 59.4 ml per minute). Biopsy-proven acute rejection was lowest with low-dose tacrolimus (12.3%), versus 25.8% on standard-dose cyclosporine, 24.0% on low-dose cyclosporine and 37.2% on low-dose sirolimus. Allograft survival differed significantly among the four groups (P=0.02) and was highest with low-dose tacrolimus (94.2%), followed by low-dose cyclosporine (93.1%), standard-dose cyclosporine (89.3%) and low-dose sirolimus (89.3%). Serious adverse events were more common with low-dose sirolimus (53.2% vs a range of 43.4 to 44.3% in the other groups), while the proportion with at least one adverse event was similar across groups (86.3 to 90.5%).
cards.watchOut: A single 2007 trial whose induction agent (daclizumab) is no longer the modern standard, with a calculated-GFR primary endpoint at 12 months: it set the low-dose tacrolimus backbone, but it is one trial from one era of transplant practice.
cards.source: Ekberg H et al. Reduced exposure to calcineurin inhibitors in renal transplantation. N Engl J Med. 2007;357(25):2562-75. PMID: 18094377. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00231764, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one four-arm trial built the modern backbone — POSSIBLE, capped by the single-trial rule
cards.summary: One four-arm trial built the modern backbone — POSSIBLE, capped by the single-trial rule.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ELITE-Symphony 2007 (1,645 renal-transplant recipients, four regimens).
cards.result: Within one randomised comparison, low-dose tacrolimus with daclizumab induction, mycophenolate and steroids simultaneously produced the best graft function, the fewest rejections and the best 12-month graft survival of the four regimens — a coherent sweep that explains why it became the reference regimen. The synthesis fences the neighbouring questions: belatacept versus ciclosporin after transplantation lives on Shelf #590, and later agent-specific transplant trials are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: A four-arm win in 2007 is not a verdict on every modern variation (different induction, steroid withdrawal, or newer agents); those questions need their own shelves.

shelves.title: Atrasentan for diabetic kidney disease
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with CKD already on maximum RAS blockade, does the endothelin antagonist atrasentan slow kidney progression in the enriched responder population SONAR selected — at what fluid-retention cost?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Atrasentan/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Creatinine/blood,urine · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Diabetic Nephropathies/blood,prevention & control,urine · Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Glomerular Filtration Rate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind trial with an enrichment design (SONAR: 2,648 randomised responders) found the primary renal composite — doubling of serum creatinine or end-stage kidney disease — in 6.0% on atrasentan versus 7.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.88 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the design caveat belongs on the shelf face: only patients who first responded to atrasentan in an enrichment period (albuminuria down at least 30% without substantial fluid retention) were randomised. The harm side is printed with the benefit: fluid retention and anaemia were more frequent, heart-failure hospital admission was 3.5% versus 2.6% (hazard ratio 1.33, 0.85 to 2.07 — not significant), and deaths were 4.4% versus 3.9% (hazard ratio 1.09, 0.75 to 1.59) — the heart-failure figures are always shown beside the mortality figures, and no heart-failure or mortality benefit is claimed.

cards.headline: SONAR 2019: in enriched responders, atrasentan cut the renal composite — 6.0% vs 7.9%, relative hazard 0.65 — with more fluid retention
cards.summary: SONAR 2019: in enriched responders, atrasentan cut the renal composite — 6.0% vs 7.9% , relative hazard 0.65 — with more fluid retention; heart-failure admission 3.5% vs 2.6% beside deaths 4.4% vs 3.9%, both non-significant, printed together on the card.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial with a pre-randomisation enrichment period
cards.people: Adults aged 18–85 years with type 2 diabetes, eGFR 25–75 mL/min per 1.73 m2 and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 300–5000 mg/g on maximum labelled or tolerated renin-angiotensin system inhibition: 11,087 screened, 5,117 entered enrichment on atrasentan 0.75 mg daily, and the 2,648 who responded (UACR down at least 30% without substantial fluid retention) were randomised to atrasentan (1,325) or placebo (1,323) across 689 sites in 41 countries; median follow-up 2.2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite renal endpoint (doubling of serum creatinine sustained at least 30 days, or end-stage kidney disease) occurred in 79 (6.0%) of 1,325 patients on atrasentan and 105 (7.9%) of 1,323 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% confidence interval 0.49 to 0.88; p=0.0047 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). Fluid retention and anaemia adverse events were more frequent with atrasentan. Hospital admission for heart failure occurred in 47 (3.5%) on atrasentan and 34 (2.6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, 0.85 to 2.07; p=0.208), and 58 (4.4%) versus 52 (3.9%) patients died (hazard ratio 1.09, 0.75 to 1.59; p=0.65) — heart-failure and mortality figures are reported together here, and neither favours atrasentan.
cards.watchOut: The enrichment design is the caveat: the randomised result applies only to the roughly half of screened patients who tolerated atrasentan and responded during run-in. Results in an unselected diabetic CKD population would be expected to look worse on fluid retention and no better on efficacy.

shelves.title: Vaptans for SIADH: raising sodium with tolvaptan
shelves.question: In euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia (SIADH and heart failure), does tolvaptan raise serum sodium versus placebo — and does faster correction translate into outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Area Under Curve · Benzazepines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heart Failure/complications · Hyponatremia/blood,drug therapy,etiology · Inappropriate ADH Syndrome/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY that tolvaptan raises serum sodium — the twin SALT-1 and SALT-2 trials (448 patients combined, reported together) both found significantly greater increases in serum sodium at day 4 and day 30 versus placebo (P<0.001 for all comparisons). MAYBE (weak evidence) that this translates into outcomes: the carded record reports a biochemical primary endpoint, recurrence of hyponatremia within a week of stopping, and a mental-component health-survey improvement in a planned combined analysis — no trial on this shelf randomised patients to tolvaptan and measured mortality, falls, cognition outcomes or length of stay as its primary question. The abstract reports no mean sodium-change figure, so none is printed. Symptomatic hyponatremia treated with hypertonic-saline bolus strategy is a different question and stays home on Shelf #126.

cards.headline: SALT-1/-2 2006: tolvaptan raised serum sodium significantly more than placebo at day 4 and day 30 in the twin trials — and hyponatremia recurred within a week of stopping
cards.summary: SALT-1/-2 2006: tolvaptan raised serum sodium significantly more than placebo at day 4 and day 30 in the twin trials — the abstracts report no mean sodium change, so no mmol/L figure is printed.
cards.type: Two multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together (SALT-1 and SALT-2)
cards.people: Patients with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (from SIADH, heart failure or cirrhosis): 225 assigned to oral tolvaptan (15 mg daily, titrated to 30 or 60 mg by sodium response) and 223 to placebo, across the two trials, treated for 30 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Serum sodium concentrations increased more in the tolvaptan group than the placebo group during the first 4 days (P<0.001) and after the full 30 days of therapy (P<0.001); the condition of patients with mild or marked hyponatremia improved (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The record's abstract reports these comparisons as P values without a mean sodium-change figure, so no mmol/L magnitude is printed on this card. During the week after tolvaptan was discontinued at day 30, hyponatremia recurred. Side effects associated with tolvaptan included increased thirst, dry mouth and increased urination. A planned combined analysis of the two trials showed significant improvement to day 30 in the Mental Component score of the SF-12 health survey in the tolvaptan group.
cards.watchOut: A biochemical-endpoint programme: the twin trials prove aquaresis raises sodium while the drug is taken (and that sodium falls again when it stops), not that patients live longer, fall less, or leave hospital sooner.
cards.source: Schrier RW et al. Tolvaptan, a selective oral vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist, for hyponatremia. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(20):2099-112. PMID: 17105757. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00072683 (SALT-1) and NCT00201994 (SALT-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Sodium, yes — outcomes, unproven: LIKELY for the biochemical effect, MAYBE (weak evidence) for outcomes.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: SALT-1 and SALT-2 (448 patients combined across the twin trials).
cards.result: The shelf's two halves must not be merged. Half one: two concordant blinded trials found tolvaptan superior to placebo on sodium at day 4 and day 30 (both P<0.001) — LIKELY for the biochemical effect, with the honest footnote that the abstract gives no mean change to quote. Half two: no carded trial tested whether correcting sodium with a vaptan changes a patient outcome, and the one patient-reported signal (an SF-12 mental-component improvement in a planned pooling) is hypothesis-grade — MAYBE (weak evidence). shelves.title: Which beta-lactam partner for vancomycin: cefepime versus piperacillin–tazobactam and the kidney (ACORN)
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults receiving an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, does cefepime versus piperacillin–tazobactam change the risk of acute kidney injury or death — the randomised test of the 'vanco–pip-tazo nephrotoxicity' argument?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Cefepime/adverse effects · Coma · Piperacillin/adverse effects · Drug Therapy, Combination · Retrospective Studies · Piperacillin, Tazobactam Drug Combination/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single large randomised trial (ACORN, 2,511 patients, single academic centre), the highest stage of acute kidney injury or death by day 14 did not differ between cefepime and piperacillin–tazobactam (odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13) — the long-suspected piperacillin–tazobactam kidney harm did not appear under randomisation. Cefepime patients had fewer days alive and free of delirium and coma (odds ratio 0.79, a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band). Single-centre and single-trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ACORN (Qian 2023): piperacillin–tazobactam did not increase acute kidney injury or death versus cefepime (OR 0.95); cefepime carried more neurological dysfunction
cards.summary: ACORN 2023: piperacillin–tazobactam did not increase acute kidney injury or death vs cefepime (odds ratio 0.95); cefepime carried more neurological dysfunction.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (pragmatic, single academic centre)
cards.people: 2,511 adults included in the primary analysis, for whom a clinician ordered antipseudomonal antibiotics within 12 hours of presentation in the emergency department or medical ICU of one US academic medical centre; randomised 1:1 to cefepime (1,214) or piperacillin–tazobactam (1,297); median age 58 years (IQR 43–69), 42.7% female, 77.2% receiving vancomycin at enrolment.
cards.result: The primary outcome — highest stage of acute kidney injury or death by day 14 on a 5-level ordinal scale — did not differ: stage 3 acute kidney injury occurred in 85 patients (7.0%) in the cefepime group and 97 (7.5%) in the piperacillin–tazobactam group, and death in 92 (7.6%) versus 78 (6.0%) (odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13; P=0.56 — a relative measure). Major adverse kidney events at day 14 did not differ (10.2% versus 8.8%; absolute difference 1.4%, 95% CI −1.0% to 3.8%). Patients in the cefepime group had fewer days alive and free of delirium and coma within 14 days (mean 11.9 versus 12.2 days; odds ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.95 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so not solid evidence on its own).
cards.watchOut: Single centre, and enrolment hinged on the initial antibiotic order; the delirium/coma signal is a secondary outcome with a modest relative effect. Mortality was a component of the composite and is reported as such — no mortality-benefit claim is made for either drug, so this shelf is not Tier C.
cards.source: Qian ET et al. Cefepime vs Piperacillin-Tazobactam in Adults Hospitalized With Acute Infection: The ACORN Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;330(16):1557-1567. PMID: 37837651. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05094154, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Under randomisation, the vancomycin–pip-tazo kidney signal vanished; the open question moved to cefepime and the brain — POSSIBLE. (Ruled NOT Tier C: mortality is a composite component, reported as such, with no claim.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ACORN (2,511 hospitalised adults).
cards.result: ACORN is the randomised answer to a decade of observational 'vancomycin plus piperacillin–tazobactam causes AKI' reports: the kidney-or-death composite was flat (odds ratio 0.95), as were major adverse kidney events (10.2% versus 8.8%). The counterweight is neurological: fewer delirium/coma-free days with cefepime (odds ratio 0.79, inside the caution band). One centre and one trial cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. The dialysis-timing and dialysis-dose AKI shelves (#195, #754) test different questions and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Observational nephrotoxicity comparisons of these drugs are confounded by indication and creatinine-assay effects; ACORN's null should be quoted from the randomised record, not from the older cohort literature.

shelves.title: Regional citrate versus systemic heparin anticoagulation for continuous kidney replacement (RICH)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with acute kidney injury on continuous kidney replacement therapy, does regional citrate anticoagulation prolong filter life and change mortality versus systemic heparin anticoagulation?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/blood,mortality,therapy · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Calcium/blood · Citric Acid/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy/instrumentation,mortality · Critical Illness · Early Termination of Clinical Trials
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C at build: 90-day mortality was a coprimary outcome of RICH, so the shelf carries a mortality outcome on its face even though no mortality benefit is claimed). In RICH (596 patients, terminated early), regional citrate prolonged median filter life (47 versus 26 hours; P<0.001) and halved-plus bleeding complications (5.1% versus 16.9%), but 90-day mortality did not differ significantly (51.2% versus 53.6% Kaplan–Meier; adjusted hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.004; P=0.054) in a trial the authors state was underpowered for mortality after early termination, and new infections were more frequent with citrate (68.0% versus 55.4%). Single trial, early stop: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RICH (Zarbock 2020): citrate prolonged filter life (47 vs 26 hours) and cut bleeding, but 90-day mortality was not significantly different and infections rose
cards.summary: RICH 2020: citrate prolonged filter life (47 vs 26 hours) and cut bleeding (5.1% vs 16.9%); 90-day mortality — a coprimary outcome — was 51.2% vs 53.6%, not significant in an early-terminated trial.
cards.type: Parallel-group, randomised multicentre trial (26 centres, Germany), terminated early
cards.people: 596 critically ill patients with severe acute kidney injury or indications for kidney replacement therapy completed the trial (638 randomised), assigned to regional citrate anticoagulation (300) or systemic heparin anticoagulation (296) during continuous kidney replacement therapy; mean age 67.5 years, 30.7% women (183 of 596).
cards.result: Median filter life span was 47 hours (IQR 19–70) with citrate versus 26 hours (IQR 12–51) with heparin (difference 15 hours, 95% CI 11 to 20; P<0.001). Ninety-day all-cause mortality — the coprimary outcome — occurred in 150 of 300 versus 156 of 296 patients (Kaplan–Meier 51.2% versus 53.6%; unadjusted hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.13; adjusted hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.004; adjusted P=0.054). Bleeding complications were fewer with citrate (15/300 [5.1%] versus 49/296 [16.9%]; difference −11.8%, 95% CI −16.8% to −6.8%; P<0.001); new infections were more frequent (204/300 [68.0%] versus 164/296 [55.4%]; difference 12.6%, 95% CI 4.9% to 20.3%; P=0.002). Of 38 prespecified secondary end points, 34 showed no significant difference.
cards.watchOut: The trial was terminated early and was therefore underpowered for mortality, as the authors state — the adjusted mortality P of 0.054 is not a near-miss benefit claim. The infection excess with citrate is part of the balance, not a footnote.
cards.source: Zarbock A et al. Effect of Regional Citrate Anticoagulation vs Systemic Heparin Anticoagulation During Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy on Dialysis Filter Life Span and Mortality Among Critically Ill Patients With Acute Kidney Injury: The RICH Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(16):1629-1639. PMID: 33095849. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02669589, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: citrate is the better circuit anticoagulant for filter life and bleeding; a mortality effect is unproven — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Citrate is the better circuit anticoagulant for filter life and bleeding; a mortality effect is unproven — POSSIBLE, Tier C (coprimary mortality), proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: RICH (596 critically ill patients on continuous kidney replacement therapy).
cards.result: RICH separates a circuit outcome from a patient outcome: filter life up by a median 21 hours and bleeding down from 16.9% to 5.1%, against a null-on-significance mortality coprimary (51.2% versus 53.6%) in an early-terminated trial, plus more new infections with citrate (68.0% versus 55.4%). Tier C ruling at build: mortality was a coprimary outcome, so the stamp is PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict; no mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf. Dialysis dose/intensity is home on Shelf #754 and dialysis timing on Shelves #195/#292 — none is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Guideline first-line status for citrate rests heavily on this one early-stopped trial plus older small trials and meta-analyses; the shelf stamp reflects the randomised record carded here, not the guideline consensus.
