shelves.title: Complement factor B inhibition with iptacopan in IgA nephropathy (APPLAUSE-IgAN)
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy at risk of progression despite supportive care, does the oral factor B inhibitor iptacopan reduce proteinuria and slow kidney-function decline — in its phase 2 trial, the APPLAUSE-IgAN phase 3 interim analysis, and the trial's final 24-month analysis?
shelves.mesh: Glomerulonephritis, IGA/pathology · Complement Pathway, Alternative · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Biomarkers · Complement Inactivating Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Complement Pathway, Alternative/drug effects,immunology · Creatinine/urine
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A randomised programme in three reports — a phase 2 dose-ranging trial (dose–response on proteinuria, 23% relative reduction at the 200 mg dose at 3 months), the APPLAUSE-IgAN phase 3 interim analysis (proteinuria 38.3% relatively lower than placebo at month 9), and the APPLAUSE-IgAN final 24-month analysis (annualised eGFR slope −3.10 versus −6.12 mL/min/1.73 m²/year; composite kidney-failure end point 21.4% versus 33.5%, hazard ratio 0.57, relative). Two randomised blinded trials plus a hard kidney-function outcome in the final analysis carry LIKELY; the kidney-failure composite includes death from kidney failure as one component and no mortality benefit is claimed, so this shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Iptacopan phase 2 (2024): a dose–response on proteinuria — 23% relative reduction at 200 mg twice daily at 3 months
cards.summary: Iptacopan phase 2 2024: a dose–response on proteinuria — a 23% relative reduction at 200 mg twice daily at 3 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group adaptive phase 2 trial
cards.people: 112 patients with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy (within the previous three years), eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73 m² or over and urine protein 0.75 g/24 hours or over on stable renin–angiotensin-system inhibitors, randomised to iptacopan 10, 50, 100 or 200 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months (Part 1, 46 patients) or 6 months (Part 2, 66 patients); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was a statistically significant dose–response effect, with a 23% reduction in 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio achieved with iptacopan 200 mg twice daily (80% CI 8 to 34%) at 3 months — a relative measure; the abstract does not print the absolute proteinuria rates for this comparison. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased further through 6 months in the 100 mg and 200 mg arms (from a mean of 1.3 g/g at baseline to 0.8 g/g at 6 months in the 200 mg arm). Complement biomarkers (plasma Bb, serum Wieslab, urinary C5b-9) fell in a sustained manner. Iptacopan was well tolerated, with no deaths, treatment-related serious adverse events or bacterial infections reported.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, small, and proteinuria-only: a dose-ranging signal that justified the phase 3 trial, not an outcome result. Its 23% figure is relative and sits on a surrogate.
cards.source: Perkovic V et al. Results of a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled Phase 2 study propose iptacopan as a promising treatment for IgA nephropathy. Kidney Int. 2024;105(1):189-199. PMID: 37914086. Registry ID: NCT03373461, stated in the record's abstract (the record's databank fields carry NCT04578834, the phase 3 APPLAUSE-IgAN trial).

cards.headline: APPLAUSE-IgAN interim (Perkovic 2025): proteinuria 38.3% relatively lower with iptacopan than placebo at month 9
cards.summary: APPLAUSE-IgAN interim 2025: proteinuria 38.3% relatively lower with iptacopan than placebo at month 9.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial — prespecified interim analysis
cards.people: Adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy and proteinuria (24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1 or higher) despite optimised supportive therapy, randomised 1:1 to oral iptacopan 200 mg or placebo twice daily for 24 months; the main trial population comprised 222 patients (iptacopan) and 221 (placebo), and the interim efficacy analysis covered the first 250 randomised patients (125 per group) reaching month 9; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At month 9, the adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 38.3% (95% CI 26.0 to 48.6; P<0.001) lower with iptacopan than with placebo — a relative measure; secondary end-point analyses were consistent, including the proportion reaching a ratio below 1 without rescue therapy. There were no unexpected safety findings; adverse-event incidence was similar between groups, most events were mild to moderate and reversible, and no increased risk of infection was observed. The effect on kidney function was reserved for the end of the 2-year double-blind period — reported in the final analysis carded below.
cards.watchOut: An interim, proteinuria-only read of an unfinished trial when published: on its own it would cap at POSSIBLE. It is carded here as the middle report of one programme, superseded on outcomes by the final analysis below.

cards.headline: APPLAUSE-IgAN final analysis (2026): iptacopan slowed eGFR decline — slope −3.10 versus −6.12 per year; kidney-failure composite 21.4% versus 33.5% (HR 0.57, relative)

cards.people: 477 patients included in the final analysis (238 iptacopan, 239 placebo): adults with IgA nephropathy, eGFR at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1 or higher despite supportive care, randomised to oral iptacopan 200 mg or placebo twice daily; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised total eGFR slope over 24 months was −3.10 mL/min/1.73 m² per year with iptacopan versus −6.12 with placebo (difference 3.02, 95% CI 2.02 to 4.01; adjusted P<0.001). A composite kidney-failure end-point event (sustained eGFR decline of 30% or more, sustained eGFR below 15, maintenance dialysis, kidney transplant, or death from kidney failure) occurred in 21.4% of the iptacopan group versus 33.5% of the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.81; adjusted P=0.003 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). Adverse events occurred in 87.0% versus 89.1%; serious adverse events in 12.2% versus 11.7%; serious infections in 6.7% versus 2.1%. No deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: One phase 3 trial's final analysis: the eGFR-slope primary is a function measure over 24 months, and the serious-infection imbalance (6.7% versus 2.1%) is part of the record. Longer and post-marketing follow-up will test durability.

shelves.title: Tenapanor for hyperphosphataemia in maintenance dialysis (AMPLIFY and the phase 3 monotherapy trial)
shelves.question: In patients on maintenance dialysis with hyperphosphataemia, does the intestinal NHE3 inhibitor tenapanor — alone or added to phosphate binders — lower serum phosphate versus binders or placebo alone?
shelves.mesh: Chelating Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Hyperphosphatemia/blood,drug therapy · Isoquinolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Phosphorus/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two double-blind phase 3 trials agree that tenapanor lowers serum phosphate: added to binders in AMPLIFY (mean change −0.84 versus −0.19 mg/dL at 4 weeks) and as monotherapy in the Block phase 3 trial (phosphate rose 0.85 mg/dL on withdrawal to placebo versus 0.02 mg/dL on continued tenapanor). Both are short (4–12 weeks) and the outcome is a laboratory surrogate with no event data; diarrhoea/softened stool is the mechanism's price. Surrogate-only and short: POSSIBLE despite two concordant trials. No albumin claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: AMPLIFY (Pergola 2021): tenapanor added to binders lowered phosphate more than binders alone at 4 weeks (−0.84 versus −0.19 mg/dL)
cards.summary: AMPLIFY 2021: tenapanor added to binders lowered phosphate more than binders alone at 4 weeks (−0.84 vs −0.19 mg/dL).
cards.type: Double-blind phase 3 randomised trial (4-week randomised period)
cards.people: 236 patients on maintenance dialysis with hyperphosphataemia (serum phosphorus 5.5–10 mg/dL) despite phosphate-binder therapy, randomised to oral tenapanor 30 mg twice daily (116) or placebo (119) added to their binders for 4 weeks; mean age 54.5 years, 40.9% women (full analysis set, 235 patients).
cards.result: Patients treated with tenapanor plus binder achieved a larger mean change in serum phosphorus from baseline to week 4 than placebo plus binder (−0.84 versus −0.19 mg/dL; P<0.001). A total of 228 patients (96.6%) completed the 4-week period. Diarrhoea was the most commonly reported adverse event, leading to study-drug discontinuation in 4 of 119 (3.4%) patients receiving tenapanor plus binder and 2 of 116 (1.7%) receiving placebo plus binder (group sizes as printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, one laboratory outcome, in patients already on binders: AMPLIFY shows dual-mechanism phosphate lowering, nothing about fractures, cardiovascular events or survival.
cards.source: Pergola PE et al. A Randomized Trial of Tenapanor and Phosphate Binders as a Dual-Mechanism Treatment for Hyperphosphatemia in Patients Receiving Maintenance Dialysis (AMPLIFY). cards.headline: Block 2019 (phase 3 monotherapy): tenapanor lowered phosphate by about 1 mg/dL over 8 weeks, and withdrawal to placebo let it rebound (+0.85 versus +0.02 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Block 2019: tenapanor lowered phosphate by about 1 mg/dL over 8 weeks, and withdrawal to placebo let it rebound (+0.85 mg/dL).
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind trial with a randomised withdrawal period
cards.people: 219 patients with hyperphosphataemia receiving maintenance haemodialysis, randomised to twice-daily oral tenapanor 3, 10 or 30 mg (the last down-titrated if needed) for 8 weeks, then re-randomised 1:1 to their dose or placebo for a 4-week withdrawal period; 152 completed both phases; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: During the initial 8 weeks, all three dose groups had significant decreases in mean serum phosphate (reductions of 1.00, 1.02 and 1.19 mg/dL for the 3, 10 and 30 mg groups). During withdrawal, phosphate rose by a mean of 0.85 mg/dL in the placebo group versus 0.02 mg/dL in the pooled tenapanor group — the trial's primary end point. Adverse events were largely limited to softened stool and a modest increase in bowel-movement frequency, reflecting the drug's mechanism (increased stool sodium and water).
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design proves the drug was doing the lowering; it does not add duration — total exposure was 12 weeks, and the outcome remains a laboratory surrogate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two blinded trials, one laboratory outcome, twelve weeks at most — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Two blinded trials, one laboratory outcome, twelve weeks at most — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: AMPLIFY (236 patients, add-on design) and Block 2019 (219 patients, monotherapy with randomised withdrawal).
cards.result: Tenapanor lowers serum phosphate by roughly 0.65 mg/dL beyond binders at 4 weeks (AMPLIFY: −0.84 versus −0.19 mg/dL) and by about 1 mg/dL as monotherapy over 8 weeks, with the withdrawal rebound confirming causality. What no trial here shows is any effect on the cardiovascular and bone outcomes that make hyperphosphataemia matter — hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY despite two concordant blinded trials. Calcium-free versus calcium-based binder comparisons are home on Shelf #295 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Phosphate is a surrogate with a historically weak record of predicting event benefit from lowering it; quote the mg/dL changes, not an implied outcome benefit.

shelves.title: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for predialysis hyperkalaemia in haemodialysis (DIALIZE)
shelves.question: In patients on maintenance haemodialysis with recurrent predialysis hyperkalaemia, does sodium zirconium cyclosilicate on non-dialysis days increase the proportion maintaining predialysis potassium in range without rescue therapy?
shelves.mesh: Hyperkalemia/drug therapy,etiology,prevention & control · Ion Exchange Resins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications,therapy · Potassium/blood · Renal Dialysis · Silicates/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pivotal trial (DIALIZE, 196 patients), sodium zirconium cyclosilicate on non-dialysis days produced treatment responders (predialysis potassium 4.0–5.0 mmol/L on at least three of four post-long-interval treatments, without rescue therapy) in 41.2% versus 1.0% on placebo (P<0.001). That is a potassium-control outcome over a 4-week evaluation period in one trial — no event outcomes — so POSSIBLE. Binders used to enable RAAS inhibitors in CKD/heart failure are a different question, home on Shelf #301.

cards.headline: DIALIZE (Fishbane 2019): responders 41.2% on sodium zirconium cyclosilicate versus 1.0% on placebo for predialysis potassium control
cards.summary: DIALIZE 2019: responders 41.2% on sodium zirconium cyclosilicate vs 1.0% on placebo for predialysis potassium control.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3b multicentre randomised trial
cards.people: 196 adults with end-stage renal disease on three-times-weekly haemodialysis with predialysis hyperkalaemia, randomised to sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 5 g once daily on non-dialysis days (97), titrated in 5 g increments to a maximum of 15 g to maintain normokalaemia, or placebo (99); mean age 58.1 years (SD 13.7); the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: During the 4-week stable-dose evaluation period, 41.2% of patients receiving sodium zirconium cyclosilicate met the primary end point (predialysis serum potassium 4.0–5.0 mmol/L during at least three of four haemodialysis treatments after the long interdialytic interval, without urgent rescue therapy) and were deemed treatment responders, compared with 1.0% on placebo (P<0.001). Rescue therapy was required by 2.1% of the sodium zirconium cyclosilicate group versus 5.1% of the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred in 7% and 8% respectively; interdialytic weight gain was comparable, and hypokalaemia episodes were few.
cards.watchOut: Single pivotal trial, 4-week evaluation window, and a responder definition built on potassium values: DIALIZE shows control of a number in the dialysis population, not fewer arrhythmias, hospitalisations or deaths.
cards.source: Fishbane S et al. A Phase 3b, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study of Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate for Reducing the Incidence of Predialysis Hyperkalemia. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2019;30(9):1723-1733. PMID: 31201218. Registry ID: NCT03303521, stated in the record's abstract (the record carries no databank fields).

cards.headline: Synthesis: potassium control in dialysis patients is real; outcome benefit is untested — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Potassium control in dialysis patients is real; outcome benefit is untested — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: DIALIZE (196 patients on maintenance haemodialysis).
cards.result: The responder gap (41.2% versus 1.0%) is large because placebo almost never holds predialysis potassium in range across the long interdialytic interval — the trial cleanly proves pharmacological control. It does not test whether that control prevents events, and at one trial the stamp is POSSIBLE. The RAAS-inhibitor-enabling binder trials (OPAL-HK, DIAMOND, REALIZE-K) are home on Shelf #301 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not extrapolate DIALIZE's responder rate to non-dialysis CKD hyperkalaemia; the population, dosing days and end point are dialysis-specific.

shelves.title: Gepotidacin for uncomplicated urinary tract infection (EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3)
shelves.question: Is oral gepotidacin non-inferior (and in one trial superior) to nitrofurantoin for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women?
shelves.mesh: Nitrofurantoin/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy · Research · Acenaphthenes · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel double-blind, double-dummy phase 3 trials (EAGLE-2: 1,531 randomised; EAGLE-3: 1,605 randomised) both found oral gepotidacin non-inferior to nitrofurantoin for therapeutic success at test-of-cure (EAGLE-2: 50.6% vs 47.0%, adjusted difference 4.3%, 95% CI −3.6 to 12.1; EAGLE-3: 58.5% vs 43.6%, adjusted difference 14.6%, 95% CI 6.4 to 22.8 — superior in EAGLE-3). Two randomised blinded trials of the same question support LIKELY. The cost is gastrointestinal: diarrhoea in 14–18% on gepotidacin versus nausea in 4% on nitrofurantoin. Both trials were stopped early for efficacy at a prospectively agreed interim analysis, which is why the primary populations are subsets of those randomised.

cards.headline: EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3 2024: gepotidacin was non-inferior to nitrofurantoin in both trials and superior in EAGLE-3 (therapeutic success 58.5% vs 43.6%)
cards.summary: EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3 (2024): gepotidacin non-inferior to nitrofurantoin in both trials and superior in EAGLE-3 (therapeutic success 58.5% vs 43.6% ).
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, phase 3, non-inferiority trials (219 centres worldwide; 10% margin)
cards.people: Adolescent and adult female patients (assigned female at birth, non-pregnant, aged 12 years or older, weighing at least 40 kg) with uncomplicated urinary tract infection: 1,531 randomised in EAGLE-2 (767 gepotidacin, 764 nitrofurantoin) and 1,605 in EAGLE-3 (805 vs 800), receiving gepotidacin 1,500 mg twice daily or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days. Because both trials stopped for efficacy at an interim analysis, the primary analysis populations were 320 versus 287 (EAGLE-2) and 277 versus 264 (EAGLE-3) patients with nitrofurantoin-susceptible uropathogens. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Therapeutic success at test-of-cure (day 10–13; complete symptom resolution plus uropathogen reduction below 10^3 CFU/mL without other systemic antimicrobials) was 162 (50.6%) of 320 on gepotidacin versus 135 (47.0%) of 287 on nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-2 (adjusted difference 4.3%, 95% CI −3.6 to 12.1) and 162 (58.5%) of 277 versus 115 (43.6%) of 264 in EAGLE-3 (adjusted difference 14.6%, 95% CI 6.4 to 22.8). Gepotidacin was non-inferior in both studies and superior in EAGLE-3. The most common adverse event with gepotidacin was diarrhoea (111 [14%] of 766 in EAGLE-2; 147 [18%] of 804 in EAGLE-3) and with nitrofurantoin nausea (29 [4%] of 760; 35 [4%] of 798); events were mostly mild or moderate and no life-threatening or fatal events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Both trials stopped early for efficacy and the primary population is restricted to nitrofurantoin-susceptible uropathogens — the comparison that matters most for resistant phenotypes is outside the primary analysis; success rates near 50% also show how often uncomplicated UTI fails the strict combined clinical-plus-microbiological definition in both arms.
cards.source: Wagenlehner F et al. Oral gepotidacin versus nitrofurantoin in patients with uncomplicated urinary tract infection (EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3): two randomised, controlled, double-blind, double-dummy, phase 3, non-inferiority trials. Lancet. 2024 Feb 24;403(10428):741-755. PMID: 38342126. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04020341 (EAGLE-2) and NCT04187144 (EAGLE-3), from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Daprodustat for anaemia of dialysis-dependent kidney disease (ASCEND-D)
shelves.question: In patients on dialysis with anaemia, is the oral hypoxia-inducible-factor stabiliser daprodustat non-inferior to injectable epoetin alfa for haemoglobin control — and non-inferior on the cardiovascular safety composite of death, myocardial infarction and stroke (ASCEND-D)?
shelves.mesh: Anemia/drug therapy,etiology · Barbiturates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology,etiology,mortality · Darbepoetin alfa/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Epoetin Alfa/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Glycine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Hematinics/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (non-inferiority) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the headline claim is cardiovascular-safety non-inferiority on a composite of death, myocardial infarction and stroke). Two large open-label phase 3 trials with prespecified non-inferiority margins agree: ASCEND-D (2,964 patients on dialysis: haemoglobin change difference 0.18 g/dL, margin −0.75; MACE 25.2% versus 26.7%, hazard ratio 0.93 [95% CI 0.81 to 1.07], margin 1.25) and ASCEND-ND (3,872 patients not on dialysis: haemoglobin difference 0.08 g/dL; MACE 19.5% versus 19.2%, hazard ratio 1.03 [0.89 to 1.19], margin 1.25) — oral daprodustat is non-inferior to injectable ESAs for haemoglobin control and on the cardiovascular composite in both populations. Non-inferiority is the claim and it is printed as such everywhere on this shelf: neither trial shows superiority on any outcome, both are open-label, and the MACE confidence intervals still include up to 7% and 19% relative harm respectively against margins of 1.25.

cards.headline: ASCEND-D (Singh 2021): daprodustat was non-inferior to injectable ESA for haemoglobin and for the death/MI/stroke composite in dialysis patients
cards.summary: ASCEND-D (2021): daprodustat was non-inferior to injectable ESA for haemoglobin and for the death/MI/stroke composite in dialysis patients.
cards.people: 2,964 patients with chronic kidney disease undergoing dialysis (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) with haemoglobin 8.0 to 11.5 g/dL, randomised to oral daprodustat or injectable ESA (epoetin alfa on haemodialysis, darbepoetin alfa on peritoneal dialysis); mean baseline haemoglobin was 10.4 (SD 1.0) g/dL overall; median follow-up 2.5 years. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The mean change in haemoglobin from baseline to weeks 28 through 52 was 0.28 (SE 0.02) g/dL on daprodustat and 0.10 (0.02) on ESA (difference 0.18 g/dL, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.24), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin of −0.75 g/dL. During follow-up, a major adverse cardiovascular event (death from any cause, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke) occurred in 374 of 1,487 patients (25.2%) on daprodustat and 394 of 1,477 (26.7%) on ESA (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07), which also met the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1.25. Percentages of patients with other adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a wide non-inferiority margin (1.25): 'non-inferior' here means 'not shown to be more than 25% relatively worse on MACE', and the observed interval (0.81 to 1.07) is the honest summary — not proof of equal safety.

cards.result: Read together, the pair support one sentence: in 6,836 randomised patients, oral daprodustat controlled haemoglobin as well as injectable ESAs and was not shown to exceed the prespecified 1.25 relative margin on death, myocardial infarction or stroke. shelves.title: RNA interference for primary hyperoxaluria: lumasiran (ILLUMINATE-A) and nedosiran (PHYOX2)
shelves.question: In primary hyperoxaluria, where the liver overproduces the oxalate that destroys the kidneys, do the two RNA-interference drugs — lumasiran and nedosiran — lower urinary oxalate?
shelves.mesh: Creatinine/urine · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Hyperoxaluria, Primary/blood,complications,drug therapy,urine · Kidney Calculi/prevention & control · Oxalates/blood,metabolism,urine · RNA, Small Interfering/adverse effects,therapeutic use · RNAi Therapeutics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small pivotal trials of two different molecular targets in the same disease each lowered urinary oxalate decisively — lumasiran by a least-squares mean difference of -53.5 percentage points vs placebo in PH1 (39 patients), and nedosiran on its AUC endpoint in PH1/PH2 (35 participants), with the PH1 subgroup responding and no consistent PH2 effect. Both are surrogate-endpoint trials (urinary oxalate, not kidney survival), both are small, and neither is a trial of the other's drug — POSSIBLE is the honest stamp. No kidney-survival or mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: ILLUMINATE-A 2021: lumasiran cut urinary oxalate in PH1 — between-group difference -53.5 percentage points; 84% reached near-normal excretion vs 0% on placebo
cards.summary: ILLUMINATE-A (2021): lumasiran cut urinary oxalate in PH1 — between-group difference −53.5 percentage points ; 84% reached near-normal excretion.
cards.type: Double-blind, phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (6 months)
cards.people: 39 patients with primary hyperoxaluria type 1 aged 6 years or older, randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous lumasiran (26) or placebo (13), dosed at baseline and months 1, 2, 3 and 6. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in percent change in 24-hour urinary oxalate (lumasiran minus placebo, averaged over months 3-6) was -53.5 percentage points (P<0.001), with a 65.4% reduction in the lumasiran group and an effect seen as early as month 1. The difference in percent change in plasma oxalate was -39.5 percentage points (P<0.001). In the lumasiran group, 84% of patients had urinary oxalate no higher than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal at month 6, vs 0% on placebo (P<0.001). Mild, transient injection-site reactions occurred in 38% of lumasiran-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine patients and a biochemical endpoint over 6 months: urinary oxalate is the proven mediator of kidney damage in PH1, but stone events, kidney failure and systemic oxalosis were not trial outcomes here.
cards.source: Garrelfs SF et al. Lumasiran, an RNAi Therapeutic for Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 1. The New England journal of medicine. 2021;384(13):1216-1226. PMID: 33789010. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03681184, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PHYOX2 2023: nedosiran lowered urinary oxalate in PH1 (normal/near-normal excretion on repeated visits 50% vs 0%), with no consistent effect in the small PH2 subgroup
cards.summary: PHYOX2 (2023): nedosiran lowered urinary oxalate in PH1 (normal/near-normal excretion on repeated visits 50% vs 0%).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled pivotal study (monthly dosing, 6 months)
cards.people: 35 participants with PH1 (29) or PH2 (6) and eGFR at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous nedosiran or placebo once monthly. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The area under the curve of percent reduction in 24-hour urinary oxalate (day 90-180) was significantly greater with nedosiran than placebo (least-squares mean +3507 [SE 788] vs -1664 [1190]; difference 5172; 95% CI 2929 to 7414; P<0.001). cards.headline: Synthesis: two silencers, one mediator, both surrogate trials — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: two silencers, one mediator, both surrogate trials — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ILLUMINATE-A (39 patients, PH1) and PHYOX2 (35 participants, PH1 and PH2).
cards.result: Silencing glycolate oxidase (lumasiran) or lactate dehydrogenase A, the final common step of oxalate synthesis (nedosiran), each cut urinary oxalate by half or more against placebo in PH1. The drugs have not been compared, and nedosiran's PH2 signal was inconsistent. Human data only are carded, per the library rule — the animal knockdown work behind both drugs is not carded. cards.watchOut: Normalising a urine test in 6 months is not the same as preventing kidney failure over years; long-term registries, not these trials, will answer the outcome question.

shelves.title: Adrenal vein sampling versus CT to choose treatment in primary aldosteronism (SPARTACUS)
shelves.question: In primary aldosteronism, does choosing between adrenalectomy and mineralocorticoid-antagonist therapy by adrenal vein sampling produce better one-year outcomes than choosing by CT?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Neoplasms/blood,complications,diagnostic imaging,surgery · Adrenal Glands/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Adrenalectomy · Adrenocortical Adenoma/blood,complications,diagnostic imaging,surgery · Hyperaldosteronism/blood,diagnostic imaging,etiology,therapy · Hyperplasia/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference for AVS superiority): One outcome-based randomised diagnostic-strategy trial (SPARTACUS, 200 patients) found no difference at 1 year between AVS-based and CT-based management in antihypertensive drug intensity (median 3.0 vs 3.0 defined daily doses), target-blood-pressure attainment (45% vs 42%), quality of life or biochemical cure after adrenalectomy (89% vs 80%, not significant) — while AVS cost significantly more (€2,285 per patient). A single trial caps the null at POSSIBLE. The randomisation is to the test, not the treatment, and the shelf states that plainly. The long-term follow-up report sought at build could not be pinned — a relevance-ranked search returned only the original trial record — so the shelf rests on the 1-year trial (see summary). Blood-pressure and medication outcomes only; no event claim is made.

cards.headline: SPARTACUS 2016: AVS-based management was no better than CT-based management at 1 year — drug intensity 3.0 vs 3.0 daily defined doses; AVS cost €2,285 more per patient
cards.summary: SPARTACUS (2016): AVS-based management was no better than CT-based management at 1 year — drug intensity 3.0 vs 3.0 daily defined doses (the long-term follow-up remains unpinned, disclosed).
cards.people: 200 patients with primary aldosteronism recruited 2010-2013; 184 completed follow-up (92 CT-based, 92 AVS-based), with exactly 46 adrenalectomies and 46 mineralocorticoid-antagonist treatments in each arm. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Intensity of antihypertensive treatment at 1 year did not differ: median daily defined doses 3.0 (IQR 1.0-5.0) with CT-based vs 3.0 (1.1-5.9) with AVS-based management (p=0.52); median number of drugs 2 in both arms. Target blood pressure was reached in 39 (42%) CT-based vs 41 (45%) AVS-based patients (p=0.82). After adrenalectomy, hyperaldosteronism resolved in 37 (80%) CT-based vs 41 (89%) AVS-based patients (p=0.25). Quality of life did not differ. The quality-adjusted life-year difference (0.05, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.13) favoured AVS non-significantly, at a significant extra cost of €2,285 per patient (1323 to 3248); at €30,000 per QALY, the probability that AVS was cost-effective was less than 0.2. Adverse events were similar (159 events, 9 serious, vs 187, 12 serious).
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic-strategy trial of 184 completers: it tests the management pathway's average outcome, not AVS's accuracy in expert hands or in the individual difficult case, and 1 year is short for blood-pressure-mediated event differences.
cards.source: Dekkers T et al. Adrenal vein sampling versus CT scan to determine treatment in primary aldosteronism: an outcome-based randomised diagnostic trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2016;4(9):739-746. PMID: 27325147. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01096654, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the invasive reference standard did not buy better outcomes — POSSIBLE the null
cards.summary: Synthesis: the invasive reference standard did not buy better outcomes — POSSIBLE the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: SPARTACUS (200 patients with primary aldosteronism).
cards.result: When the test itself was randomised, choosing surgery by adrenal vein sampling rather than CT produced identical medication burden and blood-pressure control at 1 year at significantly higher cost — challenging the recommendation to perform AVS in all patients with primary aldosteronism. The fourth-drug question in resistant hypertension is home on Shelf #278 and aldosterone-synthase inhibition on drafted Shelf #743; neither is re-carded here. Nothing on this shelf invokes albumin as a dietary measure; where albumin appears in this library it reflects inflammation or injury, never diet.
cards.watchOut: A single-trial challenge to a guideline-embedded practice: centres with low CT accuracy or high AVS expertise may reasonably ask for replication before changing pathways.

shelves.title: Migalastat, a chaperone pill, in Fabry disease (FACETS and ATTRACT)
shelves.question: In Fabry disease with amenable GLA variants, does oral migalastat match enzyme replacement — against placebo on kidney substrate inclusions in FACETS, and head-to-head against agalsidase infusions on kidney function in ATTRACT?
shelves.mesh: 1-Deoxynojirimycin/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy,etiology · Fabry Disease/complications,drug therapy · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Heart Ventricles/diagnostic imaging · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular/diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Kidney/chemistry,physiopathology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — comparability with enzyme replacement in amenable mutations (ATTRACT: similar renal-function effects over 18 months, left-ventricular-mass index falling on migalastat) · MAYBE (weak evidence) — placebo-controlled substrate benefit, because FACETS missed its primary endpoint in the full randomised population (response 41% vs 28%, P=0.30) and its supportive data come from the amenable-mutation subset followed open-label. Neither trial was powered for clinical events, and the shelf says so.

cards.headline: FACETS 2016: migalastat missed its primary endpoint — kidney substrate response 41% vs 28% on placebo (P=0.30) in the full randomised population
cards.summary: FACETS (2016): migalastat missed its primary endpoint — kidney substrate response 41% vs 28% on placebo (P=0.30) in the full randomised population.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (6-month stage 1, then open-label migalastat to 24 months)
cards.people: 67 patients with Fabry disease randomised to migalastat or placebo for 6 months; a validated assay completed before unblinding showed 50 of the 67 had migalastat-amenable mutant alpha-galactosidase forms. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. (The companion record carries no erratum relevant here.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥50% reduction in globotriaosylceramide inclusions per kidney interstitial capillary at 6 months) did not differ significantly: 13 of 32 patients (41%) on migalastat vs 9 of 32 (28%) on placebo had a response (P=0.30). Among amenable-mutation patients treated with migalastat for up to 24 months (open-label follow-up), annualised changes in estimated GFR were -0.30±0.66 and in measured GFR -1.51±1.33 ml/min/1.73 m2, and the left-ventricular-mass index decreased significantly from baseline (-7.7 g/m2; 95% CI -15.4 to -0.01), particularly with baseline hypertrophy (-18.6 g/m2, -38.2 to 1.0). Diarrhoea, reflux and indigestion severity decreased.
cards.watchOut: The trial's first assay misclassified amenability — the randomised comparison includes patients whose enzyme the drug cannot rescue — and the encouraging renal and cardiac figures come from uncontrolled open-label follow-up of the amenable subset, which is why this half of the shelf is MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: ATTRACT 2017: switching from enzyme replacement to migalastat gave similar renal effects over 18 months; left-ventricular-mass index fell on migalastat (-6.6 g/m2)
cards.summary: ATTRACT (2017): switching from enzyme replacement to migalastat gave similar renal effects over 18 months.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, active-controlled phase 3 trial (18 months)
cards.people: 57 adults with Fabry disease previously treated with enzyme replacement therapy (56% women; 88% with multiorgan disease), randomised 1.5:1 to switch to oral migalastat or remain on enzyme replacement; 4 patients with non-amenable mutations on the validated assay were excluded from primary efficacy analyses only. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 29661968; not a retraction.)
cards.result: Migalastat and enzyme replacement had similar effects on renal function over 18 months (the abstract reports the comparison qualitatively, without a between-group eGFR figure, so none is printed). Left-ventricular-mass index decreased significantly with migalastat (-6.6 g/m2; 95% CI -11.0 to -2.2), with no significant change on enzyme replacement. Predefined renal, cardiac or cerebrovascular events occurred in 29% of migalastat vs 44% of enzyme-replacement patients (small numbers, not a powered comparison). Plasma globotriaosylsphingosine remained low and stable after the switch. Patient-reported outcomes were comparable, and migalastat was generally safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-seven patients, open-label, 18 months, in patients already stabilised on enzyme replacement: comparability here is 'no detected loss of control after switching', not proof of equal long-term organ protection, and it applies only to amenable mutations.
cards.source: Hughes DA et al. Oral pharmacological chaperone migalastat compared with enzyme replacement therapy in Fabry disease: 18-month results from the randomised phase III ATTRACT study. Journal of medical genetics. 2017;54(4):288-296. PMID: 27834756. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01218659, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Bardoxolone methyl in diabetic kidney disease: BEACON's cardiovascular harm and the TSUBAKI shadow
shelves.question: Did bardoxolone methyl, an Nrf2 activator that raised measured eGFR, help or harm patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease, and what do the later Japanese trials' eGFR rises mean under that shadow?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology,mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetic Nephropathies/drug therapy · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Failure, Chronic/etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the harm, and no benefit on the primary outcome) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf IS a cardiovascular-harm claim from a trial stopped for harm). BEACON (2,185 patients) was terminated early: its primary composite of ESRD or cardiovascular death was identical (6% vs 6%; relative hazard ratio 0.98), while hospitalisation for heart failure or heart-failure death was higher on bardoxolone (96 vs 55 patients; relative hazard ratio 1.83; absolute 8.8% vs 5.0%). The later phase 2 TSUBAKI trial showed a genuine measured-GFR rise (+6.64 ml/min/1.73 m2 vs placebo) in patients screened to exclude heart-failure risk — a surrogate result that cannot launder BEACON's outcome harm, and the shelf presents bardoxolone as a cautionary exhibit, not an option. Nothing on this shelf re-sequences diabetes therapy.

cards.headline: BEACON 2013: bardoxolone did not reduce ESRD or cardiovascular death (6% vs 6%) and increased heart-failure hospitalisation or heart-failure death (96 vs 55 patients; relative hazard ratio 1.83) — the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: BEACON (2013): bardoxolone did not reduce ESRD or cardiovascular death ( 6% vs 6% ) and increased heart-failure hospitalisation or heart-failure death (8.8% vs 5.0%) — the trial was stopped.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, terminated early on the data and safety monitoring committee's recommendation (median follow-up 9 months)
cards.people: 2,185 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 15 to <30 ml/min/1.73 m2), randomised to bardoxolone methyl 20 mg daily (1,088) or placebo (1,097). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite (end-stage renal disease or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 69 of 1,088 patients (6%) on bardoxolone and 69 of 1,097 (6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.37; P=0.92) — cardiovascular death itself occurred in 27 bardoxolone patients vs 19 on placebo, and ESRD in 43 vs 51 (components of the composite, printed beside the heart-failure figures per the library's pairing rule). Hospitalisation for heart failure or death from heart failure occurred in 96 bardoxolone patients (8.8%) vs 55 (5.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.83; 1.32 to 2.55; P<0.001) — a relative measure with absolute counts beside it. Estimated GFR, blood pressure and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio rose significantly, and body weight fell significantly, on bardoxolone.
cards.watchOut: The eGFR rise that made the drug look promising coexisted with fluid-retention harm: BEACON is the library's standing lesson that a filtration-marker rise (with rising albuminuria and blood pressure) is not kidney protection.
cards.source: de Zeeuw D et al. Bardoxolone methyl in type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2013;369(26):2492-503. PMID: 24206459. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01351675, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TSUBAKI 2020: in patients screened to exclude heart-failure risk, bardoxolone raised measured (inulin) GFR by 6.64 ml/min/1.73 m2 vs placebo at 16 weeks — no heart failure occurred
cards.summary: TSUBAKI (2020): in patients screened to exclude heart-failure risk, bardoxolone raised measured (inulin) GFR by 6.64 ml/min/1.73 m² vs placebo.
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (16 weeks; dose titration)
cards.people: 120 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 3-4 CKD in Japan (cohort G3: bardoxolone 41, placebo 41; cohort G4: bardoxolone 24, placebo 14), enrolled after BEACON identified elevated baseline BNP (>200 pg/mL) and prior heart-failure hospitalisation as the fluid-overload risk factors to exclude; 40 G3 patients were in the prespecified primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. This record's MeSH list is empty in the MEDLINE record.
cards.result: Mean change in GFR measured by inulin clearance at week 16 (cohort G3) was +5.95 ml/min/1.73 m2 (95% CI 2.29 to 9.60) on bardoxolone vs -0.69 (-3.83 to 2.45) on placebo, an intergroup difference of 6.64 (P=0.008). The albumin-to-creatinine ratio increased on bardoxolone. Peripheral oedema occurred in 4 bardoxolone patients vs 1 on placebo (all mild, self-limiting); no patient died or experienced heart failure. Discontinuations were more frequent on bardoxolone (G3: 8; G4: 7) than placebo (G3: 1; G4: 0). Common adverse events included liver-enzyme rises and viral upper respiratory infection.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks, 120 pre-screened patients, a filtration endpoint: TSUBAKI shows the GFR effect is pharmacologically real in selected patients; it cannot and does not overturn BEACON's outcome-level harm in unselected stage 4 disease.
cards.source: Nangaku M et al. Randomized Clinical Trial on the Effect of Bardoxolone Methyl on GFR in Diabetic Kidney Disease Patients (TSUBAKI Study). Kidney international reports. 2020;5(6):879-890. PMID: 32518870. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank entry and no MeSH list.

cards.result: Bardoxolone's dossier is a parable in two acts: an outcome trial stopped for an 83% relative excess of heart-failure hospitalisation or heart-failure death (absolute 8.8% vs 5.0%) with a null primary endpoint, followed by smaller screened-population trials (TSUBAKI carded here; the AYAME phase 3 study's design-and-baseline report, PMID 36002026, is fenced here as a design paper with no outcomes) showing real measured-GFR rises that remain surrogates. shelves.title: Etelcalcetide, an intravenous calcimimetic at dialysis: twin placebo trials and the cinacalcet head-to-head
shelves.question: Does intravenous etelcalcetide, given thrice weekly at dialysis, lower parathyroid hormone in secondary hyperparathyroidism more than placebo, and how does it compare with oral cinacalcet — at what cost in hypocalcaemia and gut symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Calcimimetic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Calcium/blood · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Fibroblast Growth Factors/blood · Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary/blood,drug therapy,etiology · Infusions, Intravenous/methods · Parathyroid Hormone/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for PTH lowering — a surrogate): Two parallel placebo-controlled trials in one report (1,023 patients) each found >30% PTH reduction in about three-quarters on etelcalcetide vs under 10% on placebo, and a randomised head-to-head (683 patients) found etelcalcetide noninferior — indeed superior on the primary comparison — to cinacalcet (68.2% vs 57.7% achieving >30% reduction), with more decreased blood calcium (68.9% vs 59.8%). All are PTH-surrogate trials, stated on the shelf face; no calcimimetic trial of this generation showed a mortality benefit, no outcome claim is made, and EVOLVE's null stays home on Shelf #296.

cards.headline: Block 2017 (twin trials): etelcalcetide achieved >30% PTH reduction in 74.0% and 75.3% of patients vs 8.3% and 9.6% on placebo
cards.summary: Block (2017, twin trials): etelcalcetide achieved >30% PTH reduction in 74.0% and 75.3% of patients vs 8.3% and 9.6% on placebo.
cards.type: Two parallel phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials reported together (26 weeks)
cards.people: 1,023 patients receiving haemodialysis with moderate-to-severe secondary hyperparathyroidism (trial A: 508 patients at 111 sites; trial B: 515 at 97 sites, across North America, Europe, Israel, Russia and Australia); mean age 58.2 (SD 14.4) years, 60.4% men. Intravenous etelcalcetide or placebo after each dialysis session.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (>30% reduction in mean PTH during weeks 20-27) was achieved in trial A by 188 of 254 patients (74.0%) on etelcalcetide vs 21 of 254 (8.3%) on placebo (difference 65.7 percentage points; 95% CI 59.4 to 72.1; P<0.001) and in trial B by 192 of 255 (75.3%) vs 25 of 260 (9.6%) (difference 65.7 points, 59.3 to 72.1; P<0.001). PTH of 300 pg/mL or lower was achieved by 49.6% vs 5.1% (trial A) and 53.3% vs 4.6% (trial B). Mean PTH fell from ~845-849 to ~363-384 pg/mL on etelcalcetide while rising or holding on placebo. Muscle spasms (12.0%/11.1% vs 7.1%/6.2%), nausea (12.4%/9.1% vs 5.1%/7.3%) and vomiting (10.4%/7.5% vs 7.1%/3.1%) were more common with etelcalcetide.
cards.watchOut: PTH is a surrogate: these registration trials were not designed or powered to test fractures, cardiovascular events or death, and the report says so. (The record's databank fields carry one registry number, NCT01788046, for the twin-trial report.)
cards.source: Block GA et al. Effect of Etelcalcetide vs Placebo on Serum Parathyroid Hormone in Patients Receiving Hemodialysis With Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: Two Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2017;317(2):146-155. PMID: 28097355. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01788046, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Block 2017 (head-to-head): etelcalcetide was noninferior and superior to cinacalcet for >30% PTH reduction (68.2% vs 57.7%), with more hypocalcaemia (68.9% vs 59.8%)
cards.summary: Block (2017, head-to-head): etelcalcetide was noninferior and superior to cinacalcet for >30% PTH reduction ( 68.2% vs 57.7% ), with more hypocalcaemia.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-comparator trial (26 weeks)
cards.people: 683 patients receiving haemodialysis with PTH above 500 pg/mL on active therapy, at 164 sites; mean age 54.7 (SD 14.1) years, 56.2% men; intravenous etelcalcetide plus oral placebo (340) or oral cinacalcet plus IV placebo (343).
cards.result: The primary endpoint (>30% reduction in mean predialysis PTH during weeks 20-27) was achieved by 232 of 340 patients (68.2%) on etelcalcetide vs 198 of 343 (57.7%) on cinacalcet — etelcalcetide was noninferior (margin 12.0%; P for noninferiority <0.001) and met superiority (difference -10.5% as printed for cinacalcet minus etelcalcetide; P for superiority 0.004). More than 50% PTH reduction was achieved by 52.4% vs 40.2% (P=0.001; difference 12.2 points, 4.7 to 19.5). The most common adverse effect was decreased blood calcium (68.9% vs 59.8%). Self-reported nausea/vomiting endpoints were assessed as secondary outcomes. (The abstract text prints the registry number once as 'NCT1896232', an evident typographical slip; the record's databank fields carry NCT01896232, which is what this card cites.)
cards.watchOut: Superiority on a biochemical endpoint between two drugs of the same class, neither with an outcomes win in this generation: the clinical case for the IV drug rests on adherence and administration at dialysis, which the trial design assumes rather than tests.

shelves.title: Zibotentan on top of dapagliflozin in chronic kidney disease (ZENITH-CKD)
shelves.question: Does adding low-dose zibotentan, a selective endothelin-A antagonist, to dapagliflozin reduce albuminuria more than dapagliflozin alone in chronic kidney disease, and can the SGLT2 inhibitor contain the fluid retention that sank earlier endothelin blockers?
shelves.mesh: Albuminuria · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications,drug therapy · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Benzhydryl Compounds
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2b trial (ZENITH-CKD, 447 treated patients, 12 weeks) found zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin reduced urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by -33.7% relative to dapagliflozin alone, and the 0.25 mg dose by -27.0% (both relative measures) — with fluid-retention events in 18% on the higher dose vs 8% on dapagliflozin alone. An albuminuria-surrogate trial; no outcome trial exists yet and the shelf says so. Albuminuria here is a kidney-damage marker and trial surrogate; no claim connects it to diet. No kidney-survival or cardiovascular claim is made.

cards.headline: ZENITH-CKD 2023: zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin cut albuminuria by -33.7% relative to dapagliflozin alone at 12 weeks; fluid retention occurred in 18% vs 8%
cards.summary: ZENITH-CKD (2023): zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin cut albuminuria by −33.7% relative to dapagliflozin alone at 12 weeks; fluid retention roughly doubled at the higher dose.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase 2b trial (12 weeks; 170 sites, 18 countries)
cards.people: 447 treated adults with CKD (eGFR at least 20 mL/min/1.73 m2, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 150-5000 mg/g), on ACE inhibitor or ARB if tolerated; mean age 62.8 (SD 12.1) years, 31% women, mean eGFR 46.7, median UACR 565.5 mg/g; zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin (179), zibotentan 0.25 mg plus dapagliflozin (91), or dapagliflozin plus placebo (177).
cards.result: At week 12, the difference in UACR versus dapagliflozin plus placebo was -33.7% (90% CI -42.5 to -23.5; p<0.0001) for zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin and -27.0% (90% CI -38.4 to -13.6; p=0.0022) for zibotentan 0.25 mg plus dapagliflozin — both relative differences in the albuminuria surrogate. Fluid-retention events (prespecified definition: weight gain mostly from body water, or large BNP rise above threshold) occurred in 33 (18%) of 179 participants on the 1.5 mg combination, 8 (9%) of 91 on the 0.25 mg combination, and 14 (8%) of 177 on dapagliflozin plus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a urine surrogate, with the class's signature harm (fluid retention) still visibly dose-related despite the SGLT2 inhibitor aboard: the trial shows the pharmacology works, not that kidneys or hearts fare better.
cards.source: Heerspink HJL et al. Zibotentan in combination with dapagliflozin compared with dapagliflozin in patients with chronic kidney disease (ZENITH-CKD): a multicentre, randomised, active-controlled, phase 2b, clinical trial. Lancet (London, England). 2023;402(10416):2004-2017. PMID: 37931629. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724837, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Exercise training in haemodialysis patients (EXCITE; CYCLE-HD)
shelves.question: In adults on maintenance haemodialysis, does a personalised low-intensity exercise programme improve physical performance (six-minute walk distance) versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Fitness · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Walking
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two dialysis exercise trials test different deliveries against different primary endpoints, and the cards do not average them. EXCITE (n=296): a personalised, low-intensity home walking programme improved six-minute walk distance (328 to 367 m) versus usual care (321 to 324 m; P<0.001 between groups) and sit-to-stand time at 6 months — LIKELY for walk performance. CYCLE-HD (n=130): six months of intradialytic cycling significantly reduced left ventricular mass (−11.1 g between groups) — a cardiac surrogate — but had no significant effect on physical function or quality of life, its secondary outcomes — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the functional question this shelf asks. Neither trial reports clinical-event outcomes, and neither shelf claim touches mortality, so the shelf is not Tier C. Attrition was material in both (EXCITE: 227 of 296 repeated the 6-month evaluations; CYCLE-HD: 101 of 130 completed).

cards.headline: EXCITE: home walking improved six-minute walk distance (328→367 m versus 321→324 m) and sit-to-stand at 6 months
cards.summary: EXCITE: home walking improved six-minute walk distance (328→367 m versus 321→324 m) and sit-to-stand at 6 months
cards.people: 296 adults on dialysis randomised to a personalised, low-intensity home walking programme managed by dialysis staff (151) or normal physical activity (145); 227 patients (104 exercise, 123 control) repeated the 6-month evaluations. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Six-minute walk distance improved in the exercise group (baseline 328±96 m to 367±113 m at 6 months) but not in controls (321±107 to 324±116 m; P<0.001 between groups). Five-times sit-to-stand time improved likewise (20.5→18.2 s versus 20.9→20.2 s; P=0.001). Cognitive-function (P=0.04) and social-interaction (P=0.01) scores on the kidney-disease quality-of-life instrument also improved more with exercise.
cards.watchOut: About 23% of randomised patients did not repeat the 6-month evaluations, and the analysis is in completers of the assessments; the programme was home-based and staff-managed, so the result is about this supported delivery, not exercise advice in general. shelves.title: Ferric pyrophosphate citrate in dialysate (CRUISE 1 and 2)
shelves.question: In iron-deficient adults on haemodialysis, does ferric pyrophosphate citrate delivered via the dialysate maintain haemoglobin and reduce intravenous iron and ESA requirements versus placebo dialysate?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Dialysis Solutions · Dietary Supplements · Diphosphates · Female · Ferric Compounds · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Iron · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two identical phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials reported together (599 iron-replete chronic haemodialysis patients). Haemoglobin was maintained from baseline to end of treatment on ferric pyrophosphate citrate (FPC) dialysate but fell by 0.4 g/dL on placebo (P<0.001, combined results); reticulocyte haemoglobin and ferritin also fell less on FPC, and adverse and serious adverse event proportions were similar between groups. The outcomes are haemoglobin and iron indices — maintenance-of-iron-balance surrogates — not transfusion or clinical-event outcomes, and the shelf claims nothing beyond them. Correction printed on the card: the topic file's pinned anchor (PMID 28371161) is a narrative review of FPC by two authors, not the trials' results report; it is fenced by name, and this shelf cards the CRUISE trials' combined report (PMID 26175145), pinned at build.

cards.headline: CRUISE 1 and 2 (combined report): haemoglobin maintained on FPC dialysate, fell 0.4 g/dL on placebo
cards.summary: CRUISE 1 and 2 (combined report): haemoglobin maintained on FPC dialysate, fell 0.4 g/dL on placebo
cards.type: Two identical phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials (combined report)
cards.people: 599 iron-replete chronic haemodialysis patients across CRUISE 1 and CRUISE 2, dialysed with dialysate containing 2 µM FPC-iron or standard dialysate (placebo) for up to 48 weeks; oral and intravenous iron were prohibited and ESA doses held constant. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Haemoglobin concentration was maintained from baseline to end of treatment in the FPC group but decreased by 0.4 g/dL in the placebo group (P<0.001, combined results; 95% CI 0.2 to 0.6). Placebo patients had larger falls in reticulocyte haemoglobin content (−0.9 versus −0.4 pg; P<0.001) and serum ferritin (−133.1 versus −69.7 µg/L; P<0.001). Proportions of patients with adverse and serious adverse events were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The trials were designed so the placebo arm slowly became iron-deficient (no other iron allowed, ESA frozen) — the comparison proves FPC replaces ongoing iron losses, in a setting engineered to show exactly that. No transfusion, hospitalisation, or mortality outcomes are reported.

shelves.title: Incremental twice-weekly haemodialysis start (TWOPLUS)
shelves.question: In patients starting dialysis with residual kidney function, does a twice-weekly haemodialysis start with adjuvant pharmacotherapy and planned transition to thrice-weekly treatment match conventional thrice-weekly start on patient-reported outcomes and safety?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Pilot Projects · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small pilot trial whose carded report (patient-reported outcomes) prints no between-group comparisons at all. Both arms' symptom scores improved over the first 6 weeks (Dialysis Symptom Index change −9.7 in the incremental group versus −13.8 in the conventional group; PHQ-9 −2.5 versus −3.5; GAD-7 −1.9 versus −1.5), with the P values in the record being within-group, and week-6-to-12 changes small and non-significant in both arms. The authors' conclusion of a 'possible mitigating effect' of the incremental start on anxiety and depression is flagged on the card: no between-group estimate in the abstract supports it, and on the printed changes the conventional arm improved at least as much on most measures. This was a feasibility and safety pilot (about 20 patients per group in the outcome analyses); it generates the hypothesis for a definitive trial and answers nothing yet. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped.

cards.headline: TWOPLUS pilot: symptoms improved in both arms; the record prints no between-group comparison
cards.summary: TWOPLUS pilot: symptoms improved in both arms; the record prints no between-group comparison

cards.people: Incident patients with kidney failure requiring dialysis and residual kidney function at 14 dialysis units, assigned to incremental start (twice-weekly haemodialysis for 6 weeks, then thrice-weekly) or conventional thrice-weekly start. Patient-reported outcome analyses included 20 patients per group at week 6, and 21 patients at week 12 as printed in the record.
cards.result: Change from baseline to week 6 (incremental versus conventional): Dialysis Symptom Index −9.7 versus −13.8; GAD-7 anxiety −1.9 versus −1.5; PHQ-9 depression −2.5 versus −3.5 (lower scores denote lower symptom burden). Changes from week 6 to week 12 were small in both groups. Most surveyed participants felt their healthcare was not jeopardised by the incremental schedule.
cards.watchOut: The P values printed in the record are within-group changes from baseline; no between-group effect estimate or P value appears in the abstract, so the authors' conclusion of a 'possible mitigating effect' on anxiety and depression goes beyond the printed analysis and is flagged as such. A feasibility pilot of about 40 analysed patients cannot establish equivalence of the schedules on any outcome.

shelves.title: Buttonhole versus stepladder cannulation (MacRae)
shelves.question: In conventional (in-centre) haemodialysis patients with an arteriovenous fistula, does buttonhole cannulation reduce pain and complications versus standard (rope-ladder) cannulation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alberta · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Arteriovenous Shunt, Surgical · Chi-Square Distribution · Female · Hematoma · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Pain Measurement · Punctures · Renal Dialysis · Risk Factors · Staphylococcal Infections · Staphylococcus aureus · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — a single randomised trial (n=140) found no pain benefit and a clear infection cost. Pain at 8 weeks was similar (median VAS 1.5 on buttonhole versus 1.2 on standard needling; P=0.57). Buttonhole produced fewer haematomas (295 versus 436 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.03) but more localised infection signs (50 versus 22.4 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.003), one Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia during the 8-week trial versus none, and — within 12 months of follow-up — two further buttonhole bacteraemias and nine needling-site abscesses requiring intravenous antibiotics versus zero in the standard group (P=0.003). Question re-scoped to the record and disclosed here: the topic file frames the population as home haemodialysis patients, but the trial enrolled conventional in-centre haemodialysis patients. The shelf's claim is a harm/null claim resting on one trial; it is stated as such on the face.

cards.headline: MacRae: no pain difference (P=0.57); infection signs doubled and bacteraemias clustered in the buttonhole arm
cards.summary: MacRae: no pain difference (P=0.57); infection signs doubled and bacteraemias clustered in the buttonhole arm
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (8-week primary outcome; 12-month infection follow-up)
cards.people: 140 conventional haemodialysis patients with arteriovenous fistulas, randomised to buttonhole or standard (rope-ladder) needling. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Median pain score at 8 weeks (0–10 cm visual analogue scale) was 1.5 (IQR 0.5–3.4) for buttonhole versus 1.2 (0.4–2.4) for standard needling (P=0.57). Haematoma formation was less frequent with buttonhole (295 versus 436 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.03). Localised signs of infection were more frequent with buttonhole (50 versus 22.4 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.003). One episode of S. aureus bacteraemia occurred during the 8 weeks with buttonhole and none with standard needling; within 12 months, two further buttonhole bacteraemias and nine buttonhole needling-site abscesses requiring intravenous antibiotics occurred, versus zero standard-needling episodes (P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: The infection signal grows with follow-up beyond the 8-week primary window — the trial's most important numbers are in its 12-month data. A single-centre-group trial; cannulation technique and hygiene protocols vary between units, which bounds generalisation.

shelves.title: Gentamicin–citrate catheter lock (Moran; Dogra)
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with tunneled central venous catheters, does a gentamicin–citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection versus a heparin lock?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Anticoagulants · Catheter-Related Infections · Catheterization, Central Venous · Citric Acid · Female · Gentamicins · Heparin · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials, a decade apart, agree strongly. Moran 2012 (n=303): catheter-related bloodstream infection at 0.28 episodes per 1,000 catheter-days on gentamicin 320 µg/mL in 4% citrate versus 0.91 on heparin (P=0.003), with thrombolytic use no different. Dogra 2002 (112 catheters in 83 patients): infection at 0.03 versus 0.42 per 100 catheter-days (P=0.003) with gentamicin–citrate filling. The caution travels with the benefit and is printed on the Dogra card: the concentrations differ about a hundredfold between the trials (40 mg/mL versus 320 µg/mL), and Dogra's record itself shows measurable predialysis gentamicin levels and warns of aminoglycoside exposure and ototoxicity risk — these records establish that gentamicin–citrate locks prevent bacteraemia, not which concentration is safe for long-term use.

cards.headline: Moran: bloodstream infection 0.28 versus 0.91 per 1,000 catheter-days with gentamicin–citrate lock (P=0.003)

cards.type: Parallel-group, randomised, multicentre clinical trial (patients blinded)
cards.people: 303 adult maintenance haemodialysis patients using tunneled cuffed central venous catheters at 16 free-standing facilities in Northern California; the treatment lock was gentamicin 320 µg/mL in 4% sodium citrate and the control lock heparin 1,000 U/mL; both groups received triple-antibiotic ointment at the exit site. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Catheter-related bloodstream infection occurred at 0.28 episodes per 1,000 catheter-days in the gentamicin–citrate group versus 0.91 in the heparin group (P=0.003), and time to first bacteraemia was significantly delayed (P=0.005). Tissue plasminogen activator use for clotting was similar (2.36 versus 3.42 events per 1,000 catheter-days; P=0.2).
cards.watchOut: Facility staff prepared the lock, so the study could not be completely blinded (the record's own stated limitation). Registry ID: none in this record's databank fields — stated, not filled.

shelves.title: Depression treatment in dialysis: sertraline versus CBT (ASCEND)
shelves.question: In patients on maintenance dialysis with depression, is chairside cognitive behavioural therapy as effective as sertraline for depressive symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Depression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Interview, Psychological · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Patient Compliance · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Renal Dialysis · Sertraline
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label randomised trial (120 patients in the treatment phase) found sertraline modestly superior to chairside CBT on the primary symptom measure: QIDS-C scores at 12 weeks favoured sertraline by 1.84 points (95% CI −3.54 to −0.13; P=0.035), with adverse events more frequent on sertraline. Correction printed on the card: the topic file states symptoms improved 'with no significant difference between CBT and sertraline' — the record shows a statistically significant difference, and the card follows the record. Two bounds on the claim: the 1.84-point difference is below the 2-point minimal clinically important difference used for this scale in the CAST trial (Shelf #1736), and ASCEND had no untreated control group, so neither arm's absolute efficacy — only their comparison — is established here. The trial's phase 1 found an engagement interview did not increase treatment acceptance (66% versus 64%).

cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, open-label randomised controlled trial (two phases)
cards.people: Patients on maintenance haemodialysis for at least 3 months with Beck Depression Inventory-II score of 15 or more, at 41 dialysis facilities in three US metropolitan areas: 184 patients took part in phase 1 (engagement interview versus control visit) and 120 in phase 2 (12 weeks of chairside CBT versus sertraline). cards.result: Phase 1: treatment initiation did not differ after the engagement interview versus control visit (66% versus 64%; P=0.77). Phase 2: compared with CBT, sertraline produced lower QIDS-C depression scores at 12 weeks (effect estimate −1.84 [95% CI, −3.54 to −0.13]; P=0.035). Adverse events were more frequent in the sertraline group than the CBT group.
cards.watchOut: The record's own stated limitations: no randomised comparison with no treatment, and persistence of effect was not assessed. The topic file's claim of 'no significant difference' between the arms is contradicted by the record and is corrected on this card; the honest reading is a small, statistically real advantage for sertraline of uncertain clinical importance.

shelves.title: Sertraline for depression in non-dialysis CKD (CAST)
shelves.question: In patients with non-dialysis chronic kidney disease and major depression, does sertraline improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Depression · Major Depressive Disorder · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Sertraline · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=201) found no improvement: QIDS-C16 scores changed by −4.1 on sertraline versus −4.2 on placebo over 12 weeks (between-group difference 0.1, 95% CI −1.1 to 1.3; P=0.82). The interval is informative — it excludes the 2-point minimal clinically important difference the trial prespecified — so this is a measured null, not an absence of data. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on sertraline (nausea or vomiting 22.7% versus 10.4%; diarrhoea 13.4% versus 3.1%). The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) because the shelf rests on this one trial. Read beside Shelf #1735 (ASCEND), where sertraline modestly beat CBT in dialysis patients without a placebo arm — the two records together do not establish that sertraline works in kidney disease at all.

shelves.title: Antibiotic exit-site cream in peritoneal dialysis (Bernardini)
shelves.question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does daily gentamicin cream at the catheter exit site prevent exit-site infection and peritonitis compared with mupirocin cream?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Catheters, Indwelling · Confidence Intervals · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gentamicins · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections · Humans · Incidence · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Mupirocin · Ointments · Peritoneal Dialysis · Probability · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single double-blind randomised trial (n=133) with consistent, organism-specific advantages for gentamicin cream: catheter infection rates 0.23 versus 0.54 episodes per dialysis-year (P=0.005), peritonitis 0.34 versus 0.52 per year (P=0.03), no Pseudomonas catheter infections on gentamicin versus 0.11 per year on mupirocin (P<0.003), and Gram-negative peritonitis 0.02 versus 0.15 per year (P=0.003), while Staphylococcus aureus exit-site infections were equally infrequent in both groups (0.06 versus 0.08 per year). The comparison is against mupirocin — an active prophylactic — not against no prophylaxis. The topic file's wider double-A framing rests on other mupirocin-prophylaxis randomised trials that were not separately pinned in this build; the stamp therefore rests on this trial alone, and that is stated here rather than borrowed.

cards.headline: Bernardini: catheter infections 0.23 versus 0.54 per year and peritonitis 0.34 versus 0.52 per year on gentamicin versus mupirocin cream
cards.summary: Bernardini: catheter infections 0.23 versus 0.54 per year and peritonitis 0.34 versus 0.52 per year on gentamicin versus mupirocin cream
cards.people: 133 peritoneal dialysis patients from three centres (53% incident, 47% prevalent), randomised to daily gentamicin cream (67) or mupirocin cream (66) at the catheter exit site, with infections tracked prospectively by organism. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Catheter infection rates were 0.23 per year with gentamicin versus 0.54 with mupirocin (P=0.005), and time to first catheter infection was longer (P=0.03). There were no Pseudomonas aeruginosa catheter infections on gentamicin versus 0.11 per year on mupirocin (P<0.003). S. aureus exit-site infections were infrequent in both groups (0.06 versus 0.08 per year; P=0.44). Peritonitis rates were 0.34 versus 0.52 per year (P=0.03), with Gram-negative peritonitis 0.02 versus 0.15 per year (P=0.003); gentamicin use predicted lower peritonitis rates after adjustment (relative risk 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.93; P<0.03).
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial: it shows gentamicin cream is the better prophylactic of the two, driven by Gram-negative and Pseudomonas coverage — it does not measure either cream against no prophylaxis. Single trial from 2005; registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era), stated rather than filled.

shelves.title: Neutral-pH low-GDP peritoneal dialysis fluid (balANZ)
shelves.question: In incident peritoneal dialysis patients, does a neutral-pH, low-glucose-degradation-product solution preserve residual kidney function versus conventional acidic solution?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biocompatible Materials · Confidence Intervals · Cross-Over Studies · Dialysis Solutions · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Glucose · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Peritoneal Dialysis · Peritonitis · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Analysis · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — balANZ (n=185) splits cleanly between its primary question and its secondary findings. On the shelf's question, the answer is no: the slope of GFR decline did not differ between biocompatible and conventional fluid (year 1: −0.22 versus −0.28 mL/min/1.73 m² per month, P=0.17; year 2: −0.09 versus −0.10, P=0.9) — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for preserving residual kidney function. On secondary outcomes, the biocompatible group had a longer time to anuria (P=0.009) and fewer peritonitis episodes (30% versus 49% of patients; 0.30 versus 0.49 episodes per year, P=0.01), confirmed in the trial's secondary microbiology analysis (IRR 0.61 relative) — POSSIBLE. Correction printed on the cards: the topic file pinned the trial's secondary peritonitis analysis (PMID 22991015) as the anchor; this shelf is led by the primary report (PMID 22440906), pinned at build, with the pinned paper carded second as the same trial's secondary analysis (counted once).

cards.headline: balANZ primary report: GFR decline slopes identical (P=0.17 and P=0.9); anuria delayed and peritonitis reduced

cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, parallel-group randomised controlled trial (2 years)
cards.people: 185 incident adult peritoneal dialysis patients with residual renal function, randomised to biocompatible (neutral-pH, low-glucose-degradation-product) or conventional solution for 2 years. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary outcome — slope of renal function decline — did not differ: GFR slopes were −0.22 versus −0.28 mL/min/1.73 m² per month in year 1 (P=0.17) and −0.09 versus −0.10 in year 2 (P=0.9), biocompatible versus conventional. The biocompatible group had significantly longer times to anuria (P=0.009) and to first peritonitis (P=0.01), fewer patients developing peritonitis (30% versus 49%), and lower peritonitis rates (0.30 versus 0.49 episodes per year; P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the headline depends on the outcome chosen: the kidney-function question this shelf asks is answered null by the trial's own primary analysis, while the infection and anuria findings are secondary. Registry ID: none in this record's databank fields — stated, not filled.

shelves.title: Icodextrin for the long dwell in peritoneal dialysis
shelves.question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does icodextrin for the long dwell improve ultrafiltration and fluid status versus glucose-based solutions?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Icodextrin · Peritoneal Dialysis · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Dialysis Solutions · Adult · Glucose · Glucans · Aged · Kidney Failure, Chronic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the quantitative case rests on the classic MIDAS report (Wolfson 2002; two randomised double-blind studies reported together): net ultrafiltration on the long dwell was 587 versus 346 mL per exchange versus 2.5% dextrose (P<0.001), with higher urea and creatinine clearances, no weight gain over 52 weeks versus about 2 kg gained on dextrose, and less oedema (6.3% versus 17.9%). The recent trial the topic file pins (Li 2025, n=40, 4 months) points the same way — greater nighttime ultrafiltration, P<0.05 — but its abstract prints no effect sizes at all, so no figures from it are carded; that absence is flagged on its card. Two randomised comparisons in the same direction, one of them small and numberless: POSSIBLE. Outcomes are ultrafiltration and fluid-status surrogates; neither record reports mortality or technique-survival endpoints.

cards.headline: MIDAS (Wolfson 2002): net ultrafiltration 587 versus 346 mL; no weight gain at 52 weeks versus ~2 kg on dextrose
cards.summary: MIDAS (Wolfson 2002): net ultrafiltration 587 versus 346 mL; no weight gain at 52 weeks versus ~2 kg on dextrose
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, controlled studies reported together (4-week efficacy study; 52-week safety study)
cards.people: The 4-week efficacy study enrolled 175 CAPD patients comparing 7.5% icodextrin with 2.5% dextrose for the once-daily long dwell; a parallel 52-week study in CAPD and APD patients examined long-term safety, weight, and quality of life (its enrolment is not printed in the abstract). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Mean net ultrafiltration was 587.2 mL on icodextrin versus 346.2 mL on dextrose (P<0.001); clearances of urea nitrogen (4.5 versus 4.1 mL/min) and creatinine (4.0 versus 3.5 mL/min) were also higher (both P<0.001). After 52 weeks, icodextrin patients had no increase in weight versus a gain of almost 2 kg on dextrose (P<0.05), and fewer reported oedema (6.3% versus 17.9%; P<0.01). Adverse events did not differ significantly; small decreases in sodium and chloride and increases in alkaline phosphatase occurred on icodextrin.
