shelves.title: Paricalcitol and cardiac structure in CKD (OPERA; PRIMO)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and left ventricular hypertrophy, does paricalcitol reduce left ventricular mass versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Echocardiography · Ergocalciferols · Female · Humans · Hypercalcemia · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone · Prospective Studies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with the same primary endpoint agree. PRIMO (n=227, 48 weeks): change in left ventricular mass index was +0.34 g/m^2.7 on paricalcitol versus −0.07 on placebo — no difference, and diastolic measures likewise. OPERA (n=60, 52 weeks): LV mass index changed by −2.59 on paricalcitol versus −4.85 g/m² on placebo — again no significant difference, numerically favouring placebo. Both trials confirm paricalcitol suppresses parathyroid hormone; PRIMO found more hypercalcaemia on the drug. Question re-scoped to the records and disclosed here: the topic file also asks about left atrial volume, but neither carded record's abstract reports a left-atrial-volume result — OPERA's record in particular does not support the file's statement that it 'reduced left atrial volume index'; a separate small vitamin-D trial reports an LA-volume finding and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded. OPERA's fewer cardiovascular-related hospitalisations on paricalcitol are a secondary observation printed without figures in its abstract and carry no stamp weight.

cards.headline: PRIMO: left ventricular mass index change +0.34 versus −0.07 g/m^2.7 — no effect of paricalcitol (48 weeks)
cards.summary: PRIMO: left ventricular mass index change +0.34 versus −0.07 g/m^2.7 — no effect of paricalcitol (48 weeks)
cards.people: 227 patients with CKD (eGFR 15–60 mL/min/1.73 m²), mild-to-moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, and preserved ejection fraction, in 11 countries; randomised to oral paricalcitol 2 µg/day (115) or placebo (112) for 48 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Change in left ventricular mass index by cardiac MRI did not differ between groups: +0.34 g/m^2.7 (95% CI −0.14 to 0.83) on paricalcitol versus −0.07 (−0.55 to 0.42) on placebo. Doppler measures of diastolic function also did not differ. Paricalcitol reduced parathyroid hormone within 4 weeks and maintained it in the normal range. Episodes of hypercalcaemia were more frequent on paricalcitol.
cards.watchOut: An imaging-surrogate trial powered for structure, not events: the null is a statement that paricalcitol does not remodel the ventricle measurably in a year, not a statement about cardiovascular outcomes.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline in diabetic kidney disease (PREDIAN)
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic kidney disease on RAAS blockade, does pentoxifylline slow eGFR decline and reduce albuminuria versus control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albumins/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetic Nephropathies/drug therapy/urine · Disease Progression · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Inflammation · Kidney/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Pentoxifylline/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Research Design · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two randomised trials point the same way on surrogate outcomes, and neither reports a hard kidney outcome. PREDIAN (open-label, n=169, 2 years): eGFR fell by 2.1 ml/min/1.73 m² on pentoxifylline versus 6.5 on control (between-group difference 4.3, 95% CI 3.1 to 5.5; P<0.001), with albuminuria falling 14.9% against a 5.7% rise. Han 2015 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=174, 6 months): proteinuria fell 23% versus 4% (P=0.012). Both trials were add-ons to RAAS blockade; dialysis, kidney failure and death were not endpoints in either record, so no progression-to-ESRD claim is made. Surrogate endpoints in modest-sized trials cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PREDIAN: pentoxifylline slowed eGFR decline (2.1 vs 6.5 ml/min/1.73 m² over 2 years) and reduced albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease
cards.summary: PREDIAN: pentoxifylline slowed eGFR decline (2.1 vs 6.5 ml/min/1.73 m² over 2 years) and reduced albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease
cards.people: 169 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 3–4 CKD, all on renin-angiotensin system inhibitors: 82 received pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day and 87 were controls. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Over 2 years, eGFR decreased by a mean of 2.1 ± 0.4 ml/min/1.73 m² in the pentoxifylline group versus 6.5 ± 0.4 in controls — a between-group difference of 4.3 ml/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 3.1 to 5.5; P<0.001). The proportion declining faster than the median rate was 33.3% versus 68.2% (P<0.001). Urinary albumin excretion changed by −14.9% (95% CI −20.4 to −9.4) on pentoxifylline versus +5.7% (−0.3 to 11.1) on control (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo, and both outcomes are surrogates (eGFR slope and albuminuria); the trial reports no dialysis, kidney-failure or mortality endpoints, so the result cannot be read as protection against ESRD. Single-country (Spanish) population.

shelves.title: Sparsentan in paediatric focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (DUPLEX subgroup)
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, does sparsentan reduce proteinuria versus irbesartan?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Biomarkers · Creatinine · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Glomerulosclerosis, Focal Segmental/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Irbesartan/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Proteinuria/drug therapy/etiology · Child · Adolescent · Young Adult · Adult · Middle Aged · Aged · Remission Induction · Spiro Compounds · Sulfonamides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with two disclosures on the face of the shelf. First, the paediatric evidence is a POST HOC subgroup analysis of the DUPLEX trial (35 children), not a standalone paediatric randomised trial as the topic draft implied. Second, the parent DUPLEX trial (n=371, ages 8–75) MISSED its primary endpoint: eGFR slope at 108 weeks did not differ significantly between sparsentan and irbesartan (total-slope difference 0.3 ml/min/1.73 m²/year, 95% CI −1.7 to 2.4), even though the proteinuria surrogate favoured sparsentan (partial remission 42.0% vs 26.0% at 36 weeks, P=0.009). In the paediatric subgroup, proteinuria fell more on sparsentan (mean UPCR reduction 39.5% vs 24.9% at 108 weeks; partial remission endpoint 56.3% vs 36.8%), consistent with the parent trial's surrogate result; no paediatric kidney-function outcome is reported. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: the whole shelf rests on one trial programme, and the paediatric claim on a 35-patient post hoc subgroup — it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: DUPLEX paediatric subgroup (post hoc): proteinuria fell more on sparsentan (UPCR −39.5% vs −24.9% at 108 weeks) in 35 children
cards.summary: DUPLEX paediatric subgroup (post hoc): proteinuria fell more on sparsentan (UPCR −39.5% vs −24.9% at 108 weeks) in 35 children
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of the DUPLEX randomised trial (paediatric patients aged 8 to <18 years)
cards.people: 35 paediatric patients enrolled in DUPLEX: 16 received sparsentan and 19 irbesartan. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: UPCR reductions appeared by week 6 and were sustained: mean reduction at 108 weeks 39.5% on sparsentan versus 24.9% on irbesartan. More sparsentan patients reached low-proteinuria thresholds, including complete remission (UPCR <0.3 g/g) in 12.5% versus 5.3% and the FSGS partial remission endpoint (UPCR ≤1.5 g/g with >40% reduction) in 56.3% versus 36.8%. Safety profiles were similar. The record lists kidney-failure rates among its outcomes but prints no figures for them, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: This is a post hoc analysis of 35 children inside an adult-powered trial — not a paediatric trial in its own right, and the topic draft's description of it as 'a randomised trial in paediatric FSGS' overstates the design; the randomisation is inherited from DUPLEX. Proteinuria is a surrogate; no paediatric eGFR or kidney-failure result is reported. shelves.title: Apixaban versus phenprocoumon in haemodialysis patients with atrial fibrillation (AXADIA–AFNET 8)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation on chronic haemodialysis, is apixaban as safe and effective as the vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon for bleeding and thromboembolic outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Phenprocoumon/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Stroke/prevention & control · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Pyridones/adverse effects · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Pyrazoles
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Both of the trial's primary composites embed all-cause death — the safety composite (major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, or all-cause death) and the efficacy composite (ischaemic stroke, all-cause death, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) — so the shelf is Tier C even though no mortality claim is made or supported by the data. AXADIA–AFNET 8 randomised only 97 patients and stopped early: the safety composite occurred in 45.8% on apixaban versus 51.0% on phenprocoumon (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.65) and noninferiority was NOT established (P for noninferiority = 0.157); the efficacy composite occurred in 20.8% versus 30.6% (P=0.51), with all-cause mortality 18.8% versus 24.5%. The confidence intervals are wide enough to include important benefit and important harm, so the record earns MAYBE (weak evidence): an underpowered trial cannot settle anticoagulant choice in dialysis.

cards.headline: AXADIA–AFNET 8: no significant difference between apixaban and phenprocoumon in 97 dialysis patients — and noninferiority was not established
cards.summary: AXADIA–AFNET 8: no significant difference between apixaban and phenprocoumon in 97 dialysis patients — and noninferiority was not established
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) trial, stopped early
cards.people: 97 patients with atrial fibrillation on chronic haemodialysis at 39 sites (30% women; mean age 75 years; mean CHA2DS2-VASc score 4.5): 48 received apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily and 49 the vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon (target INR 2.0 to 3.0). Median follow-up was 429 days on apixaban versus 506 days on VKA; median time in therapeutic range on VKA was 50.7%.
cards.result: The composite primary safety outcome (major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, or all-cause death) occurred in 22 patients (45.8%) on apixaban and 25 (51.0%) on VKA (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.65; P for noninferiority = 0.157 — noninferiority not shown). The composite primary efficacy outcome (ischaemic stroke, all-cause death, myocardial infarction, DVT or PE) occurred in 10 (20.8%) versus 15 (30.6%) (P=0.51). Individual outcomes: all-cause mortality 18.8% versus 24.5%; major bleeding 10.4% versus 12.2%; myocardial infarction 4.2% versus 6.1%.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped early with 97 of its planned patients, event rates were very high in both arms, and VKA control was mediocre (median time in range 50.7%) — the comparison is imprecise in both directions and its own authors conclude larger trials are needed. Event rates this high also mean the composites are dominated by the frailty of the population, not only by drug effects.

shelves.title: Hydroxychloroquine in IgA nephropathy
shelves.question: In patients with IgA nephropathy and persistent proteinuria despite supportive care, does hydroxychloroquine reduce proteinuria versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Creatinine/blood · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Glomerulonephritis, IGA/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Humans · Hydroxychloroquine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Immunologic Factors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Protective Agents/administration & dosage · Proteinuria/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Renal Elimination/drug effects · Renin-Angiotensin System/drug effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one small double-blind phase 2 trial with a large surrogate effect and no hard outcome. In 60 patients with IgA nephropathy on optimised RAAS inhibition, hydroxychloroquine changed proteinuria by −48.4% at 6 months against +10.0% on placebo (P<0.001), with no serious adverse events recorded. Six months, 60 patients, a single centre, and a proteinuria endpoint — with no eGFR or kidney-failure data — cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single small trial with no second randomised test; it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Steroids, targeted budesonide and sparsentan in IgA nephropathy, and complement inhibition, are different questions homed on their own shelves.

cards.headline: Liu 2019: hydroxychloroquine halved proteinuria at 6 months in IgA nephropathy (−48.4% vs +10.0%; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Liu 2019: hydroxychloroquine halved proteinuria at 6 months in IgA nephropathy (−48.4% vs +10.0%; P<0.001)
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial (6 months)
cards.people: 60 patients with IgA nephropathy (protein excretion 0.75–3.5 g/day, eGFR >30 ml/min/1.73 m²) on optimised RAAS inhibitor therapy: 30 received hydroxychloroquine and 30 placebo. Mean eGFR was 53.8 ml/min/1.73 m² and median urine protein excretion 1.7 g/day; the abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Percentage change in proteinuria at 6 months was −48.4% (IQR −64.2 to −30.5) on hydroxychloroquine versus +10.0% (IQR −38.7 to +30.6) on placebo (P<0.001). Median proteinuria at 6 months was 0.9 (IQR 0.6 to 1.0) versus 1.9 (0.9 to 2.6) g/day (P=0.002). No serious adverse events were recorded in either group.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient, 6-month, single-centre phase 2 trial with a proteinuria surrogate: its own authors state the findings require confirmation in larger trials, and the short follow-up without post-withdrawal observation says nothing about long-term kidney protection or long-term safety (including retinal screening, which the record does not address).

shelves.title: AST-120 oral adsorbent for CKD progression (EPPIC-1 and EPPIC-2)
shelves.question: In patients with progressive chronic kidney disease, does the oral adsorbent AST-120 slow progression (composite of dialysis initiation, kidney transplantation, or creatinine doubling) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Carbon/therapeutic use · Confidence Intervals · Creatinine/blood · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/prevention & control · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Oxides/therapeutic use · Predictive Value of Tests · Proportional Hazards Models · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two large multinational double-blind trials, 2,035 patients, agree: EPPIC-1 HR 1.03 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.27; P=0.78) and EPPIC-2 HR 0.91 (0.74 to 1.12; P=0.37) for the primary progression composite, with a similar pooled result. Disclosure: the topic draft described death as a component of the composite and flagged the shelf Tier C; the published record's primary endpoint is a composite of dialysis initiation, kidney transplantation, and serum creatinine doubling — it contains no mortality component — so on the record the shelf is NOT Tier C, and the question above follows the record. Progression in the trial populations was slower than expected (placebo median times to endpoint 189.0 and 170.3 weeks against 124 assumed), but the point estimates sit on the null in both trials.

cards.headline: EPPIC-1 and EPPIC-2: AST-120 did not slow CKD progression in either trial (HR 1.03 and 0.91)
cards.summary: EPPIC-1 and EPPIC-2: AST-120 did not slow CKD progression in either trial (HR 1.03 and 0.91)
cards.type: Two multinational, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together
cards.people: 2,035 adults with moderate-to-severe CKD (screening serum creatinine 2.0–5.0 mg/dl in men, 1.5–5.0 mg/dl in women) received AST-120 9 g/day or placebo on top of standard therapy; each trial continued until 291 primary endpoints had accrued. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Time to the primary endpoint — a composite of dialysis initiation, kidney transplantation, and serum creatinine doubling, as printed in the record — was similar between groups in both trials: EPPIC-1 HR 1.03 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.27; P=0.78); EPPIC-2 HR 0.91 (0.74 to 1.12; P=0.37); the pooled analysis was similar. Disease progression was more gradual than expected (placebo median times 189.0 and 170.3 weeks versus 124 weeks assumed in the power calculations).
cards.watchOut: The composite as printed in the record contains no death component — the topic draft's description of the endpoint (with death, without transplantation) does not match the record, and the record governs; that correction is also why this shelf is not Tier C. No registry IDs appear in the record.

shelves.title: Low-dose ('renal-dose') dopamine in early renal dysfunction (ANZICS)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with early renal dysfunction, does low-dose ('renal-dose') dopamine prevent worsening renal failure versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Biomarkers · Creatinine/blood · Dopamine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kidney Diseases/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Agents/therapeutic use · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive placebo-controlled trial found nothing: in 328 critically ill patients with early renal dysfunction, low-dose dopamine (2 µg/kg/min) did not differ from placebo on peak creatinine (245 vs 249 µmol/L (≈2.77 vs 2.82 mg/dL); p=0.93), creatinine above 300 µmol/L (≈3.39 mg/dL) (56 vs 56 patients), renal replacement therapy (35 vs 40; p=0.55), ICU or hospital stay, and deaths were 69 versus 66 as printed counts. Mortality was not the trial's primary endpoint (peak creatinine was) and no mortality claim is made; the shelf is not Tier C. The subsequent meta-analytic record points the same way and is fenced, not carded.

cards.headline: ANZICS: low-dose dopamine did not protect the kidneys — peak creatinine 245 vs 249 µmol/L (≈2.77 vs 2.82 mg/dL), dialysis 35 vs 40 patients
cards.summary: ANZICS: low-dose dopamine did not protect the kidneys — peak creatinine 245 vs 249 µmol/L (≈2.77 vs 2.82 mg/dL), dialysis 35 vs 40 patients
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (23 ICUs)
cards.people: 328 critically ill patients with at least two systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and early renal dysfunction (oliguria or rising creatinine): 161 analysed on dopamine 2 µg/kg/min by central infusion and 163 on placebo (4 of 328 excluded for major protocol violations). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Peak serum creatinine during treatment was 245 (SD 144) µmol/L (≈2.77 mg/dL) on dopamine versus 249 (147) on placebo (p=0.93); the rise from baseline was 62 (107) versus 66 (108) µmol/L (≈0.70 versus 0.75 mg/dL) (p=0.82). Creatinine exceeded 300 µmol/L (≈3.39 mg/dL) in 56 patients in each group (p=0.92); renal replacement therapy was required by 35 versus 40 (p=0.55). ICU stay (13 vs 14 days; p=0.67) and hospital stay (29 vs 33 days; p=0.29) were similar. There were 69 deaths in the dopamine group and 66 in the placebo group, printed as counts without a comparative statistic.
cards.watchOut: A year-2000 trial from the pre-registration era (no registry ID in the record). Dopamine increased urine output in earlier physiological studies without improving renal outcomes — the distinction between making urine and protecting kidneys is the whole lesson of this shelf.

shelves.title: Ferric citrate in non-dialysis CKD: iron indices and haemoglobin
shelves.question: In patients with non-dialysis CKD and iron deficiency, does ferric citrate improve haemoglobin and iron indices versus control — and what does it do to phosphate-related markers?
shelves.mesh: No MeSH terms in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with a re-scoping disclosure: the topic draft framed this shelf around phosphate lowering, but neither carded record prints a phosphate-lowering effect size against control. The anchor trial (Wu 2026, double-blind, n=141, Taiwanese patients with iron-deficiency anaemia) was powered on haemoglobin and met that endpoint (between-group difference 0.62 ± 0.15 g/dL; p<0.0001); phosphate, iPTH and FGF23 changes are reported only as significant secondary/exploratory differences (all p<0.05) with no magnitudes printed, so none are carded. The Japanese trial (Iguchi 2018, open-label, n=40) enrolled NORMOphosphataemic patients and found FGF23 unchanged (P=0.1764), with a within-group PTH fall. So the honest claim is: ferric citrate improves haemoglobin and iron indices in non-dialysis CKD (POSSIBLE); its phosphate and FGF23 effects are unquantified or null in these records. Ferric citrate as a phosphate binder in dialysis is a different population and is not imported here.

cards.headline: Wu 2026: ferric citrate raised haemoglobin more than placebo in non-dialysis CKD with iron-deficiency anaemia (+0.62 g/dL; p<0.0001)

cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: haemoglobin rose significantly more on ferric citrate than placebo (intergroup difference 0.62 ± 0.15 g/dL; p<0.0001). shelves.title: Nicotinamide-based phosphate lowering in CKD (COMBINE)
shelves.question: In patients with CKD and hyperphosphataemia, does nicotinamide-based phosphate lowering (with lanthanum carbonate) reduce serum phosphate and FGF23 versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Fibroblast Growth Factors/blood/drug effects · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Lanthanum/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Monte Carlo Method · Niacinamide/administration & dosage · Phosphates/blood · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the only randomised test of this strategy was null on both of its dual primary endpoints: over 12 months in 205 patients with stage 3b/4 CKD, serum phosphate and FGF23 changes did not differ significantly across the nicotinamide, lanthanum carbonate, combination, and double-placebo arms (phosphate in fact rose slightly in all groups). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate in reverse: the shelf rests on one trial, and should be revisited if a second test appears.

cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2×2 factorial trial (12 months)
cards.people: 205 patients with stage 3b/4 CKD (eGFR 20–45 ml/min/1.73 m²; mean eGFR 32), randomised to nicotinamide 750 mg twice daily plus lanthanum carbonate 1000 mg three times daily, nicotinamide alone, lanthanum alone, or double placebo. cards.result: Neither dual primary endpoint separated: mean phosphate change over 12 months rose slightly in all arms and did not differ significantly across arms, and FGF23 percent change rose in all arms except lanthanum-alone, again without significant between-arm differences. cards.watchOut: Adherence limited by gastrointestinal intolerance means the trial tests the strategy as tolerated, not as prescribed at full dose; the endpoints are biochemical surrogates (phosphate, FGF23), not cardiovascular events. shelves.title: Sodium bicarbonate after kidney transplantation (PRESERVE-TRANSPLANT)
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with metabolic acidosis, does sodium bicarbonate preserve graft function (eGFR trajectory) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Female · Adolescent · Sodium Bicarbonate/therapeutic use · Bicarbonates/therapeutic use · Switzerland · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects · Single-Blind Method · Double-Blind Method · COVID-19 · Acidosis/drug therapy/etiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single well-run phase 3 trial with a precise null: in 242 transplant recipients with metabolic acidosis treated for 2 years, the eGFR slope difference between sodium bicarbonate and placebo was 0.032 ml/min/1.73 m²/year (95% CI −1.644 to 1.707), even though bicarbonate corrected the acidosis itself (serum bicarbonate 21.3 to 23.0 mmol/L). Correcting the number did not protect the graft. The stamp is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), not LIKELY, because one trial — however clean — is one trial. Scope boundary: this shelf is transplant recipients only; bicarbonate in non-transplant CKD is a different question, homed on its own shelf, and neither shelf's result should be read onto the other. Three deaths occurred during the trial (2 placebo, 1 bicarbonate, as printed); mortality was not an endpoint and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: PRESERVE-TRANSPLANT: bicarbonate corrected acidosis but did not slow eGFR decline in transplant recipients (difference 0.032 ml/min/1.73 m²/yr)
cards.summary: PRESERVE-TRANSPLANT: bicarbonate corrected acidosis but did not slow eGFR decline in transplant recipients (difference 0.032 ml/min/1.73 m²/yr)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial (2 years)
cards.people: 242 long-term kidney transplant recipients (>1 year post-transplant, eGFR 15–89 ml/min/1.73 m², serum bicarbonate ≤22 mmol/L) at three Swiss university hospitals: 120 received sodium bicarbonate 1.5–4.5 g/day and 122 placebo; 240 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. The abstract does not print mean age or the overall sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — eGFR slope over 24 months — did not differ: mean slopes −1.830 (SD 6.233) ml/min/1.73 m²/year on bicarbonate versus −1.862 (6.344) on placebo; mean difference 0.032 (95% CI −1.644 to 1.707); Wilcoxon p=0.51, Welch t-test p=0.97. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses agreed. Serum bicarbonate rose from 21.3 (SD 2.6) to 23.0 (2.7) mmol/L on treatment. Adverse and serious adverse events were similar; three participants died (placebo: one SARS-CoV-2 respiratory failure, one cardiac arrest after severe dehydration; bicarbonate: one sudden cardiac death).
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (participants) rather than double-blind, and the endpoint is an eGFR slope — a surrogate for graft survival, which the trial was not powered to measure. The deaths printed above are safety reporting, not an efficacy signal in either direction.
cards.source: Mohebbi N et al. Sodium bicarbonate for kidney transplant recipients with metabolic acidosis in Switzerland: a multicentre, randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 36708734. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03102996, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Voclosporin in active lupus nephritis (AURORA 1)
shelves.question: In adults with active lupus nephritis, does voclosporin added to mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose steroids increase complete renal response versus mycophenolate and steroids alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Calcineurin Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Creatinine/urine · Cyclosporine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic · Lupus Nephritis/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in the single phase 3 trial, adding the calcineurin inhibitor voclosporin to mycophenolate and rapidly tapered steroids nearly doubled complete renal response at 52 weeks (41% versus 23%), with a balanced overall adverse-event profile; deaths were few and numerically fewer on voclosporin (1 versus 5, none judged treatment-related — printed beside the efficacy results, as a secondary count). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: AURORA 1 is one trial (its continuation study was not placebo-controlled); the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: AURORA 1: complete renal response at 52 weeks in 41% on voclosporin versus 23% on placebo (OR 2.65)
cards.summary: AURORA 1: complete renal response at 52 weeks in 41% on voclosporin versus 23% on placebo (OR 2.65)
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (142 sites in 27 countries; 52 weeks)
cards.people: 357 adults with systemic lupus erythematosus and biopsy-proven active lupus nephritis (class III, IV or V, alone or combined), randomised 1:1 to voclosporin 23.7 mg twice daily (179) or placebo (178), all on mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily with rapidly tapered low-dose oral steroids. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, complete renal response at week 52 (urine protein-creatinine ratio 0.5 mg/mg or less with stable renal function, no rescue medication and no prolonged higher-dose prednisone), was achieved by 73 (41%) of 179 patients on voclosporin versus 40 (23%) of 178 on placebo (odds ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.64 to 4.27; p<0.0001 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). Serious adverse events occurred in 21% of each group; the most frequent serious infection was pneumonia (4% in each group). Six patients died during the study or follow-up: 1 (<1%) on voclosporin and 5 (3%) on placebo; investigators judged none of the deaths treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Complete renal response is a composite surrogate for long-term kidney survival; the trial does not report end-stage kidney disease or mortality as efficacy outcomes, and 52 weeks is short in a relapsing lifelong disease. As a calcineurin inhibitor, voclosporin carries the class's renal-function and drug-interaction baggage, which a one-year trial only partly maps.
cards.source: Rovin BH et al. Efficacy and safety of voclosporin versus placebo for lupus nephritis (AURORA 1): a double-blind, randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2021. PMID: 33971155. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03021499, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Obinutuzumab in active lupus nephritis (REGENCY)
shelves.question: In adults with active lupus nephritis, does obinutuzumab added to standard therapy (mycophenolate and prednisone) increase complete renal response versus standard therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacokinetics · Creatinine/urine · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects/methods · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacokinetics · Lupus Nephritis/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology/urine · Mycophenolic Acid/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Prednisone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Proteinuria/diagnosis/drug therapy/urine · Infusions, Intravenous · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Tract Infections/epidemiology/immunology · Gastroenteritis/epidemiology/immunology · Pneumonia/epidemiology/immunology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in the single phase 3 trial, adding the type II anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab to mycophenolate and prednisone raised complete renal response at week 76 from 33.1% to 46.4% (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points), with consistent secondary renal endpoints; more serious adverse events, mainly infections, occurred with obinutuzumab (the abstract reports this qualitatively, without arm-level rates). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Scope boundary: obinutuzumab in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia combinations is a different question (Shelf #676).

cards.headline: REGENCY: complete renal response at week 76 in 46.4% on obinutuzumab versus 33.1% on placebo (adjusted difference 13.4 points; P=0.02)
cards.summary: REGENCY: complete renal response at week 76 in 46.4% on obinutuzumab versus 33.1% on placebo (adjusted difference 13.4 points; P=0.02)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (obinutuzumab 1000 mg in one of two dose schedules, on a background of mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone tapered to 5 mg/day by week 24; primary endpoint at week 76)
cards.people: 271 adults with biopsy-proven active lupus nephritis were randomised (135 obinutuzumab across two dose schedules, 136 placebo). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: A complete renal response at week 76 (urine protein-creatinine ratio below 0.5, eGFR at least 85% of baseline, and no intercurrent event such as rescue therapy, treatment failure, death or early withdrawal) occurred in 46.4% on obinutuzumab versus 33.1% on placebo (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points, 95% CI 2.0 to 24.8; P=0.02). Secondary endpoints agreed: complete renal response with prednisone at 7.5 mg/day or lower during weeks 64-76 in 42.7% versus 30.9% (adjusted difference 11.9 points, 95% CI 0.6 to 23.2; P=0.04), and urine protein-creatinine ratio below 0.8 without an intercurrent event in 55.5% versus 41.9% (adjusted difference 13.7 points, 95% CI 2.0 to 25.4; P=0.02). No unexpected safety signals were identified; more serious adverse events, mainly infections and COVID-19-related events, occurred with obinutuzumab — the abstract does not print the arm-level serious-adverse-event rates.
cards.watchOut: The two obinutuzumab dose schedules are pooled in the analysis, so this record cannot say whether the week-50 dose matters. Complete renal response at 76 weeks is a surrogate for long-term kidney survival. The infection excess is real in direction but unquantified in this record — do not attach a number to it.
cards.source: Furie RA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Obinutuzumab in Active Lupus Nephritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39927615. shelves.title: Dietary protein restriction in chronic kidney disease (MDRD)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease, does dietary protein restriction (with usual- versus low-dose blood-pressure control) slow the decline in glomerular filtration rate versus usual protein intake?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure · Chronic Disease · Dietary Proteins · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypertension · Kidney Diseases · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Polycystic Kidney Diseases
shelves.balance: The Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) study remains the definitive randomised test of protein restriction: 840 patients in two studies, each crossing diet with blood-pressure target. In Study 1 (585 patients, GFR 25–55), the projected three-year GFR decline did not differ significantly between usual-protein (1.3 g/kg/day) and low-protein (0.58 g/kg/day) diets, or between usual and low blood-pressure targets; the low-protein group declined faster in the first four months (a haemodynamic effect of eating less protein) and slower thereafter, a pattern the authors read as suggesting at most a small benefit. In Study 2 (255 patients, GFR 13–24), a very-low-protein diet (0.28 g/kg/day with keto-acid supplements) was only marginally slower than low protein (P=0.07), and in neither study was there any delay in end-stage renal disease or death. The one positive interaction: patients with heavier baseline proteinuria declined significantly more slowly in the low-blood-pressure group. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for protein restriction as a progression-slowing strategy.

cards.headline: MDRD: 840 patients — protein restriction did not significantly slow GFR decline, and did not delay dialysis or death
cards.summary: MDRD: 840 patients — protein restriction did not significantly slow GFR decline, and did not delay dialysis or death
cards.type: Randomized trial (two studies, factorial diet × blood pressure)
cards.people: 840 patients with various chronic renal diseases. Study 1: 585 patients with GFR 25–55 ml/min/1.73 m² randomised to a usual-protein diet (1.3 g/kg/day) or a low-protein diet (0.58 g/kg/day) and to a usual or low blood-pressure target (mean arterial pressure 107 or 92 mm Hg). Study 2: 255 patients with GFR 13–24 randomised to the low-protein diet or a very-low-protein diet (0.28 g/kg/day) with a keto acid–amino acid supplement, and to the same blood-pressure targets. Mean follow-up was 2.2 years; the outcome was rate of decline in glomerular filtration rate, with time to end-stage renal disease or death recorded.
cards.result: In Study 1, the projected mean decline in GFR at three years did not differ significantly between the diet groups or between the blood-pressure groups; the low-protein and low-blood-pressure groups declined more rapidly during the first four months and more slowly thereafter. In Study 2, the very-low-protein group had a marginally slower GFR decline than the low-protein group (P=0.07). There was no delay in the time to end-stage renal disease or death in either study. In both studies, patients in the low-blood-pressure group who had more pronounced proteinuria at baseline had a significantly slower rate of GFR decline.
cards.watchOut: A GFR-slope trial from the pre-ACE-inhibitor-standard era (published 1994): background therapy today differs, and the early rapid decline on protein restriction complicates slope interpretation, as the investigators themselves noted. The record carries no registry ID — MDRD predates trial registration. The proteinuria–blood-pressure interaction is a subgroup finding, hypothesis-generating rather than a carded prescription.
cards.source: Klahr S et al. The effects of dietary protein restriction and blood-pressure control on the progression of chronic renal disease. Modification of Diet in Renal Disease Study Group. N Engl J Med. 1994. PMID: 8114857. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Biomarker-guided KDIGO bundle after cardiac surgery (PrevAKI): fewer severe injuries, overall AKI unchanged in the multicentre trial
shelves.question: In cardiac-surgery patients identified as high-risk by urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7], does implementing the KDIGO care bundle (haemodynamic optimisation, nephrotoxin avoidance, glycaemic control) reduce AKI within 72 hours compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Biomarkers · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Proteins · Patient Care Bundles · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinase-2
shelves.balance: The two trials of the same idea point in different directions depending on which outcome you read, so this stamp is split. In the single-centre PrevAKI trial, cardiac-surgery patients flagged high-risk by urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] who received the KDIGO bundle developed AKI within 72 hours in 55.1% of cases versus 71.7% with standard care (absolute reduction 16.6 percentage points). In the multicentre PrevAKI trial (278 patients), overall AKI did not differ (46.3% bundle versus 41.5% control), but moderate-to-severe AKI was less frequent with the bundle (14.0% versus 23.9%; absolute reduction 10.0 points), and the trial's primary purpose was feasibility — bundle adherence was 65.4% versus 4.2%. The specific tested programme is the KDIGO care bundle (haemodynamic optimisation, nephrotoxin avoidance, glycaemic control) triggered by the [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] biomarker test. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit for moderate-to-severe AKI; (the treatment made no difference) for overall AKI in the multicentre trial.

cards.headline: PrevAKI single-centre (Meersch 2017): KDIGO bundle in biomarker-positive patients cut AKI within 72 hours — 55.1% vs 71.7% (absolute reduction 16.6 points)
cards.summary: PrevAKI single-centre (Meersch 2017): KDIGO bundle in biomarker-positive patients cut AKI within 72 hours — 55.1% vs 71.7% (absolute reduction 16.6 points)
cards.people: Cardiac-surgery patients at a single German centre (University of Münster) identified as high-risk by urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] >0.3 after cardiopulmonary bypass, randomised to the KDIGO bundle — optimisation of volume status and haemodynamics, avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs, and prevention of hyperglycaemia — or standard care. Primary endpoint: AKI by KDIGO criteria within 72 hours of surgery. (The PubMed abstract does not state the randomised total.)
cards.result: AKI was significantly reduced with the intervention compared with controls: 55.1% versus 71.7%, an absolute risk reduction of 16.6% (95% CI 5.5 to 27.9%; p=0.004). Rates of moderate-to-severe AKI were also significantly reduced; haemodynamic parameters, hyperglycaemia, and ACE-inhibitor/ARB use differed in the bundle's favour, with no significant effects on other secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, unblinded bundle care, and an endpoint (any AKI within 72 hours) dominated by mild creatinine-defined injury; the authors themselves called for adequately powered multicentre trials of mortality and long-term renal outcomes.
cards.source: Meersch M et al. Prevention of cardiac surgery-associated AKI by implementing the KDIGO guidelines in high risk patients identified by biomarkers: the PrevAKI randomized controlled trial. Intensive Care Med. 2017. PMID: 28110412. No registry ID appears in the record's abstract. cards.headline: PrevAKI multicentre (Zarbock 2021): bundle was feasible and cut moderate-to-severe AKI (14.0% vs 23.9%), but overall AKI did not differ (46.3% vs 41.5%)
cards.summary: PrevAKI multicentre (Zarbock 2021): bundle was feasible and cut moderate-to-severe AKI (14.0% vs 23.9%), but overall AKI did not differ (46.3% vs 41.5%)
cards.people: 278 high-risk cardiac-surgery patients (urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7]-positive) in a multicentre, multinational randomised trial of the KDIGO bundle versus control. Primary endpoint: adherence to the bundle protocol (a feasibility trial preparing a definitive trial).
cards.result: Complete bundle adherence was 65.4% in the intervention group versus 4.2% in controls (absolute risk reduction 61.2; 95% CI 52.6 to 69.9; P<.001). AKI rates did not differ: 46.3% intervention versus 41.5% control (absolute risk reduction −4.8%; 95% CI −16.4 to 6.9; P=.423). Moderate-to-severe AKI was significantly lower with the bundle: 14.0% versus 23.9% (absolute reduction 10.0%; 95% CI 0.9 to 19.1; P=.034). No significant effects on other secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial, not powered as the definitive outcome trial: the moderate-to-severe AKI difference is a secondary endpoint, and even in the intervention arm only about two-thirds of patients received the complete bundle.

shelves.title: Continuous versus intermittent dialysis in ICU AKI (Hemodiafe): survival was the same either way
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with AKI as part of multiple-organ dysfunction, does continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration improve survival compared with intermittent haemodialysis delivered to the same tolerance and metabolic-control standards?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Hemodiafiltration · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Multiple Organ Failure · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: One multicentre randomised trial, now two decades old, found no survival advantage for the continuous mode when both modes were delivered carefully. In 360 critically ill patients with AKI as part of multiple-organ dysfunction in 21 French ICUs, 60-day survival was 32% with intermittent haemodialysis versus 33% with continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration — essentially identical, and the same at every other time point. The trial's own interpretation was narrower than 'mode does not matter': with strict guidelines to improve tolerance and metabolic control, almost all such patients could be treated intermittently. THIN: a single trial from 1999–2003, before modern membranes, dosing, and hybrid modes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one well-run multicentre trial, but old and unconfirmed by a second modality trial.

cards.headline: Vinsonneau 2006 (Hemodiafe): 60-day survival was 32% with intermittent haemodialysis versus 33% with continuous haemodiafiltration — no difference
cards.summary: Vinsonneau 2006 (Hemodiafe): 60-day survival was 32% with intermittent haemodialysis versus 33% with continuous haemodiafiltration — no difference
cards.people: 360 patients with acute renal failure as part of multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome, randomised in 21 medical or multidisciplinary ICUs in France (1999–2003) to intermittent haemodialysis or continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration. Both groups used the same polymer membrane and bicarbonate-based buffer, with guidelines to achieve optimum haemodynamic tolerance and solute removal. Primary endpoint: 60-day survival, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Survival at 60 days did not differ between groups: 32% in the intermittent haemodialysis group versus 33% in the continuous group (95% CI for the difference −8.8 to 11.1), nor at any other time point. The authors concluded that, provided strict guidelines to improve tolerance and metabolic control are used, almost all patients with acute renal failure as part of multiple-organ dysfunction can be treated with intermittent haemodialysis.
cards.watchOut: Era effect: enrolment ran 1999–2003; membranes, delivered dose, anticoagulation, and hybrid techniques (such as prolonged intermittent therapy) have all moved on. The confidence interval (−8.8 to 11.1 points) also cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction.
cards.source: Vinsonneau C et al. Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration versus intermittent haemodialysis for acute renal failure in patients with multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome: a multicentre randomised trial. Lancet. 2006. PMID: 16876666. No registry ID appears in the record (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Far-infrared therapy for arteriovenous fistula maturation: one small positive trial, effects unquantified
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with a new arteriovenous fistula, does far-infrared therapy improve fistula maturation, blood flow, and 12-month patency compared with usual care?
shelves.balance: The evidence here is small and fragile, and this stamp stays weak. In one single-centre randomised trial of 80 haemodialysis patients (40 per group), adding far-infrared therapy to mucopolysaccharide polysulfonate cream for 3 months was followed by significantly larger vein diameter, higher pump-controlled and brachial-artery blood flow, shorter maturation time, lower pain scores, fewer fistula complications, and a higher primary patency rate than cream alone — but the PubMed abstract reports these only as statistically significant (P<0.05), without the actual values, so no effect size can be quoted or checked from the record. A second randomised trial named in the drafting notes (PMID 35887935) could not be gate-verified in this build session and is therefore not carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small single-centre trial, qualitative reporting only.

cards.headline: Huang 2023: far-infrared therapy plus cream beat cream alone on fistula maturation measures at 3 months — but the abstract gives no numbers, only P<0.05
cards.summary: Huang 2023: far-infrared therapy plus cream beat cream alone on fistula maturation measures at 3 months — but the abstract gives no numbers, only P<0.05
cards.people: 80 haemodialysis patients at a single Chinese hospital (the 900th Hospital, Fuzhou), randomised 40 to far-infrared therapy plus mucopolysaccharide polysulfonate cream and 40 to the cream alone, for 3 months. Outcomes: vein diameter, fistula maturation time, pump-controlled and brachial-artery blood flow during dialysis, fistula complications (oozing, occlusion, infection), and pain (numerical rating scale).
cards.result: After 3 months, vein diameter, pump-controlled blood flow, and brachial-artery blood flow were significantly higher in the intervention group, and maturation time, pain score, and complication rate were significantly lower (all P<0.05); the primary patency rate was higher and overall patency differed significantly (P<0.05). The abstract reports no absolute values, rates, or confidence intervals for any of these outcomes, so the size of every effect is unverifiable from the record.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 80 patients, unblinded device therapy, a cream co-intervention in both arms, and abstract reporting without a single effect size — this is hypothesis-supporting evidence, not a basis for purchasing equipment or changing access practice.
cards.source: Huang J et al. Effect of far-infrared therapy device on arteriovenous fistula maturation and lifespan in hemodialysis patients: a randomized controlled clinical trial. Front Surg. 2023. PMID: 37753529. No registry ID and no MeSH terms are listed on the PubMed record.

shelves.title: Intradialytic parenteral nutrition for protein-energy wasting: albumin up in one small trial, primary endpoint null in another
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting who cannot tolerate oral supplements, does intradialytic parenteral nutrition improve nutritional status compared with intensive dietary counselling alone?
shelves.mesh: Cachexia · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Malnutrition · Nutritional Status · Parenteral Nutrition · Prealbumin · Renal Dialysis · Serum Albumin
shelves.balance: Two small randomised trials of intradialytic parenteral nutrition (IDPN) disagree on their primary nutritional markers, so this stamp is split and weak. In a Thai trial of 38 haemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting who could not tolerate oral supplements, 3 months of fish-oil-based IDPN raised serum albumin (3.5 to 3.8 g/dL) while intensive dietary counselling did not (3.6 to 3.5 g/dL; p=0.01 between patterns as reported), with improved dietary intake, body weight, and malnutrition-inflammation score in the IDPN group only. In the multicentre ENEFLUID study — the specific tested product is named here for clarification, as it is a single proprietary formulation (ENEFLUID) — 39 analysed patients showed no difference in the primary endpoint, change in serum transthyretin at 12 weeks (difference 1.3 mg/dL; 95% CI −1.7 to 4.3; P=0.41), although protein intake fell less with IDPN. Neither trial measured survival or hospitalisation. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for short-term nutritional markers in supplement-intolerant patients; (the treatment made no difference) on the ENEFLUID trial's transthyretin primary endpoint. THIN: 38 and 39 patients.

cards.headline: Kittiskulnam 2022: 3 months of IDPN raised albumin (3.5→3.8 g/dL) versus counselling (3.6→3.5 g/dL) in 38 supplement-intolerant dialysis patients
cards.summary: Kittiskulnam 2022: 3 months of IDPN raised albumin (3.5→3.8 g/dL) versus counselling (3.6→3.5 g/dL) in 38 supplement-intolerant dialysis patients
cards.people: 38 maintenance haemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting who could not tolerate oral nutritional supplements (mean age 67.6 years), randomised to 3 months of concentrated 3-in-1 fish-oil-based parenteral nutrition infused during dialysis, or intensive dietary counselling once weekly for 3 months; both groups were followed for a further 3 months. 18 patients in the IDPN group contributed to the 3-month albumin comparison as reported.
cards.result: At 3 months, serum albumin was significantly higher with IDPN, rising from 3.5±0.3 to 3.8±0.2 g/dL versus 3.6±0.3 to 3.5±0.3 g/dL with counselling (p=0.01). Spontaneous dietary intake (p=0.04), body weight (p=0.01), and malnutrition-inflammation score (p=0.01) improved in the IDPN group but not the control group; muscle mass, strength, prealbumin, interleukin-6, hs-CRP, and acylated ghrelin did not differ significantly. At 6 months albumin in the IDPN group remained above baseline (p=0.04). No volume overload or uncontrolled hyperglycaemia occurred.
cards.watchOut: Very small, single-country, unblinded, and built on nutritional surrogates — albumin in dialysis patients also tracks inflammation, so an albumin rise is not proof of better survival or fewer admissions, as the authors themselves state in calling for larger, longer studies.
cards.source: Kittiskulnam P et al. The beneficial effects of intradialytic parenteral nutrition in hemodialysis patients with protein energy wasting: a prospective randomized controlled trial. Sci Rep. 2022. PMID: 35296793. No registry ID appears in the record's abstract. cards.headline: ENEFLUID (Kabasawa 2024): IDPN with the ENEFLUID formulation did not improve transthyretin at 12 weeks (difference 1.3 mg/dL; P=0.41), though protein intake fell less
cards.summary: ENEFLUID (Kabasawa 2024): IDPN with the ENEFLUID formulation did not improve transthyretin at 12 weeks (difference 1.3 mg/dL; P=0.41), though protein intake fell less
cards.people: 40 adults on maintenance haemodialysis with mild-to-moderate malnutrition (Nutritional Risk Index-Japanese Hemodialysis score 5–10) in a multicentre, open-label Japanese trial; one patient withdrew before intervention, leaving 20 receiving IDPN with ENEFLUID (310 kcal, 550 mL) three times weekly for 12 weeks and 19 controls receiving none. Primary endpoint: change in serum transthyretin.
cards.result: Change in serum transthyretin at 12 weeks did not differ: +1.0 mg/dL (95% CI −1.1 to 3.2) with IDPN versus −0.3 (−2.4 to 1.9) in controls; between-group difference 1.3 (−1.7 to 4.3); P=0.41. Food protein intake rose with IDPN and fell in controls (changes +0.12 versus −0.18 g/kg/day; difference 0.30; 0.00 to 0.60; P=0.050). No adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Self-described as exploratory, open-label, and industry-involved (authors include employees of the product's manufacturer); 39 analysed patients cannot settle a nutritional question, and its primary endpoint was null.

shelves.title: Blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration for intradialytic hypotension: no reduction in the crossover trial
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients whose sessions are frequently complicated by symptomatic intradialytic hypotension, does blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration biofeedback reduce hypotensive episodes compared with best clinical practice alone?
shelves.mesh: Blood Volume · Cross-Over Studies · Feedback, Physiological · Humans · Hypotension · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Renal Dialysis · Ultrafiltration
shelves.balance: One small crossover trial in exactly the patients the technology is meant for found no benefit — if anything, the point estimate ran the wrong way. In 32 randomised haemodialysis patients whose sessions were frequently complicated by symptomatic intradialytic hypotension, the rate of symptomatic hypotension was 0.10 episodes per hour with blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration biofeedback versus 0.07 per hour with best clinical practice alone (P=0.29), with no differences in asymptomatic episodes, symptoms alone, weight gain, cardiac biomarkers, or recovery time. THIN: 26 patients completed the study, from a single programme in Calgary. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a properly randomised test in the right population, but small enough that a modest effect in either direction cannot be excluded.

cards.headline: Leung 2017: biofeedback did not reduce symptomatic intradialytic hypotension — 0.10 episodes/hour with biofeedback vs 0.07/hour with best clinical practice (P=0.29)
cards.summary: Leung 2017: biofeedback did not reduce symptomatic intradialytic hypotension — 0.10 episodes/hour with biofeedback vs 0.07/hour with best clinical practice (P=0.29)
cards.people: Patients on maintenance haemodialysis at five centres in Calgary, Canada, with more than 30% of sessions complicated by symptomatic intradialytic hypotension: 35 entered, 32 were randomised, and 26 completed a 22-week single-blind crossover trial (4-week run-in, 8 weeks of best clinical practice with or without blood-volume-guided ultrafiltration biofeedback, 2-week washout, then crossover). Primary outcome: rate of symptomatic intradialytic hypotension.
cards.result: The rate of symptomatic intradialytic hypotension was 0.10/h (95% confidence interval 0.06 to 0.14) with biofeedback and 0.07/h (0.05 to 0.10) during control (P=0.29). There were no differences in asymptomatic hypotension or symptoms alone, and results were consistent after adjustment for randomisation order and study week. Interdialytic weight gain, brain natriuretic peptide, cardiac troponins, extracellular-to-intracellular water ratio, ultrafiltration rate, and dialysis recovery time also did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Only 26 completers and a single regional programme; a crossover design in a symptomatic population is efficient but cannot exclude carryover or period effects, and the confidence intervals leave room for a modest benefit or harm.
cards.source: Leung KCW et al. Randomized Crossover Trial of Blood Volume Monitoring-Guided Ultrafiltration Biofeedback to Reduce Intradialytic Hypotensive Episodes with Hemodialysis. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017. PMID: 29018100. No registry ID appears in the record's abstract. shelves.title: Machine perfusion versus cold storage for deceased-donor kidneys: hypothermic perfusion helps, a 1-hour normothermic add-on does not
shelves.question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does hypothermic machine perfusion of the graft reduce delayed graft function compared with static cold storage?
shelves.mesh: Delayed Graft Function · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Organ Preservation · Perfusion · Tissue Donors
shelves.balance: The answer depends on which machine perfusion is meant. In the international paired trial (Moers 2009), one kidney from each of 336 deceased donors was randomised to hypothermic machine perfusion and the other to static cold storage: delayed graft function occurred in 70 recipients on machine perfusion versus 89 on cold storage (20.8% versus 26.5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.57, a relative effect), and 1-year graft survival was 94% versus 90%. In the later DCD trial (Hosgood 2023), adding just 1 hour of normothermic machine perfusion at the end of cold storage made no difference: delayed graft function was 60.7% with normothermic perfusion versus 58.5% with cold storage alone (adjusted odds ratio 1.13). So sustained hypothermic perfusion reduced delayed graft function, while a brief normothermic perfusion period after cold storage did not. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for hypothermic machine perfusion reducing delayed graft function / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for 1-hour normothermic perfusion added to cold storage — two large randomised trials, but testing two different perfusion strategies, so the verdict is split by technique rather than pooled.

cards.headline: Moers 2009: hypothermic machine perfusion cut delayed graft function (70 vs 89 cases) and improved 1-year graft survival (94% vs 90%)
cards.summary: Moers 2009: hypothermic machine perfusion cut delayed graft function (70 vs 89 cases) and improved 1-year graft survival (94% vs 90%)
cards.people: 672 recipients of kidneys from 336 consecutive deceased donors in an international randomised trial: one kidney from each donor was assigned to hypothermic machine perfusion and the paired kidney to static cold storage, with 1 year of follow-up. The primary end point was delayed graft function (dialysis required in the first week after transplantation).
cards.result: Delayed graft function developed in 70 patients in the machine-perfusion group versus 89 in the cold-storage group (20.8% versus 26.5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.57; P=0.01 — a relative effect, with the absolute rates given here). Machine perfusion also shortened delayed graft function, lowered serum creatinine in the first 2 weeks, and reduced graft failure (hazard ratio 0.52; P=0.03); 1-year allograft survival was 94% versus 90% (P=0.04). No serious adverse events were directly attributable to machine perfusion.
cards.watchOut: The paired design is strong — each donor contributes one kidney to each arm — but the comparison is hypothermic perfusion for the whole preservation period, not a short perfusion episode added at the end. Effects on delayed graft function were clearer than effects on other secondary end points, most of which did not differ.
cards.source: Moers C et al. Machine perfusion or cold storage in deceased-donor kidney transplantation. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19118301. Registry ID: ISRCTN83876362, from the record. cards.headline: Hosgood 2023: 1 hour of normothermic machine perfusion after cold storage did not reduce delayed graft function in DCD kidneys (60.7% vs 58.5%)
cards.summary: Hosgood 2023: 1 hour of normothermic machine perfusion after cold storage did not reduce delayed graft function in DCD kidneys (60.7% vs 58.5%)
cards.people: 338 kidneys from donation after circulatory death (DCD) donors randomised to static cold storage alone (n=168) or cold storage plus 1 hour of normothermic machine perfusion (n=170); 277 kidneys were included in the final intention-to-treat analysis. The primary end point was delayed graft function (dialysis in the first 7 days).
cards.result: Delayed graft function occurred in 82 of 135 (60.7%) normothermic-perfusion kidneys versus 83 of 142 (58.5%) cold-storage kidneys (adjusted odds ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.84; P=0.624 — a relative effect, with the absolute rates given here). Normothermic perfusion was not associated with more transplant thrombosis, infectious complications, or other adverse events, and was shown to be feasible and safe, but it did not reduce delayed graft function.
cards.watchOut: This trial tests a different intervention from Moers: a single 1-hour normothermic episode at the end of cold storage, in DCD kidneys with a much higher baseline delayed-graft-function rate (~59%). Its null result does not overturn the hypothermic-perfusion finding, and its confidence interval (0.69 to 1.84, relative) cannot exclude a moderate benefit or harm.
cards.source: Hosgood SA et al. Normothermic machine perfusion versus static cold storage in donation after circulatory death kidney transplantation: a randomized controlled trial. Nat Med. 2023. shelves.title: Donor hypothermia for delayed graft function: helps without machine perfusion, adds nothing to it, loses to it head-to-head
shelves.question: In deceased (brain-dead) kidney donors, does therapeutic hypothermia (34–35°C) reduce delayed graft function in recipients — and how does it compare with hypothermic machine perfusion?
shelves.mesh: Delayed Graft Function · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced · Kidney Transplantation · Tissue Donors
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials give a context-dependent answer. Where kidneys were not routinely machine-perfused, donor hypothermia helped: Niemann 2015 (370 donors, 572 recipients) found delayed graft function in 28% of recipients of hypothermia-donor kidneys versus 39% with normothermia (odds ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.92; P=0.02) — though that trial was stopped early for efficacy, which tends to inflate effects. Where machine perfusion was routine, hypothermia added nothing detectable: HYPOREME (Canet 2024; 526 recipients of expanded-criteria donor kidneys, all machine-perfused) found delayed graft function in 16% versus 21% (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.13; P=0.14), with 1-year creatinine slightly favouring hypothermia. And head-to-head, hypothermia lost: Malinoski 2023 (1,349 kidneys) found delayed graft function in 30% with donor hypothermia versus 19% with machine perfusion (adjusted risk ratio 1.72; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.17 — a relative measure, against absolute rates of 30% and 19%), with the combination (22%) no better than machine perfusion alone, and 1-year graft survival similar in all groups. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for hypothermia reducing delayed graft function when machine perfusion is not used / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) when added to routine machine perfusion, and inferior to machine perfusion in direct comparison.

cards.headline: Niemann 2015: delayed graft function 28% with donor hypothermia versus 39% with normothermia (OR 0.62) — trial stopped early for efficacy
cards.summary: Niemann 2015: delayed graft function 28% with donor hypothermia versus 39% with normothermia (OR 0.62) — trial stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 370 deceased organ donors after declaration of death by neurologic criteria (180 hypothermia, 190 normothermia) from two large US donation service areas, randomised to a targeted temperature of 34–35°C or 36.5–37.5°C from authorisation until organ recovery; 572 patients received kidney transplants (285 from hypothermia donors, 287 from normothermia donors). Primary outcome: delayed graft function, defined as dialysis during the first week after transplantation.
cards.result: Delayed graft function developed in 79 recipients (28%) in the hypothermia group and 112 (39%) in the normothermia group (odds ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.92; P=0.02). The trial was terminated early on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board after an interim analysis showed efficacy of hypothermia.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for efficacy at an interim analysis — early-stopped trials systematically overestimate benefit, and the later trials on this shelf did not reproduce an effect of this size. Conducted before machine perfusion became routine in the participating programmes, which is exactly the context that later proved to matter.

cards.headline: HYPOREME (Canet 2024): with routine machine perfusion, delayed graft function 16% with hypothermia versus 21% without (P=0.14)
cards.summary: HYPOREME (Canet 2024): with routine machine perfusion, delayed graft function 16% with hypothermia versus 21% without (P=0.14)
cards.people: 365 expanded-criteria deceased donors at 53 centres in France, randomised to hypothermia or normothermia, with hypothermic machine perfusion used routinely for the kidneys; 298 donors provided kidneys to 526 recipients (251 from hypothermia donors, 275 from normothermia donors). Primary outcome: delayed graft function in recipients.
cards.result: Delayed graft function occurred in 40 of 251 recipients (16%) in the hypothermia group versus 58 of 275 (21%) in the normothermia group (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.13; P=0.14; absolute difference −5.2 percentage points). At 1 year, serum creatinine was lower in the hypothermia group (152.4 versus 169.7 µmol/L (≈1.72 versus 1.92 mg/dL); P=0.0351) and creatinine clearance slightly higher (42.3 versus 40.5 mL/min; P=0.0414).
cards.watchOut: The population is expanded-criteria donors and every kidney was machine-perfused — the null here answers 'does hypothermia add to machine perfusion', not 'does hypothermia work at all'. The 1-year creatinine differences are secondary outcomes in a trial whose primary outcome was not significant.

cards.headline: Malinoski 2023: delayed graft function 30% with hypothermia versus 19% with machine perfusion — hypothermia inferior head-to-head
cards.summary: Malinoski 2023: delayed graft function 30% with hypothermia versus 19% with machine perfusion — hypothermia inferior head-to-head
cards.people: 725 brain-dead kidney donors at six US organ-procurement facilities randomised to therapeutic hypothermia, ex situ hypothermic machine perfusion, or both; 1,349 kidneys transplanted (359 hypothermia, 511 machine perfusion, 479 combination). Primary outcome: delayed graft function (dialysis in the first 7 days after transplantation). A secondary question was whether hypothermia alone was noninferior to machine perfusion alone.
cards.result: Delayed graft function occurred in 109 patients (30%) in the hypothermia group, 99 (19%) in the machine-perfusion group, and 103 (22%) in the combination group. Adjusted risk ratios (relative measures, against the absolute rates just given) were 1.72 (95% CI 1.35 to 2.17) for hypothermia versus machine perfusion, 1.57 (1.26 to 1.96) for hypothermia versus combination therapy, and 1.09 (0.85 to 1.40) for combination versus machine perfusion. Graft survival at 1 year was similar in the three groups. Ten adverse events were reported, including cardiovascular instability in 9 donors and organ loss in 1 donor owing to perfusion malfunction.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a different comparison from Niemann 2015: hypothermia versus machine perfusion, not versus ordinary normothermic management. Its result — machine perfusion superior, combination no better — is the strongest evidence on this shelf for centres choosing between the two strategies. A later subset report in low-risk nonpumped donors under the same registration exists but is not carded here; the draft for this shelf specified these three trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: hypothermia helps only where machine perfusion is absent; it adds nothing to, and loses against, machine perfusion — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: hypothermia helps only where machine perfusion is absent; it adds nothing to, and loses against, machine perfusion — SPLIT
cards.people: 572 recipients without routine machine perfusion (Niemann 2015), 526 recipients with routine machine perfusion (Canet 2024), and 1,349 kidneys in a three-way comparison (Malinoski 2023).
cards.result: Delayed graft function: 28% versus 39% favouring hypothermia without machine perfusion (OR 0.62); 16% versus 21% with machine perfusion (OR 0.71, not significant); 30% hypothermia versus 19% machine perfusion head-to-head (adjusted RR 1.72). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit without machine perfusion) / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (added to machine perfusion; inferior to machine perfusion alone).
cards.watchOut: The discordance is explained by context, not by any trial being 'wrong': perfusion status of the kidney differs across trials, and the positive trial stopped early. Delayed graft function is an early outcome; none of these trials shows a graft-survival difference.

shelves.title: Early corticosteroid cessation after kidney transplantation: matched graft outcomes, more mild rejection (Woodle trial, 5- and ~16-year results)
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients without delayed graft function, does stopping corticosteroids at day 7 match long-term low-dose prednisone (5 mg/day) on the 5-year composite of death, graft loss, and moderate/severe acute rejection?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Graft Rejection · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Prednisone · Tacrolimus
shelves.balance: One double-blind programme answers this, followed for a very long time. In 386 kidney transplant recipients without delayed graft function, randomised to stop corticosteroids at day 7 or continue low-dose prednisone (5 mg/day), the 5-year composite of death, graft loss, or moderate/severe acute rejection was 15.7% with early cessation versus 14.4% with continued steroids — no difference (Woodle 2008). Registry-linked follow-up to a median of 15.8 years still showed no difference in allograft failure (adjusted hazard ratio 0.83, relative; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10). The trade-off was rejection: biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was more frequent after early cessation (17.8% versus 10.8% at 5 years), but the extra episodes were mainly mild, steroid-sensitive Banff 1A rejections, while metabolic markers (triglycerides, weight gain, diabetes needing insulin) favoured stopping. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the death/graft-loss composite / POSSIBLE (harm) for biopsy-confirmed acute rejection — a single (THIN) double-blind programme, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite the long follow-up.

cards.headline: Woodle 2008: no difference in the 5-year composite (15.7% vs 14.4%) when steroids stopped at day 7, but more mild biopsy-confirmed rejection (17.8% vs 10.8%)
cards.summary: Woodle 2008: no difference in the 5-year composite (15.7% vs 14.4%) when steroids stopped at day 7, but more mild biopsy-confirmed rejection (17.8% vs 10.8%)
cards.people: 386 adult recipients of deceased- or living-donor kidney transplants without delayed graft function, randomised double-blind to early corticosteroid withdrawal at day 7 (n=191) or chronic corticosteroid therapy tapering to prednisone 5 mg/day (n=195), on tacrolimus/mycophenolate with antibody induction, blinded for 5 years. Primary end point: composite of death, graft loss, or moderate/severe acute rejection.
cards.result: At 5 years the primary composite occurred in 30/191 (15.7%) with withdrawal versus 28/195 (14.4%) with continued steroids; patient death 5.8% versus 6.7% and death-censored graft loss 5.8% versus 3.6% did not differ. Biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was higher with withdrawal (34/191, 17.8%, versus 21/195, 10.8%; P=0.058; Kaplan–Meier P=0.04), mainly mild Banff 1A steroid-sensitive episodes; antibody-treated rejection was similar (5.8% versus 6.7%). Renal function was identical (mean creatinine 1.5 mg/dL in both). Withdrawal favoured triglycerides, weight gain (median change 5.1 versus 7.7 kg; P=0.05), and diabetes requiring insulin (3.7% versus 11.6%; P=0.049).
cards.watchOut: Recipients had no delayed graft function and were selected for a tacrolimus/mycophenolate/antibody-induction backbone; the result does not automatically extend to higher-immunological-risk recipients or other regimens. 'No difference' on the composite coexists with a real increase in mild rejection — the two findings should not be merged.
cards.source: Woodle ES et al. A prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial comparing early (7 day) corticosteroid cessation versus long-term, low-dose corticosteroid therapy. Ann Surg. 2008. PMID: 18936569. Registry ID: NCT00650468, from the record. cards.headline: Woodle 2021: at a median of 15.8 years, allograft failure still did not differ (adjusted HR 0.83, relative; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10)
cards.summary: Woodle 2021: at a median of 15.8 years, allograft failure still did not differ (adjusted HR 0.83, relative; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10)
cards.people: The same trial cohort (385 analysed: 191 assigned to withdraw corticosteroids, 194 to continue), followed by linkage to a mandatory national registry until June 2018; median follow-up 15.8 years. Participants were low- to moderate-immune-risk adults without delayed graft function or rejection in the first week.
cards.result: The adjusted hazard ratio for allograft failure from any cause including death was 0.83 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.10; P=.19) and for allograft failure censored for patient death 0.78 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.19; P=.25) — relative effects; the abstract reports no absolute failure rates. Per-protocol results among 223 patients who stayed on their assigned treatment for at least 5 years were consistent.
cards.watchOut: This is a follow-up report of the same single trial, not an independent replication — the evidence remains one programme (THIN for replication, strong for duration). Registry ascertainment captures graft failure and death, not the milder rejection or metabolic outcomes reported at 5 years.
