shelves.title: Everolimus with calcineurin-inhibitor elimination after kidney transplantation (ZEUS): better GFR, more early rejection
shelves.question: In de novo kidney transplant recipients, does converting at 4.5 months from ciclosporin to an everolimus-based, calcineurin-inhibitor-free regimen improve renal function without losing efficacy (biopsy-proven rejection, graft loss, death)?
shelves.mesh: Calcineurin Inhibitors · Cyclosporine · Everolimus · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection · Humans · Kidney Transplantation
shelves.balance: In the single ZEUS trial, 503 de novo kidney transplant recipients were started on ciclosporin-based therapy and 300 were randomised at 4.5 months to eliminate the calcineurin inhibitor (everolimus-based regimen) or continue ciclosporin (Budde 2011). At 12 months, estimated GFR was clearly better after conversion (71.8 versus 61.9 mL/min/1.73 m², mean difference 9.8), and a living-donor subgroup report found the gap persisted at 5 years (67.2 versus 60.8; Sommerer 2016). The cost was rejection and tolerability: biopsy-proven acute rejection after randomisation was 10% versus 3% (full-period rates were equal at 15%), and everolimus brought more lipid elevation, proteinuria, low haemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, mouth ulcers, and diarrhoea. Patient and graft survival did not differ. This is one trial programme (THIN), with a surrogate renal-function primary end point. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for improved renal function / POSSIBLE (harm) for post-conversion rejection and adverse effects — the function benefit and the rejection/tolerability cost come from the same single programme and should not be merged into one stamp.

cards.headline: Budde 2011 (ZEUS): everolimus conversion improved 12-month GFR (71.8 vs 61.9 mL/min/1.73 m²) but post-randomisation rejection was 10% vs 3%
cards.summary: Budde 2011 (ZEUS): everolimus conversion improved 12-month GFR (71.8 vs 61.9 mL/min/1.73 m²) but post-randomisation rejection was 10% vs 3%
cards.people: 503 de novo kidney transplant recipients aged 18–65 enrolled on ciclosporin, enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium, corticosteroids, and basiliximab induction; 300 were randomised at 4.5 months to calcineurin-inhibitor elimination with everolimus (trough 6–10 ng/mL) plus mycophenolate and steroids, or to continue standard ciclosporin-based treatment. Primary objective: renal function (GFR, Nankivell formula) at 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 months GFR was 71.8 mL/min/1.73 m² on everolimus versus 61.9 on ciclosporin (mean difference 9.8 mL/min/1.73 m²; the abstract prints the 95% CI as −12.2 to −7.5). Biopsy-proven acute rejection after randomisation was higher with everolimus (15/154, 10%, versus 5/146, 3%; p=0.036) but similar over the full study period (15% versus 15%). Completion of study drug to 12 months was 118/155 (76%) versus 117/145 (81%). Everolimus was associated with higher mean lipids, slightly increased urinary protein excretion, lower haemoglobin, and more thrombocytopenia, aphthous stomatitis, and diarrhoea; hyperuricaemia was more common with ciclosporin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, industry-funded (Novartis Pharma, per the record), with an estimated-GFR primary end point rather than graft survival. The randomised population was the 300 of 503 enrolled patients who reached 4.5 months eligible for conversion — a selected, stable subgroup, not all de novo recipients.
cards.source: Budde K et al. Everolimus-based, calcineurin-inhibitor-free regimen in recipients of de-novo kidney transplants: an open-label, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21334736. Registry ID: NCT00154310, from the record. cards.headline: Sommerer 2016 (ZEUS living-donor subgroup, 5 years): GFR gap persisted (67.2 vs 60.8) in those who stayed on everolimus; rejection 22.0% vs 7.5% (not significant)
cards.summary: Sommerer 2016 (ZEUS living-donor subgroup, 5 years): GFR gap persisted (67.2 vs 60.8) in those who stayed on everolimus; rejection 22.0% vs 7.5% (not significant)
cards.type: Randomised trial subgroup long-term follow-up (ZEUS living-donor recipients)
cards.people: The living-donor subgroup of ZEUS: 80 living-donor recipients randomised at 4.5 months to convert to everolimus or continue cyclosporine; 75 completed the 1-year core study and 60 attended the 5-year follow-up visit. Outcomes: 5-year efficacy, renal function, and safety.
cards.result: At year 5, mean adjusted eGFR was 67.2 versus 60.8 mL/min/1.73 m² (mean difference 6.4; p=0.031); among patients who remained on study drug the difference was 13.2 (p=0.003), while in those who had switched off study drug it was −2.6 (p=0.701). Only 15/31 (48.4%) everolimus patients versus 20/29 (69.0%) cyclosporine patients remained on study drug at year 5. Patient and graft survival were similar; biopsy-proven acute rejection occurred in 22.0% versus 7.5% (p=0.116). One living-donor patient discontinued everolimus for adverse events during years 1–5.
cards.watchOut: This is a small subgroup report of the same ZEUS programme (60 patients at the 5-year visit), not the trial's full 5-year population and not an independent trial. The renal benefit was concentrated in patients who tolerated and stayed on everolimus — about half had left the drug by year 5.
cards.source: Sommerer C et al. Early conversion from cyclosporine to everolimus following living-donor kidney transplantation: outcomes at 5 years posttransplant in the randomized ZEUS trial. Clin Nephrol. 2016. PMID: 26932178. shelves.title: Switching to sirolimus to prevent further skin cancers after kidney transplantation (TUMORAPA, 5-year results)
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients on a calcineurin inhibitor who have had at least one cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, does switching to sirolimus prolong skin-cancer-free survival compared with maintaining calcineurin-inhibitor therapy?
shelves.mesh: Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Sirolimus · Skin Neoplasms · Transplant Recipients
shelves.balance: In the single TUMORAPA randomised trial, kidney transplant recipients who had already had at least one cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma were switched from a calcineurin inhibitor to sirolimus (n=64) or kept on the calcineurin inhibitor (n=56). At 5 years, survival free of squamous cell carcinoma was significantly longer with sirolimus (P=.007), and far fewer switched patients had developed new skin cancers: 22% versus 59% for squamous cell carcinoma, 34% versus 66% for other skin cancers, and 20% versus 37.5% for basal cell carcinoma (absolute rates). Kidney function and patient and graft survival were similar. This is one small trial (THIN) in a rare, high-risk population, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite the large absolute differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a benefit claim resting on a single small randomised trial with 5-year follow-up.

cards.headline: Dantal 2018 (TUMORAPA 5-year): switching to sirolimus — new squamous cell carcinomas in 22% vs 59% of patients at 5 years
cards.summary: Dantal 2018 (TUMORAPA 5-year): switching to sirolimus — new squamous cell carcinomas in 22% vs 59% of patients at 5 years
cards.people: 120 kidney transplant recipients receiving calcineurin inhibitors who had at least one cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, randomised to substitute sirolimus for calcineurin inhibitors (n=64) or maintain calcineurin-inhibitor treatment (n=56). Primary end point: survival free of squamous cell carcinoma at 5 years.
cards.result: Survival free of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma was significantly longer in the sirolimus group (P=.007). The proportion of patients with new skin cancers was lower with sirolimus: 22% versus 59% for squamous cell carcinomas (P<.001), 34% versus 66% for other skin cancers (P<.001), and 20% versus 37.5% for basal cell carcinomas (P<.05) — absolute rates. Kidney graft function and patient and graft survival were similar in both groups. In the sirolimus group the mean number of serious adverse effects per patient fell from 1.16 in the first 2 years to 0.83 between years 2 and 5.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (THIN): 120 patients, one trial programme, and a population defined by prior squamous cell carcinoma — the result does not address primary skin-cancer prevention or switching for other reasons. The 5-year report extends the trial's earlier 2-year report; it is not an independent second trial.
cards.source: Dantal J et al. Sirolimus for Secondary Prevention of Skin Cancer in Kidney Transplant Recipients: 5-Year Results. J Clin Oncol. 2018. PMID: 30016177. shelves.title: High-dose versus low-dose vitamin D after kidney transplantation (VITALE): no extraskeletal benefit; fewer fractures
shelves.question: In non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients with low vitamin D levels, does high-dose cholecalciferol (100,000 IU) versus low-dose (12,000 IU) reduce diabetes, major cardiovascular events, cancer, or death — and does it prevent fractures?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholecalciferol · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Vitamin D Deficiency
shelves.balance: VITALE (Courbebaisse 2023) randomised 536 non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients with 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 ng/mL to high-dose cholecalciferol (100,000 IU) or low-dose (12,000 IU), given every 2 weeks for 2 months then monthly for 22 months. Levels rose much more on high dose (+23 versus +6 ng/mL), but the primary composite — diabetes, major cardiovascular events, cancer, and death — occurred in 15% versus 16% (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.48; P=.78): no difference. The one positive finding was secondary: incident symptomatic fractures in 1% versus 4% (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.86; P=.03), an absolute difference of about 3 percentage points on small event numbers. Adverse-event incidence was similar. This is a dose-comparison trial with no placebo or untreated arm (THIN for the broader 'does vitamin D help' question). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the extraskeletal composite / POSSIBLE for fewer symptomatic fractures. This shelf does not add references to the held dietary-supplements shelves (#48–#60); it is the transplant-specific dose question only.

cards.headline: Courbebaisse 2023 (VITALE): high-dose vitamin D made no difference to diabetes, cardiovascular events, cancer or death (15% versus 16%); fractures 1% versus 4%
cards.summary: Courbebaisse 2023 (VITALE): high-dose vitamin D made no difference to diabetes, cardiovascular events, cancer or death (15% versus 16%); fractures 1% versus 4%
cards.people: 536 non-diabetic adult kidney transplant recipients, randomised 12 to 48 months after transplantation, with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 ng/mL, to high-dose cholecalciferol 100,000 IU (n=269) or low-dose 12,000 IU (n=267), every 2 weeks for 2 months and then monthly for 22 months. Primary outcome: composite of diabetes mellitus, major cardiovascular events, cancer, and death (intention-to-treat).
cards.result: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose by 23 ng/mL on high dose versus 6 ng/mL on low dose (P<.0001). A first composite event occurred in 15% of the high-dose group versus 16% of the low-dose group (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.48; P=.78). Incident symptomatic fracture occurred in 1% versus 4% (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.86; P=.03) — an odds ratio (relative measure) alongside absolute rates of 1% and 4%. The incidence of adverse events was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received vitamin D — there is no placebo group, so the trial cannot say whether any supplementation beats none. The fracture result is a secondary outcome based on roughly 3 versus 11 events; treat it as a signal, not proof. Participants were non-diabetic recipients 1–4 years post-transplant with low vitamin D levels.

shelves.title: Early basal insulin after kidney transplantation: pilot promised less post-transplant diabetes; the multicentre trial found none
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients without prior diabetes, does early postoperative basal insulin (treating glucose from 140 mg/dL) reduce post-transplant diabetes compared with standard threshold-based care?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin, Isophane · Kidney Transplantation · Postoperative Care
shelves.balance: A promising pilot did not hold up at scale. The single-centre proof-of-concept trial (Hecking 2012; 50 recipients) randomised patients to immediate postoperative basal (isophane) insulin whenever evening glucose reached 140 mg/dL, versus standard care treating at 180–250 mg/dL, and reported 73% lower odds of new-onset diabetes after transplantation with the early-insulin strategy (odds ratio 0.27 — a relative odds measure; the abstract reports no absolute diabetes rates), HbA1c on average 0.38% lower, and no treatment-group patient needing antidiabetic agents at 12 months versus 7 of 25 controls (28%). The multicentre trial designed to confirm it (Schwaiger 2021, ITP-NODAT; 263 recipients) found post-transplant diabetes at 12 months in 12.2% versus 14.7% on intention-to-treat (odds ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.76) and 13.4% versus 17.4% at 24 months (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.49) — no significant difference — with a lower odds only in per-protocol and adjusted analyses (adjusted odds ratio 0.21; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.62), and more hypoglycaemia (mostly asymptomatic or mild) on early insulin. Per-protocol findings cannot rescue a null intention-to-treat result. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the multicentre intention-to-treat analysis / MAYBE (weak evidence) for the pilot's suggested benefit. Wording note: this is post-transplant diabetes arising in people without prior diabetes, not prediabetes; the outcome is described as its occurrence, per the trials.

cards.headline: Hecking 2012 (pilot): early basal insulin associated with 73% lower odds of new-onset diabetes (OR 0.27) in 50 recipients
cards.summary: Hecking 2012 (pilot): early basal insulin associated with 73% lower odds of new-onset diabetes (OR 0.27) in 50 recipients
cards.people: 50 renal transplant recipients without a history of diabetes, all receiving tacrolimus, randomised at a single centre (Vienna) to immediate-postoperative isophane insulin for evening blood glucose of at least 140 mg/dL, or standard-of-care control (short-acting insulin and/or oral antidiabetic agents for blood glucose of 180–250 mg/dL). Follow-up 1 year. Mean insulin dose in the treatment group during the first 3 weeks was 17±11 IU/day.
cards.result: Throughout follow-up, the treatment group had 73% lower odds of new-onset diabetes after transplantation than the control group (odds ratio 0.27 — a relative odds measure; the abstract does not report the absolute diabetes rates), and HbA1c was on average 0.38% lower. At 12 months, all treatment-group patients were insulin-independent, whereas 7 of 25 controls (28%) required antidiabetic agents. Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia occurred five times in the treatment group and once in the control group. Beta-cell function was better in the treatment group throughout follow-up; insulin sensitivity did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, one centre, and the headline is an odds ratio without absolute event rates in the abstract — the size of any real benefit cannot be judged from this report alone. Essentially all treated patients qualified for insulin by the third evening, so the comparison is close to 'insulin for everyone' versus threshold-based care. This pilot is the hypothesis, not the answer; the next card is the answer attempted at scale.
cards.source: Hecking M et al. Early basal insulin therapy decreases new-onset diabetes after renal transplantation. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2012. PMID: 22343119. Registry ID: NCT00830297, from the article's PMC record. cards.headline: Schwaiger 2021 (ITP-NODAT): post-transplant diabetes 12.2% versus 14.7% at 12 months on intention-to-treat — no significant difference
cards.summary: Schwaiger 2021 (ITP-NODAT): post-transplant diabetes 12.2% versus 14.7% at 12 months on intention-to-treat — no significant difference
cards.people: 263 kidney transplant recipients without pretransplant diabetes at four European centres, randomised to early postoperative basal insulin (isophane insulin for afternoon glucose of at least 140 mg/dL; n=133) or standard of care (short-acting insulin for fasting glucose of at least 200 mg/dL; n=130). Primary outcome: post-transplant diabetes mellitus at 12 months, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Post-transplant diabetes occurred in 12.2% of the treatment group versus 14.7% of controls at 12 months (odds ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.76) and in 13.4% versus 17.4% at 24 months (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.49) — neither significant. In per-protocol analysis the odds ratio was 0.40 (95% CI 0.16 to 1.01) at 12 months, and an analysis adjusted for polycystic kidney disease gave an odds ratio of 0.21 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.62). Hypoglycaemia, mostly asymptomatic or mild, was more frequent in the treatment group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the control threshold (fasting glucose ≥200 mg/dL) differs from the pilot's control definition, so the two trials are not perfectly parallel. The favourable adjusted and per-protocol analyses are hypothesis-generating only — the prespecified intention-to-treat comparison is the result that counts, and it is null. More hypoglycaemia is the demonstrated cost of the strategy.

shelves.title: CMV prevention after kidney transplant: prophylaxis suppresses the virus better than preemptive therapy, without a rejection or graft advantage
shelves.question: In cytomegalovirus-seropositive kidney transplant recipients, does universal valganciclovir prophylaxis beat preemptive therapy (treatment triggered by DNAemia) on acute rejection, CMV disease, and long-term graft outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Cytomegalovirus Infections · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Transplant Recipients · Valganciclovir
shelves.balance: Two independent randomised trials point the same way on CMV itself but not on rejection or graft survival. In VIPP (Witzke 2018, 7-year results), valganciclovir prophylaxis in CMV-positive recipients cut CMV infection to 11.5% versus 39.7% and CMV disease to 4.7% versus 15.9% compared with preemptive therapy, while graft loss (7.4% versus 8.6%), death (9.5% versus 11.3%), and rejection (29.1% versus 28.5%) did not differ. In the OVERT trial (Reischig 2023), acute rejection at 12 months — its primary outcome — was 13% on prophylaxis versus 23% on preemptive therapy, a difference that was not statistically significant; subclinical rejection was less frequent with prophylaxis (13% versus 29%), DNAemia was much more frequent under preemptive therapy (75% versus 44%), CMV disease was 4% in both groups, and preemptive therapy meant less drug exposure and less neutropenia. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for prophylaxis preventing CMV infection and disease / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute rejection and long-term graft outcomes — two independent trials (DOUBLE-A) agree that prophylaxis suppresses the virus better, and neither shows a rejection or graft-survival advantage.

cards.headline: Reischig 2023 (OVERT): acute rejection not significantly lower with prophylaxis (13% vs 23%); subclinical rejection lower (13% vs 29%); DNAemia far more common preemptively (75% vs 44%)
cards.summary: Reischig 2023 (OVERT): acute rejection not significantly lower with prophylaxis (13% vs 23%); subclinical rejection lower (13% vs 29%); DNAemia far more common preemptively (75% vs 44%)
cards.people: 140 kidney transplant recipients (excluding CMV-seronegative recipients of seronegative-donor kidneys) at a single centre, randomised 1:1 to valganciclovir prophylaxis 900 mg daily for 3 months (6 months for seronegative recipients of seropositive-donor kidneys) or preemptive therapy — valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily started at CMV DNA ≥1000 IU/mL on weekly PCR for 4 months and stopped after two negative tests. Primary outcome: biopsy-confirmed acute rejection at 12 months.
cards.result: Acute rejection occurred in 9/70 (13%) on prophylaxis versus 16/70 (23%) on preemptive therapy — lower, but not statistically significant. Subclinical rejection at 3 months was 13% versus 29% (P=0.027). Both regimens prevented CMV disease (4% of patients in both groups). CMV DNAemia was significantly more frequent with preemptive therapy (75% versus 44%; P<0.001), with more high-viral-load episodes (≥2000 IU/mL), but preemptive therapy gave significantly lower valganciclovir exposure and less neutropenia.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and open-label, with 140 patients — underpowered for its rejection primary outcome, whose confidence interval is not given in the abstract. The population excluded the lowest-risk (D−/R−) group, and the preemptive arm used intensive weekly monitoring, which is part of the strategy being tested.
cards.source: Reischig T et al. A Randomized Trial of Valganciclovir Prophylaxis Versus Preemptive Therapy in Kidney Transplant Recipients. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2023. PMID: 36749127. Registry ID: ACTRN12613000554763, from the record. cards.headline: Witzke 2018 (VIPP, 7-year): prophylaxis cut CMV infection (11.5% vs 39.7%) and disease (4.7% vs 15.9%); graft loss, death, and rejection did not differ
cards.summary: Witzke 2018 (VIPP, 7-year): prophylaxis cut CMV infection (11.5% vs 39.7%) and disease (4.7% vs 15.9%); graft loss, death, and rejection did not differ
cards.people: 299 CMV-positive (R+) renal transplant recipients in a multicentre open-label trial (148 prophylaxis, 151 preemptive in the intention-to-treat/safety population), stratified by donor CMV status. Prophylaxis: valganciclovir 2 × 450 mg/day for 100 days, adjusted to renal function. Preemptive: valganciclovir 2 × 900 mg/day started at a viral load ≥400 copies/mL for at least 14 days, followed by secondary prophylaxis. Follow-up to 84 months; 47% completed follow-up.
cards.result: By month 84, CMV infection had occurred in 11.5% (95% CI 6.8 to 17.8) on prophylaxis versus 39.7% (31.9 to 48.0) on preemptive therapy (P<0.0001), and CMV disease in 4.7% (1.9 to 9.5) versus 15.9% (10.5 to 22.7) (P=0.002) — absolute rates. Graft loss (7.4% versus 8.6%), death (9.5% versus 11.3%), rejection (29.1% versus 28.5%), and eGFR (58.2 versus 59.9 mL/min/1.73 m²) did not differ significantly. Tolerability was comparable.
cards.watchOut: VIPP enrolled only CMV-positive recipients (intermediate risk) and used what its authors call a low-intensity surveillance protocol in the preemptive arm — more intensive monitoring, as in OVERT, narrows the gap in CMV disease. Only 47% completed the full 84-month follow-up.
cards.source: Witzke O et al. Valganciclovir Prophylaxis Versus Preemptive Therapy in Cytomegalovirus-Positive Renal Allograft Recipients: Long-term Results After 7 Years of a Randomized Clinical Trial. Transplantation. 2018. PMID: 29166336. Registry ID: NCT00372229, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis suppresses CMV better in both trials; neither shows less rejection or better graft survival — SPLIT verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis suppresses CMV better in both trials; neither shows less rejection or better graft survival — SPLIT verdict
cards.people: 140 recipients (Reischig 2023) and 299 CMV-positive recipients followed to 7 years (Witzke 2018).
cards.result: CMV infection 11.5% versus 39.7% and CMV disease 4.7% versus 15.9% with prophylaxis in VIPP; CMV disease 4% in both arms in OVERT. Acute rejection 13% versus 23% (not significant, OVERT) and 29.1% versus 28.5% (VIPP); graft loss and death similar in VIPP. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for prophylaxis preventing CMV infection and disease / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute rejection and long-term graft outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The two trials differ in risk group (VIPP: R+ only; OVERT: also D+/R−), monitoring intensity, and treatment thresholds — read the CMV-disease advantage as applying to prophylaxis versus the preemptive protocols actually tested, not versus any possible monitoring schedule. Drug cost, exposure, and neutropenia favour the preemptive side and are part of the real decision.

shelves.title: LCP-tacrolimus once daily versus immediate-release tacrolimus twice daily: noninferior, no outcome advantage
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients, does once-daily LCP-tacrolimus (extended-release formulation) prevent rejection and preserve graft function as well as twice-daily immediate-release tacrolimus — de novo and after conversion in stable patients?
shelves.mesh: Drug Administration Schedule · Graft Rejection · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Kidney Transplantation · Tacrolimus · Transplant Recipients
shelves.balance: The honest answer from the trials is equivalence, not advantage. In the primary de novo phase 3 trial (Budde 2014; 543 recipients), once-daily LCP-tacrolimus — the specific extended-release MeltDose formulation tested, named here because the question is about that formulation — met its noninferiority margin against twice-daily tacrolimus: treatment failure at 12 months was 18.3% versus 19.6%, with the upper 95% confidence limit of the difference (+5.27%) below the predefined +10% margin, and no significant differences in individual efficacy events or adverse events. Target troughs were reached faster and at a 14% lower cumulative dose. In stable recipients converting from immediate-release tacrolimus, the carded evidence is thinner: a post hoc Hispanic subgroup analysis of the conversion phase 3 trial (Faravardeh 2021; only 55 patients) found composite treatment failure in 4% versus 3%, with similar kidney function, troughs, and adverse events; a post hoc metaboliser analysis of the de novo trial (Suwelack 2020) likewise found no outcome differences in any metaboliser stratum. So there is no outcome the once-daily formulation improves — the case for it is convenience and pharmacokinetics, not better graft outcomes (THIN on the conversion side, where only subgroup analyses are carded). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for clinical outcomes in both settings, with noninferiority formally shown de novo.

cards.headline: Budde 2014: de novo treatment failure 18.3% on once-daily LCP-tacrolimus versus 19.6% on twice-daily tacrolimus — noninferiority met
cards.summary: Budde 2014: de novo treatment failure 18.3% on once-daily LCP-tacrolimus versus 19.6% on twice-daily tacrolimus — noninferiority met
cards.type: Phase III double-blind randomised trial (de novo)
cards.people: 543 de novo kidney transplant recipients randomised in a phase III double-blind trial to once-daily LCP-tacrolimus starting at 0.17 mg/kg/day (n=268) or twice-daily tacrolimus starting at 0.1 mg/kg/day (n=275). Primary end point: treatment failure (death, graft failure, biopsy-proven acute rejection, or lost to follow-up) within 12 months, against a predefined noninferiority margin of +10%.
cards.result: Treatment failure at 12 months was 18.3% with LCP-tacrolimus and 19.6% with twice-daily tacrolimus; the upper 95% confidence limit of the treatment difference was +5.27%, below the +10% noninferiority criterion. There were no significant differences in the incidence of individual efficacy events or adverse events. After the initial dose, 36.6% of the LCP-tacrolimus group had trough levels within 6–11 ng/mL versus 18.5% of the twice-daily group (troughs below 6 ng/mL in 33.5% versus 74.7%), and the cumulative study dose was 14% lower with LCP-tacrolimus.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority design: it shows LCP-tacrolimus is not unacceptably worse, within a generous +10% margin — it does not show superiority on any clinical outcome. The faster trough attainment and lower dose are pharmacokinetic advantages, not graft-outcome advantages. Industry-linked formulation trial.
cards.source: Budde K et al. Novel once-daily extended-release tacrolimus (LCPT) versus twice-daily tacrolimus in de novo kidney transplants: one-year results of Phase III, double-blind, randomized trial. Am J Transplant. 2014. PMID: 25278376. Registry ID: NCT01187953 — the record itself does not print the ID; it is the registration of this de novo phase 3 trial as given in the trial's post hoc analysis record (Suwelack 2020, PMID: 32719307). cards.headline: Faravardeh 2021: in the Hispanic subgroup of the conversion trial, failure was 4% after switching to LCP-tacrolimus versus 3% staying on immediate-release
cards.summary: Faravardeh 2021: in the Hispanic subgroup of the conversion trial, failure was 4% after switching to LCP-tacrolimus versus 3% staying on immediate-release
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a phase 3 conversion trial
cards.people: Post hoc subgroup analysis of the phase 3 conversion trial (NCT00817206): 55 stable adult kidney transplant recipients who self-identified as Hispanic or Latino, randomised to convert from immediate-release tacrolimus to a reduced dose of LCP-tacrolimus (n=26) or to remain on immediate-release tacrolimus (n=29), followed for 12 months. Outcomes: composite treatment failure, estimated glomerular filtration rate, and tacrolimus trough concentrations.
cards.result: Composite treatment failure occurred in 1 patient (4%) who converted to LCP-tacrolimus and 1 patient (3%) who remained on immediate-release tacrolimus. Estimated glomerular filtration rate was stable over time and similar in the two groups (P=0.08), as were tacrolimus trough levels (P=0.98). Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc subgroup of 55 patients with one failure event per arm — this can show the absence of a large signal, nothing finer. It is not the conversion trial's primary report, and several authors are employees of the formulation's manufacturer (Veloxis, per the record's affiliations). Do not generalise the subgroup to all stable recipients without the primary report.
cards.source: Faravardeh A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Once-Daily LCP-Tacrolimus Versus Twice-Daily Immediate-Release Tacrolimus in Adult Hispanic Stable Kidney Transplant Recipients: Sub-Group Analysis from a Phase 3 Trial. Ann Transplant. 2021. PMID: 33859155. Registry ID: NCT00817206, from the record. shelves.title: Bortezomib for late antibody-mediated rejection after kidney transplantation (BORTEJECT): no benefit, real toxicity
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with late donor-specific-antibody-positive antibody-mediated rejection, do two cycles of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib halt GFR decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Bortezomib · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Proteasome Inhibitors
shelves.balance: The only randomised trial in late antibody-mediated rejection is a clean negative. In BORTEJECT (Eskandary 2018), 44 kidney transplant recipients with donor-specific-antibody-positive late antibody-mediated rejection (median 5 years after transplant) received two cycles of bortezomib or placebo. The primary end point — the slope of eGFR decline — differed by 0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI −4.8 to 5.8; P=0.86), and nothing else separated the groups: measured GFR at 24 months, 2-year graft survival (81% versus 96%, not significant), proteinuria, donor-specific antibody levels, and biopsy morphology or molecular phenotypes were all similar. Bortezomib did cause gastrointestinal and haematologic toxicity. This is a single small trial (THIN), but it is placebo-controlled and internally consistent across every end point, and its confidence interval centres on no effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a null verdict on one small but rigorous trial, with documented toxicity on the harm side of the ledger.

cards.headline: Eskandary 2018 (BORTEJECT): bortezomib did not slow GFR decline in late antibody-mediated rejection (slope difference 0.5; P=0.86)
cards.summary: Eskandary 2018 (BORTEJECT): bortezomib did not slow GFR decline in late antibody-mediated rejection (slope difference 0.5; P=0.86)
cards.people: 44 donor-specific-antibody-positive kidney transplant recipients with characteristic antibody-mediated rejection morphology (median 5.0 years after transplantation; identified by screening 741 patients), randomised to two cycles of bortezomib (1.3 mg/m² intravenously on days 1, 4, 8, and 11 per cycle; n=21) or placebo (n=23). Primary end point: eGFR slope.
cards.result: The difference in eGFR slope between bortezomib and placebo was 0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI −4.8 to 5.8; P=0.86). There were no significant differences in median measured GFR at 24 months (33 versus 42 mL/min/1.73 m²; P=0.31), 2-year graft survival (81% versus 96%; P=0.12), urinary protein concentration, donor-specific antibody levels, or morphologic or molecular rejection phenotypes on 24-month biopsies. Bortezomib was associated with gastrointestinal and haematologic toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Small (44 patients) and single-centre-led — a modest benefit cannot be excluded statistically, but the point estimates favour placebo on several end points and toxicity is real. The record gives no registry ID in its abstract, so none is claimed here. The trial addresses late, established antibody-mediated rejection, not early or acute episodes.
cards.source: Eskandary F et al. A Randomized Trial of Bortezomib in Late Antibody-Mediated Kidney Transplant Rejection. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2018. PMID: 29242250. shelves.title: Kidney transplant recipients: fluvastatin missed its primary endpoint but cut cardiac death and MI (ALERT)
shelves.question: In renal transplant recipients, does fluvastatin versus placebo reduce major adverse cardiac events?
shelves.mesh: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Kidney Transplantation · Cardiovascular Diseases · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — a single trial, and its two layers point different ways, so this shelf splits. In ALERT, 2,102 renal transplant recipients were randomised to fluvastatin or placebo for a mean of 5.1 years; LDL cholesterol fell 32% relative on fluvastatin. The primary endpoint — cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention — was not significantly reduced (risk ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.06; p=0.139). But the prespecified secondary composite of cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction did differ: 70 versus 104 events (6.7% versus 9.9% in absolute terms; RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.88; p=0.005). Other secondary endpoints, including overall mortality and graft outcomes, did not differ significantly. The coronary-intervention component counted in the primary endpoint but not the secondary one is the most likely reason the two disagree. PROPOSED SPLIT — MAYBE (weak evidence) on the trial's own primary question; POSSIBLE for cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (Tier C: a mortality-containing endpoint).

cards.headline: ALERT 2003: primary endpoint RR 0.83 (p=0.139, not significant); cardiac death or nonfatal MI RR 0.65 (p=0.005)
cards.summary: ALERT 2003: primary endpoint RR 0.83 (p=0.139, not significant); cardiac death or nonfatal MI RR 0.65 (p=0.005)
cards.people: 2,102 renal transplant recipients with total cholesterol 4.0 to 9.0 mmol/L (≈155 to 348 mg/dL) (fluvastatin n=1,050; placebo n=1,052), followed for a mean of 5.1 years in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Primary endpoint: occurrence of a major adverse cardiac event — cardiac death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention procedure — over the follow-up period.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell 32% relative on fluvastatin versus placebo. For the primary endpoint the risk ratio was 0.83 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.06; p=0.139) — not significant. The prespecified secondary endpoint of cardiac death or definite non-fatal myocardial infarction occurred in 70 patients on fluvastatin versus 104 on placebo (6.7% vs 9.9% absolute; RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.88; p=0.005). Other secondary endpoints did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: THIN: one trial, and the significant result is a secondary endpoint while the primary endpoint — the question the trial was powered and designed to answer — was not significant. An open-label extension and later pooled analyses exist but are not randomised evidence and are not carded here.
cards.source: Holdaas H et al. Effect of fluvastatin on cardiac outcomes in renal transplant recipients: a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (ALERT). Lancet. 2003. PMID: 12814712. Registry ID: none in the fetched record (2003 trial).

shelves.title: Spironolactone on dialysis: two large blinded trials found no cardiovascular benefit — overturning a small open-label trial that had claimed mortality was cut by two thirds
shelves.question: In patients receiving maintenance dialysis for kidney failure, does spironolactone reduce cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · *Heart Failure/prevention & control/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · *Kidney Failure, Chronic/therapy/complications/mortality · *Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Renal Dialysis · *Spironolactone/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This shelf replaces the assigned allopurinol-in-CKD question, which the library already covers on shelf #168 (CKD-FIX and PERL). For a decade the case for spironolactone on dialysis rested on one small open-label trial (Matsumoto 2014, PMID: 24184249) reporting cardiovascular death or hospitalisation in 5.7% versus 12.5% of patients and all-cause mortality of 6.4% versus 19.7%. The two large double-blind trials reported in 2025 did not reproduce any of it: in ACHIEVE (Walsh 2025, PMID: 40818850; 2,538 randomised patients), the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred at 10.46 versus 11.33 events per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.09), all-cause mortality was similar (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.09), and the trial was stopped early for futility; in ALCHEMIST (Rossignol 2025, PMID: 40818851; 644 high-risk haemodialysis patients), major cardiovascular events occurred in 24% of both groups (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.36), and potassium above 6 mmol/L was as common on placebo as on spironolactone (41% versus 42%) in this run-in-selected population. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two adequately sized blinded trials agree on no benefit. Tier C: taken to the developer personally (a cardiovascular-event and mortality question).

cards.headline: Walsh 2025 (ACHIEVE): cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10.46 versus 11.33 per 100 patient-years on spironolactone versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.92) — stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Walsh 2025 (ACHIEVE): cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10.46 versus 11.33 per 100 patient-years on spironolactone versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.92) — stopped early for futility
cards.type: International randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 2,538 patients on maintenance dialysis (ACHIEVE, Walsh 2025)
cards.people: Adults on maintenance dialysis for at least three months (aged 45 or over, or 18 or over with diabetes) at 143 dialysis programmes in 12 countries. Of 3,565 patients who entered an open-label run-in, the 2,538 who tolerated and adhered to spironolactone 25 mg daily were randomised (1,260 spironolactone, 1,278 placebo) to continue it or switch to matching placebo; median follow-up was 1.8 years. The primary outcome was the composite of cardiovascular mortality or hospitalisation for heart failure.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 258 spironolactone patients (10.46 events per 100 patient-years) and 276 placebo patients (11.33 per 100 patient-years) — hazard ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.09; p = 0.35). Death from any cause was similar (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.09), as was hospitalisation for any cause (0.96, 0.87 to 1.06). After a planned interim analysis at 75% of expected events, the monitoring committee recommended stopping the trial early for futility.
cards.watchOut: The run-in design means everyone randomised had already tolerated spironolactone, so the trial cannot speak to starting it in unselected dialysis patients — and its safety results flatter the drug for the same reason. Even so, in this best-case population there was no efficacy signal at all.
cards.source: Walsh M et al. Spironolactone versus placebo in patients undergoing maintenance dialysis (ACHIEVE): an international, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40818850. Registry ID: NCT03020303, from the record. cards.headline: Rossignol 2025 (ALCHEMIST): major cardiovascular events in 24% of both groups (hazard ratio 1.00); potassium above 6 mmol/L in 42% on spironolactone and 41% on placebo
cards.summary: Rossignol 2025 (ALCHEMIST): major cardiovascular events in 24% of both groups (hazard ratio 1.00); potassium above 6 mmol/L in 42% on spironolactone and 41% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 644 high-risk haemodialysis patients (ALCHEMIST, Rossignol 2025)
cards.people: Adults on chronic haemodialysis with at least one cardiovascular comorbidity or risk factor, at 64 centres in France, Belgium and Monaco. After a four-week open-label run-in on spironolactone 25 mg every other day, 644 patients were randomised to spironolactone titrated to 25 mg daily (320) or placebo (324); median follow-up was 32.6 months. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, stroke or heart-failure hospitalisation.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 78 of 320 spironolactone patients (24%; 10.66 per 100 patient-years) and 79 of 324 placebo patients (24%; 10.70 per 100 patient-years) — hazard ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.36; p = 0.98). Hyperkalaemia above 6 mmol/L was reported in 135 patients (42%) on spironolactone and 134 (41%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.43). The trial's updated meta-analysis of blinded trials found mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists did not reduce all-cause or cardiovascular mortality in dialysis patients. The trial stopped prematurely when sponsor funding ran out.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than ACHIEVE and stopped early for funding, so its confidence interval (0.73 to 1.36) cannot exclude a moderate benefit on its own — its weight comes from pointing the same way as ACHIEVE. As in ACHIEVE, the run-in means randomised patients were pre-selected tolerators, which is the likely explanation for the unexpectedly similar hyperkalaemia rates between arms.
cards.source: Rossignol P et al. Spironolactone in patients on chronic haemodialysis at high risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes (ALCHEMIST): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial and updated meta-analysis. The Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40818851. Registry ID: NCT01848639, from the record. cards.headline: Matsumoto 2014: the small open-label trial behind a decade of use — cardiovascular events 5.7% versus 12.5% and death 6.4% versus 19.7% favouring spironolactone
cards.summary: Matsumoto 2014: the small open-label trial behind a decade of use — cardiovascular events 5.7% versus 12.5% and death 6.4% versus 19.7% favouring spironolactone
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial without placebo, 309 haemodialysis patients (Matsumoto 2014)
cards.people: 309 oligoanuric haemodialysis patients at five Japanese clinics, randomised to spironolactone 25 mg daily without dietary potassium restriction (157 patients) or to a control group receiving no spironolactone (152), followed for three years. The primary outcome was the composite of death from cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events or hospitalisation for them; the secondary outcome was all-cause death.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 5.7% of the spironolactone group versus 12.5% of controls (hazard ratio 0.404, 95% CI 0.202 to 0.809; adjusted 0.379). All-cause death occurred in 6.4% versus 19.7% (hazard ratio 0.355, 95% CI 0.191 to 0.662; adjusted 0.335). Gynaecomastia or breast pain was reported in 16 patients (10.2%) on spironolactone, and serious hyperkalaemia led to discontinuation in three patients (1.9%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, unblinded, no placebo, 309 patients and few events: the mortality gap (6.4% versus 19.7%) is far larger than any plausible drug effect and is the classic signature of a small trial with baseline imbalance or co-intervention differences. It is carded because it drove practice — and because ACHIEVE and ALCHEMIST, with eight times the patients and proper blinding, found nothing. Read this shelf as a cautionary tale about small open-label trials, not as a tie between equals.
cards.source: Matsumoto Y et al. Spironolactone reduces cardiovascular and cerebrovascular morbidity and mortality in hemodialysis patients. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014. cards.headline: Synthesis: the two blinded trials agree — spironolactone does not reduce cardiovascular events or death on dialysis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the two blinded trials agree — spironolactone does not reduce cardiovascular events or death on dialysis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Three randomised records in maintenance dialysis: two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials reported in 2025 (2,538 and 644 randomised patients, both with tolerability run-ins) and one small open-label Japanese trial from 2014 (309 patients).
cards.result: ACHIEVE: hazard ratio 0.92 (0.78 to 1.09) for cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation, and 0.95 (0.83 to 1.09) for all-cause death, stopped for futility. ALCHEMIST: hazard ratio 1.00 (0.73 to 1.36) for major cardiovascular events. Matsumoto: hazard ratios of 0.40 for cardiovascular events and 0.36 for death — effects of a size the blinded trials exclude. Hyperkalaemia above 6 mmol/L was common in ALCHEMIST but no commoner on spironolactone than placebo among run-in tolerators (42% versus 41%).
cards.watchOut: Both big trials pre-selected patients who tolerated spironolactone in a run-in, so neither answers what happens when it is started in all-comers, and neither was powered for dialysis-specific harms such as gynaecomastia (10.2% in Matsumoto). The null applies to cardiovascular prevention; it says nothing about other uses of the drug.
cards.source: Synthesis of Walsh M et al. The Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40818850); Rossignol P et al. The Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40818851); Matsumoto Y et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014 (PMID: 24184249).

shelves.title: Hepatitis B vaccination in dialysis patients: adjuvanted vaccines and intradermal rescue raise seroprotection in individual trials, but the pooled adjuvant advantage is not significant
shelves.question: In patients on dialysis, do intensified hepatitis B vaccine regimens (high-dose, four-dose, or adjuvanted) achieve seroprotection?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Follow-Up Studies · Hepatitis B/prevention & control · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens/blood · Hepatitis B Vaccines/immunology · Lipid A/analogs & derivatives/immunology · Renal Dialysis · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — intensified regimens beat the standard schedule in individual trials on the seroprotection surrogate, but the pooled evidence is equivocal and no trial measures clinical hepatitis B. The reference intensified regimen is four double doses of standard vaccine; against that benchmark, the AS04-adjuvanted vaccine (HBV-AS04) produced an earlier antibody response, higher titres and significantly higher seroprotection rates throughout 42 months of follow-up in pre-dialysis and haemodialysis patients, with slower decline and fewer boosters needed (Kong 2008, PMID: 18160963). A TLR9-agonist-adjuvanted vaccine (HBsAg-1018, the vaccine later licensed as Heplisav-B) given as 3 single doses achieved a seroprotection rate of 89.9% at week 28 versus 81.8% for four double doses of standard vaccine in 467 evaluable patients with chronic kidney disease — meeting both non-inferiority and superiority — with geometric mean antibody concentrations of 587.1 versus 156.5 mIU/mL (Janssen 2013, PMID: 23727422). For patients who have already failed a primary course, route matters: in 59 haemodialysis nonresponders, intradermal revaccination (10 µg weekly for 8 weeks) produced seroconversion in 79% versus 40% with intramuscular revaccination (odds ratio 5.5, 95% CI 1.6 to 18.4), with higher peak titres (Barraclough 2009, PMID: 19481320). Against all this stands the meta-analysis of adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccines in chronic kidney disease: across 10 randomised trials with 1,228 patients, the pooled odds ratio for seroprotection with adjuvants was 1.47 (95% CI 0.88 to 2.46) — not significant, including in the AS04/AS02 subgroup (Fabrizi 2012, PMID: 22285268). The fair reading: seroprotection is achievable in most dialysis patients with intensified schedules; adjuvanted products won their own trials but not the pooled analysis, possibly because trials differed in populations and comparators; and seroprotection (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) is a surrogate whose durability on dialysis is itself imperfect. Hepatitis B vaccination of healthcare workers who fail a first series is a different population, held as a separate question in the slate.

cards.headline: Kong 2008: the AS04-adjuvanted vaccine gave earlier, higher and longer-lasting seroprotection than four double doses of standard vaccine in dialysis patients
cards.summary: Kong 2008: the AS04-adjuvanted vaccine gave earlier, higher and longer-lasting seroprotection than four double doses of standard vaccine in dialysis patients
cards.people: Pre-haemodialysis and haemodialysis patients in the primary vaccination study of HBV-AS04 (hepatitis B vaccine with the AS04 adjuvant system) versus four double doses of standard hepatitis B vaccine, with antibody persistence followed for up to 42 months and booster responses assessed in patients who lost seroprotection.
cards.result: HBV-AS04 elicited an earlier antibody response and higher antibody titres than the standard regimen, and seroprotection rates were significantly higher in HBV-AS04 recipients throughout the study. The decline in seroprotection over time was significantly less in the HBV-AS04 group, and significantly fewer primed patients required a booster dose during follow-up. Solicited and unsolicited adverse events were rare after booster doses; 57 patients had a serious adverse event during follow-up, none vaccine-related. (The record reports these comparisons without pooled percentages; no figures beyond the abstract's are claimed here.)
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports direction and significance rather than the actual seroprotection percentages, so the size of the advantage cannot be quoted from this record — a real limitation when comparing against the meta-analysis at card 4. The population mixes pre-dialysis with haemodialysis patients, whose responsiveness differs.
cards.source: Kong NC et al. A new adjuvant improves the immune response to hepatitis B vaccine in hemodialysis patients. Kidney international. 2008. PMID: 18160963. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Janssen 2013: three doses of the TLR9-adjuvanted vaccine beat four double doses of standard vaccine — seroprotection 89.9% versus 81.8% at week 28
cards.summary: Janssen 2013: three doses of the TLR9-adjuvanted vaccine beat four double doses of standard vaccine — seroprotection 89.9% versus 81.8% at week 28
cards.people: Observer-blind, randomised, active-controlled multicentre trial in 521 patients aged 18–75 with chronic kidney disease (467 in the modified intention-to-treat population): 3 single doses of HBsAg-1018 (20 µg antigen plus 3,000 µg of the TLR9 agonist adjuvant 1018) at weeks 0, 4 and 24, versus 4 double doses of licensed vaccine (HBsAg-Eng) at weeks 0, 4, 8 and 24 — 8 injections. Follow-up 1 year; primary endpoint seroprotection (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) at week 28.
cards.result: Seroprotection at week 28 was 89.9% with HBsAg-1018 versus 81.8% with HBsAg-Eng, meeting criteria for both non-inferiority and superiority. The proportion reaching anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL was 73.6% versus 63.2%, and geometric mean concentration was 587.1 versus 156.5 mIU/mL. Seroprotection was significantly higher with HBsAg-1018 as early as weeks 8 and 12 and remained higher at 52 weeks. Tolerability was similar between groups. This vaccine was later licensed as Heplisav-B (Dynavax).
cards.watchOut: The population is chronic kidney disease broadly, not exclusively dialysis patients — responsiveness in the trial is better than a pure haemodialysis cohort would show. The absolute seroprotection advantage is 8.1 percentage points on a surrogate endpoint; whether it converts into fewer clinical hepatitis B infections on dialysis units is untested.
cards.source: Janssen RS et al. Immunogenicity and safety of an investigational hepatitis B vaccine with a toll-like receptor 9 agonist adjuvant (HBsAg-1018) compared with a licensed hepatitis B vaccine in patients with chronic kidney disease. Vaccine. 2013. PMID: 23727422. Registry ID: NCT00985426. cards.headline: Barraclough 2009: in haemodialysis patients who had failed primary vaccination, intradermal revaccination seroconverted 79% versus 40% intramuscularly
cards.summary: Barraclough 2009: in haemodialysis patients who had failed primary vaccination, intradermal revaccination seroconverted 79% versus 40% intramuscularly
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in vaccine nonresponders (Barraclough 2009)
cards.people: Prospective open-label randomised controlled trial in 59 haemodialysis patients nonresponsive to primary hepatitis B vaccination: revaccination intradermally (10 µg weekly for 8 weeks) versus intramuscularly (40 µg at weeks 1 and 8). Primary outcome: anti-HBs ≥10 IU/L within 2 months of the course; titres followed to 24 months.
cards.result: Seroconversion was 79% with intradermal versus 40% with intramuscular revaccination (P = 0.002); the unadjusted odds ratio was 5.5 (95% CI 1.6 to 18.4), and route was the only predictor of seroconversion. Geometric mean peak titre was 239 IU/L (95% CI 131 to 434) intradermally versus 78 IU/L (36 to 168) intramuscularly (P < 0.001), with a trend toward longer seroprotection. Intradermal vaccine was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A single small open-label trial (59 patients), and its design cannot separate the effect of the intradermal route from the effect of eight weekly injections — cumulative dose and repetition may be doing some of the work. The authors themselves flag the surrogate endpoint and the absence of long-term clinical protection data.
cards.source: Barraclough KA et al. randomised controlled trial in vaccine nonresponders (barraclough 2009) prospective open-label randomised controlled trial in 59 haemodialysis patients nonresponsive to primary hepatitis b vaccination: revaccination intradermally (10 µg weekly for 8 weeks) versus intramuscularly (40 µg at weeks 1 and 8). primary outcome: anti-hbs ≥10 iu/l within 2 months of the course; titres followed to 24 months. seroconversion was 79% with intradermal versus 40% with intramuscular revaccination (p = 0.002); the unadjusted odds ratio was 5.5 (95% ci 1.6 to 18.4), and route was the only predictor of seroconversion. geometric mean peak titre was 239 iu/l (95% ci 131 to 434) intradermally versus 78 iu/l (36 to 168) intramuscularly (p < 0.001), with a trend toward longer seroprotection. intradermal vaccine was safe and well tolerated. a single small open-label trial (59 patients), and its design cannot separate the effect of the intradermal route from the effect of eight weekly injections — cumulative dose and repetition may be doing some of the work. the authors themselves flag the surrogate endpoint and the absence of long-term clinical protection data. barraclough ka et al. intradermal versus intramuscular hepatitis b vaccination in hemodialysis patients: a prospective open-label randomized controlled trial in nonresponders to primary vaccination. american journal of kidney diseases. 2009. pmid: 19481320. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · antibodies, viral/blood · chronic disease · female · hepatitis b/prevention & control · hepatitis b vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · humans · injections, intradermal · injections, intramuscular · kaplan-meier estimate · kidney diseases/therapy · male · middle aged · prospective studies · renal dialysis · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Fabrizi 2012: pooling 10 randomised trials (1,228 patients), adjuvanted vaccines did NOT significantly improve seroprotection (odds ratio 1.47, 0.88 to 2.46)
cards.summary: Fabrizi 2012: pooling 10 randomised trials (1,228 patients), adjuvanted vaccines did NOT significantly improve seroprotection (odds ratio 1.47, 0.88 to 2.46)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of prospective randomised trials of recombinant hepatitis B vaccine with adjuvants versus recombinant vaccine alone in patients with chronic kidney disease: 10 studies, 1,228 unique patients. Primary endpoint: seroprotection rate after vaccination; random-effects pooling with heterogeneity and subgroup analyses.
cards.result: The pooled odds ratio for seroprotection with adjuvanted versus non-adjuvanted vaccine was 1.47 (95% CI 0.88 to 2.46) — not significant. In the subgroup of trials using the novel adjuvant systems HBV-AS04 or HBV-AS02, the pooled odds ratio was 2.22 (95% CI 0.72 to 6.78), also not significant, with significant heterogeneity (Q = 10.819, P = 0.004). The authors concluded the results do not support adjuvantation as a general approach to improving immunogenicity in this population.
cards.watchOut: The pooled null sits in visible tension with the positive individual trials carded above it — the likely explanations are heterogeneity (different adjuvants, doses, comparators and CKD stages across small trials) rather than proof that no adjuvant works. This meta-analysis predates the Janssen 2013 TLR9 trial, so the newest adjuvant class is not in its pool.
cards.source: Fabrizi F et al. Hepatitis B virus vaccine in chronic kidney disease: improved immunogenicity by adjuvants? A meta-analysis of randomized trials. Vaccine. 2012. PMID: 22285268. cards.headline: Synthesis: intensified schedules raise seroprotection, adjuvants win their own trials but not the pooled analysis — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: intensified schedules raise seroprotection, adjuvants win their own trials but not the pooled analysis — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three randomised trials (an AS04-adjuvanted vaccine in dialysis patients; a TLR9-adjuvanted vaccine in 521 CKD patients; intradermal rescue in 59 haemodialysis nonresponders) and one meta-analysis of 10 adjuvant trials (1,228 patients).
cards.result: Seroprotection: 89.9% versus 81.8% for the TLR9-adjuvanted vaccine versus four double doses (week 28); significantly higher and more durable seroprotection with HBV-AS04 versus the same standard comparator; 79% versus 40% seroconversion for intradermal versus intramuscular rescue in nonresponders. Pooled adjuvant effect: odds ratio 1.47 (0.88–2.46), not significant. Every endpoint is the anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL surrogate; no study measures clinical hepatitis B.
cards.watchOut: Seroprotection is a laboratory threshold, and dialysis patients lose antibody over time — a regimen that wins at week 28 may need boosters the trials only partly map. The stamp reflects surrogate-endpoint, partly contradictory evidence: enough to justify intensified schedules in practice, not enough to declare any single product superior for patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kong NC et al. Kidney international. 2008 (PMID: 18160963); Janssen RS et al. Vaccine. 2013 (PMID: 23727422); Barraclough KA et al. American journal of kidney diseases. 2009 (PMID: 19481320); Fabrizi F et al. Vaccine. 2012 (PMID: 22285268).

shelves.title: Sucroferric oxyhydroxide: the same phosphate control as sevelamer on roughly a third of the tablets — paid for with more diarrhoea and more early withdrawals
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia, does sucroferric oxyhydroxide control phosphate with fewer pills than sevelamer?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chelating Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Constipation/chemically induced · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Female · Ferric Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperphosphatemia/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Induction Chemotherapy · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced · Patient Dropouts · Peritoneal Dialysis · Phosphorus/blood · Polyamines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/therapy · Sevelamer
shelves.balance: Yes — on the evidence of two randomised phase 3 trials, sucroferric oxyhydroxide (PA21 in the trial reports) lowers serum phosphate as effectively as sevelamer, and the tablet count is not close. In the global trial (Floege 2014, PMID: 24646861), phosphate fell −0.71 versus −0.79 mmol/L at 12 weeks, meeting non-inferiority, on an average of about 3 tablets a day against 8; in the Japanese trial (Koiwa 2017, PMID: 27496336) end-of-treatment phosphate was 1.62 versus 1.72 mmol/L on 5.6 versus 18.7 tablets a day. Recorded non-adherence was lower on sucroferric oxyhydroxide (15.1% vs 21.3%) — but so was tolerability at the margin: more patients withdrew for adverse events (15.7% vs 6.6%), with diarrhoea and discoloured faeces the typical price, against nausea and constipation on sevelamer. The 1-year post hoc analysis of the same global programme (Ketteler 2019, PMID: 29846719 — a repeat report of the Floege trial, flagged on its card) found phosphate down 30% relative and FGF-23 down a median 64% relative across both binders pooled; that is a class effect of phosphate lowering, not an advantage of one drug. What none of this answers is whether any binder changes death, cardiovascular events or fractures — the hard-outcome comparison of non-calcium versus calcium binders is shelf #295, and no sucroferric-versus-sevelamer trial has tested clinical endpoints.

cards.headline: Floege 2014 (phase 3): phosphate fell −0.71 vs −0.79 mmol/L at 12 weeks — non-inferior — on an average of 3 tablets of sucroferric oxyhydroxide a day against 8 of sevelamer
cards.summary: Floege 2014 (phase 3): phosphate fell −0.71 vs −0.79 mmol/L at 12 weeks — non-inferior — on an average of 3 tablets of sucroferric oxyhydroxide a day against 8 of sevelamer
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Floege 2014, PA21 Study Group)
cards.people: 707 patients randomised to PA21 (sucroferric oxyhydroxide) 1.0–3.0 g/day and 348 to sevelamer carbonate 4.8–14.4 g/day — haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia, open-label: 8 weeks of dose titration, 4 weeks fixed, 12 weeks maintenance. Afterwards, 99 haemodialysis patients on PA21 were re-randomised for 3 weeks to their maintenance dose or a low (ineffective) dose of 250 mg/day.
cards.result: Serum phosphorus reduction at week 12 was −0.71 mmol/L on PA21 versus −0.79 mmol/L on sevelamer, meeting non-inferiority, and control was maintained to week 24; in the re-randomised subset the maintenance dose held phosphate control better than the low dose. The average tablet burden was about 3 PA21 tablets a day versus 8 sevelamer tablets. Non-adherence was 15.1% on PA21 versus 21.3% on sevelamer. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 83.2% versus 76.1%; withdrawal for adverse events was higher on PA21 (15.7% vs 6.6%). Mild transient diarrhoea, discoloured faeces and hyperphosphataemia were more frequent with PA21; nausea and constipation were more frequent with sevelamer.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the endpoint is a blood level, not a clinical event: this trial cannot say whether either binder changes death, fractures or cardiovascular events (that comparison, non-calcium versus calcium binders, is shelf #295). Note the tension inside the result — adherence was better on PA21 among those who stayed on it, yet more than twice as many PA21 patients withdrew for adverse events (15.7% vs 6.6%).
cards.source: Floege J et al. A phase III study of the efficacy and safety of a novel iron-based phosphate binder in dialysis patients. Kidney Int. 2014. PMID: 24646861. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Koiwa 2017 (Japanese phase 3): end-of-treatment phosphate 1.62 vs 1.72 mmol/L — non-inferior — on 5.6 tablets a day against 18.7
cards.summary: Koiwa 2017 (Japanese phase 3): end-of-treatment phosphate 1.62 vs 1.72 mmol/L — non-inferior — on 5.6 tablets a day against 18.7
cards.people: 213 Japanese haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia randomised open-label to PA21 (sucroferric oxyhydroxide) or sevelamer hydrochloride for 12 weeks; primary outcome the adjusted serum phosphorus concentration at end of treatment, with a non-inferiority margin of 0.32 mmol/L.
cards.result: Adjusted mean serum phosphorus at end of treatment was 1.62 mmol/L on PA21 versus 1.72 mmol/L on sevelamer (difference −0.11 mmol/L, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.02), confirming non-inferiority. Mean daily tablet intake was 5.6 ± 2.6 tablets on PA21 versus 18.7 ± 7.1 on sevelamer. Incidences of adverse events and adverse drug reactions did not differ significantly between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks only, and the comparator is sevelamer hydrochloride at Japanese doses — the 18.7-tablet figure reflects that formulation and dosing practice, so the tablet contrast is larger than in the global trial (about 3 vs 8). The direction, not the exact ratio, is the transportable finding.
cards.source: Koiwa F et al. Efficacy and safety of sucroferric oxyhydroxide compared with sevelamer hydrochloride in Japanese haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia: A randomized, open-label, multicentre, 12-week phase III study. Nephrology (Carlton). 2017. PMID: 27496336. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ketteler 2019 (post hoc, SAME phase 3 programme as Floege 2014 — flagged): over 1 year, both binders together cut phosphate by 30% relative and FGF-23 by a median 64% relative
cards.summary: Ketteler 2019 (post hoc, SAME phase 3 programme as Floege 2014 — flagged): over 1 year, both binders together cut phosphate by 30% relative and FGF-23 by a median 64% relative
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial — a repeat report of the Floege 2014 trial programme, flagged as such (Ketteler 2019)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the Floege phase 3 programme (1,059 patients randomised 2:1 to sucroferric oxyhydroxide or sevelamer carbonate), restricted to the 549 patients who completed at least 1 year of continuous treatment; because CKD-MBD outcomes were similar between the two binders, the analysis pooled both arms.
cards.result: One year of binder treatment was associated with a significant, sustained 30% relative reduction in serum phosphorus (P < 0.001) and a significant median 64% relative decrease in intact FGF-23 (P < 0.001). Intact PTH fell significantly by week 24 (P < 0.001) but returned to near baseline by week 52; serum calcium changed minimally. The bone-resorption marker TRAP5b fell significantly; CTx rose transiently and returned to baseline; bone-formation markers (bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin) rose over the year.
cards.watchOut: This card reports the same trial programme as the Floege 2014 card above, not an independent trial — and it pools the two drugs precisely because they did not differ, so it cannot support any claim that sucroferric oxyhydroxide beats sevelamer on mineral-and-bone markers. It is also a completers analysis (549 of 1,059 randomised), so the 1-year picture is drawn from patients who tolerated and stayed on treatment.
cards.source: Ketteler M et al. Effects of sucroferric oxyhydroxide and sevelamer carbonate on chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder parameters in dialysis patients. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2019. PMID: 29846719. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal phosphate control, a third of the tablets, a different side-effect profile — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal phosphate control, a third of the tablets, a different side-effect profile — LIKELY
cards.people: Two randomised open-label phase 3 trials (global, 707 vs 348 patients; Japanese, 213 patients) plus a flagged post hoc 1-year analysis of the global trial programme (549 completers).
cards.result: Phosphate lowering was non-inferior in both trials (−0.71 vs −0.79 mmol/L at 12 weeks; 1.62 vs 1.72 mmol/L at end of treatment). Tablet burden: ~3 vs ~8 per day (global) and 5.6 vs 18.7 per day (Japanese, against sevelamer hydrochloride). Non-adherence 15.1% vs 21.3%, but withdrawal for adverse events 15.7% vs 6.6%, both from the global trial. Over 1 year, pooled across both drugs: phosphate −30% relative, FGF-23 −64% relative (median).
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint here is biochemical. A clinician choosing between these binders is choosing tablet burden and gut tolerability, not proven survival — and a patient who cannot tolerate sucroferric oxyhydroxide's diarrhoea gets no benefit from its lower pill count, as the withdrawal figures show.
cards.source: Synthesis of Floege J et al. Kidney Int. 2014 (PMID: 24646861); Koiwa F et al. Nephrology (Carlton). 2017 (PMID: 27496336); Ketteler M et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2019 (PMID: 29846719).

shelves.title: Vadadustat in non-dialysis CKD: the haemoglobin matched darbepoetin exactly, the cardiovascular safety did not — MACE hazard ratio 1.17 against a 1.25 non-inferiority margin
shelves.question: In non-dialysis CKD anaemia, does vadadustat match darbepoetin for haemoglobin control and cardiovascular safety?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anemia/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced · Darbepoetin alfa/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Glycine/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Hematinics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hemoglobins/analysis · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Picolinic Acids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prolyl-Hydroxylase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/mortality
shelves.balance: Half of the question gets a clean yes, and the other half gets a clean no. In the two PRO2TECT trials (Chertow 2021, PMID: 33913637; 3,476 patients with non-dialysis CKD), vadadustat's haemoglobin control was non-inferior to darbepoetin alfa in both the ESA-untreated and ESA-treated trials, with mean differences of +0.05 and −0.01 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin. But the pooled primary safety analysis gave a hazard ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events of 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.36), failing the prespecified 1.25 non-inferiority margin — and because the interval excludes 1.0, it reads as a harm signal in this population, not just an unmet formality. The contrast with the companion dialysis programme is part of the evidence and is cross-referenced, not carded, here: in INNO2VATE (Eckardt 2021, PMID: 33913638), vadadustat in dialysis patients was non-inferior to darbepoetin for cardiovascular safety (MACE hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11) as well as for haemoglobin. So the class story is population-specific: the safety failure belongs to the non-dialysis trials. The wider HIF-stabiliser class shelf, led by the roxadustat trials, is #731.

cards.headline: Chertow 2021 (PRO2TECT, two trials): haemoglobin non-inferiority met in both — but pooled MACE hazard ratio 1.17 (1.01 to 1.36) missed the 1.25 cardiovascular safety margin
cards.summary: Chertow 2021 (PRO2TECT, two trials): haemoglobin non-inferiority met in both — but pooled MACE hazard ratio 1.17 (1.01 to 1.36) missed the 1.25 cardiovascular safety margin
cards.type: Two randomised open-label phase 3 non-inferiority trials reported together (Chertow 2021, PRO2TECT)
cards.people: Two phase 3 randomised open-label non-inferiority trials of oral vadadustat versus darbepoetin alfa in non-dialysis-dependent CKD: 1,751 ESA-untreated patients (haemoglobin < 10 g/dL) and 1,725 ESA-treated patients (haemoglobin 8–11 g/dL in the US, 9–12 g/dL elsewhere). Primary safety endpoint: first major adverse cardiovascular event (death from any cause, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke), pooled across both trials; prespecified non-inferiority margin 1.25 for safety and −0.75 g/dL for the haemoglobin change.
cards.result: In the pooled analysis (1,739 vadadustat, 1,732 darbepoetin alfa), the hazard ratio for MACE was 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.36), which did not meet the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1.25 — cardiovascular non-inferiority was not demonstrated. Haemoglobin efficacy was non-inferior in both trials: mean between-group differences in haemoglobin change at weeks 24–36 were +0.05 g/dL (95% CI −0.04 to 0.15) in the ESA-untreated trial and −0.01 g/dL (95% CI −0.09 to 0.07) in the ESA-treated trial, both well inside the −0.75 g/dL margin.
cards.watchOut: The MACE confidence interval (1.01 to 1.36) excludes 1.0: in these trials the pooled estimate is not merely 'non-inferiority unproven' but a statistically significant excess of cardiovascular events on vadadustat, driven by the non-dialysis population studied here. The trials were open-label, and the safety analysis was pooled across two trials with different ESA histories by design — the paper's prespecified primary safety analysis, not a post hoc choice.
cards.source: Chertow GM et al. Vadadustat in Patients with Anemia and Non-Dialysis-Dependent CKD. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33913637. Registry ID: NCT02648347 and NCT02680574 (PRO2TECT). cards.headline: Synthesis: haemoglobin yes, cardiovascular safety no — a SPLIT verdict confined to non-dialysis CKD
cards.summary: Synthesis: haemoglobin yes, cardiovascular safety no — a SPLIT verdict confined to non-dialysis CKD
cards.people: One report of two pooled phase 3 trials (PRO2TECT; 3,476 randomised patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD), read against the cross-referenced dialysis programme (INNO2VATE) in the balance.
cards.result: Haemoglobin: non-inferior in both trials (differences +0.05 and −0.01 g/dL; margin −0.75). Cardiovascular safety: pooled MACE hazard ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.36); non-inferiority margin 1.25 not met. In dialysis patients (cross-referenced INNO2VATE), the same comparison gave a MACE hazard ratio of 0.96 (0.83 to 1.11) and met non-inferiority — the harm signal is specific to the non-dialysis programme as run.
cards.watchOut: A single trial programme carries this shelf (Tier C): two trials, but one sponsor, one design, one pooled safety analysis. The result should not be read across to dialysis patients — where the same drug passed the same safety test — nor across the HIF class, whose other members have their own trial records (shelf #731).
cards.source: Synthesis of Chertow GM et al. N Engl J Med. 2021 (PMID: 33913637).

shelves.title: Ferric maltol in stage 3–4 CKD: haemoglobin 0.5 g/dL higher than placebo at 16 weeks — a single trial, a modest gain, and a gastrointestinal price
shelves.question: In non-dialysis CKD with iron deficiency, does oral ferric maltol raise haemoglobin versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: *Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy/etiology · Female · Ferric Compounds · Humans · *Iron Deficiencies · Pyrones · *Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications
shelves.balance: On the one placebo-controlled trial that exists, yes — modestly. In AEGIS-CKD (Pergola 2021, PMID: 34029682; 167 patients with stage 3–4 CKD and iron-deficiency anaemia), ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily raised haemoglobin by 0.5 g/dL more than placebo at 16 weeks (95% CI 0.1 to 0.9), with ferritin, transferrin saturation and serum iron all rising on the drug while they fell on placebo. The cost was gastrointestinal: adverse events in 41% versus 30% during the blinded phase, though withdrawals for adverse events were no higher than on placebo (6% vs 9%). The open-label extension suggests the gain persists to a year, but with no comparator that part is description, not proof. This shelf is deliberately narrow — ferric maltol against placebo. The neighbouring questions live elsewhere: whether intravenous iron given proactively or at higher ferritin targets improves outcomes in CKD and dialysis is shelf #294, and IV versus oral iron beyond the blood count in non-dialysis CKD is shelf #369.

cards.headline: Pergola 2021 (AEGIS-CKD): haemoglobin rose 0.5 g/dL more on ferric maltol than placebo at 16 weeks (95% CI 0.1 to 0.9), and iron indices rose while placebo's fell
cards.summary: Pergola 2021 (AEGIS-CKD): haemoglobin rose 0.5 g/dL more on ferric maltol than placebo at 16 weeks (95% CI 0.1 to 0.9), and iron indices rose while placebo's fell
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with open-label extension (Pergola 2021, AEGIS-CKD)
cards.people: 167 adults with stage 3 or 4 CKD and iron-deficiency anaemia at 30 US centres, randomised 2:1 to oral ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily (n = 111) or placebo (n = 56) for 16 weeks, followed by an open-label extension in which all patients received ferric maltol for up to 36 further weeks. Funded by Shield Therapeutics (UK) Ltd.
cards.result: At week 16 the least-squares mean difference in haemoglobin change was +0.5 g/dL in favour of ferric maltol (SE 0.2; 95% CI 0.1 to 0.9; P = 0.01). Ferritin, transferrin saturation and serum iron increased on ferric maltol and declined on placebo (all P < 0.05). Haemoglobin was sustained to week 52 in patients continuing ferric maltol and rose in those switching from placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent (41% vs 30% in the randomised phase); adverse events led to withdrawal in 6% on ferric maltol and 9% on placebo during double-blind treatment.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 167 patients, a 16-week primary endpoint and a haemoglobin surrogate: the 0.5 g/dL average gain is real but modest, and the 52-week extension had no control group, so 'sustained' cannot be separated from natural history or co-treatment. The trial enrolled a high proportion of women and had heterogeneous baseline ferritin. It says nothing about transfusion, hospitalisation or symptoms.
cards.source: Pergola PE et al. Oral Ferric Maltol for the Treatment of Iron-Deficiency Anemia in Patients With CKD: A Randomized Trial and Open-Label Extension. Am J Kidney Dis. 2021. PMID: 34029682. Registry ID: NCT02968368 (AEGIS-CKD).
