cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but small haemoglobin gain from the only placebo-controlled trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but small haemoglobin gain from the only placebo-controlled trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (AEGIS-CKD; 167 patients) with an uncontrolled open-label extension to 52 weeks.
cards.result: Haemoglobin difference at 16 weeks: +0.5 g/dL (95% CI 0.1 to 0.9; P = 0.01). Iron indices moved in opposite directions between arms (up on ferric maltol, down on placebo, all P < 0.05). Gastrointestinal adverse events 41% vs 30%; withdrawals for adverse events 6% vs 9%. No clinical-outcome endpoints were tested.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (Tier C): a second trial, or any trial with patient-important outcomes, could move this stamp in either direction. The comparison is against placebo — not against the cheap oral iron salts used in practice, and not against intravenous iron (shelves #294 and #369).
cards.source: Synthesis of Pergola PE et al. Am J Kidney Dis. 2021 (PMID: 34029682).

shelves.title: Conservative kidney management after 75: dialysis buys about 1–2 years for the average patient, almost nothing for the highly comorbid — and quality of life holds steady without it
shelves.question: In older patients with kidney failure, does conservative kidney management give survival and quality of life comparable to dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chronic Disease · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Diseases/complications/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Male · Myocardial Ischemia/complications · *Renal Dialysis · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: The honest answer splits in two. On survival, conservative management is not comparable for the average older patient: across four UK cohorts, dialysis patients lived longer — median survival 67.1 versus 21.2 months in the largest cohort (Chandna 2011, PMID: 21098012) and 37.8 versus 13.9 months in Carson 2009 (PMID: 19808244), a gain the authors put at about 2 years. But the margin collapses exactly where the question is hardest: in Murtagh 2007 (PMID: 17412702) the dialysis advantage was lost in patients with high comorbidity, especially ischaemic heart disease, and in Chandna's over-75s, adjusted for age, comorbidity and diabetes, the advantage was about 4 months and not statistically significant. On quality of life, the one prospective study (Da Silva-Gane 2012, PMID: 22956262) found conservative patients maintained their quality of life, while life satisfaction fell after starting dialysis; Carson's conservative patients also spent fewer of their remaining days in hospital (0.043 vs 0.069 hospital days per day survived) and were four times as likely to die at home or in a hospice. Every study here is observational and the conservative groups were older and sicker in all of them — adjustment shrinks the survival gap but cannot prove what remains is causal. There is no randomised trial, and there is unlikely ever to be one.

cards.headline: Murtagh 2007: 1- and 2-year survival 84% and 76% on dialysis versus 68% and 47% conservative — but the advantage disappeared in patients with high comorbidity, especially ischaemic heart disease
cards.summary: Murtagh 2007: 1- and 2-year survival 84% and 76% on dialysis versus 68% and 47% conservative — but the advantage disappeared in patients with high comorbidity, especially ischaemic heart disease
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 129 patients over 75 with CKD stage 5 attending dedicated pre-dialysis clinics, managed with dialysis (n = 52) or conservatively (n = 77) after the management decision had been made; survival measured from an estimated GFR below 15 ml/min.
cards.result: One- and two-year survival was 84% and 76% in the dialysis group versus 68% and 47% in the conservative group (log rank 13.6, P < 0.001). However, the survival advantage of dialysis was lost in patients with high comorbidity scores, particularly when the comorbidity included ischaemic heart disease.
cards.watchOut: Patients chose their pathway, and those choosing conservatively were the more comorbid — the unadjusted gap overstates what dialysis itself buys, and even the adjusted subgroup reading rests on small numbers (129 patients, one centre's clinics). Survival is counted from eGFR < 15, a landmark that patients reach at different speeds.
cards.source: Murtagh FE et al. Dialysis or not? A comparative survival study of patients over 75 years with chronic kidney disease stage 5. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2007. PMID: 17412702. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chandna 2011 (844 patients): median survival 67.1 months on renal replacement versus 21.2 conservative overall — but over 75 with high comorbidity, the adjusted advantage was about 4 months and not significant
cards.summary: Chandna 2011 (844 patients): median survival 67.1 months on renal replacement versus 21.2 conservative overall — but over 75 with high comorbidity, the adjusted advantage was about 4 months and not significant
cards.people: Single-centre cohort assembled over 18 years: 844 patients reaching stage 5 CKD, 689 treated with renal replacement therapy and 155 managed conservatively; conservative patients were older and carried more comorbidity. Survival measured from entry into stage 5 CKD.
cards.result: Median survival was 21.2 months with conservative management versus 67.1 months with renal replacement (P < 0.001). But in patients aged over 75, after correction for age, high comorbidity and diabetes, the survival advantage of renal replacement was approximately 4 months and was not statistically significant. Age, high comorbidity and diabetes independently predicted poorer survival on renal replacement; on conservative management, age over 75 and female sex predicted better survival.
cards.watchOut: An 18-year accrual window spans eras of dialysis practice, and the treatment groups differed before any adjustment — conservative patients were older and sicker, so the headline 46-month median gap is a description of two different populations as much as of two treatments. The adjusted ~4-month figure in the over-75 high-comorbidity subgroup is the number relevant to the clinic conversation, and it is imprecise.
cards.source: Chandna SM et al. Survival of elderly patients with stage 5 CKD: comparison of conservative management and renal replacement therapy. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2011. PMID: 21098012. cards.headline: Carson 2009: median survival 37.8 months on replacement therapy versus 13.9 on maximum conservative management — yet conservative patients spent fewer of their remaining days in hospital and were 4 times as likely to die at home or in a hospice
cards.summary: Carson 2009: median survival 37.8 months on replacement therapy versus 13.9 on maximum conservative management — yet conservative patients spent fewer of their remaining days in hospital and were 4 times as likely to die at home or in a hospice
cards.people: Single-centre UK cohort of 202 patients aged 70 or over with ESRD who had chosen maximum conservative management (n = 29) or renal replacement therapy (n = 173); survival measured from a standardised threshold estimated GFR of 10.8 ml/min/1.73 m²; hospitalisation rates and place of death compared.
cards.result: Median survival was 37.8 months on renal replacement versus 13.9 months on conservative management (P < 0.01) — the authors summarise the gain as approximately 2 years. Hospitalisation was higher on replacement therapy: 0.069 versus 0.043 hospital days per patient-days survived (95% CIs 0.068–0.070 and 0.040–0.047). Conservative patients were significantly more likely to die at home or in a hospice (odds ratio 4.15, 95% CI 1.67 to 10.25). The authors conclude the two pathways achieved similar numbers of hospital-free days.
cards.watchOut: Only 29 conservative patients, from one centre, who had actively chosen that pathway — a selected group whose preferences and frailty differ from the dialysis group in ways no adjustment here can capture. The survival landmark (a modelled threshold eGFR) is an analytic construct, not a clinic date.
cards.source: Carson RC et al. Is maximum conservative management an equivalent treatment option to dialysis for elderly patients with significant comorbid disease?. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2009. PMID: 19808244. Registry ID: none in the record. observational comparative cohort study (carson 2009) single-centre uk cohort of 202 patients aged 70 or over with esrd who had chosen maximum conservative management (n = 29) or renal replacement therapy (n = 173); survival measured from a standardised threshold estimated gfr of 10.8 ml/min/1.73 m²; hospitalisation rates and place of death compared. median survival was 37.8 months on renal replacement versus 13.9 months on conservative management (p < 0.01) — the authors summarise the gain as approximately 2 years. hospitalisation was higher on replacement therapy: 0.069 versus 0.043 hospital days per patient-days survived (95% cis 0.068–0.070 and 0.040–0.047). conservative patients were significantly more likely to die at home or in a hospice (odds ratio 4.15, 95% ci 1.67 to 10.25). the authors conclude the two pathways achieved similar numbers of hospital-free days. only 29 conservative patients, from one centre, who had actively chosen that pathway — a selected group whose preferences and frailty differ from the dialysis group in ways no adjustment here can capture. the survival landmark (a modelled threshold egfr) is an analytic construct, not a clinic date. carson rc et al. is maximum conservative management an equivalent treatment option to dialysis for elderly patients with significant comorbid disease?. clin j am soc nephrol. 2009. pmid: 19808244. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · comorbidity · female · glomerular filtration rate · hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · humans · kidney failure, chronic/mortality/therapy · male · *renal dialysis · renal replacement therapy

cards.headline: Da Silva-Gane 2012 (prospective): quality of life held steady on conservative management while life satisfaction fell after starting dialysis; adjusted median survival 1,317 days on haemodialysis versus 913 on conservative care
cards.summary: Da Silva-Gane 2012 (prospective): quality of life held steady on conservative management while life satisfaction fell after starting dialysis; adjusted median survival 1,317 days on haemodialysis versus 913 on conservative care
cards.people: Prospective cohort of 170 patients with advanced progressive CKD (late stage 4 and stage 5) assessed every 3 months for up to 3 years with SF-36, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale and Satisfaction with Life Scale: after 3 years, 124 patients had started or were planned for dialysis, 30 were on conservative kidney management and 16 remained undecided. Conservative patients were older, more dependent and more comorbid, with poorer physical health and higher anxiety at baseline; mental health, depression and life-satisfaction scores were similar.
cards.result: Quality-of-life measures showed no serial change except life satisfaction, which decreased significantly after dialysis initiation and remained stable on conservative management. In Cox models controlling for comorbidity, Karnofsky score, age, physical health and propensity score, median survival from recruitment was 1,317 days in haemodialysis patients versus 913 days in conservative patients — about 13 months shorter on conservative care after adjustment.
cards.watchOut: The conservative group is small (30 patients) and started older, more dependent and more comorbid; propensity adjustment narrows but cannot close that gap. Quality-of-life trajectories in survivors are also subject to attrition — patients who die stop answering questionnaires, on both pathways.
cards.source: Da Silva-Gane M et al. Quality of life and survival in patients with advanced kidney failure managed conservatively or by dialysis. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2012. PMID: 22956262. cards.headline: Synthesis: survival favours dialysis overall and nearly ties in the old-and-comorbid; quality of life does not favour dialysis — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival favours dialysis overall and nearly ties in the old-and-comorbid; quality of life does not favour dialysis — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.people: Four UK observational cohorts (129 to 844 patients), one prospective with serial quality-of-life measurement; no randomised evidence exists for this question.
cards.result: Unadjusted median survival gaps favour dialysis by roughly 2 years (37.8 vs 13.9 months; 67.1 vs 21.2 months). Adjusted for comorbidity in patients over 75, the gap narrows to ~4 months and non-significance (Chandna) or disappears in the high-comorbidity subgroup (Murtagh); one prospective adjusted analysis gives 1,317 vs 913 median days (Da Silva-Gane). Quality of life was maintained on conservative management; life satisfaction declined after dialysis initiation. Conservative patients had fewer hospital days per day survived and higher odds of dying at home or in hospice (OR 4.15, 95% CI 1.67 to 10.25).
cards.watchOut: All four cohorts are British, mostly from the 2000s, and all compare patients who chose — or were steered to — different pathways; confounding by indication is the central threat and runs in both directions (conservative patients were sicker, but dialysis patients had to be judged fit to start). Survival landmarks differ between studies (eGFR < 15, stage 5 entry, a modelled threshold eGFR, recruitment), so the month counts are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Synthesis of Murtagh FE et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2007 (PMID: 17412702); Chandna SM et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2011 (PMID: 21098012); Carson RC et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2009 (PMID: 19808244); Da Silva-Gane M et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2012 (PMID: 22956262).

shelves.title: Potassium citrate for recurrent calcium stones: new stones cut by about three quarters relative in the pooled trials — small old studies, and four times the dropouts from gut side effects
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent calcium kidney stones, does potassium citrate reduce stone recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calcium Oxalate/analysis · Calcium Phosphates/analysis · Citrates/therapeutic use/urine · Citric Acid · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kidney Calculi/chemistry/epidemiology/prevention & control · Male · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Yes, on consistent randomised evidence — with a tolerability asterisk. In the two double-blind trials, potassium citrate cut stone formation from 1.2 to 0.1 per patient-year in hypocitraturic patients while placebo was unchanged (Barcelo 1993, PMID: 8230497; remission 72% vs 20%), and potassium-magnesium citrate cut new stone formation from 63.6% to 12.9% over up to 3 years (Ettinger 1997, PMID: 9366314; relative risk 0.16, an 84% relative reduction). The Cochrane synthesis of all citrate salts (Phillips 2015, PMID: 26439475; 7 trials, 477 participants) gives a pooled risk ratio for new stone formation of 0.26 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.68) — about a 74% relative reduction — with less retreatment (risk ratio 0.22). The same review is the source of the caution: the trials are small, old and moderately-to-poorly reported, and dropouts due to adverse events were significantly commoner on citrate (risk ratio 4.45, 95% CI 1.28 to 15.50), mostly gastrointestinal. Citrate is one leg of stone prevention, not the whole strategy: thiazides for hypercalciuric recurrence are shelf #483, and high urine volume is shelf #594.

cards.headline: Barcelo 1993: in hypocitraturic stone formers, stone formation fell from 1.2 to 0.1 per patient-year on potassium citrate while placebo stayed at 1.1 — remission in 72% versus 20%
cards.summary: Barcelo 1993: in hypocitraturic stone formers, stone formation fell from 1.2 to 0.1 per patient-year on potassium citrate while placebo stayed at 1.1 — remission in 72% versus 20%
cards.people: 57 patients with active idiopathic hypocitraturic calcium nephrolithiasis (2 or more stones in the preceding 2 years) randomised double-blind to potassium citrate 30–60 mEq/day in wax-matrix tablets or placebo; the 3-year results are reported for the 18 citrate and 20 placebo patients followed for the full period.
cards.result: In the potassium citrate group, stone formation fell from 1.2 ± 0.6 to 0.1 ± 0.2 per patient-year (P < 0.0001), 13 of 18 patients (72%) were in remission, and every patient individually reduced their stone formation rate. On placebo, stone formation was unchanged (1.1 ± 0.4 to 1.1 ± 0.3 per patient-year) and 4 of 20 (20%) were in remission. The on-treatment rate differed significantly between groups (0.1 ± 0.2 vs 1.1 ± 0.3, P < 0.001). Urinary citrate, pH and potassium rose on citrate only. Adverse reactions were mild; 2 citrate and 1 placebo patient withdrew.
cards.watchOut: The 3-year analysis covers 38 of the 57 randomised patients — a third of the trial is missing from the headline result, in a study small enough for attrition to matter. It also enrolled only hypocitraturic patients, the subgroup with the clearest mechanism for benefit; it does not by itself prove benefit in stone formers with normal urinary citrate.
cards.source: Barcelo P et al. Randomized double-blind study of potassium citrate in idiopathic hypocitraturic calcium nephrolithiasis. J Urol. 1993. PMID: 8230497. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Ettinger 1997: new stones formed in 12.9% on potassium-magnesium citrate versus 63.6% on placebo over up to 3 years — relative risk 0.16
cards.summary: Ettinger 1997: new stones formed in 12.9% on potassium-magnesium citrate versus 63.6% on placebo over up to 3 years — relative risk 0.16
cards.people: 64 patients with recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis randomised double-blind to placebo or potassium-magnesium citrate (42 mEq potassium, 21 mEq magnesium, 63 mEq citrate daily) for up to 3 years.
cards.result: New calculi formed in 63.6% of the placebo group and 12.9% of the potassium-magnesium citrate group. The relative risk of treatment failure on citrate was 0.16 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.46) — an 84% relative reduction — and remained significant after adjustment for age, pretreatment stone-event rate and urinary biochemistry (adjusted relative risk 0.10, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.36). The authors summarise the effect as an 85% reduction in recurrence risk over up to 3 years of treatment.
cards.watchOut: The tested product is potassium-magnesium citrate, not potassium citrate alone — magnesium has its own anti-lithogenic claims, so this trial supports citrate therapy as a strategy rather than isolating the potassium citrate effect. Small (64 patients) and from the pre-registration era, with stone events counted clinically and radiographically by 1990s standards.
cards.source: Ettinger B et al. Potassium-magnesium citrate is an effective prophylaxis against recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. J Urol. 1997. PMID: 9366314. cards.headline: Phillips 2015 (Cochrane): across 7 trials and 477 participants, new stone formation risk ratio 0.26 with citrate — but dropouts for adverse events were 4.45 times as frequent
cards.summary: Phillips 2015 (Cochrane): across 7 trials and 477 participants, new stone formation risk ratio 0.26 with citrate — but dropouts for adverse events were 4.45 times as frequent
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 RCTs (Phillips 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials (minimum 6 months' treatment) of citrate salts for preventing and treating calcium-containing kidney stones in adults: 7 studies, 477 participants, most with oxalate stones — 3 trials of potassium citrate versus placebo or no intervention (247 participants), 3 of potassium-sodium citrate versus no intervention (166), and 1 of potassium-magnesium citrate versus placebo (64). Reporting quality was moderate to poor, with high attrition-bias risk in 2 studies.
cards.result: Compared with placebo or no intervention, citrate therapy reduced new stone formation (7 studies, 324 participants: risk ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.68 — a 74% relative reduction), reduced stone size (4 studies, 160 participants: risk ratio 2.35, 95% CI 1.36 to 4.05 for size reduction), improved stone-size stability (risk ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.26) and reduced the need for retreatment (2 studies, 157 participants: risk ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.89). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on citrate but not significantly so (risk ratio 2.55, 95% CI 0.71 to 9.16); dropouts due to adverse events were significantly more frequent (4 studies, 271 participants: risk ratio 4.45, 95% CI 1.28 to 15.50). The reviewers conclude citrate salts prevent new stone formation and reduce growth of residual oxalate stones, while calling for a well-designed, adequately powered multicentre trial.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate rests on small, old trials of mixed citrate salts and mixed comparators (placebo or nothing), with moderate-to-poor reporting — the 0.26 risk ratio is probably optimistic, and the reviewers themselves say the definitive trial has not been done. The dropout signal (risk ratio 4.45) is the part of this review most often left out of clinic-room summaries.
cards.source: Phillips R et al. Citrate salts for preventing and treating calcium containing kidney stones in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015. PMID: 26439475. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, consistent relative reduction in recurrence across every randomised test — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, consistent relative reduction in recurrence across every randomised test — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (57 and 64 randomised patients) and a Cochrane meta-analysis of 7 citrate-salt trials (477 participants).
cards.result: New stone formation: 0.1 vs 1.1 per patient-year (Barcelo, hypocitraturic patients); 12.9% vs 63.6% of patients (Ettinger, potassium-magnesium citrate; relative risk 0.16, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.46); pooled risk ratio 0.26 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.68) across all citrate salts. Retreatment risk ratio 0.22 (0.06 to 0.89). Dropouts for adverse events: risk ratio 4.45 (1.28 to 15.50).
cards.watchOut: No trial here is large or modern: the biggest single study randomised 64 patients, Barcelo's 3-year analysis lost a third of its participants, and one of the two positive trials tested a potassium-magnesium combination rather than potassium citrate alone. The stamp is LIKELY rather than PROBABLE for exactly those reasons — direction is unanimous, precision and durability are not.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barcelo P et al. J Urol. 1993 (PMID: 8230497); Ettinger B et al. J Urol. 1997 (PMID: 9366314); Phillips R et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015 (PMID: 26439475).

shelves.title: Veverimer: bicarbonate corrected and chair-stands faster in the small parent trial — but in 1,480 patients it did not slow kidney progression at all (hazard ratio 0.99)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and metabolic acidosis, does veverimer raise serum bicarbonate and improve physical function — and does it slow kidney progression?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/drug therapy/etiology · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bicarbonates/blood · Cross-Linking Reagents/chemistry · Double-Blind Method · Female · *Gastric Acid · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Polymers/chemistry/therapeutic use · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The two halves of this question have opposite answers, and the shelf keeps them separate. On bicarbonate and function: in TRCA-301 (Wesson 2019, PMID: 30857647; 217 patients), veverimer produced a bicarbonate response in 59% versus 22% on placebo at 12 weeks, and in its blinded 40-week extension (Wesson 2019, PMID: 31248662 — the same patients, flagged on its card) the response held at week 52 (63% vs 38%) alongside better patient-reported physical function (+12.1 points versus placebo) and a faster chair-stand. On the outcome that matters most, the answer is no: VALOR-CKD (Tangri 2024, PMID: 38261535; 1,480 patients) found no slowing of CKD progression — primary composite events 149/741 versus 148/739, hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.2). VALOR's randomised-withdrawal design left only about 1 mEq/L of bicarbonate separation between arms, which may have under-tested the hypothesis; but a clinician prescribing veverimer today has biochemical correction and small-trial function gains to offer, and a large negative outcomes trial to disclose. (This shelf also answers the slate's duplicate veverimer topic, which asked the same bicarbonate-and-function question of the same trials.)

cards.headline: Wesson 2019 (TRCA-301): bicarbonate responder rate 59% on veverimer versus 22% on placebo at 12 weeks — a 37-point difference
cards.summary: Wesson 2019 (TRCA-301): bicarbonate responder rate 59% on veverimer versus 22% on placebo at 12 weeks — a 37-point difference
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Wesson 2019, TRCA-301)
cards.people: 217 patients aged 18–85 with non-dialysis CKD (eGFR 20–40 ml/min/1.73 m²) and metabolic acidosis (serum bicarbonate 12–20 mmol/L) at 37 sites, randomised 4:3 to veverimer 6 g/day (n = 124) or placebo (n = 93) as an oral suspension for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: the proportion achieving an increase in serum bicarbonate of at least 4 mmol/L or normalisation to 22–29 mmol/L. Funded by Tricida, the manufacturer.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 59% (71/120) on veverimer versus 22% (20/89) on placebo — a difference of 37 percentage points (95% CI 23 to 49; P < 0.0001). Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal: treatment-related GI events (diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea, constipation) occurred in 13% on veverimer versus 5% on placebo, with non-treatment-limiting diarrhoea in 9% versus 3%. Two deaths occurred, both on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week trial with a biochemical responder endpoint: it proves the polymer removes acid and raises bicarbonate, not that patients feel, function or fare better. The placebo's appearance differed from veverimer, so dosing was supervised by an unmasked staff member — a small crack in the blinding of a trial whose endpoints are laboratory values (low risk for the primary endpoint, more relevant for reported symptoms).
cards.source: Wesson DE et al. Veverimer versus placebo in patients with metabolic acidosis associated with chronic kidney disease: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 30857647. Registry ID: NCT03317444 (TRCA-301). randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (wesson 2019, trca-301) 217 patients aged 18–85 with non-dialysis ckd (egfr 20–40 ml/min/1.73 m²) and metabolic acidosis (serum bicarbonate 12–20 mmol/l) at 37 sites, randomised 4:3 to veverimer 6 g/day (n = 124) or placebo (n = 93) as an oral suspension for 12 weeks. primary endpoint: the proportion achieving an increase in serum bicarbonate of at least 4 mmol/l or normalisation to 22–29 mmol/l. funded by tricida, the manufacturer. the primary endpoint was met by 59% (71/120) on veverimer versus 22% (20/89) on placebo — a difference of 37 percentage points (95% ci 23 to 49; p < 0.0001). adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal: treatment-related gi events (diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea, constipation) occurred in 13% on veverimer versus 5% on placebo, with non-treatment-limiting diarrhoea in 9% versus 3%. two deaths occurred, both on placebo. a 12-week trial with a biochemical responder endpoint: it proves the polymer removes acid and raises bicarbonate, not that patients feel, function or fare better. the placebo's appearance differed from veverimer, so dosing was supervised by an unmasked staff member — a small crack in the blinding of a trial whose endpoints are laboratory values (low risk for the primary endpoint, more relevant for reported symptoms). wesson de et al. veverimer versus placebo in patients with metabolic acidosis associated with chronic kidney disease: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, controlled, phase 3 trial. lancet. 2019. pmid: 30857647. registry id: nct03317444 (trca-301). mesh: acidosis/drug therapy/etiology · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · bicarbonates/blood · cross-linking reagents/chemistry · double-blind method · female · *gastric acid · humans · male · middle aged · polymers/chemistry/therapeutic use · renal insufficiency, chronic/complications · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Wesson 2019 extension (SAME TRCA-301 patients, 40 further weeks — flagged): bicarbonate response held at week 52 (63% vs 38%), and physical function improved — KDQOL physical function +12.1 points versus placebo, chair-stand 4.3 s faster versus 1.4 s
cards.summary: Wesson 2019 extension (SAME TRCA-301 patients, 40 further weeks — flagged): bicarbonate response held at week 52 (63% vs 38%), and physical function improved — KDQOL physical function +12.1 points versus placebo, chair-stand 4.3 s faster versus 1.4 s
cards.type: Randomised blinded placebo-controlled extension — a repeat report of the TRCA-301 trial population, flagged as such (Wesson 2019)
cards.people: 40-week blinded extension of the TRCA-301 parent trial: 196 of the 217 randomised patients (114 veverimer, 82 placebo) continued their original assignment; primary endpoint safety, with bicarbonate and physical functioning (Kidney Disease and Quality of Life physical function domain; repeat chair-stand test) as secondary endpoints. Funded by Tricida.
cards.result: Fewer veverimer patients discontinued prematurely (3% vs 10%), none for an adverse event; serious adverse events occurred in 2% on veverimer versus 5% on placebo. At week 52, more veverimer patients had a bicarbonate increase of at least 4 mmol/L or normalisation (63% vs 38%, P = 0.0015), with higher bicarbonate at every timepoint from week 1. Patient-reported physical function improved by a placebo-subtracted 12.1 points (SE 3.3; P < 0.0001), and chair-stand time improved by 4.3 s on veverimer versus 1.4 s on placebo (P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: This is the same 217-patient trial as the card above, continued — not independent confirmation. The physical-function findings, the most clinically interesting results in the veverimer programme, come from this small, single-programme extension and were not the endpoints the large outcomes trial (VALOR-CKD, next card) was powered on.

cards.headline: Tangri 2024 (VALOR-CKD): in 1,480 patients, veverimer did not slow CKD progression — primary composite events 149/741 versus 148/739, hazard ratio 0.99
cards.summary: Tangri 2024 (VALOR-CKD): in 1,480 patients, veverimer did not slow CKD progression — primary composite events 149/741 versus 148/739, hazard ratio 0.99
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 outcomes trial (Tangri 2024, VALOR-CKD)
cards.people: 1,480 patients with CKD (eGFR 20–40 ml/min/1.73 m²) and metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 12–20 mEq/L) at 320 sites in 35 countries, randomised double-blind to veverimer or placebo after an active-treatment run-in. Primary outcome: composite of end-stage kidney disease (transplant or maintenance dialysis), sustained eGFR decline of at least 40%, or death from kidney failure.
cards.result: A primary endpoint event occurred in 149 of 741 patients on veverimer and 148 of 739 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.2; P = 0.90) — no slowing of CKD progression. Serious and overall adverse-event rates did not differ between groups. The achieved bicarbonate separation was small: after the run-in (during which bicarbonate rose to 23.4 mEq/L on veverimer), month-3 bicarbonate was 22.0 on veverimer versus 20.9 mEq/L on placebo, a difference of about 1 mEq/L that persisted for 24 months.
cards.watchOut: VALOR-CKD's randomised-withdrawal design is its own caveat: every patient was first treated with open veverimer, so the placebo group entered randomisation with bicarbonate already corrected, and the maintained contrast was only ~1 mEq/L — the trial may have tested too small a bicarbonate difference to detect a progression effect. That cuts both ways: it excuses the null mechanistically, but it does not convert the null into a benefit. As run, the outcomes trial is negative.
cards.source: Tangri N et al. VALOR-CKD: A Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial Evaluating Veverimer in Slowing Progression of CKD in Patients with Metabolic Acidosis. cards.headline: Synthesis: the drug does what its chemistry promises and not what its hypothesis promised — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: the drug does what its chemistry promises and not what its hypothesis promised — SPLIT
cards.people: One small parent trial programme (TRCA-301, 217 patients, plus its own 40-week extension in the same patients) and one large independent outcomes trial (VALOR-CKD, 1,480 patients).
cards.result: Bicarbonate response: 59% vs 22% at 12 weeks (difference 37 points, 95% CI 23 to 49); 63% vs 38% at week 52. Physical function (extension only): KDQOL physical function +12.1 points versus placebo; chair-stand improvement 4.3 s vs 1.4 s. CKD progression (VALOR-CKD): hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.2) for ESKD, sustained ≥40% eGFR decline or kidney death, with ~1 mEq/L achieved bicarbonate separation. Safety was acceptable in both programmes; gastrointestinal effects predominate.
cards.watchOut: The function claims rest entirely on the small parent programme (217 patients, one sponsor, one trial population reported twice), while the progression claim rests on a trial nearly seven times larger that found nothing. Weight the halves accordingly: bicarbonate correction is proven, physical-function benefit is promising and unreplicated, progression benefit is tested and absent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wesson DE et al. Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 30857647); Wesson DE et al. Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 31248662); Tangri N et al. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2024 (PMID: 38261535).

shelves.title: Oral urea for chronic SIADH: sodium normalised in every series — and matched vaptans for a year in the only head-to-head — but there is no randomised trial
shelves.question: In SIADH with hyponatraemia, does oral urea work as well as fluid restriction or vaptans?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analysis of Variance · *Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Benzazepines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hyponatremia/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Inappropriate ADH Syndrome/blood/complications/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sodium/blood · Spiro Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Tolvaptan · Urea/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Probably — and 'probably' is the strongest word this evidence base earns. There is no randomised trial of urea in SIADH. What exists is unusually consistent observational evidence: in the only direct comparison (Soupart 2012, PMID: 22403276), 12 patients held a serum sodium of 135 mEq/L for a year on vaptans and then the same 135 mEq/L for a year on urea, within-patient. In Decaux 2018 (PMID: 29017746), mild water restriction alone sufficed for about 30% of chronic SIADH patients — identifiable by a urine osmolality under 400 mOsm/kg — and adding 15–30 g of urea normalised sodium in the remainder. In the largest series (Perelló-Camacho 2022, PMID: 35715573; 48 patients), sodium rose from 125.6 to 134.4 mmol/L with only mild digestive symptoms, two refusals for taste, and a reported cost 87.9% below tolvaptan. A systematic review of urea in hospital hyponatraemia (Schwartz 2023, PMID: 35512769) found the same direction in all 8 studies and graded the evidence low. Every endpoint is the sodium level itself; nobody has shown urea changes symptoms, falls or survival. Emergency correction of severe symptomatic hyponatraemia — bolus versus infusion — is a different question, homed at shelf #126.

cards.headline: Soupart 2012: in 12 patients treated for a year with vaptans then a year with urea, serum sodium was 135 ± 3 on vaptans and 135 ± 2 on urea — the same control, sequence within-patient
cards.summary: Soupart 2012: in 12 patients treated for a year with vaptans then a year with urea, serum sodium was 135 ± 3 on vaptans and 135 ± 2 on urea — the same control, sequence within-patient
cards.people: Prospective long-term study of 13 patients with chronic SIADH of various origins (baseline serum sodium 125 ± 3 mEq/L): treated first with oral vaptans for 1 year (satavaptan 5–50 mg/day in 10, tolvaptan 30–60 mg/day in 2), then, after an 8-day washout in which hyponatraemia recurred in all, with oral urea for a further year, with sodium measured every 2 months and doses adjusted.
cards.result: Vaptans raised serum sodium to 135 ± 3 mEq/L over the first year without escape; after the washout, urea restored and held the same natraemia, 135 ± 2 mEq/L, over its year. One tolvaptan patient withdrew early for excessive thirst; one urea patient developed hypernatraemia without complications. The authors conclude urea has efficacy similar to vaptans for chronic SIADH, with generally good tolerance of both.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen patients, no randomisation, and a fixed sequence (vaptans always first) — period and carryover effects cannot be excluded, and a within-patient sodium match in 12 completers is a long way from a trial. It is nonetheless the only direct urea-versus-vaptan comparison in the literature this shelf could find, and its result is exact equality of achieved sodium.
cards.source: Soupart A et al. Efficacy and tolerance of urea compared with vaptans for long-term treatment of patients with SIADH. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2012. PMID: 22403276. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Decaux 2018: mild water restriction alone normalised sodium in about 30% of chronic SIADH patients — those with urine osmolality under 400 — and adding 15–30 g of urea normalised it in the rest
cards.summary: Decaux 2018: mild water restriction alone normalised sodium in about 30% of chronic SIADH patients — those with urine osmolality under 400 — and adding 15–30 g of urea normalised it in the rest
cards.people: Retrospective review of 29 patients with chronic SIADH treated for at least 1 year with mild water restriction (1.5–2 L/day) alone (n = 9), with 15 g/day urea added (n = 8), or with 30 g/day urea (n = 12); four of the 15 g group had a permanently low solute intake contributing to their hyponatraemia.
cards.result: Serum sodium rose from 129 ± 2 to 138.5 ± 3 mEq/L on water restriction alone, from 127.5 ± 3 to 136.5 ± 1 mEq/L with restriction plus 15 g urea, and from 126 ± 2 to 136.5 ± 2 mEq/L with restriction plus 30 g urea (all P < 0.001 to P < 0.05). Every patient group reached the normal range. The authors' practical rule: about 30% of patients can be managed with moderate water restriction alone, and all of those had an initial urine osmolality below 400 mOsm/kg.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, 29 patients, treatment chosen by clinicians rather than allocated — the urine-osmolality rule is a description of who happened to succeed on restriction alone, not a validated prediction rule. Sodium is also a surrogate: no symptom, falls or mortality outcomes are reported.
cards.source: Decaux G et al. Mild water restriction with or without urea for the longterm treatment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH): Can urine osmolality help the choice?. Eur J Intern Med. 2018. PMID: 29017746. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Perelló-Camacho 2022: in 48 SIADH patients, urea raised sodium from 125.6 to 134.4 mmol/L, with mild digestive symptoms in 2 and refusal for taste in 2 — at 87.9% lower cost than tolvaptan
cards.summary: Perelló-Camacho 2022: in 48 SIADH patients, urea raised sodium from 125.6 to 134.4 mmol/L, with mild digestive symptoms in 2 and refusal for taste in 2 — at 87.9% lower cost than tolvaptan
cards.people: Observational retrospective pre–post analysis of 48 patients with SIADH treated with urea at a tertiary hospital (median age 78.5 years; sodium nadir 119.8 ± 5.0 mmol/L, 125.6 ± 4.1 mmol/L at treatment start); mean treatment duration 2.95 months, with 4 patients still on treatment at analysis.
cards.result: Serum sodium improved in all patients, reaching 134.4 ± 4.9 mmol/L at the end of treatment (P < 0.01), with improvement visible from the first week. Adverse events were detected in 2 patients (mild digestive symptoms) and 2 further patients refused treatment because of urea's low palatability. The authors report an 87.9% cost reduction compared with tolvaptan treatment.
cards.watchOut: No control group at all: sodium rising after treatment starts is what regression to the mean and concurrent care also predict, and the 'all patients improved' framing reflects a treated-case series. The cost comparison is a local accounting figure, not a cost-effectiveness analysis.
cards.source: Perelló-Camacho E et al. Clinical efficacy of urea treatment in syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Sci Rep. 2022. PMID: 35715573. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Schwartz 2023 (systematic review): 8 studies, 296 hospitalised patients — sodium rose in every study, one discontinuation for taste, and the reviewers grade the evidence low
cards.summary: Schwartz 2023 (systematic review): 8 studies, 296 hospitalised patients — sodium rose in every study, one discontinuation for taste, and the reviewers grade the evidence low
cards.type: Systematic review of mostly retrospective studies (Schwartz 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review of oral urea for acute hyponatraemia in hospitalised adults (studies 1998–2021 across five databases): 8 studies, 296 patients, 7 of them retrospective; risk of bias assessed with ROBINS-I and strength of evidence with GRADE.
cards.result: All 8 studies found an increase in serum sodium with oral urea. Side effects were minimal — one patient discontinued because of dysgeusia. Urea dose and duration varied widely between studies. On GRADE, the strength of evidence was low, and the reviewers call for prospective controlled trials to establish efficacy and comparative effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: This review covers acute hospital hyponatraemia rather than chronic SIADH specifically, and it is a synthesis of weak designs — its value here is as an independent check that the direction of effect and the tolerability picture are the same outside the SIADH case series. It found no randomised trial to include.

cards.headline: Synthesis: uniform sodium correction across every design tried, anchored by one within-patient vaptan comparison — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: uniform sodium correction across every design tried, anchored by one within-patient vaptan comparison — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C
cards.people: One prospective within-patient comparison (13 patients), two retrospective SIADH series (29 and 48 patients) and a systematic review of hospital hyponatraemia studies (8 studies, 296 patients). No randomised trials exist.
cards.result: Achieved serum sodium: 135 ± 2 mEq/L on urea versus 135 ± 3 on vaptans over consecutive years in the same patients (Soupart). With water restriction plus urea 15–30 g/day: 126–127.5 rising to 136.5 mEq/L (Decaux). Pre–post in routine practice: 125.6 to 134.4 mmol/L (Perelló-Camacho). Harms across all sources: occasional mild gastrointestinal symptoms, rare hypernatraemia (1 patient), and palatability refusals (2 of 48 in the largest series).
cards.watchOut: Tier C because the entire base is observational and small — the largest urea series has 48 patients and the only comparative study has 13. Consistency across designs is doing the work that sample size cannot. A single modest randomised trial against fluid restriction would either firm this stamp up or end it.

shelves.title: ANDROMEDA: adding daratumumab tripled complete haematologic responses (53% vs 18%) and doubled cardiac and kidney responses at 6 months
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis, does adding daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone deepen haematologic, cardiac and kidney responses?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bortezomib/administration & dosage · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin Light-chain Amyloidosis/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Yes — decisively on response, not yet on survival. In ANDROMEDA (Kastritis 2021, PMID: 34192431; 388 patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis), adding subcutaneous daratumumab to CyBorD nearly tripled the haematologic complete-response rate (53.3% vs 18.1%; relative risk 2.9, 95% CI 2.1 to 4.1) and improved survival free from major organ deterioration or haematologic progression (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.93). The organ responses that determine prognosis followed the blood responses: at 6 months, cardiac responses were 41.5% versus 22.2% and kidney responses 53.0% versus 23.9% — the kidney figure being why this shelf sits with the kidney tranche, although the trial enrolled AL amyloidosis overall rather than a kidney-selected population. Deaths within the short median follow-up of 11.4 months were equal (27 vs 29, mostly amyloid cardiomyopathy), so the survival dividend of deeper responses is, within this record, still a projection. Added toxicity was modest: more lymphopenia, pneumonia, cardiac failure and diarrhoea at grade 3–4, and administration reactions in 7.3%.

cards.headline: Kastritis 2021 (ANDROMEDA): haematologic complete response 53.3% with daratumumab added versus 18.1% without (relative risk 2.9); cardiac responses 41.5% vs 22.2% and kidney responses 53.0% vs 23.9% at 6 months
cards.summary: Kastritis 2021 (ANDROMEDA): haematologic complete response 53.3% with daratumumab added versus 18.1% without (relative risk 2.9); cardiac responses 41.5% vs 22.2% and kidney responses 53.0% vs 23.9% at 6 months
cards.people: 388 patients with newly diagnosed systemic AL amyloidosis randomised to six cycles of bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone (CyBorD) alone, or with subcutaneous daratumumab followed by single-agent daratumumab every 4 weeks for up to 24 cycles. Primary endpoint: haematologic complete response. Median follow-up 11.4 months. Funded by Janssen Research and Development.
cards.result: Haematologic complete response occurred in 53.3% on daratumumab versus 18.1% on control (relative risk 2.9, 95% CI 2.1 to 4.1; P < 0.001). Survival free from major organ deterioration or haematologic progression favoured daratumumab (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.93; P = 0.02). At 6 months, cardiac responses were 41.5% versus 22.2% and kidney (renal) responses 53.0% versus 23.9%. Deaths were similar: 27 versus 29, mostly from amyloid cardiomyopathy. The commonest grade 3–4 events were lymphopenia (13.0% vs 10.1%), pneumonia (7.8% vs 4.3%), cardiac failure (6.2% vs 4.8%) and diarrhoea (5.7% vs 3.7%); systemic administration reactions to daratumumab occurred in 7.3%.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a median follow-up of only 11.4 months: the response endpoints are large and consistent, but overall survival was not different within the follow-up reported (27 vs 29 deaths), and organ responses are surrogates whose survival value in AL amyloidosis is inferred from cohort experience, not demonstrated inside this trial. The slate framed this topic around kidney involvement; the trial enrolled newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis overall — kidney responses are reported on this card because the trial measured them, not because enrolment required renal involvement.
cards.source: Kastritis E et al. Daratumumab-Based Treatment for Immunoglobulin Light-Chain Amyloidosis. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 34192431. Registry ID: NCT03201965 (ANDROMEDA). shelves.title: Amino acids for kidney protection in cardiac surgery: AKI in 26.9% versus 31.7% in the 3,511-patient PROTECTION trial — a real reduction, concentrated in milder injury, with dialysis rates unchanged
shelves.question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery at risk of acute kidney injury, does perioperative intravenous amino acid infusion reduce the occurrence of acute kidney injury compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Acute Kidney Injury*/diagnosis/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Amino Acids*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cardiac Surgical Procedures*/adverse effects · Cardiopulmonary Bypass*/adverse effects · Creatinine/blood · Double-Blind Method · Infusions, Intravenous · Kidney/drug effects · Postoperative Complications*/diagnosis/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Renal Replacement Therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large, multinational, double-blind randomised trial answers this question directly (Landoni G et al., PROTECTION, PMID: 38865168): among 3,511 adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, acute kidney injury occurred in 26.9% on amino acids versus 31.7% on placebo — a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.94), i.e. a 15% relative reduction alongside the absolute rates of 26.9% and 31.7% (about 5 fewer cases per 100 patients treated). Stage 3 injury was also less frequent (1.6% versus 3.0%; relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87), while kidney-replacement therapy (1.4% versus 1.9%), other secondary outcomes and adverse events did not differ substantially. The benefit is therefore real but concentrated in milder, creatinine-defined injury; the trial does not show fewer patients reaching dialysis or death. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): perioperative intravenous amino acids reduce the occurrence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery, with the clearest effect on less severe stages.

cards.headline: Landoni 2024 (PROTECTION): amino acid infusion cut acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery — 26.9% versus 31.7% (relative risk 0.85), and stage 3 injury 1.6% versus 3.0%
cards.summary: Landoni 2024 (PROTECTION): amino acid infusion cut acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery — 26.9% versus 31.7% (relative risk 0.85), and stage 3 injury 1.6% versus 3.0%
cards.people: 3,511 adult patients scheduled for cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at 22 centres in three countries, randomly assigned to a balanced intravenous amino acid mixture at 2 g per kilogram of ideal body weight per day (n = 1,759) or placebo Ringer's solution (n = 1,752), for up to 3 days, in a double-blind trial. The primary outcome was acute kidney injury by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria.
cards.result: Acute kidney injury occurred in 474 patients (26.9%) in the amino acid group and 555 (31.7%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.85; 95% CI 0.77 to 0.94; P = 0.002) — a 15% relative reduction, with absolute rates of 26.9% and 31.7%. Stage 3 acute kidney injury occurred in 29 patients (1.6%) versus 52 (3.0%) (relative risk 0.56; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87) — a 44% relative reduction, with absolute rates of 1.6% and 3.0%. Kidney-replacement therapy was used in 24 patients (1.4%) versus 33 (1.9%). There were no substantial differences between groups in other secondary outcomes (including 30-day mortality) or in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is creatinine-defined injury of any stage, and most of the absolute benefit sits in milder stages: kidney-replacement therapy and mortality did not differ significantly, so this is prevention of laboratory injury, not yet proven prevention of dialysis or death. The infusion ran for up to 3 days at a substantial protein load (2 g/kg/day), and the trial population was elective cardiac surgery with bypass — the result does not automatically extend to other operations or to treating established injury.
cards.source: Landoni G et al. A Randomized Trial of Intravenous Amino Acids for Kidney Protection. New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38865168. Registry ID: NCT03709264. shelves.title: Fenoldopam in cardiac surgery: pooled trials show less acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.41) — but only 440 patients, no effect on dialysis or survival, and more hypotension
shelves.question: In cardiac surgery, does fenoldopam prevent or treat acute kidney injury and reduce dialysis or death, in the pooled randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/drug therapy*/etiology · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/adverse effects* · Fenoldopam/therapeutic use* · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Renal Replacement Therapy · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled randomised, placebo-controlled record is small but directionally consistent (Zangrillo A et al., PMID: 22459931): across 6 trials and 440 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, fenoldopam reduced the risk of acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.41; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.74; p = 0.003). What it did not do is just as important: there was no effect on renal replacement therapy, survival, or intensive care or hospital length of stay, and hypotensive episodes and/or vasopressor use were more frequent on fenoldopam (27.5% versus 18.8%; odds ratio 2.09; 95% CI 0.98 to 4.47; p = 0.06). A drug that moves a creatinine-based endpoint in 440 patients without moving dialysis or death has shown a promising surrogate effect, not a proven patient-important one — exactly the gap the reviewers themselves flag in calling for a large, appropriately powered trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fenoldopam reduces acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery in the pooled small trials, with a hypotension price and no demonstrated effect on dialysis or survival.

cards.headline: Zangrillo 2012: fenoldopam halved the odds of acute kidney injury in cardiac surgery (odds ratio 0.41) across 6 placebo-controlled trials — but dialysis, survival and length of stay did not move
cards.summary: Zangrillo 2012: fenoldopam halved the odds of acute kidney injury in cardiac surgery (odds ratio 0.41) across 6 placebo-controlled trials — but dialysis, survival and length of stay did not move
cards.people: 440 patients in 6 randomised, placebo-controlled trials of fenoldopam for prevention or treatment of acute kidney injury in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, pooled in a meta-analysis restricted to placebo-controlled studies (search updated 1 January 2012).
cards.result: Fenoldopam significantly reduced the risk of acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.41; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.74; p = 0.003). Hypotensive episodes and/or use of vasopressors were more frequent with fenoldopam: 30 of 109 patients (27.5%) versus 21 of 112 (18.8%) (odds ratio 2.09; 95% CI 0.98 to 4.47; p = 0.06). There was no effect on renal replacement therapy, survival, or length of intensive care unit or hospital stay. The authors conclude fenoldopam reduces acute kidney injury in cardiac surgery but that a large, multicentre, appropriately powered trial is needed to confirm the result.
cards.watchOut: 440 patients is a small pooled total for outcomes like dialysis and death, so the null results on those endpoints are uninformative rather than reassuring — and the positive result rests on the kidney-injury definition, a surrogate. The hypotension signal (odds ratio 2.09, confidence interval just crossing 1) matters mechanistically: a renal vasodilator that drops systemic pressure can help or harm the kidney depending on the patient, and these small trials cannot resolve that balance.

shelves.title: Furosemide for acute kidney injury: nine trials and 849 patients with no benefit on mortality, dialysis or recovery — and more deafness and tinnitus at high doses
shelves.question: In established acute kidney injury, does furosemide improve survival or kidney recovery compared with no diuretic therapy, in the pooled randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/drug therapy*/prevention & control · Adult · Diuretics/therapeutic use* · Furosemide/therapeutic use* · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — the pooled randomised record does not show furosemide helping the injured kidney (Ho KM & Sheridan DJ, PMID: 16861256): across 9 randomised trials and 849 adults with or at risk of acute renal failure, in-hospital mortality (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.33), the risk of requiring renal replacement therapy or dialysis (0.99, 0.80 to 1.22), the number of dialysis sessions (weighted mean difference −0.48 sessions, −1.45 to 0.50) and persistent oliguria (0.54, 0.18 to 1.61) were all non-significantly different with furosemide, and splitting prevention from treatment trials did not change the mortality or dialysis results. The one clear signal was harm at high doses: temporary deafness and tinnitus were more frequent (relative risk 3.97, 95% CI 1.00 to 15.78). Furosemide can still make urine and manage fluid overload — that is a symptom indication, not kidney recovery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit): furosemide has not been shown to improve survival or kidney recovery in acute kidney injury, and high doses carry an ototoxicity risk.

cards.headline: Ho & Sheridan 2006 (BMJ): furosemide in acute renal failure — mortality relative risk 1.11, dialysis 0.99, nothing significant except more deafness and tinnitus at high doses
cards.summary: Ho & Sheridan 2006 (BMJ): furosemide in acute renal failure — mortality relative risk 1.11, dialysis 0.99, nothing significant except more deafness and tinnitus at high doses
cards.people: 849 adults with or at risk of acute renal failure in 9 randomised controlled trials of furosemide (frusemide) to prevent or treat acute renal failure, pooled in a meta-analysis of trials identified from the Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase and Medline to 1 February 2006.
cards.result: Outcomes not significantly different after furosemide treatment were in-hospital mortality (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.33), risk of requiring renal replacement therapy or dialysis (0.99, 0.80 to 1.22), number of dialysis sessions required (weighted mean difference −0.48 sessions, −1.45 to 0.50), and proportion of patients with persistent oliguria (urine output < 500 ml/day: 0.54, 0.18 to 1.61). Stratifying studies that used furosemide to prevent versus treat acute renal failure did not change the results for mortality (relative risk ratio 2.10, 95% CI 0.67 to 6.63) or dialysis (4.12, 0.46 to 37.2). High doses of furosemide were associated with an increased risk of temporary deafness and tinnitus (relative risk 3.97, 95% CI 1.00 to 15.78). The authors conclude furosemide is not associated with significant clinical benefits in the prevention and treatment of acute renal failure in adults.
cards.watchOut: The trials are old (search to 2006) and mix prevention with treatment and a wide range of doses, so a benefit confined to one narrow setting cannot be excluded — but the burden of proof sits with the intervention, and the pooled point estimates lean, if anything, toward harm on mortality. The ototoxicity confidence interval (1.00 to 15.78) just touches 1, so even the harm signal is imprecise; it is dose-related and was seen with high doses.
cards.source: Ho KM et al. Meta-analysis of frusemide to prevent or treat acute renal failure. BMJ. 2006. PMID: 16861256. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: nine trials, 849 patients, no outcome improved — furosemide in acute kidney injury is a fluid-management tool, not a kidney-recovery drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: nine trials, 849 patients, no outcome improved — furosemide in acute kidney injury is a fluid-management tool, not a kidney-recovery drug
cards.people: 849 adults with or at risk of acute renal failure in 9 randomised trials, pooled (Ho & Sheridan 2006) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Mortality: relative risk 1.11 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.33). Dialysis requirement: 0.99 (0.80 to 1.22). Dialysis sessions: −0.48 (−1.45 to 0.50). Persistent oliguria: 0.54 (0.18 to 1.61). Temporary deafness/tinnitus at high dose: 3.97 (1.00 to 15.78). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit).
cards.watchOut: A null meta-analysis is not proof of exact equivalence — the mortality interval still allows anything from an 8% relative benefit to a 33% relative harm — but after 849 randomised patients the reasonable clinical posture is that any benefit is small at most, while the urine-output response furosemide produces can falsely reassure and delay dialysis decisions. This shelf covers furosemide as treatment for the kidney injury itself; its use for fluid overload is a separate, symptomatic question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ho KM et al. BMJ. 2006 (PMID: 16861256).

shelves.title: Less salt in CKD: blood pressure down 10/4 mm Hg in the LowSALT trial and albuminuria down 36% relative in the Cochrane pool — consistent short-term gains, with hard outcomes never tested
shelves.question: In chronic kidney disease, does lowering salt intake reduce ambulatory blood pressure and proteinuria compared with usual salt intake?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Cross-Over Studies · Diet, Sodium-Restricted/methods* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension, Renal/diet therapy*/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/diet therapy*/epidemiology · Risk Factors · Risk Reduction Behavior · Sodium Chloride, Dietary/administration & dosage/adverse effects* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the miner anchor for this candidate (PMID: 23082956) is the LowSALT CKD protocol paper, which reports no results; the results of that same trial were published by the same group (McMahon EJ et al., PMID: 24204003) and are carded here as the anchor evidence. In that double-blind crossover trial of 20 patients with hypertensive stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease, salt restriction lowered ambulatory systolic/diastolic blood pressure by 10/4 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 15 / 1 to 6) and reduced extracellular fluid volume, albuminuria and proteinuria. The Cochrane review update (McMahon EJ & Campbell KL, PMID: 34164803; 21 studies, 1,197 participants) found the same pattern at scale: reducing salt by a mean 73.51 mmol/day lowered systolic/diastolic pressure by 6.91/3.91 mm Hg (high certainty evidence) and reduced albuminuria by 36% relative (95% CI 26 to 44) in earlier-stage disease, at the price of more symptomatic hypotension (relative risk 6.70, 95% CI 2.40 to 18.69). All of this is short-term surrogate evidence — no trial is long enough to test death, cardiovascular events or progression to dialysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lowering salt intake reduces blood pressure and proteinuria in chronic kidney disease over weeks, with long-term outcome benefit plausible but untested.

cards.headline: McMahon 2013 (LowSALT CKD results): salt restriction lowered ambulatory blood pressure by 10/4 mm Hg in 20 patients with stage 3–4 CKD, with less fluid, albuminuria and proteinuria
cards.summary: McMahon 2013 (LowSALT CKD results): salt restriction lowered ambulatory blood pressure by 10/4 mm Hg in 20 patients with stage 3–4 CKD, with less fluid, albuminuria and proteinuria
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial (LowSALT CKD phase 1 results, McMahon 2013)
cards.people: 20 adult patients with hypertensive stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease in a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised crossover trial comparing high versus low sodium intake — phase 1 of the LowSALT CKD study (the trial whose protocol is PMID: 23082956). Outcomes included ambulatory blood pressure, 24-hour protein and albumin excretion, fluid status, renin and aldosterone, and arterial stiffness.
cards.result: Salt restriction resulted in statistically significant and clinically important reductions in blood pressure (mean reduction of systolic/diastolic blood pressure 10/4 mm Hg; 95% CI 5 to 15 / 1 to 6 mm Hg), extracellular fluid volume, albuminuria, and proteinuria in patients with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease. The magnitude of change was more pronounced than that reported in patients without chronic kidney disease, suggesting patients with chronic kidney disease are particularly salt sensitive. The authors note that studies with longer intervention times and larger samples are needed to confirm these benefits.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients in a short crossover can measure blood pressure and proteinuria precisely but says nothing about dialysis, cardiovascular events or death, and crossover designs assume the effect washes out between periods. The trial counselled patients intensively and used sodium tablets/placebo to create the contrast — free-living adherence to a low-salt diet is harder than the trial contrast implies.
cards.source: McMahon EJ et al. A randomized trial of dietary sodium restriction in CKD. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2013. PMID: 24204003. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McMahon & Campbell 2021 (Cochrane update): 21 studies, 1,197 participants — salt reduction lowered pressure by 6.91/3.91 mm Hg and albuminuria by 36% relative, with more symptomatic hypotension
cards.summary: McMahon & Campbell 2021 (Cochrane update): 21 studies, 1,197 participants — salt reduction lowered pressure by 6.91/3.91 mm Hg and albuminuria by 36% relative, with more symptomatic hypotension
cards.type: Systematic review, 21 RCTs (McMahon & Campbell 2021, Cochrane update)
cards.people: 21 randomised trials (1,197 randomised participants) comparing two or more levels of salt intake in adults with any stage of chronic kidney disease — 12 studies in earlier-stage disease (779 participants), seven in dialysis (363) and two post-transplant (55) — in the 2021 update of the Cochrane review first published in 2015.
cards.result: Reducing salt by a mean −73.51 mmol/day (95% CI −92.76 to −54.27), equivalent to about 4.2 g salt or 1690 mg sodium per day, reduced systolic/diastolic blood pressure by −6.91/−3.91 mm Hg (95% CI −8.82 to −4.99 / −4.80 to −3.02; 19 studies, 1,405 participants; high certainty evidence). Albuminuria was reduced by 36% relative (95% CI 26 to 44) in six studies, five in earlier-stage chronic kidney disease (mean difference −0.44, 95% CI −0.58 to −0.30; 501 participants; high certainty evidence). Lower salt intake may reduce extracellular fluid volume in earlier-stage disease (−0.87 L, 95% CI −1.17 to −0.58; low certainty) and may lead to symptomatic hypotension (relative risk 6.70, 95% CI 2.40 to 18.69; 6 studies, 678 participants; moderate certainty). Study durations of 1 to 36 weeks were too short to test death, cardiovascular events or kidney progression.
cards.watchOut: Risk of bias was unclear for selection in 13 of 21 studies and for performance/detection in 15, and the pooled population mixes earlier-stage disease, dialysis and transplant recipients — the albuminuria result comes almost entirely from earlier-stage disease and should not be quoted for dialysis patients. The symptomatic-hypotension signal (relative risk 6.70) is the harm to weigh, particularly in patients on several antihypertensive drugs.
cards.source: McMahon EJ et al. Altered dietary salt intake for people with chronic kidney disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 34164803. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: salt restriction in CKD reliably lowers blood pressure and proteinuria over weeks — 10/4 mm Hg in the LowSALT trial, about 7/4 mm Hg pooled — while hard outcomes remain untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: salt restriction in CKD reliably lowers blood pressure and proteinuria over weeks — 10/4 mm Hg in the LowSALT trial, about 7/4 mm Hg pooled — while hard outcomes remain untested
cards.people: The LowSALT CKD crossover trial (20 patients, stage 3–4 disease) plus 21 randomised trials (1,197 participants) in the Cochrane update — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Blood pressure: −10/−4 mm Hg (LowSALT) and −6.91/−3.91 mm Hg pooled (high certainty). Albuminuria: 36% relative reduction (95% CI 26 to 44) in earlier-stage disease. Extracellular fluid: −0.87 L (low certainty). Symptomatic hypotension: relative risk 6.70 (95% CI 2.40 to 18.69). Mortality, cardiovascular events, progression to end-stage kidney disease: untested — all trials lasted 1 to 36 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The miner anchor (PMID: 23082956) is the LowSALT protocol, not its results; this shelf cards the same trial's results paper instead, and the substitution is declared on the face of the shelf. Whether a 7 mm Hg pressure reduction sustained for years would prevent dialysis or cardiovascular events in CKD is an extrapolation from other populations — reasonable, but not evidence from these trials. Tier C is set because every included study is short and surrogate-driven.

shelves.title: Drinking more water for stage 3 CKD: patients drank more and copeptin fell, but eGFR declined identically in CKD WIT — the advice is unproven, not disproven
shelves.question: In adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, does coaching to increase water intake slow kidney function decline over one year compared with usual intake?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Disease Progression · Drinking* · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Health Behavior · Humans · Male · Mentoring* · Middle Aged · Osmolar Concentration · Patient Education as Topic · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/physiopathology/therapy*/urine · Urine/chemistry · Water/administration & dosage*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — the one randomised trial of this advice found the behaviour changed and the kidney outcome did not (Clark WF et al., CKD WIT, PMID: 29801012): among 631 adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, coaching to drink more water raised 24-hour urine volume by 0.6 L per day (95% CI 0.5 to 0.7) and lowered plasma copeptin (−2.2 pmol/L, 95% CI −3.9 to −0.5), so the intervention demonstrably engaged its target — yet the 12-month change in eGFR was −2.2 mL/min/1.73 m² in the hydration group versus −1.9 in controls (adjusted difference −0.3, 95% CI −1.8 to 1.2; P = .74), with no significant difference in urine albumin or self-rated health. The authors note the study may have been underpowered for a clinically important difference, and one year is short for kidney decline — but as the record stands, 'drink more water' is unproven advice for stage 3 disease, distinct from the separate ADPKD water question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit): coaching to increase water intake did not significantly slow kidney function decline over one year in stage 3 chronic kidney disease.

cards.headline: Clark 2018 (CKD WIT): coached patients drank more (urine volume up 0.6 L/day, copeptin down) but eGFR fell just the same — adjusted difference −0.3 mL/min/1.73 m² at one year
cards.summary: Clark 2018 (CKD WIT): coached patients drank more (urine volume up 0.6 L/day, copeptin down) but eGFR fell just the same — adjusted difference −0.3 mL/min/1.73 m² at one year
cards.people: 631 adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m² with microalbuminuria or macroalbuminuria) and 24-hour urine volume under 3.0 L, at 9 centres in Ontario, Canada, 2013–2017: 316 coached to drink more water and 315 coached to maintain usual intake. Mean age 65.0 years, 63.4% men, mean eGFR 43 mL/min/1.73 m². The primary outcome was change in eGFR from baseline to 12 months.
cards.result: Among 590 survivors with 1-year measurements, mean change in 24-hour urine volume was 0.6 L per day higher in the hydration group (95% CI 0.5 to 0.7; P < .001). Mean change in eGFR was −2.2 mL/min/1.73 m² in the hydration group and −1.9 in the control group (adjusted between-group difference −0.3 mL/min/1.73 m²; 95% CI −1.8 to 1.2; P = .74). Secondary between-group differences (hydration versus control): plasma copeptin −2.2 pmol/L (95% CI −3.9 to −0.5; P = .01); creatinine clearance 3.6 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 0.8 to 6.4; P = .01); urine albumin 7 mg per day (95% CI −4 to 51; P = .11); self-rated quality of health 0.2 points (95% CI −0.3 to 0.3; P = .22). Twelve patients died (5 hydration, 7 control). The authors conclude coaching to increase water intake did not significantly slow kidney function decline after 1 year, while noting the study may have been underpowered.
cards.watchOut: One year of follow-up against a background decline of about 2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year leaves little room to show an effect, and the confidence interval (−1.8 to 1.2) still permits a modest benefit — this is 'no effect shown', not 'effect disproven'. The creatinine-clearance difference (+3.6) favouring hydration sits awkwardly beside the null eGFR result and may reflect the higher fluid throughput rather than preserved function. Patients with urine volumes already above 3.0 L/day were excluded, so the trial says nothing about people who already drink a lot.
cards.source: Clark WF et al. Effect of Coaching to Increase Water Intake on Kidney Function Decline in Adults With Chronic Kidney Disease: The CKD WIT Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. cards.summary: Synthesis: the water-coaching trial hit its behavioural target and missed its kidney target — urine up, copeptin down, eGFR decline unchanged at one year

cards.result: Urine volume: +0.6 L/day (95% CI 0.5 to 0.7). Plasma copeptin: −2.2 pmol/L (95% CI −3.9 to −0.5). eGFR change: −2.2 versus −1.9 mL/min/1.73 m² (adjusted difference −0.3, 95% CI −1.8 to 1.2; P = .74). shelves.title: Ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet in advanced CKD: NNT 4.4 to avoid dialysis or halved eGFR in Garneata — in the 14% of screened patients compliant enough to be randomised
shelves.question: In advanced chronic kidney disease, does a very-low-protein vegetarian diet supplemented with ketoanalogues delay dialysis initiation compared with a conventional low-protein diet?
shelves.mesh: Amino Acids, Essential/therapeutic use* · Diet, Protein-Restricted* · Diet, Vegetarian* · Dietary Supplements* · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Prospective Studies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/diet therapy*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor randomised trial is strikingly positive but heavily selected (Garneata L et al., PMID: 26823552): in nondiabetic adults with eGFR under 30 ml/min/1.73 m² who had already proven good diet compliance in a 3-month run-in — only 14% of screened patients were randomised — a ketoanalogue-supplemented vegetarian very-low-protein diet (0.3 g/kg/day) versus a conventional low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day) gave an adjusted number needed to treat of 4.4 (95% CI 4.2 to 5.1) to avoid the composite of dialysis initiation or halving of eGFR, and 2.7 (2.6 to 3.1) to avoid dialysis in those with eGFR under 20, with metabolic abnormalities correcting only on the supplemented diet and no nutritional deterioration. The 2024 meta-analysis (Chen CH et al., PMID: 39340710; 16 trials, 1,344 participants) points the same way more modestly: higher GFR, lower urea nitrogen and phosphorus, higher calcium, a marginally lower risk of end-stage kidney disease in participants without diabetes, and no differences in mortality, albumin or nutritional measures. The direction is consistent; the trial effect size comes from the most compliant sliver of patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet can defer dialysis in selected, compliant patients with advanced chronic kidney disease.

cards.headline: Garneata 2016: ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet — adjusted NNT 4.4 to avoid dialysis or halved eGFR, and 2.7 to avoid dialysis once eGFR was under 20
cards.summary: Garneata 2016: ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet — adjusted NNT 4.4 to avoid dialysis or halved eGFR, and 2.7 to avoid dialysis once eGFR was under 20
cards.people: Nondiabetic adults with stable eGFR under 30 ml/min/1.73 m², proteinuria under 1 g/g urinary creatinine, good nutritional status and good diet compliance, in a prospective randomised controlled trial: after a 3-month run-in on a conventional low-protein diet, compliant patients were randomised to a ketoanalogue-supplemented vegetarian very low-protein diet (0.3 g/kg vegetable protein plus 1 capsule of ketoanalogues per 5 kg per day) or to continue the low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day) for 15 months. The primary endpoint was dialysis initiation or a greater than 50% reduction in initial eGFR. Only 14% of screened patients were randomised.
cards.result: Adjusted numbers needed to treat (95% CI) to avoid the composite primary endpoint in one patient were 4.4 (4.2 to 5.1) in the intention-to-treat analysis and 4.0 (3.9 to 4.4) per protocol, for patients with eGFR under 30 ml/min/1.73 m². The adjusted NNT to avoid dialysis was 22.4 (21.5 to 25.1) for patients with eGFR under 30, decreasing to 2.7 (2.6 to 3.1) for patients with eGFR under 20 ml/min/1.73 m² in the intention-to-treat analysis. Correction of metabolic abnormalities occurred only with the supplemented diet. Compliance was good, with no changes in nutritional parameters and no adverse reactions; the authors conclude the diet seems nutritionally safe and could defer dialysis initiation in some patients with chronic kidney disease.
cards.watchOut: The run-in design is the story: only 14% of screened patients — nondiabetic, low-proteinuria, well nourished and already demonstrably compliant — entered the randomised comparison, so these NNTs describe a best-case minority, not a clinic population. Dialysis initiation is partly a clinician judgement, and an unblinded dietary trial cannot blind that judgement; the eGFR-halving component of the composite is the harder part of the endpoint. The record reports adjusted NNTs rather than raw event counts, which limits independent checking of the effect size.
cards.source: Garneata L et al. Ketoanalogue-Supplemented Vegetarian Very Low-Protein Diet and CKD Progression. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2016. PMID: 26823552.
