cards.headline: Chen 2024 meta-analysis: 16 trials, 1,344 participants — ketoanalogues with protein restriction gave higher GFR, lower urea and phosphorus, and a marginally lower end-stage kidney disease risk in people without diabetes
cards.summary: Chen 2024 meta-analysis: 16 trials, 1,344 participants — ketoanalogues with protein restriction gave higher GFR, lower urea and phosphorus, and a marginally lower end-stage kidney disease risk in people without diabetes
cards.people: 16 randomised trials comprising 1,344 participants with stage 3–5 chronic kidney disease (median follow-up 13 months), comparing ketoanalogue supplementation added to a low- or very low-protein diet against a low-protein diet alone, in a systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023465754) searching to 3 June 2024.
cards.result: Compared with a low-protein diet alone, ketoanalogues supplemented to a protein-restricted diet resulted in a significantly higher GFR and decreased levels of urea nitrogen and phosphorus, with increased levels of calcium. Ketoanalogues combined with a protein-restricted diet showed a marginally lower risk of end-stage kidney disease in participants without diabetes. No significant differences were observed in all-cause mortality, albumin, mid-arm muscle circumference, lean body mass, or subjective global assessment. The authors conclude the combination may help postpone dialysis initiation, improve calcium-phosphate homeostasis and slow GFR decline while maintaining similar nutritional status and survival, and that larger long-term studies are needed, especially in patients with diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports directions and significance rather than pooled effect sizes for most outcomes, so the size of the GFR and end-stage kidney disease effects cannot be weighed precisely from the record. The end-stage kidney disease signal was confined to participants without diabetes and described as marginal — the population in which Garneata also worked — leaving the diabetic majority of advanced CKD effectively untested.
cards.source: Chen CH et al. Efficacy and safety of ketoanalogue supplementation combined with protein-restricted diets in advanced chronic kidney disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Nephrology. 2024. PMID: 39340710. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diets defer dialysis in the patients who can follow them — a consistent direction across one selected trial and a 16-trial pool, with nutrition preserved
cards.summary: Synthesis: ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diets defer dialysis in the patients who can follow them — a consistent direction across one selected trial and a 16-trial pool, with nutrition preserved
cards.people: One randomised trial in highly selected compliant nondiabetic patients with eGFR under 30 (Garneata 2016) plus 16 trials and 1,344 participants with stage 3–5 disease (Chen 2024) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Dialysis/composite endpoint: adjusted NNT 4.4 (Garneata, eGFR < 30) and 2.7 to avoid dialysis at eGFR < 20; marginally lower end-stage kidney disease risk without diabetes (Chen). Biochemistry: higher GFR, lower urea nitrogen and phosphorus, higher calcium with supplementation. Nutrition and mortality: no differences in albumin, lean body mass, subjective global assessment or all-cause mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both sources agree the unanswered population is the typical one: patients with diabetes, heavier proteinuria, or ordinary adherence. A very-low-protein diet is a demanding, dietitian-dependent intervention, and 'deferring dialysis' must not become delaying needed dialysis — the trials monitored nutrition closely, which is part of the intervention, not an optional extra. Tier C is set because the pivotal trial randomised only 14% of those screened.
cards.source: Synthesis of Garneata L et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2016 (PMID: 26823552); Chen CH et al. Journal of Nephrology. 2024 (PMID: 39340710).

shelves.title: Treating PD peritonitis: intraperitoneal antibiotics beat intravenous in the one small head-to-head study and glycopeptides cured more completely — across 42 studies the Cochrane verdict is still low-quality evidence
shelves.question: In peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis, do intraperitoneal antibiotics achieve cure as reliably as intravenous or oral routes, in the pooled randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage* · Drug Administration Routes · Fibrinolytic Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunoglobulins/therapeutic use · Infusions, Parenteral · Injections, Intravenous · Peritoneal Dialysis/adverse effects* · Peritoneal Lavage · Peritonitis/drug therapy/etiology/therapy* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Urokinase-Type Plasminogen Activator/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the Cochrane record on treating peritoneal dialysis peritonitis is broad but shallow (Ballinger AE et al., PMID: 24771351): 42 studies in 2,433 participants, yet most comparisons rest on one or a few small trials with generally high risk of bias and inconsistent outcome definitions. The two positive findings are narrow: intraperitoneal glycopeptide regimens were more likely to achieve complete cure than first-generation cephalosporins (3 studies, 370 episodes: relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.72) with uncertain effects on response, relapse and catheter removal, and intraperitoneal antibiotics were superior to intravenous antibiotics for treatment failure in a single small study (relative risk 3.52, 95% CI 1.26 to 9.81, favouring the intraperitoneal route). Continuous and intermittent intraperitoneal dosing performed similarly; for relapsing or persistent peritonitis, simultaneous catheter removal and replacement beat urokinase in one small study. No optimal agent, combination or duration was identified. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intraperitoneal administration and glycopeptide regimens have the best — still low-quality — support for treating peritoneal dialysis peritonitis.

cards.headline: Ballinger 2014 (Cochrane): 42 studies, 2,433 participants — intraperitoneal beat intravenous in one small study, glycopeptides beat first-generation cephalosporins for complete cure, and no optimal regimen emerged
cards.summary: Ballinger 2014 (Cochrane): 42 studies, 2,433 participants — intraperitoneal beat intravenous in one small study, glycopeptides beat first-generation cephalosporins for complete cure, and no optimal regimen emerged
cards.people: 42 eligible studies in 2,433 participants (adults and children) with peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis: antimicrobial agents (36 studies), urokinase (4), peritoneal lavage (1) and intraperitoneal immunoglobulin (1), comparing routes (oral, intraperitoneal, intravenous), agents, doses, schedules and durations, in the 2014 update of the Cochrane review.
cards.result: No optimal antibiotic agent or combination was identified. Intraperitoneal glycopeptides (vancomycin or teicoplanin) had uncertain effects on primary treatment response, relapse and catheter removal versus first-generation cephalosporins, although glycopeptide regimens were more likely to achieve complete cure (3 studies, 370 episodes: relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.72). Intraperitoneal antibiotics were superior to intravenous antibiotics in reducing treatment failure in one small study (relative risk 3.52, 95% CI 1.26 to 9.81). Continuous and intermittent intraperitoneal dosing schedules had similar treatment failure and relapse rates. Longer treatment (21 versus 10 days of intravenous vancomycin and intraperitoneal gentamicin) had uncertain effects on relapse (1 study, 49 patients: relative risk 1.56, 95% CI 0.60 to 3.95) although it may have increased ototoxicity. For relapsing or persistent peritonitis, simultaneous catheter removal and replacement was better than urokinase at reducing treatment failure (relative risk 2.35, 95% CI 1.13 to 4.91) in a single small study. The reviewers conclude the evidence was low quality and insufficient to identify the optimal agent, route or duration.
cards.watchOut: Almost every actionable number here comes from a single small study or a handful of episodes, with generally high risk of bias, heterogeneous interventions and inconsistent definitions — the intraperitoneal-versus-intravenous result (relative risk 3.52) has a confidence interval running from 1.26 to 9.81. Many included studies are old, there were no randomised trials of catheter-removal timing, and data for automated peritoneal dialysis were absent, so the review maps uncertainty more than it resolves it.
cards.source: Ballinger AE et al. Treatment for peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24771351. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for PD peritonitis the route has better support than the drug choice — intraperitoneal administration and glycopeptides lead a low-quality field, and relapsing infection is a catheter problem
cards.summary: Synthesis: for PD peritonitis the route has better support than the drug choice — intraperitoneal administration and glycopeptides lead a low-quality field, and relapsing infection is a catheter problem
cards.people: 42 studies and 2,433 participants across all randomised treatment comparisons for peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis (Cochrane 2014) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Complete cure: glycopeptides versus first-generation cephalosporins, relative risk 1.66 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.72). Treatment failure: intraperitoneal superior to intravenous in one small study (relative risk 3.52, 95% CI 1.26 to 9.81). Dosing schedule: continuous versus intermittent intraperitoneal dosing similar. Duration: 21 versus 10 days uncertain for relapse, possible added ototoxicity. Relapsing/persistent peritonitis: catheter removal and replacement superior to urokinase (relative risk 2.35, 95% CI 1.13 to 4.91). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Guideline practice (empirical gram-positive plus gram-negative cover, intraperitoneal where feasible) rests substantially on pharmacological reasoning and observational experience rather than on these trials — the shelf grades the randomised record, not the whole rationale for standard care. Organism-specific treatment (for example fungal or mycobacterial peritonitis) is outside this review's comparisons.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ballinger AE et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24771351).

shelves.title: Dialysate sodium in haemodialysis: 23 studies show a trade — higher sodium, more fluid gained between sessions; lower sodium, more hypotension during them — and no winner on blood pressure or survival
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a lower dialysate sodium concentration reduce interdialytic weight gain and blood pressure compared with standard or higher dialysate sodium, in the pooled trials?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure · Chronic Disease · Dialysis Solutions/metabolism* · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Hospitalization · Humans · Outcome Assessment, Health Care* · Renal Dialysis* · Sodium/blood* · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this literature cannot currently crown either prescription (Basile C et al., PMID: 25843783): 23 studies and 76,635 subjects sounds substantial, but the studies were highly heterogeneous in size, quality, follow-up, dialysate sodium levels and even in what counted as 'high' or 'low'. The only three mortality studies were observational, and the apparent relation between death and the plasma-to-dialysate sodium gradient was confounded by indication — sicker patients get different prescriptions. Blood pressure was not markedly affected by higher or lower dialysate sodium; interdialytic weight gain was overall higher with higher dialysate sodium; and three studies reported significantly more intradialytic hypotensive episodes with low dialysate sodium — the physiological trade at the heart of the question. Data on hospitalisations and antihypertensive use were sparse and inconclusive. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): lower dialysate sodium reduces interdialytic weight gain but may provoke intradialytic hypotension, and no definite evidence shows superiority of either uniform prescription on outcomes patients feel.

cards.headline: Basile 2016: 23 studies, 76,635 patients — higher dialysate sodium meant more interdialytic weight gain, lower dialysate sodium meant more intradialytic hypotension in three studies, and blood pressure barely moved
cards.summary: Basile 2016: 23 studies, 76,635 patients — higher dialysate sodium meant more interdialytic weight gain, lower dialysate sodium meant more intradialytic hypotension in three studies, and blood pressure barely moved
cards.people: 23 studies (76,635 subjects) comparing low versus high dialysate sodium concentrations in chronic haemodialysis patients, identified from MEDLINE and CENTRAL, in a systematic review examining mortality, blood pressure, interdialytic weight gain, plasma sodium, hospitalisations, antihypertensive use and intradialytic complications.
cards.result: There was high heterogeneity in the number of patients analysed, overall study quality, duration of follow-up, dialysate sodium concentration, and even in the definition of 'high' or 'low' dialysate sodium. The only three studies looking at mortality were observational; the risk of death was related to the plasma–dialysate sodium gradient but was also shown to be confounded by indication from the dialysate sodium prescription itself. Blood pressure was not markedly affected by high or low dialysate sodium. Patients treated with higher dialysate sodium had overall higher interdialytic weight gain than those with lower dialysate sodium. Three studies reported a significant increase in intradialytic hypotensive episodes in patients receiving low dialysate sodium. Data on hospitalisations and use of antihypertensive agents were sparse and inconclusive. The authors conclude there is no definite evidence proving the superiority of a low or high uniform dialysate sodium on hard or surrogate endpoints, and that adequately powered trials of patient-centred outcomes are needed.
cards.watchOut: The headline denominator (76,635) is dominated by observational data; the randomised subset is far smaller, and with definitions of high and low sodium differing between studies, pooling is more narrative than numeric — the review reports directions, not pooled effect sizes, for its main outcomes. Confounding by indication runs through the mortality data in both directions, so no mortality claim in either direction should be quoted from this shelf.

shelves.title: Medium cut-off dialysers: quality of life up 16.7 points and recovery time down 420 minutes in the pooled record, fewer infections in the pilot — paid for with albumin leak and no survival difference
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a medium cut-off dialyser improve clearance of large middle molecules and patient-reported outcomes compared with a high-flux dialyser?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two complementary records support the medium cut-off membrane. The anchor pilot crossover (Cozzolino M et al., PMID: 33564442) randomised the order of treatment in 20 prevalent haemodialysis patients for 3 months on each membrane: the medium cut-off dialyser (the tested product was the Theranova 400 membrane, named in the record) was associated with fewer infections (7 of 19 patients versus 14 of 20 on conventional high-flux haemodialysis; P = 0.03) and lower interleukin-1β and interleukin-6 levels, at the cost of a significant fall in serum albumin (median reduction −0.45 g/dL; P = 0.025), though median albumin stayed at or above 3.5 g/dL and no patient developed symptoms of hypoalbuminaemia or needed intravenous albumin. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Kandi M et al., PMID: 35083060; 22 studies, 1,811 patients) found moderate-certainty improvements in quality of life (mean difference 16.7 of 100 points), pruritus and restless legs syndrome, and a high-certainty reduction in post-dialysis recovery time (−420 minutes), with little to no difference in all-cause mortality (−0.4%, 95% CI −2.8 to 2.1). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): medium cut-off dialysers improve several patient-reported outcomes and recovery time versus high-flux membranes, with albumin leak the measurable price and no mortality difference shown.

cards.headline: Cozzolino 2021: medium cut-off dialyser crossover in 20 patients — fewer infections (7/19 versus 14/20) and lower inflammatory markers, but serum albumin fell by a median 0.45 g/dL
cards.summary: Cozzolino 2021: medium cut-off dialyser crossover in 20 patients — fewer infections (7/19 versus 14/20) and lower inflammatory markers, but serum albumin fell by a median 0.45 g/dL
cards.people: 20 prevalent haemodialysis patients in a prospective, open-label, controlled crossover pilot study: 10 began on conventional high-flux haemodialysis and 10 on expanded haemodialysis with the medium cut-off membrane (Theranova 400, the tested product named in the record) for 3 months, then switched to the other treatment for a further 3 months. Biochemical, dialysis adequacy and safety measures (adverse events, infections, hospitalisation) were recorded.
cards.result: Treatment with the medium cut-off dialyser was associated with a significant reduction in serum albumin concentration (median reduction −0.45 g/dL, interquartile range −0.575 to −0.05; P = 0.025); however, median albumin levels were ≥ 3.5 g/dL, no patient had clinical symptoms of hypoalbuminaemia, and none needed intravenous albumin. The number of infections was lower with the medium cut-off dialyser (7 of 19 patients) than with conventional haemodialysis (14 of 20; P = 0.03). Interleukin-1β levels were lower on the medium cut-off membrane (0.06 ± 0.02 pg/mL versus 0.28 ± 0.18 pg/mL) and interleukin-6 likewise (6.45 ± 1.57 versus 9.48 ± 2.15 pg/mL), while tumour necrosis factor-α was unchanged. The authors conclude chronic use appears safe and well tolerated, with fewer infections, and that larger randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, open-label, 3 months per period: the infection difference (7/19 versus 14/20) rests on small counts in a crossover where period and carryover effects are hard to exclude, and the denominators differ between periods. The albumin fall is the mechanistically expected price of a more open membrane — benign over 3 months at these levels, but the long-term nutritional balance in frailer patients is exactly what a pilot cannot show. The record carries no MeSH list, so none is quoted.

cards.headline: Kandi 2022 meta-analysis: 22 studies, 1,811 patients — medium cut-off improved quality of life by 16.7 points and cut recovery time by 420 minutes (high certainty), with no mortality difference
cards.summary: Kandi 2022 meta-analysis: 22 studies, 1,811 patients — medium cut-off improved quality of life by 16.7 points and cut recovery time by 420 minutes (high certainty), with no mortality difference
cards.people: 22 eligible studies (6 randomised, 16 non-randomised; 1,811 patients, 1,546 patient-years) comparing the medium cut-off dialyser (Theranova, Baxter Healthcare — the product named in the record) with high-flux membranes in adults on maintenance haemodialysis, in a systematic review and meta-analysis with GRADE certainty ratings (searches to July 2020).
cards.result: The medium cut-off dialyser improved quality of life (mean difference 16.7 of 100 points; 95% CI 6.9 to 26.4; moderate certainty), Kidney Disease Quality of Life burden (4.0; 1.1 to 6.9; moderate) and effects (5.4; 3.2 to 7.6; moderate) subscales, pruritus (−4.4; −7.1 to −1.7; moderate), recovery time (−420 minutes; −541 to −299; high certainty) and restless legs syndrome (odds ratio 0.39; 0.29 to 0.53; moderate). There was little to no difference in all-cause mortality (risk difference −0.4%; −2.8 to 2.1; moderate) and serious adverse events (rate ratio 0.63; 0.38 to 1.04; low). Medium cut-off dialysis reduced hospitalisation (rate ratio 0.48; 0.27 to 0.84; low), infection (0.38; 0.17 to 0.85; moderate) and hospitalisation days (−1.5 days; −2.22 to −0.78; moderate). The authors conclude the dialyser improves several patient-important outcomes with no apparent harms, while more definitive studies are needed for mortality and other rare events.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen of the 22 studies were non-randomised, so the patient-reported gains (quality of life, pruritus, recovery time) come mostly from designs open to selection and expectation effects — the moderate and high GRADE ratings should be read against that mix. Mortality and serious adverse events are imprecisely estimated, and albumin loss — the anchor pilot's clearest laboratory finding — is not the focus of this review's pooled outcomes. The record carries no MeSH list, so none is quoted.

cards.people: A 20-patient crossover pilot (Cozzolino 2021) plus 22 studies and 1,811 patients in meta-analysis (Kandi 2022) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Patient-reported outcomes: quality of life +16.7 of 100 points (moderate certainty); recovery time −420 minutes (high certainty); pruritus −4.4; restless legs odds ratio 0.39. shelves.title: Midodrine for dialysis hypotension: pressures up about 12 mmHg and symptoms better in six of ten small studies — coherent, but built on the weakest designs in the library
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with dialysis-induced hypotension, does prophylactic midodrine reduce intradialytic hypotensive episodes, in the pooled small trials?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Humans · Hypotension/drug therapy*/etiology* · Midodrine/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled record is a systematic review of small studies, and its numbers favour midodrine (Prakash S et al., PMID: 15280522): across 10 studies (9 published, 1 unpublished) of haemodialysis patients with dialysis-induced hypotension, midodrine 2.5 to 10 mg given 15–30 minutes before dialysis was associated with post-dialysis systolic pressure higher by 12.4 mmHg (95% CI 7.5 to 17.7), diastolic higher by 7.3 mmHg (3.7 to 10.9), nadir systolic higher by 13.3 mmHg (8.6 to 18.0) and nadir diastolic higher by 5.9 mmHg (2.7 to 9.1); six of 10 studies reported improvement in hypotensive symptoms, and no serious adverse events were ascribed to midodrine. Those are surrogate pressure outcomes from observational, crossover and pre–post designs as well as small trials — the review itself warns its conclusion must be viewed with caution given the quality and sample size of the included studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylactic midodrine raises intra- and post-dialysis blood pressure and probably reduces hypotensive symptoms, on low-quality small-study evidence.

cards.headline: Prakash 2004: midodrine before dialysis raised post-dialysis systolic pressure by 12.4 mmHg and the nadir by 13.3 mmHg across 10 small studies, with symptoms better in six of them
cards.summary: Prakash 2004: midodrine before dialysis raised post-dialysis systolic pressure by 12.4 mmHg and the nadir by 13.3 mmHg across 10 small studies, with symptoms better in six of them
cards.people: 10 studies (9 meeting published selection criteria plus 1 unpublished) of haemodialysis patients with dialysis-induced (intradialytic) hypotension — observational studies, randomised controlled trials, crossover studies and pre–post intervention designs with at least 5 patients each — in a systematic review searching MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings and industry sources. Midodrine doses ranged from 2.5 to 10 mg given 15–30 minutes before dialysis.
cards.result: Post-dialysis systolic blood pressure was higher by 12.4 mmHg (95% CI 7.5 to 17.7) and diastolic pressure higher by 7.3 mmHg (95% CI 3.7 to 10.9) during midodrine treatment versus control. The nadir systolic blood pressure was higher by 13.3 mmHg (95% CI 8.6 to 18.0), with a difference in nadir diastolic pressure of 5.9 mmHg (95% CI 2.7 to 9.1). Six of 10 studies reported improvement in symptoms of intradialytic hypotension, and there were no reported serious adverse events ascribed to midodrine. The authors conclude midodrine appears to have a role in haemodialysis patients experiencing intradialytic hypotension, while cautioning that the conclusion must be viewed with caution given the quality and sample size of the studies included.
cards.watchOut: Most included designs (observational, crossover, pre–post) cannot separate drug effect from session-to-session variability and regression to the mean in patients selected for bad sessions, and the pooled outcomes are pressures, not the harder endpoints of session completion, hospitalisation or death. 'No serious adverse events reported' in small short studies is weak safety evidence for a vasopressor used thrice weekly for years — supine hypertension between sessions is the concern this literature barely measures.
cards.source: Prakash S et al. Midodrine appears to be safe and effective for dialysis-induced hypotension: a systematic review. Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. 2004. PMID: 15280522. 'no serious adverse events reported' in small short studies is weak safety evidence for a vasopressor used thrice weekly for years — supine hypertension between sessions is the concern this literature barely measures. prakash s et al. midodrine appears to be safe and effective for dialysis-induced hypotension: a systematic review. nephrology dialysis transplantation. 2004. pmid: 15280522. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adrenergic alpha-agonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · humans · hypotension/drug therapy*/etiology* · midodrine/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · renal dialysis/adverse effects* · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: midodrine lifts the dialysis-session pressure curve by roughly 12–13 mmHg systolic and helps symptoms in most small studies — a physiologically coherent benefit resting on low-quality designs
cards.summary: Synthesis: midodrine lifts the dialysis-session pressure curve by roughly 12–13 mmHg systolic and helps symptoms in most small studies — a physiologically coherent benefit resting on low-quality designs
cards.people: 10 small studies of haemodialysis patients with intradialytic hypotension (Prakash 2004) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Post-dialysis pressure: +12.4/+7.3 mmHg versus control. Nadir pressure: +13.3/+5.9 mmHg. Symptoms: improved in 6 of 10 studies. Serious adverse events: none reported. Dose range studied: 2.5–10 mg, 15–30 minutes before dialysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Midodrine's other homes in this library are different questions — vasovagal syncope (#1557), ICU vasopressor weaning (#1942) and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (#2498) — and none of their results should be imported here: the intradialytic setting adds ultrafiltration and rapid fluid shifts that those populations do not have. A large blinded trial with session-completion and symptom endpoints remains the missing evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Prakash S et al. Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. 2004 (PMID: 15280522).

shelves.title: Gabapentin versus levodopa for restless legs on dialysis: scores improved about 17 versus 13 points in four weeks — one small trial, no placebo, and augmentation never measured
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome, does gabapentin improve symptoms compared with levodopa?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Amines/therapeutic use* · Carbidopa/therapeutic use* · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/therapeutic use* · Drug Combinations · Gabapentin · Humans · Iran · Levodopa/therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/drug effects · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects* · Restless Legs Syndrome/diagnosis/drug therapy*/etiology/physiopathology · Sleep/drug effects · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small, single-centre randomised trial is the whole comparative record in dialysis patients (Razazian N et al., PMID: 25758874): over four weeks, both gabapentin 200 mg and levodopa-carbidopa 110 mg improved restless legs symptoms and sleep in haemodialysis patients, with gabapentin improving the International Restless Legs Study Group score more (change from baseline approximately −17 versus approximately −13; P = 0.016); both drugs improved sleep parameters (P < 0.0001 within groups). A four-point difference on the symptom scale, in a trial whose record does not even state its sample size, over four weeks, with no placebo arm and no augmentation follow-up, is a hint rather than an answer — augmentation on dopaminergic therapy is precisely the long-term harm a four-week trial cannot see, and it is the main clinical reason to prefer a non-dopaminergic drug in this population. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): gabapentin improved restless legs scores slightly more than levodopa-carbidopa over four weeks in one small dialysis trial.

cards.headline: Razazian 2015: gabapentin beat levodopa-carbidopa on restless legs score over 4 weeks in dialysis patients — improvement about −17 versus about −13 points (P = 0.016)
cards.summary: Razazian 2015: gabapentin beat levodopa-carbidopa on restless legs score over 4 weeks in dialysis patients — improvement about −17 versus about −13 points (P = 0.016)
cards.people: Haemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome diagnosed by International Restless Legs Study Group criteria, in a four-week randomised clinical trial in Iran (sample size not stated in the record). After a four-week washout of previous restless legs treatments, subjects were randomly assigned to gabapentin 200 mg or levodopa-carbidopa 110 mg for four weeks. Outcomes were the International Restless Legs Study Group (IRLS) questionnaire, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, administered before and after treatment.
cards.result: Both drugs were effective for restless legs symptoms, but the effect of gabapentin was more significant: gabapentin improved the IRLS total score (change from baseline to post-treatment approximately −17) compared with levodopa-carbidopa (approximately −13) (P = 0.016). For sleep parameters, levodopa improved sleep quality, sleep latency and sleep duration (P < 0.0001), and gabapentin was also effective on sleep parameters (P < 0.0001). The authors conclude gabapentin is a safe and effective therapy for restless legs syndrome among haemodialysis patients and may be considered as an alternative or additive treatment.
cards.watchOut: The record does not state how many patients were randomised, reports the headline scores only as approximate changes (≈ −17 versus ≈ −13), and gives within-group P values for sleep rather than between-group differences — so the precision of the gabapentin advantage cannot be judged. Four weeks cannot capture augmentation (paradoxical worsening on dopaminergic drugs), the outcome that most influences long-term choice in restless legs syndrome, and there is no placebo group to size either drug's absolute effect in a population whose symptoms fluctuate with dialysis adequacy and iron status.
cards.source: Razazian N et al. Gabapentin versus levodopa-c for the treatment of restless legs syndrome in hemodialysis patients: a randomized clinical trial. Saudi Journal of Kidney Diseases and Transplantation. 2015. PMID: 25758874. Registry ID: IRCT201112078323N1. cards.headline: Synthesis: in dialysis restless legs, gabapentin edged levodopa-carbidopa over four weeks in a single small trial — both helped sleep, and the long-term augmentation question was never asked
cards.summary: Synthesis: in dialysis restless legs, gabapentin edged levodopa-carbidopa over four weeks in a single small trial — both helped sleep, and the long-term augmentation question was never asked
cards.people: Haemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome in one four-week randomised trial (Razazian 2015; sample size not stated in the record) — the carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: IRLS total score change: approximately −17 on gabapentin versus approximately −13 on levodopa-carbidopa (P = 0.016). Sleep quality, latency and duration: improved within both groups (P < 0.0001). Placebo comparison, augmentation, durability beyond four weeks: untested. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The general-population restless legs shelves (#498, #929) compare alpha-2-delta ligands with dopamine agonists over much longer periods in non-dialysis patients; their augmentation data are relevant background but are not dialysis evidence and are not imported into this stamp. Gabapentin dosing in kidney failure needs renal adjustment — the 200 mg dose here was the trial's dialysis-population dose, not a general prescription. Tier C is set because the evidence is one small, incompletely reported trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Razazian N et al. Saudi Journal of Kidney Diseases and Transplantation. 2015 (PMID: 25758874).

shelves.title: Citrate versus heparin catheter locks: the infection win belongs to citrate locks carrying an antimicrobial — plain citrate's proven prize is less bleeding
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with tunnelled catheters, does a citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection and dysfunction compared with a heparin lock, in the pooled trials?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Catheter-Related Infections/etiology/prevention & control · Catheters/adverse effects · Central Venous Catheters/adverse effects · Citrates/therapeutic use · Heparin/therapeutic use · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects/instrumentation
shelves.balance: The pooled randomised record separates into two different products wearing one name. Where the citrate lock contained an antimicrobial, catheter-related bloodstream infection fell sharply against heparin (relative risk 0.34, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.49, in Mai H et al., PMID: 31012037), and tunnelled cuffed catheters showed the clearest benefit (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69); citrate in non-tunnelled catheters cut exit-site infection (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.75), and bleeding episodes were lower with citrate in tunnelled catheters (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86) and with citrate alone (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.85). What did not move: catheter removal for poor flow, thrombolytic use, thrombocytopenia, access-related admission, or mortality. So the infection headline belongs largely to antimicrobial-containing locks, while plain citrate's own clearest gain is less bleeding — a heparin-sparing effect, not proof that citrate alone prevents bloodstream infection. PROPOSED SPLIT: antimicrobial-containing citrate locks likely prevent catheter-related bloodstream infection and citrate locks bleed less than heparin, but citrate alone has not been shown to deliver the infection benefit, and no lock strategy changed mortality or catheter survival for flow.

cards.headline: Mai 2019 (meta-analysis of RCTs): antimicrobial-containing citrate locks cut catheter-related bloodstream infection versus heparin (RR 0.34) — plain citrate's proven gain was less bleeding (RR 0.51), not infection
cards.summary: Mai 2019 (meta-analysis of RCTs): antimicrobial-containing citrate locks cut catheter-related bloodstream infection versus heparin (RR 0.34) — plain citrate's proven gain was less bleeding (RR 0.51), not infection
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Mai 2019)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of citrate lock versus heparin lock for haemodialysis catheters, pooled in an updated systematic review and meta-analysis (Mai H et al. 2019), covering tunnelled cuffed and non-tunnelled cuffed catheters; primary outcomes were catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBI), exit-site infection, bleeding, catheter removal for poor flow, and thrombolytic treatment.
cards.result: Citrate lock containing antimicrobials reduced the relative risk of CRBI compared with heparin lock (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.49; I²=0%; P<0.00001), and tunnelled cuffed catheters benefited most for CRBI prevention (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69; I²=40%; P=0.0007). Citrate lock with non-tunnelled catheters reduced exit-site infection versus heparin (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.75; I²=0%; P=0.001). Bleeding episodes were reduced with citrate in tunnelled catheters (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86; P=0.01) and with citrate alone (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.85; I²=12%; P=0.010). No significant difference was found for catheter removal for poor flow (P=0.91), thrombolytic treatment (P=0.76), thrombocytopenia (P=0.37), access-related admission (P=0.10), or all-cause mortality (P=0.62). A microbiological analysis suggested CRBI occurrence was closely related to Staphylococcus aureus in citrate-locked catheters (P=0.015) rather than heparin-locked ones (P=0.868).
cards.watchOut: The headline infection result is for citrate locks containing antimicrobials — pooling them with plain citrate overstates what citrate alone does, and the abstract reports no separate CRBI estimate for citrate without an antimicrobial. Relative risks are printed without the underlying absolute infection rates, so the absolute number of infections prevented per catheter-year cannot be read off this record. The gentamicin–citrate antibiotic lock comparison is a different question, carded at shelf #1734.
cards.source: Mai H et al. Citrate versus heparin lock for prevention of hemodialysis catheter-related complications: updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. International Urology and Nephrology. 2019. PMID: 31012037. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: split the lock by its contents — infection prevention tracks with the antimicrobial in the lock; bleeding reduction tracks with citrate replacing heparin
cards.summary: Synthesis: split the lock by its contents — infection prevention tracks with the antimicrobial in the lock; bleeding reduction tracks with citrate replacing heparin
cards.people: The pooled randomised trials of citrate versus heparin haemodialysis catheter locks, as meta-analysed by Mai et al. 2019 — the whole comparative record for citrate alone versus heparin and for antimicrobial-containing citrate versus heparin.
cards.result: CRBI: RR 0.34 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.49) for antimicrobial-containing citrate versus heparin; RR 0.42 in tunnelled cuffed catheters. Exit-site infection: RR 0.48 for citrate in non-tunnelled catheters. Bleeding: RR 0.51 to 0.53 favouring citrate. Catheter removal for poor flow, thrombolytic treatment, thrombocytopenia, access-related admission, all-cause mortality: no significant differences. PROPOSED SPLIT — the benefit splits by lock composition and by outcome.
cards.watchOut: A unit choosing a lock on this evidence should name which product it means: 'citrate' alone, citrate with an antimicrobial, and the catheter type all change which benefit is on offer. None of the pooled outcomes shows a mortality or catheter-longevity advantage, and antimicrobial locks carry the usual stewardship question about resistance that these trials were not designed to answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mai H et al. International Urology and Nephrology. 2019 (PMID: 31012037).

shelves.title: Stent graft versus balloon for a failing dialysis graft: patency doubled at six months in REVISE and the pooled trials agree — the access still fails eventually, just later and with fewer redos
shelves.question: In failing dialysis arteriovenous grafts, does a stent graft improve patency compared with balloon angioplasty alone?
shelves.mesh: Angioplasty, Balloon*/adverse effects · Arteriovenous Shunt, Surgical*/methods · Catheters, Indwelling/adverse effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Graft Occlusion, Vascular/etiology/therapy · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Renal Dialysis* · Stents*/adverse effects · Treatment Failure · Vascular Patency
shelves.balance: For a failing prosthetic dialysis graft narrowed at the venous anastomosis, adding an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene stent graft to balloon angioplasty roughly doubled six-month patency in the REVISE trial (Haskal ZJ et al., PMID: 20147715): treatment-area patency 51% versus 23% and access-circuit patency 38% versus 20%, with binary restenosis in 28% versus 78%. The pooled record since (Ng B et al., PMID: 34108161; seven studies, 1,147 patients, 867 with grafts) points the same way, with covered stents associated with lower loss of patency at 6, 12, and 24 months and better access-circuit primary patency at 6 and 12 months — but no significant difference in loss of secondary patency at 12 or 24 months, meaning the graft is not ultimately saved more often, it is kept primarily patent longer with fewer repeat procedures (freedom from subsequent intervention at six months 32% versus 16% in REVISE). Adverse events in REVISE were equivalent apart from restenosis itself. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for venous anastomotic stenosis in a failing prosthetic graft, a stent graft is the better revision — expect longer primary patency and fewer re-interventions, not a longer-lived access in the end. Drug-coated balloons in native fistulas are a different question (shelf #1594).

cards.headline: Haskal 2010 (REVISE): stent graft doubled six-month treatment-area patency versus balloon angioplasty alone — 51% versus 23% — and halved the need for repeat intervention
cards.summary: Haskal 2010 (REVISE): stent graft doubled six-month treatment-area patency versus balloon angioplasty alone — 51% versus 23% — and halved the need for repeat intervention
cards.people: 190 patients undergoing haemodialysis with a prosthetic arteriovenous graft and venous anastomotic stenosis, in a prospective multicentre randomised trial, assigned to balloon angioplasty alone or balloon angioplasty plus an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene stent graft; primary end points were patency of the treatment area and of the entire access circuit at six months.
cards.result: At six months, patency of the treatment area was 51% in the stent-graft group versus 23% with balloon angioplasty alone (P<0.001), and patency of the access circuit was 38% versus 20% (P=0.008). Freedom from subsequent interventions at six months was 32% versus 16% (P=0.03 by log-rank test). Binary restenosis at six months occurred in 28% of the stent-graft group versus 78% of the angioplasty group (P<0.001). Adverse events at six months were equivalent between groups except for restenosis, which was more frequent with angioplasty alone (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Six months is the trial's horizon: even in the winning arm, half the treatment areas had lost patency and two-thirds of patients had needed another intervention by then — this is a better revision, not a cure for graft failure. The population is prosthetic grafts with anastomotic stenosis only; nothing here speaks to native fistulas or to central venous stenosis.
cards.source: Haskal ZJ et al. Stent graft versus balloon angioplasty for failing dialysis-access grafts. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20147715. Registry ID: NCT00678249. randomised controlled trial (revise; haskal 2010) 190 patients undergoing haemodialysis with a prosthetic arteriovenous graft and venous anastomotic stenosis, in a prospective multicentre randomised trial, assigned to balloon angioplasty alone or balloon angioplasty plus an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene stent graft; primary end points were patency of the treatment area and of the entire access circuit at six months. at six months, patency of the treatment area was 51% in the stent-graft group versus 23% with balloon angioplasty alone (p<0.001), and patency of the access circuit was 38% versus 20% (p=0.008). freedom from subsequent interventions at six months was 32% versus 16% (p=0.03 by log-rank test). binary restenosis at six months occurred in 28% of the stent-graft group versus 78% of the angioplasty group (p<0.001). adverse events at six months were equivalent between groups except for restenosis, which was more frequent with angioplasty alone (p<0.001). six months is the trial's horizon: even in the winning arm, half the treatment areas had lost patency and two-thirds of patients had needed another intervention by then — this is a better revision, not a cure for graft failure. the population is prosthetic grafts with anastomotic stenosis only; nothing here speaks to native fistulas or to central venous stenosis. haskal zj et al. stent graft versus balloon angioplasty for failing dialysis-access grafts. the new england journal of medicine. 2010. pmid: 20147715. registry id: nct00678249. mesh: angioplasty, balloon*/adverse effects · arteriovenous shunt, surgical*/methods · catheters, indwelling/adverse effects · female · follow-up studies · graft occlusion, vascular/etiology/therapy · humans · intention to treat analysis · kaplan-meier estimate · male · middle aged · recurrence · renal dialysis* · stents*/adverse effects · treatment failure · vascular patency

cards.headline: Ng 2021 (meta-analysis, 7 studies, 1,147 patients): covered stents beat angioplasty on primary patency out to 24 months in failing grafts — but secondary patency (the access ultimately saved) did not differ
cards.summary: Ng 2021 (meta-analysis, 7 studies, 1,147 patients): covered stents beat angioplasty on primary patency out to 24 months in failing grafts — but secondary patency (the access ultimately saved) did not differ
cards.people: Seven studies including 1,147 patients with failing arteriovenous access (867 arteriovenous grafts, 280 fistulas), pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis registered as CRD42018069955; the meta-analyses of patency were performed in patients with failing grafts only, and overall risk of bias was moderate.
cards.result: Covered stents were associated with lower loss of patency versus angioplasty alone at 6 months (OR 4.48, 95% CI 1.98 to 10.14; P<0.001), 12 months (OR 4.07, 95% CI 1.74 to 9.54; P=0.001), and 24 months (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.17 to 4.29; P=0.01). Access-circuit primary patency was superior with covered stents at 6 months (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.80; P<0.001) and 12 months (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.41; P=0.02) but not significant at 24 months. There was no significant difference in loss of secondary patency at 12 months (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.23; P=0.25) or 24 months (OR 0.67; P=0.34).
cards.watchOut: One included study was an ongoing trial and the pooled odds ratios for patency are large with wide intervals — the direction is consistent but the exact size is not precise. The null result for secondary patency is the honest ceiling on the claim: covered stents postpone failure and re-intervention rather than preventing eventual access loss.
cards.source: Ng B et al. Covered stents versus balloon angioplasty for failure of arteriovenous access: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. 2021. PMID: 34108161. cards.headline: Synthesis: a stent graft is the better revision for a stenosed prosthetic graft — longer primary patency, fewer repeat procedures, same eventual access fate
cards.summary: Synthesis: a stent graft is the better revision for a stenosed prosthetic graft — longer primary patency, fewer repeat procedures, same eventual access fate
cards.people: One multicentre RCT of 190 patients (REVISE, Haskal 2010) and a seven-study meta-analysis of 1,147 patients (Ng 2021) on covered stents versus balloon angioplasty alone for failing dialysis grafts.
cards.result: Treatment-area patency at six months 51% versus 23% (REVISE); pooled lower loss of patency at 6, 12, and 24 months (OR 4.48, 4.07, 2.24); freedom from re-intervention at six months 32% versus 16%; binary restenosis 28% versus 78%. Secondary patency: no significant difference at 12 or 24 months. Adverse events: equivalent apart from restenosis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the outcome is a patency surrogate in a single large trial plus small pooled studies, and because device iterations since 2010 may not match the tested stent graft exactly. The claim to carry away is procedural — fewer re-interventions per graft-year — not longer access survival, which the evidence does not show.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haskal ZJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20147715); Ng B et al. BMJ Open. 2021 (PMID: 34108161).

shelves.title: Antithymocyte globulin versus basiliximab for transplant induction: rejection 15.6% versus 25.5%, infections 85.8% versus 75.2% — a trade that turns on how high-risk the recipient is
shelves.question: In kidney transplantation, does rabbit antithymocyte globulin induction reduce acute rejection compared with basiliximab induction, and at what infection cost?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Animals · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antilymphocyte Serum/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Basiliximab · Blood Cell Count · Cadaver · Delayed Graft Function/prevention & control · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Graft Rejection/prevention & control · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Kidney Transplantation*/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Rabbits · Receptors, Interleukin-2/antagonists & inhibitors · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: In the head-to-head randomised trial in high-risk deceased-donor recipients (Brennan DC et al., PMID: 17093248; 278 patients on ciclosporin, mycophenolate, and prednisone), rabbit antithymocyte globulin beat basiliximab on the outcome induction exists for: acute rejection 15.6% versus 25.5% (P=0.02), and rejection severe enough to need antibody treatment 1.4% versus 8.0% (P=0.005) — while the composite of rejection, delayed graft function, graft loss, and death did not differ (P=0.34), nor did graft loss (9.2% versus 10.2%), delayed graft function (40.4% versus 44.5%), or death (4.3% versus 4.4%). The price was infection overall: 85.8% versus 75.2% (P=0.03) — though cytomegalovirus disease ran the other way, 7.8% versus 17.5% (P=0.02), under the prophylaxis used. Pooled patient-level reanalysis of two international trials (Alloway RR et al., PMID: 30838775; 508 recipients) found treatment failure 25.1% with antithymocyte globulin versus 36.0% with interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (absolute difference −10.9%, 95% CI −18.8 to −2.9). PROPOSED SPLIT: in high-risk recipients antithymocyte globulin prevents more — and more severe — rejection than basiliximab, at the cost of more infections overall, with no demonstrated survival or graft-survival advantage at one year.

cards.headline: Brennan 2006: antithymocyte globulin cut acute rejection to 15.6% versus 25.5% on basiliximab and antibody-treated rejection to 1.4% versus 8.0% — but infections rose to 85.8% versus 75.2%, and survival and graft loss were identical
cards.summary: Brennan 2006: antithymocyte globulin cut acute rejection to 15.6% versus 25.5% on basiliximab and antibody-treated rejection to 1.4% versus 8.0% — but infections rose to 85.8% versus 75.2%, and survival and graft loss were identical
cards.people: 278 patients at high risk for acute rejection or delayed graft function receiving a deceased-donor kidney transplant, in a prospective randomised international study; all received ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone, and were assigned to rabbit antithymocyte globulin 1.5 mg/kg daily on days 0–4 (141 patients) or basiliximab 20 mg on days 0 and 4 (137 patients). The primary end point was a composite of acute rejection, delayed graft function, graft loss, and death at 12 months.
cards.result: The composite end point did not differ between groups (P=0.34). Acute rejection was lower with antithymocyte globulin than basiliximab (15.6% vs 25.5%, P=0.02), as was acute rejection requiring antibody treatment (1.4% vs 8.0%, P=0.005). Graft loss (9.2% vs 10.2%), delayed graft function (40.4% vs 44.5%), and death (4.3% vs 4.4%) were similar. All adverse events, serious adverse events, and cancers were similar overall, but infection was more frequent with antithymocyte globulin (85.8% vs 75.2%, P=0.03) while cytomegalovirus disease was less frequent (7.8% vs 17.5%, P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A high-risk, deceased-donor, ciclosporin-era population: the rejection gap may shrink in lower-risk recipients or under tacrolimus-based maintenance, and the CMV result depends on the prophylaxis protocol of the time. Twelve months cannot show whether fewer early rejections become longer graft survival — in this trial they had not, yet.
cards.source: Brennan DC et al. Rabbit antithymocyte globulin versus basiliximab in renal transplantation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2006. PMID: 17093248. Registry ID: NCT00235300. cards.headline: Alloway 2019 (pooled reanalysis, 508 recipients): treatment failure 25.1% with antithymocyte globulin versus 36.0% with interleukin-2 receptor antagonists — a 10.9-point absolute gap meeting noninferiority and superiority
cards.summary: Alloway 2019 (pooled reanalysis, 508 recipients): treatment failure 25.1% with antithymocyte globulin versus 36.0% with interleukin-2 receptor antagonists — a 10.9-point absolute gap meeting noninferiority and superiority
cards.type: Pooled patient-level reanalysis of 2 RCTs plus meta-analysis (Alloway 2019)
cards.people: Patient-level pooled data from two international randomised trials totalling 508 kidney transplant recipients, reanalysed to compare rabbit antithymocyte globulin against interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (the basiliximab class) on a quadruple end point of biopsy-proven acute rejection, graft loss, death, or loss to follow-up, assembled for United States regulatory approval.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 25.1% of the antithymocyte globulin group and 36.0% of the interleukin-2 receptor antagonist group, an absolute difference of −10.9% (95% CI −18.8 to −2.9), supporting both noninferiority (margin 10%) and superiority. In a meta-analysis of seven trials, the difference in biopsy-proven acute rejection at 12 months was −4.8% (95% CI −8.6 to −0.9) in favour of antithymocyte globulin.
cards.watchOut: This is a reanalysis assembled for a regulatory submission, and its composite counts loss to follow-up as failure — a conservative but non-clinical component. It pools the interleukin-2 antagonist class rather than basiliximab alone, and like the anchor trial it speaks to rejection and treatment failure, not to long-term graft survival or the infection ledger in modern prophylaxis eras.
cards.source: Alloway RR et al. Rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin for the prevention of acute rejection in kidney transplantation. American Journal of Transplantation. 2019. PMID: 30838775. cards.headline: Synthesis: the depleting agent wins on rejection, loses on total infections, and ties on everything a patient would count at one year
cards.summary: Synthesis: the depleting agent wins on rejection, loses on total infections, and ties on everything a patient would count at one year
cards.people: One randomised trial of 278 high-risk deceased-donor recipients (Brennan 2006) and a pooled reanalysis of 508 recipients across two trials (Alloway 2019), comparing rabbit antithymocyte globulin with basiliximab or its class for kidney transplant induction.
cards.result: Acute rejection: 15.6% versus 25.5% (Brennan); biopsy-proven rejection difference −4.8% across seven trials (Alloway). Antibody-treated rejection: 1.4% versus 8.0%. Treatment failure: 25.1% versus 36.0%. Infection overall: 85.8% versus 75.2%; cytomegalovirus disease: 7.8% versus 17.5%. Graft loss, delayed graft function, death: no differences. PROPOSED SPLIT — the trade is rejection against infection, and it resolves by recipient risk.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the anchor trial is from the ciclosporin era in a deliberately high-risk population, and no trial here follows recipients long enough to convert the rejection advantage into graft-years. For a low-risk living-donor recipient, the absolute rejection gap — and therefore the case for accepting more infection — is likely smaller than these numbers suggest.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brennan DC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2006 (PMID: 17093248); Alloway RR et al. American Journal of Transplantation. 2019 (PMID: 30838775).

shelves.title: Skipping or stopping steroids after kidney transplant: rejection rises by half to three-quarters in relative terms across 48 trials — graft loss and death have not followed, within follow-up that ends too soon to be sure
shelves.question: After kidney transplantation, does steroid avoidance or early withdrawal increase rejection or graft loss compared with maintenance steroids, in the pooled randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Graft Rejection/immunology/prevention & control · Graft Survival/drug effects/immunology · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Kidney Transplantation*/mortality · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Steroids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: Across 48 randomised studies and 7,803 kidney transplant recipients, the Cochrane review (Haller MC et al., PMID: 27546100) gives steroid avoidance or withdrawal a consistent signature: acute rejection rises — relative risk 1.58 (95% CI 1.08 to 2.30) when steroids were given for less than 14 days, and relative risk 1.77 (95% CI 1.20 to 2.61) when steroids were withdrawn later — while patient mortality and graft loss show no significant difference out to the follow-up available: death at one year, relative risk 0.68 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.30) for withdrawal versus maintenance and 0.96 (0.52 to 1.80) for avoidance versus maintenance; graft loss excluding death with a functioning graft, relative risk 1.17 (0.72 to 1.92) and 1.09 (0.64 to 1.86) respectively. There was also no evidence of a difference in infection or malignancy in adults, and the effect in children (three studies, 346 participants) is unclear. So the rejection harm is real and measured; the feared downstream cost in lost grafts has not appeared within five years — but the reviewers stress that no prospective long-term studies exist, so 'not yet seen' is not 'never'. PROPOSED SPLIT: steroid avoidance or withdrawal buys freedom from long-term steroids at a proven price in acute rejection, with graft loss and mortality unchanged so far — the split is between a certain early harm and an unproven late one, in both directions.

cards.headline: Haller 2016 (Cochrane, 48 studies, 7,803 recipients): avoiding or withdrawing steroids raised acute rejection (RR 1.58–1.77) — mortality and graft loss did not differ in any comparison
cards.summary: Haller 2016 (Cochrane, 48 studies, 7,803 recipients): avoiding or withdrawing steroids raised acute rejection (RR 1.58–1.77) — mortality and graft loss did not differ in any comparison
cards.people: 48 randomised and quasi-randomised studies (224 reports) involving 7,803 kidney transplant recipients — three studies in children (346 participants) — comparing steroid avoidance or withdrawal at any time point against steroid maintenance, and avoidance against withdrawal; this is the 2016 update of a 2009 review, searched to 15 February 2016.
cards.result: In adults there was no significant difference in mortality: steroid withdrawal versus maintenance, death at one year relative risk 0.68 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.30; 10 studies, 1,913 participants); steroid avoidance versus maintenance, RR 0.96 (0.52 to 1.80; 10 studies, 1,462 participants). Graft loss excluding death with a functioning graft at one year likewise did not differ: withdrawal versus maintenance RR 1.17 (0.72 to 1.92; 8 studies, 1,817 participants); avoidance versus maintenance RR 1.09 (0.64 to 1.86; 7 studies, 1,211 participants). Acute rejection risk significantly increased when steroids were given for less than 14 days after transplantation (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.30; 7 studies, 835 participants) and when steroids were withdrawn at a later time point (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.61; 10 studies, 1,913 participants). No evidence suggested a difference in infection or malignancy in adults; the effect of withdrawal in children is unclear.
cards.watchOut: Risk of bias was low for sequence generation in only 19 studies and allocation concealment in 14, and follow-up in the underlying trials rarely reaches the horizon where rejection episodes might convert into graft loss — the authors state plainly that long-term consequences remain unclear because prospective long-term studies have not been conducted. The review also cannot show the benefit side of the ledger (diabetes, bone, cardiovascular effects of steroid freedom) with the same rigour, because the trials measured rejection far better than steroid harms.
cards.source: Haller MC et al. Steroid avoidance or withdrawal for kidney transplant recipients. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27546100. Registry ID: none in the record. 7 studies, 835 participants) and when steroids were withdrawn at a later time point (rr 1.77, 95% ci 1.20 to 2.61; 10 studies, 1,913 participants). no evidence suggested a difference in infection or malignancy in adults; cards.headline: Synthesis: rejection is the proven price of steroid freedom; graft loss is the unproven fear — and the trials end before either late benefit or late harm can declare itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: rejection is the proven price of steroid freedom; graft loss is the unproven fear — and the trials end before either late benefit or late harm can declare itself
cards.people: 48 randomised studies, 7,803 kidney transplant recipients (Haller 2016, Cochrane) — the entire randomised record on steroid avoidance or withdrawal after kidney transplantation.
cards.result: Acute rejection: relative risk 1.58 (steroids under 14 days) and 1.77 (later withdrawal). Mortality at one year: RR 0.68 and 0.96, both non-significant. Graft loss at one year: RR 1.17 and 1.09, both non-significant. Infection and malignancy: no demonstrated difference in adults. Children: unclear. PROPOSED SPLIT — a certain early harm against unproven long-term effects on both sides.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the null graft-loss result as proof of long-term safety: confidence intervals include up to a 92% relative increase for withdrawal, and chronic antibody-mediated injury from extra rejection episodes is exactly the kind of harm five-year trial horizons miss. Equally, do not quote the rejection increase as proof steroid freedom is reckless — for a recipient with steroid-driven diabetes or bone disease, the trade may be worth making with eyes open and monitoring close.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haller MC et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27546100).

shelves.title: Mannitol around kidney transplantation: less delayed graft function in the pooled trials (RR as low as 0.25) — from eight small, dated studies the reviewers themselves grade cautiously
shelves.question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does donor or recipient mannitol improve early graft function and reduce delayed graft function, in the pooled trials?
shelves.mesh: Graft Rejection · Graft Survival · Humans · Kidney · Kidney Transplantation*/adverse effects · Mannitol
shelves.balance: The pooled record is small, old, and pointed in a friendly direction. Van de Laar SCV et al. (PMID: 34412911) found eight eligible studies among 3,570 references — one examining mannitol during kidney donation and seven during transplantation, six of them meta-analysable, totalling 1,143 patients — and reported significantly less acute renal failure with mannitol (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.79; P<0.01) and less delayed graft function in the analyses reported (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.77; and RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.94), while graft survival, rejection, renal failure, creatinine clearance, diuresis, and serum creatinine showed no significant differences. The authors themselves close with the caveats that decide the stamp: the quality of the underlying evidence must temper interpretation, only one study addresses donor-side administration, and more up-to-date research is needed. A cheap, familiar osmotic diuretic with pooled relative risks like these would normally earn more — but the trials predate modern donor, preservation, and recipient practice. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mannitol around transplantation is associated with less delayed graft function in the pooled older trials, and that is all the record can honestly carry.

cards.headline: Van de Laar 2021 (systematic review, 8 studies, 1,143 patients): mannitol was associated with less acute renal failure (RR 0.45) and less delayed graft function — and with nothing else, in trials the authors call low quality and dated
cards.summary: Van de Laar 2021 (systematic review, 8 studies, 1,143 patients): mannitol was associated with less acute renal failure (RR 0.45) and less delayed graft function — and with nothing else, in trials the authors call low quality and dated
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (van de Laar 2021)
cards.people: Eight studies (six eligible for meta-analysis) of mannitol given during kidney donation (one study) or during kidney transplantation (seven studies), totalling 1,143 patients, identified from 3,570 references across five databases to 12 July 2021; outcomes included graft survival, rejection, acute renal failure, delayed graft function, creatinine clearance, diuresis, and serum creatinine.
cards.result: Acute renal failure was significantly less frequent with mannitol than control (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.79; P<0.01). Delayed graft function analyses also favoured mannitol (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.77; P=0.02, and RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.94, as reported). Differences in graft survival, rejection, renal failure, creatinine clearance, diuresis, and serum creatinine were not significant. The authors conclude mannitol during kidney transplantation leads to a lower incidence of acute renal failure and delayed graft function, while emphasising that evidence quality must be considered, that donor-side use rests on a single study, and that more up-to-date research is needed.
cards.watchOut: The two delayed-graft-function estimates are reported side by side in the record without the subgroup structure that would explain them, and the second is printed with a P value (0.94) inconsistent with its own confidence interval — treat the precise size of the DGF effect as unsettled even though both point estimates favour mannitol. The underlying studies are small and largely predate contemporary machine perfusion and donor practice (the interventions carded at shelves #2100 and #2101), so transportability to a modern deceased-donor programme is assumed, not shown.
cards.source: Laar SCV et al. Effect of Mannitol on Kidney Function After Kidney Transplantation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Transplantation Proceedings. 2021. PMID: 34412911. cards.headline: Synthesis: a favourable signal on early graft function from a thin, ageing evidence base — enough to keep using a cheap drug, not enough to promise it works
cards.summary: Synthesis: a favourable signal on early graft function from a thin, ageing evidence base — enough to keep using a cheap drug, not enough to promise it works
cards.people: Eight studies, 1,143 patients, one systematic review and meta-analysis (van de Laar 2021) — the whole pooled record on mannitol in kidney donation and transplantation.
cards.result: Acute renal failure: RR 0.45 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.79). Delayed graft function: RR 0.25 and RR 0.69 in the analyses reported. Graft survival, rejection, creatinine clearance, diuresis, serum creatinine: no significant differences. Donor administration: one study only. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Delayed graft function is an early, partly surrogate outcome; a reduction that never surfaces in graft survival or creatinine may reflect the diuretic making urine sooner rather than the graft being injured less. Any centre weighing mannitol should weigh it as a low-cost, low-risk habit with supportive-but-weak evidence, not as a proven graft-preservation intervention alongside perfusion and hypothermia strategies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Laar SCV et al. Transplantation Proceedings. 2021 (PMID: 34412911).

shelves.title: Eculizumab in atypical HUS: platelets up 73×10⁹/L, 80% event-free, four of five dialysis patients off dialysis — prospective evidence with no control arm, in a disease that rarely allows one
shelves.question: In atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, does terminal complement blockade with eculizumab improve kidney function and haematological remission in open-label prospective trials?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/blood/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Complement C5/antagonists & inhibitors · Female · Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome/blood/drug therapy/genetics/therapy · Humans · Kidney Diseases/drug therapy/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Plasma Exchange · Platelet Count · Quality of Life · Thrombotic Microangiopathies/prevention & control · Young Adult
shelves.balance: There is no randomised trial of eculizumab in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and there is unlikely ever to be one: the disease is rare, genetic, and life-threatening, and plasma therapy does not treat its underlying complement-driven microangiopathy. What exists is two prospective open-label phase 2 trials totalling 37 patients aged 12 and over (Legendre CM et al., PMID: 23738544). In trial 1 — patients with low platelets and renal damage — the platelet count rose by a mean of 73×10⁹ per litre by week 26 (P<0.001) and dialysis was discontinued in four of five patients on it. In trial 2 — patients with renal damage progressing despite at least eight weeks of plasma exchange or infusion — 80% achieved thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status. Estimated GFR improved continuously and in a time-dependent way in both trials, earlier treatment was associated with significantly greater GFR improvement, health-related quality of life improved, and through median exposures of 64 and 62 weeks there was no cumulative toxicity and no meningococcal or other serious infection-related adverse event. Before-and-after evidence in a disease this stereotyped carries real weight, but it cannot quantify the effect the way a control arm would, and spontaneous or plasma-related improvement cannot be fully excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): terminal complement blockade reverses the haematology and improves kidney function in most treated patients — start early — on prospective but uncontrolled evidence.

cards.headline: Legendre 2013, trial 1: in aHUS with low platelets and renal damage, eculizumab raised the platelet count by a mean 73×10⁹/L by week 26 — and 4 of 5 patients on dialysis came off it
cards.summary: Legendre 2013, trial 1: in aHUS with low platelets and renal damage, eculizumab raised the platelet count by a mean 73×10⁹/L by week 26 — and 4 of 5 patients on dialysis came off it
cards.people: 17 patients aged 12 years or older with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, low platelet counts, and renal damage, treated with eculizumab for 26 weeks and a long-term extension (median exposure 64 weeks) in a prospective phase 2 trial; the primary end point was change in platelet count.
cards.result: The mean increase in platelet count from baseline to week 26 was 73×10⁹ per litre (P<0.001). Eculizumab was associated with significant improvement in all secondary end points, with continuous, time-dependent increases in estimated GFR, and dialysis was discontinued in four of five patients receiving it. Earlier intervention was associated with significantly greater improvement in estimated GFR, and health-related quality of life improved. No cumulative toxicity or serious infection-related adverse events, including meningococcal infections, were observed through the extension period.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients, no control arm: in a disease where plasma therapy alone can transiently normalise haematology, an uncontrolled before-and-after rise in platelets and GFR cannot be wholly credited to the drug, and the dialysis-discontinuation figure rests on five patients. The association between earlier treatment and greater GFR recovery is observational within the trial — patients treated earlier may simply have had more recoverable kidney.
cards.source: Legendre CM et al. Terminal complement inhibitor eculizumab in atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23738544. cards.headline: Legendre 2013, trial 2: in aHUS with renal damage progressing despite plasma therapy, 80% of patients reached thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status on eculizumab
cards.summary: Legendre 2013, trial 2: in aHUS with renal damage progressing despite plasma therapy, 80% of patients reached thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status on eculizumab
cards.people: 20 patients aged 12 years or older with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and renal damage but no fall in platelet count greater than 25% during at least eight weeks of plasma exchange or infusion — that is, disease not controlled by plasma therapy — treated with eculizumab for 26 weeks and a long-term extension (median exposure 62 weeks); the primary end point was thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status (no platelet fall over 25%, no plasma exchange or infusion, no new dialysis).
cards.result: 80% of patients achieved thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status. As in trial 1, eculizumab was associated with significant improvement in all secondary end points, continuous time-dependent increases in estimated GFR, and improvement in health-related quality of life, with earlier intervention associated with significantly greater GFR improvement. No cumulative toxicity of therapy or serious infection-related adverse events, including meningococcal infections, were observed through the extension period.
cards.watchOut: Event-free status is a composite built partly from the treatment decisions the open-label design itself influences (whether to give plasma therapy or start dialysis), and again there is no concurrent control. These two trials also predate the ravulizumab era and say nothing about how long treatment must continue — the question families ask next — or about genetically negative or complement-negative phenotypes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: uncontrolled but coherent — haematology normalises, kidneys recover in a time-dependent way, and delay costs GFR; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because no control arm exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: uncontrolled but coherent — haematology normalises, kidneys recover in a time-dependent way, and delay costs GFR; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because no control arm exists
cards.people: Two prospective phase 2 trials, 37 patients aged 12 and over with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (Legendre 2013) — the entire prospective evidence base for terminal complement blockade in this disease.
cards.result: Platelet count: mean +73×10⁹/L at week 26 (trial 1). TMA event-free status: 80% (trial 2). Dialysis discontinued: 4 of 5 patients on dialysis in trial 1. Estimated GFR: continuous time-dependent improvement in both trials, greater with earlier treatment. Safety through a median of roughly 62–64 weeks: no cumulative toxicity, no meningococcal infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the evidence is two small open-label trials without comparators. In a rare, otherwise devastating disease this design may be all that is ethically available, and the internal coherence (haematology, GFR trajectory, dialysis independence, quality of life all moving together) is genuinely reassuring — but any number quoted from this shelf is a before-and-after change, not a treatment effect measured against what would have happened anyway. Complement blockade in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a different shelf (#845, #1804).
