shelves.title: Iptacopan in C3 glomerulopathy: proteinuria down by a third against placebo in the first phase 3 trial — six months, 74 patients, and no kidney-function result yet
shelves.question: In C3 glomerulopathy, does oral factor B inhibition with iptacopan reduce proteinuria and stabilise kidney function compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Complement C3*/metabolism · Young Adult · Adolescent · Treatment Outcome · Glomerulonephritis*/drug therapy · Complement Inactivating Agents*/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Proteinuria · Benzoates · Indoles · Piperidines
shelves.balance: APPEAR-C3G (Kavanagh D et al., PMID: 41016405) is the first placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in C3 glomerulopathy, and on its chosen ground it succeeded clearly: in 74 randomised adults with biopsy-confirmed disease, low serum C3, and proteinuria of at least 1 g/g, six months of oral iptacopan 200 mg twice daily — on top of renin–angiotensin blockade and immunosuppression — changed 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −30.2% against +7.6% on placebo, a 35.1% relative reduction (95% CI 13.8 to 51.1; P=0.0014) in the between-group comparison. Tolerability in this small sample was reassuring: treatment-emergent adverse events in 79% versus 67%, mostly mild or moderate; serious adverse events in three participants (8%) versus one (3%); no deaths, no discontinuations for adverse events, and no meningococcal infections in a vaccinated population. What the record does not yet contain is the kidney-function half of the question: the published primary analysis reports proteinuria, not an eGFR benefit, and six months in 74 patients cannot show slowed progression in an ultra-rare disease whose harm accrues over years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): iptacopan reduces proteinuria meaningfully at six months; whether that becomes preserved kidney function is the open-label and longer-term question still running. Iptacopan in IgA nephropathy is a different shelf (#1056).

cards.headline: Kavanagh 2025 (APPEAR-C3G): iptacopan cut proteinuria by a 35.1% relative reduction versus placebo at six months (UPCR −30.2% versus +7.6%; P=0.0014) in 74 randomised adults
cards.summary: Kavanagh 2025 (APPEAR-C3G): iptacopan cut proteinuria by a 35.1% relative reduction versus placebo at six months (UPCR −30.2% versus +7.6%; P=0.0014) in 74 randomised adults
cards.people: 74 adults aged 18–60 with biopsy-confirmed C3 glomerulopathy, reduced serum C3 (below 77 mg/dL), urine protein-to-creatinine ratio at least 1.0 g/g, and eGFR at least 30 ml/min per 1.73 m², enrolled at 35 centres in 18 countries, vaccinated against meningococcus and pneumococcus, and randomised 1:1 to iptacopan 200 mg twice daily (38 patients) or placebo (36 patients) for six months double-blind, both on top of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors and immunosuppression, followed by six months of open-label iptacopan for all.
cards.result: The 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio changed by −30.2% (95% CI −42.8 to −14.8) with iptacopan versus +7.6% (−11.9 to +31.3) with placebo — a relative reduction of 35.1% (95% CI 13.8 to 51.1; P=0.0014), meeting the primary end point. Geometric mean UPCR fell from 3.33 g/g at baseline to 2.17 g/g at six months on iptacopan, and rose from 2.58 to 2.80 g/g on placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 30 of 38 iptacopan participants (79%) versus 24 of 36 on placebo (67%), mostly mild or moderate; serious adverse events in three (8%) versus one (3%); there were no deaths, no discontinuations due to adverse events, and no meningococcal infections.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-four patients and six blinded months: the trial is powered for a proteinuria surrogate, and this record reports no eGFR result — 'stabilises kidney function' in the shelf question is not yet answered by the primary publication. Baseline proteinuria was also somewhat higher in the iptacopan arm (geometric mean 3.33 versus 2.58 g/g), which the ratio-to-baseline analysis handles statistically but which small trials cannot fully balance. Adolescent and transplant-recurrence cohorts sit outside this adult native-kidney result.

shelves.title: Atrasentan in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria −38.1% versus −3.1% at the ALIGN interim — a big surrogate win with the 132-week kidney verdict still outstanding
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy at risk of progression despite supportive care, does the endothelin antagonist atrasentan reduce proteinuria and slow kidney-function decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Atrasentan*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Creatinine/urine · Double-Blind Method · Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Glomerulonephritis, IGA*/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy/urine · Proteinuria*/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology/urine · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The ALIGN trial's prespecified interim analysis (Heerspink HJL et al., PMID: 39460694) answers the proteinuria half of the question decisively and the kidney-protection half not at all — yet. Among the first 270 patients with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, at least 1 g/day of proteinuria, and eGFR at least 30, atrasentan 0.75 mg daily changed the 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −38.1% at week 36 against −3.1% on placebo, a between-group difference of −36.1 percentage points (95% CI −44.6 to −26.4; P<0.001). The class-level pooled record (Tian Z et al., PMID: 40130231; four randomised trials, 1,346 patients with endothelin A receptor antagonists) agrees on proteinuria (mean difference −31.89 in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio) but adds the price list ALIGN's interim was too small to itemise: higher odds of anaemia (OR 2.38), fluid retention (OR 1.46), hypotension (OR 2.39), dizziness (OR 2.37), cough (OR 2.27), and acute kidney injury (OR 3.12), with the pooled eGFR difference (mean difference 4.10, 95% CI −0.76 to 8.96) not significant. In ALIGN itself fluid retention was reported in 11.2% versus 8.2% and led to no discontinuations, with no apparent cardiac failure or severe oedema. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): atrasentan is a potent proteinuria-lowering drug in IgA nephropathy whose defining trial has not yet reported whether kidneys are saved — that answer is scheduled at 132 weeks, and the endothelin class history in diabetic kidney disease (shelf #738) is exactly why it must be awaited rather than assumed.

cards.headline: Heerspink 2025 (ALIGN, interim): atrasentan cut the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −38.1% versus −3.1% on placebo at week 36 — a −36.1-point gap (P<0.001) — with fluid retention in 11.2% versus 8.2%
cards.summary: Heerspink 2025 (ALIGN, interim): atrasentan cut the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −38.1% versus −3.1% on placebo at week 36 — a −36.1-point gap (P<0.001) — with fluid retention in 11.2% versus 8.2%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, prespecified interim analysis (ALIGN; Heerspink 2025)
cards.people: Adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, total urinary protein excretion at least 1 g per day, and eGFR at least 30 ml/min per 1.73 m², in a phase 3 multinational double-blind randomised trial of atrasentan 0.75 mg daily versus placebo for 132 weeks; the primary outcome was assessed at a prespecified interim analysis of the first 270 patients in the main stratum (135 per group) completing week 36, of 340 recruited into the main stratum, with a separate exploratory stratum of patients on sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors analysed separately.
cards.result: The geometric mean percentage change in the 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio from baseline to week 36 was −38.1% with atrasentan versus −3.1% with placebo, a geometric mean between-group difference of −36.1 percentage points (95% CI −44.6 to −26.4; P<0.001). The percentage of patients with adverse events did not differ substantially between groups. Fluid retention was reported by 19 of 169 patients (11.2%) on atrasentan and 14 of 170 (8.2%) on placebo and did not lead to discontinuation of the trial regimen. No apparent cases of cardiac failure or severe oedema occurred.
cards.watchOut: This is an interim look at a surrogate: the trial runs to 132 weeks precisely because proteinuria at week 36 is not kidney survival, and patients in the separate sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor stratum — increasingly the real-world background — are not in these numbers. Safety denominators (169 and 170) cover the whole main stratum while efficacy covers the first 270, and an 11.2% fluid-retention signal in a young, cardiac-healthy trial population may behave differently in clinic patients.

cards.headline: Tian 2025 (meta-analysis, 4 RCTs, 1,346 patients): endothelin A antagonists in IgA nephropathy cut proteinuria (MD −31.89) but raised the odds of acute kidney injury (OR 3.12), anaemia (OR 2.38), and fluid retention (OR 1.46); the eGFR difference was not significant
cards.summary: Tian 2025 (meta-analysis, 4 RCTs, 1,346 patients): endothelin A antagonists in IgA nephropathy cut proteinuria (MD −31.89) but raised the odds of acute kidney injury (OR 3.12), anaemia (OR 2.38), and fluid retention (OR 1.46); the eGFR difference was not significant
cards.people: Four randomised controlled trials comprising 1,346 patients with IgA nephropathy, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis of endothelin A receptor antagonists (searched to 31 October 2024) — the class that includes atrasentan and the dual endothelin–angiotensin antagonist studied in this disease.
cards.result: Compared with control, endothelin A receptor antagonists achieved a greater reduction in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (mean difference −31.89, 95% CI −37.50 to −26.28), lower systolic blood pressure (MD −2.78, 95% CI −4.11 to −1.44) and diastolic pressure (MD −4.12, −5.24 to −2.99), and a smaller reduction in eGFR that was not significant (MD 4.10, 95% CI −0.76 to 8.96). Harms were higher: anaemia OR 2.38 (95% CI 1.54 to 3.69), cough OR 2.27 (1.24 to 4.15), dizziness OR 2.37 (1.51 to 3.71), hypotension OR 2.39 (1.56 to 3.67), fluid retention OR 1.46 (1.04 to 2.05), and acute kidney injury OR 3.12 (1.31 to 7.42).
cards.watchOut: A class pool, not an atrasentan pool: the four trials mix selective endothelin A blockade with a dual endothelin–angiotensin agent, so the harm odds ratios describe the class's centre of gravity rather than atrasentan's exact profile, and the proteinuria mean difference is on the trials' reported ratio scale. Its value here is as the safety ledger and the reminder that pooled eGFR effects remain unproven — not as a substitute for ALIGN's final analysis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: proteinuria falls hard and consistently; kidney protection is scheduled, not shown; the class charges fluid, blood pressure, and haemoglobin for the effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: proteinuria falls hard and consistently; kidney protection is scheduled, not shown; the class charges fluid, blood pressure, and haemoglobin for the effect
cards.people: One phase 3 interim analysis of 270 patients (ALIGN, Heerspink 2025) and a four-trial class meta-analysis of 1,346 patients (Tian 2025) on endothelin A receptor antagonism in IgA nephropathy.
cards.result: Proteinuria: −38.1% versus −3.1% at week 36 in ALIGN (difference −36.1 points, P<0.001); pooled class mean difference −31.89. Kidney function: pooled eGFR difference 4.10 (95% CI −0.76 to 8.96), not significant; ALIGN's 132-week outcome unreported. Harms: fluid retention 11.2% versus 8.2% in ALIGN; pooled odds raised for anaemia, hypotension, dizziness, and acute kidney injury. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the anchor result is an interim surrogate analysis. The honest sentence for clinic is: atrasentan lowers proteinuria by about a third beyond placebo — and in IgA nephropathy that surrogate has a better track record than most, but the endothelin class has previously converted proteinuria wins into fluid-retention problems at scale (SONAR, shelf #738), so the stamp waits for ALIGN's final kidney outcome.

shelves.title: Rigorous blood pressure in early ADPKD: kidney growth slowed from 6.6% to 5.6% a year in HALT-PKD — eGFR unmoved, dizziness up, and a second blocker proven useless alongside
shelves.question: In early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does rigorous blood-pressure control slow total kidney volume growth and kidney-function decline compared with standard control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/therapeutic use · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Benzimidazoles/therapeutic use · Benzoates/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy/etiology · Kidney/pathology · Lisinopril/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Size/drug effects · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant/drug therapy/pathology/physiopathology · Telmisartan · Young Adult
shelves.balance: HALT-PKD Study A (Schrier RW et al., PMID: 25399733) randomised 558 hypertensive patients aged 15–49 with early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (eGFR above 60) in a two-by-two design: a low blood-pressure target (95/60 to 110/75 mm Hg) versus a standard target (120/70 to 130/80), crossed with lisinopril plus telmisartan versus lisinopril plus placebo. Rigorous control slowed the primary outcome — total kidney volume grew 5.6% per year versus 6.6% (P=0.006) — and improved two secondary measures: left-ventricular-mass index fell faster (−1.17 versus −0.57 g/m² per year; P<0.001) and urinary albumin excretion fell 3.77% where it rose 2.43% on standard control (P<0.001). But the outcome patients feel, eGFR, showed no overall benefit — a negative short-term slope difference (P<0.001) and only a marginally positive long-term one (P=0.05) — and dizziness and light-headedness were commoner on the low target (80.7% versus 69.4%; P=0.002). Adding telmisartan to lisinopril changed nothing in Study A, and the companion Study B in later disease (Torres VE et al., PMID: 25399731; 486 patients, eGFR 25–60, followed five to eight years) found dual blockade identical to lisinopril alone on the composite of death, end-stage kidney disease, or halving of eGFR (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.42). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in young patients with early ADPKD and preserved function, aiming low slows kidney growth and helps the heart and albuminuria — a real but surrogate-level gain, bought with more dizziness, and not a licence to add a second renin–angiotensin blocker.

cards.headline: Schrier 2014 (HALT-PKD Study A): a low blood-pressure target slowed kidney growth to 5.6% versus 6.6% per year (P=0.006) — eGFR did not improve overall, and dizziness rose to 80.7% versus 69.4%
cards.summary: Schrier 2014 (HALT-PKD Study A): a low blood-pressure target slowed kidney growth to 5.6% versus 6.6% per year (P=0.006) — eGFR did not improve overall, and dizziness rose to 80.7% versus 69.4%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (HALT-PKD Study A; Schrier 2014)
cards.people: 558 hypertensive participants aged 15–49 with early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and eGFR above 60 ml/min per 1.73 m², in a double-blind two-by-two factorial trial: standard blood-pressure target (120/70 to 130/80 mm Hg) versus low target (95/60 to 110/75), crossed with lisinopril plus telmisartan versus lisinopril plus placebo; the primary outcome was the annual percentage change in total kidney volume.
cards.result: Total kidney volume increased 5.6% per year in the low-blood-pressure group versus 6.6% in the standard group (P=0.006), with no significant difference between the lisinopril–telmisartan and lisinopril–placebo groups. The eGFR slope showed a negative difference in the short term in the low-pressure group (P<0.001) and a marginally positive difference in the long term (P=0.05), with no overall change. Left-ventricular-mass index decreased more with the low target (−1.17 vs −0.57 g per square metre per year; P<0.001), and urinary albumin excretion changed by −3.77% versus +2.43% (P<0.001). Dizziness and light-headedness were more common with the low target (80.7% vs 69.4%; P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Total kidney volume is a growth surrogate: the trial's own kidney-function outcome refused to confirm an overall benefit within its horizon, and the early eGFR dip on intensive lowering is the familiar haemodynamic price that can alarm patients into stopping treatment. The population was young with preserved function and able to tolerate targets most older, comorbid patients could not — do not export 95/60–110/75 beyond that phenotype. Vasopressin blockade with tolvaptan is a separate question (shelf #297).

cards.headline: Torres 2014 (HALT-PKD Study B): in later ADPKD, adding telmisartan to lisinopril at a standard target changed nothing — composite outcome hazard ratio 1.08 over five to eight years
cards.summary: Torres 2014 (HALT-PKD Study B): in later ADPKD, adding telmisartan to lisinopril at a standard target changed nothing — composite outcome hazard ratio 1.08 over five to eight years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (HALT-PKD Study B; Torres 2014)
cards.people: 486 patients aged 18–64 with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and eGFR 25–60 ml/min per 1.73 m², in a double-blind trial of lisinopril plus telmisartan versus lisinopril plus placebo, doses adjusted to a blood pressure of 110/70 to 130/80 mm Hg, followed for five to eight years; the composite primary outcome was time to death, end-stage kidney disease, or a 50% reduction in eGFR.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the composite primary outcome (hazard ratio with lisinopril–telmisartan 1.08, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.42). The two treatments controlled blood pressure and lowered urinary aldosterone excretion similarly, and the rates of eGFR decline, urinary albumin excretion change, other secondary outcomes, and adverse events — including hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury — were also similar.
cards.watchOut: Study B did not randomise the blood-pressure target, so it cannot refute Study A's low-target finding in early disease — it answers the drug-combination question in a later-stage population. Its real service to this shelf is negative and valuable: whatever benefit rigorous control offers comes from the pressure achieved, not from doubling renin–angiotensin blockade.
cards.source: Torres VE et al. Angiotensin blockade in late autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25399731. Registry ID: NCT01885559. cards.headline: Synthesis: push the pressure, not the pill count — rigorous control slows early cyst growth on surrogate measures, dual blockade adds nothing at any stage
cards.summary: Synthesis: push the pressure, not the pill count — rigorous control slows early cyst growth on surrogate measures, dual blockade adds nothing at any stage
cards.people: Two companion factorial-era trials totalling 1,044 patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: Study A in early disease (558 patients, eGFR above 60) and Study B in stage 3 disease (486 patients, eGFR 25–60).

shelves.title: Extended-release calcifediol in stage 3–4 CKD: vitamin D normalised in over 95% and parathyroid hormone down by a third in 40% at six months — all biochemistry, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does extended-release calcifediol raise 25-hydroxyvitamin D and lower parathyroid hormone compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 24,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D 3/blood · Aged · Calcifediol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Calcium/blood/urine · Creatinine/urine · Delayed-Action Preparations/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Fibroblast Growth Factors/blood · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone/blood · Phosphorus/blood · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/physiopathology · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives/blood · Vitamin D Deficiency/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Vitamins/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: The evidence here is two identical placebo-controlled trials wearing one publication. Sprague SM et al. (PMID: 27676085) randomised 429 adults with stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and vitamin D insufficiency, 2:1 to extended-release calcifediol 30 or 60 µg at bedtime or placebo for 26 weeks across 89 United States sites: the drug normalised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (above 30 ng/ml) in over 95% of per-protocol participants, reduced intact parathyroid hormone by at least 10% in 72%, and produced parathyroid hormone reductions of at least 30% in a proportion that climbed with time on treatment — 22% at 12 weeks, 40% at 26 weeks, and 50% at 52 weeks in the open-label extension — with lowering significantly greater than placebo and independent of CKD stage, and with what the authors call an inconsequential impact on serum calcium, phosphorus, fibroblast growth factor 23, and adverse events. The anchor review (Sprague SM et al., PMID: 30058895) frames why the formulation matters: ordinary nutritional vitamin D has proven ineffective for secondary hyperparathyroidism, and active vitamin D receptor activators suppress parathyroid hormone at the price of hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia risk, whereas gradual-release calcifediol corrected the hormone without meaningfully raising calcium or phosphorus in its trials. Every outcome here is a laboratory value — no trial shows fewer fractures, less cardiovascular disease, or slower dialysis onset. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): extended-release calcifediol reliably repletes 25-hydroxyvitamin D and lowers parathyroid hormone in stage 3–4 CKD without disturbing calcium or phosphate — a biochemical benefit, honestly labelled. Active vitamin D analogues such as paricalcitol are carded at shelves #1740 and #2047.

cards.headline: Sprague 2016 (two identical RCTs, 429 patients): extended-release calcifediol normalised vitamin D in over 95% and cut parathyroid hormone by at least 30% in 40% at 26 weeks — calcium and phosphorus essentially unmoved
cards.summary: Sprague 2016 (two identical RCTs, 429 patients): extended-release calcifediol normalised vitamin D in over 95% and cut parathyroid hormone by at least 30% in 40% at 26 weeks — calcium and phosphorus essentially unmoved
cards.people: 429 adults with stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and vitamin D insufficiency, in two identical multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies at 89 United States sites, randomised 2:1 to oral extended-release calcifediol (30 or 60 µg) or placebo once daily at bedtime for 26 weeks; 354 participants (83%) completed dosing and 298 (69%) entered a 26-week open-label extension on the drug.
cards.result: Extended-release calcifediol normalised serum total 25-hydroxyvitamin D (above 30 ng/ml) in over 95% of per-protocol participants and reduced plasma intact parathyroid hormone by at least 10% in 72%. The proportion achieving parathyroid hormone reductions of at least 30% rose progressively with treatment duration, reaching 22% at 12 weeks, 40% at 26 weeks, and 50% at 52 weeks; parathyroid hormone lowering was independent of CKD stage and significantly greater than with placebo. The drug had an inconsequential impact on serum calcium, phosphorus, fibroblast growth factor 23, and adverse events, and the authors conclude it is safe and effective for treating secondary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin D insufficiency in CKD.
cards.watchOut: The record reports responder proportions for the drug arm and states the parathyroid hormone effect was significantly greater than placebo, but does not print the placebo arm's responder rate or a mean hormone difference — so the exact placebo-adjusted size of the effect cannot be quoted from this record, and the 52-week figure comes from an uncontrolled extension in the 69% who chose to continue. All end points are biochemical; nothing here measures bone, cardiovascular, or kidney outcomes.
cards.source: Sprague SM et al. Use of Extended-Release Calcifediol to Treat Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in Stages 3 and 4 Chronic Kidney Disease. American Journal of Nephrology. 2016. PMID: 27676085. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sprague 2017 (review): the formulation is the argument — gradual-release calcifediol corrects vitamin D insufficiency and suppresses parathyroid hormone where plain nutritional vitamin D failed, without the calcium and phosphate price of active analogues
cards.summary: Sprague 2017 (review): the formulation is the argument — gradual-release calcifediol corrects vitamin D insufficiency and suppresses parathyroid hormone where plain nutritional vitamin D failed, without the calcium and phosphate price of active analogues
cards.type: Review of the randomised trial programme (Sprague 2017)
cards.people: Adults with stage 3–4 (not stage 5) chronic kidney disease and vitamin D insufficiency (serum total 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 ng/mL) with secondary hyperparathyroidism — the population for which extended-release calcifediol 30 µg capsules were approved in the United States, as reviewed by Sprague and Strugnell 2017.
cards.result: The review records that randomised trials have demonstrated nutritional vitamin D to be ineffective for treating secondary hyperparathyroidism, whereas vitamin D receptor activators can correct elevated parathyroid hormone but with increased risk of hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia; extended-release calcifediol, a lipophilic-fill capsule that gradually releases 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, corrects vitamin D insufficiency, increases serum calcitriol, and suppresses parathyroid hormone production without perturbing normal vitamin D and mineral metabolism, and was demonstrated in randomised trials to be safe and effective for controlling secondary hyperparathyroidism without meaningfully increasing serum calcium or phosphorus.
cards.watchOut: This is a narrative expert review by the trial programme's own investigator — its comparative claims about nutritional vitamin D and active analogues are framing, not head-to-head trial results, and no calcifediol trial has randomised patients against paricalcitol or another active analogue. The record carries no MeSH terms and no new numbers; the quantitative evidence for this shelf is the 2016 trial report carded above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a reliable laboratory effect — vitamin D repleted, parathyroid hormone down, minerals undisturbed — with patient-level outcomes entirely untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: a reliable laboratory effect — vitamin D repleted, parathyroid hormone down, minerals undisturbed — with patient-level outcomes entirely untested
cards.people: Two identical randomised placebo-controlled trials of 429 patients with stage 3–4 CKD (Sprague 2016) and the programme review (Sprague 2017) — the evidence base for extended-release calcifediol in secondary hyperparathyroidism.
cards.result: 25-hydroxyvitamin D normalised (above 30 ng/ml) in over 95% of per-protocol participants. Intact parathyroid hormone: reductions of at least 10% in 72%, at least 30% in 40% at 26 weeks and 50% at 52 weeks (extension), significantly greater than placebo. Calcium, phosphorus, fibroblast growth factor 23: inconsequential impact. Fractures, cardiovascular events, dialysis onset, mortality: not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Five units instead of ten for hyperkalaemia: hypoglycaemia odds nearly halved and potassium fell just as far — in ten retrospective studies and not one randomised trial
shelves.question: In acute hyperkalaemia, does a reduced insulin dose (5 units, or weight-based) lower potassium as effectively as the standard 10 units, with less hypoglycaemia, in the pooled studies?
shelves.mesh: Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Humans · Hyperkalemia*/drug therapy · Hypoglycemia*/epidemiology · Insulin*/administration & dosage · Potassium Deficiency*/epidemiology · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: Everyone who treats acute hyperkalaemia knows the standard 10 units of intravenous insulin is a hypoglycaemia machine; the question is whether halving the dose surrenders potassium control. The pooled answer (Moussavi K et al., PMID: 33993515) comes from ten retrospective cohort studies and 3,437 patients — no randomised trials — comparing 10 units against alternatives of 5 units, 0.1 units/kg, or anything under 10 units. The reduced strategies were associated with lower pooled odds of hypoglycaemia (odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69; I²=8%) and of severe hypoglycaemia (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.64; I²=0%), and potassium reduction was indistinguishable: mean difference −0.02 mmol/L (95% CI −0.11 to 0.07), albeit with moderate heterogeneity (I²=53%). Included studies carried low or moderate risk of bias on the scales used. That is a reassuring pattern — less of the harm, none of the efficacy lost — resting entirely on retrospective comparisons in which clinicians may have chosen smaller doses for patients they judged frailer or more hypoglycaemia-prone, a confounding direction that would actually work against the reduced dose on potassium and for it on hypoglycaemia, and which only a prospective trial can untangle; the authors say exactly that. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): reduced insulin dosing for hyperkalaemia appears to halve the odds of hypoglycaemia without compromising potassium lowering, on retrospective evidence that prospective studies have yet to confirm.

cards.headline: Moussavi 2021 (meta-analysis, 10 retrospective studies, 3,437 patients): reduced insulin dosing halved the odds of severe hypoglycaemia (OR 0.41) with potassium reduction identical to 10 units (difference −0.02 mmol/L)
cards.summary: Moussavi 2021 (meta-analysis, 10 retrospective studies, 3,437 patients): reduced insulin dosing halved the odds of severe hypoglycaemia (OR 0.41) with potassium reduction identical to 10 units (difference −0.02 mmol/L)
cards.people: 3,437 patients treated for hyperkalaemia with standard intravenous insulin (10 units) or alternative reduced dosing (5 units, 0.1 units/kg, or under 10 units), in ten retrospective cohort studies identified from PubMed/MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Ovid, and ClinicalTrials.gov to November 2020; only studies reporting hypoglycaemia (glucose below 70 mg/dl), severe hypoglycaemia (below 50 mg/dl), and post-treatment potassium reduction were included, with bias assessed by Cochrane and Newcastle–Ottawa tools and rated low or moderate.
cards.result: Alternative dosing was associated with lower pooled odds of hypoglycaemia (odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69; I²=8%) and severe hypoglycaemia (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.64; I²=0%) than standard 10-unit dosing. No difference in potassium reduction was detected (mean difference −0.02 mmol/L, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.07; I²=53%). The authors conclude that alternative insulin dosing strategies resulted in less hypoglycaemia and severe hypoglycaemia without compromising potassium reduction, and that prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.
cards.watchOut: Not one randomised trial sits inside this pool. In retrospective data the dose was chosen by clinicians who could see the patient — plausibly giving 5 units to the frail, the low-weight, and the already-low-glucose, which biases the hypoglycaemia comparison in the reduced dose's favour and the potassium comparison against it. The pooled alternatives also lump three different strategies (flat 5 units, weight-based, any dose under 10) that are not interchangeable prescriptions, and odds ratios are printed without the absolute hypoglycaemia rates a clinician needs to counsel a patient.
cards.source: Moussavi K et al. Reduced alternative insulin dosing in hyperkalemia: A meta-analysis of effects on hypoglycemia and potassium reduction. Pharmacotherapy. 2021. PMID: 33993515. cards.headline: Synthesis: the dose can probably come down — the harm signal is consistent and the efficacy signal is flat — but 'probably' is doing real work in that sentence
cards.summary: Synthesis: the dose can probably come down — the harm signal is consistent and the efficacy signal is flat — but 'probably' is doing real work in that sentence
cards.people: Ten retrospective cohort studies, 3,437 hyperkalaemia patients (Moussavi 2021) — the entire comparative record on reduced versus standard insulin dosing for acute hyperkalaemia.
cards.result: Hypoglycaemia: pooled OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.69). Severe hypoglycaemia: OR 0.41 (0.27 to 0.64). Potassium reduction: mean difference −0.02 mmol/L (−0.11 to 0.07) — no detectable loss of effect. Randomised evidence: none. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Insulin is only the shifting half of hyperkalaemia treatment — this shelf says nothing about potassium removal, binders, or dialysis timing, and a smaller insulin dose is not a reason to relax glucose monitoring, since the pooled data show less hypoglycaemia, not none. Patients with the highest potassiums and ECG changes are also the least represented in elective dose-reduction cohorts; the record should not be read as permission to under-dose a crashing patient.

shelves.title: Drinking more water for polycystic kidneys: PREVENT-ADPKD's three-year answer is no — urine diluted, copeptin unmoved, kidneys grew 6.8% versus 7.8% a year
shelves.question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does prescribed increased water intake slow kidney growth and function decline compared with usual intake over three years?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant* · Drinking* · Male · Female · Adult · Middle Aged · Kidney/pathology
shelves.balance: The logic was impeccable — vasopressin drives cyst growth, water suppresses vasopressin — and PREVENT-ADPKD (Rangan GK et al., PMID: 38319283) tested it properly: 184 adults with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in Mayo imaging subclasses 1B–1E and eGFR at least 30, randomised for three years to water prescribed to drive 24-hour urine osmolality to 270 mOsmol/kg or below, or to drinking ad libitum. The intervention did dilute the urine (between-group difference in mean 24-hour urine osmolality −91 mOsmol/kg, 95% CI −127 to −54), yet kidney growth did not slow: height-corrected total kidney volume grew 6.8% per year on prescribed water versus 7.8% ad libitum, a mean difference of −0.97% per year (95% CI −2.37 to 0.44; P=0.18). Two internal findings explain the miss: only 52.3% of the prescribed group actually achieved the target urine osmolality, and serum copeptin — the vasopressin surrogate the whole strategy aimed to suppress — did not fall over three years. Adverse events were similar between groups, so the prescription is safe; it is the efficacy that failed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): prescribed high water intake, as actually achieved in this trial, does not slow kidney growth in ADPKD — reasonable hydration advice, not a treatment, and no substitute for therapies with positive trials. Water coaching in non-ADPKD stage 3 CKD is a different population and question (a separate candidate in this programme); tolvaptan in ADPKD is shelf #297.

cards.headline: Rangan 2022 (PREVENT-ADPKD): three years of prescribed water did not slow kidney growth — 6.8% versus 7.8% per year (P=0.18) — despite urine osmolality falling by 91 mOsmol/kg, because copeptin never fell
cards.summary: Rangan 2022 (PREVENT-ADPKD): three years of prescribed water did not slow kidney growth — 6.8% versus 7.8% per year (P=0.18) — despite urine osmolality falling by 91 mOsmol/kg, because copeptin never fell
cards.people: 184 adults with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, height-corrected total kidney volume in Mayo imaging subclasses 1B to 1E, and eGFR at least 30 ml/min per 1.73 m², randomised (92 per group) for three years to water intake prescribed to reduce 24-hour urine osmolality to 270 mOsmol/kg or less, or to ad libitum water intake; the primary end point was the annualised percentage rate of change in height-corrected total kidney volume.
cards.result: There was no difference in the annualised rate of change in height-corrected total kidney volume: 7.8% per year (95% CI 6.6 to 9.0) with ad libitum intake versus 6.8% per year (5.8 to 7.7) with prescribed intake — mean difference −0.97% per year (95% CI −2.37 to 0.44; P=0.18). The prescribed group achieved a mean 24-hour urine osmolality 91 mOsmol/kg lower than the ad libitum group (difference −91, 95% CI −127 to −54), but only 52.3% of patients achieved the target urine osmolality, and there was no reduction in serum copeptin over three years. The frequency of adverse events was similar between groups, and the authors conclude prescribed water intake was not associated with excess adverse events but did not slow total kidney volume growth.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial of an imperfectly delivered intervention: with barely half the prescribed group reaching the urine target and copeptin unmoved, the trial refutes prescribed water as prescribed — it cannot refute the vasopressin hypothesis itself, which pharmacological blockade tests separately. Three years and 184 patients also leave room for a small effect (the interval runs to a 2.37-point slowing), so the honest verdict is 'no demonstrated benefit', not 'proof of none'.
cards.source: Rangan GK et al. Prescribed Water Intake in Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease. NEJM Evidence. 2022. PMID: 38319283. Registry ID: ACTRN12614001216606 (ANZCTR). cards.headline: Synthesis: the water prescription diluted urine but not vasopressin, and kidneys grew at the same rate — hydration advice survives, water-as-treatment does not
cards.summary: Synthesis: the water prescription diluted urine but not vasopressin, and kidneys grew at the same rate — hydration advice survives, water-as-treatment does not
cards.people: One three-year randomised trial of 184 adults with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PREVENT-ADPKD, Rangan 2022) — the entire randomised record on prescribed water intake in this disease.
cards.result: Kidney volume growth: 6.8% versus 7.8% per year (difference −0.97%, 95% CI −2.37 to 0.44; P=0.18). Urine osmolality: −91 mOsmol/kg between groups; target achieved by 52.3%. cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because a single trial with incomplete intervention delivery is the whole base. Patients should not be told to force water to targets that the trial shows are hard to sustain and unrewarded — and clinicians should be alert to the opposite harm in advanced disease or hyponatraemia risk, which this eGFR-at-least-30 population does not address. Rigorous blood-pressure control, the other 'simple lever' in ADPKD, has its own (positive-on-surrogates) trial at shelf #2931.

shelves.title: The low-calcium diet for stones, overturned: normal calcium with less meat and salt recurred in 20% versus 38% over five years — because cutting calcium raised urinary oxalate
shelves.question: In idiopathic hypercalciuria with recurrent calcium stones, does a normal-calcium diet low in animal protein and salt prevent recurrence better than a traditional low-calcium diet?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calcium/urine · Calcium Oxalate/urine · Calcium, Dietary/administration & dosage · Diet Therapy* · Diet, Sodium-Restricted* · Dietary Proteins/administration & dosage · Humans · Incidence · Kidney Calculi/etiology/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Oxalates/urine · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: The traditional advice — restrict calcium — was tested head-to-head against the counter-intuitive alternative and lost. Borghi L et al. (PMID: 11784873) randomised 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and idiopathic hypercalciuria for five years: a normal-calcium diet (30 mmol/day) with reduced animal protein (52 g/day) and reduced salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride/day), versus the traditional low-calcium diet (10 mmol/day). Relapse struck 12 of 60 men on the normal-calcium, low-protein, low-salt diet versus 23 of 60 on low calcium — an unadjusted relative risk of recurrence of 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.98; P=0.04), i.e. a 51% relative reduction in recurrence, printed beside the absolute rates of 20% versus 38%. Urinary calcium fell by about 170 mg/day in both groups, which is what makes the result interesting: the low-calcium diet matched on calcium excretion but lost on stones, because urinary oxalate rose by an average of 5.4 mg/day on low calcium while falling by 7.2 mg/day on the normal-calcium diet — dietary calcium binds gut oxalate, and removing it frees oxalate for absorption. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for men with hypercalciuric recurrent calcium oxalate stones, keep calcium normal and cut animal protein and salt — five-year randomised evidence from a single trial, in men only. Drug prevention with thiazides (shelf #483) and potassium citrate (shelf #2645) answers different questions.

cards.headline: Borghi 2002: over five years, stones recurred in 12 of 60 men on a normal-calcium, low-protein, low-salt diet versus 23 of 60 on a low-calcium diet — relative risk 0.49 — while urinary oxalate moved in opposite directions
cards.summary: Borghi 2002: over five years, stones recurred in 12 of 60 men on a normal-calcium, low-protein, low-salt diet versus 23 of 60 on a low-calcium diet — relative risk 0.49 — while urinary oxalate moved in opposite directions
cards.people: 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and idiopathic hypercalciuria, in a five-year randomised trial: 60 assigned to a diet with normal calcium (30 mmol per day) but reduced animal protein (52 g per day) and salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride per day), and 60 to the traditional low-calcium diet (10 mmol of calcium per day).
cards.result: At five years, 12 of the 60 men on the normal-calcium, low-animal-protein, low-salt diet and 23 of the 60 men on the low-calcium diet had had relapses — absolute rates of 20% versus 38% — giving an unadjusted relative risk of recurrence of 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.98; P=0.04), a 51% relative reduction in recurrence. Urinary calcium fell significantly in both groups by approximately 170 mg per day (4.2 mmol per day). Urinary oxalate excretion rose in the low-calcium group (by an average of 5.4 mg per day) but fell in the normal-calcium, low-protein, low-salt group (by an average of 7.2 mg per day). The authors conclude that restricted animal protein and salt, combined with normal calcium intake, provides greater protection than the traditional low-calcium diet.
cards.watchOut: Men only, one country, one trial, and an unadjusted headline relative risk whose confidence interval (0.24 to 0.98) only just excludes 1 — the finding is biologically coherent (the oxalate mechanism is visible in the trial's own urine data) but fragile in the statistical sense. The winning diet is a bundle: the trial cannot apportion credit among normal calcium, less animal protein, and less salt, and five years of dietary adherence in a trial outruns what most clinic patients sustain.
cards.source: Borghi L et al. Comparison of two diets for the prevention of recurrent stones in idiopathic hypercalciuria. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 11784873. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: ROSE-AHF: neither low-dose dopamine nor low-dose nesiritide added urine or protected the kidney — 72-hour urine 8,524 and 8,574 mL vs 8,296 mL on placebo
shelves.question: In acute heart failure with kidney dysfunction, does low-dose dopamine or nesiritide improve kidney function and urine output compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cystatin C/blood · Diuretics/therapeutic use · Dopamine/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Heart Failure/complications/drug therapy · Humans · Kidney/physiopathology · Kidney Diseases/complications/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Agents/administration & dosage · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Urine · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two beloved 'renal-dose' strategies, tested properly in the same trial, both flat. ROSE randomised 360 hospitalised patients with acute heart failure and an eGFR of 15–60 mL/min/1.73 m² to low-dose dopamine (2 µg/kg/min), low-dose nesiritide (0.005 µg/kg/min), or pooled placebo, each added to diuretic therapy. At 72 hours, cumulative urine volume was 8,524 mL on dopamine and 8,574 mL on nesiritide versus 8,296 mL on placebo (P=0.59 and P=0.49), and the change in cystatin C — the kidney co-primary endpoint — was likewise indistinguishable (dopamine difference 0.01 mg/L, P=0.72; nesiritide difference -0.04 mg/L, P=0.36). No secondary decongestion, renal, or clinical endpoint favoured either drug. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction, neither low-dose dopamine nor low-dose nesiritide enhances decongestion or preserves kidney function when added to diuretics.

cards.headline: ROSE (Chen 2013): dopamine urine 8,524 vs 8,296 mL placebo (P=0.59), cystatin C difference 0.01 mg/L (P=0.72) — a clean null
cards.summary: ROSE (Chen 2013): dopamine urine 8,524 vs 8,296 mL placebo (P=0.59), cystatin C difference 0.01 mg/L (P=0.72) — a clean null
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Chen 2013, ROSE — dopamine strategy)
cards.people: Within the ROSE trial's 360 hospitalised patients with acute heart failure and renal dysfunction (eGFR 15–60 mL/min/1.73 m²) at 26 North American sites, 122 patients were assigned to the dopamine strategy and randomised 2:1 to low-dose dopamine (2 µg/kg/min) or placebo, added to diuretic therapy within 24 hours of admission.
cards.result: Compared with the pooled placebo group (n=119), low-dose dopamine had no significant effect on 72-hour cumulative urine volume (dopamine 8,524 mL, 95% CI 7,917 to 9,131 vs placebo 8,296 mL, 95% CI 7,762 to 8,830; difference 229 mL, 95% CI -714 to 1,171; P=0.59) or on change in cystatin C (0.12 vs 0.11 mg/L; difference 0.01, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.10; P=0.72). No secondary endpoint reflective of decongestion, renal function, or clinical outcomes favoured dopamine.
cards.watchOut: The trial tests 'renal-dose' dopamine at 2 µg/kg/min for 72 hours in patients already receiving diuretics — it does not test dopamine as a vasopressor or in cardiogenic shock, and its confidence intervals still allow a few hundred millilitres of urine either way, just nothing a clinician would notice.
cards.source: Chen HH et al. Low-dose dopamine or low-dose nesiritide in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction: the ROSE acute heart failure randomized trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 24247300. cards.people: Within the same ROSE population of 360 hospitalised patients with acute heart failure and eGFR 15–60 mL/min/1.73 m², 119 patients were assigned to the nesiritide strategy and randomised 2:1 to low-dose nesiritide (0.005 µg/kg/min without bolus) or placebo, added to diuretic therapy.
cards.result: Compared with pooled placebo, low-dose nesiritide had no significant effect on 72-hour cumulative urine volume (nesiritide 8,574 mL, 95% CI 8,014 to 9,134 vs placebo 8,296 mL, 95% CI 7,762 to 8,830; difference 279 mL, 95% CI -618 to 1,176; P=0.49) or on change in cystatin C (0.07 vs 0.11 mg/L; difference -0.04, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.05; P=0.36). No secondary decongestion, renal, or clinical endpoint favoured nesiritide.
cards.watchOut: The dose was deliberately low (no bolus, 0.005 µg/kg/min) to chase the renal hypothesis without hypotension — this shelf judges that renal strategy, not the higher-dose dyspnoea use examined in ASCEND-HF, which has its own shelf.

shelves.title: A statin load before angiography prevents contrast kidney injury in two trials: 6.7% vs 15.1% in acute coronary syndrome, 2.3% vs 3.9% in diabetes with CKD
shelves.question: In patients undergoing coronary angiography or PCI, does a high-dose statin beforehand prevent contrast-associated acute kidney injury compared with placebo or low-dose statin?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Acute Kidney Injury/chemically induced/prevention & control · Aged · Contrast Media/adverse effects · Coronary Angiography/adverse effects/methods · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluorobenzenes/administration & dosage · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Male · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage · Rosuvastatin Calcium · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials, two different at-risk populations, the same direction. In PRATO-ACS, statin-naïve patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome randomised to high-dose rosuvastatin on admission (40 mg, then 20 mg/day) developed contrast-induced acute kidney injury in 6.7% versus 15.1% without statin (adjusted odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.71; p=0.003), and the 30-day composite of death, dialysis, myocardial infarction, stroke, or persistent renal damage was 3.6% versus 7.9% (p=0.036). In TRACK-D, 2,998 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg/day for five days around angiography developed contrast injury in 2.3% versus 3.9% on standard care (p=0.01), with less worsening heart failure at 30 days (2.6% vs 4.3%; p=0.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short rosuvastatin course around contrast exposure reduces contrast-associated kidney injury; the absolute gains are modest where baseline risk is low (1.6 points in TRACK-D) and larger where it is high (8.4 points in PRATO-ACS).

cards.headline: PRATO-ACS (Leoncini 2014): contrast injury 6.7% vs 15.1% (adjusted OR 0.38, p=0.003) with on-admission high-dose rosuvastatin
cards.summary: PRATO-ACS (Leoncini 2014): contrast injury 6.7% vs 15.1% (adjusted OR 0.38, p=0.003) with on-admission high-dose rosuvastatin
cards.people: 504 consecutive statin-naïve patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome scheduled for an early invasive strategy, randomised to rosuvastatin 40 mg on admission followed by 20 mg/day (n=252) or no statin treatment (n=252), on top of standard preventive measures.
cards.result: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (creatinine rise ≥0.5 mg/dL or ≥25% within 72 hours of contrast) occurred in 6.7% of the statin group versus 15.1% of controls (adjusted odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.71; p=0.003) — an absolute reduction of 8.4 percentage points — consistently across CI-AKI definitions and pre-specified risk categories. The 30-day incidence of adverse cardiovascular and renal events (death, dialysis, myocardial infarction, stroke, or persistent renal damage) was 3.6% versus 7.9% (p=0.036); death or nonfatal myocardial infarction at 6 months was 3.6% versus 7.2% (p=0.07).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo, single-centre programme, and a control group denied a statin class that acute coronary syndrome patients would ordinarily receive anyway — the trial measures early high-dose loading against none, in the era before universal immediate statin therapy in ACS.
cards.source: Leoncini M et al. Early high-dose rosuvastatin for contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in acute coronary syndrome: Results from the PRATO-ACS Study (Protective Effect of Rosuvastatin and Antiplatelet Therapy On contrast-induced acute kidney injury and myocardial damage in patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 24076283. Registry ID: NCT01185938. cards.headline: TRACK-D (Han 2014): contrast injury 2.3% vs 3.9% (p=0.01) with five days of rosuvastatin 10 mg in diabetes with CKD — 2,998 patients
cards.summary: TRACK-D (Han 2014): contrast injury 2.3% vs 3.9% (p=0.01) with five days of rosuvastatin 10 mg in diabetes with CKD — 2,998 patients
cards.people: 2,998 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease undergoing coronary or peripheral arterial angiography with or without intervention, randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg/day for 5 days (2 days before and 3 days after the procedure; n=1,498) or standard care (n=1,500).
cards.result: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury occurred in 2.3% of the rosuvastatin group versus 3.9% of controls (p=0.01) — an absolute reduction of 1.6 percentage points. During 30 days of follow-up, worsening heart failure was less frequent with rosuvastatin (2.6% vs 4.3%; p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The dose was modest (10 mg) and the control event rate low, so the number needed to treat is around 63; the trial was conducted in China in patients with diabetes and CKD, and whether the effect is a class effect, a rosuvastatin effect, or a pleiotropic loading effect remains unresolved. The record's printed CI-AKI definition contains an apparent typographical error in its percentage threshold; the rates above are as reported.
cards.source: Han Y et al. Short-term rosuvastatin therapy for prevention of contrast-induced acute kidney injury in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 24076297. Registry ID: NCT00786136. cards.headline: Synthesis: the same drug, the same direction, in a high-risk ACS cohort and a large diabetic CKD cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: the same drug, the same direction, in a high-risk ACS cohort and a large diabetic CKD cohort
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 3,502 patients: PRATO-ACS (504 statin-naïve ACS patients, high-dose rosuvastatin vs none) and TRACK-D (2,998 patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, rosuvastatin 10 mg for 5 days vs standard care).
cards.result: Contrast-induced AKI: 6.7% vs 15.1% (adjusted OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.71) in PRATO-ACS; 2.3% vs 3.9% in TRACK-D. Clinical composites at 30 days favoured statin in both (3.6% vs 7.9% cardiovascular-renal events in PRATO-ACS; worsening heart failure 2.6% vs 4.3% in TRACK-D). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was placebo-blinded, and most patients in modern practice receive a statin for the underlying disease anyway — the live question is timing and dose around the procedure, which is what these trials actually randomised. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the claim.

shelves.title: POSEIDON: letting the left-ventricular filling pressure set the drip rate cut contrast kidney injury from 16.3% to 6.7% (RR 0.41)
shelves.question: In patients at risk of contrast-associated kidney injury, does hydration guided by left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure prevent kidney injury better than standard hydration?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/chemically induced/physiopathology/prevention & control · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers/blood · Cardiac Catheterization/methods · Clinical Protocols · Contrast Media/adverse effects · Creatinine/blood · Female · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects/methods · Hemodynamics/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Replacement Therapy · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Volume/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted trial, a large relative effect, and a mechanism that makes sense: give more fluid to the hearts that can take it, less to those that cannot. POSEIDON randomised 396 patients with eGFR ≤60 mL/min/1.73 m² plus at least one risk factor, undergoing cardiac catheterisation, to hydration titrated to left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure or a standard protocol; contrast-induced acute kidney injury occurred in 6.7% (12/178) of the guided group versus 16.3% (28/172) of controls (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.79; p=0.005) — a 59% relative reduction and 9.6 absolute points. Hydration was stopped for shortness of breath in three patients in each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the result rests on a single trial, and the strategy requires the filling pressure the catheterisation itself provides — it generalises to the cath lab, not to every contrast study.

cards.headline: POSEIDON (Brar 2014): contrast injury 6.7% (12/178) vs 16.3% (28/172), RR 0.41 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.79), p=0.005
cards.people: 396 patients aged 18 or older undergoing cardiac catheterisation with eGFR ≤60 mL/min/1.73 m² and at least one risk factor (diabetes, heart failure history, hypertension, or age over 75), randomised to LVEDP-guided volume expansion (n=196) or a standard fluid protocol (n=200) at Kaiser Permanente Southern California; both groups received saline 3 mL/kg for 1 hour before catheterisation. Primary-outcome data were available for 178 guided and 172 control patients.
cards.result: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (creatinine rise >25% or >0.5 mg/dL) occurred less frequently with LVEDP-guided hydration: 6.7% (12/178) versus 16.3% (28/172) (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.79; p=0.005). Hydration was terminated prematurely for shortness of breath in three patients in each group.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, single health system, and the intervention is inseparable from its setting — LVEDP is measured during the catheterisation it protects. Proceduralists were unmasked (patients and laboratory staff were masked), and the endpoint is a creatinine definition, not dialysis or death. Tier C: one trial carries the benefit claim.
cards.source: Brar SS et al. Haemodynamic-guided fluid administration for the prevention of contrast-induced acute kidney injury: the POSEIDON randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24856027. Registry ID: NCT01218828. shelves.balance: SPLIT — AASK answered its two questions in opposite directions. In 1,094 Black adults with hypertensive kidney disease (GFR 20–65 mL/min/1.73 m²) randomised in a 3×2 factorial design, the lower blood-pressure goal (mean arterial pressure ≤92 mmHg; achieved 128/78) did not slow GFR decline versus the usual goal (achieved 141/85): slopes -2.21 vs -1.95 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (P=0.24), and the clinical composite (GFR halving, kidney failure, or death) differed by 2% (95% CI -22% to 21%; P=0.85). The drug comparison did separate: ramipril reduced the clinical composite by 22% versus metoprolol (95% CI 1% to 38%; P=0.04) and by 38% versus amlodipine (95% CI 14% to 56%; P=0.004), though GFR slopes did not differ consistently by drug. The trial's cardiovascular analysis found 202 cardiovascular events (4.5% per patient-year) with no significant relation to either randomised drug class or blood-pressure goal. PROPOSED SPLIT: ACE inhibition first for the kidney in this population; pushing below the usual target bought no renal protection in AASK.

cards.headline: AASK (Wright 2002): lower BP goal null on GFR slope (P=0.24) and composite (P=0.85); ramipril beat metoprolol by 22% and amlodipine by 38% on the composite
cards.summary: AASK (Wright 2002): lower BP goal null on GFR slope (P=0.24) and composite (P=0.85); ramipril beat metoprolol by 22% and amlodipine by 38% on the composite
cards.people: 1,094 African American adults aged 18–70 with hypertensive renal disease (GFR 20–65 mL/min/1.73 m²) at 21 US centres, enrolled 1995–1998 and followed 3 to 6.4 years; randomised to a usual mean arterial pressure goal of 102–107 mmHg (n=554) or lower goal ≤92 mmHg (n=540), and to initial metoprolol 50–200 mg/day (n=441), ramipril 2.5–10 mg/day (n=436), or amlodipine 5–10 mg/day (n=217), with open-label agents added to reach goal.
cards.result: Achieved blood pressure averaged 128/78 mmHg in the lower group and 141/85 in the usual group. GFR slope did not differ by blood-pressure goal (-2.21 vs -1.95 mL/min/1.73 m² per year; P=0.24), and the lower goal did not significantly reduce the clinical composite (risk reduction 2%, 95% CI -22% to 21%; P=0.85). No drug comparison showed consistent GFR-slope differences, but ramipril reduced the clinical composite (GFR reduction ≥50% or ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m², kidney failure, or death) by 22% versus metoprolol (95% CI 1% to 38%; P=0.04) and 38% versus amlodipine (95% CI 14% to 56%; P=0.004); amlodipine versus metoprolol did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The amlodipine arm was smaller and its early GFR rise (a haemodynamic effect) complicates slope comparisons — which is why the composite, not the slope, carries the drug verdict. The composite includes death, so this shelf is Tier C under the mortality-claim rule despite the trial's size. Open-label add-on therapy was needed in all arms to reach goal.
cards.source: Wright JT Jr et al. Effect of blood pressure lowering and antihypertensive drug class on progression of hypertensive kidney disease: results from the AASK trial. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12435255. cards.headline: AASK cardiovascular outcomes (Norris 2006): 202 events, 4.5% per patient-year — neither drug class nor BP goal predicted them
cards.summary: AASK cardiovascular outcomes (Norris 2006): 202 events, 4.5% per patient-year — neither drug class nor BP goal predicted them
cards.people: The same 1,094 AASK participants with hypertensive nephrosclerosis, followed a mean of 4.1 years for the cardiovascular composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure, in a trial powered for renal outcomes.
cards.result: Thirty-one patients died of cardiovascular disease (0.7% per patient-year) and 149 experienced at least one cardiovascular outcome (3.3% per patient-year); 202 cardiovascular events occurred overall (4.5% per patient-year). The cardiovascular outcome rate was not related significantly to the randomised drug class or blood-pressure goal. Baseline pulse pressure, hypertension duration, abnormal electrocardiogram, non-HDL cholesterol, serum urea nitrogen, urine protein-creatinine and sodium-potassium ratios, and income under $15,000 independently predicted events.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for renal endpoints, so the cardiovascular null is a power statement as much as a biology statement — it should not be read as proof that class and target are cardiovascularly interchangeable, only that AASK could not separate them.
cards.source: Norris K et al. Cardiovascular outcomes in the African American Study of Kidney Disease and Hypertension (AASK) Trial. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2006. PMID: 17059993. cards.headline: Synthesis: choose the ACE inhibitor for the kidney; AASK gives no renal reason to chase the lower target
cards.summary: Synthesis: choose the ACE inhibitor for the kidney; AASK gives no renal reason to chase the lower target
cards.people: One 1,094-patient factorial RCT in Black adults with hypertensive CKD (3 drug classes × 2 blood-pressure goals, 3–6.4 years) and its cardiovascular-outcomes analysis (mean 4.1 years).
cards.result: Blood-pressure goal: GFR slope -2.21 vs -1.95 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr (P=0.24); composite risk reduction 2% (P=0.85). Drug class on the composite: ramipril 22% relative reduction vs metoprolol (P=0.04) and 38% vs amlodipine (P=0.004). Cardiovascular events: 202 (4.5%/patient-year), unrelated to randomised assignment. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C because the winning composite contains death.
cards.watchOut: AASK enrolled patients with hypertensive nephrosclerosis and mostly low-level proteinuria; its drug verdict should not be silently extended to heavily proteinuric or diabetic kidney disease, where other shelves govern. Its target verdict predates SPRINT-era intensive control and applies to the goals actually compared (achieved 128/78 vs 141/85).
cards.source: Synthesis of Wright JT Jr et al. JAMA. 2002 (PMID: 12435255); Norris K et al. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2006 (PMID: 17059993).

shelves.title: Sibeprenlimab in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria halved at 9 months, and the final analysis shows eGFR slope 0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min per year on placebo
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy at risk of progression, does the anti-APRIL antibody sibeprenlimab reduce proteinuria compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Creatinine/urine · Double-Blind Method · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Glomerulonephritis, IGA/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/urine · Hematuria/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/urine · Immunoglobulin A/blood · Injections, Subcutaneous · Proteinuria/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/urine · Tumor Necrosis Factor Ligand Superfamily Member 13/antagonists & inhibitors/blood · Adolescent · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the APRIL hypothesis, confirmed at every step it has been tested. In the phase 2 ENVISION trial, 12 months of sibeprenlimab cut the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 47.2%, 58.8%, and 62.0% at 2, 4, and 8 mg/kg versus 20.0% on placebo, with eGFR changes of -2.7, 0.2, and -1.5 versus -7.4 mL/min/1.73 m². In the phase 3 VISIONARY interim analysis, proteinuria fell 50.2% on sibeprenlimab while rising 2.1% on placebo at 9 months (adjusted ratio 51.2% lower; P<0.001), and the trial's final analysis delivered the kidney-function endpoint: an annualised eGFR slope of 0.3 versus -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (difference 4.5; P<0.001), with a composite kidney event in 0.4% versus 11.2% (hazard ratio 0.029, 95% CI 0.004 to 0.214). Serious adverse events were no commoner on drug (8.1% vs 12.7% in the final analysis) and no deaths were reported. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): sibeprenlimab halves proteinuria and, over 24 months, essentially flattens eGFR decline in IgA nephropathy at risk of progression.

cards.headline: ENVISION phase 2 (Mathur 2024): proteinuria down 47–62% across doses vs 20% on placebo; eGFR -1.5 to 0.2 vs -7.4 at the higher doses
cards.summary: ENVISION phase 2 (Mathur 2024): proteinuria down 47–62% across doses vs 20% on placebo; eGFR -1.5 to 0.2 vs -7.4 at the higher doses
cards.people: 155 adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy at high risk of progression despite standard care, randomised 1:1:1:1 to intravenous sibeprenlimab 2, 4, or 8 mg/kg (n=38, 41, 38) or placebo (n=38) monthly for 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 months, the geometric mean ratio reduction in 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 47.2% (±8.2) at 2 mg, 58.8% (±6.1) at 4 mg, 62.0% (±5.7) at 8 mg, and 20.0% (±12.6) on placebo. Least-squares mean eGFR change was -2.7 ± 1.8, 0.2 ± 1.7, -1.5 ± 1.8, and -7.4 ± 1.8 mL/min/1.73 m² respectively. Adverse events occurred in 78.6% of pooled sibeprenlimab patients and 71.1% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A dose-ranging trial with about 40 patients per arm — its eGFR separation is encouraging but imprecise, and the intravenous monthly regimen differs from the subcutaneous regimen carried into phase 3.
cards.source: Mathur M et al. A Phase 2 Trial of Sibeprenlimab in Patients with IgA Nephropathy. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 37916620. Registry ID: NCT04287985; EudraCT:2019-002531-29. cards.headline: VISIONARY interim (Perkovic 2026): proteinuria -50.2% vs +2.1% at 9 months (P<0.001); serious adverse events 3.5% vs 4.4%
cards.summary: VISIONARY interim (Perkovic 2026): proteinuria -50.2% vs +2.1% at 9 months (P<0.001); serious adverse events 3.5% vs 4.4%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, interim analysis (Perkovic 2026, VISIONARY)
cards.people: 510 adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous sibeprenlimab 400 mg (n=259) or placebo (n=251) every 4 weeks for 100 weeks; the prespecified interim analysis covered the first 320 patients (152 sibeprenlimab, 168 placebo) reaching the 9-month proteinuria evaluation.
cards.result: At 9 months, the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell 50.2% with sibeprenlimab and rose 2.1% with placebo — an adjusted geometric least-squares mean ratio 51.2% lower with sibeprenlimab (96.5% CI 42.9 to 58.2; P<0.001). APRIL and galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 95.8% and 67.1% from baseline at week 48 on drug. No deaths were reported; serious adverse events during treatment occurred in 3.5% on sibeprenlimab and 4.4% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis on a proteinuria endpoint in the first 320 of 510 patients — the proteinuria result was never in doubt after phase 2; the trial's meaning hinged on the eGFR endpoint reported in the final analysis (next card).
cards.source: Perkovic V et al. Sibeprenlimab in IgA Nephropathy - Interim Analysis of a Phase 3 Trial. The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 41211929. Registry ID: NCT05248646. cards.headline: VISIONARY final (Rizk 2026): eGFR slope 0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr (difference 4.5, P<0.001); composite kidney events 0.4% vs 11.2%
cards.summary: VISIONARY final (Rizk 2026): eGFR slope 0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr (difference 4.5, P<0.001); composite kidney events 0.4% vs 11.2%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, final analysis (Rizk 2026, VISIONARY)
cards.people: The full VISIONARY population: 510 adults with IgA nephropathy randomised to subcutaneous sibeprenlimab 400 mg every 4 weeks (n=259) or placebo (n=251), followed for the 24-month eGFR-slope endpoint.
cards.result: The annualised eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 (95% CI -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference 4.5, 95% CI 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001); the least-squares mean difference in eGFR change at 24 months was 9.2 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 7.1 to 11.4). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) on sibeprenlimab and 28 (11.2%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.029, 95% CI 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 90.7% vs 90.0%; serious adverse events in 8.1% vs 12.7%; serious infections in 1.9% vs 4.0%; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The composite kidney endpoint is driven by few events (1 vs 28) and the hazard ratio's confidence interval is correspondingly wide (0.004 to 0.214); 24 months of slope is strong evidence of slowed progression, not yet proof of prevented kidney failure over a lifetime of treatment. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Rizk DV et al. Sibeprenlimab in IgA Nephropathy - Final Phase 3 Trial Analysis. The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 42911185. Registry ID: NCT05248646. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: proteinuria, slope, and events all point the same way — the strongest IgA dataset on this shelf's row
cards.summary: Synthesis: proteinuria, slope, and events all point the same way — the strongest IgA dataset on this shelf's row
cards.people: A 155-patient phase 2 dose-ranging RCT and a 510-patient phase 3 RCT (interim proteinuria analysis in 320; final 24-month analysis in all 510) of the anti-APRIL antibody sibeprenlimab in IgA nephropathy at risk of progression.
cards.result: Proteinuria: -47 to -62% across phase 2 doses vs -20% placebo; -50.2% vs +2.1% at 9 months in phase 3. eGFR slope over 24 months: 0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr (difference 4.5; P<0.001). Composite kidney events: 0.4% vs 11.2% (HR 0.029). Serious adverse events no higher on drug in either trial; no deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials were industry-funded, enrolled biopsy-confirmed patients already on standard care, and ran 12–24 months; cost, access, and very-long-term infection safety of chronic APRIL suppression are outside the records carded here. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials, including a phase 3 with a kidney-function endpoint, carry the claim.

shelves.title: Atacicept in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria down 35% vs placebo at 36 weeks, and the phase 3 final analysis shows eGFR slope -0.6 vs -5.6 per year
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL inhibitor atacicept reduce proteinuria compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Glomerulonephritis, IGA/drug therapy/urine/diagnosis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Male · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Adult · Middle Aged · Creatinine/urine/blood · Treatment Outcome · Proteinuria/drug therapy/urine · Receptors, Fc/therapeutic use · Young Adult · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the second B-cell-targeting strategy in IgA nephropathy to clear both the proteinuria bar and the eGFR bar. In the ORIGIN phase 2b trial (116 patients), atacicept reduced the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 34% at week 36 while placebo rose 2% — a 35% reduction versus placebo — with galactose-deficient IgA1 down 60% and eGFR stabilised (between-group difference about 5.7 mL/min/1.73 m²). In the ORIGIN 3 phase 3 final analysis (431 randomised), the annualised eGFR slope through week 104 was -0.60 versus -5.60 mL/min/1.73 m² per year on placebo (difference 5.00; P<0.001), composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 5.1% versus 17.8% (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.48), and no atacicept patient progressed to dialysis, transplantation, or death versus 7 on placebo. Serious adverse events were fewer on drug (7.0% vs 15.4%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): atacicept reduces proteinuria and slows eGFR decline over two years in IgA nephropathy.

cards.headline: ORIGIN phase 2b (Lafayette 2024): proteinuria -34% vs +2% at week 36 (35% vs placebo); Gd-IgA1 down 60%; eGFR stabilised
cards.summary: ORIGIN phase 2b (Lafayette 2024): proteinuria -34% vs +2% at week 36 (35% vs placebo); Gd-IgA1 down 60%; eGFR stabilised
cards.people: 116 individuals with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy randomised to weekly subcutaneous atacicept 150, 75, or 25 mg or placebo for up to 36 weeks; primary and key secondary endpoints assessed the combined 150 mg and 75 mg groups versus placebo.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met at week 24: mean urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell 31% from baseline in the combined atacicept group versus 8% on placebo (a 25% reduction versus placebo). At week 36 the ratio fell 34% on atacicept versus a 2% rise on placebo (a 35% reduction versus placebo). eGFR stabilised on atacicept against a placebo decline (between-group geometric mean difference 11%, about 5.7 mL/min/1.73 m² absolute), and galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 60% versus placebo. The safety profile was like placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 116-patient dose-ranging trial with a 36-week horizon — enough to justify phase 3, not to settle kidney protection; the eGFR difference is a geometric-mean contrast over months, not a slope over years.

cards.headline: ORIGIN 3 final (Barratt 2026): eGFR slope -0.60 vs -5.60/yr (difference 5.00, P<0.001); progression 5.1% vs 17.8% (HR 0.24)
cards.summary: ORIGIN 3 final (Barratt 2026): eGFR slope -0.60 vs -5.60/yr (difference 5.00, P<0.001); progression 5.1% vs 17.8% (HR 0.24)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, final efficacy analysis (Barratt 2026, ORIGIN 3)
cards.people: 431 adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy randomised to weekly subcutaneous atacicept 150 mg or placebo (428 treated, 214 per group), with hierarchically tested endpoints of eGFR change at week 52 and annualised eGFR slope through week 104.
cards.result: At week 52, mean eGFR change was -0.11 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI -1.44 to 1.22) on atacicept versus -5.69 (95% CI -7.04 to -4.35) on placebo (difference 5.58, 95% CI 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104 the annualised slope was -0.60 (95% CI -1.62 to 0.41) versus -5.60 (95% CI -6.64 to -4.57) (difference 5.00 per year, 95% CI 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) versus 38 (17.8%) (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death occurred in 0 versus 7 patients. Adverse events: 74.8% vs 78.0%; serious adverse events 7.0% vs 15.4%; one death, on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The final-analysis record is an abstract-length report without MeSH terms; event counts for the hardest outcomes remain small (0 vs 7), and two years of slope preservation is not the same as lifetime kidney survival. The proteinuria result for this trial was reported in an earlier analysis not carded here.
