shelves.title: Fish oil in IgA nephropathy: one positive 1994 trial (kidney failure or death 10% vs 40% at four years) that the pooled trials never confirmed for kidney function
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy, does fish oil slow the loss of kidney function compared with placebo or control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Creatinine/metabolism · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Glomerulonephritis, IGA/complications/diet therapy/metabolism · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy · Kidney Failure, Chronic/etiology/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the shelf splits between its founding trial and everything pooled since. Donadio's 1994 multicentre placebo-controlled trial (106 patients, fish oil 12 g/day for two years) found a ≥50% creatinine rise in 6% on fish oil versus 33% on olive-oil placebo (P=0.002), and death or kidney failure in 10% versus 40% by four years (P=0.006). But when the same group later randomised 73 patients with severe disease to high-dose versus low-dose omega-3, the doses were indistinguishable (creatinine slope 0.10 vs 0.08 mg/dL per year; P=0.51; kidney failure 8 vs 10 patients), and the meta-analysis of five randomised trials (233 patients) concluded omega-3 fatty acids ameliorate proteinuria but have no beneficial effect on preserving renal function, at any dose. PROPOSED SPLIT: fish oil lowers proteinuria modestly across trials, but the kidney-protection claim rests on a single small 1994 trial whose result the pooled evidence does not confirm — Tier C, because the positive claim is single-trial and includes mortality.

cards.headline: Donadio 1994: ≥50% creatinine rise in 6% vs 33% (P=0.002); death or kidney failure 10% vs 40% at four years (P=0.006)
cards.summary: Donadio 1994: ≥50% creatinine rise in 6% vs 33% (P=0.002); death or kidney failure 10% vs 40% at four years (P=0.006)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Donadio 1994, Mayo Nephrology Collaborative Group)
cards.people: 106 patients with IgA nephropathy and persistent proteinuria (55 fish oil, 51 placebo) in a multicentre trial; serum creatinine was already elevated in 68% at baseline. Fish oil dose was 12 g daily; the placebo was a similar dose of olive oil; treatment and creatinine follow-up ran two years, with the death/kidney-failure tally reported at four years.
cards.result: By Kaplan-Meier estimation, 3 patients (6%) on fish oil and 14 (33%) on placebo had increases of 50% or more in serum creatinine during treatment (P=0.002). Annual median creatinine change was 0.03 mg/dL on fish oil versus 0.14 mg/dL on placebo. The cumulative percentage who died or developed end-stage renal disease was 10% in the fish-oil group and 40% in the placebo group after four years (P=0.006). Proteinuria was slightly reduced and hypertension controlled comparably in both groups; no patient stopped fish oil for adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: A strikingly positive result from 106 patients in the pre-RAS-blockade-standard era, with a placebo (olive oil) that may not be inert and event counts small enough (3 vs 14 on the primary endpoint) for chance and era effects to matter — the reason this shelf cannot rest on it alone. The mortality component makes the claim Tier C.
cards.source: Donadio JV Jr et al. A controlled trial of fish oil in IgA nephropathy. Mayo Nephrology Collaborative Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1994. PMID: 7935657. cards.headline: Donadio 2001: high-dose vs low-dose omega-3 in severe IgA — slopes 0.10 vs 0.08 mg/dL/yr (P=0.51), kidney failure 8 vs 10: no dose effect
cards.summary: Donadio 2001: high-dose vs low-dose omega-3 in severe IgA — slopes 0.10 vs 0.08 mg/dL/yr (P=0.51), kidney failure 8 vs 10: no dose effect
cards.people: 73 patients with severe IgA nephropathy (86% with creatinine 1.5–2.9 mg/dL; 14% with 3.0–4.9 mg/dL) randomised open-label to high-dose omega-3 (EPA 3.76 g + DHA 2.94 g daily) or low-dose (EPA 1.88 g + DHA 1.47 g) as a purified ethyl-ester concentrate, for at least two years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — within-patient rate of creatinine change — showed an annualised median increase of 0.10 mg/dL per year on high dose and 0.08 on low dose (P=0.51). No patient died; 18 developed end-stage renal disease (10 low-dose, 8 high-dose; P=0.56). Compliance was excellent and no serious adverse events were noted.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm: this trial can only say the doses match, not that either works. Its authors' favourable comparison against the earlier trial's placebo group is a historical-control argument — the weakest card on this shelf, included because it is the trial most often quoted as confirmatory.

cards.headline: Chou 2012 meta-analysis: five RCTs, 233 patients — proteinuria reduced, renal function not preserved, no dose gradient
cards.summary: Chou 2012 meta-analysis: five RCTs, 233 patients — proteinuria reduced, renal function not preserved, no dose gradient
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials totalling 233 patients with IgA nephropathy treated with omega-3 fatty acids versus control, including dose-effect analyses split at 3 g/day.
cards.result: Omega-3 fatty acids did not have any beneficial effect in preserving renal function in IgA nephropathy, while proteinuria was significantly reduced. Patients receiving high-dose omega-3 (>3 g/day) did not differ from those receiving low-dose (≤3 g/day) in renal function or proteinuria — the effects on proteinuria were not dose dependent.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials and 233 patients is a thin pool — the meta-analysis can dilute the 1994 result but cannot definitively bury it; what it establishes is that the average randomised effect on kidney function, across all trials run, is null.
cards.source: Chou HH et al. Omega-3 fatty acids ameliorate proteinuria but not renal function in IgA nephropathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nephron. Clinical practice. 2012. PMID: 23095320. cards.people: Two randomised trials from one research programme (106 placebo-controlled; 73 dose-comparison) and a meta-analysis of five RCTs (233 patients) of omega-3 fatty acids in IgA nephropathy.
cards.result: Placebo-controlled trial: ≥50% creatinine rise 6% vs 33% (P=0.002); death or kidney failure at 4 years 10% vs 40% (P=0.006). Dose trial: no difference between doses on slope or kidney failure. Meta-analysis: proteinuria significantly reduced; renal function not preserved; no dose effect. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by study design. The only multicentre randomised trial (72 patients) compared tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses with steroid pulses alone over 12 months: the percentage fall in proteinuria was significantly larger with tonsillectomy, but the frequency of disappearance of proteinuria, haematuria, or both (clinical remission) was not statistically different between groups, and the authors concluded the added operation had no beneficial effect on haematuria or remission, with the antiproteinuric difference marginal. Against that, the meta-analysis of 14 studies (1,794 patients) — mostly retrospective cohorts — reports far higher odds of clinical remission with tonsillectomy (pooled OR 3.40, 95% CI 2.58 to 4.48) and lower odds of kidney failure (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52), including for tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses versus pulses alone (remission OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.99 to 5.01). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: randomised evidence says the operation adds little to steroid pulses; the large observational effects are exactly the size that confounding by indication manufactures, and kidney survival has never been randomised.

cards.headline: Kawamura 2014 RCT: proteinuria fell further with tonsillectomy, but remission did not differ — 'no beneficial effect' on the endpoints that define it
cards.summary: Kawamura 2014 RCT: proteinuria fell further with tonsillectomy, but remission did not differ — 'no beneficial effect' on the endpoints that define it
cards.people: 72 patients with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, proteinuria, and low serum creatinine, randomised to tonsillectomy combined with steroid pulses (n=33) or steroid pulses alone (n=39), followed for 12 months; primary endpoints were urinary protein excretion and disappearance of proteinuria and/or haematuria.
cards.result: The percentage decrease in urinary protein excretion over 12 months was significantly larger in the tonsillectomy group (P<0.05). However, the frequency of disappearance of proteinuria, haematuria, or both (clinical remission) at 12 months was not statistically different between the groups. Logistic regression identified assigned treatment as an independent factor for disappearance of proteinuria (odds ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.01 to 8.83; P=0.049) but not for haematuria or clinical remission. The authors concluded tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses has no beneficial effect over pulses alone on haematuria or clinical remission, and that the antiproteinuric difference was marginal.
cards.watchOut: Small (72 patients) and short (12 months): it cannot speak to kidney survival at all, and a borderline proteinuria-disappearance odds ratio whose confidence interval starts at 1.01 is fragile. But it is the only randomised evidence, and Japanese practice — where this combination is most used — is what it tested.
cards.source: Kawamura T et al. A multicenter randomized controlled trial of tonsillectomy combined with steroid pulse therapy in patients with immunoglobulin A nephropathy. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association. 2014. PMID: 24596084. Registry ID: JPRN:C000000384. cards.headline: Liu 2015 meta-analysis: remission OR 3.40 and kidney-failure OR 0.25 with tonsillectomy — from 14 studies that were mostly retrospective
cards.summary: Liu 2015 meta-analysis: remission OR 3.40 and kidney-failure OR 0.25 with tonsillectomy — from 14 studies that were mostly retrospective
cards.people: Fourteen prospective and retrospective studies totalling 1,794 patients with IgA nephropathy treated with or without tonsillectomy, as adjunct or independent therapy; outcomes were clinical remission and end-stage renal disease.
cards.result: Tonsillectomy was associated with greater odds of clinical remission (10 studies, 1,431 patients; pooled OR 3.40, 95% CI 2.58 to 4.48; P<0.001), robust to excluding renin-angiotensin inhibitor effects (OR 2.80, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.09). In subgroups, tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses beat pulses alone (7 studies, 783 patients; OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.99 to 5.01), and tonsillectomy was associated with lower odds of end-stage renal disease (9 studies, 873 patients; OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52; P<0.001). The authors note most included studies were retrospective cohorts and confounding could not be uniformly adjusted.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes of OR 3.40 and 0.25 from retrospective data, in a literature where healthier, earlier-stage patients are selected for surgery, are the classic signature of confounding by indication — and they sit directly against the one randomised trial's null on the same remission outcome. Observational ratios this large still cannot carry a shelf past the RCT under this library's rules.
cards.source: Liu LL et al. Tonsillectomy for IgA nephropathy: a meta-analysis. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2015. PMID: 25446024. cards.headline: Synthesis: an operation whose randomised trial is null and whose reputation is observational
cards.summary: Synthesis: an operation whose randomised trial is null and whose reputation is observational
cards.people: One multicentre RCT (72 patients, 12 months) of tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses versus pulses alone, and one meta-analysis of 14 mostly retrospective studies (1,794 patients) of tonsillectomy in IgA nephropathy.
cards.result: Randomised: remission not significantly different; proteinuria fall larger (P<0.05); proteinuria-disappearance OR 2.98 (95% CI 1.01 to 8.83). Observational pool: remission OR 3.40 (95% CI 2.58 to 4.48); kidney failure OR 0.25 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.52). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — the positive side of the split is observational.
cards.watchOut: Practice differs sharply by country (routine in Japan, rare elsewhere), and ethnicity and biopsy-timing differences may make both bodies of evidence partly right in different populations; a large randomised trial with kidney-survival follow-up remains the missing arbiter.

shelves.title: Mycophenolate in IgA nephropathy: the largest trial cut progression from 21.2% to 7.1% (aHR 0.23) — while the meta-analysis of nine earlier trials found nothing
shelves.question: In IgA nephropathy with persistent proteinuria, does mycophenolate mofetil reduce proteinuria and slow progression compared with control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Glomerulonephritis, IGA/drug therapy · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Kidney Failure, Chronic/therapy · Mycophenolic Acid/therapeutic use · Proteinuria/drug therapy/complications · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: SPLIT — this shelf is two literatures facing each other. The MAIN trial randomised 170 Chinese patients with progressive IgA nephropathy (proteinuria >1 g/day, eGFR 30–60 or persistent hypertension), all after three months of optimised supportive care with losartan, to mycophenolate plus supportive care or supportive care alone for three years: the composite of creatinine doubling, kidney failure, or kidney/cardiovascular death occurred in 7.1% versus 21.2% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63), and chronic kidney disease progression in 8.2% versus 27.1% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57). Yet the meta-analysis of the nine earlier randomised trials (587 patients) found mycophenolate — alone or with low/medium-dose steroid — did not differ from full-dose steroid or placebo on remission, proteinuria, or creatinine, with more infection but less Cushing syndrome and diabetes. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: a single large positive trial in one population against a null pooled literature — the honest stamp is that mycophenolate's benefit in IgA nephropathy is population- and protocol-dependent and unconfirmed outside China.

cards.headline: MAIN trial (Hou 2023): composite progression 7.1% vs 21.2% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63) over three years, on top of optimised losartan care
cards.summary: MAIN trial (Hou 2023): composite progression 7.1% vs 21.2% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63) over three years, on top of optimised losartan care
cards.people: 170 adults with IgA nephropathy, proteinuria >1.0 g/day and eGFR >30 and <60 mL/min/1.73 m² or persistent hypertension, enrolled after a 3-month run-in of optimised supportive care including losartan (238 patients entered run-in; those still excreting ≥0.75 g/day were randomised) to mycophenolate (1.5 g/day for 12 months, then 0.75–1.0 g/day for at least 6 months) plus supportive care (n=85) or supportive care alone (n=85), treated 3 years and followed a median of 60 months post-trial.
cards.result: The primary composite (doubling of serum creatinine, end-stage kidney disease, or death from kidney or cardiovascular cause) occurred in 6 patients (7.1%) on mycophenolate and 18 (21.2%) on supportive care (adjusted hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63). Progression of chronic kidney disease occurred in 7 (8.2%) versus 23 (27.1%) (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57), consistently across subgroups. After the trial, eGFR loss accelerated in those who stopped mycophenolate (annual loss 6.1 mL/min/1.73 m² off drug vs 2.9 on it). Serious adverse events were not more frequent with mycophenolate.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (blinded endpoints), single-country, and the benefit faded when the drug stopped — suggesting suppression rather than cure, and a treatment commitment measured in years. Event counts are small (6 vs 18), so the aHR of 0.23 carries a wide interval.
cards.source: Hou FF et al. Effectiveness of Mycophenolate Mofetil Among Patients With Progressive IgA Nephropathy: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2023. PMID: 36745456. Registry ID: NCT01854814. cards.headline: Peng 2021 meta-analysis: nine RCTs, 587 patients — no significant difference in remission, proteinuria, or creatinine; more infection, less steroid harm
cards.summary: Peng 2021 meta-analysis: nine RCTs, 587 patients — no significant difference in remission, proteinuria, or creatinine; more infection, less steroid harm
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials enrolling 587 patients with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, comparing mycophenolate (alone or with medium/low-dose steroid) against full-dose steroid alone or placebo.
cards.result: Mycophenolate-based regimens showed no significant difference from comparators in complete or partial remission, proteinuria reduction, serum creatinine, doubling of creatinine, or end-stage kidney disease. The risk of Cushing syndrome and diabetes was significantly lower with mycophenolate-treated patients, while the risk of infection was increased. The authors concluded larger randomised studies were needed.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials predate MAIN, were smaller, used varied doses and comparators (including full-dose steroids, an active treatment), and mixed ethnic populations in whom mycophenolate responses are reported to differ — a null pool does not erase a positive trial, just as the trial does not erase the pool.
cards.source: Peng XJ et al. Efficacy and safety of mycophenolate mofetil in the treatment for IgA nephropathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Clinical and experimental nephrology. 2021. PMID: 33710500. cards.headline: Synthesis: one strong trial in progressive Chinese disease versus a null international pool — split, and flagged
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial in progressive Chinese disease versus a null international pool — split, and flagged
cards.people: One 170-patient randomised trial in progressive IgA nephropathy after optimised supportive care, and one meta-analysis of nine earlier RCTs with 587 patients across mixed populations and comparators.
cards.result: MAIN: composite progression 7.1% vs 21.2% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63); CKD progression 8.2% vs 27.1% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57). Meta-analysis: no significant difference on remission, proteinuria, creatinine, or kidney failure; infection risk increased, steroid-type harms decreased. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.

shelves.title: LUNAR: adding rituximab to mycophenolate and steroids did not significantly raise renal response at one year — 56.9% vs 45.8% (P=0.18), primary endpoint missed
shelves.question: In proliferative lupus nephritis, does adding rituximab to mycophenolate and steroids increase complete renal remission compared with mycophenolate and steroids alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lupus Nephritis/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Rituximab · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a biologically beautiful idea that missed its endpoint. LUNAR randomised 144 patients with class III or IV lupus nephritis to rituximab (1,000 mg on days 1, 15, 168, and 182) or placebo, both on mycophenolate and corticosteroids. At week 52 the overall (complete plus partial) renal response rate was 56.9% on rituximab versus 45.8% on placebo (P=0.18) — a numerical gap carried mostly by partial responses that did not reach significance, so the primary endpoint was not achieved. Rituximab did what it does to blood tests: B cells were depleted in 71 of 72 patients, complement C3 and C4 rose and anti-dsDNA fell significantly, and no rituximab patient needed cyclophosphamide rescue versus eight on placebo. Serious adverse events, including infections, were similar; neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension were commoner on rituximab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: a single trial, and its lesson is that depleting B cells on top of mycophenolate improves serology without proven clinical gain at one year.

cards.headline: LUNAR (Rovin 2012): renal response 56.9% vs 45.8% (P=0.18) — primary endpoint not achieved; rescue cyclophosphamide 0 vs 8 patients
cards.summary: LUNAR (Rovin 2012): renal response 56.9% vs 45.8% (P=0.18) — primary endpoint not achieved; rescue cyclophosphamide 0 vs 8 patients
cards.people: 144 patients with class III or class IV lupus nephritis randomised 1:1 to rituximab 1,000 mg or placebo on days 1, 15, 168, and 182, all receiving mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids; primary endpoint was renal response status at week 52.
cards.result: Overall (complete and partial) renal response rates were 56.9% among the 72 rituximab patients and 45.8% among the 72 placebo patients (P=0.18); partial responses accounted for most of the difference, and the primary endpoint (superior response rate with rituximab) was not achieved. Rituximab depleted peripheral CD19+ B cells in 71 of 72 patients. Eight placebo patients and no rituximab patients required cyclophosphamide rescue through week 52. Serum C3, C4, and anti-dsDNA improved significantly more with rituximab. Serious adverse events, including infections, were similar between groups; neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension occurred more frequently with rituximab.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for a larger response gap than it found; an 11-point difference with P=0.18 in 144 patients is 'not proven', not 'proven absent' — but the burden of proof sits with the add-on drug, and one year may also be short for a B-cell strategy whose serological effects were clear. Tier C: single trial.
cards.source: Rovin BH et al. Efficacy and safety of rituximab in patients with active proliferative lupus nephritis: the Lupus Nephritis Assessment with Rituximab study. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2012. PMID: 22231479. Registry ID: NCT00282347. cards.headline: Synthesis: serology obeyed, the kidney endpoint did not — rituximab as add-on remains unproven, not disproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: serology obeyed, the kidney endpoint did not — rituximab as add-on remains unproven, not disproven
cards.people: One randomised double-blind phase 3 trial of 144 patients with proliferative lupus nephritis, rituximab versus placebo added to mycophenolate and corticosteroids, 52 weeks.
cards.result: Overall renal response 56.9% vs 45.8% (P=0.18); complete responses did not drive the difference. B-cell depletion 71/72; cyclophosphamide rescue 0 vs 8; serious adverse events similar; neutropenia, leukopenia, hypotension commoner on rituximab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — single-trial shelf, flagged for the developer.
cards.watchOut: This shelf judges rituximab added to full mycophenolate-based therapy in trial-eligible proliferative disease. It does not judge rituximab in refractory or relapsing lupus nephritis, where the evidence is observational and the clinical logic differs — that use remains uncarded here rather than condemned.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rovin BH et al. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2012 (PMID: 22231479).

shelves.title: Multitarget therapy for lupus nephritis: complete remission 45.9% vs 25.6% with IV cyclophosphamide at 24 weeks — and 65% vs 15% in the earlier class V+IV trial
shelves.question: In proliferative lupus nephritis, does multitarget therapy with tacrolimus plus mycophenolate induce remission faster than intravenous cyclophosphamide?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Biopsy · Cyclophosphamide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Kidney/pathology · Lupus Nephritis/drug therapy/pathology · Male · Methylprednisolone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Pilot Projects · Prednisone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Remission Induction · Tacrolimus/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same research tradition, both clearly positive on remission, both short. In the 362-patient multicentre trial, multitarget therapy (tacrolimus 4 mg/day plus mycophenolate 1.0 g/day plus steroids) produced complete remission at 24 weeks in 45.9% versus 25.6% on intravenous cyclophosphamide (difference 20.3 percentage points, 95% CI 10.0 to 30.6; P<0.001), with overall response 83.5% versus 63.0% and a median time to response 4.1 weeks shorter; adverse events were similar (50.3% vs 52.5%). In the earlier 40-patient trial in class V+IV disease, complete remission on multitarget therapy reached 50% at 6 months and 65% at 9 months versus 5% and 15% on cyclophosphamide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): multitarget induction induces remission faster and more often than IV cyclophosphamide in the populations studied — with the standing caveat that both trials are Chinese, the larger one is open-label, and neither follows patients long enough to judge kidney survival or relapse.

cards.headline: Liu 2015: complete remission 45.9% vs 25.6% (difference 20.3 points, P<0.001); overall response 83.5% vs 63.0%; adverse events 50.3% vs 52.5%
cards.summary: Liu 2015: complete remission 45.9% vs 25.6% (difference 20.3 points, P<0.001); overall response 83.5% vs 63.0%; adverse events 50.3% vs 52.5%
cards.people: 362 adults (18–65 years) with biopsy-proven lupus nephritis at 26 renal centres in China, randomised to multitarget therapy (tacrolimus 4 mg/day plus mycophenolate mofetil 1.0 g/day) or intravenous cyclophosphamide (starting 0.75 g/m², adjusted 0.5–1.0, every 4 weeks for 6 months); both groups received 3 days of pulse methylprednisolone then tapering oral prednisone. Primary endpoint: complete remission at 24 weeks.
cards.result: After 24 weeks, complete remission occurred in 45.9% of the multitarget group versus 25.6% of the cyclophosphamide group (difference 20.3 percentage points, 95% CI 10.0 to 30.6; P<0.001). Overall response (complete plus partial) was 83.5% versus 63.0% (difference 20.4 points, 95% CI 10.3 to 30.6; P<0.001), and median time to overall response was 4.1 weeks shorter with multitarget therapy (95% CI -7.9 to -2.1). Adverse-event incidence did not differ (50.3% (91/181) vs 52.5% (95/181)).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 24 weeks only, one country, and mycophenolate dosed at 1.0 g/day — lower than Western practice — while the cyclophosphamide comparator was a full-dose monthly regimen; remission at 6 months is a milestone, not kidney survival, and relapse after induction is where this strategy must still prove itself.
cards.source: Liu Z et al. Multitarget therapy for induction treatment of lupus nephritis: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2015. PMID: 25383558. Registry ID: NCT00876616. cards.headline: Bao 2008: in class V+IV disease, complete remission 50% vs 5% at 6 months and 65% vs 15% at 9 months with multitarget therapy
cards.summary: Bao 2008: in class V+IV disease, complete remission 50% vs 5% at 6 months and 65% vs 15% at 9 months with multitarget therapy
cards.people: 40 patients with class V+IV lupus nephritis randomised to induction with mycophenolate, tacrolimus, and steroids (multitarget) or intravenous cyclophosphamide, treated 6 months and extended to 9 months if complete remission was not achieved.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat complete remission was higher with multitarget therapy at both 6 months (50% vs 5%) and 9 months (65% vs 15%). Partial remission at 6 months occurred in eight patients (40%) in each group; at 9 months, six patients (30%) on multitarget therapy and eight (40%) on cyclophosphamide were in partial remission. There were no deaths. Most adverse events were less frequent in the multitarget group; calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity was not observed, though three patients developed new-onset hypertension on multitarget therapy.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, one centre, one histological subgroup — the effect sizes (50% vs 5%) are larger than small trials can reliably sustain, and this card supports direction, not magnitude. Class V+IV (membranous plus proliferative) disease is also the subgroup where tacrolimus has its strongest independent rationale.
cards.source: Bao H et al. Successful treatment of class V+IV lupus nephritis with multitarget therapy. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2008. PMID: 18596121. cards.headline: Synthesis: remission comes faster and oftener with two drugs aimed at two targets — durability is the open question
cards.summary: Synthesis: remission comes faster and oftener with two drugs aimed at two targets — durability is the open question
cards.people: Two randomised trials (362 and 40 patients) in Chinese patients with lupus nephritis comparing multitarget tacrolimus plus mycophenolate plus steroids with intravenous cyclophosphamide plus steroids, over 24 weeks to 9 months.
cards.result: Complete remission: 45.9% vs 25.6% at 24 weeks (difference 20.3 points, P<0.001) in the large trial; 65% vs 15% at 9 months in the small class V+IV trial. Overall response in the large trial: 83.5% vs 63.0%. Adverse events: 50.3% vs 52.5% in the large trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial reports beyond 9 months, neither is blinded, and tacrolimus brings its own renal and metabolic toxicities that a 24-week window cannot price. Tier C is not set — two concordant randomised trials — but the developer should note both come from one country's trial programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Liu Z et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25383558); Bao H et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2008 (PMID: 18596121).

shelves.title: Pegcetacoplan in C3 glomerulopathy: proteinuria down 67.2% vs up 2.9% on placebo at 26 weeks — composite renal endpoint met by 49% vs 3%
shelves.question: In C3 glomerulopathy, does the C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan reduce proteinuria and stabilise kidney function compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Complement C3/analysis/antagonists & inhibitors/immunology · Creatinine/urine · Double-Blind Method · Glomerulonephritis, Membranoproliferative/drug therapy/immunology/pathology/urine · Kidney Glomerulus/pathology · Proteinuria/drug therapy/immunology/pathology/urine · Peptides, Cyclic/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a rare-disease trial with an unusually unambiguous primary result. VALIANT randomised 124 adolescents and adults with C3 glomerulopathy or primary immune-complex MPGN (including post-transplant recurrence) to pegcetacoplan or placebo for 26 weeks: proteinuria fell 67.2% on drug while rising 2.9% on placebo, a 68.1% relative reduction (95% CI 57.3 to 76.2). The composite renal endpoint (eGFR stabilisation plus ≥50% proteinuria reduction) was met by 49% versus 3%, and ≥50% proteinuria reduction by 60% versus 5%. In the open-label extension, patients switched from placebo cut proteinuria 53.9% within 26 weeks of starting drug, and the treated group held its 67.2% reduction at week 52. Pegcetacoplan was not associated with more adverse events than placebo; no serious infections from encapsulated bacteria occurred, and one pegcetacoplan patient died of COVID-19 pneumonia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: one randomised trial in a rare disease, with proteinuria — not kidney survival — as its proven endpoint.

cards.headline: VALIANT (Fakhouri 2025): proteinuria -67.2% vs +2.9% (relative reduction 68.1%); composite renal endpoint 49% vs 3%; ≥50% reduction 60% vs 5%
cards.summary: VALIANT (Fakhouri 2025): proteinuria -67.2% vs +2.9% (relative reduction 68.1%); composite renal endpoint 49% vs 3%; ≥50% reduction 60% vs 5%
cards.people: 124 adolescents and adults with C3 glomerulopathy or primary immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis — native kidney disease or recurrence after transplantation — randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous pegcetacoplan or placebo for 26 weeks; primary endpoint was the log-transformed ratio of urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 26 versus baseline.
cards.result: Proteinuria fell significantly more with pegcetacoplan (geometric mean change -67.2%, 95% CI -74.9 to -57.2) than placebo (+2.9%, 95% CI -8.6 to 15.9) — a relative reduction of 68.1% (95% CI 57.3 to 76.2). Significantly more pegcetacoplan patients met the composite renal endpoint (eGFR stabilisation plus ≥50% proteinuria reduction): 49% vs 3%; and achieved ≥50% proteinuria reduction: 60% vs 5%. Among 69 patients with evaluable biopsies, the C3 glomerulopathy histologic activity score did not differ significantly. Pegcetacoplan was not associated with more adverse events; no serious infections from encapsulated bacteria occurred; one pegcetacoplan patient died from COVID-19 pneumonia; no allograft rejection or loss occurred.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six weeks, 124 patients, and a proteinuria primary endpoint in diseases whose natural history runs over years — eGFR 'stabilisation' inside a composite at 26 weeks is encouraging, not proof of prevented kidney failure. Tier C: single-trial benefit claim in a rare disease.
cards.source: Fakhouri F et al. Trial of Pegcetacoplan in C3 Glomerulopathy and Immune-Complex MPGN. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 41337715. Registry ID: NCT05067127. cards.headline: VALIANT open-label extension (Nester 2026): benefit held at week 52 (-67.2%); placebo-switchers fell 53.9% after starting drug
cards.summary: VALIANT open-label extension (Nester 2026): benefit held at week 52 (-67.2%); placebo-switchers fell 53.9% after starting drug
cards.people: VALIANT participants entering the 26-week open-label period in which all received pegcetacoplan: 59 who had received pegcetacoplan and 55 who had received placebo in the randomised period completed it.
cards.result: The pegcetacoplan-to-pegcetacoplan group maintained its proteinuria reduction at week 52 (-67.2%, 95% CI -75.8 to -55.4, versus -67.1% at week 26). The placebo-to-pegcetacoplan group moved from +3.2% on placebo to -53.9% (95% CI -64.5 to -40.1) after 26 weeks on drug. eGFR change at week 52 was -3.7 mL/min/1.73 m² in the continuous group and -4.7 in the switch group (whose week-26-to-52 change was +3.0). A post hoc pooled analysis of 52 weeks of pegcetacoplan (n=118) showed proteinuria -63.0% and eGFR change +0.1 mL/min/1.73 m². No new safety concerns, encapsulated meningococcal infections, deaths, or allograft losses were identified in the extension.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, completer-based, with post hoc elements — the switchers' response is the strongest internal replication this shelf has, but it is not a second randomised trial. This record carries no MeSH terms.

shelves.title: Ravulizumab in atypical HUS: complete TMA response in 53.6% of adults and 77.8% of children — from single-arm trials with no comparator
shelves.question: In atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, does the long-acting C5 inhibitor ravulizumab achieve haematological normalisation and improve kidney function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome/drug therapy · Complement Inactivating Agents/adverse effects · Complement System Proteins · Humans · Thrombotic Microangiopathies/diagnosis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dramatic responses in a disease that does not remit on its own, from trials with no control arm. In Study 311, 58 complement-inhibitor-naïve adults with atypical HUS received ravulizumab every 8 weeks: complete thrombotic microangiopathy response (platelet and LDH normalisation plus ≥25% creatinine improvement) was achieved by 53.6%, with platelet normalisation in 83.9%, LDH normalisation in 76.8%, creatinine improvement in 58.9%, and eGFR improvement by at least one stage in 68.1% by day 183; four deaths occurred, none judged treatment-related. In Study 312, 18 naïve children achieved complete response in 77.8% by week 26 and 94.4% by week 50, with a median eGFR increase of 80 mL/min/1.73 m² by week 26 and no deaths or meningococcal infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the evidence is two single-arm phase 3 studies — persuasive against the known natural history of untreated aHUS, but incapable of pricing the drug against eculizumab or of excluding selection effects.

cards.headline: Study 311 (Rondeau 2020): complete TMA response 53.6%; platelets normalised 83.9%, LDH 76.8%, creatinine improved ≥25% in 58.9%
cards.summary: Study 311 (Rondeau 2020): complete TMA response 53.6%; platelets normalised 83.9%, LDH 76.8%, creatinine improved ≥25% in 58.9%
cards.people: Complement-inhibitor-naïve adults (≥18 years) with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome presenting with thrombotic microangiopathy, treated globally with ravulizumab through a 26-week initial evaluation period; the safety analysis set comprised 58 patients. Primary endpoint: complete TMA response — platelet and LDH normalisation plus ≥25% improvement in serum creatinine.
cards.result: Ravulizumab produced immediate, complete, and sustained C5 inhibition in all patients. Complete TMA response was achieved in 53.6% of patients. Platelet normalisation occurred in 83.9%, LDH normalisation in 76.8%, and ≥25% creatinine improvement in 58.9%. Improvement in eGFR by one or more stages was achieved by 68.1% by day 183. No unexpected adverse events were reported; four deaths occurred (three within a month of starting, including one patient excluded on eligibility after the first dose), none considered treatment-related by investigators.

cards.headline: Study 312 (Ariceta 2021): complete TMA response 77.8% at week 26 and 94.4% at week 50 in 18 children; median eGFR up 80 points
cards.summary: Study 312 (Ariceta 2021): complete TMA response 77.8% at week 26 and 94.4% at week 50 in 18 children; median eGFR up 80 points
cards.people: 18 complement-inhibitor-naïve children (median age 5.2 years) with atypical HUS — 72.2% with extrarenal symptoms and 38.9% previously in intensive care; baseline eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m² — treated with ravulizumab every 8 weeks (every 4 weeks if under 20 kg) for 26 weeks, with follow-up to week 50.
cards.result: By week 26, 77.8% achieved complete TMA response; platelet normalisation occurred in 94.4%, LDH normalisation in 88.9%, and ≥25% creatinine improvement in 83.3%. By week 50, 94.4% had achieved complete response. Median eGFR increase above baseline was 80 mL/min/1.73 m² at week 26 and 94 at week 50. No unexpected adverse events, deaths, or meningococcal infections occurred.
cards.watchOut: Eighteen children, no control group, and a baseline eGFR of 22 leaves enormous room for recovery with any effective therapy plus modern supportive care; the trial establishes that ravulizumab can deliver these outcomes in children, not the size of its advantage over eculizumab, which was never randomised against it.

shelves.title: Somatostatin analogues in ADPKD: kidneys grow more slowly on octreotide and lanreotide — but the largest trial found eGFR falling at exactly the same rate
shelves.question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, do somatostatin analogues (octreotide or lanreotide) slow kidney growth and function decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cholecystitis, Acute/chemically induced · Cholelithiasis/chemically induced · Disease Progression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Italy · Kidney/drug effects/pathology · Kidney Failure, Chronic/prevention & control · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Organ Size/drug effects · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant/drug therapy/pathology · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the class splits by drug, by trial, and by endpoint. On kidney growth the signal is consistent: in ALADIN, octreotide-LAR limited total kidney volume growth at one year (46.2 vs 143.7 mL on placebo; p=0.032), though the three-year difference was not significant (220.1 vs 454.3 mL; p=0.25); in ALADIN 2, in later-stage disease, octreotide reduced volume growth by 96.8 mL at one year (p=0.027) and 422.6 mL at three years (p=0.002) and cut progression to creatinine doubling or kidney failure (9 vs 21 patients; HR 0.307, 95% CI 0.127 to 0.742; p=0.009), while its GFR-decline difference (0.56 mL/min/1.73 m² per year) was not significant (p=0.295). Then DIPAK 1 — the largest trial, 309 patients — found lanreotide did not slow eGFR decline at all (-3.53 vs -3.46 mL/min/1.73 m² per year; difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.71 to 0.56; P=0.81), even though kidney growth was slower (4.15% vs 5.56% per year; P=0.02), at the cost of loose stools in 91% and hepatic cyst infections in 5.2%. PROPOSED SPLIT: somatostatin analogues reliably slow cyst growth; whether they preserve kidney function is unproven — positive only as a secondary composite in one small octreotide trial, null as the primary endpoint of the large lanreotide trial.

cards.headline: ALADIN (Caroli 2013): kidney growth at 1 year 46.2 vs 143.7 mL (p=0.032); at 3 years 220.1 vs 454.3 mL (p=0.25) — significance faded
cards.summary: ALADIN (Caroli 2013): kidney growth at 1 year 46.2 vs 143.7 mL (p=0.032); at 3 years 220.1 vs 454.3 mL (p=0.25) — significance faded
cards.people: 79 adults with ADPKD and eGFR ≥40 mL/min/1.73 m² at five Italian hospitals, randomised to octreotide-LAR (two 20 mg intramuscular injections every 28 days; n=40) or saline placebo (n=39) for 3 years; participants and outcome assessors were masked. Primary endpoint: change in total kidney volume by MRI at 1 and 3 years.
cards.result: At 1 year (38 vs 37 evaluable), mean total kidney volume increased less on octreotide-LAR (46.2 mL, SE 18.2) than placebo (143.7 mL, SE 26.0; p=0.032). At 3 years (35 per group), the increase remained numerically smaller (220.1 mL, SE 49.1 vs 454.3 mL, SE 80.8) but was not significant (p=0.25). At least one adverse event occurred in 92.5% on octreotide and 82.1% on placebo; four cases of cholelithiasis or acute cholecystitis on octreotide were probably treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: A 79-patient trial whose primary endpoint lost significance by year 3 as numbers thinned — it proves a growth effect at one year and suggests, but cannot confirm, durability; renal function decline was not its endpoint.
cards.source: Caroli A et al. Effect of longacting somatostatin analogue on kidney and cyst growth in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ALADIN): a randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. Lancet (London, England). 2013. PMID: 23972263. Registry ID: NCT00309283. cards.headline: ALADIN 2 (Perico 2019): in later-stage disease, volume growth cut by 422.6 mL at 3 years (p=0.002) and progression events 9 vs 21 (HR 0.307) — but GFR slope not significant
cards.summary: ALADIN 2 (Perico 2019): in later-stage disease, volume growth cut by 422.6 mL at 3 years (p=0.002) and progression events 9 vs 21 (HR 0.307) — but GFR slope not significant
cards.people: 100 adults with later-stage ADPKD (GFR 15–40 mL/min/1.73 m²) at four Italian nephrology units, randomised to octreotide-LAR (two 20 mg injections every 28 days; n=51) or saline placebo (n=49) for 3 years; co-primary outcomes were 1-year total kidney volume growth and 3-year measured GFR decline.
cards.result: Octreotide-LAR reduced median total kidney volume growth by 96.8 mL (95% CI 10.8 to 182.7) at 1 year (p=0.027) and 422.6 mL (95% CI 150.3 to 695.0) at 3 years (p=0.002) versus placebo. The reduction in rate of GFR decline (0.56 mL/min/1.73 m² per year, 95% CI -0.63 to 1.75) was not significant (p=0.295). Over a median 36 months, 9 octreotide and 21 placebo patients progressed to creatinine doubling or kidney failure (adjusted HR 0.307, 95% CI 0.127 to 0.742; p=0.009) — one event prevented for every 4 treated; among CKD stage 4 patients, kidney failure occurred in 3 vs 8 (adjusted HR 0.121, 95% CI 0.017 to 0.866; p=0.036).
cards.watchOut: The trial's own co-primary GFR endpoint missed; the impressive composite is a secondary analysis in 100 patients with 30 events, and the authors name the small sample as the main limitation. This is the strongest pro-function card on the shelf and it still does not carry a LIKELY.

cards.headline: DIPAK 1 (Meijer 2018): lanreotide did not slow eGFR decline (-3.53 vs -3.46/yr, P=0.81) in 309 patients — despite slower kidney growth (4.15% vs 5.56%/yr)
cards.summary: DIPAK 1 (Meijer 2018): lanreotide did not slow eGFR decline (-3.53 vs -3.46/yr, P=0.81) in 309 patients — despite slower kidney growth (4.15% vs 5.56%/yr)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded endpoint assessment (Meijer 2018, DIPAK 1)
cards.people: 309 patients with ADPKD aged 18–60 with eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m² at four Dutch nephrology clinics, randomised to lanreotide 120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks plus standard care (n=153) or standard care alone (n=152) for 2.5 years; 261 (85.6%) completed. Primary outcome: annual change in eGFR (slope).
cards.result: Annual eGFR decline was -3.53 on lanreotide versus -3.46 mL/min/1.73 m² per year on control (difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.71 to 0.56; P=0.81). Worsening kidney function (dialysis or 30% eGFR fall) did not differ (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.52; P=0.87), nor did quality of life. Total kidney volume grew more slowly on lanreotide (4.15% vs 5.56% per year; difference -1.33% per year, 95% CI -2.41 to -0.24; P=0.02). Adverse events on lanreotide included injection-site discomfort (32% vs 0.7%), loose stools (91% vs 6.6%), abdominal discomfort (79% vs 20%), and hepatic cyst infections (5.2% vs 0%). The authors concluded the findings do not support lanreotide for later-stage ADPKD.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (though endpoints were blinded) and a different drug, dose route, and population from the ALADIN trials — DIPAK refutes lanreotide for function preservation directly, and octreotide only by class inference. Its size and primary-endpoint discipline make it the shelf's anchor of doubt.
cards.source: Meijer E et al. Effect of Lanreotide on Kidney Function in Patients With Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease: The DIPAK 1 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30422235. Registry ID: NCT01616927. cards.headline: Synthesis: growth and function come apart — the class slows cysts, and only octreotide has even a secondary claim on outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: growth and function come apart — the class slows cysts, and only octreotide has even a secondary claim on outcomes
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 488 patients with ADPKD: ALADIN (79, octreotide, early disease), ALADIN 2 (100, octreotide, later-stage), and DIPAK 1 (309, lanreotide, later-stage), each 2.5–3 years.
cards.result: Kidney growth: slower on drug in all three trials (significant at 1 year in ALADIN, at 1 and 3 years in ALADIN 2, and as %/year in DIPAK 1). eGFR decline: not significantly different in ALADIN 2 (difference 0.56/yr, p=0.295) and null in DIPAK 1 (difference -0.08/yr, P=0.81). Hard composite: 9 vs 21 events in ALADIN 2 (HR 0.307). Harms: gallstones/cholecystitis (octreotide), loose stools 91% and hepatic cyst infections 5.2% (lanreotide). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Tolvaptan — the ADPKD drug with proven function benefit — has its own shelf and is the correct comparator in clinic; this shelf exists because patients still ask about somatostatin analogues, and the honest answer is 'smaller kidneys, unproven function'. Tier C is not set: three randomised trials, openly split, carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Caroli A et al. Lancet (London, England). 2013 (PMID: 23972263); Perico N et al. PLoS medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30951521); Meijer E et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 30422235).

shelves.title: TAME-PKD: metformin was safe and tolerable in ADPKD, but the efficacy signals were not significant — eGFR decline -1.71 vs -3.07 per year in a 97-patient phase 2 trial
shelves.question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does metformin slow kidney-function decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cysts · Disease Progression · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney · Metformin/adverse effects · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — a safety trial that answered its safety question and could not answer the efficacy one. TAME-PKD randomised 97 adults with ADPKD and eGFR above 50 mL/min/1.73 m² to metformin or placebo twice daily for two years, with safety and tolerability as primary outcomes: serious adverse events were similar, gastrointestinal symptom scores stayed low, and dose reductions for intolerance occurred in 21 metformin versus 14 placebo participants (not significant). The secondary efficacy signals leaned toward metformin on function — annual eGFR change -1.71 versus -3.07 mL/min/1.73 m² (mean difference 1.37, 95% CI -0.70 to 3.44) — and against it on growth (height-adjusted kidney volume +3.87% versus +2.16% per year; difference 1.68%, 95% CI -2.11 to 5.62), neither significant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): metformin in ADPKD is safe and tolerable at the doses tested; whether it slows progression is unknown and awaits an adequately powered trial.

cards.headline: TAME-PKD (Perrone 2021): eGFR -1.71 vs -3.07/yr (difference 1.37, 95% CI -0.70 to 3.44); kidney growth 3.87% vs 2.16%/yr — both non-significant
cards.summary: TAME-PKD (Perrone 2021): eGFR -1.71 vs -3.07/yr (difference 1.37, 95% CI -0.70 to 3.44); kidney growth 3.87% vs 2.16%/yr — both non-significant
cards.people: 97 patients aged 18–60 with ADPKD and eGFR >50 mL/min/1.73 m², randomised 1:1 to metformin or placebo twice daily for 2 years; primary outcomes were medication safety and tolerability; 38 metformin and 39 placebo participants remained on study product at 24 months.
cards.result: Proportions experiencing serious adverse events were similar between groups, and Gastrointestinal Symptoms Rating Scale scores were low at baseline and did not change significantly. Twenty-one metformin participants reduced dose for intolerance versus 14 on placebo (not significant). Annual eGFR change was -1.71 with metformin and -3.07 mL/min/1.73 m² per year with placebo (mean difference 1.37, 95% CI -0.70 to 3.44). Mean annual height-adjusted total kidney volume change was 3.87% on metformin and 2.16% on placebo (mean difference 1.68%, 95% CI -2.11 to 5.62). The authors concluded metformin was safe and tolerable, with efficacy requiring a larger trial.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, 97 patients, and efficacy endpoints the trial never powered — the eGFR point estimate (1.37/yr slower decline) would be clinically important if real, and the kidney-volume estimate points the other way; both intervals comfortably include zero and each other. This record carries no registry identifier.

shelves.title: Pravastatin in children and young adults with ADPKD: the composite progression endpoint hit 69% vs 88% on placebo over three years — driven by slower kidney growth
shelves.question: In children with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does pravastatin slow kidney growth and left-ventricular mass increase compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Albuminuria/urine · Child · Creatinine/blood/urine · Double-Blind Method · Heart Ventricles/drug effects/pathology · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Kidney/drug effects/pathology · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Organ Size/drug effects · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant/drug therapy/urine · Pravastatin/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the only randomised trial of early intervention in paediatric ADPKD, and it met its endpoint. In 110 children and young adults with ADPKD and normal kidney function — all receiving lisinopril — pravastatin versus placebo over three years produced the composite primary endpoint (a ≥20% change in height-corrected total kidney volume, left ventricular mass index, or urine microalbumin excretion) in 69% versus 88% (P=0.03). The driver was kidney growth: a ≥20% rise in height-corrected kidney volume occurred in 46% versus 68% (P=0.03), and adjusted three-year kidney-volume growth was 23% ± 3% versus 31% ± 3% (P=0.02). Left ventricular mass progression (25% vs 38%; P=0.18) and microalbuminuria progression (47% vs 39%; P=0.50) did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial, on structural endpoints, in young patients with normal kidney function — it shows early pravastatin slows the anatomical march of ADPKD, not yet that it prevents kidney failure decades later.

cards.headline: Cadnapaphornchai 2014: composite endpoint 69% vs 88% (P=0.03); kidney-volume progression 46% vs 68% (P=0.03); growth 23% vs 31% over 3 years (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Cadnapaphornchai 2014: composite endpoint 69% vs 88% (P=0.03); kidney-volume progression 46% vs 68% (P=0.03); growth 23% vs 31% over 3 years (P=0.02)
cards.people: 110 paediatric participants with ADPKD and normal kidney function, all receiving lisinopril, randomised to pravastatin or placebo for 3 years (2007–2012) with MRI and urine assessments at 0, 18, and 36 months; 91 participants (83%) completed. Primary outcome: a ≥20% change in height-corrected total kidney volume (HtTKV), left ventricular mass index (LVMI), or urine microalbumin excretion (UAE).
cards.result: Fewer pravastatin participants reached the primary endpoint (69% vs 88%; P=0.03), driven by kidney volume: HtTKV progression in 46% vs 68% (P=0.03), with similar findings for LVMI (25% vs 38%; P=0.18) and UAE (47% vs 39%; P=0.50) that were not significant individually. The adjusted percent change in HtTKV over 3 years was significantly lower with pravastatin (23% ± 3% vs 31% ± 3%; P=0.02). The authors concluded pravastatin slows progression of structural kidney disease in children and young adults with ADPKD.
cards.watchOut: A composite in which two of three components were individually null, structural (imaging and urine) endpoints rather than kidney function, and every participant on background lisinopril — the trial tests pravastatin as an add-on in early disease, and no trial can yet connect a 3-year growth difference at age 15 to dialysis at age 50. This record carries no registry identifier. Tier C: single trial.
cards.source: Cadnapaphornchai MA et al. Effect of pravastatin on total kidney volume, left ventricular mass index, and microalbuminuria in pediatric autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2014. PMID: 24721893. cards.headline: Synthesis: early statin therapy bends the growth curve in young ADPKD — a structural promise awaiting a functional payoff
cards.summary: Synthesis: early statin therapy bends the growth curve in young ADPKD — a structural promise awaiting a functional payoff
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial of 110 children and young adults with ADPKD and normal kidney function, pravastatin versus placebo on background lisinopril, 3 years.
cards.result: Composite ≥20% progression (kidney volume, ventricular mass, or microalbuminuria): 69% vs 88% (P=0.03). Kidney-volume progression: 46% vs 68% (P=0.03); adjusted 3-year growth 23% vs 31% (P=0.02). Ventricular mass and microalbuminuria components: not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Adult statin trials in ADPKD ask a different question in different kidneys and are not carded here; nor should this paediatric structural result be read across to adults with established disease, where the neighbouring shelves (tolvaptan; somatostatin analogues) govern.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cadnapaphornchai MA et al. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2014 (PMID: 24721893).

shelves.title: Kidneys from hepatitis-C-viremic donors: every recipient cured in THINKER (20/20) and MYTHIC (30/30) with direct-acting antivirals — graft function matching HCV-negative kidneys
shelves.question: In kidney transplantation, can kidneys from hepatitis-C-viremic donors be used safely when recipients receive direct-acting antivirals?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Benzofurans/therapeutic use · Creatinine/blood · Drug Combinations · End Stage Liver Disease/complications/physiopathology/surgery · Female · Genotype · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Hepacivirus/genetics · Hepatitis C/drug therapy · Humans · Imidazoles/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Quality of Life · Quinoxalines/therapeutic use · RNA, Viral/blood · Tissue Donors · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a discarded organ supply, reclaimed in two prospective trials with a perfect cure record. In THINKER, 20 hepatitis-C-negative recipients of genotype-1 HCV-viremic kidneys received elbasvir-grazoprevir from post-transplant day 3: all 20 achieved HCV cure, complications were transient or manageable, and 12-month eGFR (median 72.8 mL/min/1.73 m²) matched recipients of HCV-negative kidneys (67.2). In the multicentre MYTHIC trial, 30 recipients of HCV-viremic deceased-donor kidneys received 8 weeks of glecaprevir-pibrentasvir starting about day 3: all 30 achieved sustained virologic response, median eGFR at 6 months was 57 mL/min/1.73 m², three developed acute cellular rejection, and one recipient died of sepsis four months after achieving cure — with no severe adverse event judged likely related to HCV or its treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-arm trials without randomised comparators — the claim is feasibility and safety of the strategy, and on that claim 50 consecutive cures is strong evidence.

cards.headline: THINKER (Reese 2018): 20/20 recipients cured; 12-month eGFR 72.8 vs 67.2 in matched HCV-negative-kidney recipients
cards.summary: THINKER (Reese 2018): 20/20 recipients cured; 12-month eGFR 72.8 vs 67.2 in matched HCV-negative-kidney recipients
cards.type: Single-arm open-label trial with matched comparison (Reese 2018, THINKER-1)
cards.people: 20 HCV-negative transplant candidates (mean age 56.3 years; 70% male) at a single centre who received kidneys infected with genotype 1 HCV and elbasvir-grazoprevir from post-transplant day 3; renal function was compared with a 1:5 matched sample of recipients of HCV-negative kidneys. The report covers 12-month outcomes for the first 10 recipients and 6-month data for 10 more.
cards.result: All 20 participants achieved HCV cure. Hepatic and renal complications were transient or successfully managed. Quality-of-life physical scores dipped at 4 weeks then rose above pre-transplant values; mental scores returned to baseline. eGFR was similar to matched HCV-negative-kidney recipients at 6 months (median 67.5 vs 66.2 mL/min/1.73 m²) and 12 months (median 72.8 vs 67.2).
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, one centre, genotype 1 only, and a sponsor with a product in the protocol (Merck) — THINKER proves a concept in carefully consented, closely monitored patients; it cannot price rare harms or generalise to every donor genotype and recipient. The trial's first brief report (Goldberg 2017) carries no abstract data and is not carded; this 12-month report is the THINKER record of substance.
cards.source: Reese PP et al. Twelve-Month Outcomes After Transplant of Hepatitis C-Infected Kidneys Into Uninfected Recipients: A Single-Group Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2018. PMID: 30083748. Registry ID: NCT02743897. cards.headline: MYTHIC (Sise 2020): 30/30 sustained virologic responses across seven centres; median eGFR 57 at 6 months; one late sepsis death after cure
cards.summary: MYTHIC (Sise 2020): 30/30 sustained virologic responses across seven centres; median eGFR 57 at 6 months; one late sepsis death after cure
cards.people: 30 HCV-uninfected recipients of kidneys from HCV-viremic deceased donors (median donor profile index 53%) at seven centres, transplanted May–October 2019 after a median 6.3 weeks from consent, treated with once-daily glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks targeted to start 3 days post-transplant.
cards.result: All 30 recipients achieved sustained virologic response (undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment). All had good allograft function at 6 months (median creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; median eGFR 57 mL/min/1.73 m²). Three recipients developed acute cellular rejection (one borderline) and three developed BK viremia that resolved with reduced immunosuppression. One recipient died of sepsis complications 4 months after achieving sustained response. No severe adverse event in any patient was deemed likely related to HCV infection or antiviral treatment.
cards.watchOut: Still single-arm and small; the sepsis death — after cure, on immunosuppression — is a reminder that the strategy's risks are the ordinary lethal risks of transplantation, now accepted in exchange for a much shorter wait (median 6.3 weeks from consent here). Longer-term graft and liver outcomes rest on registry follow-up, not these trials.
cards.source: Sise ME et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: 50 transplants, 50 cures, graft function intact — the question has moved from 'can we?' to 'who should be offered it?'
cards.summary: Synthesis: 50 transplants, 50 cures, graft function intact — the question has moved from 'can we?' to 'who should be offered it?'
cards.people: Two prospective single-arm trials (20 single-centre and 30 seven-centre recipients) of HCV-viremic deceased-donor kidneys into HCV-negative recipients, with direct-acting antivirals started about day 3 post-transplant.
cards.result: HCV cure: 20/20 (THINKER, elbasvir-grazoprevir) and 30/30 sustained virologic response (MYTHIC, glecaprevir-pibrentasvir 8 weeks). Graft function: 12-month median eGFR 72.8 vs 67.2 matched (THINKER); 6-month median eGFR 57 (MYTHIC). Deaths: one, from sepsis 4 months after cure (MYTHIC). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — non-randomised evidence, flagged for personal review.
cards.watchOut: Both trials required informed recipients, assured antiviral access, and intensive early monitoring; where any of those is missing, the 100% cure figure should not be assumed. Neither trial randomised against waiting for an HCV-negative kidney — the true comparator — so the benefit is framed as access and time, which the records support, rather than survival, which they do not measure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Reese PP et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30083748); Sise ME et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2020 (PMID: 32843477).

shelves.title: Imlifidase for highly sensitised transplant candidates: 89.5% of positive crossmatches turned negative within 24 hours — and 38.9% then had early antibody-mediated rejection
shelves.question: In highly sensitised patients awaiting kidney transplantation, does imlifidase enable transplantation and improve graft outcomes compared with remaining on dialysis or conventional desensitisation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bacterial Proteins/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Desensitization, Immunologic/methods · Female · Graft Rejection · Graft Survival · Histocompatibility Testing · Humans · Isoantibodies/blood · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Tissue Donors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — imlifidase unquestionably does the thing it is designed to do, for about a day; what happens next is the honest uncertainty. In the international phase 2 Highdes trial, imlifidase converted a positive crossmatch to negative within 24 hours in 89.5% of transplanted, highly sensitised patients (median calculated panel-reactive antibody 99.83%), enabling transplantation that conventional desensitisation could not offer; patient survival was 100% and graft survival 88.9% at 6 months — but donor-specific antibodies rebounded at 3–14 days and 38.9% developed early biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection. In the first French real-world series of 9 deceased-donor recipients (cPRA 99–100%, on dialysis a mean of 123 months), all crossmatches turned negative after one injection, five patients had antibody rebound within 14 days (four with clinical or subclinical rejection), and eGFR at about 7 months was 56 ± 22 mL/min/1.73 m² with no graft loss or death. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): imlifidase opens a transplant window for patients with essentially no other route to a deceased-donor kidney; comparative outcomes against remaining on dialysis are untested in any controlled design, and early rejection is the rule's price, not its exception.

cards.headline: Highdes phase 2 (Jordan 2021): crossmatch converted in 89.5% within 24 hours; graft survival 88.9% at 6 months; early rejection 38.9%
cards.summary: Highdes phase 2 (Jordan 2021): crossmatch converted in 89.5% within 24 hours; graft survival 88.9% at 6 months; early rejection 38.9%
cards.people: Highly sensitised kidney transplant candidates with a positive crossmatch against a living or deceased donor at five transplant centres, treated with imlifidase to create a negative crossmatch within 24 hours; median calculated panel-reactive antibody among transplanted patients was 99.83%.
cards.result: Of the transplanted patients, 89.5% demonstrated conversion of baseline positive crossmatch to negative within 24 hours of imlifidase. Donor-specific antibodies most often rebounded 3–14 days post-dose, with substantial interpatient variability. Patient survival was 100% and graft survival 88.9% at 6 months; 38.9% had early biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection with onset 2–19 days post-transplant. Serum IgG began to normalise after about 3–7 days. Seven adverse events in 6 patients were classified as possibly or probably treatment-related and were mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, small, and six months long: there is no 'remaining on dialysis' or 'conventional desensitisation' comparator anywhere in this evidence, so the benefit claim is mechanistic (a window opened) rather than comparative (outcomes improved). The 38.9% early rejection rate is part of the intervention's real cost, not a footnote.
cards.source: Jordan SC et al. Imlifidase Desensitization in Crossmatch-positive, Highly Sensitized Kidney Transplant Recipients: Results of an International Phase 2 Trial (Highdes). Transplantation. 2021. PMID: 33093408. Registry ID: NCT02790437. cards.headline: Kamar 2024 real-world series: 9/9 deceased-donor crossmatches negatived; 5 antibody rebounds, 4 with rejection; eGFR 56 ± 22 at ~7 months; no graft loss
cards.summary: Kamar 2024 real-world series: 9/9 deceased-donor crossmatches negatived; 5 antibody rebounds, 4 with rejection; eGFR 56 ± 22 at ~7 months; no graft loss
cards.people: The first 9 highly sensitised patients transplanted with a deceased donor after imlifidase in France (cPRA ≥98%, at least 3 years on the waiting list — mean dialysis duration 123 ± 41 months; cPRA 99% in 2 and 100% in 7), all receiving polyclonal antibodies, IVIG, rituximab, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate alongside.
cards.result: Before imlifidase, flow-cytometry crossmatch was positive in all 9 and complement-dependent cytotoxic crossmatch in 2; after one injection, all were negative. Five patients had donor-specific antibody rebound within 14 days: two with concomitant clinical antibody-mediated rejection, two with subclinical rejection, and one with isolated C4d staining; no rejection occurred without rebound. eGFR at last follow-up (7 ± 2.8 months) was 56 ± 22 mL/min/1.73 m². No graft loss or death occurred; four patients developed at least one infection.
cards.watchOut: Nine patients, heavy protocolised co-therapy (rituximab, IVIG, polyclonal antibodies), and seven months of follow-up — this series shows the strategy is deliverable outside a trial, and its rejection pattern matches the trial's; it adds no comparative information. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Kamar N et al. Imlifidase in Highly Sensitized Kidney Transplant Recipients With a Positive Crossmatch Against a Deceased Donor. Kidney international reports. 2024. PMID: 39430184. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Clazakizumab for chronic antibody-mediated rejection: the phase 3 IMAGINE trial was stopped for futility — eGFR fell 8.0 points on drug vs 5.2 on placebo
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, does the anti-interleukin-6 antibody clazakizumab slow the decline in kidney function compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a phase 2 promise that phase 3 dismantled. The phase 2 study (10 patients, open-label) had shown eGFR stabilising after clazakizumab (38.1 mL/min/1.73 m² at initiation, 41.6 at 12 months, 38.1 at 24 months) with falling donor-specific antibodies and biopsy inflammation scores — enough to launch IMAGINE, the largest placebo-controlled trial in chronic active antibody-mediated rejection. IMAGINE randomised kidney transplant recipients to clazakizumab 12.5 mg monthly or placebo; its one-year interim analysis (115 patients) showed the trial was unlikely to meet its primary outcome, and it was terminated early. In the final analysis (191 patients), eGFR change at week 52 was -8.0 mL/min/1.73 m² on clazakizumab versus -5.2 on placebo (P=0.959 as reported), and allograft loss or irreversible loss of function occurred in 28.3% versus 22.2% — numerically worse on drug, with no safety concerns and the expected fall in C-reactive protein. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): interleukin-6 blockade with clazakizumab does not slow kidney-function decline in chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, and this shelf stands as the library's record of a phase 2 signal that did not survive randomisation.

cards.headline: IMAGINE phase 3 (Djamali 2026): terminated for futility at interim; final eGFR change -8.0 vs -5.2 mL/min/1.73 m²; graft loss/irreversible loss 28.3% vs 22.2%
cards.summary: IMAGINE phase 3 (Djamali 2026): terminated for futility at interim; final eGFR change -8.0 vs -5.2 mL/min/1.73 m²; graft loss/irreversible loss 28.3% vs 22.2%
cards.people: Kidney transplant recipients with chronic active antibody-mediated rejection randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous clazakizumab 12.5 mg every 4 weeks or placebo; a one-year interim analysis included 115 patients, and the final analysis 191.
cards.result: The one-year interim analysis of eGFR (N=115) indicated the trial was unlikely to meet its primary outcome (time to all-cause allograft loss or irreversible loss of allograft function), resulting in early termination. In the final analysis (N=191), least-squares mean eGFR change to week 52 was -8.0 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI -10.2 to -5.8) on clazakizumab versus -5.2 (95% CI -7.4 to -3.1) on placebo (P=0.959 as reported in the record). Allograft loss or irreversible loss of function occurred in 28.3% on clazakizumab and 22.2% on placebo. C-reactive protein fell with treatment; no safety concerns were noted.
cards.watchOut: Early termination truncates follow-up, and the reported P value sits oddly beside the point estimates — both are reproduced as the record gives them. The substantive reading is unaffected: no endpoint favoured clazakizumab, and the trial's own futility analysis closed it. This record carries no MeSH terms and no registry identifier in its databank fields (the phase 2 record gives NCT03744910 for the programme).
cards.source: Djamali A et al. Clazakizumab in the treatment of chronic active antibody-mediated kidney transplant rejection: Results from the IMAGINE phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. American journal of transplantation : official journal of the American Society of Transplantation and the American Society of Transplant Surgeons. 2026. PMID: 42035994. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Jordan 2022): in 10 patients, eGFR stabilised (38.1 → 41.6 at 12 months) and antibodies fell — the signal IMAGINE was built to test
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Jordan 2022): in 10 patients, eGFR stabilised (38.1 → 41.6 at 12 months) and antibodies fell — the signal IMAGINE was built to test
cards.people: 10 adults with biopsy-proven, treatment-resistant chronic active antibody-mediated rejection at a single centre, treated with clazakizumab 25 mg subcutaneously monthly for 12 months with a 6-month protocol biopsy, stable patients entering a long-term extension beyond 2.5 years.
cards.result: Mean eGFR had fallen significantly in the 24 months before enrolment (52.8 ± 14.6 to 38.11 ± 12.23 mL/min/1.73 m²; P=0.03) and then stabilised on treatment (41.6 ± 14.2 at 12 months and 38.1 ± 20.3 at 24 months). Biopsy g+ptc and C4d scores fell, and donor-specific antibodies fell in most patients. Adverse events were minimal; two graft losses occurred, both in patients who had discontinued clazakizumab at 6 and 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Ten uncontrolled patients, enrolled at a moment of decline — regression to the mean and survivor selection can manufacture exactly this picture, and did: the randomised trial is the correction. This card is retained so the shelf shows why IMAGINE was run, not as evidence of effect.
cards.source: Jordan SC et al. Evaluation of Clazakizumab (Anti-Interleukin-6) in Patients With Treatment-Resistant Chronic Active Antibody-Mediated Rejection of Kidney Allografts. Kidney international reports. 2022. PMID: 35497778. Registry ID: NCT03744910. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: IL-6 blockade lowered CRP and antibodies, and changed nothing the graft could feel
cards.summary: Synthesis: IL-6 blockade lowered CRP and antibodies, and changed nothing the graft could feel
cards.people: One terminated-for-futility phase 3 RCT (191 patients in final analysis) and the 10-patient single-arm phase 2 study that motivated it, of monthly clazakizumab in chronic active antibody-mediated rejection after kidney transplantation.
cards.result: Phase 3: eGFR change at week 52 -8.0 vs -5.2 mL/min/1.73 m²; allograft loss or irreversible loss 28.3% vs 22.2%; trial stopped at interim for futility. Phase 2: eGFR stabilisation and antibody reduction in 10 uncontrolled patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The verdict is specific to clazakizumab at 12.5 mg monthly in established chronic active AMR; it does not adjudicate IL-6 blockade earlier in the rejection course or other agents in this class, none of which are carded here. Tier C is not set: the claim is a null carried by a randomised phase 3 trial.

shelves.title: Rituximab added to IVIG for desensitisation: the one randomised trial stopped early at 15 patients — rejection episodes clustered in the IVIG-only arm, but nothing was significant
shelves.question: In sensitised kidney transplant candidates, does rituximab plus intravenous immunoglobulin reduce panel-reactive antibodies and improve transplantation rates compared with immunoglobulin alone?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Desensitization, Immunologic/methods · Drug Combinations · Female · Graft Rejection · HLA Antigens/immunology · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Isoantibodies/blood · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects · Male · Rituximab · Tissue Donors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the randomised evidence for adding rituximab to IVIG is one small trial that was stopped early. Vo AA et al. (PMID: 24770617) randomised 15 highly HLA-sensitised deceased-donor candidates to IVIG plus rituximab or IVIG plus placebo; 13 received transplants, but entry was discontinued after five serious adverse events. No significant difference was seen in donor-specific antibody levels at transplant, and all antibody-mediated rejection episodes occurred in the IVIG-plus-placebo arm (P=0.06), with the two graft losses also in the placebo group; renal function at 6 and 12 months favoured IVIG plus rituximab (P=0.04). The systematic review by Macklin PS et al. (PMID: 25321163) found only two randomised trials among 21 studies of rituximab desensitisation and concluded the evidence in highly sensitised recipients was of limited quality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): rituximab added to IVIG may prevent antibody rebound and rejection after desensitisation, but the claim rests on a single stopped-early trial of 15 patients.

cards.headline: Vo 2014: 15 sensitised candidates randomised, trial stopped after five serious adverse events — all rejection episodes in the IVIG-plus-placebo arm (P=0.06), no significant antibody difference
cards.summary: Vo 2014: 15 sensitised candidates randomised, trial stopped after five serious adverse events — all rejection episodes in the IVIG-plus-placebo arm (P=0.06), no significant antibody difference
cards.people: 15 highly HLA-sensitised deceased-donor kidney transplant candidates randomised to IVIG plus rituximab or IVIG plus placebo (7 IVIG plus placebo, 6 IVIG plus rituximab among those transplanted); 13 received transplants. Study entry was discontinued after five serious adverse events were observed and the study was unblinded.
cards.result: No significant differences were seen in donor-specific HLA antibody levels at transplant. All antibody-mediated rejection episodes occurred in the IVIG-plus-placebo arm and required intense therapy (P=0.06). The two graft losses were in the placebo group. Donor-specific antibody rebound with severe antibody-mediated rejection was seen in three patients in the IVIG-plus-placebo group and in none of the IVIG-plus-rituximab group. Renal function at 6 and 12 months showed a significant benefit for IVIG plus rituximab (P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: Fifteen randomised patients, entry stopped early for serious adverse events, and unblinding mid-trial: every effect here is a handful of events, and the headline comparisons (P=0.06) did not reach significance. Transplantation rates themselves were not shown to differ.
cards.source: Vo AA et al. Benefits of rituximab combined with intravenous immunoglobulin for desensitization in kidney transplant recipients. Transplantation. 2014. PMID: 24770617.
