cards.headline: Macklin 2014 systematic review: 21 studies of rituximab desensitisation, only two randomised — evidence in highly sensitised recipients judged limited quality
cards.summary: Macklin 2014 systematic review: 21 studies of rituximab desensitisation, only two randomised — evidence in highly sensitised recipients judged limited quality
cards.people: 45 records relating to 21 individual studies (two randomised controlled trials and 19 retrospective cohort studies) of rituximab for desensitisation in ABO-incompatible and highly sensitised renal transplant recipients; a lack of randomised evidence precluded meta-analysis.
cards.result: In ABO-incompatible patients, most studies found no significant differences in patient and graft outcomes for rituximab versus (most often) splenectomy-based protocols. Nine studies of limited quality in highly sensitised recipients demonstrated some benefits in graft survival, acute and chronic rejection, and sensitisation levels with rituximab. Two studies combining both populations found no statistically significant increase in infectious complications with rituximab.
cards.watchOut: Almost everything outside the one small trial is retrospective cohort data, where fitter patients get the newer protocol; the review itself calls for further randomised trials to define efficacy, long-term safety, and dosing.
cards.source: Macklin PS et al. A systematic review of the use of rituximab for desensitization in renal transplantation. Transplantation. 2014. PMID: 25321163. cards.headline: Synthesis: a biologically plausible add-on whose entire randomised base is 15 patients and a stopped trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: a biologically plausible add-on whose entire randomised base is 15 patients and a stopped trial
cards.people: One placebo-controlled randomised trial of 15 highly sensitised candidates (Vo 2014) plus a systematic review of 21 mostly retrospective studies (Macklin 2014).
cards.result: Antibody levels at transplant: no significant difference. Antibody-mediated rejection: all episodes in the IVIG-only arm (P=0.06); graft losses: two, both on IVIG alone; renal function at 6–12 months favoured adding rituximab (P=0.04). The trial was stopped after five serious adverse events. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small trial carries the benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: Desensitisation practice has largely adopted rituximab on cohort evidence; this shelf records how thin the randomised base is, not that the drug does not work. Panel-reactive antibody reduction — the question's first endpoint — was never significantly shown.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vo AA et al. Transplantation. 2014 (PMID: 24770617); Macklin PS et al. Transplantation. 2014 (PMID: 25321163).

shelves.title: Oxygenated machine perfusion of donor kidneys: fewer graft failures in DCD kidneys in one trial, no gain at all when added briefly before implantation in expanded-criteria kidneys in another
shelves.question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion reduce delayed graft function and improve graft survival compared with static cold storage or standard (non-oxygenated) perfusion?
shelves.mesh: Cold Temperature · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Preservation · Oxygen/physiology · Perfusion · Tissue Survival · Tissue and Organ Harvesting
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by how and in which kidneys the oxygen is given. In COMPARE (Jochmans I et al., PMID: 33220737), a paired double-blind phase 3 trial in kidneys donated after circulatory death, continuous oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion did not significantly improve the primary outcome — 12-month eGFR was 50.5 versus 46.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (mean difference 3.7, 95% CI -1.0 to 8.4; p=0.12) — but graft failure was lower (3 of 106 [3%] versus 11 of 106 [10%]; hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.95; p=0.028) and severe complications were fewer (11% versus 16%; p=0.032). In Husen P et al. (PMID: 33881456), short end-perfusion with oxygen after static cold storage in expanded-criteria brain-dead-donor kidneys changed nothing: 1-year graft survival was 92.1% versus 93.3% (P=.71), with no significant differences in delayed graft function, primary nonfunction, eGFR, or acute rejection. PROPOSED SPLIT: continuous oxygenation throughout preservation may protect DCD kidneys (secondary outcomes only, primary null); a brief oxygenated reconditioning at the end of cold storage does not help expanded-criteria kidneys.

cards.headline: Jochmans 2020 (COMPARE): 12-month eGFR 50.5 vs 46.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p=0.12, not significant) — but graft failure 3% vs 10% (HR 0.27) and severe complications 11% vs 16%
cards.summary: Jochmans 2020 (COMPARE): 12-month eGFR 50.5 vs 46.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p=0.12, not significant) — but graft failure 3% vs 10% (HR 0.27) and severe complications 11% vs 16%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind paired phase 3 trial (Jochmans 2020, COMPARE)
cards.people: Kidney pairs from donors aged 50 years or older donated after circulatory death at 19 European transplant centres: 197 pairs randomised, 106 pairs transplanted into eligible recipients; one kidney of each pair received oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion (HMPO2), the other standard hypothermic machine perfusion, from retrieval to implantation.
cards.result: Mean eGFR at 12 months was 50.5 mL/min per 1.73 m2 (SD 19.3) in the HMPO2 group versus 46.7 (17.1) in the HMP group (mean difference 3.7 mL/min per 1.73 m2, 95% CI -1.0 to 8.4; p=0.12) — the primary outcome was not significant. Fewer severe complications (Clavien-Dindo grade IIIb or more) were reported with HMPO2 (46 of 417, 11%, 95% CI 8% to 14%) than HMP (76 of 474, 16%, 13% to 20%; p=0.032). Graft failure was lower with HMPO2 (three [3%] of 106) compared with HMP (11 [10%] of 106; hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.95; p=0.028).
cards.watchOut: The graft-failure and complication benefits are secondary outcomes in a trial whose primary outcome was null, and 23 pairs were excluded from the primary analysis because of kidney failure or patient death — the very events the secondary analysis counts. Fourteen graft failures in total is a small base for a survival claim.
cards.source: Jochmans I et al. Oxygenated versus standard cold perfusion preservation in kidney transplantation (COMPARE): a randomised, double-blind, paired, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 33220737. Registry ID: ISRCTN32967929. cards.headline: Husen 2021: oxygenated end-perfusion after cold storage — 1-year graft survival 92.1% vs 93.3% (P=.71), and delayed graft function, eGFR and rejection all unchanged
cards.summary: Husen 2021: oxygenated end-perfusion after cold storage — 1-year graft survival 92.1% vs 93.3% (P=.71), and delayed graft function, eGFR and rejection all unchanged
cards.people: 305 kidneys from expanded criteria donors (brain-dead; median donor age 64 years, range 50–84) at centres in five European countries, randomised to static cold storage alone or cold storage followed by oxygenated end-hypothermic machine perfusion (minimum 120 minutes; median 4.7 hours) before implantation; 262 kidneys were successfully transplanted (127 end-perfusion, 135 cold storage).
cards.result: One-year graft survival was 92.1% (n=117) in the end-perfusion group versus 93.3% (n=126) in the cold-storage group (95% CI, -7.5 to 5.1; P=.71). The secondary endpoint analysis showed no significant between-group differences for delayed graft function, primary nonfunction, estimated glomerular filtration rate, and acute rejection.
cards.watchOut: The trial was single-blind and, by its authors' account, underpowered because overall graft survival was higher than expected; a null here does not exclude a small effect. But it is a direct randomised test of the add-oxygen-at-the-end strategy, and it found nothing on any endpoint.
cards.source: Husen P et al. Oxygenated End-Hypothermic Machine Perfusion in Expanded Criteria Donor Kidney Transplant: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Surgery. 2021. PMID: 33881456. Registry ID: ISRCTN63852508. cards.headline: Synthesis: oxygen throughout preservation in DCD kidneys looks protective on secondary outcomes; oxygen only at the end, in ECD kidneys, does nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: oxygen throughout preservation in DCD kidneys looks protective on secondary outcomes; oxygen only at the end, in ECD kidneys, does nothing
cards.people: Two European randomised trials: COMPARE (106 transplanted DCD kidney pairs, oxygenated vs standard perfusion throughout) and Husen 2021 (262 transplanted expanded-criteria kidneys, brief oxygenated end-perfusion vs cold storage alone).
cards.result: COMPARE primary outcome (12-month eGFR): 50.5 vs 46.7 mL/min/1.73 m2, p=0.12. COMPARE graft failure: 3% vs 10% (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.95). Husen 1-year graft survival: 92.1% vs 93.3% (P=.71), delayed graft function not significantly different. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C flagged because the positive half rests on secondary outcomes of a single trial.
cards.watchOut: The two trials differ in donor type, timing, and comparator, so the split may reflect those differences rather than oxygen itself; neither trial showed a significant delayed-graft-function benefit in its record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jochmans I et al. Lancet. 2020 (PMID: 33220737); Husen P et al. JAMA Surgery. 2021 (PMID: 33881456).

shelves.title: Everolimus with reduced-dose calcineurin inhibitor: noninferior to mycophenolate with standard-dose CNI at 12 and 24 months — fewer viral infections, far more patients stopping the drug
shelves.question: In de novo kidney transplant recipients, does everolimus with reduced-dose calcineurin inhibitor preserve kidney function without more rejection than mycophenolate with standard-dose calcineurin inhibitor?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Adult · Allografts/physiopathology · Calcineurin Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Cyclosporine/therapeutic use · Cytomegalovirus Infections/etiology · Everolimus/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection/etiology/pathology · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy/methods · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/therapeutic use · Polyomavirus Infections/etiology · Tacrolimus/therapeutic use · Tumor Virus Infections/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the TRANSFORM trial (Pascual J et al., PMID: 29752413), 2,037 de novo kidney transplant recipients were randomised to everolimus with reduced-exposure calcineurin inhibitor or mycophenolic acid with standard-exposure CNI. The primary endpoint (treated biopsy-proven acute rejection or eGFR below 50 mL/min/1.73 m2 at month 12) occurred in 48.2% versus 45.1% (difference 3.2%; 95% CI, -1.3% to 7.6%), meeting the 10% noninferiority margin. Cytomegalovirus (3.6% versus 13.3%) and BK virus infections (4.3% versus 8.0%) were less frequent with everolimus, but 23.0% versus 11.9% discontinued the study drug for adverse events. At 24 months (Berger SP et al., PMID: 31152476), noninferiority held (47.9% versus 43.7%; difference 4.2%; 95% CI -0.3 to 8.7), mean eGFR was 52.6 versus 54.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, and discontinuation for adverse events had risen to 27.2% versus 15.0%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): everolimus with reduced CNI exposure matches mycophenolate with standard CNI on efficacy and graft function for two years, trading fewer viral infections for roughly double the drug discontinuations.

cards.headline: Pascual 2018 (TRANSFORM, 12 months): primary endpoint 48.2% vs 45.1% — noninferior; CMV 3.6% vs 13.3%, but drug stopped for adverse events in 23.0% vs 11.9%
cards.summary: Pascual 2018 (TRANSFORM, 12 months): primary endpoint 48.2% vs 45.1% — noninferior; CMV 3.6% vs 13.3%, but drug stopped for adverse events in 23.0% vs 11.9%
cards.people: 2,037 de novo kidney transplant recipients at mild-to-moderate immunologic risk (everolimus arm n=1,022; mycophenolic acid arm n=1,015), randomised with induction therapy and corticosteroids to everolimus with reduced-exposure calcineurin inhibitor or mycophenolic acid with standard-exposure CNI, followed to post-transplant month 12.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — treated biopsy-proven acute rejection or eGFR <50 ml/min per 1.73 m2 at month 12 — occurred in 48.2% (493) with everolimus and 45.1% (457) with mycophenolic acid (difference 3.2%; 95% CI, -1.3% to 7.6%), within the 10% noninferiority margin. Treated biopsy-proven acute rejection, graft loss, or death occurred in 14.9% versus 12.5% (difference 2.3%; 95% CI, -1.7% to 6.4%). De novo donor-specific antibody incidence and antibody-mediated rejection did not differ. Cytomegalovirus (3.6% versus 13.3%) and BK virus infections (4.3% versus 8.0%) were less frequent with everolimus; 23.0% versus 11.9% discontinued the study drug because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against a 10% margin on a composite that is mostly the eGFR<50 component is a generous bar, and the trial was open-label; the near-quarter of everolimus patients who stopped the drug limit what 'the regimen' delivered in practice.
cards.source: Pascual J et al. Everolimus with Reduced Calcineurin Inhibitor Exposure in Renal Transplantation. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2018. PMID: 29752413. Registry ID: NCT01950819. cards.headline: Berger 2019 (TRANSFORM, 24 months): noninferiority held (47.9% vs 43.7%), eGFR 52.6 vs 54.9, de novo donor-specific antibodies lower on-treatment (12.3% vs 17.6%)
cards.summary: Berger 2019 (TRANSFORM, 24 months): noninferiority held (47.9% vs 43.7%), eGFR 52.6 vs 54.9, de novo donor-specific antibodies lower on-treatment (12.3% vs 17.6%)
cards.people: The same 2,037 de novo renal transplant recipients randomised in TRANSFORM to everolimus with reduced-exposure CNI or mycophenolate with standard-exposure CNI, followed prospectively to month 24 (open-label).
cards.result: Noninferiority of the everolimus regimen for treated biopsy-proven acute rejection or eGFR <50 mL/min per 1.73 m2 was achieved at month 24 (47.9% vs 43.7%; difference 4.2%; 95% CI -0.3 to 8.7; P=.006 for noninferiority). Mean eGFR was stable to month 24 (52.6 vs 54.9 mL/min per 1.73 m2). De novo donor-specific antibody incidence was lower with everolimus among on-treatment patients (12.3% vs 17.6%). Discontinuation due to adverse events was higher with everolimus (27.2% vs 15.0%), while cytomegalovirus (2.8% vs 13.5%) and BK virus (5.8% vs 10.3%) infections remained lower.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same single trial, not an independent replication; the on-treatment donor-specific antibody comparison excludes the many patients who had already stopped everolimus, flattering the arm with the higher dropout.

cards.headline: Synthesis: equal efficacy and graft function for two years, fewer viral infections, about double the discontinuations — a trade, not an advance
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal efficacy and graft function for two years, fewer viral infections, about double the discontinuations — a trade, not an advance
cards.people: One large randomised noninferiority trial programme (TRANSFORM, 2,037 recipients) reported at 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: Primary composite: 48.2% vs 45.1% at 12 months and 47.9% vs 43.7% at 24 months, both noninferior. eGFR at 24 months: 52.6 vs 54.9 mL/min/1.73 m2. CMV infection: 3.6% vs 13.3% at 12 months. Discontinuation for adverse events: 23.0% vs 11.9% at 12 months, 27.2% vs 15.0% at 24 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C flagged: the shelf rests on a single (very large) trial programme.
cards.watchOut: No second trial of this exact comparison exists in the record set; TRANSFORM's size is its strength and its singularity is the caveat. Results apply to mild-to-moderate immunologic risk recipients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pascual J et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2018 (PMID: 29752413); Berger SP et al. American Journal of Transplantation. 2019 (PMID: 31152476).

shelves.title: Esaxerenone on top of RAS blockade: albuminuria remission 22% versus 4% at one year in phase 3, dose-dependent albuminuria cuts in phase 2 — potassium the price
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with albuminuric kidney disease, does the mineralocorticoid antagonist esaxerenone reduce albuminuria compared with placebo on top of RAS blockade?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albuminuria/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Biomarkers/urine · Creatinine/urine · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/diagnosis · Female · Humans · Japan · Kidney/drug effects/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrroles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Remission Induction · Risk Factors · Sulfones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for albuminuria, a surrogate, in Japanese trial populations. In the phase 3 ESAX-DN trial (Ito S et al., PMID: 33239409), 455 patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria on RAS inhibitors were randomised to esaxerenone or placebo for 52 weeks: albuminuria remission was achieved by 22% versus 4% (absolute difference 18%; 95% CI, 12% to 25%; P<0.001), and the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio changed by -58% versus +8% (ratio to placebo 0.38, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.44). The earlier phase 2 trial (Ito S et al., PMID: 31248950) found dose-dependent reductions at 12 weeks — 38%, 50%, and 56% at 1.25, 2.5, and 5 mg/day versus 7% on placebo (all P<0.001). The harm is potassium: in phase 3, a serum potassium of at least 5.5–6.0 mEq/L on two consecutive measurements occurred in 9% on esaxerenone versus 2% on placebo, asymptomatic and resolving with dose reduction or discontinuation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): esaxerenone reliably and substantially reduces albuminuria on top of RAS blockade; no trial here measured kidney failure or cardiovascular outcomes.

cards.headline: Ito 2020 (ESAX-DN, phase 3): albuminuria remission 22% vs 4% at 52 weeks; UACR -58% vs +8%; potassium ≥5.5–6.0 on repeat testing in 9% vs 2%
cards.summary: Ito 2020 (ESAX-DN, phase 3): albuminuria remission 22% vs 4% at 52 weeks; UACR -58% vs +8%; potassium ≥5.5–6.0 on repeat testing in 9% vs 2%
cards.people: 455 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria (urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 45 to <300 mg/g creatinine) treated with renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, randomised to esaxerenone (started 1.25 mg/day, titrated to 2.5 mg/day on potassium monitoring) or placebo for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Albuminuria remission (UACR <30 mg/g creatinine and at least 30% reduction on two consecutive occasions) was achieved by 49 (22%) on esaxerenone and nine (4%) on placebo (absolute difference 18%; 95% CI, 12% to 25%; P<0.001). Percent change in UACR to end of treatment was -58% versus +8% (geometric least-squares mean ratio to placebo 0.38, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.44). Time to first remission favoured esaxerenone (hazard ratio 5.13; 95% CI 3.27 to 8.04), as did time to transition to UACR at least 300 mg/g (hazard ratio 0.23; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.48). Serum potassium at least 6.0, or at least 5.5 mEq/L on two consecutive measurements, occurred in 20 (9%) on esaxerenone versus five (2%) on placebo; events were asymptomatic and resolved after dose reduction or discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is albuminuria — a surrogate — over one year, in a single-country population with microalbuminuria (not advanced CKD); whether the albuminuria effect converts into slower kidney failure is untested for this drug.
cards.source: Ito S et al. Esaxerenone (CS-3150) in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes and Microalbuminuria (ESAX-DN): Phase 3 Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2020. PMID: 33239409. cards.headline: Ito 2019 (phase 2): UACR fell 38%, 50% and 56% at 1.25, 2.5 and 5 mg/day versus 7% on placebo at 12 weeks — hyperkalaemia dose-proportional
cards.summary: Ito 2019 (phase 2): UACR fell 38%, 50% and 56% at 1.25, 2.5 and 5 mg/day versus 7% on placebo at 12 weeks — hyperkalaemia dose-proportional
cards.people: 365 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria (UACR at least 45 to <300 mg/g creatinine), eGFR at least 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2, on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, randomised to esaxerenone 0.625, 1.25, 2.5, or 5 mg/day or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Esaxerenone at 1.25, 2.5, and 5 mg/day reduced UACR by 38%, 50%, and 56% respectively versus 7% on placebo (all P<0.001). UACR remission was 21% in the 2.5- and 5-mg/day groups versus 3% on placebo (both P<0.05). The most common drug-related adverse event was hyperkalaemia, which was dose proportional; drug-related adverse events and discontinuations were marginally higher at 5 mg/day.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is short, and the top dose's extra albuminuria effect came with the most hyperkalaemia — the phase 3 programme settled on 2.5 mg/day for a reason.
cards.source: Ito S et al. Efficacy and Safety of Esaxerenone (CS-3150) for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes with Microalbuminuria: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Phase II Trial. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2019. PMID: 31248950. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — a large, dose-dependent albuminuria effect with a real potassium cost and no hard-outcome data
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — a large, dose-dependent albuminuria effect with a real potassium cost and no hard-outcome data
cards.people: Phase 2 (365 patients, 12 weeks, dose-ranging) and phase 3 ESAX-DN (455 patients, 52 weeks) randomised double-blind trials of esaxerenone added to RAS blockade in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria.
cards.result: Phase 3 remission: 22% vs 4% (difference 18%; 95% CI 12% to 25%). Phase 3 UACR change: -58% vs +8%. Phase 2 UACR reductions: 38–56% across 1.25–5 mg/day vs 7% placebo. Potassium signal: 9% vs 2% reaching at least 5.5–6.0 mEq/L twice in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the (surrogate) claim.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from one development programme in one country; esaxerenone is marketed in Japan and not FDA-approved, and no outcomes trial (kidney failure, cardiovascular events, death) is in this record set.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ito S et al. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2020 (PMID: 33239409); Ito S et al. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2019 (PMID: 31248950).

shelves.title: Eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor: albuminuria down 41–48% versus 7% on ACE inhibitor alone at 12 weeks — the class review confirms the proteinuria effect and doubles hyperkalaemia
shelves.question: In diabetic kidney disease, does eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor reduce albuminuria compared with ACE inhibitor alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albuminuria/blood/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Creatinine/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enalapril/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Eplerenone · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Hyperkalemia/blood/epidemiology/etiology · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Potassium/blood · Spironolactone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for albuminuria, over 12 weeks, in the one diabetes-specific randomised trial. Epstein M et al. (PMID: 17699311) randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria, all on enalapril, to added eplerenone 50 mg, eplerenone 100 mg, or placebo: at week 12 the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio had fallen by 41.0% and 48.4% on eplerenone versus 7.4% on placebo (both P<0.001 versus placebo), with significant reductions already at week 4, and incidences of sustained and severe hyperkalaemia not significantly different between arms. The Cochrane review by Chung EY et al. (PMID: 33107592), covering 44 studies and 5,745 participants with proteinuric CKD, found aldosterone antagonists added to ACE inhibitor or ARB may reduce protein excretion (standardised mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.20) but probably increase hyperkalaemia (risk ratio 2.17, 95% CI 1.47 to 3.22) and acute kidney injury (risk ratio 2.04, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.97), with effects on kidney failure, death, and cardiovascular events uncertain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor reduces albuminuria substantially in the short term; the class price is potassium and kidney-function monitoring, and no hard-outcome benefit is established.

cards.headline: Epstein 2006: UACR -41.0% on eplerenone 50 mg and -48.4% on 100 mg versus -7.4% on placebo, all on enalapril (both P<0.001) at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Epstein 2006: UACR -41.0% on eplerenone 50 mg and -48.4% on 100 mg versus -7.4% on placebo, all on enalapril (both P<0.001) at 12 weeks
cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes and a urinary albumin:creatinine ratio of at least 50 mg/g, after open-label run-in on enalapril 20 mg/day, randomised to enalapril plus placebo, eplerenone 50 mg, or eplerenone 100 mg daily for 12 weeks (amlodipine allowed from week 4 for blood-pressure control).
cards.result: By week 12, UACR was reduced by 7.4% in the placebo group, by 41.0% in the eplerenone 50 mg group, and by 48.4% in the eplerenone 100 mg group (both eplerenone groups P<0.001 versus placebo). Both eplerenone groups significantly reduced albuminuria from baseline as early as week 4 (P<0.001), whereas placebo (enalapril alone) did not significantly reduce UACR at any point. The incidences of sustained and severe hyperkalaemia were not significantly different in any of the three treatment arms. Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly in all groups, generally similarly.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a urine surrogate; the trial was sized for albuminuria, not for hyperkalaemia events or kidney outcomes, so 'no significant difference' in potassium is a small-sample statement — the class-level review below finds the potassium risk is real.
cards.source: Epstein M et al. Selective aldosterone blockade with eplerenone reduces albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2006. PMID: 17699311. cards.headline: Chung 2020 (Cochrane): aldosterone antagonists on top of ACEi/ARB — protein excretion SMD -0.51, hyperkalaemia RR 2.17, acute kidney injury RR 2.04; kidney failure and death effects uncertain
cards.summary: Chung 2020 (Cochrane): aldosterone antagonists on top of ACEi/ARB — protein excretion SMD -0.51, hyperkalaemia RR 2.17, acute kidney injury RR 2.04; kidney failure and death effects uncertain
cards.people: 44 randomised studies (5,745 participants) of aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, canrenone, eplerenone, finerenone) added to ACE inhibitor or ARB in adults with proteinuric chronic kidney disease, searched to 13 January 2020.
cards.result: Compared with placebo or standard care, aldosterone antagonists may reduce protein excretion (14 studies, 1,193 participants: standardised mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.20; very low certainty) and systolic blood pressure (mean difference -4.98 mmHg, 95% CI -8.22 to -1.75), and probably increase hyperkalaemia (17 studies, 3,001 participants: risk ratio 2.17, 95% CI 1.47 to 3.22; moderate certainty) and acute kidney injury (5 studies, 1,446 participants: risk ratio 2.04, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.97). Effects on kidney failure (risk ratio 3.00, 95% CI 0.33 to 27.65; very low certainty), death (risk ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.10 to 3.50; low certainty), and cardiovascular events (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.26 to 3.56) were uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The review pools the whole aldosterone-antagonist class across proteinuric CKD, not eplerenone in diabetes specifically, and most included studies were at unclear or high risk of bias; the proteinuria estimate has very low certainty despite the precise-looking interval.
cards.source: Chung EY et al. Aldosterone antagonists in addition to renin angiotensin system antagonists for preventing the progression of chronic kidney disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 33107592. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, quick albuminuria effect on top of ACE inhibition — bought with the class's potassium and kidney-injury risks, hard outcomes unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, quick albuminuria effect on top of ACE inhibition — bought with the class's potassium and kidney-injury risks, hard outcomes unknown
cards.people: One diabetes-specific randomised trial of eplerenone added to enalapril (Epstein 2006, 12 weeks) read with the 44-study Cochrane review of aldosterone antagonists added to RAS blockade in proteinuric CKD (5,745 participants).
cards.result: UACR at 12 weeks: -41.0% (50 mg) and -48.4% (100 mg) vs -7.4% on ACE inhibitor alone. Class protein excretion: standardised mean difference -0.51 (95% CI -0.82 to -0.20). Class hyperkalaemia: risk ratio 2.17 (95% CI 1.47 to 3.22); acute kidney injury risk ratio 2.04 (95% CI 1.05 to 3.97). Kidney failure, death, cardiovascular events: uncertain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for albuminuria, Tier C not set: a randomised trial plus a large class review carry the claim.

shelves.question: In chronic kidney disease with albuminuria, does the aldosterone synthase inhibitor BI 690517, alone or with empagliflozin, reduce albuminuria compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Benzhydryl Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cytochrome P-450 CYP11B2 · Double-Blind Method · Glucosides/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hyperkalemia · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2 trial, 14 weeks, a urine surrogate. Tuttle KR et al. (PMID: 38109916) randomised 586 people with CKD (eGFR 30 to <90 mL/min/1.73 m2, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 200 to <5,000 mg/g, potassium at most 4.8 mmol/L, all on an ACE inhibitor or ARB) to BI 690517 3, 10, or 20 mg or placebo, after an empagliflozin-or-placebo run-in. Percentage change in first-morning UACR at week 14 was -3% (95% CI -19 to 17) on placebo, -22% (-36 to -7) on 3 mg, -39% (-50 to -26) on 10 mg, and -37% (-49 to -22) on 20 mg monotherapy, with similar reductions when BI 690517 was added to empagliflozin. Investigator-reported hyperkalaemia occurred in 10% (3 mg), 15% (10 mg), and 18% (20 mg) versus 6% on placebo, though 86% of affected participants needed no intervention; adrenal insufficiency was reported in 2% on BI 690517 versus 1% on placebo, and there were no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BI 690517 dose-dependently reduces albuminuria over 14 weeks, alone or with empagliflozin; this is a single short phase 2 trial and no kidney-outcome data exist yet.

cards.headline: Tuttle 2024: UACR change at week 14: -3% placebo, -22% (3 mg), -39% (10 mg), -37% (20 mg); hyperkalaemia 10–18% across doses vs 6% on placebo
cards.summary: Tuttle 2024: UACR change at week 14: -3% placebo, -22% (3 mg), -39% (10 mg), -37% (20 mg); hyperkalaemia 10–18% across doses vs 6% on placebo
cards.people: 586 participants (of 714 entering run-in) aged 18 or older with eGFR 30 to <90 mL/min/1.73 m2, UACR 200 to <5,000 mg/g, serum potassium at most 4.8 mmol/L, on an ACE inhibitor or ARB; after 8 weeks of empagliflozin or placebo run-in, randomised to 14 weeks of BI 690517 3, 10, or 20 mg once daily or placebo. Mean age 63.8 years, mean eGFR 51.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, median UACR 426 mg/g.
cards.result: Percentage change in first-morning-void UACR from second randomisation to week 14 was -3% (95% CI -19 to 17) with placebo, -22% (-36 to -7) with BI 690517 3 mg, -39% (-50 to -26) with 10 mg, and -37% (-49 to -22) with 20 mg monotherapy; BI 690517 produced similar UACR reductions when added to empagliflozin. Investigator-reported hyperkalaemia occurred in 10% (14/146) at 3 mg, 15% (22/144) at 10 mg, and 18% (26/146) at 20 mg, versus 6% (9/147) on placebo (with or without empagliflozin); most participants with hyperkalaemia did not require intervention (86%, 72/84). Adrenal insufficiency was reported in seven of 436 (2%) on BI 690517 and one of 147 (1%) on placebo. No treatment-related deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen weeks, a surrogate endpoint, and a potassium-selected population (entry required potassium at most 4.8 mmol/L) — the hyperkalaemia rates would plausibly be higher in unselected CKD. A single phase 2 trial from one development programme.

shelves.title: Empagliflozin in stone formers (SWEETSTONE): calcium-phosphate supersaturation down 36% in calcium stone formers and uric-acid supersaturation down 30% in uric-acid stone formers — calcium-oxalate supersaturation unmoved
shelves.question: In patients with calcium kidney stones, does empagliflozin reduce urinary supersaturation for calcium stones compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Benzhydryl Compounds/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Glucosides/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Kidney Calculi/drug therapy/urine · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Uric Acid/urine/metabolism · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Calcium · Calcium Oxalate/urine · Cross-Over Studies · Calcium Phosphates/urine
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the effect splits by stone chemistry, and it is a two-week urine-chemistry effect, not a stone-prevention result. In the SWEETSTONE trial (Anderegg MA et al., PMID: 39747681), 53 non-diabetic adults with calcium (n=28) or uric acid (n=25) stones were randomised in a double-blind crossover to empagliflozin 25 mg daily and placebo, two weeks each. In calcium stone formers, empagliflozin reduced the relative supersaturation ratio for calcium phosphate (relative difference to placebo -36%; 95% CI -48% to -21%; P<0.001) but not for calcium oxalate or uric acid. In uric acid stone formers, it reduced the uric-acid supersaturation ratio (-30%; 95% CI -44% to -12%; P=0.002) but not the calcium-oxalate or calcium-phosphate ratios. No serious or prespecified adverse events occurred. PROPOSED SPLIT: empagliflozin lowers the supersaturation that drives calcium-phosphate stones (in calcium formers) and uric-acid stones (in uric-acid formers), but leaves calcium-oxalate supersaturation — the commonest stone chemistry — unchanged; whether any of this prevents actual stones is untested.

cards.headline: Anderegg 2025 (SWEETSTONE): RSR calcium phosphate -36% relative vs placebo in calcium formers (P<0.001); RSR uric acid -30% relative in uric-acid formers (P=0.002); RSR calcium oxalate unchanged in both
cards.summary: Anderegg 2025 (SWEETSTONE): RSR calcium phosphate -36% relative vs placebo in calcium formers (P<0.001); RSR uric acid -30% relative in uric-acid formers (P=0.002); RSR calcium oxalate unchanged in both
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover phase 2 trial (Anderegg 2025, SWEETSTONE)
cards.people: 53 non-diabetic adults (at least 18 and under 75 years; HbA1c below 6.5%, no diabetes treatment) with calcium (n=28) or uric acid (n=25) kidney stones and at least one previous stone event, at a single centre, randomised to empagliflozin 25 mg once daily followed by placebo or the reverse, two weeks per treatment; primary analyses in the per-protocol set, performed separately by stone type.
cards.result: Prespecified relative supersaturation ratio (RSR) reductions of at least 15% were met in both stone-former groups. In calcium stone formers, empagliflozin reduced RSR for calcium phosphate (relative difference to placebo -36%; 95% CI -48% to -21%; P<0.001) but not RSRs for calcium oxalate or uric acid. In uric acid stone formers, empagliflozin reduced RSR for uric acid (-30%; 95% CI -44% to -12%; P=0.002) but not RSRs for calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate. No serious or prespecified adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks of treatment and urine chemistry only: supersaturation ratios are validated surrogates, but the trial's own framing notes the risk categories did not necessarily change, and no stone events were or could be measured. The question asked about calcium stones — the calcium-oxalate ratio, the dominant calcium-stone chemistry, did not move.
cards.source: Anderegg MA et al. Empagliflozin in nondiabetic individuals with calcium and uric acid kidney stones: a randomized phase 2 trial. Nature Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39747681. shelves.title: Allopurinol for hyperuricosuric calcium stones (Ettinger 1986): stone events 0.12 versus 0.26 per patient-year — but the placebo group also improved by 63%, in the only randomised trial
shelves.question: In recurrent calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria, does allopurinol reduce stone recurrence compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/therapeutic use · Calcium Oxalate/metabolism · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kidney Calculi/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Random Allocation · Recurrence · Uric Acid/urine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small double-blind trial conducted in the 1980s. Ettinger B et al. (PMID: 3534570) randomised 60 patients with hyperuricosuria and normocalciuria and a history of calcium oxalate calculi to allopurinol 100 mg three times daily or placebo. During the study the mean rate of calculous events was 0.12 per patient per year on allopurinol versus 0.26 on placebo, and actuarial analysis showed a significantly longer time before recurrence on allopurinol (P<0.02). The caution is built into the record: compared with their pre-study rates, the placebo group had 63.4 percent fewer calculi (P<0.001) and the allopurinol group 81.2 percent fewer (P<0.001) — most of the apparent improvement happened on placebo too, the 'positive treatment bias' the authors themselves flag in stone-prophylaxis trials that use historical controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): allopurinol roughly halved the on-trial stone-event rate in hyperuricosuric calcium stone formers, on the strength of one 60-patient trial; the effect has never been re-tested in a modern randomised trial.

cards.headline: Ettinger 1986: calculous events 0.12 vs 0.26 per patient per year; time to recurrence significantly longer on allopurinol (P<0.02) — in 60 patients
cards.summary: Ettinger 1986: calculous events 0.12 vs 0.26 per patient per year; time to recurrence significantly longer on allopurinol (P<0.02) — in 60 patients
cards.people: 60 patients with hyperuricosuria and normocalciuria and a history of calcium oxalate kidney calculi, randomly assigned to allopurinol 100 mg three times daily or placebo, in a double-blind study.
cards.result: The mean rate of calculous events during the study was 0.26 per patient per year in the placebo group and 0.12 in the allopurinol group. By actuarial analysis, the allopurinol group had a significantly longer time before recurrence of calculi (P<0.02). Against pre-study rates, the placebo group had 63.4 percent fewer calculi (P<0.001) and the allopurinol group 81.2 percent fewer calculi (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, one trial, four decades old, in a selected hyperuricosuric/normocalciuric subgroup. The authors' own warning stands: stone trials show a large positive treatment bias — the placebo arm improved by nearly two-thirds — so the drug's true increment is the modest gap between 0.12 and 0.26 events per year.
cards.source: Ettinger B et al. Randomized trial of allopurinol in the prevention of calcium oxalate calculi. New England Journal of Medicine. 1986. PMID: 3534570. shelves.title: Fruits and vegetables versus sodium bicarbonate for CKD acidosis: matched on acidosis correction and eGFR preservation in two trials from one research group — both beat usual care
shelves.question: In chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis, does a base-producing diet of fruits and vegetables correct acidosis and preserve kidney function as well as sodium bicarbonate?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/diagnosis/etiology/physiopathology/therapy/urine · Administration, Oral · Angiotensinogen/urine · Bicarbonates/administration & dosage · Biomarkers/blood/urine · Diet · Female · Fruit · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Kidney/drug effects/metabolism/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/diagnosis/physiopathology/therapy/urine · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vegetables
shelves.balance: SPLIT — between the two alkali strategies there is no difference that matters; against usual care, both work. In Goraya N et al. (PMID: 24694986), 108 patients with stage 3 CKD and plasma total CO2 of 22–24 mmol/l were randomised for three years to usual care, sodium bicarbonate, or fruits and vegetables dosed to halve dietary acid: plasma total CO2 fell in usual care but rose with either alkali treatment, urine angiotensinogen rose in usual care but fell with either, and eGFR loss at three years was less with bicarbonate or fruits and vegetables than with usual care, with no separation between the two alkali arms. In Goraya N et al. (PMID: 39990902), 153 patients with stage G1 CKD and normal eGFR were randomised for five years to fruits and vegetables (n=51), matched oral bicarbonate (n=51), or usual care (n=51): five-year acid accumulation was lower in the fruits-and-vegetables (-1.2 [11.0] mmol) and bicarbonate (-1.7 [10.8] mmol) groups than in usual care (5.2 [10.3] mmol, P<0.003), and urine albumin, N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine, and angiotensinogen excretion were lower in both treated groups. PROPOSED SPLIT: fruits and vegetables match bicarbonate on acidosis and kidney-injury markers wherever the two have been compared head-to-head — the benefit is in giving alkali, not in which form it takes.

cards.headline: Goraya 2014 (stage 3 CKD, 3 years): total CO2 and urine angiotensinogen moved the wrong way on usual care and the right way on either alkali; eGFR loss less on both, no difference between them
cards.summary: Goraya 2014 (stage 3 CKD, 3 years): total CO2 and urine angiotensinogen moved the wrong way on usual care and the right way on either alkali; eGFR loss less on both, no difference between them
cards.people: 108 patients with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and plasma total CO2 of 22–24 mmol/l, all treated to systolic blood pressure below 130 mm Hg with regimens including ACE inhibition, randomised to usual care or dietary-acid reduction by 50% using sodium bicarbonate or base-producing fruits and vegetables, followed for 3 years.
cards.result: Plasma total CO2 decreased in usual care but increased with bicarbonate or fruits and vegetables. Urine angiotensinogen excretion increased in usual care but decreased with bicarbonate or fruits and vegetables. Creatinine- and cystatin C-calculated eGFR decreased in all groups, but the loss was less at 3 years with bicarbonate or fruits and vegetables than with usual care; the record reports no difference between the bicarbonate and fruits-and-vegetables arms on these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports directions and significance rather than arm-by-arm numbers for the primary comparisons, the trial is open-label by necessity (you cannot blind a diet), and all patients came from one research programme. cards.headline: Goraya 2025 (stage G1 CKD, 5 years): acid accumulation -1.2 mmol on fruits and vegetables and -1.7 mmol on bicarbonate versus +5.2 mmol on usual care (P<0.003)
cards.summary: Goraya 2025 (stage G1 CKD, 5 years): acid accumulation -1.2 mmol on fruits and vegetables and -1.7 mmol on bicarbonate versus +5.2 mmol on usual care (P<0.003)
cards.people: 153 participants with macroalbuminuric, nondiabetic, hypertension-associated CKD stage G1 (mean eGFR 101 ml/min per 1.73 m2), randomised to fruits and vegetables in amounts to reduce dietary acid intake by 50% (n=51), oral sodium bicarbonate matched to the fruits-and-vegetables alkali intake (n=51), or usual care (n=51) for 5 years.
cards.result: Five-year acid accumulation (mean [SD]) was lower in the fruits-and-vegetables (-1.2 [11.0] mmol) and bicarbonate (-1.7 [10.8] mmol) groups than in usual care (5.2 [10.3] mmol, P<0.003). Five-year urine excretion of albumin, N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine, and angiotensinogen was lower in both treated groups than in usual care, consistent with less kidney injury; baseline acid accumulation, eGFR, and urine marker excretion did not differ among groups.
cards.watchOut: The population had normal eGFR and 'eubicarbonatemic' acid accumulation — a research construct measured with a bicarbonate-bolus test, not routine clinical acidosis — and the endpoints are urine injury markers, not kidney failure. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Goraya N et al. Randomized Trial of Dietary Acid Reduction and Acid-Base Status of Patients With CKD and Normal Estimated GFR. Kidney International Reports. 2025. PMID: 39990902. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two CKD stages, one message — alkali is alkali; the diet performs like the tablet wherever they were compared
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two CKD stages, one message — alkali is alkali; the diet performs like the tablet wherever they were compared
cards.people: Two randomised trials from a single research programme: stage 3 CKD with mild acidosis (108 patients, 3 years) and stage G1 CKD with normal eGFR (153 patients, 5 years), each comparing fruits and vegetables, sodium bicarbonate, and usual care.
cards.result: Stage 3: eGFR loss less and total CO2 higher on either alkali strategy than usual care, no difference between strategies. Stage G1: acid accumulation -1.2 (fruits and vegetables) and -1.7 (bicarbonate) vs +5.2 mmol (usual care), P<0.003; kidney-injury urine markers lower on both. PROPOSED SPLIT — Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the comparison.
cards.watchOut: Anchor swap declared: the candidate anchor (Goraya 2013, stage 4) is already carded on live shelf #162, so this shelf is built on the programme's two uncarded trials. All evidence comes from one investigative group; independent replication is absent, and the stage-4 head-to-head detail lives on shelf #162.

shelves.title: Higher dialysis dose and high-flux membranes (HEMO; MPO): no survival benefit overall in 2,584 randomised patients — the only signal is high-flux in patients with albumin at most 4 g/dL
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a higher dialysis dose or a high-flux membrane reduce death and hospitalisation compared with a standard dose and low-flux membrane?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Hemodialysis Solutions/administration & dosage · Hospitalization · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/metabolism/mortality/therapy · Male · Membranes, Artificial · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Renal Dialysis/instrumentation/methods · Survival Analysis · Urea/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the two definitive randomised trials agree on the main question. In the HEMO Study (Eknoyan G et al., PMID: 12490682), 1,846 patients on thrice-weekly dialysis were randomised in a two-by-two factorial design to standard or high dialysis dose and low-flux or high-flux dialyser: the relative risk of death was 0.96 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.10; P=0.53) for high versus standard dose and 0.92 (95% CI, 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.23) for high-flux versus low-flux, and none of the main secondary outcomes (cardiac hospitalisation or death, infection hospitalisation or death, albumin fall or death, all hospitalisations) differed significantly. In the MPO study (Locatelli F et al., PMID: 19092122), 738 incident patients randomised to high-flux or low-flux membranes and followed for 3 to 7.5 years showed no significant survival difference overall, but patients with serum albumin at most 4 g/dl had significantly higher survival with high-flux membranes (P=0.032), with a secondary signal in patients with diabetes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): pushing dose above standard targets, or switching flux, does not reduce death or hospitalisation for the average maintenance haemodialysis patient; the low-albumin high-flux signal is a subgroup finding, not a general rule.

cards.headline: Eknoyan 2002 (HEMO): death RR 0.96 (95% CI 0.84–1.10) for high dose and 0.92 (0.81–1.05) for high-flux — every main secondary outcome also null, in 1,846 patients
cards.summary: Eknoyan 2002 (HEMO): death RR 0.96 (95% CI 0.84–1.10) for high dose and 0.92 (0.81–1.05) for high-flux — every main secondary outcome also null, in 1,846 patients
cards.type: Randomised two-by-two factorial trial (Eknoyan 2002, HEMO Study)
cards.people: 1,846 patients undergoing thrice-weekly maintenance haemodialysis, randomised to standard or high dialysis dose (achieved single-pool Kt/V 1.32 versus 1.71; urea-reduction ratio 66.3% versus 75.2%) and to low-flux or high-flux dialyser (beta2-microglobulin clearance 3 versus 34 ml per minute).
cards.result: The primary outcome, death from any cause, was not significantly influenced by dose or flux: relative risk of death 0.96 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.10; P=0.53) for high versus standard dose, and 0.92 (95% CI, 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.23) for high-flux versus low-flux. The main secondary outcomes — first hospitalisation for cardiac causes or death, first hospitalisation for infection or death, first 15% decrease in serum albumin or death, and all hospitalisations not related to vascular access — also did not differ significantly between dose or flux groups. Possible benefits were suggested in two of seven prespecified subgroups.
cards.watchOut: HEMO tested dose above an already-adequate standard (Kt/V 1.32) — it does not say dialysis dose doesn't matter below adequacy. The trial predates widespread convective therapies, which are a different intervention from high-flux diffusive dialysis.
cards.source: Eknoyan G et al. Effect of dialysis dose and membrane flux in maintenance hemodialysis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12490682. cards.headline: Locatelli 2009 (MPO): no survival difference for high-flux versus low-flux overall in 738 incident patients — significant benefit confined to albumin at most 4 g/dl (P=0.032)
cards.summary: Locatelli 2009 (MPO): no survival difference for high-flux versus low-flux overall in 738 incident patients — significant benefit confined to albumin at most 4 g/dl (P=0.032)
cards.people: 738 incident haemodialysis patients in Europe, stratified by serum albumin (at most 4 versus above 4 g/dl) and assigned to low-flux or high-flux membranes, followed for 3 to 7.5 years.
cards.result: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed no significant difference between high-flux and low-flux membranes overall, and a Cox proportional hazards model concurred. Patients with serum albumin at most 4 g/dl had significantly higher survival rates in the high-flux group compared with the low-flux group (P=0.032). A secondary analysis suggested high-flux membranes may significantly improve survival of patients with diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The positive findings are subgroup and secondary analyses of an overall-null trial — hypothesis-generating by the authors' own framing ('requires confirmation given the post hoc nature'). The abstract reports no absolute survival rates, so the size of the subgroup benefit cannot be quantified from the record.
cards.source: Locatelli F et al. Effect of membrane permeability on survival of hemodialysis patients. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2009. PMID: 19092122. cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials, one answer for the average patient — standard dose and either flux; a low-albumin subgroup signal stands unconfirmed
cards.people: HEMO (1,846 prevalent patients, dose × flux factorial) and MPO (738 incident patients, flux), totalling 2,584 randomised maintenance haemodialysis patients.
cards.result: Death: RR 0.96 (dose) and 0.92 (flux) in HEMO, both non-significant; hospitalisation composites null. MPO overall survival: no significant difference; albumin at most 4 g/dl subgroup: P=0.032 in favour of high-flux. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C not set: two large concordant randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are old enough that dialyser technology and practice have moved on; the shelf answers the dose-and-flux question as randomised, not whether modern high-volume haemodiafiltration helps — a separate question with its own trials.

shelves.title: Extended-hours haemodialysis (ACTIVE): quality of life unchanged at 12 months — phosphate and potassium lower and fewer medicines, sleep no better, deaths 5 versus 2
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis, do extended treatment hours improve phosphate control, blood pressure, and quality of life compared with conventional hours?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis/methods · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcomes patients feel, in the one large randomised trial. In ACTIVE (Jardine MJ et al., PMID: 28151412), 200 adults on maintenance haemodialysis were randomised to extended weekly hours (at least 24 hours; median achieved 24.0) or standard hours (target 12–15; median 12.0) for 12 months. The primary outcome, change in EQ-5D quality-of-life score, did not differ (mean difference 0.04; 95% CI, -0.03 to 0.11; P=0.29), blood pressure did not differ at study end, and left ventricular mass index in a 95-patient substudy did not differ (mean difference -6.0; 95% CI, -14.8 to 2.7 g/m2; P=0.18). Extended hours were associated with lower phosphate and potassium and higher haemoglobin, and with fewer blood-pressure-lowering and phosphate-binding medicines; five deaths occurred in the extended group and two in the standard group (P=0.44). The prespecified sleep analysis (Liao JL et al., PMID: 29424935) found no significant improvement in overall sleep quality (average intervention effect 0.44, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.89; P=0.053) or the sleep subscale (3.58, 95% CI -0.02 to 7.18; P=0.051). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): doubling weekly dialysis hours buys better phosphate and potassium numbers and a smaller pill burden, but not better quality of life, blood pressure, or sleep over 12 months.

cards.headline: Jardine 2017 (ACTIVE): EQ-5D change difference 0.04 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.11; P=0.29) for at least 24 vs 12–15 hours weekly; blood pressure no different, phosphate and potassium lower
cards.summary: Jardine 2017 (ACTIVE): EQ-5D change difference 0.04 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.11; P=0.29) for at least 24 vs 12–15 hours weekly; blood pressure no different, phosphate and potassium lower
cards.people: 200 adult recipients of standard maintenance haemodialysis from in-centre and home programmes, randomised 1:1 to extended weekly haemodialysis (at least 24 hours; median achieved 24.0 hours, IQR 23.6–24.0) or standard hours (target 12–15, maximum 18; median 12.0, IQR 12.0–16.0) for 12 months.
cards.result: Change in EQ-5D quality-of-life score did not differ between groups (mean difference 0.04; 95% CI, -0.03 to 0.11; P=0.29). Extended hours were associated with lower phosphate and potassium levels and higher haemoglobin levels; blood pressure did not differ at study end. Extended hours were associated with fewer blood-pressure-lowering agents and phosphate-binding medications, but not with erythropoietin dosing. In a 95-patient substudy, left ventricular mass index did not differ (mean difference -6.0; 95% CI, -14.8 to 2.7 g/m2; P=0.18). Five deaths occurred in the extended group and two in the standard group (P=0.44); vascular access events were similar.
cards.watchOut: Two hundred patients for 12 months cannot exclude a mortality effect in either direction — the 5-versus-2 death split is noise, not signal, and the trial says so by its P value. Quality of life was the primary outcome and it was flat despite a doubled time commitment.
cards.source: Jardine MJ et al. A Trial of Extending Hemodialysis Hours and Quality of Life. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2017. PMID: 28151412. Registry ID: NCT00649298. cards.headline: Liao 2019 (ACTIVE sleep analysis): sleep quality effect 0.44 points (95% CI -0.01 to 0.89; P=0.053) — not significant, despite the extra clearance
cards.summary: Liao 2019 (ACTIVE sleep analysis): sleep quality effect 0.44 points (95% CI -0.01 to 0.89; P=0.053) — not significant, despite the extra clearance
cards.people: The 200 ACTIVE participants randomised to extended (at least 24 hours/week) or standard (target 12–15 hours/week) haemodialysis over 12 months, with sleep quality measured every 3 months by blinded telephone interview using the Kidney Disease Quality of Life Short Form.
cards.result: Baseline overall sleep quality (5.9 versus 6.3 on a 0–10 scale) and sleep subscale scores (65.0 versus 63.2 on 0–100) were similar between extended and standard groups. Extended hours led to a non-significant improvement in overall sleep quality score (average intervention effect 0.44, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.89; P=0.053) and sleep subscale (3.58, 95% CI -0.02 to 7.18; P=0.051). Poor sleep quality was associated with being female and with current smoking.
cards.watchOut: Borderline P values (0.051–0.053) in a substudy invite over-reading; the prespecified conclusion is that sleep quality was not significantly improved. Same single trial as the main report — not independent evidence.
cards.source: Liao JL et al. Effect of extended hours dialysis on sleep quality in a randomized trial. Nephrology. 2019. PMID: 29424935. cards.headline: Synthesis: the laboratory and medication benefits of longer hours are real; the patient-experience benefits were not shown in 12 months
cards.summary: Synthesis: the laboratory and medication benefits of longer hours are real; the patient-experience benefits were not shown in 12 months
cards.people: One randomised trial programme (ACTIVE, 200 participants, 12 months): main report plus prespecified sleep analysis.
cards.result: Quality of life: mean difference 0.04 (P=0.29). Blood pressure at study end: no difference. Sleep quality: effect 0.44 (P=0.053), not significant. Phosphate and potassium: lower on extended hours; blood-pressure and phosphate-binder medication counts: fewer. Deaths: 5 vs 2 (P=0.44). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for quality of life, blood pressure, and sleep, Tier C flagged: a single trial programme carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Extended hours in ACTIVE meant facility/home schedules of at least 24 hours weekly — a major life commitment; the shelf should not be read as covering nocturnal or frequent-dialysis regimens, which ask different questions.

shelves.title: Probing dry weight in haemodialysis hypertension (DRIP): about 1 kg of extra ultrafiltration lowered ambulatory systolic pressure by 6.6–6.9 mm Hg at 4–8 weeks
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with hypertension, does probing dry weight with additional ultrafiltration lower ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Pressure/physiology · Diastole/physiology · Female · Hemodiafiltration/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Hypertension/physiopathology/therapy · Kidney Failure, Chronic/physiopathology/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects/methods · Systole/physiology · Time Factors · Weight Loss/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted randomised trial, eight weeks long. In the DRIP trial (Agarwal R et al., PMID: 19153263), 150 hypertensive haemodialysis patients were randomised to additional ultrafiltration (dry weight probed without extra dialysis time; n=100) or control (physician visits only; n=50). Post-dialysis weight fell by 0.9 kg at 4 weeks, with systolic ambulatory blood pressure changing by -6.9 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.4 to -1.3; P=0.016) and diastolic by -3.1 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.2 to -0.02; P=0.048); at 8 weeks, with dry weight reduced by 1 kg, systolic changed by -6.6 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.2 to -1.0; P=0.021) and diastolic by -3.3 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.4 to -0.2; P=0.037). The combined odds ratio for a systolic reduction of at least 10 mm Hg was 2.24 (95% CI, 1.32 to 3.81; P=0.003). No domain of the kidney-disease quality-of-life survey deteriorated, despite more intradialytic signs and symptoms of hypotension. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): probing dry weight by roughly a kilogram lowers interdialytic ambulatory pressure by about 7/3 mm Hg within two months; whether the gain persists, and at what long-term cost in cramps and access or myocardial stunning, the trial does not say.

cards.headline: Agarwal 2009 (DRIP): systolic ambulatory BP -6.9 mm Hg at 4 weeks and -6.6 mm Hg at 8 weeks (both significant); odds ratio 2.24 for a fall of at least 10 mm Hg
cards.summary: Agarwal 2009 (DRIP): systolic ambulatory BP -6.9 mm Hg at 4 weeks and -6.6 mm Hg at 8 weeks (both significant); odds ratio 2.24 for a fall of at least 10 mm Hg
cards.people: 150 long-term hypertensive haemodialysis patients randomised to additional ultrafiltration (n=100; dry weight probed without increasing dialysis time or duration) or control (n=50; physician visits only). Primary outcome: change in systolic interdialytic ambulatory blood pressure.
cards.result: Post-dialysis weight was reduced by 0.9 kg at 4 weeks, resulting in a -6.9 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.4 to -1.3; P=0.016) change in systolic BP and -3.1 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.2 to -0.02; P=0.048) in diastolic BP. At 8 weeks, dry weight was reduced by 1 kg, systolic BP changed by -6.6 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.2 to -1.0; P=0.021), and diastolic BP by -3.3 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.4 to -0.2; P=0.037). The Mantel-Haenszel combined odds ratio for systolic BP reduction of at least 10 mm Hg was 2.24 (95% CI, 1.32 to 3.81; P=0.003). No deterioration was seen in any domain of the kidney disease quality of life health survey, despite an increase in intradialytic signs and symptoms of hypotension.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is the whole horizon: durability, and the long-term trade-offs of chronic extra ultrafiltration (cramps, intradialytic hypotension, possible myocardial stunning), are outside this record. A single trial from the investigator group that has championed the method.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a simple, effective manoeuvre on an 8-week evidence base — about 7 mm Hg systolic for about 1 kg
cards.people: One randomised controlled trial, 150 hypertensive haemodialysis patients, 8 weeks (DRIP).
cards.result: Dry weight: -0.9 kg at 4 weeks, -1 kg at 8 weeks. Ambulatory systolic BP: -6.9 mm Hg (P=0.016) and -6.6 mm Hg (P=0.021). shelves.title: Intravenous L-carnitine in haemodialysis: 49 randomised trials pooled — no improvement in haemoglobin, erythropoietin dose, or quality of life; LDL and CRP shifts too small or too soft to act on
shelves.question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does intravenous L-carnitine improve anaemia, muscle symptoms, cramps, or hypotension compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Carnitine/administration & dosage · Cholesterol/blood · Databases, Factual · Dietary Supplements · Erythropoietin/blood · Hemoglobins/metabolism · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Renal Dialysis · Triglycerides/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two independent meta-analyses of the randomised literature land in the same place. Chen Y et al. (PMID: 24368434) pooled 49 randomised trials (1,734 participants) of L-carnitine in maintenance haemodialysis: no significant differences in haemoglobin (mean difference 0.68 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.14 to 1.50 — an interval the authors read as failing to confirm an anaemia benefit), haematocrit, albumin, or required erythropoietin dose (-0.76 KU/week; 95% CI, -1.75 to 0.23); LDL cholesterol fell slightly (-5.82 mg/dL; 95% CI, -11.61 to -0.04) and C-reactive protein by -3.65 mg/L (95% CI, -6.19 to -1.12), changes the authors call clinically irrelevant (LDL) or of unclear relevance to hard endpoints (CRP). Yang SK et al. (PMID: 24535997), in a separate meta-analysis, found L-carnitine did not improve quality-of-life total score (standardised mean difference 0.76; 95% CI, -0.13 to 1.65; P=0.09), CRP, oxidised LDL, albumin, haemoglobin, cholesterol, triglycerides, or parathyroid hormone, concluding there is no evidence of benefit for inflammation, nutrition, anaemia, dyslipidaemia, or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine L-carnitine in haemodialysis has no demonstrated benefit on anaemia, erythropoietin requirements, or quality of life; cramps and intradialytic hypotension were never adequately measured in the pooled trials.

cards.headline: Chen 2014: 49 RCTs, 1,734 patients — haemoglobin MD 0.68 g/dL (95% CI 0.14 to 1.50) and erythropoietin dose MD -0.76 KU/week (CI -1.75 to 0.23), neither confirming benefit; LDL -5.82 mg/dL, CRP -3.65 mg/L
cards.summary: Chen 2014: 49 RCTs, 1,734 patients — haemoglobin MD 0.68 g/dL (95% CI 0.14 to 1.50) and erythropoietin dose MD -0.76 KU/week (CI -1.75 to 0.23), neither confirming benefit; LDL -5.82 mg/dL, CRP -3.65 mg/L
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Chen 2014)
cards.people: 49 randomised controlled trials (1,734 participants) of L-carnitine supplementation (intravenous or oral) versus control in adults with end-stage kidney disease requiring maintenance haemodialysis, searched to 31 December 2012.
cards.result: L-Carnitine significantly decreased LDL cholesterol (mean difference -5.82 mg/dL; 95% CI, -11.61 to -0.04) and C-reactive protein (-3.65 mg/L; 95% CI, -6.19 to -1.12). There were no significant differences in triglycerides (-0.89 mg/dL; 95% CI, -29.32 to 27.53), total cholesterol (0.14 mg/dL; 95% CI, -6.15 to 6.42), HDL cholesterol (1.13 mg/dL; 95% CI, -2.44 to 4.70), haemoglobin (0.68 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.14 to 1.50), haematocrit (2.04%; 95% CI, -1.39 to 5.48), albumin (1.65 g/L; 95% CI, -0.22 to 3.51), or required erythropoietin dose (-0.76 KU/week; 95% CI, -1.75 to 0.23). No adverse effects were reported. The authors state the meta-analysis failed to confirm previous findings on haemoglobin and erythropoietin dose.
cards.watchOut: Many included trials are small and short, and the symptom outcomes patients ask about — cramps, muscle symptoms, intradialytic hypotension — were not pooled endpoints at all; absence of measurement is not proof of absence of effect, but it is absence of evidence after decades of use.
cards.source: Chen Y et al. L-Carnitine supplementation for adults with end-stage kidney disease requiring maintenance hemodialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2014. PMID: 24368434. cards.headline: Yang 2014: quality of life SMD 0.76 (95% CI -0.13 to 1.65; P=0.09) — and CRP, albumin, haemoglobin, lipids and PTH all non-significant
cards.summary: Yang 2014: quality of life SMD 0.76 (95% CI -0.13 to 1.65; P=0.09) — and CRP, albumin, haemoglobin, lipids and PTH all non-significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Yang 2014)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of L-carnitine versus placebo in maintenance haemodialysis patients, identified from Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register (number of trials and participants as reported in each pooled analysis).
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed L-carnitine could not increase the total SF-36 quality-of-life score (standardised mean difference 0.76; 95% CI, -0.13 to 1.65; P=0.09) and did not improve CRP (SMD -0.37; 95% CI, -0.88 to 0.14; P=0.16), oxidised LDL (SMD 0.04), albumin (SMD 0.25; P=0.38), haemoglobin (SMD 0.23; 95% CI, -0.23 to 0.68; P=0.33), cholesterol (SMD -0.24; P=0.33), triglycerides (SMD 0.02; P=0.91), or parathyroid hormone (SMD 0.21; P=0.46). The authors conclude there is no evidence L-carnitine improves inflammation, oxidative stress, nutrition, anaemia, dyslipidaemia, hyperparathyroidism, or quality of life in haemodialysis patients.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses disagree on CRP (significant in Chen, not in Yang) — a reminder that the pooled small-trial literature is fragile; they agree on every patient-centred endpoint, which is what this shelf rests on.
cards.source: Yang SK et al. Effect of L-carnitine therapy on patients in maintenance hemodialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Nephrology. 2014. PMID: 24535997. cards.summary: Synthesis: after 49 randomised trials, the measurable benefits are two laboratory shifts; anaemia, EPO dose, and quality of life are null in both syntheses
cards.people: Two independent meta-analyses of randomised L-carnitine trials in maintenance haemodialysis (Chen 2014: 49 trials, 1,734 participants; Yang 2014).
cards.result: Haemoglobin: MD 0.68 g/dL (95% CI 0.14 to 1.50) / SMD 0.23 (P=0.33) — not confirmed. Erythropoietin dose: MD -0.76 KU/week (95% CI -1.75 to 0.23). Quality of life: SMD 0.76 (P=0.09). shelves.title: Nalfurafine for uraemic pruritus: itch, sleep disturbance, and excoriations significantly better than placebo in two pooled trials — a 9.5 mm advantage on a 100 mm itch scale, over 2–4 weeks
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with uraemic pruritus, does the kappa-opioid agonist nalfurafine reduce itch severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antipruritics/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications/diagnosis/therapy · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/therapeutic use · Probability · Pruritus/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Receptors, Opioid, kappa/antagonists & inhibitors · Reference Values · Renal Dialysis · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Uremia/complications/diagnosis/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest itch reduction, measured over weeks. Wikström B et al. (PMID: 16251241) report two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies enrolling 144 haemodialysis patients with uraemic pruritus, treated with post-dialysis intravenous nalfurafine or placebo for 2 to 4 weeks: a meta-analytic assessment found statistically significant reductions in worst itching (P=0.0212), itching intensity (P=0.0410), and sleep disturbances (P=0.0003), with improvements in itching (P=0.0025) and excoriations (P=0.0060), and drug-related adverse events of similar type and incidence to placebo. The systematic review by Jaiswal D et al. (PMID: 28270926) pooled the nalfurafine trials and found a 9.50 mm (95% CI, 6.27 to 12.74; P<0.001) greater reduction in itch severity on a 100-mm visual analogue scale than placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nalfurafine reduces uraemic itch by roughly a tenth of the scale over a few weeks — meaningful for a symptom with few options, but the trials are short, small, and largely from the Japanese development programme where the drug is approved.

cards.headline: Wikström 2005: two pooled placebo-controlled studies (144 patients) — worst itching P=0.0212, sleep disturbances P=0.0003, excoriations P=0.0060, all favouring nalfurafine
cards.summary: Wikström 2005: two pooled placebo-controlled studies (144 patients) — worst itching P=0.0212, sleep disturbances P=0.0003, excoriations P=0.0060, all favouring nalfurafine
cards.type: Two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies with meta-analytic pooling (Wikström 2005)
cards.people: 144 patients with uraemic pruritus undergoing routine haemodialysis, enrolled across two multicentre studies, treated with post-dialysis intravenous nalfurafine or placebo for 2 to 4 weeks.
cards.result: A meta-analysis approach across the two studies found statistically significant reductions in worst itching (P=0.0212), itching intensity (P=0.0410), and sleep disturbances (P=0.0003) in the nalfurafine group compared with placebo, with improvements in itching (P=0.0025) and excoriations (P=0.0060). Nalfurafine showed similar types and incidences of drug-related adverse events to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The record reports P values without effect sizes, and 2–4 weeks is a very short window for a chronic symptom; the pooled analysis was performed by the investigators reporting both studies. Effect magnitude has to come from the independent review below.

cards.headline: Jaiswal 2016 meta-analysis: nalfurafine beat placebo by 9.50 mm (95% CI 6.27 to 12.74; P<0.001) on a 100-mm itch scale, across the two randomised trials
cards.summary: Jaiswal 2016 meta-analysis: nalfurafine beat placebo by 9.50 mm (95% CI 6.27 to 12.74; P<0.001) on a 100-mm itch scale, across the two randomised trials
cards.people: Five randomised studies of opioid-pathway treatments for uraemic pruritus in adult chronic dialysis patients (three of naltrexone, two of nalfurafine), identified from 3,587 screened records; study durations ranged from 2 to 9 weeks. Only the nalfurafine studies could be pooled.
cards.result: Pooled analysis using a random-effects model found that nalfurafine resulted in a 9.50 mm (95% CI, 6.27 to 12.74; P<0.001) greater reduction of itch severity (100-mm visual analogue scale) than placebo. Data from the naltrexone studies could not be pooled because of heterogeneity in outcome reporting. The authors conclude nalfurafine holds some promise but that more long-term randomised trials are required.
cards.watchOut: The entire pooled estimate rests on the same two short trials; a 9.5 mm average advantage on a 100 mm scale is modest, and individual response varies — the review predates the later difelikefalin trials, which are a different drug and a different shelf. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Jaiswal D et al. Targeting the Opioid Pathway for Uremic Pruritus: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Canadian Journal of Kidney Health and Disease. 2016. PMID: 28270926. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Endovascular fistula creation: 87% physiologically suitable and 84% cumulative patency at 12 months in the single-arm NEAT study — but no randomised comparison with surgical fistulas exists
shelves.question: In patients needing a new arteriovenous fistula, does endovascular fistula creation achieve maturation and patency comparable to surgical creation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arteriovenous Fistula · Arteriovenous Shunt, Surgical/methods · Endovascular Procedures · Female · Forearm/blood supply · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the technology works in its own series; the comparison the question asks for has never been randomised. In the NEAT study (Lok CE et al., PMID: 28624422), a prospective single-arm multicentre study of 60 full-analysis-set patients, endovascular fistulas were created in 98%, 87% were physiologically suitable for dialysis within 3 months (mean brachial artery flow 918 mL/min, vein diameter 5.2 mm), functional usability was 64% among participants who received dialysis, and 12-month primary and cumulative patencies were 69% and 84%; 8% had a serious procedure-related adverse event (2% device-related). The meta-analysis by Sun JB et al. (PMID: 36148078), pooling 14 case series and 5 cohort studies with 1,929 patients, found endovascular technique success of 98.00% and maturation of 87.00%, with no statistically significant differences versus surgical fistulas in the three cohort studies reporting procedural success (odds ratio 0.69; 95% CI, 0.04 to 11.98; P=0.80) or maturation (odds ratio 0.73; 95% CI, 0.20 to 2.63; P=0.63) — intervals so wide they exclude neither substantial inferiority nor superiority. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): endovascular creation reliably produces usable fistulas in selected anatomy, but 'comparable to surgery' is an unproven claim resting on non-randomised cohorts.

cards.headline: Lok 2017 (NEAT): fistula created in 98%, physiologically suitable in 87%, functional usability 64%, 12-month cumulative patency 84% — single-arm, no surgical comparator
cards.summary: Lok 2017 (NEAT): fistula created in 98%, physiologically suitable in 87%, functional usability 64%, 12-month cumulative patency 84% — single-arm, no surgical comparator
cards.people: 80 patients enrolled (20 roll-in; 60 in the full analysis set) — consecutive adult dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis-dependent patients referred for vascular access creation at nine centres in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand — receiving an endovascular arteriovenous fistula created with a catheter-based radiofrequency system between the proximal forearm vessels.
cards.result: Endovascular fistulas were created in 98% of participants; 8% had a serious procedure-related adverse event (2% device-related). 87% were physiologically suitable for dialysis within 3 months (mean brachial artery flow 918 mL/min; endoAVF vein diameter 5.2 mm). Functional usability (prescribed dialysis via two-needle cannulation) was 64% in participants who received dialysis. Twelve-month primary and cumulative patencies were 69% and 84% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm by design — the authors state the unique anatomy precluded a surgical comparator — so every percentage here is a description, not a comparison. Functional usability (64%) is notably lower than physiological suitability (87%): a fistula that measures well is not always a fistula that gets used.
cards.source: Lok CE et al. Endovascular Proximal Forearm Arteriovenous Fistula for Hemodialysis Access: Results of the Prospective, Multicenter Novel Endovascular Access Trial (NEAT). American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2017. PMID: 28624422.
