cards.headline: Sun 2022 meta-analysis: maturation 87% pooled for endovascular fistulas; versus surgery, odds ratios 0.69 for procedural success and 0.73 for maturation — neither significant, both uninformative
cards.summary: Sun 2022 meta-analysis: maturation 87% pooled for endovascular fistulas; versus surgery, odds ratios 0.69 for procedural success and 0.73 for maturation — neither significant, both uninformative
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of case series and cohort studies (Sun 2022)
cards.people: 14 case series and 5 cohort studies, 1,929 patients with kidney failure receiving endovascular arteriovenous fistula creation, some cohorts comparing with surgical creation; no randomised controlled studies were available to include.
cards.result: Technique success for endovascular fistula was 98.00% (95% CI, 0.97 to 0.99) and the maturation rate 87.00% (95% CI, 0.79 to 0.93). In three cohort studies, there was no statistically significant difference between endovascular and surgical fistulas for procedural success (odds ratio 0.69; 95% CI, 0.04 to 11.98; P=0.80) or maturation (odds ratio 0.73; 95% CI, 0.20 to 2.63; P=0.63). Procedure-related complications for endovascular fistulas were 7%, not significantly different from surgery in four cohort studies (odds ratio 1.85; 95% CI, 0.37 to 9.16; P=0.45). The authors state further research is greatly necessary due to the lack of randomised controlled studies. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: Cohort comparisons of a new device against surgery are confounded by anatomy and operator selection in both directions, and heterogeneity was high (I² up to 88% for maturation). 'No significant difference' here means 'no usable information', not 'equivalent'.
cards.source: Sun JB et al. Percutaneous endovascular arteriovenous fistula: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36148078. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a feasible technology with respectable single-arm numbers and an entirely open comparative question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a feasible technology with respectable single-arm numbers and an entirely open comparative question
cards.people: One prospective single-arm multicentre study (NEAT, 60 analysed patients) and one meta-analysis of 19 non-randomised studies (1,929 patients).
cards.result: Creation success: 98%. Physiological suitability/maturation: 87%. Twelve-month cumulative patency (NEAT): 84%. Versus surgery (cohorts only): procedural success OR 0.69 (95% CI 0.04 to 11.98); maturation OR 0.73 (95% CI 0.20 to 2.63) — both non-significant and uninformative. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C: the shelf rests on observational and single-arm evidence.
cards.watchOut: Device iterations (two commercial systems with different anatomy) are pooled in this literature as if one intervention; centre experience effects are likely large and unmeasured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lok CE et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2017 (PMID: 28624422); Sun JB et al. Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36148078).

shelves.title: Exercise for fistula maturation: isometric hand exercise improved maturation (RR 1.56–1.80) and vein diameter (+0.84 mm) in small trials; ordinary isotonic exercise barely moved ultrasound maturation (RR 1.09)
shelves.question: After arteriovenous fistula creation, does a programme of hand and arm exercise improve fistula maturation and usable diameter compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Arteriovenous Fistula · Exercise · Humans · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency · Upper Extremity
shelves.balance: SPLIT — it splits by exercise type, and the certainty is low throughout. The Cochrane review by Nantakool S et al. (PMID: 36184076) included nine studies (579 participants) of upper-limb exercise around fistula creation. Compared with no intervention, isotonic exercise may make little or no difference to ultrasound maturation (two studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.09; 95% CI, 0.94 to 1.25) but may improve clinical maturation (risk ratio 1.14; 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.27), both low-certainty. Compared with isotonic exercise, isometric exercise may improve ultrasound maturation (three studies, 160 participants: risk ratio 1.56; 95% CI, 1.21 to 2.00) and clinical maturation (risk ratio 1.80; 95% CI, 1.18 to 2.76), with greater venous diameter (mean difference 0.84 mm; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.23) and inflow-artery blood flow (mean difference 140.62 mL/min; 95% CI, 38.72 to 242.52). The systematic review by Ramanarayanan S et al. (PMID: 36805738) found hand exercise increased distal cephalic vein calibre by 0.24 mm (95% CI, 0.03 to 0.45) overall, and by 0.29 mm (95% CI, 0.11 to 0.47) when restricted to the two randomised trials with independent control groups, and was well tolerated, especially in the first four weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: isometric hand exercise probably helps maturation modestly; generic isotonic exercise has little measurable effect on ultrasound maturation — all on low-certainty evidence from small trials.

cards.headline: Nantakool 2022 (Cochrane): isometric vs isotonic — ultrasound maturation RR 1.56, clinical maturation RR 1.80, vein diameter +0.84 mm; isotonic vs none — ultrasound RR 1.09, clinical RR 1.14
cards.summary: Nantakool 2022 (Cochrane): isometric vs isotonic — ultrasound maturation RR 1.56, clinical maturation RR 1.80, vein diameter +0.84 mm; isotonic vs none — ultrasound RR 1.09, clinical RR 1.14
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Nantakool 2022)
cards.people: Nine randomised and quasi-randomised studies (579 participants) of upper-limb exercise programmes before or after arteriovenous fistula creation in people with kidney failure requiring permanent haemodialysis access; seven studies (519 participants) of post-operative exercise could be meta-analysed. Searched to 15 March 2022.
cards.result: Compared with no intervention, isotonic exercise may make little or no difference to ultrasound maturation (2 studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.09; 95% CI, 0.94 to 1.25; low certainty) but may improve clinical maturation (2 studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.14; 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.27; low certainty). Compared with isotonic exercise, isometric exercise may improve ultrasound maturation (3 studies, 160 participants: risk ratio 1.56; 95% CI, 1.21 to 2.00) and clinical maturation (3 studies, 160 participants: risk ratio 1.80; 95% CI, 1.18 to 2.76), with greater venous diameter (3 studies, 160 participants: mean difference 0.84 mm; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.23) and blood flow in the inflow artery (mean difference 140.62 mL/min; 95% CI, 38.72 to 242.52). Whether isometric exercise reduces vascular access complications is uncertain (risk ratio 2.54; 95% CI, 0.38 to 17.08; very low certainty). No included study reported time to mature or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Every estimate is low or very low certainty, from a handful of small trials with varying programmes; the isometric advantage is measured against another exercise, not against usual care, so its absolute value over doing nothing is inferred, not shown.

cards.headline: Ramanarayanan 2023: hand exercise increased cephalic vein calibre by 0.24 mm (95% CI 0.03 to 0.45); 0.29 mm in the two properly controlled RCTs; well tolerated
cards.summary: Ramanarayanan 2023: hand exercise increased cephalic vein calibre by 0.24 mm (95% CI 0.03 to 0.45); 0.29 mm in the two properly controlled RCTs; well tolerated
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of preoperative interventions (Ramanarayanan 2023)
cards.people: Eight eligible studies of preoperative interventions to support fistula maturation in advanced chronic kidney disease — six of hand exercise, one of cholecalciferol supplementation, one of pneumatic compression (Fist Assist device) — with meta-analysis of the hand-exercise studies.
cards.result: The overall effect size of hand exercise on distal cephalic vein calibre was 0.24 mm (95% CI, 0.03 to 0.45). Restricted to the two randomised controlled trials with independent control groups, the effect size was higher, at 0.29 mm (95% CI, 0.11 to 0.47). Hand exercise was well tolerated, especially when confined to the first four weeks. The authors note methodological heterogeneity and call for well-designed prospective randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: A quarter of a millimetre of vein calibre is a surrogate of a surrogate; whether it converts into more fistulas successfully cannulated is exactly what the larger Cochrane analysis could only answer at low certainty.
cards.source: Ramanarayanan S et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of preoperative interventions to support the maturation of arteriovenous fistulae in patients with advanced kidney disease. shelves.title: Taurolidine–citrate catheter locks: pooled citrate-lock data favour antimicrobial locks for bloodstream infection, but the one double-blind taurolidine trial missed its primary endpoint and doubled thrombolytic use
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with central venous catheters, does a taurolidine–citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection compared with a heparin lock?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents/therapeutic use · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Bacteremia/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Catheters, Indwelling/microbiology · Citric Acid/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gram-Positive Bacterial Infections/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Heparin/therapeutic use · Humans · Incidence · Kidney Failure, Chronic/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods · Taurine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Thiadiazines/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pooled and the best-blinded evidence point in different directions. The double-blind randomised trial by Solomon LR et al. (PMID: 20207458) assigned 110 haemodialysis patients with new tunneled catheters to taurolidine-citrate or heparin locks: there were 11 bacteraemic episodes on taurolidine-citrate versus 23 on heparin (1.4 versus 2.4 episodes per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.1), no significant benefit for time to first bacteraemia (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI, 0.2 to 1.6; P=0.4), fewer Gram-negative infections (0.2 versus 1.1 per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.02) but no difference for Gram-positive organisms — and a greater need for thrombolytic therapy (hazard ratio 2.5; 95% CI, 1.3 to 5.2; P=0.008). The smaller randomised trial by Betjes MG et al. (PMID: 14993498), covering 76 catheters in 58 patients, found catheter colonisation and exit-site infections similar between locks, with four cases of catheter-related sepsis on heparin versus none on citrate-taurolidine, a difference the record does not show to be statistically significant. The meta-analysis by Zhao Y et al. (PMID: 24125729) of 13 citrate-lock trials (1,770 patients) found citrate locks reduced catheter-related bloodstream infection overall (risk ratio 0.39; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.56), with the advantage confined to antimicrobial-containing citrate locks (including citrate plus taurolidine) rather than citrate alone. PROPOSED SPLIT: antimicrobial citrate locks probably reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection on pooled evidence, but taurolidine-citrate's own double-blind trial was null on its primary endpoint and cost more thrombolytic use.

cards.headline: Solomon 2010 (double-blind RCT): bacteraemia 1.4 vs 2.4 episodes per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.1); time to first bacteraemia HR 0.66 (NS); thrombolytic therapy HR 2.5 (P=0.008)
cards.summary: Solomon 2010 (double-blind RCT): bacteraemia 1.4 vs 2.4 episodes per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.1); time to first bacteraemia HR 0.66 (NS); thrombolytic therapy HR 2.5 (P=0.008)
cards.people: 110 adult haemodialysis patients with tunneled cuffed intravascular catheters inserted at three centres in Northwest England, randomised at catheter insertion to interdialytic locking with taurolidine-citrate (1.35% taurolidine and 4% citrate) or heparin (5,000 U/mL). Primary endpoints: time to first bacteraemia episode from any cause and time to first thrombolytic therapy.
cards.result: There were 11 bacteraemic episodes in the taurolidine-citrate group and 23 in the heparin group (1.4 and 2.4 episodes per 1,000 patient-days respectively; P=0.1). There was no significant benefit for time to first bacteraemia (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI, 0.2 to 1.6; P=0.4). Taurolidine-citrate was associated with fewer Gram-negative infections (0.2 vs 1.1 infections per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.02) but no difference for Gram-positive organisms (1.1 vs 1.2 per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.8). The need for thrombolytic therapy was greater with taurolidine-citrate (hazard ratio 2.5; 95% CI, 1.3 to 5.2; P=0.008). The authors note the small sample size and that bacteraemia from all causes, not only catheter-related, was counted.
cards.watchOut: The trial counted all-cause bacteraemia, diluting any catheter-specific effect, and was small; but it is the only double-blind test of this exact lock, and its primary endpoint was missed while its harm endpoint (thrombolytics) was hit.
cards.source: Solomon LR et al. A randomized double-blind controlled trial of taurolidine-citrate catheter locks for the prevention of bacteremia in patients treated with hemodialysis. cards.headline: Betjes 2004: 76 catheters — colonisation and exit-site infections similar; catheter-related sepsis four cases on heparin versus none on citrate-taurolidine
cards.summary: Betjes 2004: 76 catheters — colonisation and exit-site infections similar; catheter-related sepsis four cases on heparin versus none on citrate-taurolidine
cards.people: 58 patients receiving a dialysis catheter (76 catheters in total), randomised to catheter locking with heparin or a citrate-taurolidine-containing solution, with routine catheter-lumen blood cultures every two weeks and at removal, and registration of catheter-related sepsis and exit-site infections.
cards.result: The incidence of catheter colonisation progressed slowly over time with no differences between heparin and citrate-taurolidine catheters, and exit-site infections were also similar. In the heparin group, four cases of catheter-related sepsis occurred, as opposed to no sepsis episodes in patients whose catheters were locked with the citrate-taurolidine solution; the record reports this as P<0.5, i.e. not statistically significant. No side effects with the citrate-taurolidine lock were noted.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-six catheters and four events in one arm: the sepsis contrast that makes this trial look positive is a 4-versus-0 split in a small unblinded study, and its own colonisation endpoint — the mechanism the lock is supposed to interrupt — showed no difference.
cards.source: Betjes MG et al. Prevention of dialysis catheter-related sepsis with a citrate-taurolidine-containing lock solution. Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. 2004. PMID: 14993498. cards.headline: Zhao 2014 meta-analysis: citrate locks cut CRBSI (RR 0.39; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.56) across 13 RCTs — but the benefit sits in antimicrobial-containing locks, not citrate alone
cards.summary: Zhao 2014 meta-analysis: citrate locks cut CRBSI (RR 0.39; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.56) across 13 RCTs — but the benefit sits in antimicrobial-containing locks, not citrate alone
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Zhao 2014)
cards.people: 13 randomised controlled trials (1,770 patients, 221,064 catheter-days) comparing citrate locks with heparin locks in haemodialysis patients with central venous catheters.
cards.result: Citrate locks significantly reduced catheter-related bloodstream infection (risk ratio 0.39; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.56; P<0.001). In subgroup analysis, antimicrobial-containing citrate locks (citrate plus gentamicin, citrate plus taurolidine, and citrate plus methylene blue/parabens) were superior to heparin for preventing CRBSI, whereas citrate alone was not (P=0.2). Bleeding episodes were fewer with citrate locks (risk ratio 0.48; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.76; P=0.002); exit-site infection, catheter removal for poor flow, thrombolytic treatment, thrombosis, and all-cause death did not differ. All included studies were performed in Western countries.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate mixes different antimicrobial partners (an antibiotic, taurolidine, a dye combination) and mostly open-label trials; attributing the pooled benefit to taurolidine specifically goes beyond what the subgroup analysis can separate.
cards.source: Zhao Y et al. Citrate versus heparin lock for hemodialysis catheters: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2014. PMID: 24125729. cards.headline: Synthesis: class-level pooled benefit, product-level double-blind null — the honest shelf is a split
cards.summary: Synthesis: class-level pooled benefit, product-level double-blind null — the honest shelf is a split
cards.people: Two randomised taurolidine-citrate trials (110 and 58 patients) and a 13-trial meta-analysis of citrate-based locks (1,770 patients).
cards.result: Taurolidine-citrate double-blind RCT: bacteraemia HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.2 to 1.6), episodes 1.4 vs 2.4 per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.1); thrombolytic HR 2.5 (P=0.008). Small RCT: sepsis 0 vs 4 cases, not significant. Citrate-lock meta-analysis: CRBSI risk ratio 0.39 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.56), driven by antimicrobial-containing locks. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C not set: randomised and meta-analytic evidence both exist but conflict at the level of the named product.
cards.watchOut: Catheter care bundles and exit-site practice changed substantially over the decades these trials span; absolute infection rates from older trials overstate what a lock can add in a modern unit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solomon LR et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2010 (PMID: 20207458); Betjes MG et al. Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. 2004 (PMID: 14993498); Zhao Y et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2014 (PMID: 24125729).

shelves.title: Acute peritoneal dialysis versus haemodialysis for AKI: mortality 58% versus 53% and kidney recovery 28% versus 26% in the one head-to-head trial — the Cochrane pool agrees there is little or no difference
shelves.question: In acute kidney injury needing dialysis in low-resource or critical-care settings, does acute peritoneal dialysis match haemodialysis for survival and kidney recovery?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/metabolism/therapy · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Creatinine/blood · Female · Humans · Kidney/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Peritoneal Dialysis/methods · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on survival and recovery, the two modalities match wherever they have been compared head-to-head. In Gabriel DP et al. (PMID: 18379555), 120 patients with acute tubular necrosis were randomised to high-volume peritoneal dialysis or daily haemodialysis: mortality was 58% versus 53% and renal function recovery 28% versus 26%, both similar, although delivered weekly Kt/V was lower with peritoneal dialysis (3.6 versus 4.7; P<0.01) and time to recovery of renal function was significantly shorter with peritoneal dialysis. The Cochrane review by Liu L et al. (PMID: 29199769), pooling six studies (484 participants), found peritoneal dialysis probably makes little or no difference to all-cause mortality versus extracorporeal therapy (four studies, 383 participants: risk ratio 1.12; 95% CI, 0.81 to 1.55; moderate certainty) or to kidney function recovery (three studies, 333 participants: risk ratio 0.95; 95% CI, 0.68 to 1.35; moderate certainty), with probably slightly less fluid removal (mean difference -0.59 L/day; 95% CI, -1.19 to 0.01; low certainty) and little or no difference in infectious complications (risk ratio 1.03; 95% CI, 0.60 to 1.78). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): acute peritoneal dialysis is a legitimate substitute for haemodialysis in AKI where machines, water, or vascular access are limiting — accepting somewhat weaker clearance and fluid removal.

cards.headline: Gabriel 2008: mortality 58% on high-volume PD vs 53% on daily HD; recovery 28% vs 26%; delivered Kt/V lower on PD (3.6 vs 4.7; P<0.01) but recovery faster
cards.summary: Gabriel 2008: mortality 58% on high-volume PD vs 53% on daily HD; recovery 28% vs 26%; delivered Kt/V lower on PD (3.6 vs 4.7; P<0.01) but recovery faster
cards.people: 120 patients with acute tubular necrosis at a tertiary-care university hospital, assigned to high-volume peritoneal dialysis (n=60) or daily haemodialysis (n=60). Groups were similar for age (64.2 versus 62.5 years), sepsis (42% versus 47%), haemodynamic instability (61% versus 63%), severity scores, and pre-dialysis urea and creatinine. Primary endpoints: hospital survival and renal function recovery.
cards.result: Weekly delivered Kt/V was 3.6 (SD 0.6) with high-volume peritoneal dialysis and 4.7 (SD 0.6) with daily haemodialysis (P<0.01). Metabolic control, mortality rate (58% and 53%), and renal function recovery (28% and 26%) were similar in both groups, whereas peritoneal dialysis was associated with a significantly shorter time to recovery of renal function. The authors conclude both can be considered alternative forms of renal replacement therapy in AKI.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 120 patients from 2008, in acute tubular necrosis specifically; the confidence intervals around a 58%-versus-53% mortality split are wide, and modern continuous therapies were not the comparator. 'Similar' here means 'no difference detected', not 'proven equivalent'.
cards.source: Gabriel DP et al. High volume peritoneal dialysis vs daily hemodialysis: a randomized, controlled trial in patients with acute kidney injury. Kidney International Supplement. 2008. PMID: 18379555. cards.headline: Liu 2017 (Cochrane): PD vs extracorporeal therapy — mortality RR 1.12 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.55), recovery RR 0.95 (0.68 to 1.35), infections RR 1.03; fluid removal slightly less with PD
cards.summary: Liu 2017 (Cochrane): PD vs extracorporeal therapy — mortality RR 1.12 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.55), recovery RR 0.95 (0.68 to 1.35), infections RR 1.03; fluid removal slightly less with PD
cards.people: Six randomised studies (484 participants) of peritoneal dialysis for acute kidney injury: five comparing high-volume PD with daily haemodialysis, extended daily haemodialysis, or continuous renal replacement therapy, and one comparing PD intensities. Overall risk of bias low to unclear.
cards.result: Compared with extracorporeal therapy, PD probably made little or no difference to all-cause mortality (4 studies, 383 participants: risk ratio 1.12; 95% CI, 0.81 to 1.55; I²=69%; moderate certainty) or kidney function recovery (3 studies, 333 participants: risk ratio 0.95; 95% CI, 0.68 to 1.35; I²=0%; moderate certainty). PD probably slightly reduces fluid removal (3 studies, 313 participants: mean difference -0.59 L/day; 95% CI, -1.19 to 0.01; low certainty) and probably made little or no difference to infectious complications (2 studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.03; 95% CI, 0.60 to 1.78; low certainty). Effects on weekly Kt/V, acidosis correction, and dialysis duration were uncertain (very low certainty), with high heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The pooled comparators mix intermittent haemodialysis with continuous therapies, and heterogeneity for mortality was substantial (I²=69%); the moderate-certainty 'little or no difference' is the review's judgement, not a tight equivalence bound — the mortality interval still includes a 55% relative increase.

cochrane systematic review (liu 2017) six randomised studies (484 participants) of peritoneal dialysis for acute kidney injury: five comparing high-volume pd with daily haemodialysis, extended daily haemodialysis, or continuous renal replacement therapy, and one comparing pd intensities. overall risk of bias low to unclear. compared with extracorporeal therapy, pd probably made little or no difference to all-cause mortality (4 studies, 383 participants: risk ratio 1.12; 95% ci, 0.81 to 1.55; i²=69%; moderate certainty) or kidney function recovery (3 studies, 333 participants: risk ratio 0.95; 95% ci, 0.68 to 1.35; i²=0%; moderate certainty). pd probably slightly reduces fluid removal (3 studies, 313 participants: mean difference -0.59 l/day; 95% ci, -1.19 to 0.01; low certainty) and probably made little or no difference to infectious complications (2 studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.03; 95% ci, 0.60 to 1.78; low certainty). effects on weekly kt/v, acidosis correction, and dialysis duration were uncertain (very low certainty), with high heterogeneity. the pooled comparators mix intermittent haemodialysis with continuous therapies, and heterogeneity for mortality was substantial (i²=69%); the moderate-certainty 'little or no difference' is the review's judgement, not a tight equivalence bound — the mortality interval still includes a 55% relative increase. liu l et al. peritoneal dialysis for acute kidney injury. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. pmid: 29199769. mesh: acidosis/therapy · acute kidney injury/mortality/therapy · cause of death · humans · peritoneal dialysis/adverse effects/mortality/statistics & numerical data · randomized controlled trials as topic · recovery of function · renal dialysis/methods

cards.headline: Synthesis: survival and recovery match; clearance and ultrafiltration are weaker — a resource question, not an efficacy gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival and recovery match; clearance and ultrafiltration are weaker — a resource question, not an efficacy gap
cards.people: One head-to-head randomised trial (120 patients, high-volume PD vs daily HD) within a six-study Cochrane pool (484 participants) spanning HD, extended HD, and continuous therapies.
cards.result: Mortality: 58% vs 53% (Gabriel); pooled RR 1.12 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.55). Kidney recovery: 28% vs 26%; pooled RR 0.95 (95% CI 0.68 to 1.35). Delivered Kt/V: 3.6 vs 4.7 (P<0.01) favouring HD. Fluid removal: -0.59 L/day with PD (low certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C not set: a randomised trial plus a Cochrane review carry the claim.
cards.watchOut: Most trial data predate modern PD catheter and cycler practice in AKI programmes; in hypercatabolic or severely fluid-overloaded patients the weaker clearance and ultrafiltration are the operative limits, and the trials were not powered for those subgroups.

shelves.title: Antifungal prophylaxis during antibiotic treatment in peritoneal dialysis: fungal peritonitis 0.92% versus 6.45% of treated bacterial-peritonitis episodes with fluconazole; pooled risk ratio 0.28
shelves.question: In peritoneal dialysis patients receiving antibiotics for peritonitis, does antifungal prophylaxis prevent fungal peritonitis compared with no prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Candidiasis/drug therapy/prevention & control · Catheters, Indwelling/adverse effects · Chemoprevention · Coinfection · Female · Fibrosis · Fluconazole/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Gram-Positive Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/therapy · Laparoscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Peritoneal Dialysis/adverse effects/instrumentation · Peritoneum/pathology · Peritonitis/microbiology/prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Prosthesis-Related Infections/drug therapy · Tissue Adhesions/etiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the specific, dangerous niche of fungal peritonitis following an antibiotic course. In the randomised trial by Restrepo C et al. (PMID: 20634438), patients in a peritoneal dialysis programme who developed bacterial peritonitis, exit-site infection, or tunnel infection were randomised to oral fluconazole 200 mg every 48 hours throughout antibiotic treatment or no prophylaxis: among bacterial-peritonitis episodes, fungal peritonitis followed in 0.92% of fluconazole-covered episodes versus 6.45% without prophylaxis (p=0.0051), with three occurrences of fungal peritonitis in the prophylaxis group versus 15 in the control group within 30–150 days across the studied infections. The Cochrane review by Campbell D et al. (PMID: 28390069) pooled the randomised evidence: antifungal prophylaxis with oral nystatin or fluconazole, compared with placebo or no treatment, may reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis occurring after an antibiotic course (two studies, 817 patients: risk ratio 0.28; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.63; low quality evidence). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): covering antibiotic courses with an oral antifungal substantially reduces subsequent fungal peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis; the evidence is two trials and rated low quality, and it does not extend to preventing bacterial peritonitis or preserving the catheter.

cards.headline: Restrepo 2010: fungal peritonitis in 0.92% of fluconazole-covered bacterial-peritonitis episodes vs 6.45% uncovered (p=0.0051); 3 vs 15 occurrences overall
cards.summary: Restrepo 2010: fungal peritonitis in 0.92% of fluconazole-covered bacterial-peritonitis episodes vs 6.45% uncovered (p=0.0051); 3 vs 15 occurrences overall
cards.people: Patients in a single peritoneal dialysis programme (Colombia, 2004–2007) who developed bacterial peritonitis, exit-site infection, or tunnel infection, randomised to oral fluconazole 200 mg every 48 hours throughout therapeutic antibiotic administration or no prophylaxis (236 patients received prophylaxis and 236 did not, across peritonitis and exit-site/tunnel episodes); 434 peritonitis episodes were analysed, of which 402 (92.6%) were bacterial and 32 (7.3%) mycotic, mainly Candida species.
cards.result: Of the fungal peritonitis cases, 14 (43.73%) were primary (without prior antibiotic use) and 18 (56.25%) secondary. In the prophylaxis group, only three occurrences of fungal peritonitis were observed within 30–150 days of administration, versus 15 in the group without prophylaxis. Among patients with bacterial peritonitis, fungal peritonitis proportions were 0.92% with fluconazole versus 6.45% without (p=0.0051). For exit-site or tunnel infection, one patient in each group developed fungal peritonitis, which was not statistically significant.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial analysed partly by episode rather than by patient, in a programme with a high baseline fungal-peritonitis rate (7.3% of episodes) — the absolute benefit will be smaller where fungal peritonitis is rarer. Primary fungal peritonitis (no preceding antibiotics) is untouched by this strategy by definition.
cards.source: Restrepo C et al. Fungal peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis patients: successful prophylaxis with fluconazole, as demonstrated by prospective randomized control trial. Peritoneal Dialysis International. 2010. PMID: 20634438. cards.headline: Campbell 2017 (Cochrane): antifungal prophylaxis after an antibiotic course — fungal peritonitis risk ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.63), two studies, 817 patients, low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Campbell 2017 (Cochrane): antifungal prophylaxis after an antibiotic course — fungal peritonitis risk ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.63), two studies, 817 patients, low-quality evidence
cards.people: 39 randomised studies (4,435 patients) of antimicrobial strategies to prevent peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis; the antifungal comparison (oral nystatin or fluconazole versus placebo or no treatment, given with antibiotic courses) rests on two studies with 817 patients.
cards.result: Antifungal prophylaxis with oral nystatin/fluconazole compared with placebo/no treatment may reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis occurring after a patient has had an antibiotic course (2 studies, 817 patients: risk ratio 0.28; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.63; low quality evidence). No intervention in the review reduced the risk of catheter removal or replacement. The review notes most available studies were small and of suboptimal quality, with only six enrolling 200 or more patients.
cards.watchOut: A 72% relative reduction sounds decisive, but it is two trials, low quality, with few events, in high-baseline-risk settings; the review's broader verdict is that almost no antimicrobial strategy in PD has proven efficacy beyond this and peri-operative vancomycin for early peritonitis.
cards.source: Campbell D et al. Antimicrobial agents for preventing peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis patients. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28390069. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large relative effect on a rare, catastrophic outcome — worth doing during antibiotic courses, on low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large relative effect on a rare, catastrophic outcome — worth doing during antibiotic courses, on low-quality evidence
cards.people: One single-centre randomised trial of fluconazole prophylaxis (434 peritonitis episodes) pooled in a Cochrane review with one further study (817 patients total across the antifungal comparison).
cards.result: Fungal peritonitis after bacterial peritonitis: 0.92% vs 6.45% (p=0.0051). Pooled risk ratio: 0.28 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.63), low-quality evidence. Catheter removal: not reduced by any intervention in the review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C not set: two randomised studies and a Cochrane pool carry the claim, with the low-quality rating on the face of the shelf.

shelves.title: Vitamin K1 in haemodialysis (VitaVasK): aortic calcification progression 56% lower and coronary 68% lower at 18 months — in a trial stopped early with only 40 of 60 patients analysed
shelves.question: In patients on dialysis, does vitamin K supplementation slow the progression of vascular calcification compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a promising signal from a trial that could not finish. In VitaVasK (Saritas T et al., PMID: 37216675), 60 haemodialysis patients with pre-existing coronary calcification were randomised to standard care alone or with vitamin K1 5 mg orally three times weekly, with calcification progression on CT at 18 months as the hierarchically ordered primary endpoints. Twenty patients dropped out for reasons unrelated to vitamin K1, leaving 23 control and 17 vitamin K1 patients; the trial was stopped early for slow recruitment. Average thoracic aortic calcification progression at 18 months was 56% lower in the vitamin K1 group than control (p=.039); coronary artery calcification progressed significantly within the control group but not within the vitamin K1 group, with average progression 68% lower than control (P=.072 — not significant). Vitamin K1 reduced plasma uncarboxylated matrix Gla protein by 69% at 18 months, and no treatment-related adverse events were noted. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): vitamin K1 may slow vascular calcification progression in haemodialysis, but the entire result rests on 40 analysed patients in an open-label trial stopped early — a hypothesis, not a basis for practice.

cards.headline: Saritas 2022 (VitaVasK): TAC progression 56% lower on vitamin K1 (p=.039); CAC progression 68% lower (P=.072); uncarboxylated MGP down 69% — 20 of 60 randomised patients dropped out
cards.summary: Saritas 2022 (VitaVasK): TAC progression 56% lower on vitamin K1 (p=.039); CAC progression 68% lower (P=.072); uncarboxylated MGP down 69% — 20 of 60 randomised patients dropped out
cards.people: 60 haemodialysis patients with pre-existing coronary artery calcification, randomised to standard care or standard care plus vitamin K1 5 mg orally thrice weekly, with CT calcification scans at baseline, 12, and 18 months. Twenty patients dropped out for reasons unrelated to vitamin K1, leaving 23 control and 17 vitamin K1 patients analysed; the trial was stopped early due to slow recruitment. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: At 18 months, average thoracic aortic calcification progression was 56% lower in the vitamin K1 group compared with control (p=.039). Coronary artery calcification significantly progressed within the control group but not within the vitamin K1 group; average progression at 18 months was 68% lower in the vitamin K1 group (P=.072). Vitamin K1 reduced plasma levels of pro-calcific uncarboxylated matrix Gla protein by 69% at 18 months. No treatment-related adverse events were noted.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, stopped early, one-third of patients missing from the analysis, and a surrogate imaging endpoint with relative percentage changes on small absolute scores — every classic fragility marker is present. The coronary endpoint, first in the hierarchy alongside aortic, did not reach significance (P=.072).
cards.source: Saritas T et al. Vitamin K1 and progression of cardiovascular calcifications in hemodialysis patients: the VitaVasK randomized controlled trial. Clinical Kidney Journal. 2022. PMID: 37216675. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Early ramipril in children with Alport syndrome (EARLY PRO-TECT): progression hazard ratio 0.51 — not significant in the 22 randomised children, with a clean safety record over 216 patient-years
shelves.question: In children with Alport syndrome, does early ramipril delay progression to kidney failure compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects · Bayes Theorem · Child · Double-Blind Method · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Nephritis, Hereditary/genetics · Prospective Studies · Ramipril/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direction is consistent, the randomised numbers are tiny, and the firmest finding is safety. In EARLY PRO-TECT (Gross O et al., PMID: 32299679), 66 oligosymptomatic children with Alport syndrome were enrolled at 14 German sites; only 22 could be randomised to ramipril or placebo for three to six years, while 44 joined an open-arm comparison. In the randomised arm, ramipril decreased the risk of disease progression by almost half (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.12 to 2.20 — not significant), diminished the slope of albuminuria progression, and slowed glomerular filtration decline. Adjusted analysis of the open-label treated children versus untreated children again suggested progression reduced by almost half (0.53; 95% CI 0.22 to 1.29), and Bayesian synthesis combining the data gave a hazard ratio of 0.52 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.39). Safety was the co-primary endpoint and was met: over 216.4 patient-years on ramipril there were no safety issues (adverse event rate-ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.53). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): early ramipril appears safe in children with Alport syndrome and may halve progression, but the randomised evidence is 22 children and every efficacy interval crosses 1.

cards.headline: Gross 2020 (EARLY PRO-TECT): randomised progression HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.12 to 2.20); adverse-event rate-ratio 1.00 (0.66 to 1.53) over 216.4 patient-years on ramipril
cards.summary: Gross 2020 (EARLY PRO-TECT): randomised progression HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.12 to 2.20); adverse-event rate-ratio 1.00 (0.66 to 1.53) over 216.4 patient-years on ramipril
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with open-arm comparison (Gross 2020, EARLY PRO-TECT Alport)
cards.people: 66 oligosymptomatic children with Alport syndrome at 14 German sites: 22 randomised to ramipril or placebo for three to six years plus six months' follow-up, and 44 (pretreated children and those whose parents refused randomisation) in an open-arm comparison against prospective real-world data from untreated children. Co-primary endpoints: safety (adverse drug reactions) and efficacy (time to progression).
cards.result: Ramipril therapy showed no safety issues (total of 216.4 patient-years on ramipril; adverse event rate-ratio 1.00; 95% CI, 0.66 to 1.53). In the randomised arm, ramipril decreased the risk of disease progression by almost half (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.12 to 2.20), diminished the slope of albuminuria progression, and slowed the decline in glomerular filtration — none of it statistically significant. In adjusted analysis, open-label treated children versus untreated children again suggested progression reduced by almost half (0.53; 95% CI 0.22 to 1.29). Bayesian evidence synthesis incorporating these data gave a hazard ratio of 0.52 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.39).
cards.watchOut: A rare-disease trial that could randomise only a third of its enrolled children; the efficacy case leans on non-randomised open-arm comparisons and a Bayesian synthesis of them, which is exactly the structure that inflates treatment effects. The safety finding — the co-primary endpoint actually met — is the solid part.

adverse event rate-ratio 1.00; 95% ci, 0.66 to 1.53). in the randomised arm, ramipril decreased the risk of disease progression by almost half (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% ci 0.12 to 2.20), diminished the slope of albuminuria progression, and slowed the decline in glomerular filtration — none of it statistically significant. in adjusted analysis, open-label treated children versus untreated children again suggested progression reduced by almost half (0.53; 95% ci 0.22 to 1.29). bayesian evidence synthesis incorporating these data gave a hazard ratio of 0.52 (95% ci 0.19 to 1.39). a rare-disease trial that could randomise only a third of its enrolled children; the efficacy case leans on non-randomised open-arm comparisons and a bayesian synthesis of them, which is exactly the structure that inflates treatment effects. the safety finding — the co-primary endpoint actually met — is the solid part. gross o et al. a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial with open-arm comparison indicates safety and efficacy of nephroprotective therapy with ramipril in children with alport's syndrome. kidney international. 2020. pmid: 32299679. registry id: nct01485978. mesh: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/adverse effects · bayes theorem · child · double-blind method · glomerular filtration rate · humans · nephritis, hereditary/genetics · prospective studies · ramipril/adverse effects

cards.headline: Synthesis: safety established about as well as a rare-disease trial can; efficacy a consistent, unproven halving of progression
cards.summary: Synthesis: safety established about as well as a rare-disease trial can; efficacy a consistent, unproven halving of progression
cards.people: One randomised trial programme in 66 children with Alport syndrome (22 randomised, 44 open-arm), three to six years of treatment.
cards.result: Progression hazard ratio: 0.51 randomised (95% CI 0.12 to 2.20); 0.53 open-arm adjusted (0.22 to 1.29); 0.52 Bayesian synthesis (0.19 to 1.39) — all intervals include 1. Safety: adverse event rate-ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.53) over 216.4 patient-years. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claim in a rare disease.
cards.watchOut: Progression here is a composite of albuminuria and function stages over years, not kidney failure itself; children treated today will be followed for decades on the strength of this signal plus adult ACE-inhibitor evidence outside this record set.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gross O et al. Kidney International. 2020 (PMID: 32299679).

shelves.title: Nasal mupirocin in peritoneal dialysis carriers: S. aureus exit-site infections cut from 44 to 14 episodes — total exit-site infections and peritonitis not significantly changed
shelves.question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does nasal mupirocin eradication of Staphylococcus aureus carriage reduce exit-site infection and peritonitis compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Catheterization/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Mupirocin/administration & dosage · Ointments · Peritoneal Dialysis, Continuous Ambulatory/instrumentation · Prospective Studies · Staphylococcal Infections/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Staphylococcus aureus/isolation & purification · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for staphylococcal exit-site infection specifically, in proven nasal carriers; not for peritonitis. The Mupirocin Study Group trial (PMID: 8959632) screened 1,144 continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients in nine European centres and randomised 267 confirmed nasal carriers of Staphylococcus aureus to calcium mupirocin 2% nasal ointment or placebo, used twice daily for five days every four weeks for up to 18 months. Nasal carriage fell to 10% on mupirocin versus 48% on placebo. Total exit-site infections were 33 in 1,390 patient-months on mupirocin versus 55 in 1,236 patient-months on placebo (not significant), but S. aureus caused 14 episodes in the mupirocin group versus 44 in the control group (P=0.006); there were no differences in tunnel infection or peritonitis, and no progressive increase in mupirocin resistance over time. The meta-analysis by Tacconelli E et al. (PMID: 14689344), pooling ten studies and 2,445 dialysis patients, found mupirocin reduced S. aureus infections by 68% relative (95% CI, 57% to 76%) overall, with relative reductions among peritoneal dialysis patients of 66% for peritonitis and 62% for exit-site infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in PD patients who carry S. aureus in the nose, periodic nasal mupirocin prevents staphylococcal exit-site infections; the one large trial did not significantly reduce all-cause exit-site infection or peritonitis.

cards.headline: Mupirocin Study Group 1996: carriage 10% vs 48%; S. aureus exit-site infections 14 vs 44 episodes (P=0.006); all exit-site infections 33 vs 55 (NS); peritonitis no different
cards.summary: Mupirocin Study Group 1996: carriage 10% vs 48%; S. aureus exit-site infections 14 vs 44 episodes (P=0.006); all exit-site infections 33 vs 55 (NS); peritonitis no different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Mupirocin Study Group 1996)
cards.people: 267 confirmed nasal carriers of Staphylococcus aureus (from 1,144 screened continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients in nine European centres), randomised to calcium mupirocin 2% nasal ointment (n=134) or placebo ointment (n=133), each used twice daily for five consecutive days every four weeks, followed for up to 18 months. Groups did not differ in demographics, cause of renal failure, catheter type, system used, or exit-site care method.
cards.result: Nasal carriage fell to 10% in the mupirocin group and 48% in the placebo group. There were 55 exit-site infections in 1,236 patient-months in the control group and 33 in 1,390 patient-months in the treatment group (not significant). S. aureus caused 14 episodes of exit-site infection in the mupirocin group and 44 in the control group (P=0.006, mixed-effects Poisson regression). There were no differences in the rate of tunnel infection or peritonitis, no differences in patient outcome or adverse events, and no evidence of a progressive increase in resistance to mupirocin with time.
cards.watchOut: Only nasal carriers were randomised — the result does not cover non-carriers — and the headline success is organism-specific: the all-cause exit-site infection endpoint, the one a programme actually feels, did not reach significance, and peritonitis was flat. The trial is from 1996, before current exit-site care standards.
cards.source: Mupirocin Study Group. Nasal mupirocin prevents Staphylococcus aureus exit-site infection during peritoneal dialysis. Mupirocin Study Group. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 1996. PMID: 8959632. cards.headline: Tacconelli 2003 meta-analysis: mupirocin reduced S. aureus infections by 68% relative (95% CI 57% to 76%); in PD patients, peritonitis down 66% relative and exit-site infections 62% relative
cards.summary: Tacconelli 2003 meta-analysis: mupirocin reduced S. aureus infections by 68% relative (95% CI 57% to 76%); in PD patients, peritonitis down 66% relative and exit-site infections 62% relative
cards.people: Ten studies (nine articles; randomised trials and cohort studies) totalling 2,445 adults undergoing haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, comparing mupirocin prophylaxis (nasal or exit-site) with placebo or no therapy for prevention of S. aureus infection.
cards.result: Use of mupirocin reduced the rate of S. aureus infections by 68% (95% CI, 57% to 76%) among all patients undergoing dialysis; risk reductions were 80% (95% CI, 65% to 89%) among haemodialysis patients and 63% (95% CI, 50% to 73%) among peritoneal dialysis patients — these are relative reductions. Stratified by infection type, S. aureus bacteraemia was reduced by 78% among haemodialysis patients, and peritonitis and exit-site infections were reduced by 66% and 62% respectively among peritoneal dialysis patients (relative reductions). The authors note optimal regimens that minimise emergence of mupirocin resistance need exploration.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes nasal with exit-site application, randomised with cohort studies, and haemodialysis with peritoneal dialysis; its peritonitis estimate for PD (66% relative reduction) is more optimistic than the one large nasal-mupirocin PD trial above, which found no peritonitis difference — the discrepancy is visible on the face of this shelf.
cards.source: Tacconelli E et al. Mupirocin prophylaxis to prevent Staphylococcus aureus infection in patients undergoing dialysis: a meta-analysis. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2003. PMID: 14689344. cards.headline: Synthesis: decolonising carriers prevents staphylococcal exit-site infections; peritonitis prevention is claimed by the pool and denied by the biggest trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: decolonising carriers prevents staphylococcal exit-site infections; peritonitis prevention is claimed by the pool and denied by the biggest trial
cards.people: One large double-blind trial in 267 PD nasal carriers (18 months) and a ten-study meta-analysis across dialysis modalities (2,445 patients).
cards.result: S. aureus exit-site infections: 14 vs 44 episodes (P=0.006). All exit-site infections: 33 vs 55 (not significant). Peritonitis: no difference in the trial; 66% relative reduction in the PD subgroup of the meta-analysis. Carriage eradication: 10% vs 48% still carriers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for S. aureus exit-site infection in carriers, Tier C not set: a randomised trial plus a meta-analysis carry the shelf, with their disagreement on peritonitis stated.
cards.watchOut: Programmes must screen for carriage to use this evidence, and widespread periodic mupirocin raises the resistance question the 1996 trial could only answer for 18 months.

shelves.title: Antimicrobial urinary catheters: silver-alloy catheters did not reduce symptomatic catheter infection at all (12.5% versus 12.6%) in a 7,102-patient trial; nitrofural catheters fell short of the worthwhile threshold
shelves.question: In adults needing short-term urinary catheterisation in hospital, do antimicrobial catheters (silver alloy-coated or nitrofural-impregnated) reduce symptomatic catheter-associated urinary tract infection compared with a standard catheter?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Catheter-Related Infections/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrofurazone/administration & dosage · Urinary Catheterization/adverse effects · Urinary Tract Infections/prevention & control · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one very large pragmatic trial settles the silver question and nearly settles the nitrofural one. Among 7,102 randomised adults needing short-term catheterisation, symptomatic urinary tract infection for which an antibiotic was prescribed occurred by 6 weeks in 263 (12.5%) of 2,097 patients with a silver alloy-coated catheter versus 271 (12.6%) of 2,144 with a standard PTFE catheter (difference -0.1% [95% CI -2.4 to 2.2]), and in 228 (10.6%) of 2,153 with a nitrofural-impregnated catheter (difference -2.1% [-4.2 to 0.1]) — short of the 3.3% absolute reduction the trialists had set as the threshold for recommending routine use, and bought with higher rates of catheter-related discomfort. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine antimicrobial catheters are not supported for short-term hospital catheterisation — silver alloy does not work, and nitrofural's smaller, uncertain effect comes with more discomfort.

cards.headline: Pickard 2012: symptomatic UTI in 12.5% (silver alloy) and 10.6% (nitrofural) versus 12.6% (standard catheter) — differences -0.1% and -2.1%, against a 3.3% worthwhile threshold
cards.summary: Pickard 2012: symptomatic UTI in 12.5% (silver alloy) and 10.6% (nitrofural) versus 12.6% (standard catheter) — differences -0.1% and -2.1%, against a 3.3% worthwhile threshold
cards.people: 7,102 adults (aged 16 years or older) requiring short-term (up to 14 days) catheterisation at 24 UK hospitals, randomised 1:1:1 to a silver alloy-coated catheter, a nitrofural-impregnated catheter or a standard PTFE-coated catheter; participants and staff were unmasked, outcomes collected by trial staff and patient questionnaires for 6 weeks; 708 (10%) were not catheterised, did not confirm consent or withdrew and were excluded from the primary analyses.
cards.result: The primary outcome — symptomatic urinary tract infection for which an antibiotic was prescribed by 6 weeks — occurred in 263 (12.5%) of 2,097 silver-alloy patients versus 271 (12.6%) of 2,144 controls (difference -0.1% [95% CI -2.4 to 2.2]), and in 228 (10.6%) of 2,153 nitrofural patients (difference -2.1% [-4.2 to 0.1]). The trialists had postulated that a 3.3% absolute reduction would justify routine use; neither catheter met it. Catheter-related discomfort rates were higher in the nitrofural group than in the other groups.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked allocation and a symptom-plus-prescription outcome leave room for ascertainment bias, though that bias would be expected to favour the novel catheters, not the null. The trial covers short-term hospital catheterisation only — it does not address long-term or intermittent catheterisation.
cards.source: Pickard R et al. Antimicrobial catheters for reduction of symptomatic urinary tract infection in adults requiring short-term catheterisation in hospital: a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2012. PMID: 23134837. Registry ID: ISRCTN75198618. cards.headline: Synthesis: one definitive pragmatic trial — antimicrobial coatings are not the answer to catheter infection
cards.summary: Synthesis: one definitive pragmatic trial — antimicrobial coatings are not the answer to catheter infection
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial (7,102 randomised adults, 6,394 in the primary analyses) comparing silver alloy-coated, nitrofural-impregnated and standard catheters for short-term hospital catheterisation.
cards.result: Symptomatic UTI by 6 weeks: 12.5% (silver alloy), 10.6% (nitrofural), 12.6% (standard). Differences: -0.1% (95% CI -2.4 to 2.2) and -2.1% (-4.2 to 0.1), against a prespecified 3.3% worthwhile threshold. Discomfort: higher with nitrofural. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: this is a null result from a single very large trial, following the library's precedent for large single-trial nulls; the nitrofural confidence interval does not exclude a small benefit, which the discomfort penalty and the missed threshold argue against chasing.

shelves.title: Sevelamer versus calcium-based binders in non-dialysis CKD: the single INDEPENDENT pilot programme (212 patients) found lower mortality and slower calcification signals with sevelamer — with no effect sizes in its records and no replication trial
shelves.question: In non-dialysis chronic kidney disease with hyperphosphataemia, does sevelamer improve phosphate control, vascular calcification, or survival compared with calcium-based binders?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Aged · Biomarkers · Calcium Carbonate · Cause of Death · Chelating Agents · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Italy · Kidney Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphates · Phosphorus · Pilot Projects · Polyamines · Renal Dialysis · Sevelamer · Survival Analysis · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Calcification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small trial programme (INDEPENDENT), and its records report direction more often than effect sizes. In the INDEPENDENT pilot randomised trial (212 patients with stage 3–4 CKD), all-cause mortality and the composite of death or dialysis inception were lower on sevelamer than calcium carbonate, with only a non-significant trend for dialysis inception alone; the record reports no effect size or event counts (Di Iorio 2012, PMID: 22241819). A post hoc analysis of the 113 participants with coronary calcification found sevelamer independently predicted lower risk only when calcification progression was absent or moderate (Russo 2015, PMID: 24599830). The programme's patient-level economic analysis found sevelamer gained 0.06 life-years and saved €5,615 per patient over 3 years, driven by the mortality difference (Ruggeri 2014, PMID: 25171148). On phosphate control itself, the trial record states only the target range both arms were held to (2.7–4.6 mg/dL in stage 3–4 CKD) and reports no comparative phosphate levels. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pilot trial programme; larger trials needed, as the trial's own authors state.

cards.headline: Di Iorio 2012 (INDEPENDENT pilot trial): in 212 stage 3–4 CKD patients, mortality and the death-or-dialysis composite were lower on sevelamer than calcium carbonate — the record reports no effect size or event counts
cards.summary: Di Iorio 2012 (INDEPENDENT pilot trial): in 212 stage 3–4 CKD patients, mortality and the death-or-dialysis composite were lower on sevelamer than calcium carbonate — the record reports no effect size or event counts
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial — INDEPENDENT programme (Di Iorio 2012)
cards.people: 212 consecutive outpatients with stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease, randomised to sevelamer (n = 107) or calcium carbonate (n = 105) in a multicentre, nonblinded pilot study; phosphate was maintained at 2.7–4.6 mg/dL for stage 3–4 CKD, coronary calcification was scored by CT at entry and 6, 12, 18 and 24 months, and outcomes were recorded for up to 36 months.
cards.result: In patients randomised to sevelamer, all-cause mortality (the primary end point) and the composite end point of mortality or dialysis inception were lower than with calcium carbonate; a non-significant trend was noted for dialysis inception alone. The record reports no hazard ratio, relative risk, or event counts for these outcomes. The authors conclude sevelamer provided benefits on mortality and the composite but not on dialysis inception, and that larger studies are needed to confirm these results.
cards.watchOut: A nonblinded pilot of 212 patients whose abstract reports the direction of the mortality result without its size — a mortality claim of unknown magnitude from a single small programme should not be quoted as an established survival benefit.
cards.source: Di Iorio B et al. Mortality in kidney disease patients treated with phosphate binders: a randomized study. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2012. PMID: 22241819. cards.headline: Russo 2015: in the 113 INDEPENDENT participants with coronary calcification, calcium carbonate was associated with faster calcification progression and more events; sevelamer predicted lower risk only when calcification progression was absent or moderate
cards.summary: Russo 2015: in the 113 INDEPENDENT participants with coronary calcification, calcium carbonate was associated with faster calcification progression and more events; sevelamer predicted lower risk only when calcification progression was absent or moderate
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised trial — INDEPENDENT programme (Russo 2015)
cards.people: 113 patients with stage 3–4 CKD and evidence of coronary artery calcification, a post hoc subgroup of the phosphorus-binder study, all on a phosphorus-restricted diet and randomised to added calcium carbonate or sevelamer, followed to first event or 36 months.
cards.result: Treatment with calcium carbonate was associated with increased coronary calcification progression and with occurrence of all-cause mortality, dialysis initiation, and the composite end point. After adjustment, sevelamer use was the only independent predictive factor of reduced risk of each end point, but only if calcification progression was either absent or moderate; accelerated progression (annual increase above the cohort's 75th percentile) increased the risk of all-cause mortality and the composite end point (p = 0.01) independently of sevelamer use. The record reports no effect sizes for the binder comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and subgroup-only: the sevelamer advantage is conditional on a calcification-progression category measured during the trial, which is exactly the kind of analysis that can manufacture apparent benefit — hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
cards.source: Russo D et al. Effects of phosphorus-restricted diet and phosphate-binding therapy on outcomes in patients with chronic kidney disease. Journal of Nephrology. 2015. PMID: 24599830. cards.headline: Ruggeri 2014: patient-level INDEPENDENT data made sevelamer cost-saving versus calcium carbonate in Italy — 0.06 extra life-years and €5,615 saved per patient over 3 years, dominant in 87.1% of bootstrap replicates
cards.summary: Ruggeri 2014: patient-level INDEPENDENT data made sevelamer cost-saving versus calcium carbonate in Italy — 0.06 extra life-years and €5,615 saved per patient over 3 years, dominant in 87.1% of bootstrap replicates
cards.type: Patient-level cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised trial — INDEPENDENT programme (Ruggeri 2014)
cards.people: All 212 INDEPENDENT-CKD participants (107 sevelamer, 105 calcium carbonate) with patient-level data on mortality, dialysis inception and binder dose, plus post hoc chart-review hospitalisation and dialysis data; costs in 2012 euros from the Italian National Health Service perspective over the 3-year study period.
cards.result: Sevelamer was associated with 0.06 additional life-years (95% CI −0.04 to 0.16) and cost savings of €5,615 per patient (95% CI −10,066 to −1,164) versus calcium carbonate, and was dominant (more effective and less costly) in 87.1% of 10,000 bootstrap replicates; results were similar in patients who did not start dialysis. The authors state the results were driven by a significant reduction in all-cause mortality and significantly fewer hospitalisations in the sevelamer group, offsetting sevelamer's higher acquisition cost.
cards.watchOut: The economics inherit the trial's mortality result wholesale: the life-year confidence interval crosses zero (−0.04 to 0.16), so if the mortality difference is a small-trial artefact, the cost-saving conclusion falls with it.
cards.source: Ruggeri M et al. Sevelamer is cost-saving vs. calcium carbonate in non-dialysis-dependent CKD patients in italy: a patient-level cost-effectiveness analysis of the INDEPENDENT study. Blood Purification. 2014. PMID: 25171148. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one Italian pilot programme (212 patients) points the same way on mortality, calcification and cost — but reports few effect sizes, and phosphate levels themselves are not compared in its records
cards.summary: Synthesis: one Italian pilot programme (212 patients) points the same way on mortality, calcification and cost — but reports few effect sizes, and phosphate levels themselves are not compared in its records
cards.people: The carded evidence is a single trial programme: the INDEPENDENT pilot randomised trial (212 patients), its post hoc calcification subgroup (113 patients), and its patient-level cost-effectiveness analysis (the same 212 patients). No independent second trial is carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Mortality and the death-or-dialysis composite favoured sevelamer over calcium carbonate, with dialysis inception alone not significantly different (Di Iorio 2012 — no effect size in the record). Calcification progression was greater on calcium carbonate, and sevelamer's lower risk was confined to patients without accelerated progression (Russo 2015). The economic analysis found sevelamer dominant in most replicates, driven by that same mortality signal (Ruggeri 2014). Whether sevelamer controls phosphate better is not answered by these records: both arms were titrated to the same target range (2.7–4.6 mg/dL in stage 3–4 CKD) and no comparative phosphate levels are reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
cards.watchOut: All three cards trace back to the same 212 randomised patients — agreement between them is not replication, and the shelf's survival claim rests entirely on one nonblinded pilot trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Di Iorio B et al. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2012 (PMID: 22241819); Russo D et al. Journal of Nephrology. 2015 (PMID: 24599830); Ruggeri M et al. Blood Purification. 2014 (PMID: 25171148).

shelves.title: Finerenone and blood pressure in resistant hypertension with CKD: a modest reduction (about 6 mmHg vs placebo), smaller than spironolactone's but with far less hyperkalaemia — indirect comparison only
shelves.question: Does finerenone lower blood pressure in resistant hypertension with CKD?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Albuminuria · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Naphthyridines · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (FIDELIO-DKD / FIGARO-DKD / ARTS-DN), capped at POSSIBLE. In the subgroup that answers this shelf's question directly — 624 FIDELITY patients with treatment-resistant hypertension and CKD meeting AMBER-trial eligibility — finerenone lowered systolic blood pressure by a least-squares mean of 7.1 mmHg versus 1.3 mmHg on placebo (between-group difference −5.74 mmHg, 95% CI −7.99 to −3.49) at about 17 weeks, a smaller reduction than spironolactone achieved in AMBER (−11.7 and −10.8 mmHg in its two arms) but with far less hyperkalaemia: serum potassium 5.5 mmol/L (5.5 mEq/L) or above in 12% on finerenone versus 3% on placebo, against 35% and 64% in the spironolactone arms, and hyperkalaemia discontinuation of 0.3% versus 7% and 23% (Agarwal 2023, PMID: 36864892). The parent FIDELIO-DKD analysis (N = 5,669) confirms finerenone reduced office systolic pressure across all baseline quartiles, though blood-pressure change explained only 13.8% of its kidney-outcome effect (Ruilope 2022, PMID: 36252131), and 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in ARTS-DN showed placebo-adjusted systolic reductions of about 8–11 mmHg at the 10–20 mg doses in a 240-patient subset (Agarwal 2023, PMID: 36583355). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): finerenone lowers blood pressure modestly in resistant hypertension with CKD — less than spironolactone in indirect comparison, with a lower hyperkalaemia burden; there is no head-to-head randomised trial against spironolactone.

cards.headline: Ruilope 2022 (FIDELIO-DKD, N = 5,669): finerenone reduced office systolic blood pressure across every baseline quartile in CKD with type 2 diabetes, but blood-pressure change explained only 13.8% of its kidney-outcome benefit
cards.summary: Ruilope 2022 (FIDELIO-DKD, N = 5,669): finerenone reduced office systolic blood pressure across every baseline quartile in CKD with type 2 diabetes, but blood-pressure change explained only 13.8% of its kidney-outcome benefit
cards.type: Prespecified analysis of a randomised controlled trial, FIDELIO-DKD (Ruilope 2022)
cards.people: Patients in the FIDELIO-DKD trial with type 2 diabetes, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 30 to 5000 mg/g, and estimated glomerular filtration rate of 25 to <75 mL/min per 1.73 m2 receiving optimized renin-angiotensin system blockade, randomized to finerenone or placebo; for this analysis patients (N = 5669) were grouped by baseline office systolic blood pressure (SBP) quartiles.
cards.result: Finerenone reduced office SBP across the baseline office SBP quartiles, including patients with baseline office SBP of >148 mm Hg. Patients with lower baseline office SBP quartile and greater declines from baseline in SBP had better cardiorenal outcomes. The risk of the primary kidney and key secondary cardiovascular composite outcomes was consistently reduced with finerenone versus placebo irrespective of baseline office SBP quartiles (P for interaction 0.87 and 0.78, respectively). A time-varying analysis attributed 13.8% of the treatment effect on the primary kidney composite outcome and 12.6% of the effect on the key secondary cardiovascular outcome to the change in office SBP. The record reports no single pooled mmHg effect size for this analysis — printed plainly here rather than estimated.
cards.watchOut: This is a blood-pressure analysis inside a kidney-outcomes trial in diabetic CKD, not a hypertension trial: it establishes that finerenone lowers office pressure modestly and consistently, not that it is an antihypertensive of first resort.
cards.source: Ruilope LM et al. Blood Pressure and Cardiorenal Outcomes With Finerenone in Chronic Kidney Disease in Type 2 Diabetes. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2022. PMID: 36252131. Registry ID: NCT02540993. cards.headline: Agarwal 2023: in 624 patients with treatment-resistant hypertension and CKD, finerenone lowered systolic pressure by 5.74 mmHg more than placebo — less than spironolactone in indirect comparison, but with far less hyperkalaemia (12% vs 35%–64% reaching potassium 5.5 mmol/L or above)
cards.summary: Agarwal 2023: in 624 patients with treatment-resistant hypertension and CKD, finerenone lowered systolic pressure by 5.74 mmHg more than placebo — less than spironolactone in indirect comparison, but with far less hyperkalaemia (12% vs 35%–64% reaching potassium 5.5 mmol/L or above)
cards.type: Post hoc indirect comparison across trial programmes (Agarwal 2023)
cards.people: Post hoc indirect comparison: a subgroup of 624 patients in FIDELITY (the pooled FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD analysis) with treatment-resistant hypertension and chronic kidney disease meeting the eligibility criteria of the AMBER trial, compared at about 17 weeks with 295 AMBER patients treated with spironolactone plus patiromer or spironolactone plus placebo at 12 weeks.
cards.result: The least squares mean change in systolic blood pressure was −7.1 mmHg for finerenone and −1.3 mmHg for placebo (between-group difference −5.74 [95% CI −7.99 to −3.49], P < .0001), versus −11.7 mmHg for spironolactone + patiromer and −10.8 mmHg for spironolactone + placebo (between-group difference −1.0 [95% CI −4.4 to 2.4], P = .58). The incidence of serum potassium ≥5.5 mmol/L (5.5 mEq/L) was 12% for finerenone and 3% for placebo versus 35% with spironolactone + patiromer and 64% with spironolactone + placebo. Treatment discontinuation due to hyperkalaemia was 0.3% for finerenone and 0% for placebo versus 7% for spironolactone + patiromer and 23% for spironolactone + placebo. The authors conclude finerenone was associated with a lower systolic reduction and a lower risk of hyperkalaemia and discontinuation than spironolactone with or without patiromer.
cards.watchOut: This is a post hoc, cross-trial indirect comparison — finerenone and spironolactone were never randomised against each other, the timepoints differ (about 17 versus 12 weeks), and the resistant-hypertension subgroup was selected to match another trial's eligibility, so the contrast is hypothesis-grading, not head-to-head proof.
cards.source: Agarwal R et al. A comparative post hoc analysis of finerenone and spironolactone in resistant hypertension in moderate-to-advanced chronic kidney disease. cards.headline: Agarwal 2023 (ARTS-DN ambulatory substudy): finerenone lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by 8.3 to 11.2 mmHg versus placebo at the 10–20 mg doses over 90 days
cards.summary: Agarwal 2023 (ARTS-DN ambulatory substudy): finerenone lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by 8.3 to 11.2 mmHg versus placebo at the 10–20 mg doses over 90 days
cards.type: Ambulatory blood pressure substudy of a phase 2b randomised trial, ARTS-DN (Agarwal 2023)
cards.people: ARTS-DN was a phase 2b trial that randomized 823 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g and estimated glomerular filtration rate 30–90 ml/min per 1.73 m2) to placebo or finerenone 1.25–20 mg once daily for 90 days; 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was performed in a subset of 240 patients at screening, Day 60, and Day 90.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted change in 24-h ambulatory systolic blood pressure at Day 90 was −8.3 mmHg (95% CI, −16.6 to 0.1) for finerenone 10 mg (n = 27), −11.2 mmHg (95% CI, −18.8 to −3.6) for finerenone 15 mg (n = 34), and −9.9 mmHg (95% CI, −17.7 to −2.0) for finerenone 20 mg (n = 31). Mean daytime and night-time systolic recordings were similarly reduced, finerenone did not increase the incidence of systolic dipping, and despite a short half-life the reduction persisted over the entire 24-hour interval with once-daily morning dosing.
cards.watchOut: The ambulatory subset is small (240 of 823 patients, with 27–34 patients per dose group reported) and the treatment period is 90 days in diabetic CKD — it characterises the pressure effect precisely but says nothing about resistant hypertension specifically or about long-term outcomes.
cards.source: Agarwal R et al. Effect of finerenone on ambulatory blood pressure in chronic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes. Journal of hypertension. 2023. PMID: 36583355. Registry ID: NCT01874431. cards.headline: Synthesis: finerenone lowers blood pressure in CKD by roughly 6 mmHg on office measurement in resistant hypertension and 8–11 mmHg on ambulatory measurement at higher doses — a real but modest effect, smaller than spironolactone's, bought with less hyperkalaemia
cards.summary: Synthesis: finerenone lowers blood pressure in CKD by roughly 6 mmHg on office measurement in resistant hypertension and 8–11 mmHg on ambulatory measurement at higher doses — a real but modest effect, smaller than spironolactone's, bought with less hyperkalaemia
cards.people: The carded evidence, all from one development programme: the FIDELIO-DKD blood-pressure analysis (N = 5,669), a post hoc resistant-hypertension subgroup of the pooled FIDELITY population (624 patients) indirectly compared with the AMBER spironolactone trial (295 patients), and the ARTS-DN ambulatory monitoring substudy (240 of 823 randomised patients). Total carded participants exceed 6,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the single programme and the indirect spironolactone comparison, printed here.
cards.result: Finerenone reduced office systolic pressure across all baseline quartiles in FIDELIO-DKD, with pressure change mediating only 13.8% of its kidney benefit (Ruilope 2022). In treatment-resistant hypertension with CKD the placebo-adjusted office reduction was −5.74 mmHg, against about −11 mmHg for spironolactone in AMBER, while potassium ≥5.5 mmol/L (5.5 mEq/L) occurred in 12% on finerenone versus 35%–64% on spironolactone and hyperkalaemia discontinuation in 0.3% versus 7%–23% (Agarwal 2023). Ambulatory monitoring showed placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic reductions of −8.3 to −11.2 mmHg at 10–20 mg doses (Agarwal 2023, ARTS-DN). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised finerenone against spironolactone head-to-head, and none of the carded trials was designed as a resistant-hypertension treatment trial — the resistant-hypertension number comes from a post hoc subgroup built to resemble the AMBER population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ruilope LM et al. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2022 (PMID: 36252131); Agarwal R et al. Clinical kidney journal. 2023 (PMID: 36864892); Agarwal R et al. Journal of hypertension. 2023 (PMID: 36583355).
