shelves.title: Peritoneal dialysis versus hemodialysis survival in the first 2 years (SPLIT, observational only): similar or slightly better overall, worse in diabetic cohorts
shelves.question: In adults with end-stage kidney disease, is peritoneal dialysis associated with similar survival to hemodialysis in the first 2 years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Logistic Models · Male · Matched-Pair Analysis · Middle Aged · Peritoneal Dialysis · Proportional Hazards Models · Renal Dialysis · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face; the evidence divides by diabetes status. In the largest matched comparison, 6,337 propensity-matched pairs of incident US dialysis patients, survival modestly favoured peritoneal dialysis (PD) in exactly this shelf's window — 85.8% versus 80.7% at 12 months and 71.1% versus 68.0% at 24 months, overall hazard ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.00) — with the PD advantage concentrated in patients under 65, without cardiovascular disease and without diabetes, and no difference from day 90 in the overall sensitivity analysis (HR 1.05) (Weinhandl 2010, PMID: 20133483). A Canary Islands incident cohort (1,469 patients) likewise found higher early survival on PD, including at 24 months (90% versus 65% unadjusted), though its adjusted first-year relative risk of 0.509 and its unadjusted gaps are large enough to suggest residual selection differences (Rufino 2011, PMID: 21461011). In patients with diabetes the direction reverses: a meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies in diabetic end-stage kidney disease found PD associated with a 20% relative higher mortality than hemodialysis (HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.30) (Xue 2019, PMID: 31216914). PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only: in the first 2 years survival on PD is similar to, or slightly better than, hemodialysis overall, but worse in diabetic cohorts; no randomised comparison exists and modality choice is heavily confounded by who is offered and who chooses each therapy.

cards.headline: Weinhandl 2010: in 6,337 propensity-matched pairs, survival at 12 and 24 months was higher on peritoneal dialysis (85.8% vs 80.7%; 71.1% vs 68.0%; HR 0.92) — with the advantage in younger, non-diabetic patients without cardiovascular disease
cards.summary: Weinhandl 2010: in 6,337 propensity-matched pairs, survival at 12 and 24 months was higher on peritoneal dialysis (85.8% vs 80.7%; 71.1% vs 68.0%; HR 0.92) — with the advantage in younger, non-diabetic patients without cardiovascular disease
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 98,875 adults who initiated dialysis in 2003 in the United States, from which 6,337 incident hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patient pairs were propensity-matched; primary analysis was intention-to-treat survival from day 0, with subsets defined by age, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes.
cards.result: In the primary intention-to-treat analysis, cumulative survival was higher for peritoneal dialysis patients than for hemodialysis patients (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.00, P = 0.04) — an 8% relative lower mortality risk. Cumulative survival probabilities for peritoneal dialysis versus hemodialysis were 85.8% versus 80.7% (P < 0.01) at 12 months, 71.1% versus 68.0% (P < 0.01) at 24 months, 58.1% versus 56.7% (P = 0.25) at 36 months, and 48.4% versus 47.3% (P = 0.50) at 48 months. Peritoneal dialysis was associated with improved survival among subgroups aged <65 years, without cardiovascular disease, and without diabetes. In a sensitivity analysis of survival from 90 days after initiation, no overall difference was detected (hazard ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.96 to 1.16), but hemodialysis was associated with improved survival among subgroups with cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
cards.watchOut: Observational and era-bound (patients starting dialysis in 2003): matching balances measured factors only, patients who start on peritoneal dialysis differ systematically from those who start on hemodialysis, and the hazard ratio was not constant over follow-up — the early PD advantage is exactly where selection and catheter-related early hemodialysis deaths weigh most.
cards.source: Weinhandl ED et al. Propensity-matched mortality comparison of incident hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2010. PMID: 20133483. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rufino 2011 (Canary Islands, 1,469 incident patients): survival was higher on peritoneal dialysis at 12 months (96% vs 80%) and 24 months (90% vs 65%) in unadjusted intention-to-treat analysis, with an adjusted first-year relative mortality risk of 0.509
cards.summary: Rufino 2011 (Canary Islands, 1,469 incident patients): survival was higher on peritoneal dialysis at 12 months (96% vs 80%) and 24 months (90% vs 65%) in unadjusted intention-to-treat analysis, with an adjusted first-year relative mortality risk of 0.509
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of incident dialysis patients starting treatment in the Canary Islands between January 1, 2006 and December 31, 2009, recorded in the RERCAN registry: 1,469 patients (173 peritoneal dialysis and 1,296 hemodialysis), mean age 62.5 years, 65% male, mean follow-up 16.2 months; analyses used propensity-score adjustment and Cox models, overall and by age, sex and diabetes subgroups.
cards.result: Cumulative mortality in the intention-to-treat analysis was 27.1% in the hemodialysis group and 8.7% in the peritoneal dialysis group (P < .0001). Cumulative survival on PD versus HD was 96.6% versus 89% at 6 months, 96% versus 80% at 12 months, 90% versus 65% at 24 months, 82% versus 58% at 36 months and 73% versus 45% at 46 months (all P < .001). In subgroup analysis, survival was also higher in PD patients over and under 65 years, in diabetic and non-diabetic patients, and in both genders, with similar results from day 90 onward. The Cox-adjusted mortality risk for PD was 61% lower in relative terms than for HD (RR: 0.398, 95% CI 0.237-0.669, P = .001); broken down by year, the relative risk of death for PD versus HD in the first year was 0.509 (95% CI: 0.259-0.999, P = .049), and from year 2 onwards only age was a risk factor, with no difference between techniques.
cards.watchOut: The PD group is small (173 of 1,469) and strongly selected — younger age and province predicted choosing PD — and unadjusted survival gaps of 16–25 percentage points are far larger than any plausible modality effect, marking substantial residual confounding despite propensity adjustment.
cards.source: Rufino JM et al. [Current peritoneal dialysis compared with haemodialysis: medium-term survival analysis of incident dialysis patients in the Canary Islands in recent years]. Nefrologia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola Nefrologia. 2011. PMID: 21461011. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Xue 2019: in diabetic end-stage kidney disease, a meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies found peritoneal dialysis associated with a 20% relative higher mortality than hemodialysis (HR 1.20) — the opposite direction from the general-population cohorts
cards.summary: Xue 2019: in diabetic end-stage kidney disease, a meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies found peritoneal dialysis associated with a 20% relative higher mortality than hemodialysis (HR 1.20) — the opposite direction from the general-population cohorts
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cohort studies, diabetic ESKD only (Xue 2019)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of cohort studies comparing risk of death among diabetic patients with end-stage kidney disease receiving peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis, identified by searching Medline and Embase; 17 studies were included, with overall estimates calculated using a random-effects model and intention-to-treat estimates examined separately.
cards.result: Mortality comparison between PD and HD in diabetic ESRD patients showed PD significantly increased mortality rate (hazard ratio (HR) 1.20; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.10-1.30; I2 = 89.1%) — a 20% relative higher mortality risk. The overall HR using an intention-to-treat analysis was 1.23 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.34). Meta-regression demonstrated that PD patients from Asian countries were associated with increased mortality risk (coefficient = 0.270, SE = 0.112, p = .033). The authors note the high heterogeneity (I2 = 89.1%) undermined the robustness of the findings, and conclude that ESRD patients with diabetes may benefit more from HD than PD.
cards.watchOut: All underlying studies are observational cohorts with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 89.1%): diabetic patients channelled to PD differ from those channelled to HD in ways registries record imperfectly, so the 20% relative excess is an association in a selected population, not a randomised effect.
cards.source: Xue J et al. Comparison of peritoneal dialysis with hemodialysis on survival of diabetic patients with end-stage kidney disease: a meta-analysis of cohort studies. Renal failure. 2019. PMID: 31216914. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Diabetic Nephropathies · Disease Progression · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Peritoneal Dialysis · Renal Dialysis · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: in the first 2 years, peritoneal dialysis survival is similar to or slightly better than hemodialysis in general incident populations (HR 0.92; 71.1% vs 68.0% alive at 24 months in matched US pairs) — but diabetic cohorts point the other way (HR 1.20)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the first 2 years, peritoneal dialysis survival is similar to or slightly better than hemodialysis in general incident populations (HR 0.92; 71.1% vs 68.0% alive at 24 months in matched US pairs) — but diabetic cohorts point the other way (HR 1.20)
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational: one propensity-matched US cohort (6,337 matched pairs from 98,875 incident patients, 2003 starts), one Canary Islands registry cohort (1,469 incident patients, 2006–2009 starts), and one meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies restricted to diabetic ESKD. Total carded participants exceed 100,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is confounding by modality selection, printed here and on every card.
cards.result: At 12 and 24 months — this shelf's window — matched US survival favoured PD modestly (85.8% vs 80.7%; 71.1% vs 68.0%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.00), with no overall difference in the from-day-90 sensitivity analysis (HR 1.05) (Weinhandl 2010). The Canary cohort found larger early PD advantages that its own design cannot fully separate from selection (Rufino 2011). In diabetic patients specifically, pooled cohorts associate PD with higher mortality (HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.30) (Xue 2019). PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only: similar-or-better early survival on PD overall; worse in diabetes.
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised trial of PD versus HD survival and there almost certainly never will be: every number on this shelf carries the imprint of who gets offered, and who chooses, each modality — read the subgroup split (age, cardiovascular disease, diabetes) as the shelf's real content.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weinhandl ED et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2010 (PMID: 20133483); Rufino JM et al. Nefrologia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola Nefrologia. 2011 (PMID: 21461011); Xue J et al. Renal failure. 2019 (PMID: 31216914).

shelves.title: More frequent hemodialysis and left ventricular mass: imaging improves in small trials (15.3 g difference; −11% end-diastolic volume), on surrogate outcomes over 6–12 months
shelves.question: In adults on hemodialysis, does more frequent dialysis improve left ventricular mass versus conventional thrice-weekly dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anemia · Blood Pressure · Calcium Phosphates · Circadian Rhythm · Erythropoietin · Female · Hematocrit · Humans · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small randomised trials, concordant on the imaging outcome. The FHN Daily Trial's primary report (PMID: 21091062) is already homed on live shelf #293 and is NOT re-carded here; this shelf cards the trials' cardiac-imaging reports and the independent nocturnal trial. Culleton 2007 (PMID: 17878421), a randomised trial of 52 patients, found frequent nocturnal hemodialysis six times weekly improved left ventricular mass versus conventional thrice-weekly dialysis, with a between-group difference in mass change of 15.3 g (95% CI 1.0 to 29.6, P = .04) over 6 months, alongside fewer blood-pressure medications (16/26 versus 3/25 patients reducing or stopping). The FHN cardiac magnetic resonance analysis (Chan 2013, PMID: 23970131) found frequent in-center dialysis reduced left ventricular end-diastolic volume by 11.0% and end-systolic volume by 14.8% relative to conventional therapy in the Daily Trial (245 patients), and reduced left ventricular mass, while the FHN Nocturnal Trial (87 patients) showed no significant volume changes and neither trial changed the mass-to-volume remodeling ratio. A small non-randomised in-center nocturnal study (MIDNIGHT, 25 patients) found left ventricular mass falling by 14.75 g versus rising 6.54 g on conventional dialysis over 6 months (Graham-Brown 2017, PMID: 29084397). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): more frequent dialysis improves left ventricular mass and volumes on imaging over 6–12 months; the trials are small, short, and powered for surrogates, not for death or hospitalisation.

cards.headline: Culleton 2007 (randomised trial, 52 patients): frequent nocturnal hemodialysis six times weekly improved left ventricular mass versus conventional dialysis — between-group difference 15.3 g over 6 months
cards.summary: Culleton 2007 (randomised trial, 52 patients): frequent nocturnal hemodialysis six times weekly improved left ventricular mass versus conventional dialysis — between-group difference 15.3 g over 6 months
cards.people: A 2-group, parallel, randomized controlled trial at 2 Canadian university centers between August 2004 and December 2006: 52 patients undergoing hemodialysis were randomly assigned 1:1 to nocturnal hemodialysis 6 times weekly or conventional hemodialysis 3 times weekly. The primary outcome was change in left ventricular mass measured by cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging over 6 months.
cards.result: Frequent nocturnal hemodialysis significantly improved the primary outcome (mean left ventricular mass difference between groups, 15.3 g, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.0 to 29.6 g; P = .04). It did not significantly improve quality of life (difference of change in EuroQol 5-D index, 0.05; 95% CI, −0.07 to 0.17; P = .43), though selected kidney-specific quality-of-life domains improved (P = .01 and P = .02). Frequent nocturnal dialysis was also associated with improvement in systolic blood pressure (P = .01 after adjustment) and with reduction or discontinuation of antihypertensive medications (16/26 patients in the nocturnal group vs 3/25 in the conventional group; P < .001) and oral phosphate binders (19/26 vs 3/25; P < .001). No benefit in anemia management was seen.
cards.watchOut: A preliminary trial of 52 patients over 6 months with an imaging endpoint: the confidence interval for the mass difference runs from 1.0 to 29.6 g, and nocturnal six-times-weekly treatment bundles more hours with more sessions, so the trial cannot separate frequency from total dialysis time.
cards.source: Culleton BF et al. Effect of frequent nocturnal hemodialysis vs conventional hemodialysis on left ventricular mass and quality of life: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17878421. Registry ID: ISRCTN25858715. cards.summary: Chan 2013 (FHN cardiac imaging analysis, 245 + 87 patients): frequent in-center dialysis reduced left ventricular volumes (−11.0% end-diastolic, −14.8% end-systolic) and mass, but the nocturnal trial showed no significant volume change and neither trial improved the remodeling ratio
cards.type: Cardiac imaging analysis of two randomised trials, FHN Daily and Nocturnal (Chan 2013)
cards.people: Cardiac magnetic resonance analysis of the two Frequent Hemodialysis Network trials: the Daily Trial randomized 245 patients to 12 months of six times per week versus three times per week in-center hemodialysis, and the Nocturnal Trial randomized 87 patients to 12 months of six times per week nocturnal hemodialysis versus three times per week predominantly home-based hemodialysis. Left and right ventricular volumes, left ventricular mass, and ejection fraction were measured at baseline and end of study; the left ventricular mass/end-diastolic volume ratio indexed remodeling.
cards.result: In the Daily Trial, frequent hemodialysis resulted in significant reductions in left ventricular end diastolic volume (−11.0% [95% confidence interval, −16.1% to −5.5%]), left ventricular end systolic volume (−14.8% [−22.7% to −6.2%]), and right ventricular end diastolic volume (−11.6% [−19.0% to −3.6%]) compared with conventional therapy, with a trend for right ventricular end systolic volume (−11.3% [−21.4% to 0.1%]); reductions were accentuated among patients with residual urine output <100 ml/d (P for interaction = 0.02). In the Nocturnal Trial, there were no significant changes in left or right ventricular volumes. The frequent dialysis interventions had no substantial effect on the ratio of left ventricular mass/left ventricular end diastolic volume in either trial; the authors summarise that frequent in-center hemodialysis reduces ventricular volumes as well as left ventricular mass, but does not affect left ventricular remodeling.
cards.watchOut: This is the imaging report of the FHN programme whose primary Daily Trial report is homed on live shelf #293 (not re-carded here); within the programme the two trials disagree — the in-center daily schedule moved volumes and mass, the home nocturnal schedule did not reach significance — so 'frequent dialysis' is not one uniform intervention.
cards.source: Chan CT et al. Effects of frequent hemodialysis on ventricular volumes and left ventricular remodeling. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2013. PMID: 23970131. Registry ID: NCT00264758, NCT00271999. cards.headline: Graham-Brown 2017 (MIDNIGHT, non-randomised, 25 patients — small N on the face): in-center nocturnal hemodialysis reduced left ventricular mass by 14.75 g while conventional dialysis gained 6.54 g over 6 months
cards.summary: Graham-Brown 2017 (MIDNIGHT, non-randomised, 25 patients — small N on the face): in-center nocturnal hemodialysis reduced left ventricular mass by 14.75 g while conventional dialysis gained 6.54 g over 6 months
cards.people: A 6-month, non-randomized controlled trial (ISRCTN16672784) recruiting 13 patients on in-centre nocturnal haemodialysis (INHD) and 12 control patients on conventional HD; left ventricular structure, function and myocardial fibrosis were assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and native T1 mapping, with quality-of-life and clinical measures also collected. Total N = 25.
cards.result: INHD led to significant reductions in left ventricular mass (−14.75 vs. +6.54 g; p = 0.02), global T1 (−30.62 vs. 0.4 ms; p = 0.05) and non-septal native T1 values (−30.93 vs. 8.96 ms; p = 0.02) over time. There were also significant improvements in serum phosphate (−0.39 vs. +0.02 mmol/L [approximately −1.2 vs. +0.1 mg/dL]; p = 0.03) and reductions in ultrafiltration rates (−2.32 vs. +0.70 mL/h/kg; p = 0.05) between INHD and controls. The authors conclude that 6 months of INHD was associated with favourable LV remodelling and reduced myocardial fibrosis compared with conventional haemodialysis.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised with 25 patients total: patients on in-center nocturnal schedules are a selected group, and with numbers this small the study can only corroborate the randomised trials' direction, not estimate an effect.
cards.source: Graham-Brown MPM et al. Cardiac Remodelling in Patients Undergoing in-Centre Nocturnal Haemodialysis: Results from the MIDNIGHT Study, a Non-Randomized Controlled Trial. Blood purification. 2017. PMID: 29084397. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: more frequent dialysis improves left ventricular mass and volumes on cardiac imaging over 6–12 months (15.3 g between-group mass difference in the nocturnal RCT; −11.0% end-diastolic volume in FHN Daily) — small, short, surrogate-outcome trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: more frequent dialysis improves left ventricular mass and volumes on cardiac imaging over 6–12 months (15.3 g between-group mass difference in the nocturnal RCT; −11.0% end-diastolic volume in FHN Daily) — small, short, surrogate-outcome trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised nocturnal trial (52 patients, 6 months), the cardiac imaging analysis of the two FHN randomised trials (245 Daily + 87 Nocturnal patients, 12 months; the FHN Daily primary report itself is homed on live shelf #293 and was not re-carded), and one non-randomised in-center nocturnal study (25 patients, 6 months). Total unique carded participants are about 400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies at shelf level; each study's small size is printed on its card.
cards.result: Frequent nocturnal dialysis improved left ventricular mass versus conventional dialysis by a between-group difference of 15.3 g (95% CI 1.0 to 29.6) (Culleton 2007). Frequent in-center dialysis reduced left ventricular end-diastolic volume by 11.0% and end-systolic volume by 14.8% and reduced mass, while the FHN nocturnal comparison and the remodeling ratio showed no significant change (Chan 2013). In-center nocturnal dialysis reduced mass by 14.75 g against a 6.54 g gain on conventional treatment in a 25-patient non-randomised study (Graham-Brown 2017). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for left ventricular mass and volumes — imaging surrogates only.
cards.watchOut: Left ventricular mass is a surrogate: none of the carded trials was powered for mortality or hospitalisation, treatment burden of six-times-weekly dialysis is substantial, and the FHN programme's own two schedules did not agree — benefit is best supported for frequent in-center dialysis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Culleton BF et al. JAMA. 2007 (PMID: 17878421); Chan CT et al. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2013 (PMID: 23970131); Graham-Brown MPM et al. Blood purification. 2017 (PMID: 29084397).

shelves.title: Tacrolimus versus cyclosporine after kidney transplantation: rejection is clearly lower on tacrolimus (pooled relative risk 0.69), with more new diabetes as the trade-off
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients, is tacrolimus better than cyclosporine for preventing acute rejection?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Antilymphocyte Serum · Cadaver · Cause of Death · Clinical Protocols · Creatinine · Cross-Over Studies · Cyclosporine · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Graft Rejection · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Insulin · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Patient Selection · Regression Analysis · Tacrolimus
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for preventing acute rejection, with a diabetes harm printed on the face. Two large randomised trials agree: in the US cadaveric-transplant trial (412 patients), biopsy-confirmed acute rejection at 1 year was 30.7% on tacrolimus versus 46.4% on cyclosporine (P = 0.001), with less antilymphocyte rescue therapy (10.7% versus 25.1%) but more posttransplant diabetes (19.9% versus 4.0%) (Pirsch 1997, PMID: 9112351); in the European trial against cyclosporine microemulsion (560 patients), biopsy-proven rejection at 6 months was 19.6% versus 37.3% — an absolute difference of 17.7 percentage points (95% CI 10.3 to 25.1) — and steroid-resistant rejection 9.4% versus 21.0%, with no significant difference in patient or graft survival (Margreiter 2002, PMID: 11888584). The BMJ meta-analysis of 30 trials (4,102 patients) confirms less acute rejection at 1 year (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.79) and less graft loss (RR 0.56 at 6 months), at the cost of more insulin-requiring diabetes (RR 1.86) — treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of cyclosporine avoids 12 acute rejections and 2 graft losses but causes 5 extra cases of insulin-dependent diabetes (Webster 2005, PMID: 16157605). The later ELITE-Symphony trial (PMID: 18094377) is homed on live shelf #737 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tacrolimus prevents acute rejection better than cyclosporine, with more new diabetes as the principal trade-off.

cards.headline: Pirsch 1997 (US randomised trial, 412 cadaveric kidney recipients): biopsy-confirmed acute rejection 30.7% on tacrolimus versus 46.4% on cyclosporine at 1 year — but posttransplant diabetes 19.9% versus 4.0%
cards.summary: Pirsch 1997 (US randomised trial, 412 cadaveric kidney recipients): biopsy-confirmed acute rejection 30.7% on tacrolimus versus 46.4% on cyclosporine at 1 year — but posttransplant diabetes 19.9% versus 4.0%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, FK506 Kidney Transplant Study Group (Pirsch 1997)
cards.people: A randomized, open-label study of tacrolimus-based versus cyclosporine-based immunosuppression in patients receiving cadaveric kidney transplants: 412 patients were randomized to tacrolimus (n = 205) or cyclosporine (n = 207) and followed for 1 year for patient and graft survival and the incidence of acute rejection.
cards.result: One-year patient survival was 95.6% for tacrolimus and 96.6% for cyclosporine (P = 0.576); 1-year graft survival was 91.2% and 87.9% (P = 0.289) — the treatment made no difference to either survival outcome at 1 year. There was a significant reduction in biopsy-confirmed acute rejection in the tacrolimus group (30.7%) compared with the cyclosporine group (46.4%, P = 0.001) — an absolute difference of 15.7 percentage points — confirmed by blinded review, and in the use of antilymphocyte therapy for rejection (10.7% and 25.1%, respectively; P < 0.001). Tremor and paresthesia were more frequent in the tacrolimus group. The incidence of posttransplant diabetes mellitus was 19.9% in the tacrolimus group and 4.0% in the cyclosporine group (P < 0.001), and was reversible in some patients.
cards.watchOut: A 1997 open-label trial against the older cyclosporine formulation, in cadaveric transplants only, with 1-year follow-up: rejection was reduced without a survival or graft-survival difference within that year, and the diabetes excess (about 16 extra cases per 100) is part of the answer, not a footnote.
cards.source: Pirsch JD et al. A comparison of tacrolimus (FK506) and cyclosporine for immunosuppression after cadaveric renal transplantation. Transplantation. 1997. PMID: 9112351. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Margreiter 2002 (European randomised trial, 560 patients): biopsy-proven acute rejection at 6 months 19.6% on tacrolimus versus 37.3% on cyclosporine microemulsion — an absolute difference of 17.7 percentage points
cards.summary: Margreiter 2002 (European randomised trial, 560 patients): biopsy-proven acute rejection at 6 months 19.6% on tacrolimus versus 37.3% on cyclosporine microemulsion — an absolute difference of 17.7 percentage points
cards.people: A 6-month open randomised multicentre study in 50 European centres comparing tacrolimus with the microemulsion formulation of ciclosporin, both with azathioprine and corticosteroids: 560 patients were involved, 287 randomly assigned tacrolimus and 273 ciclosporin microemulsion (initial oral daily doses 0.30 mg/kg and 8–10 mg/kg respectively); three patients did not receive study treatment or transplantation. The primary endpoint was biopsy-proven acute rejection.
cards.result: The rate of biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was significantly lower with tacrolimus than with ciclosporin microemulsion (56 patients [19.6%] vs 101 [37.3%]; 17.7% difference [95% CI 10.3–25.1]; p < 0.0001). Biopsy-confirmed corticosteroid-resistant rejection was also significantly lower with tacrolimus (27 [9.4%] vs 57 [21.0%]; 11.6% difference [5.7–17.5]; p < 0.0001). Cross-over between therapies because of biopsy-proven rejection was judged necessary in one of 286 (0.3%) tacrolimus-group patients and 27 of 271 (10.0%) ciclosporin-group patients (p < 0.0001). There were no significant differences in survival of patients or grafts or in renal function. Hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia were more common in the ciclosporin group and tremor and hypomagnesaemia more frequent in the tacrolimus group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a 6-month primary endpoint and azathioprine-era co-therapy: it answers the rejection question against the modern (microemulsion) cyclosporine formulation, but rejection ascertainment in an open trial and the short horizon limit what it can say about graft survival.
cards.source: Margreiter R et al. Efficacy and safety of tacrolimus compared with ciclosporin microemulsion in renal transplantation: a randomised multicentre study. Lancet (London, England). 2002. PMID: 11888584. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Webster 2005 (BMJ meta-analysis, 30 trials, 4,102 patients): tacrolimus cut acute rejection at 1 year (relative risk 0.69) and graft loss (RR 0.56 at 6 months), but raised insulin-requiring diabetes (RR 1.86) — per 100 treated: 12 fewer rejections, 2 fewer graft losses, 5 extra diabetes cases
cards.summary: Webster 2005 (BMJ meta-analysis, 30 trials, 4,102 patients): tacrolimus cut acute rejection at 1 year (relative risk 0.69) and graft loss (RR 0.56 at 6 months), but raised insulin-requiring diabetes (RR 1.86) — per 100 treated: 12 fewer rejections, 2 fewer graft losses, 5 extra diabetes cases
cards.type: Meta-analysis and meta-regression of randomised trials (Webster 2005)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-regression of comparative randomised trials of tacrolimus versus ciclosporin as initial treatment for renal transplant recipients, identified from Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials, the Cochrane Renal Group Specialist Register, and conference proceedings: 123 reports from 30 trials (4,102 patients) were included, with data synthesised in a random-effects model.
cards.result: At six months, graft loss was significantly reduced in tacrolimus treated recipients (relative risk (RR) = 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.36 to 0.86) — a 44% relative reduction — and this effect persisted up to three years; the relative reduction diminished with higher tacrolimus concentrations (P = 0.04) but did not vary with ciclosporin formulation (P = 0.97). At one year, tacrolimus treated patients had less acute rejection (RR = 0.69, 0.60 to 0.79 — a 31% relative reduction) and less steroid resistant rejection (RR = 0.49, 0.37 to 0.64) but more diabetes mellitus requiring insulin (RR = 1.86, 1.11 to 3.09), tremor, headache, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, and vomiting; the relative excess of diabetes increased with higher tacrolimus concentrations (P = 0.003). No differences were seen in infection or malignancy. The authors' absolute summary: treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of ciclosporin for the first year avoids 12 patients having acute rejection and two losing their graft but causes an extra five patients to develop insulin dependent diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials span cyclosporine formulations and tacrolimus target concentrations, and the benefit–harm balance itself is concentration-dependent: higher tacrolimus exposure bought less extra rejection protection and more diabetes, so the pooled averages describe a dosing range, not a single regimen.
cards.source: Webster AC et al. Tacrolimus versus ciclosporin as primary immunosuppression for kidney transplant recipients: meta-analysis and meta-regression of randomised trial data. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2005. PMID: 16157605. Registry ID: none in the record. the relative excess of diabetes increased with higher tacrolimus concentrations (p = 0.003). no differences were seen in infection or malignancy. the authors' absolute summary: treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of ciclosporin for the first year avoids 12 patients having acute rejection and two losing their graft but causes an extra five patients to develop insulin dependent diabetes. the pooled trials span cyclosporine formulations and tacrolimus target concentrations, and the benefit–harm balance itself is concentration-dependent: higher tacrolimus exposure bought less extra rejection protection and more diabetes, so the pooled averages describe a dosing range, not a single regimen. webster ac et al. tacrolimus versus ciclosporin as primary immunosuppression for kidney transplant recipients: meta-analysis and meta-regression of randomised trial data. bmj (clinical research ed.). 2005. pmid: 16157605. registry id: none in the record. mesh: cyclosporine · forecasting · humans · immunosuppression therapy · immunosuppressive agents · kidney transplantation · randomized controlled trials as topic · regression analysis · tacrolimus · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: tacrolimus prevents acute rejection better than cyclosporine (30.7% vs 46.4% and 19.6% vs 37.3% in the two large trials; pooled relative risk 0.69 at 1 year), with more new diabetes as the consistent trade-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: tacrolimus prevents acute rejection better than cyclosporine (30.7% vs 46.4% and 19.6% vs 37.3% in the two large trials; pooled relative risk 0.69 at 1 year), with more new diabetes as the consistent trade-off
cards.people: The carded evidence: two large randomised trials (412 US cadaveric recipients, 1 year; 560 European recipients against cyclosporine microemulsion, 6 months) and a meta-analysis of 30 randomised trials (4,102 patients). Total carded participants exceed 5,000 counting the meta-analysis once, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The ELITE-Symphony trial (PMID: 18094377), which set the modern low-dose tacrolimus standard, is homed on live shelf #737 and was not re-carded.
cards.result: Biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was 30.7% versus 46.4% at 1 year (Pirsch 1997) and 19.6% versus 37.3% at 6 months (Margreiter 2002); the pooled 1-year relative risk was 0.69 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.79) with graft loss RR 0.56 at 6 months (Webster 2005). Patient and graft survival did not differ significantly within the individual trials' follow-up. Posttransplant diabetes was consistently more frequent on tacrolimus (19.9% vs 4.0% in Pirsch 1997; pooled RR 1.86 for insulin-requiring diabetes), summarised by Webster as 5 extra diabetes cases per 100 treated against 12 fewer rejections and 2 fewer graft losses. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for preventing acute rejection.
cards.watchOut: The rejection advantage is secure; what the carded evidence does not show is a patient-survival advantage, and the choice remains patient-specific — a recipient at high diabetes risk trades a real metabolic harm for the rejection benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pirsch JD et al. Transplantation. 1997 (PMID: 9112351); Margreiter R et al. Lancet (London, England). 2002 (PMID: 11888584); Webster AC et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2005 (PMID: 16157605).

shelves.title: HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors on dialysis: haemoglobin control matches ESAs in three large noninferiority programmes (vadadustat, roxadustat, daprodustat) — an oral alternative for the haemoglobin target, with shorter long-term safety experience
shelves.question: In adults on dialysis with anemia, do HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors achieve hemoglobin control as effectively as erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anemia · Cardiovascular Diseases · Darbepoetin alfa · Female · Glycine · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Picolinic Acids · Prolyl-Hydroxylase Inhibitors · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (as effective for haemoglobin control). Three large phase 3 programmes, each randomised against an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in dialysis patients, meet their haemoglobin noninferiority margins: vadadustat versus darbepoetin alfa in 3,923 patients (Eckardt 2021, PMID: 33913638 — haemoglobin differences of −0.07 to −0.31 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin, with cardiovascular safety also noninferior, MACE hazard ratio 0.96); roxadustat versus epoetin alfa in 2,133 patients (Fishbane 2022, PMID: 35361724 — haemoglobin change 0.77 versus 0.68 g/dL, difference 0.09 g/dL); and daprodustat versus darbepoetin alfa in 312 incident-dialysis patients (Singh 2022, PMID: 35377393 — adjusted difference −0.10 g/dL). A network meta-analysis of 17 phase 3 trials (Sackeyfio 2024, PMID: 38250252; 11,124 dialysis patients for the haemoglobin outcome) finds the three agents broadly comparable. The class's two biggest dialysis trials are homed elsewhere in this library — ASCEND-D on shelf #1108 and the Chen 2019 roxadustat dialysis trial within shelf #731 — and are cross-pointed here in prose, not re-carded; this shelf is built on the remaining free programme reports, a genuinely narrower class-level haemoglobin question, flagged for the developer. PROPOSED LIKELY: for haemoglobin control on dialysis, HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors match ESAs; the stamp is about haemoglobin only, not about long-term safety, where follow-up remains shorter than the decades of ESA experience.

cards.headline: Eckardt 2021 (INNO2VATE): in 3,923 dialysis patients, oral vadadustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin at both evaluation periods — and noninferior for cardiovascular safety (MACE HR 0.96)
cards.summary: Eckardt 2021 (INNO2VATE): in 3,923 dialysis patients, oral vadadustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin at both evaluation periods — and noninferior for cardiovascular safety (MACE HR 0.96)
cards.type: Two randomised noninferiority phase 3 trials (Eckardt 2021, INNO2VATE)
cards.people: Two randomised, open-label, noninferiority phase 3 trials (INNO2VATE) in patients with anaemia and incident or prevalent dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease: 3,923 patients randomised 1:1 to vadadustat or darbepoetin alfa — 369 in the incident-dialysis trial and 3,554 in the prevalent-dialysis trial. The haemoglobin noninferiority margin was −0.75 g/dL; the MACE noninferiority margin was a hazard ratio of 1.25.
cards.result: A first major adverse cardiovascular event occurred in 355 patients (18.2%) on vadadustat and 377 (19.3%) on darbepoetin alfa (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11). Mean between-group differences in haemoglobin change were −0.31 g/dL (95% CI −0.53 to −0.10) at weeks 24–36 and −0.07 g/dL (95% CI −0.34 to 0.19) at weeks 40–52 in the incident trial, and −0.17 g/dL (95% CI −0.23 to −0.10) and −0.18 g/dL (95% CI −0.25 to −0.12) in the prevalent trial — all inside the −0.75 g/dL noninferiority margin. Serious adverse events occurred in 49.7% (incident) and 55.0% (prevalent) on vadadustat versus 56.5% and 58.3% on darbepoetin alfa.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design and a noninferiority margin that tolerates up to 0.75 g/dL lower haemoglobin: 'noninferior' here means 'not unacceptably worse by a pre-set margin', and the point estimates consistently sit slightly below darbepoetin. This record was previously mentioned only as cross-referenced context in pack #2642's balance prose ('cross-referenced, not carded'); it is carded here for the first time.
cards.source: Eckardt KU et al. Safety and Efficacy of Vadadustat for Anemia in Patients Undergoing Dialysis. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 33913638. Registry ID: NCT02865850 and NCT02892149. cards.headline: Fishbane 2022 (ROCKIES): roxadustat raised haemoglobin by 0.77 g/dL versus 0.68 g/dL with epoetin alfa in 2,133 dialysis patients — noninferior, difference 0.09 g/dL
cards.summary: Fishbane 2022 (ROCKIES): roxadustat raised haemoglobin by 0.77 g/dL versus 0.68 g/dL with epoetin alfa in 2,133 dialysis patients — noninferior, difference 0.09 g/dL
cards.people: Open-label phase 3 study (ROCKIES) in patients with dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease and anaemia, randomised 1:1 to oral roxadustat three times weekly (n = 1,068) or parenteral epoetin alfa per local practice (n = 1,065); mean age 54.0 years; 89.1% on haemodialysis and 10.8% on peritoneal dialysis. The primary efficacy endpoint was mean haemoglobin change from baseline averaged over weeks 28–52, tested for noninferiority (margin −0.75 g/dL).
cards.result: Mean (95% CI) haemoglobin change from baseline was 0.77 (0.69 to 0.85) g/dL with roxadustat and 0.68 (0.60 to 0.76) g/dL with epoetin alfa, demonstrating noninferiority (least squares mean difference 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; P < 0.001). At least one adverse event occurred in 85.0% on roxadustat and 84.5% on epoetin alfa, and at least one serious adverse event in 57.6% and 57.5% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with epoetin dosed 'per local clinic practice' rather than by a fixed protocol, and adverse-event rates above 85% in both arms reflect how ill dialysis populations are rather than a drug-specific signal.
cards.source: Fishbane S et al. Roxadustat Versus Epoetin Alfa for Treating Anemia in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease on Dialysis: Results from the Randomized Phase 3 ROCKIES Study. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2022. PMID: 35361724. Registry ID: NCT02174731. cards.headline: Singh 2022 (ASCEND incident dialysis): daprodustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin in 312 patients starting dialysis (adjusted difference −0.10 g/dL)
cards.summary: Singh 2022 (ASCEND incident dialysis): daprodustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin in 312 patients starting dialysis (adjusted difference −0.10 g/dL)
cards.people: Prospective, randomised, open-label trial in 90 centres across 14 countries in incident dialysis patients — planning to start dialysis within 6 weeks or within 90 days of starting haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, haemoglobin 8.0–10.5 g/dL at screening, ESA-naive or limited prior ESA: 312 patients randomised to daprodustat (n = 157) or darbepoetin alfa (n = 155); 306 (98%) completed the trial. The noninferiority margin was −0.75 g/dL for mean haemoglobin change to weeks 28–52.
cards.result: Mean (SD) haemoglobin during the evaluation period was 10.5 (1.0) g/dL on daprodustat and 10.6 (0.9) g/dL on darbepoetin alfa, an adjusted mean treatment difference of −0.10 g/dL (95% CI −0.34 to 0.14), indicating noninferiority. Daprodustat was not superior to darbepoetin alfa in reducing monthly intravenous iron use (adjusted mean difference 19.4 mg, 95% CI −11.0 to 49.9). Adverse event rates were 76% for daprodustat versus 72% for darbepoetin alfa.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three programme trials (N = 312, printed here) and confined to patients new to dialysis; the main ASCEND-D trial in prevalent dialysis patients is homed on shelf #1108 and is not re-carded here.

JAMA internal medicine. 2022. PMID: 35377393. Registry ID: NCT03029208. cards.headline: Sackeyfio 2024: network meta-analysis of 17 phase 3 trials — in dialysis patients (n = 11,124 for haemoglobin), daprodustat and roxadustat raised haemoglobin slightly more than vadadustat, with no clinically meaningful MACE differences between agents
cards.summary: Sackeyfio 2024: network meta-analysis of 17 phase 3 trials — in dialysis patients (n = 11,124 for haemoglobin), daprodustat and roxadustat raised haemoglobin slightly more than vadadustat, with no clinically meaningful MACE differences between agents
cards.people: Network meta-analyses indirectly comparing three HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (daprodustat, roxadustat, vadadustat) in anaemia of chronic kidney disease, from 17 phase III randomised controlled trials; dialysis-population analyses included 11,124 patients for change in haemoglobin and 12,320 for time to first major adverse cardiovascular event.
cards.result: In dialysis patients, haemoglobin change from baseline was higher with daprodustat and roxadustat than with vadadustat (daprodustat 0.34 g/dL, 95% credible interval 0.22 to 0.45; roxadustat 0.38 g/dL, 95% CrI 0.27 to 0.49), while there were no clinically meaningful differences in MACE risk between the agents (daprodustat versus roxadustat HR 0.89, 95% CrI 0.73 to 1.08; daprodustat versus vadadustat HR 0.99, 95% CrI 0.82 to 1.21; roxadustat versus vadadustat HR 1.12, 95% CrI 0.92 to 1.37). The authors conclude the three agents are broadly clinically comparable in efficacy and cardiovascular safety, with low precision for the latter.
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons between agents (no head-to-head trials) with low precision for cardiovascular outcomes; the analysis compares HIF inhibitors with each other, while the ESA comparison rests on the three programme trials carded above.
cards.source: Sackeyfio A et al. Comparison of outcomes on hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) in anaemia associated with chronic kidney disease: network meta-analyses in dialysis and non-dialysis dependent populations. Clinical kidney journal. 2024. PMID: 38250252. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: three independent drug programmes each met haemoglobin noninferiority against an ESA on dialysis — the class matches ESAs for haemoglobin control, by margins that allow up to 0.75 g/dL less
cards.summary: Synthesis: three independent drug programmes each met haemoglobin noninferiority against an ESA on dialysis — the class matches ESAs for haemoglobin control, by margins that allow up to 0.75 g/dL less
cards.people: The carded evidence: two INNO2VATE trials (3,923 patients), ROCKIES (2,133 patients), the ASCEND incident-dialysis trial (312 patients), and a 17-trial network meta-analysis (11,124 dialysis patients for the haemoglobin outcome; overlapping with the programme trials). Unique randomised patients across the three programme trials total 6,368, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Vadadustat's haemoglobin differences versus darbepoetin ranged from −0.31 to −0.07 g/dL with MACE noninferiority met (HR 0.96) (Eckardt 2021). Roxadustat's haemoglobin change exceeded epoetin alfa's by 0.09 g/dL (Fishbane 2022). Daprodustat differed from darbepoetin by −0.10 g/dL in incident dialysis (Singh 2022). The network meta-analysis finds the agents broadly comparable (Sackeyfio 2024). PROPOSED LIKELY (as effective for haemoglobin control).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not identity: every programme's point estimate sits at or slightly below its ESA comparator, regulatory status differs by country, and none of these trials answers longer-horizon safety (infection, thrombosis, cancer signals) the way decades of ESA use do.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eckardt KU et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33913638); Fishbane S et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2022 (PMID: 35361724); Singh AK et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35377393); Sackeyfio A et al. shelves.title: Rituximab in frequently relapsing adult nephrotic syndrome (observational only): pooled complete remission 84.2% and relapse 27.4% in adult minimal change/FSGS series — but no randomised trial has compared it with calcineurin inhibitors in adults
shelves.question: In adults with nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab reduce relapses in frequently relapsing disease versus calcineurin inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #739 covers rituximab evidence in children with nephrotic syndrome; the uncovered slice carded here is adults, asked against calcineurin inhibitors. The honest headline is that the direct adult comparison does not exist in the records fetched: the Cochrane review of interventions for minimal change disease in adults (Azukaitis 2022; 15 randomised trials, 769 participants) evaluates calcineurin inhibitors against prednisolone (complete remission RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.05; relapse RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.03) and states that randomised data on rituximab in adults are awaited. What exists for rituximab in adults is observational: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies and case series in frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent minimal change disease/FSGS (Xue 2021; 382 adults) found a pooled complete remission rate of 84.2% (91.6% in minimal change disease, 43% in FSGS) with 27.4% relapsing during 12–43 months of follow-up, and the largest single series carded (Guitard 2014; 41 adults with minimal-change nephrotic syndrome, many previously on steroids or calcineurin inhibitors) found an overall response of 78%, with relapse in 56% of responders at a median of 18 months and renewed responses to a second course. Rituximab therefore looks effective at inducing remission and sparing steroids/CNIs in relapsing adult disease, but relapse after B-cell recovery is common, and superiority — or even equivalence — to calcineurin inhibitors is unproven in adults. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Xue 2021: pooled across 21 adult studies (382 patients with frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent MCD/FSGS), rituximab gave 84.2% complete remission — and 27.4% relapsed during follow-up
cards.summary: Xue 2021: pooled across 21 adult studies (382 patients with frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent MCD/FSGS), rituximab gave 84.2% complete remission — and 27.4% relapsed during follow-up
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies and case series (Xue 2021)
cards.people: 382 adults with difficult-to-treat (frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent, steroid-resistant excluded) nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change disease or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, pooled from 21 cohort studies or case series; median follow-up 12 to 43 months.
cards.result: Rituximab induced a pooled complete remission rate of 84.2% (95% CI 67.7–96.3%); the complete remission rate was 91.6% in minimal change disease and 43% in FSGS. However, 27.4% (95% CI 20.7–34.5%) of patients relapsed during follow-up. Pooled partial remission and no-response rates were 5.8% and 5.2%. Rituximab was associated with trivial adverse events and good tolerance. The authors conclude rituximab may be an effective alternative to displace calcineurin inhibitors or prednisone, while calling for trials comparing rituximab with other immunosuppressants — that comparison had not been done.
cards.watchOut: Every pooled study is a cohort or case series without a calcineurin-inhibitor control arm: an 84.2% remission rate in selected, previously treated patients cannot be read as superiority over CNIs, and the wide confidence interval (67.7–96.3%) reflects small, heterogeneous series.

cards.headline: Azukaitis 2022 (Cochrane, adult minimal change disease): calcineurin inhibitors match prednisolone for remission (RR 0.99) — and randomised rituximab data in adults are, in the review's words, awaited
cards.summary: Azukaitis 2022 (Cochrane, adult minimal change disease): calcineurin inhibitors match prednisolone for remission (RR 0.99) — and randomised rituximab data in adults are, in the review's words, awaited
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials in adults (Azukaitis 2022)
cards.people: Adults over 18 years with minimal change disease causing nephrotic syndrome, in 15 randomised controlled trials with 769 randomised participants: four studies of prednisolone regimens, eight of calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus or cyclosporin), two of enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium, and one of levamisole.
cards.result: Compared with prednisolone alone, calcineurin inhibitors with reduced-dose prednisolone or without prednisolone probably make little or no difference to complete remission (8 studies, 492 participants: RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.05) or complete/partial remission (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.05), and relapse was RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.03) — moderate certainty evidence; CNIs may reduce obesity/Cushing's syndrome (RR 0.11) and acne (RR 0.15). On rituximab, the review states plainly: randomised trial data on the efficacy and adverse effects of rituximab in adults with minimal change disease are awaited. No rituximab-versus-CNI trial in adults was found.
cards.watchOut: This card is carded as the state-of-the-randomised-evidence record for the comparator side of the question: it sizes what calcineurin inhibitors achieve in adult trials and documents that the head-to-head rituximab trial does not yet exist — it is not evidence about rituximab's effect.

cards.headline: Guitard 2014: in 41 adults with minimal-change nephrotic syndrome given rituximab, overall response was 78% — but 56% of responders relapsed, at a median of 18 months
cards.summary: Guitard 2014: in 41 adults with minimal-change nephrotic syndrome given rituximab, overall response was 78% — but 56% of responders relapsed, at a median of 18 months
cards.people: 41 adults with minimal-change nephrotic syndrome receiving rituximab, in a large retrospective multicentre study; complete response was defined as remission with withdrawal of all immunosuppressants and partial response as remission with withdrawal of at least one. Follow-up was 39 months (range 6–71).
cards.result: Complete and partial clinical responses were obtained in 25 and 7 patients respectively (overall response 78%), including 3 patients who received rituximab alone and had a complete response. After follow-up of 39 months, relapses occurred in 18 responder patients (56%, median time 18 months, range 3–36); 17 of these received a second rituximab course and again had complete (n = 13) or partial (n = 4) responses. Nine patients were still in remission 14 months (3–36) after B-cell recovery. No significant early or late adverse event occurred.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective, uncontrolled series in heavily pre-treated patients: the 78% response includes the effect of withdrawing other drugs over time, and the 56% relapse rate among responders is the figure that tempers any claim that rituximab durably replaces calcineurin inhibitors.
cards.source: Guitard J et al. Rituximab for minimal-change nephrotic syndrome in adulthood: predictive factors for response, long-term outcomes and tolerance. cards.headline: Synthesis: rituximab induces remission in most relapsing adults in observational data, relapse after response is common, and the randomised adult comparison with calcineurin inhibitors has never been run
cards.summary: Synthesis: rituximab induces remission in most relapsing adults in observational data, relapse after response is common, and the randomised adult comparison with calcineurin inhibitors has never been run
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of 21 observational adult studies (382 patients), a Cochrane review of 15 adult randomised trials (769 participants) covering the calcineurin-inhibitor side, and a 41-patient retrospective multicentre rituximab series. No randomised adult rituximab trial is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: Pooled complete remission after rituximab was 84.2% (91.6% minimal change disease, 43% FSGS) with 27.4% relapsing over 12–43 months (Xue 2021); in the largest single series, response was 78% with 56% of responders relapsing at a median 18 months (Guitard 2014). Calcineurin inhibitors in adult randomised trials match prednisolone for remission (RR 0.99) with a relapse RR of 0.73 whose interval crosses 1 (Azukaitis 2022), which also records that adult rituximab trial data are awaited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The versus-calcineurin-inhibitor half of this shelf's question is unanswered by direct evidence in adults; the paediatric rituximab evidence lives on live shelf #739 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded.

shelves.title: Phosphate binders versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD: mortality benefit unproven — pooled relative risks favour binders but are low-certainty and cross no effect, while calcification progressed more on binders in the largest placebo trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic kidney disease, do phosphate binders reduce mortality versus placebo in people not on dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Chelating Agents · Phosphates · Hypercalcemia · Bias · Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Lanthanum · Sevelamer · Cardiovascular Diseases · Constipation · Nausea · Calcium Compounds · Vascular Calcification · Adult · Cause of Death · Calcium Carbonate · Acetates · Hyperphosphatemia · Placebos
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of pack #5527, which compares sevelamer with calcium-based binders in non-dialysis CKD; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, binders versus placebo for mortality, and none of #5527's carded records is re-carded here. The direct answer is that no mortality benefit has been shown: the Cochrane review (Natale 2025) puts the relative risk of death versus placebo/usual care at 0.45 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.53) for sevelamer and 0.33 (0.10 to 1.05) for lanthanum — relative measures, graded low-certainty, both compatible with no effect — and cardiovascular death was not estimable because no events were reported in the placebo-controlled studies. The non-dialysis placebo trials explain why a benefit is hard to credit: binders lowered phosphate only modestly and coronary calcification progressed more on pooled binders than placebo (Block 2012); sevelamer made no difference to FGF23 or serum phosphate over 12 weeks (Liabeuf 2017, FRENCH); and lanthanum made no difference to vascular function or arterial stiffness (Jovanovich 2024). Gastrointestinal harms versus placebo are real (constipation relative risk about 3 for both binders; nausea relative risk 2.99 for lanthanum). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): phosphate binders have not been shown to reduce mortality versus placebo in people with CKD who are not on dialysis.

cards.headline: Natale 2025 (Cochrane): versus placebo or usual care, sevelamer's relative risk of death was 0.45 and lanthanum's 0.33 — but both confidence intervals cross 1, certainty is low, and no cardiovascular deaths were reported in the placebo-controlled studies at all
cards.summary: Natale 2025 (Cochrane): versus placebo or usual care, sevelamer's relative risk of death was 0.45 and lanthanum's 0.33 — but both confidence intervals cross 1, certainty is low, and no cardiovascular deaths were reported in the placebo-controlled studies at all
cards.people: Cochrane review of 134 randomised studies (20,913 adults) of phosphate binders in CKD; the binder-versus-placebo/usual-care comparisons were mostly in people with CKD not on dialysis (head-to-head binder comparisons were mostly in dialysis patients), with a median study duration of 5.4 months across the review.
cards.result: Compared with placebo/usual care, sevelamer may have little or no effect on death from any cause (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.53; 6 studies, 781 participants; low-certainty evidence) and lanthanum likewise (relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.05; 7 studies, 694 participants; low-certainty evidence) — both are relative measures whose intervals include no effect, and the review could not estimate cardiovascular death because no events were reported in those studies (3 studies, 222 participants for sevelamer). Sevelamer may increase constipation (relative risk 3.27, 1.38 to 7.74) and lanthanum may increase nausea (relative risk 2.99, 1.42 to 6.31) and constipation (relative risk 2.98, 1.21 to 7.30). The review concludes no clinically important benefits of binders were identified for cardiovascular death or coronary artery calcium score versus placebo/usual care.
cards.watchOut: The mortality analyses rest on few events in short studies (median 5.4 months) never powered for death, and 'placebo/usual care' pools different comparators — the point estimates favour binders while the evidence, as the review grades it, can support neither a benefit claim nor a claim of no benefit.

cards.headline: Block 2012: in moderate CKD with normal or near-normal phosphate, pooled binders lowered serum phosphate modestly versus placebo (3.9 vs 4.1 mg/dL) but coronary calcification progressed more on binders (median +18.1% vs +0.6%) — and mortality was not a reported outcome (N = 148)
cards.summary: Block 2012: in moderate CKD with normal or near-normal phosphate, pooled binders lowered serum phosphate modestly versus placebo (3.9 vs 4.1 mg/dL) but coronary calcification progressed more on binders (median +18.1% vs +0.6%) — and mortality was not a reported outcome (N = 148)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, three binders pooled (Block 2012)
cards.people: 148 patients with eGFR 20–45 mL/min/1.73 m² randomised to calcium acetate, lanthanum carbonate, sevelamer carbonate, or placebo for 9 months; baseline mean serum phosphorus was 4.2 mg/dL in both the pooled active and placebo arms.
cards.result: Serum phosphorus fell to 3.9 mg/dL with active therapy and 4.1 mg/dL with placebo (P = 0.03); 24-hour urine phosphorus fell by 22% on binders but not placebo, and median intact parathyroid hormone stayed stable on binders while rising on placebo (P = 0.002). Fibroblast growth factor 23 did not change significantly. However, calcification increased significantly more on active therapy in the coronary arteries (median increase 18.1% versus 0.6%, P = 0.05) and abdominal aorta (15.4% versus 3.4%, P = 0.03). The record reports no mortality outcome.
cards.watchOut: Three chemically different binders (including a calcium-based one, the likeliest calcification driver) are pooled against placebo, so the calcification signal cannot be assigned to any single binder — and with 9 months and no deaths reported, this trial cannot speak to mortality at all.
cards.source: Block GA et al. Effects of phosphate binders in moderate CKD. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2012. PMID: 22822075. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Liabeuf 2017 (FRENCH trial): 12 weeks of sevelamer versus placebo in stage 3b/4 CKD lowered urinary phosphate but made no difference to FGF23, serum phosphate or klotho (the treatment made no difference) (N = 78)
cards.summary: Liabeuf 2017 (FRENCH trial): 12 weeks of sevelamer versus placebo in stage 3b/4 CKD lowered urinary phosphate but made no difference to FGF23, serum phosphate or klotho (the treatment made no difference) (N = 78)
cards.people: 78 normophosphataemic patients with CKD stage 3b/4 (eGFR 15–45 mL/min/1.73 m², mean 27 ± 9; fasting serum phosphate over 3.1 mg/dL, mean 3.8 ± 0.5 mg/dL) randomised double-blind to sevelamer carbonate 4.8 g daily or placebo for 12 weeks; all patients received cholecalciferol at randomisation.
cards.result: Urinary phosphate-to-creatinine ratio fell significantly with sevelamer, but median change in serum C-terminal fibroblast growth factor 23 did not differ between groups (placebo +38, interquartile range −13 to +114, versus sevelamer +37, −1 to +101 relative units/mL; P = 0.77), and there was no significant difference in intact fibroblast growth factor 23, α-klotho or serum phosphate change. Total and LDL cholesterol fell significantly in the sevelamer group. The record reports no mortality outcome.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week biomarker trial in 78 patients cannot test mortality; it is carded because it removes the proposed mechanism (FGF23 lowering) that a mortality benefit in non-dialysis CKD would most plausibly run through.
cards.source: Liabeuf S et al. Randomized Clinical Trial of Sevelamer Carbonate on Serum Klotho and Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 in CKD. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2017. PMID: 29074818. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jovanovich 2024: lanthanum versus placebo for 12 weeks in CKD 3b–4 with normal phosphorus changed neither serum phosphorus, vascular function nor arterial stiffness (the treatment made no difference) (N = 54 on the face)
cards.summary: Jovanovich 2024: lanthanum versus placebo for 12 weeks in CKD 3b–4 with normal phosphorus changed neither serum phosphorus, vascular function nor arterial stiffness (the treatment made no difference) (N = 54 on the face)
cards.people: 54 participants with CKD stage 3b–4 (mean eGFR 38 ± 14 mL/min/1.73 m², mean age 65 ± 8 years) and normal phosphorus levels, randomised double-blind to lanthanum carbonate or placebo for 12 weeks; primary endpoints were change in brachial artery flow-mediated dilation and carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity.
cards.result: Serum phosphorus did not change with lanthanum (3.44 ± 0.47 to 3.44 ± 0.52 mg/dL; P = 0.94) and tended to rise with placebo (3.42 ± 0.80 to 3.74 ± 1.26 mg/dL; P = 0.09). Flow-mediated dilation and pulse wave velocity did not change in either group (between-group P = 0.67 and P = 0.77), and circulating and endothelial markers of oxidative stress and inflammation did not differ. The record reports no mortality outcome.
cards.watchOut: A small 12-week mechanistic trial in normophosphataemic patients: it shows a binder does not move vascular surrogates when phosphate is already normal, which limits — but does not by itself settle — what binders might do in hyperphosphataemic non-dialysis patients over years.
cards.source: Jovanovich A et al. Effect of Lanthanum Carbonate on Serum Phosphate, Oxidative Stress, and Vascular Dysfunction in CKD: A Mechanistic Randomized Controlled Trial. Kidney360. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: no placebo-controlled evidence shows binders reduce mortality in non-dialysis CKD — the pooled relative risks (0.45 and 0.33) are low-certainty and cross no-effect, no trial reported cardiovascular deaths, and the mechanistic trials show no FGF23 or vascular benefit while one shows more calcification on binders
cards.summary: Synthesis: no placebo-controlled evidence shows binders reduce mortality in non-dialysis CKD — the pooled relative risks (0.45 and 0.33) are low-certainty and cross no-effect, no trial reported cardiovascular deaths, and the mechanistic trials show no FGF23 or vascular benefit while one shows more calcification on binders
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of binder-versus-placebo comparisons (mortality analyses: 781 participants for sevelamer, 694 for lanthanum) and three placebo-controlled trials in non-dialysis CKD (N = 148, 78 and 54). Total carded participants exceed 1,700 across the review and trials, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is event scarcity and short follow-up, printed here.
cards.result: Versus placebo/usual care, relative risk of death was 0.45 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.53) for sevelamer and 0.33 (0.10 to 1.05) for lanthanum — relative measures, low certainty, both compatible with no effect (Natale 2025). Binders lowered serum phosphate modestly (3.9 vs 4.1 mg/dL; Block 2012) but coronary calcification progressed more on binders in that trial, and neither FGF23 (Liabeuf 2017) nor vascular function (Jovanovich 2024) improved versus placebo. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a mortality benefit of phosphate binders versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD is unproven.
cards.watchOut: The trials were short and the patients often normophosphataemic — absence of a shown benefit is not proof of no benefit in hyperphosphataemic patients treated for years, but on current records there is nothing firmer to offer a reader than 'unproven'.

shelves.title: Allopurinol for uric acid stones: unproven — no placebo trial exists; the only data bundle it with citrate and show the same recurrence rate, because acid urine, not urate load, is the main driver
shelves.question: In adults with uric acid kidney stones, does allopurinol reduce stone recurrence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Kidney Calculi · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid · Drug Monitoring
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3209, which homes allopurinol versus placebo for calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria (Ettinger 1986); this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, uric acid stones, and Ettinger 1986 is cross-pointed here in prose only and is NOT re-carded. For uric acid stones the fetched records contain no placebo-controlled trial of allopurinol at all: the comparative evidence bundles allopurinol with potassium citrate, in which form adherence was associated with smaller recurrences and fewer operations but an identical recurrence rate of 32% (Canales 2019), and a dissolution series using citrate alone or with allopurinol cleared 67% of treated patients with no comparator and no allopurinol-only arm (Gridley 2019). The standard account of this stone type (Wiederkehr 2011) attributes formation primarily to unduly acid urine — hyperuricosuria a less deciding factor — and names urinary alkalinisation to pH 6–6.5 as the essential drug treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: whether allopurinol reduces uric acid stone recurrence versus placebo is untested; its benefit for this stone type is unproven.

cards.headline: Canales 2019: in 53 uric acid stone formers cleared of stones, patients adherent to medical therapy (potassium citrate with or without allopurinol) had the same CT recurrence rate as nonadherent patients (32% in both groups) — allopurinol's own contribution was never separated
cards.summary: Canales 2019: in 53 uric acid stone formers cleared of stones, patients adherent to medical therapy (potassium citrate with or without allopurinol) had the same CT recurrence rate as nonadherent patients (32% in both groups) — allopurinol's own contribution was never separated
cards.people: 53 uric acid stone formers with complete stone clearance confirmed by CT after a stone procedure, at least one postoperative 24-hour urine collection and at least 6 months of follow-up with surveillance CT; 28 (53%) were classified adherent to medical therapy (potassium citrate with or without allopurinol, verified by pharmacy data) and 25 nonadherent (14 declined medication, 11 intolerant). Retrospective study; median follow-up 24 months.
cards.result: Stone recurrence did not differ between adherent and nonadherent groups (32%; P = .99), and 24-hour urine pH did not differ from baseline or between groups (range 5.46–5.62; P = 0.06). Adherent patients' recurrences were smaller (6.3 ± 3.8 vs 11.8 ± 6.2 mm, P = .02), they were 28% less likely to require stone surgery (P < .01), and time without recurrence trended longer (23.1 ± 18.8 vs 10.5 ± 7.5 months, P = .10). No arm received allopurinol alone or allopurinol versus placebo, so no allopurinol-specific effect can be extracted from this record.
cards.watchOut: Adherence was not randomised — patients who take therapy differ from those who decline or cannot tolerate it — and the therapy bundle mixes citrate with allopurinol in varying doses, so even the bundle's null recurrence result cannot be read as allopurinol's effect.
cards.source: Canales BK et al. Long-term Recurrence Rates in Uric Acid Stone Formers With or Without Medical Management. Urology. 2019. PMID: 31158354. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gridley 2019: dissolution therapy with potassium citrate alone or combined with allopurinol cleared stones completely in 67% of 21 treated uric acid stone patients — with no untreated or placebo group to compare against
cards.summary: Gridley 2019: dissolution therapy with potassium citrate alone or combined with allopurinol cleared stones completely in 67% of 21 treated uric acid stone patients — with no untreated or placebo group to compare against
cards.people: Retrospective review of 24 patients (14 men, 10 women) with uric acid nephrolithiasis referred for surgery but treated with medical dissolution therapy between 2007 and 2016; 3 patients (13%) did not tolerate therapy and stopped, leaving 21 maintained on potassium citrate alone or in combination with allopurinol, with serial imaging and urine pH follow-up.
cards.result: Of the 21 patients maintained on therapy, 14 (67%) had complete resolution of nephrolithiasis and 7 (33%) had partial reduction, with a mean stone-burden reduction of 68% in the partial responders. Three complications were recorded (urinary tract infection, gastrointestinal upset, throat irritation) and 4 stone recurrences occurred among the 21 patients. The record does not report outcomes separately for citrate alone versus citrate plus allopurinol, and there was no placebo or no-treatment comparator.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm series of surgery-referred patients who tolerated therapy: dissolution success under combined alkali-based treatment says nothing about whether adding allopurinol — rather than the alkalinisation itself — did any of the work.
cards.source: Gridley CM et al. Medical dissolution therapy for the treatment of uric acid nephrolithiasis. World Journal of Urology. 2019. PMID: 30810833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wiederkehr 2011: uric acid stones form primarily because urine is unduly acid — hyperuricosuria is a 'less deciding factor' — and the essential drug treatment in this review is potassium citrate to a urine pH of 6 to 6.5, not urate lowering
cards.summary: Wiederkehr 2011: uric acid stones form primarily because urine is unduly acid — hyperuricosuria is a 'less deciding factor' — and the essential drug treatment in this review is potassium citrate to a urine pH of 6 to 6.5, not urate lowering
cards.people: Narrative review of uric acid nephrolithiasis, which the authors describe as about 10% of all stone formers and characteristically a manifestation of a systemic metabolic disorder, most often metabolic syndrome; a universal finding is low baseline urine pH with insufficient urinary ammonium buffer.
cards.result: The review reports no trial of allopurinol versus placebo in uric acid stones and gives no effect size for allopurinol. Its management account is: liberal fluid intake and dietary modification, with potassium citrate to alkalinize the urine to a goal pH between 6 and 6.5 described as essential, because undissociated uric acid deprotonates into its much more soluble urate form. Stone formation is attributed primarily to unduly acid urine, with hyperuricosuria and low urine volume as less deciding factors.
cards.watchOut: A review's framing is not evidence: it is carded to document why the placebo-controlled allopurinol trial this shelf asks about does not exist in the fetched records — the field's tested lever for uric acid stones is urinary alkalinisation — not as proof that allopurinol cannot help a hyperuricosuric subgroup.
cards.source: Wiederkehr MR et al. Uric Acid Nephrolithiasis: A Systemic Metabolic Disorder. Clinical Reviews in Bone and Mineral Metabolism. 2011. PMID: 25045326. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: allopurinol has never been tested against placebo in uric acid stones in any record fetched — the only comparative data bundle it with potassium citrate and show no recurrence-rate difference, so its benefit for this stone type is unproven (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: allopurinol has never been tested against placebo in uric acid stones in any record fetched — the only comparative data bundle it with potassium citrate and show no recurrence-rate difference, so its benefit for this stone type is unproven (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective adherence cohort in uric acid stone formers (N = 53), one retrospective dissolution series (N = 24 referred, 21 treated), and one expert review documenting the alkalinisation-centred standard of care. Total carded participants are 77, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the binding limitation is the absence of any randomised or allopurinol-isolating comparison, printed here.
cards.result: In the cohort, adherence to citrate with or without allopurinol was associated with smaller recurrences and fewer operations but an identical recurrence rate (32% vs 32%; Canales 2019); in the series, citrate with or without allopurinol dissolved stones completely in 67% of treated patients with no comparator (Gridley 2019). No record separates allopurinol from the alkali it is prescribed with, and none compares it with placebo. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: allopurinol's effect on uric acid stone recurrence is untested and unproven.
cards.watchOut: Unproven is not disproven: a hyperuricosuric uric acid stone former might still benefit, but no fetched record isolates that subgroup or that drug — any stronger stamp would be manufactured, not found.
