shelves.title: Citrate intake and low urinary citrate: urinary citrate rises (lemonade +383 mg/day), but stone prevention by diet alone is unproven — no randomised trial, and the one long-term stone-rate fall missed significance
shelves.question: Does increasing citrate intake prevent kidney stones in adults with low urinary citrate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Beverages · Citric Acid · Citrus · Female · Humans · Male · Metabolic Diseases · Middle Aged · Nephrolithiasis · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2645, which homes potassium citrate drug therapy for recurrent calcium stones; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, dietary citrate intake (juices and lemonade) in people with low urinary citrate, and none of #2645's carded records is re-carded here. Intake does move the urine: long-term lemonade raised urinary citrate by a mean of 383 mg/day in hypocitraturic stone formers (Kang 2007), fruit juices raised citraturia by a pooled 167.2 mg/day across controlled studies (Pachaly 2016), and orange juice — unlike lemonade — delivered an alkali load that raised urinary pH and citrate and lowered calculated calcium oxalate supersaturation in a metabolic crossover (Odvina 2006). But prevention of stones themselves is unproven for intake: the only long-term stone-outcome report is Kang's retrospective 11-patient lemonade series, whose formation-rate fall from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient-year was reported as not statistically significant (p > 0.05), and the review authors themselves call for larger trials. A small randomised crossover of a lemonade beverage in 8 hypocitraturic stone formers exists but falls below this library's 10-human reference floor and is not carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): increasing citrate intake raises urinary citrate in low-citrate adults; whether it prevents kidney stones has not been shown in a randomised trial.

cards.headline: Kang 2007: long-term lemonade therapy raised urinary citrate by a mean of 383 mg/day in hypocitraturic stone formers and the stone formation rate fell from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient-year — but that fall was not statistically significant (p > 0.05, printed plainly) (11 lemonade patients on the face)
cards.summary: Kang 2007: long-term lemonade therapy raised urinary citrate by a mean of 383 mg/day in hypocitraturic stone formers and the stone formation rate fell from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient-year — but that fall was not statistically significant (p > 0.05, printed plainly) (11 lemonade patients on the face)
cards.people: Retrospective study of patients with hypocitraturic nephrolithiasis on long-term lemonade therapy: 11 patients (4 men, 7 women; mean age 52.7 years; mean treatment 44.4 months) met evaluation criteria, compared with an age- and sex-matched group of 11 patients treated with oral slow-release potassium citrate (mean 42.5 months). Pre- and post-therapy urinary parameters and stone formation rates were compared.
cards.result: Ten of 11 lemonade patients increased urinary citrate (mean increase +383 mg per day, p < 0.05); all 11 potassium citrate patients increased it (mean +482 mg per day, p < 0.0001). Stone burden in the lemonade group was 37.2 mm² before and 30.4 mm² after therapy (p > 0.05), and the stone formation rate fell from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient per year (p > 0.05) — a large point estimate that the record itself reports as not statistically significant in 11 patients.
cards.watchOut: Eleven retrospectively identified patients, no randomisation and no untreated control group: people who stay on lemonade therapy for nearly 4 years are a selected group, and the headline stone-rate fall did not reach significance — this card shows a citraturic effect, not proven stone prevention.
cards.source: Kang DE et al. Long-term lemonade based dietary manipulation in patients with hypocitraturic nephrolithiasis. Journal of Urology. 2007. PMID: 17382731. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Odvina 2006: in a controlled metabolic crossover, orange juice raised urinary pH and citrate and lowered calculated calcium oxalate supersaturation versus water — lemonade did not provide the same alkali load (N = 13 on the face)
cards.summary: Odvina 2006: in a controlled metabolic crossover, orange juice raised urinary pH and citrate and lowered calculated calcium oxalate supersaturation versus water — lemonade did not provide the same alkali load (N = 13 on the face)
cards.people: Randomised crossover study in 13 volunteers (9 healthy subjects and 4 stone formers) who sequentially received distilled water, orange juice or lemonade while on a constant metabolic diet, with 24-hour urine collections for acid-base parameters and stone-risk analysis.
cards.result: Orange juice, but not lemonade, provided alkali: net gastrointestinal alkali absorption and urinary pH and citrate were higher with orange juice than control. Urinary calcium did not differ significantly, urinary oxalate was higher during the orange juice phase, calculated calcium oxalate supersaturation was lower with orange juice than control, calculated undissociated uric acid was lower with orange juice than with both control and lemonade, and calculated brushite supersaturation was significantly higher with orange juice than with both other phases. The authors describe this as a short-term biochemical study and call for long-term prevention studies.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen volunteers, only four of them stone formers and none selected for low urinary citrate, studied over days on a metabolic ward: urinary chemistry moved favourably for orange juice, but no stones were formed or prevented in this study, and the brushite supersaturation moved the wrong way.
cards.source: Odvina CV et al. Comparative value of orange juice versus lemonade in reducing stone-forming risk. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2006. PMID: 17699358. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pachaly 2016: across 13 controlled studies of non-drug citrate interventions, commercial fruit juices raised urinary citrate by a pooled 167.2 mg/day — with very high heterogeneity — while other dietary interventions' pooled effects were not significant
cards.summary: Pachaly 2016: across 13 controlled studies of non-drug citrate interventions, commercial fruit juices raised urinary citrate by a pooled 167.2 mg/day — with very high heterogeneity — while other dietary interventions' pooled effects were not significant
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies of non-pharmacological interventions (commercial fruit juices, soft drinks, calcium-/magnesium-rich mineral water, high-fibre diet, low-animal-protein diet, plant extract) measuring urinary citrate or nephrolithiasis, including 358 participants with a mean age of 43 ± 11.0 years; about half the included samples were in non-stone formers.
cards.result: Commercial fruit juice interventions increased urinary citrate by 167.2 mg/day (95% CI 65.4 to 269) with high heterogeneity (I² = 88.1%, P = 0.000). Other intervention types showed no important heterogeneity but their pooled estimates were not significant. The authors conclude that further larger-scale trials are required to analyse whether non-pharmacological interventions can increase urinary citrate and act in kidney stone prevention.
cards.watchOut: The juice pooled estimate mixes different juices, doses and populations (many not hypocitraturic, many not stone formers) with I² of 88% — the average effect is real for urinary citrate but a poor predictor of what any one patient's intake change will do, and the endpoint is urine chemistry, not stones.
cards.source: Pachaly MA et al. Effects of non-pharmacological interventions on urinary citrate levels: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nephrology, Dialysis, Transplantation. 2016. PMID: 26311217. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Citrates · Diet, Protein-Restricted · Humans · Kidney Calculi · Potassium Citrate

cards.headline: Synthesis: increasing citrate intake does raise urinary citrate in people with low urinary citrate — lemonade by about 383 mg/day in the one long-term hypocitraturic series — but no randomised trial shows dietary citrate prevents stones, and the one long-term stone-rate fall was not statistically significant
cards.summary: Synthesis: increasing citrate intake does raise urinary citrate in people with low urinary citrate — lemonade by about 383 mg/day in the one long-term hypocitraturic series — but no randomised trial shows dietary citrate prevents stones, and the one long-term stone-rate fall was not statistically significant
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective long-term lemonade series in hypocitraturic stone formers (11 lemonade and 11 potassium-citrate patients), one randomised crossover metabolic study (13 volunteers, 4 stone formers), and one systematic review of non-drug interventions (13 studies, 358 participants). Total carded participants exceed 380, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small individual studies carry their Ns on their faces.
cards.result: Lemonade therapy increased urinary citrate in 10 of 11 hypocitraturic patients (mean +383 mg/day; Kang 2007) and fruit juices raised citraturia by a pooled 167.2 mg/day across controlled studies (Pachaly 2016); orange juice improved several calculated stone-risk indices versus water in the crossover study (Odvina 2006). The only stone-outcome data are Kang's formation-rate fall from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient-year, reported as p > 0.05. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): citrate intake raises urinary citrate; that it prevents stones is unproven.
cards.watchOut: Every favourable number here is a urine-chemistry surrogate except one small retrospective stone-rate estimate that missed significance — the shelf must not be read as dietary citrate being a proven substitute for potassium citrate, whose randomised evidence lives on shelf #2645.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kang DE et al. Journal of Urology. 2007 (PMID: 17382731); Odvina CV et al. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2006 (PMID: 17699358); Pachaly MA et al. Nephrology, Dialysis, Transplantation. 2016 (PMID: 26311217).

shelves.title: Stroke with high-target ESA therapy in CKD anaemia: risk was doubled in TREAT (5.0% vs 2.6%) and raised across every target-trial meta-analysis — the clearest harm of chasing a normal haemoglobin
shelves.question: In adults with anemia of CKD, does a higher hemoglobin target with ESAs increase stroke risk versus a lower target?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anemia · Case-Control Studies · Darbepoetin alfa · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Erythropoietin · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hematinics · Humans · Incidence · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Risk Factors · Risk Reduction Behavior · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #179, which covers high- versus low-target erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) therapy for cardiovascular outcomes as a composite, with stroke inside it; this shelf isolates the stroke outcome specifically, cross-pointing #179 for the primary CHOIR, CREATE and TREAT reports, which are homed there and are not re-carded here. The stroke-specific record is consistent and one-directional. In TREAT's dedicated stroke analysis (Skali 2011; a secondary analysis of the trial homed on #179, carded here as a distinct report because stroke is this shelf's question), darbepoetin alfa doubled stroke: 101 of 2,012 patients (5.0%) versus 53 of 2,026 (2.6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.9; 95% CI 1.4 to 2.7; relative measure), and no baseline feature, blood-pressure, haemoglobin, platelet or dose pattern explained or could mitigate it. Across the target trials, Palmer 2010 (27 trials, 10,452 patients) found a higher haemoglobin target increased stroke (relative risk 1.51; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.21; relative measure), and Vinhas 2012, restricting to large trials of at least a year (5 trials, 7,902 participants), found the same (relative risk 1.735; 95% CI 1.323 to 2.275; relative measure). The absolute excess in TREAT was 2.4 percentage points (5.0% versus 2.6%). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): a higher haemoglobin target with ESAs increases stroke risk versus a lower target — shown in the dedicated analysis of the largest trial and in two independent meta-analyses of the target trials.

cards.headline: Skali 2011 (TREAT stroke analysis): darbepoetin alfa doubled stroke — 5.0% versus 2.6% (hazard ratio 1.9) — and no measured factor explained or could mitigate the excess
cards.summary: Skali 2011 (TREAT stroke analysis): darbepoetin alfa doubled stroke — 5.0% versus 2.6% (hazard ratio 1.9) — and no measured factor explained or could mitigate the excess
cards.type: Secondary stroke analysis of a randomised trial (Skali 2011, TREAT)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of TREAT: 4,038 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease and anaemia randomised to darbepoetin alfa (targeting haemoglobin around 13 g/dL) or placebo (with rescue darbepoetin if haemoglobin fell below 9.0 g/dL); 154 patients had a stroke. Baseline predictors were modelled in all 4,038 patients, with a nested case-control analysis (1:10 propensity matching) for post-randomisation factors.
cards.result: Stroke occurred in 101 of 2,012 patients (5.0%) in the darbepoetin alfa arm and 53 of 2,026 (2.6%) in the placebo arm (hazard ratio 1.9; 95% CI 1.4 to 2.7; relative measure) — an absolute excess of 2.4 percentage points. Assignment to darbepoetin alfa independently predicted stroke (odds ratio 2.1; 95% CI 1.5 to 2.9), as did prior stroke (odds ratio 2.0), more proteinuria and known cardiovascular disease. In the darbepoetin arm, post-randomisation systolic and diastolic blood pressure, haemoglobin level, platelet count and dose did not differ between patients with and without stroke, and sensitivity analyses were similar; the authors conclude the two-fold increase could not be attributed to any of these factors or mitigated by them.
cards.watchOut: This is a secondary analysis of a single trial whose primary report is homed on live shelf #179 — it is carded here, as a distinct publication, only because stroke is this shelf's whole question; TREAT's placebo arm could receive rescue darbepoetin, which would bias the contrast toward the null, not create the excess.
cards.source: Skali H et al. Stroke in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and anemia treated with Darbepoetin Alfa: the trial to reduce cardiovascular events with Aranesp therapy (TREAT) experience. Circulation. 2011. PMID: 22104547. Registry ID: NCT00093015. cards.headline: Palmer 2010: across 27 target trials (10,452 patients), a higher haemoglobin target increased stroke — relative risk 1.51 — alongside hypertension and vascular access thrombosis
cards.summary: Palmer 2010: across 27 target trials (10,452 patients), a higher haemoglobin target increased stroke — relative risk 1.51 — alongside hypertension and vascular access thrombosis
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 27 randomised trials (10,452 patients) of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in chronic kidney disease, including haemoglobin-target trials and ESA-versus-no-treatment or placebo trials, across all stages of CKD (searches to March 2010).
cards.result: A higher haemoglobin target was associated with increased risks of stroke (relative risk 1.51; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.21; relative measure), hypertension (relative risk 1.67; 95% CI 1.31 to 2.12) and vascular access thrombosis (relative risk 1.33; 95% CI 1.16 to 1.53) compared with a lower target. There were no statistically significant differences in mortality (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.20), serious cardiovascular events (relative risk 1.15; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.33) or end-stage kidney disease (relative risk 1.08), though point estimates favoured the lower target. Treatment effects were consistent across subgroups, and the record reports no absolute stroke rates for the pooled comparison.
cards.watchOut: The stroke confidence interval (1.03 to 2.21) only just excludes no effect and pools target trials with ESA-versus-nothing trials; the stroke-specific estimate is corroborated, not carried, by this synthesis.
cards.source: Palmer SC et al. Meta-analysis: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in patients with chronic kidney disease. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20439566. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vinhas 2012: restricting to large, longer trials only (5 trials, 7,902 participants) strengthened the stroke signal — relative risk 1.735 with a higher haemoglobin target
cards.summary: Vinhas 2012: restricting to large, longer trials only (5 trials, 7,902 participants) strengthened the stroke signal — relative risk 1.735 with a higher haemoglobin target
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials in adults with CKD allocating patients to different ESA doses/targets, with duration of at least 1 year and more than 500 participants: 5 trials, 7,902 participants, follow-up 14 to 36 months, trial sizes 596 to 4,038.
cards.result: A higher haemoglobin target was associated with increased risk of stroke (relative risk 1.735; 95% CI 1.323 to 2.275; P = 0.0005; relative measure) and vascular access thrombosis (relative risk 1.343; 95% CI 1.162 to 1.554), with no effect on end-stage renal disease (relative risk 1.089; 95% CI 0.986 to 1.203) and no significant effect on all-cause mortality (relative risk 1.148; 95% CI 0.977 to 1.350). The record reports no pooled absolute stroke rates.
cards.watchOut: The five large trials overlap heavily with the trials in Palmer 2010 and with TREAT itself, so the three cards are concordant readings of substantially the same randomised evidence, not three independent experiments.
cards.source: Vinhas J et al. Treatment of anaemia with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in patients with chronic kidney disease does not lower mortality and may increase cardiovascular risk: a meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: stroke is the clearest harm of high-target ESA therapy — doubled in TREAT (5.0% versus 2.6%) and raised by about half to three-quarters in relative terms across the target-trial meta-analyses
cards.summary: Synthesis: stroke is the clearest harm of high-target ESA therapy — doubled in TREAT (5.0% versus 2.6%) and raised by about half to three-quarters in relative terms across the target-trial meta-analyses
cards.people: The carded evidence: one dedicated stroke analysis of the largest placebo-controlled trial (4,038 patients; 154 strokes) and two meta-analyses of the haemoglobin-target trials (27 trials, 10,452 patients; 5 large trials, 7,902 participants). The syntheses re-analyse substantially the same trials, including TREAT and CHOIR, whose primary reports are homed on live shelf #179 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Darbepoetin alfa versus placebo in TREAT: stroke 5.0% versus 2.6% (hazard ratio 1.9; absolute excess 2.4 percentage points). Higher versus lower haemoglobin target across trials: stroke relative risk 1.51 (Palmer 2010) and 1.735 in large trials only (Vinhas 2012), both relative measures. No analysis found a subgroup or on-treatment factor that removed the excess. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm).
cards.watchOut: The comparison on this shelf is target against target (and, in TREAT, ESA against placebo with rescue): it does not show that any ESA use at a low target causes stroke — it shows that pushing haemoglobin higher does.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skali H et al. Circulation. 2011 (PMID: 22104547); Palmer SC et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20439566); Vinhas J et al. Nephron Clinical Practice. 2012 (PMID: 23182871).

shelves.title: ESAs and transfusion in CKD anaemia: transfusion is reliably prevented (odds ratios ~0.2–0.3 vs placebo) — the class's most consistent benefit, with no survival gain attached
shelves.question: In adults with anemia of chronic kidney disease, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents reduce transfusion needs?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Hematinics · Epoetin Alfa · Darbepoetin alfa · Biosimilar Pharmaceuticals · Erythropoiesis · Anemia · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Hypertension · Thrombosis · Dyspnea · Myocardial Infarction
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #179, which covers erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) in CKD for haemoglobin targets and cardiovascular outcomes; this shelf covers the outcome #179 does not isolate — transfusion needs — and does not re-card #179's target trials. The transfusion evidence is the oldest and most consistent benefit of these drugs. The 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis (Chung 2023; 117 studies, 25,237 participants) found epoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.28), epoetin beta (odds ratio 0.19) and darbepoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.27) each superior to placebo for preventing blood transfusion, at low-to-moderate certainty, while effects on death were uncertain and hypertension odds rose. The 2014 edition of the same network (Palmer 2014; 56 studies, 15,596 adults) found the same pattern for every proprietary ESA (odds ratios 0.09 to 0.18 versus placebo). In pre-dialysis patients specifically, the Cochrane recombinant erythropoietin review (Cody 2016; 19 studies, 993 participants) found the number of patients requiring transfusion fell (relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.83; relative measure), alongside improved quality of life and exercise capacity. The same reviews are equally clear that preventing transfusion did not translate into a survival advantage, and that hypertension is more frequent on ESAs — and live shelf #179 and pack #5970 carry the high-target stroke harm that bounds how hard transfusion avoidance should be chased. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ESAs reduce transfusion needs in anaemia of CKD — a large, consistent effect against placebo across two Cochrane network editions and the pre-dialysis review.

cards.headline: Chung 2023 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): epoetin alfa, epoetin beta and darbepoetin alfa each prevented blood transfusion versus placebo (odds ratios 0.19–0.28) across 117 studies and 25,237 participants
cards.summary: Chung 2023 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): epoetin alfa, epoetin beta and darbepoetin alfa each prevented blood transfusion versus placebo (odds ratios 0.19–0.28) across 117 studies and 25,237 participants
cards.people: 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis update: 117 randomised studies with 25,237 adults with chronic kidney disease and anaemia, comparing epoetin alfa, epoetin beta, darbepoetin alfa, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta and biosimilar ESAs against each other, placebo or no treatment (searches to 29 April 2022). Most studies were at high or unclear risk of bias in most domains.
cards.result: For preventing blood transfusion, epoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.61; low-certainty evidence) and epoetin beta (odds ratio 0.19; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.47; low-certainty evidence) may be superior to placebo, and darbepoetin alfa was probably superior to placebo (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.67; moderate-certainty evidence); effects of methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta and biosimilar ESAs were uncertain (odds ratios 0.33 to 0.37 with intervals crossing 1). Effects on death (any cause) were uncertain for most agents and probably no different for darbepoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.21; moderate-certainty evidence). Epoetin beta probably increased hypertension versus placebo (odds ratio 2.17; 95% CI 1.17 to 4.00), and other ESAs may do so. Comparative effects between different ESAs on transfusion were uncertain. All odds ratios are relative measures; the record reports no pooled absolute transfusion rates.
cards.watchOut: Transfusion prevention is measured against placebo or no treatment — in modern practice the relevant question is usually ESA dose and target, and the same review finds no survival benefit to set against the stroke harm of high targets carried on #179 and #5970.
cards.source: Chung EY et al. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents for anaemia in adults with chronic kidney disease: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023. PMID: 36791280. Registry ID: no single registration in the record (the record lists registrations of 50 included trials). cards.headline: Palmer 2014 (first Cochrane network edition): every proprietary ESA prevented transfusion versus placebo — odds ratios 0.09 to 0.18 — across 56 studies and 15,596 adults
cards.summary: Palmer 2014 (first Cochrane network edition): every proprietary ESA prevented transfusion versus placebo — odds ratios 0.09 to 0.18 — across 56 studies and 15,596 adults
cards.people: 2014 Cochrane network meta-analysis: 56 eligible randomised studies involving 15,596 adults with CKD, comparing epoetin alfa, epoetin beta, darbepoetin alfa, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta and biosimilar ESAs against each other, placebo or no treatment (searches to 11 February 2014). Risk of bias was generally high or unclear; no study was low risk for allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessment and attrition.
cards.result: In network analyses there was moderate-to-low confidence that epoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.18; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.59), epoetin beta (odds ratio 0.09; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.38), darbepoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.17; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.57) and methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta (odds ratio 0.15; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.70) prevented blood transfusions compared with placebo; biosimilar ESA therapy was possibly no better than placebo (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.05 to 1.47, very low quality evidence). The review could not discern whether ESAs differ from each other on transfusion. All proprietary ESAs increased the odds of hypertension compared with placebo (odds ratios 1.83 to 2.57). All odds ratios are relative measures; no pooled absolute transfusion rates are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: This is the earlier edition of the same Cochrane network updated by Chung 2023 — the two cards are two readings of a growing evidence base, not independent confirmations, and the very wide intervals reflect sparse transfusion reporting in the older trials.

cards.headline: Cody 2016 (Cochrane, pre-dialysis): recombinant erythropoietin cut the number of patients requiring blood transfusion — relative risk 0.32 — in 19 studies of 993 pre-dialysis patients
cards.summary: Cody 2016 (Cochrane, pre-dialysis): recombinant erythropoietin cut the number of patients requiring blood transfusion — relative risk 0.32 — in 19 studies of 993 pre-dialysis patients
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 19 randomised or quasi-randomised studies enrolling 993 people with anaemia of chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis, comparing recombinant human erythropoietin with placebo or no treatment (searches to 29 June 2015). Most included studies were performed before 2000 and risk of bias was judged unclear in the majority of domains.
cards.result: Treatment improved haemoglobin and haematocrit and decreased the number of patients requiring blood transfusions (relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.83; relative measure). Data from studies reporting quality of life or exercise capacity showed improvement in the treatment group. Most measures of progression of kidney disease showed no statistically significant difference, and no significant increase in adverse events was identified, though the review states it was unable to assess effects on progression of kidney disease, delay in onset of dialysis, or adverse events adequately. The record's printed haemoglobin mean difference carries an internal sign inconsistency and is not relied on here.
cards.watchOut: The pre-dialysis trials are old, small and mostly pre-2000, from an era of higher transfusion thresholds; the relative reduction is large, but absolute transfusion rates in contemporary practice are lower, so the absolute benefit today is smaller than the relative figure suggests.
cards.source: Cody JD et al. Recombinant human erythropoietin versus placebo or no treatment for the anaemia of chronic kidney disease in people not requiring dialysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 26790135. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ESAs prevent transfusion in CKD anaemia with the most consistent effect in this drug class — odds ratios around 0.2–0.3 against placebo in both Cochrane network editions and relative risk 0.32 pre-dialysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: ESAs prevent transfusion in CKD anaemia with the most consistent effect in this drug class — odds ratios around 0.2–0.3 against placebo in both Cochrane network editions and relative risk 0.32 pre-dialysis
cards.people: The carded evidence: the 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis (117 studies, 25,237 participants), its 2014 first edition (56 studies, 15,596 adults) and the Cochrane pre-dialysis erythropoietin review (19 studies, 993 participants). The two network editions overlap by design (the second updates the first), so their participant counts are not independent.
cards.result: Transfusion prevention versus placebo: epoetin alfa odds ratio 0.28, epoetin beta 0.19, darbepoetin alfa 0.27 (2023); odds ratios 0.09 to 0.18 for all proprietary ESAs (2014); patients requiring transfusion relative risk 0.32 pre-dialysis (2016). Death was not reduced, and hypertension odds rose (odds ratios around 1.8 to 2.6). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for transfusion reduction.
cards.watchOut: Transfusion avoidance is a benefit with a ceiling: live shelf #179 and pack #5970 show that chasing it with high haemoglobin targets buys stroke and hypertension, so this shelf supports ESA use to avoid transfusion at conservative targets, not target escalation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chung EY et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 36791280); Palmer SC et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25486075); Cody JD et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 26790135).

shelves.title: Conservative care versus dialysis in frail older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #2644's general older-adult question): no survival advantage for dialysis was found in the frailty-defined strata — observational evidence only
shelves.question: In older adults with end-stage kidney disease and frailty, does conservative kidney management provide similar survival to dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Comorbidity · Conservative Treatment · Diagnostic Self Evaluation · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Hospitalization · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Netherlands · Patient Selection · Quality of Life · Renal Dialysis · Risk Assessment · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational only, printed on the face: in the frailest older patients, no survival advantage for dialysis has been shown. In the GOLD cohort, where frailty was measured by formal geriatric assessment (192 dialysis and 89 conservative patients), no survival benefit for dialysis could be found in patients over 80, hospitalisation was twice as common on dialysis (50% versus 24%), and quality of life held steady on dialysis while declining slightly on conservative care (van Loon 2019). In the Leeds cohort (269 renal replacement versus 172 conservative patients over 70), the survival advantage of renal replacement was lost in patients over 80 and in those with a WHO performance score of 3 or more — the frailty-defined stratum — at every level of kidney-function severity (Hussain 2013). Frailty itself, however measured, predicts shorter survival and earlier dialysis initiation in advanced kidney disease (Hussien 2024, 240 patients), which is why these comparisons are so confounded: frailer patients are both likelier to choose conservative care and likelier to die. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2644 covers older kidney failure generally (Murtagh, Chandna, Carson and Da Silva-Gane cohorts, none frailty-defined, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the frailty-defined subgroup, where the evidence is thinner and entirely observational. No randomised trial has compared the two strategies in frail patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no survival advantage shown for dialysis in frail older adults) — observational only.

cards.headline: van Loon 2019 (GOLD): in a geriatric-assessment cohort of 281 older patients, no survival benefit for dialysis over conservative management could be found over age 80 — and hospitalisation was 50% on dialysis versus 24% on conservative care
cards.summary: van Loon 2019 (GOLD): in a geriatric-assessment cohort of 281 older patients, no survival benefit for dialysis over conservative management could be found over age 80 — and hospitalisation was 50% on dialysis versus 24% on conservative care
cards.type: Prospective comparative cohort with geriatric (frailty) assessment (GOLD, van Loon 2019)
cards.people: The GOLD study (Geriatric assessment in OLder patients starting Dialysis): 192 patients starting dialysis and 89 choosing maximal conservative management, all aged 65 and over, enrolled just before dialysis initiation or after the conservative decision in the Netherlands. Baseline assessment included frailty by geriatric assessment and comorbidity (CIRS-G). Conservative patients were older (mean 82 versus 75 years) with better kidney function (eGFR 11.5 versus 8.0 mL/min/1.73m²).
cards.result: Baseline quality of life did not differ between groups. At 6 months the EQ-5D index had not improved significantly on dialysis (+0.026, P = 0.10; not clinically relevant) and showed a small clinically relevant decline on conservative care (-0.047; between-group difference P < 0.01). Hospitalisation occurred in 50% of dialysis patients versus 24% of conservative patients (P < 0.01). In patients over 80 years old, no survival benefit could be found for starting dialysis versus conservative management.
cards.watchOut: Patients chose their pathway, and the conservative group was older with better residual kidney function — 'no survival benefit found over 80' in a 281-person observational cohort is an absence of demonstrated advantage, not a randomised proof of equivalence.
cards.source: van Loon IN et al. Quality of life after the initiation of dialysis or maximal conservative management in elderly patients: a longitudinal analysis of the Geriatric assessment in OLder patients starting Dialysis (GOLD) study. BMC Nephrology. 2019. PMID: 30922246. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hussain 2013: in 441 patients over 70, renal replacement's survival advantage was lost in patients over 80 and in those with WHO performance score 3 or more, at every severity level
cards.summary: Hussain 2013: in 441 patients over 70, renal replacement's survival advantage was lost in patients over 80 and in those with WHO performance score 3 or more, at every severity level
cards.people: Retrospective observational study of patients over 70 attending a pre-dialysis clinic in Leeds, England: 172 chose conservative management and 269 chose renal replacement therapy, with survival analysed from eGFR thresholds of 20, 15 and 12 mL/min and stratified by age, performance status and Charlson Comorbidity Index.
cards.result: Overall, the renal replacement group survived longer from each eGFR threshold (P < 0.0001 at under 20 and under 15; P = 0.002 at under 12). But stratified, renal replacement failed to show a survival advantage over conservative management in patients older than 80 years or with a WHO performance score of 3 or more, and its effect shrank significantly at high comorbidity scores. The relative risk of acute hospital admission was 1.6 on renal replacement versus conservative management (95% CI 1.14-2.13); 47% of conservative patients died in hospital versus 69% on renal replacement (registry data), and 76% of the conservative group accessed community palliative care versus 0% on renal replacement.
cards.watchOut: WHO performance score is a frailty proxy, not a frailty instrument, and the choice of pathway was the patients' own — the frail stratum's lost advantage could reflect both a genuinely smaller dialysis benefit and the frailest patients never being offered or surviving to start dialysis.

cards.headline: Hussien 2024: in 240 older adults with stage 4-5 kidney disease, frailty by any of four instruments predicted shorter survival (26.8 versus 30.6 months by the physical phenotype) and earlier dialysis initiation
cards.summary: Hussien 2024: in 240 older adults with stage 4-5 kidney disease, frailty by any of four instruments predicted shorter survival (26.8 versus 30.6 months by the physical phenotype) and earlier dialysis initiation
cards.people: Prospective observational cohort of 240 patients aged 65 and over with stage 4 or 5 chronic kidney disease recruited from a nephrology outpatient department, 2020-2021. Frailty was assessed with four instruments (Physical Frailty Phenotype, PRISMA-7, Clinical Frailty Scale, FRAIL scale) and cognition with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment; outcomes were time to dialysis initiation and survival.
cards.result: Frail patients had significantly shorter time to dialysis initiation by the Physical Frailty Phenotype (28.3 versus 31.2 months; P = 0.028) and FRAIL scale (26.9 versus 30.9 months; P = 0.038), and significantly shorter survival by the phenotype, FRAIL and Clinical Frailty Scale instruments (26.8 versus 30.6 months by the phenotype; P = 0.003). Overall 37.5% of patients died during follow-up, with higher mortality in frail patients; cognitive impairment, though strongly correlated with frailty (dementia in 45.5% of frail versus 15.1% of non-frail by the FRAIL scale), did not independently predict initiation or survival.
cards.watchOut: This card establishes what frailty does to prognosis in advanced kidney disease — it does not compare dialysis with conservative care within frail patients, and it is carded so the shelf's frailty framing rests on a measured-frailty record rather than on age alone.
cards.source: Hussien H et al. The Impact of Frailty and Severe Cognitive Impairment on Survival Time and Time to Initiate Dialysis in Older Adults With Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease: A Prospective Observational Cohort Study. Cureus. 2024. PMID: 39130911. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: in frail older adults, conservative management has not been shown to cost survival versus dialysis — but every comparison is observational and confounded by who chooses which path
cards.summary: Synthesis: in frail older adults, conservative management has not been shown to cost survival versus dialysis — but every comparison is observational and confounded by who chooses which path
cards.people: The carded evidence: the GOLD geriatric-assessment cohort (281 patients), the Leeds comparative cohort (441 patients, with a performance-status frailty stratum), and a measured-frailty prognostic cohort (240 patients). Total carded participants are 962, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: No survival benefit for dialysis over 80 in GOLD; dialysis's survival advantage lost over 80 and at WHO performance score 3 or more in Leeds; frailty itself predicts shorter survival and earlier dialysis start. Hospitalisation was roughly twice as common on dialysis in both comparative cohorts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no survival advantage shown for dialysis in frail older adults) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: 'Similar survival' here means 'no advantage demonstrated in confounded cohorts', which is weaker than trial-proven equivalence — the stamp and balance keep the observational label on the claim for exactly that reason.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Loon IN et al. BMC Nephrology. 2019 (PMID: 30922246); Hussain JA et al. Palliative Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23652841); Hussien H et al. Cureus. 2024 (PMID: 39130911).

shelves.title: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio accuracy (GAP-E): no single number — sensitivity 10–100% across verified studies, respectable only at locally derived, assay-specific cutoffs
shelves.question: In adults being screened for primary aldosteronism, how accurate is the aldosterone-to-renin ratio compared with confirmatory testing?
shelves.mesh: Aldosterone · Clinical Decision-Making · Female · Humans · Hyperaldosteronism · Male · Renin · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: GAP-E test-accuracy shelf, built around the slate's warning: the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) has no single accuracy. In the most rigorous meta-analysis — restricted to studies that applied confirmatory testing to everyone, whatever the ARR result, to limit verification bias — reported sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% and specificity from 70% to 100% across ten studies (4,110 participants), three studies found sensitivity below 50%, and the authors could recommend no single threshold (Hung 2021). Performance is assay-dependent in direct comparisons too: in one 450-patient cohort the locally optimal cutoffs gave sensitivity 77% and specificity 93% for the activity-based ratio and sensitivity 80% and specificity 92% for the direct-renin ratio, with different numeric cutoffs for each assay method (Li 2019); pooling the direct-renin variant gave sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.85 (Gao 2022). The ratio is therefore a reasonable case-detection screen whose negative result can miss disease at some cutoffs and whose positive result always requires the confirmatory testing it is compared against here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence), accuracy labelled assay- and threshold-dependent on the face.

cards.headline: Hung 2021 meta-analysis: ARR sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% across studies — no single threshold could be recommended
cards.summary: Hung 2021 meta-analysis: ARR sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% across studies — no single threshold could be recommended
cards.people: Ten observational diagnostic-accuracy studies comprising 4,110 participants screened for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, selected specifically because every participant underwent dynamic confirmatory testing as the reference standard regardless of the ARR result (limiting verification bias); risk of bias and applicability were assessed with QUADAS-2.
cards.result: Reported ARR sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% and specificity from 70% to 100% across the ten studies; three of the ten studies reported sensitivity below 50%, meaning the screen missed more than half of confirmed cases at the threshold used. The population base, positivity threshold, laboratory assay and confirmatory reference standard varied substantially between studies, and potential risk of bias in patient selection was present in half of them. The authors conclude that no single ARR threshold for interpretation could be recommended and that the test's limited accuracy and reliability must be recognised in clinical decision-making.
cards.watchOut: The spread is the finding: it reflects real differences in assays, thresholds, medications at testing and who was screened — a pooled single sensitivity/specificity would be a false precision, and this review deliberately does not offer one.
cards.source: Hung A et al. Performance of the Aldosterone to Renin Ratio as a Screening Test for Primary Aldosteronism. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2021. PMID: 34008000. cards.headline: Li 2019: in 450 hypertensive patients, locally optimal cutoffs gave the ARR a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 93% — with different numbers for each renin assay
cards.summary: Li 2019: in 450 hypertensive patients, locally optimal cutoffs gave the ARR a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 93% — with different numbers for each renin assay
cards.people: 450 hypertensive patients with suspected primary aldosteronism at a single hypertension centre who underwent both screening and confirmatory testing; 64 were diagnosed with primary aldosteronism and 386 with primary hypertension. Plasma renin activity and direct renin concentration, and aldosterone by radioimmunoassay and chemiluminescent immunoassay, were measured simultaneously.
cards.result: The optimal cutoff for the aldosterone-to-direct-renin ratio (chemiluminescent assay) was 2.93 (ng/dL)/(mU/L), with sensitivity 80.33% and specificity 92.11%. The optimal cutoff for the classic aldosterone-to-renin-activity ratio was 25.28 (ng/dL)/(ng/mL/h), with sensitivity 76.92% and specificity 93.38%. Within-patient correlation between the two renin measures was high (r=0.88), but each assay pairing needed its own numeric cutoff — the accuracy figures travel with the assay and the locally derived threshold, not with the test's name.
cards.watchOut: Cutoffs derived and tested in the same single-centre cohort are optimistic ('optimal cutoff' bias), and the 64 confirmed cases limit precision; other centres using other assays cannot import these numbers directly.
cards.source: Li T et al. Feasibility of Screening Primary Aldosteronism by Aldosterone-to-Direct Renin Concentration Ratio Derived from Chemiluminescent Immunoassay Measurement: Diagnostic Accuracy and Cutoff Value. cards.headline: Gao 2022 meta-analysis: the direct-renin version of the ratio pooled at sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.85 (2,806 subjects) — better behaved, still assay-bound
cards.summary: Gao 2022 meta-analysis: the direct-renin version of the ratio pooled at sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.85 (2,806 subjects) — better behaved, still assay-bound
cards.people: Ten studies comprising 2,806 subjects evaluating the aldosterone-to-direct-renin concentration ratio (ADRR) as a screening test for primary aldosteronism, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis with QUADAS-2 quality assessment.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.87 (95% CI 0.85 to 0.89) and pooled specificity 0.85 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.86), with an area under the summary ROC curve of 0.9333, a pooled positive likelihood ratio of 5.84 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.16. The authors conclude the direct-renin ratio has good sensitivity and specificity for screening — while noting that the diagnostic efficacy reported by individual studies varied greatly, which is why pooling was attempted.
cards.watchOut: This pools the direct-renin variant only, largely in different (and partly Chinese-database) study sets from the Hung review; its tidier pooled numbers do not repeal the assay-dependence shown on the other cards — they describe one assay family under study conditions.
cards.source: Gao H et al. Aldosterone/direct renin concentration ratio as a screening test for primary aldosteronism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of translational medicine. 2022. PMID: 35845504. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: the ARR screens usefully but its accuracy is a property of the assay, the cutoff and the clinic — not a fixed number
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ARR screens usefully but its accuracy is a property of the assay, the cutoff and the clinic — not a fixed number
cards.people: The carded evidence: two diagnostic-accuracy meta-analyses (10 studies / 4,110 participants; 10 studies / 2,806 subjects) and one head-to-head assay cohort (450 patients). Total carded participants exceed 7,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Against universal confirmatory testing, ARR sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% and specificity from 70% to 100%, with no recommendable universal threshold (Hung 2021). Where cutoffs are derived locally, performance looks respectable (sensitivity 77–80%, specificity 92–93% in Li 2019; pooled 0.87/0.85 for the direct-renin variant in Gao 2022) — but those numbers belong to their assays and populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence): a positive ARR requires confirmatory testing, and a negative ARR at a high cutoff does not exclude primary aldosteronism.
cards.watchOut: Medication effects (mineralocorticoid antagonists, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors), posture, time of day and potassium all move the ratio; none of the carded accuracy figures survives careless sampling conditions, which is part of why confirmatory testing remains mandatory.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hung A et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2021 (PMID: 34008000); Li T et al. International journal of hypertension. 2019 (PMID: 31354984); Gao H et al. Annals of translational medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35845504).

shelves.title: Home haemodialysis versus in-centre haemodialysis: lower mortality in every observational comparison (very low certainty), quality of life unproven — and the FHN trials test frequency, not location
shelves.question: In adults with kidney failure, does home hemodialysis improve survival and quality of life compared with in-center hemodialysis?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hemodialysis, Home · Renal Dialysis · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Quality of Life · Cause of Death · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Bias · Renal Insufficiency · Adult · Cardiovascular Diseases · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke · Ambulatory Care Facilities · Hospitalization · Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — with the location/frequency distinction on the face. This is a GAP-E shelf: there is no randomised trial of home versus in-centre haemodialysis on survival, so the survival claim rests on observational comparisons and is capped and labelled accordingly. The Cochrane review (1 small crossover trial plus 39 non-randomised studies) found all-cause death lower with home treatment in the pooled non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.80, 58,984 patients) at very low certainty; the ANZDATA registry analysis of 26,016 patients found adjusted mortality hazard ratios of 0.51 for conventional home and 0.53 for frequent/extended home haemodialysis against conventional facility treatment; and a matched cohort of intensive home treatment found a hazard ratio of 0.55 — but that home group also received far more dialysis hours, so it tests a package, not a postcode. Quality of life is not established: the dedicated meta-analysis found a marginal physical-score advantage (SMD 0.14), no mental-score difference, and was 95% peritoneal-dialysis studies. The FHN frequent-dialysis trials test frequency, not location (Daily was in-centre; Nocturnal was at home), and are homed on live shelf #293 — they are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): home haemodialysis is associated with lower mortality than in-centre haemodialysis in every large observational comparison, with residual confounding by patient selection the standing alternative explanation, and no proven quality-of-life advantage.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2024: pooling 1 crossover trial and 39 non-randomised studies, home haemodialysis was associated with lower all-cause death (relative risk 0.80) — at very low certainty, with quality of life unpooled and uncertain
cards.summary: Cochrane 2024: pooling 1 crossover trial and 39 non-randomised studies, home haemodialysis was associated with lower all-cause death (relative risk 0.80) — at very low certainty, with quality of life unpooled and uncertain
cards.people: Adults with kidney failure receiving home haemodialysis (including community-house and self-care settings) versus in-centre haemodialysis, in the 40 studies (1 crossover randomised trial and 39 non-randomised studies of interventions) included in the 2024 Cochrane update, searched to October 2022.
cards.result: All-cause death was lower with home haemodialysis in the pooled non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95; 9 studies, 58,984 patients; very low certainty evidence), while cardiovascular death was not clearly different (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.07; 2 studies, 30,900 participants). Hospitalisation may be lower (mean difference −0.50 admissions per patient-year, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.02; 2 studies, 834 participants) and post-dialysis recovery time shorter (mean difference −2.0 hours, 95% CI −2.73 to −1.28; 2 studies, 348 participants), all at very low certainty. Quality of life could not be pooled: patient-reported outcomes used 18 different measures across 11 studies, so the review calls the quality-of-life association uncertain.
cards.watchOut: Almost everything here is observational: home patients tend to be younger with fewer comorbidities, and the review itself rates the certainty very low and warns of selection bias and residual confounding. The single randomised study was a small crossover trial, not a mortality trial.
cards.source: Cheetham MS et al. Home versus in-centre haemodialysis for people with kidney failure. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024. PMID: 38588450. Registry ID: none in the record for the review itself. cards.headline: ANZDATA 2011: in 26,016 Australian and New Zealand patients, conventional home haemodialysis carried about half the adjusted mortality of conventional facility haemodialysis (hazard ratio 0.51)
cards.summary: ANZDATA 2011: in 26,016 Australian and New Zealand patients, conventional home haemodialysis carried about half the adjusted mortality of conventional facility haemodialysis (hazard ratio 0.51)
cards.people: 26,016 adult patients starting kidney replacement therapy in Australia and New Zealand from 31 March 1996 to 31 December 2007 (856,007 patient-months of follow-up), analysed with marginal structural modelling to adjust for time-varying comorbidity; the comparison is dialysis modality, with conventional facility haemodialysis as reference.
cards.result: Adjusted mortality hazard ratios relative to conventional facility haemodialysis were 0.51 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.59) for conventional home haemodialysis and 0.53 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.68) for frequent/extended home haemodialysis, versus 1.16 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.44) for frequent/extended facility haemodialysis and 1.10 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.16) for peritoneal dialysis. The apparent home benefit was smaller in non-white, non-Asian and older patients.
cards.watchOut: A registry association, not a randomised comparison: patients who dialyse at home are selected — younger, healthier, better supported — and the registry does not collect cognition, frailty, socioeconomic or blood-pressure data, so residual confounding could explain part or all of the gap.
cards.source: Marshall MR et al. Home hemodialysis and mortality risk in Australian and New Zealand populations. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2011. PMID: 21816526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nesrallah 2012: intensive home haemodialysis matched to in-centre conventional dialysis — deaths 13% vs 21%, hazard ratio 0.55 — but 'intensive home' bundles location with much more dialysis
cards.summary: Nesrallah 2012: intensive home haemodialysis matched to in-centre conventional dialysis — deaths 13% vs 21%, hazard ratio 0.55 — but 'intensive home' bundles location with much more dialysis
cards.people: 420 patients receiving intensive home haemodialysis in France, the USA and Canada (International Quotidian Dialysis Registry, 2000–2010), of whom 338 were propensity-matched to 1,388 Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study patients receiving in-centre conventional haemodialysis; intensive meant a mean of 4.8 sessions per week at 7.4 hours per session, versus 3 sessions per week at 3.9 hours in-centre.
cards.result: Over 3,008 patient-years, 45 of 338 intensive-home patients (13%) died versus 293 of 1,388 in-centre patients (21%) — 6.1 versus 10.5 deaths per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.87), consistent across prespecified subgroups and sensitivity analyses. The authors state explicitly that whether the association is causal remains unknown.
cards.watchOut: This card cannot separate home from dose: the home group got roughly three times the weekly dialysis hours of the in-centre group. It is evidence about intensive home treatment as a package, not about location alone — the frequency question itself is homed on live shelf #293 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Nesrallah GE et al. Intensive hemodialysis associates with improved survival compared with conventional hemodialysis. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2012. PMID: 22362910. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bonenkamp 2020: home dialysis patients scored marginally better on physical quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.14) and no differently on mental quality of life — in studies that were 95% peritoneal dialysis
cards.summary: Bonenkamp 2020: home dialysis patients scored marginally better on physical quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.14) and no differently on mental quality of life — in studies that were 95% peritoneal dialysis
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Bonenkamp 2020)
cards.people: 4,158 home dialysis patients and 7,854 in-centre haemodialysis patients across 46 articles reporting 41 study populations (2007–2019); 90% of studies were cross-sectional and 95% enrolled peritoneal dialysis patients, using mainly the SF-12/SF-36 questionnaires.
cards.result: Pooled physical health-related quality-of-life scores were marginally higher in home dialysis patients (standardised mean difference 0.14, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.24) with high heterogeneity (I² >80%); Western European home patients scored higher (SMD 0.39) while Latin American home patients scored lower (SMD −0.20). Mental health-related quality of life showed no difference in any analysis (the treatment setting made no difference). More than half the studies carried moderate or high risk of bias, and no randomised trials were found.
cards.watchOut: This is the quality-of-life card, and its population is mostly peritoneal dialysis, not home haemodialysis — it should not be quoted as home-haemodialysis quality-of-life evidence. It shows at most a small, inconsistent physical-score advantage for home treatment in general.
cards.source: Bonenkamp AA et al. Health-Related Quality of Life in Home Dialysis Patients Compared to In-Center Hemodialysis Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Kidney medicine. 2020. PMID: 32734235. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: home haemodialysis is consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data, and quality of life is at best marginally better — causality is unproven for both
cards.summary: Synthesis: home haemodialysis is consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data, and quality of life is at best marginally better — causality is unproven for both
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 40 studies (1 small crossover trial, 39 non-randomised), one 26,016-patient binational registry analysis, one matched intensive-home cohort (338 vs 1,388), and one quality-of-life meta-analysis of 41 populations (mostly peritoneal dialysis). No randomised trial compares home with in-centre haemodialysis on survival.
cards.result: Every observational comparison points the same way on survival — pooled relative risk 0.80 in the Cochrane non-randomised studies, adjusted hazard ratios of 0.51–0.53 for home modalities in ANZDATA, and 0.55 in the matched intensive-home cohort — and every one of those comparisons is exposed to the same selection problem: people who dialyse at home differ from people who cannot. Quality of life is weaker still: a marginal physical-score difference (SMD 0.14) drawn mostly from peritoneal dialysis studies, and no mental-score difference. The FHN trials are not carded here: the Daily trial tested frequency in-centre and the Nocturnal trial tested frequency at home — frequency, not location — and both are homed on live shelf #293. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): home haemodialysis is associated with better survival than in-centre haemodialysis, with quality of life unproven.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade the association: there is no randomised mortality evidence for location, the intensive-home cohort confounds location with dose, and the quality-of-life pooling is mostly a different home modality (peritoneal dialysis).
cards.source: Synthesis of Cheetham MS et al. Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024 (PMID: 38588450); Marshall MR et al. American journal of kidney diseases. 2011 (PMID: 21816526); Nesrallah GE et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2012 (PMID: 22362910); Bonenkamp AA et al. Kidney medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32734235).

shelves.title: The furosemide stress test in early AKI: under 200 mL in 2 hours predicts progression to stage 3 (AUC 0.87, derivation and validation) and later dialysis
shelves.question: In adults with acute kidney injury, does the furosemide stress test predict progression to severe AKI and need for kidney replacement therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Aged · Cohort Studies · Diuretics · Exercise Test · Female · Furosemide · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis) — this is a GAP-E test/prognosis shelf, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The test is simple: one intravenous furosemide dose (1.0 mg/kg, or 1.5 mg/kg after prior exposure) and the urine produced in the next 2 hours. In the derivation cohorts (77 critically ill patients with early AKI), output under 200 mL over 2 hours predicted progression to AKIN stage III with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity 87.1% and specificity 84.1%. An independent multicentre validation in 92 ICU patients with stage I–II AKI reproduced the AUC (0.87) and the cut-off, with sensitivity 73.9% and specificity 90.0%. Pooled across 11 studies and 1,366 patients, sensitivity/specificity were 0.81/0.88 for AKI progression and 0.84/0.77 for later kidney replacement therapy, with replacement-therapy prediction better in early (stage 1–2) than in stage 3 AKI. Live shelf #195 answers when to start replacement therapy; this shelf answers the different, earlier question of who is heading towards severe AKI. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis): the furosemide stress test predicts progression to severe AKI and need for kidney replacement therapy with good discrimination, best when used early.

cards.headline: Chawla 2013 (derivation): urine output under 200 mL in the 2 hours after a furosemide stress test predicted progression to stage 3 AKI with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity 87.1% and specificity 84.1%
cards.summary: Chawla 2013 (derivation): urine output under 200 mL in the 2 hours after a furosemide stress test predicted progression to stage 3 AKI with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity 87.1% and specificity 84.1%
cards.type: Derivation cohort study (furosemide stress test, Chawla 2013)
cards.people: 77 critically ill patients with early acute kidney injury who received a standardised furosemide stress test (a single intravenous dose of 1.0 mg/kg, or 1.5 mg/kg if previously exposed to furosemide) — 23 in a retrospective cohort and 54 in a prospective multicentre cohort; 25 patients (32.4%) progressed to AKIN stage III.
cards.result: Urine output in each of the first 6 hours after the test was significantly lower in patients whose AKI progressed (P<0.001). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for total urine output over the first 2 hours predicting progression to AKIN stage III was 0.87 (P=0.001), and the best cut-off — less than 200 mL over 2 hours (100 mL/hour) — gave a sensitivity of 87.1% and a specificity of 84.1%.
cards.watchOut: This is the derivation report: the 200 mL cut-off was chosen in these same 77 patients, so its performance here is the optimistic estimate the validation studies had to reproduce.
cards.source: Chawla LS et al. Development and standardization of a furosemide stress test to predict the severity of acute kidney injury. Critical care (London, England). 2013. PMID: 24053972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rewa 2019 (validation): in 92 ICU patients with stage I–II AKI, the same under-200 mL 2-hour output predicted progression to stage III with an AuROC of 0.87, sensitivity 73.9% and specificity 90.0%
cards.summary: Rewa 2019 (validation): in 92 ICU patients with stage I–II AKI, the same under-200 mL 2-hour output predicted progression to stage III with an AuROC of 0.87, sensitivity 73.9% and specificity 90.0%
cards.people: 92 critically ill patients with stage I or II acute kidney injury (and without severe chronic kidney disease) in a multicentre prospective observational study, given the furosemide stress test at 1 mg/kg if loop-diuretic naïve or 1.5 mg/kg if previously exposed; 23 patients progressed to stage III AKI.
cards.result: Patients who progressed had significantly lower urinary flow rates (P<0.0001). Urinary flow over the first 2 hours was the most predictive window (AuROC 0.87), and the prespecified-style cut-off of less than 200 mL in the first 2 hours gave a sensitivity of 73.9% and a specificity of 90.0% for progression to stage III AKI.
cards.watchOut: Sensitivity fell from the derivation cohort's 87.1% to 73.9% on validation — roughly one in four progressors is missed by the cut-off — while specificity improved. The test stratifies risk; it does not rule progression in or out on its own.
cards.source: Rewa OG et al. The furosemide stress test for prediction of worsening acute kidney injury in critically ill patients: A multicenter, prospective, observational study. Journal of critical care. 2019. PMID: 31035185. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2020 (meta-analysis of 11 studies, 1,366 patients): pooled sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.88 for AKI progression, and sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.77 for needing kidney replacement therapy
cards.summary: Chen 2020 (meta-analysis of 11 studies, 1,366 patients): pooled sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.88 for AKI progression, and sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.77 for needing kidney replacement therapy
cards.people: Eleven studies enrolling 1,366 patients with acute kidney injury who underwent a furosemide stress test, pooled in a PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis (search to March 2020); AKI-progression outcomes were reported for 517 patients and kidney replacement therapy outcomes for 1,017 patients.
cards.result: For predicting AKI progression, pooled sensitivity was 0.81 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.87) and pooled specificity 0.88 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.92), with a diagnostic odds ratio of 29.69 (95% CI 17.00 to 51.85) and summary AUC 0.88; performance was not affected by AKI criteria or underlying chronic kidney disease. For predicting kidney replacement therapy, pooled sensitivity was 0.84 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.91) and specificity 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.87), diagnostic odds ratio 13.59 (95% CI 5.74 to 32.17), summary AUC 0.86 — and prediction of replacement therapy was better in stage 1–2 AKI than in stage 3 (relative diagnostic odds ratio 5.75, 95% CI 2.51 to 13.33).
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are small, mostly single-centre cohorts (the derivation and validation cohorts on the cards above are among them), and the test predicts a clinician-visible trajectory — progression and dialysis decisions — rather than changing it; no study here shows that acting on the test improves outcomes.
cards.source: Chen JJ et al. Furosemide stress test as a predictive marker of acute kidney injury progression or renal replacement therapy: a systemic review and meta-analysis. Critical care (London, England). 2020. PMID: 32381019. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a simple bedside test with reproducible discrimination — about 0.87 AUC for progression in both derivation and validation, and pooled sensitivity/specificity of 0.81/0.88 for progression and 0.84/0.77 for replacement therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: a simple bedside test with reproducible discrimination — about 0.87 AUC for progression in both derivation and validation, and pooled sensitivity/specificity of 0.81/0.88 for progression and 0.84/0.77 for replacement therapy
cards.people: The carded evidence: the 77-patient derivation cohorts (Chawla 2013), a 92-patient multicentre validation cohort (Rewa 2019), and an 11-study meta-analysis of 1,366 patients (Chen 2020). All are observational test-prognosis studies; there is no randomised evidence that using the test changes management or outcomes.
cards.result: The same measurement — urine output in the first 2 hours after 1.0–1.5 mg/kg furosemide, cut at 200 mL — discriminated progression to stage 3 AKI with an AUC of 0.87 in both the derivation and the independent validation cohort, with the expected trade: sensitivity fell (87.1% to 73.9%) and specificity rose (84.1% to 90.0%) on validation. Pooled across 11 studies, the test performed similarly for progression (sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.88) and somewhat less specifically for subsequent kidney replacement therapy (0.84 and 0.77), performing best when used early, in stage 1–2 AKI. Live shelf #195 covers when to start kidney replacement therapy, not this test. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis): the furosemide stress test predicts progression to severe AKI and later need for replacement therapy with good, reproducible discrimination.
cards.watchOut: Prediction is not intervention: a low output identifies patients already on a worse trajectory, and the replacement-therapy endpoint is partly a clinician's decision made in sight of the same physiology.

synthesis the carded evidence: the 77-patient derivation cohorts (chawla 2013), a 92-patient multicentre validation cohort (rewa 2019), and an 11-study meta-analysis of 1,366 patients (chen 2020). all are observational test-prognosis studies; there is no randomised evidence that using the test changes management or outcomes. the same measurement — urine output in the first 2 hours after 1.0–1.5 mg/kg furosemide, cut at 200 ml — discriminated progression to stage 3 aki with an auc of 0.87 in both the derivation and the independent validation cohort, with the expected trade: sensitivity fell (87.1% to 73.9%) and specificity rose (84.1% to 90.0%) on validation. pooled across 11 studies, the test performed similarly for progression (sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.88) and somewhat less specifically for subsequent kidney replacement therapy (0.84 and 0.77), performing best when used early, in stage 1–2 aki. live shelf #195 covers when to start kidney replacement therapy, not this test. proposed possible (observational, test-prognosis): the furosemide stress test predicts progression to severe aki and later need for replacement therapy with good, reproducible discrimination. prediction is not intervention: a low output identifies patients already on a worse trajectory, and the replacement-therapy endpoint is partly a clinician's decision made in sight of the same physiology. synthesis of chawla ls et al. critical care (london, england). 2013 (pmid: 24053972); rewa og et al. journal of critical care. 2019 (pmid: 31035185); chen jj et al. critical care (london, england). 2020 (pmid: 32381019).

shelves.title: Incremental peritoneal dialysis start: safe and no worse on survival or technique outcomes, but residual-function preservation unproven (one small randomised trial, null)
shelves.question: In adults starting peritoneal dialysis, does an incremental low-dose start preserve residual kidney function compared with a standard full-dose start?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anuria · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Peritoneal Dialysis, Continuous Ambulatory · Prospective Studies · Survival Rate · Urodynamics · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1732, which covers the incremental twice-weekly haemodialysis start; this shelf is the peritoneal-dialysis slice only, and the randomised base is thin (flagged on the slate and confirmed at build: exactly one small randomised trial). That trial (Yan 2017, 139 incident CAPD patients, 3 vs 4 exchanges) found residual GFR, urine volume and anuria-free survival identical at 24 months (the treatment made no difference), and a post-hoc dose analysis of the balANZ cohort (154 patients; the balANZ solution question itself is homed on live #1738 and not re-carded) likewise found no difference in the slope of residual-function decline (P=0.78). Against those, one small retrospective cohort found higher GFR at 24 months on incremental prescriptions — in a group that started with roughly double the GFR, the textbook signature of confounding by indication — and the 2024 systematic review of 10 comparative studies found no survival, peritonitis or technique-survival differences and conflicting residual-function data. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): incremental starts look safe and no worse on hard outcomes, but the residual-function preservation they are usually sold on has not been demonstrated in the least confounded evidence.

cards.headline: Yan 2017 (the one randomised trial): 3 versus 4 daily CAPD exchanges for 24 months — residual GFR, urine volume and time to anuria did not differ (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Yan 2017 (the one randomised trial): 3 versus 4 daily CAPD exchanges for 24 months — residual GFR, urine volume and time to anuria did not differ (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 139 incident continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients aged 18–80 years with a starting GFR of at least 2 mL/min and urine volume of at least 500 mL/day, randomised open-label at a single centre to 3 exchanges daily (n=70) or 4 exchanges daily (n=69) for 24 months — the 3-exchange arm is the incremental start.
cards.result: After 24 months, residual GFR was 1.6±2.0 mL/min on 3 exchanges versus 1.7±1.9 mL/min on 4 exchanges (P=0.8), urine volume 505±522 versus 474±442 mL/day (P=0.8), and anuria-free survival did not differ (P=0.8) — the lower-dose start made no difference to any measure of residual kidney function. Delivered dose was lower on 3 exchanges (Kt/V 1.95±0.39 vs 2.19±0.48, P=0.03; ultrafiltration 404±499 vs 742±512 mL/day, P=0.004). Peritonitis occurred in 13% versus 26% (P=0.06, not significant), and patient and technique survival were similar.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial with no formal sample-size calculation: it can rule in safety signals but is too small to exclude a modest preservation effect. Note the comparison is 3 versus 4 exchanges — a one-exchange increment — not a full low-dose programme against a maximal prescription.
cards.source: Yan H et al. Three Versus 4 Daily Exchanges and Residual Kidney Function Decline in Incident CAPD Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2017. PMID: 27751610. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hayat 2023 (balANZ dose analysis): among 154 incident PD patients, starting incremental (<56 L/week) versus full-dose made no difference to the slope of residual kidney function decline (P=0.78)
cards.summary: Hayat 2023 (balANZ dose analysis): among 154 incident PD patients, starting incremental (<56 L/week) versus full-dose made no difference to the slope of residual kidney function decline (P=0.78)
cards.type: Post-hoc dose analysis within a randomised trial cohort (Hayat 2023)
cards.people: 154 incident peritoneal dialysis patients from the balANZ randomised trial cohort who had at least one post-baseline residual kidney function measurement (mean age 57.9 years, 44% women, 34% with diabetes, mean follow-up 19.5 months), classified by the dose they actually started on: 45 (29.2%) incremental (<56 L/week) and 109 (70.8%) full-dose (≥56 L/week). This report asks the dose question inside that cohort; the balANZ solution comparison itself is homed on live shelf #1738 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Residual kidney function fell in both groups over 24 months — from 7.9±3.2 to 3.2±2.9 mL/min/1.73 m² in the incremental group and from 7.3±2.7 to 3.4±2.8 in the full-dose group — with no difference in the slope of decline (P=0.78). Urine volume likewise fell in both groups (1.81 to 0.64 L/day incremental; 1.38 to 0.71 L/day full-dose) with no difference in slope (P=0.18) — the incremental start made no difference to residual-function loss.
cards.watchOut: Dose was not randomised in this analysis — clinicians chose who started low — so this is observational evidence wearing a trial cohort's clothes, and the incremental group also started with more urine volume (1.81 vs 1.38 L/day).
cards.source: Hayat A et al. Association of Incremental peritoneal dialysis with residual kidney function decline in patients on peritoneal dialysis: The balANZ trial. Peritoneal dialysis international : journal of the International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis. 2023. PMID: 37259236. Registry ID: none in the record for this analysis. cards.headline: Fernandes 2023: a small retrospective cohort found higher GFR at 24 months on incremental PD (4.8 vs 1.9 mL/min/1.73 m²) — in patients who started with higher GFR to begin with
cards.summary: Fernandes 2023: a small retrospective cohort found higher GFR at 24 months on incremental PD (4.8 vs 1.9 mL/min/1.73 m²) — in patients who started with higher GFR to begin with
cards.people: 87 prevalent adult peritoneal dialysis patients at a single centre, grouped by their first prescription: 65.5% incremental (fewer/smaller dwells or fewer than 7 days a week, by the study's definition) and the rest standard full-dose; median follow-up 23 months.
cards.result: The incremental group had higher GFR in the first 6 months (7 vs 3.7 mL/min/1.73 m², P<0.001) and at 24 months (4.8 vs 1.9, P=0.002), and incremental prescription was independently associated with GFR ≥5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 24 months (odds ratio 13 per point, 95% CI 1.48 to 114.36). Incremental patients also had longer technique survival (P=0.026), fewer admissions per year (0.23 vs 0.5, P=0.001), lower mortality (1.8% vs 13.3%, P=0.027), and a lower hazard of technique failure (hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.098 to 0.93).
cards.watchOut: The comparison is confounded by indication on its face: patients are prescribed an incremental start because they have more residual function — the incremental group's GFR advantage (7 vs 3.7) was already present in the first 6 months — so later differences cannot be credited to the prescription. The very wide confidence interval on the headline odds ratio (1.48 to 114.36) shows how small the numbers are.
cards.source: Fernandes A et al. Incremental peritoneal dialysis: Is it better for preservation of residual kidney function and clinical outcomes? Clinical nephrology. 2023. PMID: 36472405. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Kidney · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Peritoneal Dialysis · Peritoneal Dialysis, Continuous Ambulatory · Retrospective Studies
