cards.headline: Xu 2024 (systematic review, 10 comparative studies): no difference in survival, peritonitis or technique survival — and the residual-function data conflict, some studies favouring incremental, others finding no difference
cards.summary: Xu 2024 (systematic review, 10 comparative studies): no difference in survival, peritonitis or technique survival — and the residual-function data conflict, some studies favouring incremental, others finding no difference
cards.people: Ten comparative studies of incremental versus standard (full-dose) peritoneal dialysis in end-stage kidney disease, identified across five databases to September 2023; definitions of 'incremental' varied between studies, so the synthesis is mostly qualitative with a crude-mortality meta-analysis.
cards.result: The majority of studies found no difference in patient survival between incremental and standard starts, and the meta-analysis of crude mortality data likewise found no significant difference (the treatment strategy made no difference). Peritonitis and technique survival were also not significantly different in the majority of studies. Data on residual kidney function were conflicting: some studies associated incremental starts with preservation of residual function, others found no such difference. The authors conclude incremental PD may be a safe alternative in incident patients, but that the evidence is heterogeneous and conflicting and firm conclusions cannot be drawn.
cards.watchOut: A review of mostly observational comparisons inherits their confounding by indication — patients with more residual function get incremental prescriptions — which biases the residual-function outcome in incremental PD's favour even before analysis begins.
cards.source: Xu S et al. Comparison of outcomes of incremental vs. standard peritoneal dialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC nephrology. 2024. PMID: 39285336. cards.headline: Synthesis: the preservation claim is unproven — the randomised trial and the balANZ dose analysis both found no difference in residual-function decline; the one favourable cohort started ahead; the review calls the residual-function impact questionable
cards.summary: Synthesis: the preservation claim is unproven — the randomised trial and the balANZ dose analysis both found no difference in residual-function decline; the one favourable cohort started ahead; the review calls the residual-function impact questionable
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small randomised trial (139 patients), one post-hoc dose analysis of a trial cohort (154 patients), one small retrospective cohort (87 patients), and a 10-study systematic review. Total carded primary-study participants are under 400, and only one study randomised the dose.
cards.result: On the shelf's question — does an incremental start preserve residual kidney function — the two least confounded reports say no: Yan's randomised 3-versus-4-exchange trial found identical residual GFR, urine volume and anuria-free survival at 24 months, and the balANZ dose analysis found identical slopes of decline (P=0.78). The favourable retrospective cohort's incremental group began with roughly double the GFR of its standard group, which explains its later advantage without any treatment effect. The 2024 review of all 10 comparative studies found no differences in survival, peritonitis or technique survival and conflicting residual-function data. Live shelf #1732 covers the incremental twice-weekly haemodialysis start, a different modality; this shelf is the peritoneal slice only. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): an incremental PD start appears safe and no worse on survival or technique outcomes, but preservation of residual kidney function — the reason usually given for it — has not been demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Absence of demonstrated preservation is not proof of harm: the randomised comparison tested a single-exchange difference, follow-up was 24 months, and no study was powered for technique failure or death.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yan H et al. American journal of kidney diseases. 2017 (PMID: 27751610); Hayat A et al. Peritoneal dialysis international. 2023 (PMID: 37259236); Fernandes A et al. Clinical nephrology. 2023 (PMID: 36472405); Xu S et al. BMC nephrology. 2024 (PMID: 39285336).

shelves.title: Shifting potassium in acute hyperkalaemia: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol equal alone (about 0.65 mmol/L), additive together (1.21 mmol/L) — bicarbonate alone does nothing
shelves.question: In adults with acute hyperkalemia, how do insulin-dextrose, nebulized salbutamol and sodium bicarbonate compare at shifting potassium into cells?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aerosols · Albuterol · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucose · Humans · Hyperkalemia · Injections, Intravenous · Insulin · Middle Aged · Renal Dialysis · Uremia
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a PARTIAL completion of pack #2933, which compares insulin doses (5 vs 10 units); this shelf compares the shift agents themselves, head to head. Potassium is reported in mmol/L throughout; US laboratories report potassium in mEq/L, which is numerically identical, so no conversion is needed. Glucose values are given in mmol/L with their mg/dL equivalents. The head-to-head literature is old and small, and its ordering has never changed: insulin-glucose and nebulised salbutamol each lower potassium by about 0.65 mmol/L as single agents (0.65±0.09 vs 0.66±0.12 in the 1990 crossover) and by 1.21±0.19 mmol/L combined — their effects are additive; a second crossover found the same single-agent falls (−0.85 and −0.53 to −0.71 mmol/L). Sodium bicarbonate is the outlier: alone it lowered potassium by −0.03 mmol/L (the treatment made no difference), it did not potentiate insulin or albuterol, it ranked last as a single agent in a seven-arm randomised comparison (P<0.001), and a 101-study meta-analysis found no potassium effect for bicarbonate while putting the insulin/salbutamol/combination range at 0.7–1.2 mmol/L (very low to low certainty). Insulin's cost is hypoglycaemia, seen in a fifth to three-quarters of recipients across the small trials and blunted by co-given salbutamol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol are equally effective single shift agents, best combined when the fall must be largest; bicarbonate should not be relied on to shift potassium.

cards.headline: Allon 1990: insulin-glucose and nebulised albuterol each lowered potassium by about 0.65 mmol/L in dialysis patients — and the two together lowered it by 1.21 mmol/L
cards.summary: Allon 1990: insulin-glucose and nebulised albuterol each lowered potassium by about 0.65 mmol/L in dialysis patients — and the two together lowered it by 1.21 mmol/L
cards.people: Maintenance haemodialysis patients in a crossover comparison of intravenous insulin with glucose, nebulised albuterol (salbutamol), and the combination; the report prints a denominator of 12 patients for its insulin-glucose glucose counts and no larger total in the abstract.
cards.result: Potassium fell by 0.65±0.09 mmol/L after insulin-glucose and by 0.66±0.12 mmol/L after albuterol — the two agents were equally effective — and by 1.21±0.19 mmol/L after the combination (P<0.02 versus either alone), so their effects are additive. The cost sits with insulin: plasma glucose fell to 2.8±0.3 mmol/L (about 50 mg/dL) at 1 hour after insulin-glucose, below 3 mmol/L (about 54 mg/dL) in 9 of 12 patients (without symptoms), whereas glucose rose to 6.8±0.5 mmol/L (about 122 mg/dL) with albuterol and returned to baseline (4.7±0.7 mmol/L, about 85 mg/dL) with the combination. Heart rate rose trivially with either agent alone and significantly (15.1±6.0 beats/min) with the combination.
cards.watchOut: A very small, old crossover study in dialysis patients with induced/stable hyperkalaemia — the effect sizes are the best head-to-head numbers available, but they come from a handful of patients and predate modern emergency-department populations.
cards.source: Allon M et al. Albuterol and insulin for treatment of hyperkalemia in hemodialysis patients. Kidney international. 1990. PMID: 2266671. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Allon & Shanklin 1996: sodium bicarbonate alone lowered potassium by −0.03 mmol/L — no effect — and adding it to insulin or albuterol added nothing
cards.summary: Allon & Shanklin 1996: sodium bicarbonate alone lowered potassium by −0.03 mmol/L — no effect — and adding it to insulin or albuterol added nothing
cards.people: Nondiabetic haemodialysis patients in a prospective crossover study of six protocols — isotonic bicarbonate, isotonic saline, insulin plus bicarbonate, insulin plus saline, albuterol plus bicarbonate, and albuterol plus saline — with potassium measured every 15 minutes for 1 hour. The total number of patients is not documented in the record (N not documented).
cards.result: Neither isotonic bicarbonate nor isotonic saline lowered plasma potassium significantly (−0.03±0.06 vs −0.01±0.10 mmol/L at 60 minutes, P=0.60) — bicarbonate alone made no difference. Insulin lowered potassium by the same amount whether given with bicarbonate or with saline (−0.81±0.05 vs −0.85±0.06 mmol/L, P=0.65), and albuterol likewise (−0.71±0.16 vs −0.53±0.15 mmol/L, P=0.18). Bicarbonate did raise blood bicarbonate and pH (P<0.005 and P<0.01) — it changed the acid–base numbers without shifting potassium.
cards.watchOut: These patients were not acidotic emergencies selected for bicarbonate; the result says bicarbonate does not shift potassium in stable dialysis patients, and the wider literature (next cards) has repeatedly failed to find a potassium effect for bicarbonate alone — but a severely acidotic subgroup is not what this study tested.

cards.headline: Ngugi 1997: in 70 renal-failure patients randomised across seven regimens, insulin-glucose and intravenous salbutamol were equally effective and both beat bicarbonate alone (P<0.001); combinations beat singles
cards.summary: Ngugi 1997: in 70 renal-failure patients randomised across seven regimens, insulin-glucose and intravenous salbutamol were equally effective and both beat bicarbonate alone (P<0.001); combinations beat singles
cards.type: Randomised comparative trial, seven arms of 10 (Ngugi 1997)
cards.people: 70 patients with hyperkalaemia and acute (10) or chronic (60) renal failure at a Kenyan national hospital, divided into seven treatment groups of 10: insulin-glucose alone, sodium bicarbonate alone (50 mmol of 8.4%), intravenous salbutamol alone (0.5 mg), each pair, and all three together; potassium was followed for 8 hours. The record's MeSH includes adolescents as well as adults.
cards.result: All regimens lowered potassium, with the maximum effect at 1–2 hours and a significant effect still present at 8 hours. Of the single agents, insulin-glucose and salbutamol were equieffective and both were better than bicarbonate alone (P<0.001); two-agent combinations beat the singles (P<0.001), and the triple combination was the most efficacious regimen in the study. Hypoglycaemia was the notable harm of insulin-glucose: a fall in plasma glucose was a feature of the insulin-containing regimens, with significant hypoglycaemia in 20% of patients on insulin-glucose alone and in none on insulin-glucose plus bicarbonate.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients per arm and no absolute potassium falls printed in the abstract — the rankings (singles equal, bicarbonate last, combinations best) are usable, the magnitudes are not. One of the few studies to include bicarbonate as a genuine single-agent arm.
cards.source: Ngugi NN et al. Treatment of hyperkalaemia by altering the transcellular gradient in patients with renal failure: effect of various therapeutic approaches. cards.headline: Jessen 2025 (meta-analysis, 101 studies): insulin-glucose, inhaled or intravenous salbutamol, and their combination each lowered potassium by an average of 0.7–1.2 mmol/L; bicarbonate had no effect on potassium levels
cards.summary: Jessen 2025 (meta-analysis, 101 studies): insulin-glucose, inhaled or intravenous salbutamol, and their combination each lowered potassium by an average of 0.7–1.2 mmol/L; bicarbonate had no effect on potassium levels
cards.people: 101 studies of pharmacological treatment for acute hyperkalaemia (randomised, non-randomised and observational), searched to September 2024 and graded with GRADE; the adult non-cardiac-arrest meta-analyses cover insulin with glucose, inhaled salbutamol, intravenous salbutamol in glucose, and combinations of them.
cards.result: In adults without cardiac arrest, the average potassium reduction with insulin-glucose, salbutamol (inhaled or intravenous), or the combination was between 0.7 and 1.2 mmol/L, at very low to low certainty of evidence. Bicarbonate had no effect on potassium levels (very low certainty) — the treatment made no difference. The review found no evidence of a clinical (as opposed to biochemical) benefit for calcium, which is outside this shelf's shift-agent question.
cards.watchOut: The pooled range spans different agents, doses, routes and populations, and the certainty is very low to low — read 0.7–1.2 mmol/L as the size of effect this literature supports, not as a precise ranking of insulin against salbutamol.
cards.source: Jessen MK et al. Pharmacological interventions for the acute treatment of hyperkalaemia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Resuscitation. 2025. PMID: 39761907. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Albuterol · Heart Arrest · Hyperkalemia · Insulin · Potassium

cards.headline: Synthesis: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol are interchangeable as single shift agents (about 0.65–0.85 mmol/L each), their combination is additive (about 1.2 mmol/L), and bicarbonate alone does not shift potassium
cards.summary: Synthesis: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol are interchangeable as single shift agents (about 0.65–0.85 mmol/L each), their combination is additive (about 1.2 mmol/L), and bicarbonate alone does not shift potassium
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small crossover comparisons in dialysis patients (1990, 1996), one seven-arm randomised comparison in 70 renal-failure patients (1997), and a 101-study systematic review and meta-analysis (2025). The primary trials are old and small; the pooled modern estimate carries very low to low certainty. The insulin-dose question (5 vs 10 units) is homed on pack #2933 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Three decades of small comparisons agree on the ordering. Insulin-glucose and salbutamol each lower potassium by roughly two-thirds of a mmol/L as single agents (0.65 and 0.66 mmol/L head-to-head in 1990; −0.85 and −0.53 to −0.71 mmol/L in the 1996 crossover), the combination is additive (1.21 mmol/L), and the 2025 pooling of 101 studies puts the single-agent/combination range at 0.7–1.2 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is the consistent exception: −0.03 mmol/L alone, no potentiation of insulin or albuterol, last place as a single agent in the seven-arm trial, and no effect in the meta-analysis. Insulin's price is hypoglycaemia (glucose below 3 mmol/L, about 54 mg/dL, in 9 of 12 patients in the 1990 study; significant hypoglycaemia in 20% on insulin-glucose alone in 1997), which salbutamol co-treatment appears to blunt. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: for shifting potassium into cells, use insulin-dextrose or salbutamol — expect about 0.7 mmol/L from either and about 1.2 mmol/L from both — and do not rely on bicarbonate as a shift agent.
cards.watchOut: Every carded number is a potassium fall over 1–2 hours in small or pooled studies — none of this evidence addresses arrhythmia, dialysis avoidance or death, and none of these agents removes potassium from the body.
cards.source: Synthesis of Allon M et al. Kidney international. 1990 (PMID: 2266671); Allon M et al. American journal of kidney diseases. 1996 (PMID: 8840939); Ngugi NN et al. East African medical journal. 1997 (PMID: 9487416); Jessen MK et al. Resuscitation. 2025 (PMID: 39761907).

shelves.title: Cystatin C eGFR versus creatinine eGFR: better prediction of death and kidney failure in consortium cohorts (reclassification and discordance analyses)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic kidney disease, does cystatin C based estimated GFR predict kidney failure and death better than creatinine based estimated GFR?
shelves.mesh: Creatinine · Cystatin C · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Kidney Function Tests · Reference Standards · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Risk · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — a GAP-E prognosis shelf: the evidence is cohort meta-analysis by design, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Three CKD Prognosis Consortium analyses agree. Reclassification (Shlipak 2013; 90,750 general-population and 2,960 CKD participants): cystatin C moved people to eGFR categories that matched their outcomes better than creatinine did, with a net reclassification improvement of 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease. Scale (Grams 2023; 720,736 people with creatinine–cystatin eGFR in 20 cohorts): the combined estimate was significantly associated with all 10 adverse outcomes, including kidney failure requiring replacement therapy and death. Discordance (Estrella 2025; 821,327 outpatients): the 11% whose cystatin eGFR was at least 30% below their creatinine eGFR had a mortality hazard ratio of 1.69 (28.4 vs 16.8 deaths per 1,000 person-years) and a kidney-failure hazard ratio of 1.29 — risk invisible to the creatinine estimate. Caveats on the face: the three analyses draw on overlapping consortium cohorts, cystatin C carries non-GFR influences (inflammation, adiposity), and no trial shows cystatin-guided care improves outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): cystatin-based eGFR predicts kidney failure and death better than creatinine-based eGFR.

cards.headline: Shlipak 2013 (CKD Prognosis Consortium, NEJM): cystatin C reclassification tracked risk in both directions — net reclassification improvement 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease over creatinine alone
cards.summary: Shlipak 2013 (CKD Prognosis Consortium, NEJM): cystatin C reclassification tracked risk in both directions — net reclassification improvement 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease over creatinine alone
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cohort studies (CKD Prognosis Consortium, Shlipak 2013)
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 11 general-population studies (90,750 participants) and 5 chronic kidney disease cohorts (2,960 participants), all with standardised creatinine and cystatin C measurements; outcomes included 13,202 deaths (15 cohorts), 3,471 cardiovascular deaths (12 cohorts) and 1,654 end-stage kidney disease cases (7 cohorts).
cards.result: Cystatin C classified more people as having an eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73 m² than creatinine did (prevalence 13.7% vs 9.7% in the general-population cohorts). Across all eGFR categories, people whom cystatin C reclassified to a higher (better) eGFR than creatinine had a reduced risk of death, cardiovascular death and end-stage kidney disease, and people reclassified to a lower eGFR had an increased risk — the cystatin-based estimate sorted risk more accurately in both directions. The net reclassification improvement from adding cystatin C, versus creatinine alone, was 0.23 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.28) for death and 0.10 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.21) for end-stage kidney disease, with similar results in the CKD cohorts and for the combined creatinine–cystatin equation.
cards.watchOut: Reclassification statistics show cystatin C sorts risk better; they do not by themselves show that acting on a cystatin-based stage changes treatment or outcomes, and the end-stage kidney disease improvement (0.10) has a confidence interval touching zero.
cards.source: Shlipak MG et al. Cystatin C versus creatinine in determining risk based on kidney function. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 24004120. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Grams 2023 (114 cohorts, JAMA): lower eGFR by creatinine–cystatin C, like lower eGFR by creatinine alone, was associated with higher rates of all 10 adverse outcomes including kidney failure and death
cards.summary: Grams 2023 (114 cohorts, JAMA): lower eGFR by creatinine–cystatin C, like lower eGFR by creatinine alone, was associated with higher rates of all 10 adverse outcomes including kidney failure and death
cards.type: Individual-participant data meta-analysis (CKD Prognosis Consortium, Grams 2023)
cards.people: An individual-participant data meta-analysis of 114 global cohorts (1980–2021): 27,503,140 individuals with creatinine-based eGFR, 720,736 individuals in 20 cohorts with creatinine–cystatin C eGFR (mean age 59 years, 53% women, mean follow-up 10.8 years), and 9,067,753 with albuminuria measurements; outcomes were kidney failure requiring replacement therapy, all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, acute kidney injury, hospitalisation, coronary disease, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and peripheral artery disease.
cards.result: Lower eGFR — whether calculated from creatinine alone or from creatinine combined with cystatin C — and higher albuminuria were each significantly associated with higher risk of every one of the 10 adverse outcomes, including in the mildest CKD categories. The associations were graded and consistent across the creatinine–cystatin population, supporting the combined estimate as a risk marker at least as strong as the creatinine estimate across kidney, cardiovascular and hospitalisation outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This card tests the combined creatinine–cystatin equation rather than cystatin C alone, and its role here is scale and consistency: it shows the cystatin-containing estimate carries the same graded outcome associations across 10 outcomes in three-quarters of a million people — the head-to-head 'better than' numbers are on the neighbouring cards.
cards.source: Grams ME et al. Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate, Albuminuria, and Adverse Outcomes: An Individual-Participant Data Meta-Analysis. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37787795. cards.headline: Estrella 2025: when cystatin eGFR ran at least 30% below creatinine eGFR (11% of outpatients), mortality was 28.4 vs 16.8 per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 1.69) and kidney failure hazard ratio 1.29
cards.summary: Estrella 2025: when cystatin eGFR ran at least 30% below creatinine eGFR (11% of outpatients), mortality was 28.4 vs 16.8 per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 1.69) and kidney failure hazard ratio 1.29
cards.type: Individual-level meta-analysis of cohort studies (CKD Prognosis Consortium, Estrella 2025)
cards.people: An individual-level meta-analysis from the CKD Prognosis Consortium of 821,327 individuals in 23 outpatient cohorts (mean age 59 years, 48% women; mean follow-up 11 years) and 39,639 individuals in 2 inpatient cohorts, all with concurrent creatinine and cystatin C measurements; the exposure was a large negative eGFR difference — cystatin-based eGFR at least 30% lower than creatinine-based eGFR.
cards.result: A large negative discordance was present in 11% of outpatients (range 3% to 50% across cohorts) and 35% of inpatients. Compared with patients whose two estimates agreed within 30%, outpatients with the discordance had higher rates of all-cause mortality (28.4 vs 16.8 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.57 to 1.82), cardiovascular mortality (6.1 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years; HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.48 to 1.76), heart failure (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.40 to 1.68), atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.44) and kidney failure with replacement therapy (2.7 vs 2.1 per 1,000 person-years; HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.47) — the creatinine estimate alone was missing risk that the cystatin estimate exposed.
cards.watchOut: Discordance is not pure kidney signal: cystatin C is also raised by inflammation, obesity and other non-GFR factors, so part of the extra 'risk' a low cystatin eGFR flags may be the company it keeps rather than filtration itself. The kidney-failure association (HR 1.29) is also the weakest of the outcomes reported.
cards.source: Estrella MM et al. Discordance in Creatinine- and Cystatin C-Based eGFR and Clinical Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 41202182. Registry ID: none in the record. individual-level meta-analysis of cohort studies (ckd prognosis consortium, estrella 2025) an individual-level meta-analysis from the ckd prognosis consortium of 821,327 individuals in 23 outpatient cohorts (mean age 59 years, 48% women; mean follow-up 11 years) and 39,639 individuals in 2 inpatient cohorts, all with concurrent creatinine and cystatin c measurements; the exposure was a large negative egfr difference — cystatin-based egfr at least 30% lower than creatinine-based egfr. a large negative discordance was present in 11% of outpatients (range 3% to 50% across cohorts) and 35% of inpatients. compared with patients whose two estimates agreed within 30%, outpatients with the discordance had higher rates of all-cause mortality (28.4 vs 16.8 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.69, 95% ci 1.57 to 1.82), cardiovascular mortality (6.1 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years; hr 1.61, 95% ci 1.48 to 1.76), heart failure (hr 1.54, 95% ci 1.40 to 1.68), atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (hr 1.35, 95% ci 1.27 to 1.44) and kidney failure with replacement therapy (2.7 vs 2.1 per 1,000 person-years; hr 1.29, 95% ci 1.13 to 1.47) — the creatinine estimate alone was missing risk that the cystatin estimate exposed. discordance is not pure kidney signal: cystatin c is also raised by inflammation, obesity and other non-gfr factors, so part of the extra 'risk' a low cystatin egfr flags may be the company it keeps rather than filtration itself. the kidney-failure association (hr 1.29) is also the weakest of the outcomes reported. estrella mm et al. discordance in creatinine- and cystatin c-based egfr and clinical outcomes: a meta-analysis. jama. 2025. pmid: 41202182. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · atherosclerosis · cardiovascular diseases · creatinine · cystatin c · glomerular filtration rate · heart failure · kidney failure, chronic · prognosis · renal insufficiency, chronic · renal replacement therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: across three consortium meta-analyses, cystatin-containing eGFR consistently stratifies death and kidney-failure risk better than creatinine eGFR alone — reclassification improves, and a discordantly low cystatin eGFR marks roughly 70% higher mortality hazard
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three consortium meta-analyses, cystatin-containing eGFR consistently stratifies death and kidney-failure risk better than creatinine eGFR alone — reclassification improves, and a discordantly low cystatin eGFR marks roughly 70% higher mortality hazard
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational prognosis research from one consortium's pooled cohorts: the 2013 reclassification meta-analysis (93,710 participants), the 2023 individual-participant analysis of 114 cohorts (720,736 with creatinine–cystatin eGFR), and the 2025 discordance analysis (821,327 outpatients). No study randomised anyone to cystatin-guided versus creatinine-guided care.
cards.result: The three analyses answer the question from three angles and agree. Reclassification: adding cystatin C moved people into risk categories that matched their actual outcomes, with a net reclassification improvement of 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease. Scale: the combined creatinine–cystatin estimate carried graded associations with all 10 adverse outcomes, kidney failure included. Discordance: the one patient in nine whose cystatin eGFR was at least 30% below their creatinine eGFR had a mortality hazard ratio of 1.69 and a kidney-failure hazard ratio of 1.29 relative to concordant patients — risk the creatinine number alone concealed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): cystatin C-based (and combined creatinine–cystatin) eGFR predicts kidney failure and death better than creatinine-based eGFR alone.
cards.watchOut: All three cards come from the CKD Prognosis Consortium's overlapping cohort pool, so they are three analyses of substantially the same underlying populations, not three independent literatures; and better prediction has not been shown to mean better outcomes from cystatin-guided decisions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shlipak MG et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2013 (PMID: 24004120); Grams ME et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37787795); Estrella MM et al. JAMA. 2025 (PMID: 41202182).

shelves.title: Febuxostat versus allopurinol for kidney protection in gout and CKD: positive indirect signals (FREED, small and biased direct comparisons), no rigorous head-to-head proof
shelves.question: In adults with gout and chronic kidney disease, does febuxostat protect kidney function compared with allopurinol?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiovascular Diseases · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Febuxostat · Female · Gout Suppressants · Humans · Hyperuricemia · Kidney Diseases · Male · Prospective Studies · Uric Acid
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #168, which settled that urate lowering with allopurinol does not slow CKD progression and carded FEATHER (febuxostat vs placebo: no kidney protection) inside that answer; this shelf is the febuxostat-specific, head-to-head slice. It is thin where it matters. The largest positive signal, FREED (1,070 elderly patients), compared febuxostat with conventional therapy — not allopurinol — in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia rather than gout, and its renal finding is a soft impairment composite (16.2% vs 20.5%; hazard ratio 0.745 relative) plus a post-hoc macroalbuminuria result (HR 0.44 relative), with 40% eGFR decline null. Directly against allopurinol there is one 120-patient, 6-month, low-fixed-dose trial favouring febuxostat (its abstract does not print the primary outcome's numbers) and three retrospective studies all rated at serious risk of bias. The 5,002-patient CARES post-hoc ties slower eGFR decline to achieving urate under 6 mg/dL (adjusted odds ratio 0.66 relative), whichever drug achieved it. STOP Gout's gout-and-CKD subgroup, homed on pack #2571, is cross-pointed and not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): febuxostat may protect kidney function better than allopurinol, but no direct, rigorous test has shown it.

cards.headline: FREED 2019: febuxostat versus conventional therapy in 1,070 elderly patients with hyperuricaemia — renal impairment events 16.2% vs 20.5% (hazard ratio 0.745), inside a positive composite driven by those renal events
cards.summary: FREED 2019: febuxostat versus conventional therapy in 1,070 elderly patients with hyperuricaemia — renal impairment events 16.2% vs 20.5% (hazard ratio 0.745), inside a positive composite driven by those renal events
cards.people: 1,070 elderly Japanese patients (serum uric acid over 7.0 to at most 9.0 mg/dL) at risk of cerebral, cardiovascular or renal disease through hypertension, type 2 diabetes, renal disease or prior cerebral/cardiovascular disease, randomised open-label to febuxostat (n=537) or a non-febuxostat conventional-therapy group (n=533) and followed for 36 months. The population had asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, not established gout, and the comparator was conventional therapy with lifestyle modification, not titrated allopurinol.
cards.result: The primary composite of cerebral, cardiovascular and renal events and all deaths was lower on febuxostat (hazard ratio 0.750, 95% CI 0.592 to 0.950, P=0.017), and the most frequent component was renal impairment: 16.2% on febuxostat versus 20.5% on conventional therapy (hazard ratio 0.745, 95% CI 0.562 to 0.987, P=0.041). Endpoint serum uric acid was 4.50±1.52 mg/dL on febuxostat versus 6.76±1.45 mg/dL on conventional therapy (P<0.001) — the groups differed far more in achieved urate than in drug identity alone.
cards.watchOut: This is the strongest febuxostat renal signal and it is still not the shelf's comparison: conventional therapy is not allopurinol, the patients did not have gout, and a composite 'renal impairment' event definition is softer than measured GFR slope or kidney failure.
cards.source: Kojima S et al. Febuxostat for Cerebral and CaRdiorenovascular Events PrEvEntion StuDy. European heart journal. 2019. PMID: 30844048. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01984749. cards.headline: FREED renal post-hoc 2023: developing or worsening macroalbuminuria was 56% less likely on febuxostat (hazard ratio 0.44) — but 40% eGFR decline and new microalbuminuria did not differ
cards.summary: FREED renal post-hoc 2023: developing or worsening macroalbuminuria was 56% less likely on febuxostat (hazard ratio 0.44) — but 40% eGFR decline and new microalbuminuria did not differ
cards.type: Post-hoc renal analysis of a randomised trial (Kohagura 2023)
cards.people: The same 1,070 FREED participants (febuxostat n=537, non-febuxostat n=533) — elderly patients with asymptomatic hyperuricaemia and at least one cardiovascular risk factor — re-analysed post hoc for renal outcomes: 40% decline in eGFR, new-onset microalbuminuria, and development or worsening of macroalbuminuria.
cards.result: The relative risk of developing or worsening macroalbuminuria was 56% lower in the febuxostat group (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.82, P=0.0098). The risks of the other renal outcomes — including a 40% decline in eGFR — were comparable between groups (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes).
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc analysis of the trial on the previous card — same patients, not independent evidence — and its one positive outcome is an albuminuria category change, while the harder outcome (40% eGFR decline) was null.
cards.source: Kohagura K et al. Febuxostat and renal outcomes: post-hoc analysis of a randomized trial. Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension. 2023. PMID: 36750608. Registry ID: none in the record (post-hoc analysis of FREED, NCT01984749 as on the parent trial's record). cards.headline: Yang 2022: in 120 CKD patients with hyperuricaemia, low-dose febuxostat (20 mg) versus allopurinol (200 mg) — fewer patients lost over 10% of eGFR over 6 months, with no difference in creatinine, urate or adverse events
cards.summary: Yang 2022: in 120 CKD patients with hyperuricaemia, low-dose febuxostat (20 mg) versus allopurinol (200 mg) — fewer patients lost over 10% of eGFR over 6 months, with no difference in creatinine, urate or adverse events
cards.people: 120 patients with chronic kidney disease complicated by hyperuricaemia at two centres, randomised 1:1 to low-dose febuxostat 20 mg/day or allopurinol 200 mg/day, with creatinine, uric acid and eGFR measured at baseline and at 1, 3 and 6 months; the primary outcome was the proportion with a decline in eGFR of more than 10% by 6 months. The abstract does not print the two proportions for that primary outcome.
cards.result: eGFR was higher in the febuxostat group at 6 months (but similar at baseline, 1 and 3 months), and the proportion of patients with a >10% eGFR decline was lower on febuxostat than on allopurinol; there was no difference between groups in serum creatinine or serum uric acid at any time point, and no difference in drug-related adverse events. In subgroup analysis the eGFR and urate advantages appeared in stage 3 CKD but not in stage 2.
cards.watchOut: The one direct febuxostat-versus-allopurinol randomised comparison here is small (120 patients), short (6 months), uses low fixed doses of both drugs rather than treat-to-target titration, and its abstract withholds the primary outcome's actual numbers — it can support 'maybe', not more.
cards.source: Yang N et al. Low-dose febuxostat exhibits a superior renal-protective effect and non-inferior safety profile compared to allopurinol in chronic kidney disease patients complicated with hyperuricemia: A double-centre, randomized, controlled study. cards.headline: Hu & Brown 2020: reviewing the three long-term retrospective comparisons, febuxostat patients had higher eGFR and less renal progression than allopurinol patients — in studies all rated at serious risk of bias
cards.summary: Hu & Brown 2020: reviewing the three long-term retrospective comparisons, febuxostat patients had higher eGFR and less renal progression than allopurinol patients — in studies all rated at serious risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review of retrospective studies (Hu & Brown 2020)
cards.people: A systematic review of studies with at least 12 months of follow-up comparing allopurinol with febuxostat on long-term renal outcomes in hyperuricaemia with chronic kidney disease or kidney transplantation (search to December 2019); three retrospective observational studies qualified, with follow-up of 1 to 5 years, assessed with the ROBINS-I tool.
cards.result: In the reviewed studies, febuxostat patients had a significantly higher eGFR, a reduced risk of renal disease progression, and lower serum uric acid levels than allopurinol patients. All three studies carried a serious risk of bias. The authors' conclusion is that febuxostat may be more renoprotective than allopurinol on this evidence, and that more methodologically rigorous studies are needed before the finding is clinically applicable.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective febuxostat-versus-allopurinol comparisons are confounded by prescribing: febuxostat is preferentially given to patients with worse kidney function or allopurinol intolerance, and ROBINS-I rated every included study at serious risk of bias.
cards.source: Hu AM et al. Comparative effect of allopurinol and febuxostat on long-term renal outcomes in patients with hyperuricemia and chronic kidney disease: a systematic review. cards.headline: CARES post-hoc 2025: in 5,002 patients with gout on urate-lowering therapy, keeping average urate under 6 mg/dL was associated with less eGFR decline (adjusted odds ratio 0.66) — an effect of achieved urate, not of febuxostat versus allopurinol
cards.summary: CARES post-hoc 2025: in 5,002 patients with gout on urate-lowering therapy, keeping average urate under 6 mg/dL was associated with less eGFR decline (adjusted odds ratio 0.66) — an effect of achieved urate, not of febuxostat versus allopurinol
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial (Ghang 2025)
cards.people: 5,002 patients with gout from the CARES cardiovascular-safety trial who received urate-lowering therapy with either febuxostat or allopurinol for more than 6 months, followed for a median of 2.5 years, with eGFR slope calculated by linear mixed modelling; the analysis relates achieved serum urate to kidney-function change rather than comparing the two randomised drugs on kidney outcomes.
cards.result: Over follow-up, 3,264 patients (65.3%) had an increased eGFR while on urate-lowering therapy. Higher average serum urate was significantly associated with a worse eGFR slope (per 1 mg/dL higher average urate, adjusted beta −0.1912, units as printed in the record), and in a propensity-matched analysis an average urate below 6 mg/dL was associated with a reduced risk of eGFR decline (adjusted odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.77). The abstract reports no febuxostat-versus-allopurinol difference in kidney function.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and propensity-matched: patients who achieve low urate differ from those who do not (adherence, dose tolerance, baseline health), so this card supports 'lower urate, slower decline' as an association — it does not show febuxostat protects kidneys better than allopurinol, and the parent CARES trial's kidney claims were not its randomised comparison.
cards.source: Ghang B et al. Post-hoc analysis of the CARES trial suggests delayed progression of chronic kidney disease in patients with gout during urate-lowering therapy. Kidney international. 2025. PMID: 39551133. Registry ID: none in the record (post-hoc analysis of CARES, NCT01101035 as on the parent trial's record on live shelf #382). cards.headline: Synthesis: no direct, rigorous evidence that febuxostat protects kidney function better than allopurinol — the positive signals are a non-allopurinol comparator, an albuminuria post-hoc, one small low-dose trial, and biased retrospective comparisons
cards.summary: Synthesis: no direct, rigorous evidence that febuxostat protects kidney function better than allopurinol — the positive signals are a non-allopurinol comparator, an albuminuria post-hoc, one small low-dose trial, and biased retrospective comparisons
cards.people: The carded evidence: FREED (1,070 patients, febuxostat vs conventional therapy, plus its renal post-hoc), one small direct randomised comparison (120 patients, low fixed doses, 6 months), a systematic review of 3 retrospective studies (all at serious risk of bias), and a 5,002-patient CARES post-hoc about achieved urate rather than drug choice. The direct gout-and-CKD randomised evidence — STOP Gout's stage-3 CKD subgroup — is homed on pack #2571 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded; FEATHER (febuxostat vs placebo) is homed on live shelf #168, which found no kidney protection.
cards.result: Line the comparisons up by what they actually compare. Against conventional therapy in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, febuxostat reduced a soft renal-impairment composite (16.2% vs 20.5%; HR 0.745 relative) and macroalbuminuria worsening (HR 0.44 relative), but not 40% eGFR decline. Against allopurinol directly, the evidence is one 120-patient low-dose trial favouring febuxostat on a >10%-decline outcome whose numbers its abstract does not print, plus three retrospective studies at serious risk of bias. The largest gout dataset (CARES post-hoc) attributes slower decline to achieving urate under 6 mg/dL, not to which drug achieved it — consistent with live shelf #168, where febuxostat against placebo (FEATHER) did not protect the kidney either. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): febuxostat may protect kidney function compared with allopurinol, but the claim rests on indirect and biased comparisons and has not survived a direct, adequately powered test.

shelves.title: Late belatacept conversion in established kidney transplant recipients: better graft function (two randomised trials), more early rejection, no graft-survival difference
shelves.question: In established kidney transplant recipients, does late conversion from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept improve graft function compared with continuing the calcineurin inhibitor?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept · Acute Disease · Adult · Biopsy · Calcineurin Inhibitors · Drug Substitution · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection · Graft Survival · Humans · Immunoconjugates · Immunosuppressive Agents · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2103 (everolimus-based calcineurin-inhibitor elimination in de novo recipients); this shelf is the belatacept conversion slice in established recipients, and it is distinct from live shelf #590 (de novo belatacept versus ciclosporin from the day of transplant). Two randomised trials randomised exactly this switch in stable recipients: the phase II trial (173 patients, 6–36 months post-transplant) found a better 12-month change in calculated GFR after switching, with 6 early rejections, all resolved; the phase 3b trial (446 patients, 6–60 months) quantified it — eGFR 55.5 versus 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 24 months — with survival with a functioning graft unchanged (98% vs 97%), biopsy-proven rejection roughly doubled (8% vs 4%), and fewer de novo donor-specific antibodies (1% vs 7%). A 108-patient conversion cohort adds the boundary condition: eGFR slope improved after conversion in non-sensitised recipients (+0.28/year) but declined in HLA-sensitised recipients (−0.44/year). One correction to the slate: it named the anchor 'Rostaing 2015' — the verified randomised report is Rostaing 2011 (PMID: 21051752). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: late belatacept conversion improves graft function in stable established recipients, bought with more early rejection and no demonstrated graft-survival benefit.

cards.headline: Rostaing 2011 (phase II conversion trial): switching stable recipients 6–36 months post-transplant to belatacept improved the 12-month change in calculated GFR versus continuing a calcineurin inhibitor, with 6 early rejections, all resolved
cards.summary: Rostaing 2011 (phase II conversion trial): switching stable recipients 6–36 months post-transplant to belatacept improved the 12-month change in calculated GFR versus continuing a calcineurin inhibitor, with 6 early rejections, all resolved
cards.people: 173 kidney transplant recipients with stable graft function, at least 6 and at most 36 months after transplantation and receiving a calcineurin-inhibitor-based regimen (ciclosporin or tacrolimus), randomised open-label to switch to belatacept (n=84) or continue the calcineurin inhibitor (n=89), all on background maintenance immunosuppression; the primary endpoint was the change in calculated GFR from baseline to month 12.
cards.result: At month 12 the mean change from baseline in calculated GFR was higher in the belatacept group than in the calcineurin-inhibitor group (the abstract states the direction and that the primary endpoint favoured switching, without printing the two mean changes). Six patients in the belatacept group had acute rejection episodes, all within the first 6 months and all resolved with no allograft loss; by month 12 one patient in the calcineurin group had died with a functioning graft and no belatacept patient had lost a graft. The overall safety profile was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The slate named this trial 'Rostaing 2015'; the randomised report verified on PubMed is the 2011 phase II paper carded here. It is small, open-label, and its abstract withholds the size of the GFR gain — direction only — so the magnitude has to come from the larger trial on the next card.
cards.source: Rostaing L et al. Switching from calcineurin inhibitor-based regimens to a belatacept-based regimen in renal transplant recipients: a randomized phase II study. cards.headline: Budde 2021 (phase 3b conversion trial): 446 stable recipients randomised at 6–60 months — graft survival with function 98% vs 97% at 24 months, eGFR 55.5 vs 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m², rejection 8% vs 4%, de novo donor-specific antibodies 1% vs 7%
cards.summary: Budde 2021 (phase 3b conversion trial): 446 stable recipients randomised at 6–60 months — graft survival with function 98% vs 97% at 24 months, eGFR 55.5 vs 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m², rejection 8% vs 4%, de novo donor-specific antibodies 1% vs 7%
cards.people: 446 stable adult kidney transplant recipients, 6–60 months post-transplantation on calcineurin-inhibitor-based immunosuppression, randomised 1:1 to convert to belatacept (n=223) or continue their established calcineurin inhibitor (n=223); the primary endpoint was the proportion surviving with a functioning graft at 24 months.
cards.result: Survival with a functioning graft at 24 months was 98% on belatacept conversion versus 97% on calcineurin continuation (adjusted difference 0.8, 95.1% CI −2.1 to 3.7) — no difference in the hard outcome. Kidney function favoured conversion: 24-month eGFR was 55.5 versus 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m². The costs and offsets: biopsy-proven acute rejection occurred in 8% versus 4%, while de novo donor-specific antibodies developed in 1% versus 7%. Serious adverse events, infections and discontinuations were similar, and one belatacept patient developed post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.
cards.watchOut: The GFR advantage (7 mL/min/1.73 m²) is a surrogate measured at 24 months in patients selected for stability; the trial was not powered to show a graft-survival benefit, and the doubled rejection rate (8% vs 4%) is the price that has to be set against the function gain.

cards.headline: Sethi 2020 (conversion cohort, 5 years): after conversion, eGFR slope improved in non-sensitised recipients (+0.28 mL/min/1.73 m²/year) but declined in HLA-sensitised recipients (−0.44), whose early conversions also rejected more
cards.summary: Sethi 2020 (conversion cohort, 5 years): after conversion, eGFR slope improved in non-sensitised recipients (+0.28 mL/min/1.73 m²/year) but declined in HLA-sensitised recipients (−0.44), whose early conversions also rejected more
cards.people: 108 kidney transplant recipients converted from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept at one centre between 2012 and 2017 — 29 HLA-sensitised and 79 non-sensitised — followed for 5 years for rejection-free, patient and graft survival and for eGFR slope after conversion; there is no continuing-calcineurin-inhibitor control group, so the comparison is between converted patient types.
cards.result: Rejection-free survival at 5 years did not differ overall between sensitised and non-sensitised recipients (82% vs 84.6%, P=0.30), nor did patient survival (85.7% vs 83.7%) or graft survival (78.5% vs 89.8%, P=0.17). But eGFR slope after conversion improved in non-sensitised recipients (+0.28 mL/min/1.73 m²/year, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.53) while declining in sensitised recipients (−0.44, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.03), and sensitised recipients converted within the first year after transplant had lower rejection-free survival than non-sensitised recipients converted then (55.6% vs 75.0% at 5 years, P=0.03). The authors advise caution converting high-immunologic-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Without a non-converted comparator this card cannot estimate conversion's effect — it identifies who conversion suits (stable, non-sensitised recipients) and who it may not (sensitised patients, especially converted early), which is exactly the population caveat the two randomised trials, with their stability criteria, cannot supply.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised conversion trials agree — graft function improves by about 7 mL/min/1.73 m² at 2 years with no graft-survival difference and roughly double the early rejection; cohort data say the benefit concentrates in non-sensitised recipients
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised conversion trials agree — graft function improves by about 7 mL/min/1.73 m² at 2 years with no graft-survival difference and roughly double the early rejection; cohort data say the benefit concentrates in non-sensitised recipients
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 173-patient randomised phase II conversion trial (6–36 months post-transplant), a 446-patient randomised phase 3b conversion trial (6–60 months), and a 108-patient 5-year conversion cohort. The de novo belatacept trials (BENEFIT programme, live shelf #590) and the everolimus-based de novo conversion shelf (live #2103) ask different questions and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Both randomised trials randomised the same decision — switch a stable, established recipient from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept, or stay — and both found better graft function after switching, quantified in the phase 3b trial as eGFR 55.5 versus 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 24 months, with survival with a functioning graft unchanged (98% vs 97%) and biopsy-proven rejection roughly doubled (8% vs 4%; 6 early episodes in the phase II trial, all resolved). De novo donor-specific antibodies were fewer after conversion (1% vs 7%). The cohort card adds the boundary: eGFR slope improved after conversion in non-sensitised recipients and worsened in HLA-sensitised recipients, who also rejected more when converted within the first year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: late conversion to belatacept improves graft function in stable established recipients, at the cost of more early acute rejection and with no demonstrated graft-survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: Function is a surrogate: neither trial shows patients keeping their grafts longer, follow-up is 24 months in the randomised evidence, and both trials enrolled stable recipients — the results do not extend to unstable grafts or to very late conversion beyond 5 years.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rostaing L et al. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2011 (PMID: 21051752); Budde K et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2021 (PMID: 34706967); Sethi S et al. Transplantation. 2020 (PMID: 31568398).

shelves.title: Neutral-pH, low-GDP PD solutions — peritonitis and technique failure: balANZ's benefit (homed on #1738) unreproduced across the trial programme and registry practice
shelves.question: In adults on peritoneal dialysis, do neutral-pH, low-glucose-degradation-product solutions reduce peritonitis and technique failure compared with conventional solutions?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bicarbonates · Child · Dialysis Solutions · Glucose · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Icodextrin · Kidney · Peritoneal Dialysis · Peritoneum · Pharmaceutical Solutions · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Urine
shelves.balance: SPLIT (single trial vs programme) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1738, built under the documented precedent for a homed anchor with a genuinely different slice: #1738 asks whether these solutions preserve residual kidney function (answer: no, on balANZ's primary outcome) and cards balANZ's two reports (PMIDs 22440906 and 22991015, both on the gate list and NOT re-carded here). This shelf asks the programme-wide peritonitis and technique-failure question, which #1738 touches only through balANZ's secondary peritonitis analysis. On the free reports, the answer splits: the Cochrane review of 29 neutral-pH low-GDP trials (1,971 participants) found peritonitis differences uncertain and technique failure or death little or no different (the treatment made no difference); a 50-patient randomised trial found no peritonitis difference; and the ANZDATA registry analysis found biocompatible-solution patients with a higher peritonitis rate (0.67 vs 0.47 episodes per patient-year; incidence rate ratio 1.49 relative). So balANZ's peritonitis advantage (0.30 vs 0.49 episodes per patient-year, on #1738) stands unreproduced across the wider programme, and no technique-failure benefit is shown anywhere carded. PROPOSED SPLIT (single trial vs programme): peritonitis reduction in one trial's secondary analysis; no confirmed peritonitis or technique-survival benefit programme-wide.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2018: across 29 randomised trials (1,971 participants) of neutral-pH, low-GDP solutions, peritonitis differences were uncertain and technique failure or death may make little or no difference (low certainty)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018: across 29 randomised trials (1,971 participants) of neutral-pH, low-GDP solutions, peritonitis differences were uncertain and technique failure or death may make little or no difference (low certainty)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Htay 2018)
cards.people: Adults and children on peritoneal dialysis in the 42 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (3,262 participants) of biocompatible solutions in the 2018 Cochrane update, of which 29 studies (1,971 participants) compared a neutral-pH, low-glucose-degradation-product solution with a conventional solution — the comparison this shelf asks about; icodextrin trials in the review are a different intervention and are not used here.
cards.result: For neutral-pH, low-GDP versus conventional solutions, the review found it uncertain whether there were any differences in peritonitis occurrence, hospitalisation or adverse events, and that the solutions may make little or no difference to technique failure or death (low certainty evidence) — the treatment made no difference on the technique outcome. (The same review's residual-kidney-function findings belong to live shelf #1738's question and are not re-carded here.)
cards.watchOut: The review pools the balANZ trial — whose own peritonitis result, homed on live shelf #1738, favoured the biocompatible solution — with many smaller, shorter trials; a pooled 'uncertain' can hide one large positive trial, which is precisely the split this shelf exists to display.

cards.headline: Cho 2013 (ANZDATA registry): incident Australian PD patients on biocompatible solutions had a higher peritonitis rate than patients on conventional solutions — 0.67 vs 0.47 episodes per patient-year, incidence rate ratio 1.49
cards.summary: Cho 2013 (ANZDATA registry): incident Australian PD patients on biocompatible solutions had a higher peritonitis rate than patients on conventional solutions — 0.67 vs 0.47 episodes per patient-year, incidence rate ratio 1.49
cards.people: All incident Australian patients receiving peritoneal dialysis between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2010 in the Australia and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry, classified by whether their solution was a multicompartment neutral-pH (biocompatible) product; the total number of patients is not documented in the record (N not documented). Biocompatible use was uncommon and falling (7.5% of patients in 2007 to 4.2% in 2010) and was preferentially used by smaller units and in younger patients without diabetes.
cards.result: Treatment with a biocompatible solution was associated with a significantly greater overall peritonitis rate (0.67 versus 0.47 episodes per patient-year; incidence rate ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.89) and a shorter time to first peritonitis (hazard ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.87), a finding replicated in propensity-score-matched cohorts (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.71). The authors call for randomised studies adequately powered for peritonitis as a primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Observational and opposite in direction to the balANZ trial result homed on #1738: with only 4–8% of patients on biocompatible solutions, chosen by particular units for particular patients, confounding by unit practice and case mix is a live explanation — but so is a real absence of the protection balANZ suggested.

cards.headline: Szeto 2007: in 50 new PD patients randomised to a neutral-pH, low-GDP solution or conventional solution for 12 months, peritonitis rate and hospitalisation did not differ (the treatment made no difference) — while membrane biomarkers favoured the new solution
cards.summary: Szeto 2007: in 50 new PD patients randomised to a neutral-pH, low-GDP solution or conventional solution for 12 months, peritonitis rate and hospitalisation did not differ (the treatment made no difference) — while membrane biomarkers favoured the new solution
cards.people: 50 new peritoneal dialysis patients randomised to a conventional lactate-buffered fluid or a pH-neutral, lactate-buffered, low-GDP solution (the tested product is named in the publication as 'balance') and followed for 12 months, with effluent cancer antigen-125 and hyaluronan, serum C-reactive protein, adequacy, ultrafiltration and clinical endpoints including peritonitis and hospitalisation.
cards.result: There was no difference between groups in dialysis adequacy, ultrafiltration volume, urine output, residual renal function, peritonitis rate or need for hospitalisation over 1 year (the treatment made no difference on the clinical outcomes). The biocompatibility markers did move: effluent CA-125 was higher on the neutral solution at 52 weeks (14.30±2.17 vs 7.36±2.23 U/mL, P=0.007), hyaluronan lower (1.45±0.32 vs 2.55±0.32 µg/mL, P=0.007), and serum CRP lower (1.77±0.42 vs 7.73±2.42 mg/L, P=0.026).
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients for 12 months cannot detect a peritonitis difference of the size balANZ reported, and this trial's own authors frame it as a biocompatibility-marker study: better-looking effluent markers, no clinical difference shown.

cards.headline: Synthesis: programme-wide, neutral-pH low-GDP solutions have not been shown to reduce peritonitis or technique failure — the pooled trials are null/uncertain, a small trial is null, and the largest registry analysis points the other way; the positive peritonitis result is one trial's secondary outcome, homed on #1738
cards.summary: Synthesis: programme-wide, neutral-pH low-GDP solutions have not been shown to reduce peritonitis or technique failure — the pooled trials are null/uncertain, a small trial is null, and the largest registry analysis points the other way; the positive peritonitis result is one trial's secondary outcome, homed on #1738
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of 29 neutral-pH low-GDP randomised trials (1,971 participants), a national registry cohort of incident Australian PD patients 2007–2010 (total N not documented in the record), and a 50-patient randomised trial. The balANZ trial's own reports (PMIDs 22440906 and 22991015) are homed on live shelf #1738 and are deliberately not re-carded here, in line with the one-home rule; this shelf was built on the free programme-wide reports under that precedent.
cards.result: balANZ remains the only large trial with a positive peritonitis result (0.30 vs 0.49 episodes per patient-year, on live shelf #1738, where it is a secondary outcome of a trial whose primary kidney-function outcome was null). Everything carded here qualifies or contradicts it: the Cochrane pooling of the whole neutral-pH low-GDP trial programme found peritonitis differences uncertain and technique failure or death little or no different; the small dedicated trial found no peritonitis difference; and the ANZDATA registry analysis found biocompatible-solution patients with a higher peritonitis rate (incidence rate ratio 1.49 relative) and shorter time to first peritonitis. On technique failure specifically, no carded report shows a benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT (single trial vs programme): a peritonitis reduction seen in one trial's secondary analysis has not been reproduced across the trial programme or in registry practice, and no technique-survival benefit has been shown.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane pool includes balANZ itself, so the cards are not fully independent of the homed trial; and the registry result is observational. The honest summary is not 'the solutions cause peritonitis' but 'the protection claimed from one trial is unconfirmed everywhere else'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Htay H et al. Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30362116); Cho Y et al. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2013 (PMID: 23949232); Szeto CC et al. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation. 2007 (PMID: 17005526).

shelves.title: What sets the glomerular filtration rate: glomerular pressure, arteriolar tone and Kf — the textbook equation confirmed by human protein-load and ANP studies
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what determines glomerular filtration rate — how do afferent and efferent arteriolar tone, glomerular pressure and filtration coefficient set GFR?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Creatinine · Dietary Proteins · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Inulin · Kidney · Kidney Diseases · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Plant Proteins, Dietary
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks state the governing relation: GFR equals the filtration coefficient (Kf — capillary surface area and permeability) multiplied by the net filtration pressure, which is set by glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman's capsule pressure and plasma oncotic pressure. Afferent arteriolar dilation (or efferent constriction) raises glomerular pressure and GFR; afferent constriction lowers both; efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure. The carded human studies behave exactly as that framework predicts. A protein load recruits 'renal functional reserve' and drives GFR up by roughly a third within hours (Bosch 1983; Herrera 1988: inulin-clearance GFR 107 to 146 ml/min after a meat meal, with renal blood flow rising in parallel — a predominantly afferent-side vasodilator pattern). Atrial natriuretic peptide shows the pressure/filtration-fraction dissociation the textbooks describe: at low infusion doses in normal man, GFR itself did not change while renal plasma flow fell slightly and filtration fraction rose (Richards 1988) — a pattern consistent with a relatively greater efferent than afferent effect at those doses. Herrera's indomethacin arm is the caution: blocking prostaglandin synthesis by 73% did not blunt protein-induced hyperfiltration, so no single vasodilator mediator owns the afferent response. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: in humans, GFR is set moment to moment by glomerular capillary pressure (afferent versus efferent tone), plasma flow and oncotic pressure acting through Kf, exactly as the textbook relation states.

cards.headline: Bosch 1983: a protein load raised GFR to a maximal 171.0 ± 7.7 ml/min at 2.5 hours in normal subjects — the human 'renal functional reserve'
cards.summary: Bosch 1983: a protein load raised GFR to a maximal 171.0 ± 7.7 ml/min at 2.5 hours in normal subjects — the human 'renal functional reserve'
cards.type: Human physiology study (diet and protein-load clearances, Bosch 1983)
cards.people: Normal human volunteers studied on protein versus vegetarian diets and with progressive protein intake and acute protein loads; the record does not print the number of subjects (N not documented in the record). GFR was assessed by creatinine clearance in the diet studies and in the short-term protein-load studies.
cards.result: Subjects eating a protein diet had significantly higher creatinine clearance than comparable subjects on a vegetarian diet; progressive increments in protein intake produced progressive increments in creatinine clearance, and diurnal clearance variations tracked periods of food intake. After an acute protein load, GFR rose to a maximal 171.0 ± 7.7 ml/min at two and a half hours. In patients with a reduced number of nephrons, this functional reserve was diminished or absent.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record — the abstract reports no subject count, so none is printed here. Creatinine clearance overestimates true GFR somewhat; the card's point is the direction and size of the load response, not a precise inulin value.
cards.source: Bosch JP et al. Renal functional reserve in humans. Effect of protein intake on glomerular filtration rate. The American journal of medicine. 1983. PMID: 6650549. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Herrera 1988: a meat meal raised inulin-clearance GFR from 107.2 to 146.4 ml/min in 10 normal subjects — and indomethacin did not blunt it
cards.summary: Herrera 1988: a meat meal raised inulin-clearance GFR from 107.2 to 146.4 ml/min in 10 normal subjects — and indomethacin did not blunt it
cards.type: Human physiology study (meat-meal hyperfiltration with and without indomethacin, Herrera 1988)
cards.people: 10 normal subjects on a maintenance diet (1 g protein/kg, 100 mmol sodium daily), studied before and after a meal of 86 g of meat protein, once unmedicated and once after indomethacin (150 mg daily for 3 days plus 50 mg on the test morning); a carbohydrate meal of similar caloric, sodium and potassium content served as control. GFR by inulin clearance, renal blood flow by para-aminohippurate clearance, during water diuresis.
cards.result: The protein load increased GFR from 107.2 ± 6.05 to a peak of 146.4 ± 6.79 ml/min (mean ± s.e.m., P < 0.01) and renal blood flow from 529.7 ± 42.9 to 678.9 ± 61.9 (P < 0.05). The haemodynamic changes were unrelated to urinary prostaglandin E or kallikrein excretion, and indomethacin — which inhibited prostaglandin E excretion by 73% — did not modify the protein-induced hyperfiltration.
cards.watchOut: A single 10-subject study; its negative indomethacin result argues against prostaglandins as the primary mediator of meal hyperfiltration in man, but it does not exclude a permissive prostaglandin role when afferent tone is threatened (for example in volume depletion or cirrhosis), which this fed, healthy-volunteer design did not test.
cards.source: Herrera J et al. Urinary prostaglandin E and kallikrein activity in glomerular hyperfiltration induced by a meat meal in man. Clinical nephrology. 1988. PMID: 3180523. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Richards 1988: low-dose atrial natriuretic peptide in 6 normal men left GFR unchanged while filtration fraction rose and renal plasma flow fell slightly (N = 6, below 10)
cards.summary: Richards 1988: low-dose atrial natriuretic peptide in 6 normal men left GFR unchanged while filtration fraction rose and renal plasma flow fell slightly (N = 6, below 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (low-dose ANP infusion, Richards 1988) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 normal subjects who received 2-hour low-dose (2 pmol/kg·min) infusions of both 28-amino-acid human alpha-ANP-(99-126) and 26-amino-acid human ANP-(101-126) in a placebo-controlled study. N = 6 — a small study, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Both peptides more than doubled urinary sodium, calcium and magnesium excretion. Effective renal plasma flow was slightly reduced, glomerular filtration rate did not change, and renal filtration fraction increased during the infusions. Plasma renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone concentrations fell by about 50%; arterial blood pressure and plasma catecholamines did not change.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. 'GFR unchanged with filtration fraction up' is a net whole-kidney pattern; it cannot by itself separate afferent from efferent actions, and higher ANP doses in other settings can raise GFR — the dose here was deliberately small (a roughly physiological rise).
cards.source: Richards AM et al. Low dose infusions of 26- and 28-amino acid human atrial natriuretic peptides in normal man. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1988. PMID: 2965159. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: human studies track the textbook equation — glomerular pressure and flow move GFR; filtration fraction can move without it
cards.summary: Synthesis: human studies track the textbook equation — glomerular pressure and flow move GFR; filtration fraction can move without it
cards.people: The carded evidence: protein-load/diet studies in normal volunteers (Bosch 1983, N not documented in the record), a 10-subject inulin-clearance meat-meal study with an indomethacin arm (Herrera 1988), and a 6-subject low-dose ANP infusion study (Richards 1988, N = 6 printed on the face).
cards.result: Feeding/protein raised GFR by about a third (107.2 to 146.4 ml/min by inulin clearance; maximal 171.0 ± 7.7 ml/min after a protein load in the Bosch studies) with renal blood flow rising in parallel, while a peptide that slightly reduced renal plasma flow left GFR unchanged and raised filtration fraction. That is the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account in human data: GFR = Kf × net filtration pressure, with afferent versus efferent arteriolar tone setting glomerular capillary pressure, plasma flow and oncotic pressure completing the determinants, and a recruitable reserve above baseline. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Single-nephron pressures and Kf itself cannot be measured in intact humans; the human evidence is whole-kidney clearance behaviour consistent with the micropuncture-derived textbook model (animal-derived mechanism, named here as textbook context only — no animal study is carded as evidence on this shelf).
cards.source: Synthesis of Bosch JP et al. The American journal of medicine. 1983 (PMID: 6650549); Herrera J et al. Clinical nephrology. 1988 (PMID: 3180523); Richards AM et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1988 (PMID: 2965159). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: What moves potassium between cells and blood: insulin and beta-adrenergic uptake, quantified in human infusion studies; acid-base as the textbooks give it
shelves.question: In humans, how do insulin, beta-adrenergic stimulation and acid-base status determine the distribution of potassium between the intracellular and extracellular compartments?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Aged · Aldosterone · Catecholamines · Epinephrine · Female · Homeostasis · Humans · Hyperkalemia · Insulin · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine · Potassium · Potassium Chloride · Propranolol · Receptors, Adrenergic · Receptors, Adrenergic, beta
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). Only about 2% of body potassium sits extracellularly, so plasma potassium is set less by intake or excretion minute-to-minute than by distribution: insulin and beta-2 adrenergic stimulation drive potassium into cells (via Na/K-ATPase), while acid-base status shifts it across the membrane in exchange for hydrogen ions. The carded human infusion studies quantify the hormonal legs directly. Epinephrine nearly abolished the rise from a standard potassium load (0.1 vs 0.6 mEq/L) and beta-blockade with propranolol exaggerated it (0.9 mEq/L) without any change in urinary excretion or aldosterone (Rosa 1980). Physiological insulin lowered serum potassium by about 0.3 mmol/L in healthy volunteers under clamp conditions (Gastaldelli 2000) and, in fasting dialysis patients, merely doubling plasma insulin within the physiological range completely prevented a 0.58 mmol/L fasting rise — and unmasked epinephrine's potassium-lowering effect (Allon 1993). During exercise, beta-blockade worsened the potassium rise by about 40% (Castellino 1987). The acid-base leg is presented as the textbooks give it — mineral (hyperchloraemic) acidosis shifts potassium out of cells and raises plasma potassium, alkalaemia does the reverse, with organic acidoses behaving less predictably — because no primary human acid-infusion record fetched this session reported the plasma potassium change with usable numbers; it is textbook account, not a carded result. Potassium units: US laboratories report mEq/L, which for potassium is numerically identical to mmol/L. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the insulin and beta-adrenergic determinants; the acid-base determinant is textbook-established and labelled as such.

cards.headline: Rosa 1980: in 9 healthy subjects, epinephrine blunted a potassium load's rise from 0.6 to 0.1 mEq/L and propranolol exaggerated it to 0.9 mEq/L (N = 9, below 10)
cards.summary: Rosa 1980: in 9 healthy subjects, epinephrine blunted a potassium load's rise from 0.6 to 0.1 mEq/L and propranolol exaggerated it to 0.9 mEq/L (N = 9, below 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (potassium load ± propranolol/epinephrine, Rosa 1980) — N = 9
cards.people: 9 healthy subjects given intravenous potassium chloride (0.5 mEq/kg) with and without propranolol; in a separate study the same load was given with a concomitant epinephrine infusion in 5 subjects. N = 9 (and 5) — small classic studies, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires. Potassium is reported in mEq/L, numerically identical to mmol/L for potassium.
cards.result: The potassium infusion alone raised serum potassium by 0.6 ± 0.09 mEq/L (mean ± S.E.M.). Adding propranolol augmented the rise to 0.9 ± 0.05 mEq/L and prolonged the elevation, without decreasing urinary potassium excretion. Concomitant epinephrine markedly blunted the increment to 0.1 ± 0.06 mEq/L while reducing renal potassium excretion. Plasma aldosterone was not altered by any of the procedures, and serum insulin fell only minimally with propranolol and was unaffected by epinephrine — the shifts were distributional, not excretory or aldosterone-mediated.
cards.watchOut: N = 9 and N = 5 in the two parts, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the numbers on the face. The design isolates beta-adrenergic tone cleanly, but the loads and infusions are experimental; everyday potassium excursions are smaller.
cards.source: Rosa RM et al. Adrenergic modulation of extrarenal potassium disposal. The New England journal of medicine. 1980. PMID: 6101508. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gastaldelli 2000: physiological hyperinsulinaemia under euglycaemic clamp lowered serum potassium from 3.76 to 3.44 mmol/L in 35 healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Gastaldelli 2000: physiological hyperinsulinaemia under euglycaemic clamp lowered serum potassium from 3.76 to 3.44 mmol/L in 35 healthy volunteers
cards.type: Human physiology study (euglycaemic insulin clamp, Gastaldelli 2000)
cards.people: 35 healthy volunteers studied at rest and during a euglycaemic insulin clamp (1 mU·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹) with electrocardiographic monitoring; the potassium fall was a measured accompaniment of the clamp. Potassium in mmol/L is numerically identical to mEq/L as reported by US laboratories.
cards.result: Fasting serum potassium of 3.76 ± 0.03 mmol/L declined to 3.44 ± 0.03 mmol/L during insulin infusion — a fall of about 0.3 mmol/L at physiological hyperinsulinaemia with glucose held constant, demonstrating insulin's direct cellular potassium uptake effect in healthy humans. Serum potassium was inversely related to QTc both fasting and during insulin stimulation.
cards.watchOut: The study's primary question was ventricular repolarisation, not potassium; the potassium values are nonetheless direct clamp measurements in the largest healthy-volunteer group carded here. The fall is modest — insulin redistributes potassium, it does not remove it from the body.
cards.source: Gastaldelli A et al. Insulin prolongs the QTc interval in humans. American journal of physiology. Regulatory, integrative and comparative physiology. 2000. PMID: 11080065. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
