cards.headline: Allon 1993: in 10 fasting dialysis patients, doubling plasma insulin within the physiological range completely prevented a 0.58 mmol/L potassium rise — and switched on epinephrine's effect
cards.summary: Allon 1993: in 10 fasting dialysis patients, doubling plasma insulin within the physiological range completely prevented a 0.58 mmol/L potassium rise — and switched on epinephrine's effect
cards.type: Human physiology study (insulin ± epinephrine in fasting dialysis patients, Allon 1993)
cards.people: 10 stable, nondiabetic maintenance haemodialysis patients studied prospectively after an 18-hour fast, receiving epinephrine 0.01 microgram/kg/min with and without prior propranolol beta-blockade, and restudied under identical protocols during a continuous insulin-plus-dextrose infusion. Potassium in mmol/L, numerically identical to mEq/L.
cards.result: Plasma potassium rose by 0.58 ± 0.13 mmol/L after 18 hours of fasting (P = 0.002). Insulin with dextrose at a dose that doubled plasma insulin within the physiological range (9.3 ± 1.1 to 20.2 ± 2.3 mU/L, P < 0.002) completely prevented the rise (+0.06 ± 0.13 mmol/L, P = 0.64). Epinephrine alone did not significantly change potassium during fasting (+0.05 ± 0.09 mmol/L), but lowered it significantly (−0.16 ± 0.04 mmol/L, P = 0.003) when subjects were receiving insulin with glucose — insulin and beta-adrenergic stimulation act cooperatively on extrarenal disposal.
cards.watchOut: These were patients without kidney function, in whom extrarenal disposal carries the whole load — the cleanest possible isolation of the distribution mechanism, but the absolute sizes should not be transplanted unchanged to people with normal kidneys, who also excrete.
cards.source: Allon M et al. Effect of insulin-plus-glucose infusion with or without epinephrine on fasting hyperkalemia. Kidney international. 1993. PMID: 8433561. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Castellino 1987: during exercise, beta-blockade worsened the plasma potassium rise by about 40% in control subjects
cards.summary: Castellino 1987: during exercise, beta-blockade worsened the plasma potassium rise by about 40% in control subjects
cards.type: Human physiology study (adrenergic blockade during exercise, Castellino 1987)
cards.people: Control (non-diabetic) and insulin-dependent diabetic subjects studied during moderate exercise (40% of VO2max) alone, with intravenous propranolol, and with intravenous phentolamine, plus a chronic 5-day beta-blockade protocol (propranolol versus metoprolol); the record does not print the group sizes (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Exercise alone raised plasma potassium by 0.31 ± 0.06 mEq/L in both groups, and acute propranolol exacerbated this hyperkalaemic response. With chronic blockade in the non-diabetic group, both propranolol and metoprolol were associated with a 40% greater increase in potassium than exercise alone. In no study could the altered potassium handling be explained by a change in urinary potassium excretion — again a distribution effect.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record. Exercise hyperkalaemia is normally self-limited by the same adrenergic uptake mechanisms this study blocked; the diabetic group's divergent alpha-blockade behaviour is a disease-specific detail, not part of the healthy-physiology answer.
cards.source: Castellino P et al. Adrenergic modulation of potassium metabolism during exercise in normal and diabetic humans. The American journal of physiology. 1987. PMID: 3544863. cards.headline: Synthesis: insulin and beta-2 adrenergic tone set the extracellular potassium minute to minute; acid-base shifts it as the textbooks describe
cards.summary: Synthesis: insulin and beta-2 adrenergic tone set the extracellular potassium minute to minute; acid-base shifts it as the textbooks describe
cards.people: The carded evidence: a potassium-load study in 9 healthy subjects (Rosa 1980, N on the face), a 35-volunteer insulin clamp (Gastaldelli 2000), a 10-patient fasting/insulin/epinephrine study (Allon 1993), and an exercise-blockade study (Castellino 1987, N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Across designs, the same levers move plasma potassium without any change in excretion: epinephrine cut a load's rise from 0.6 to 0.1 mEq/L while propranolol raised it to 0.9 mEq/L; physiological insulin lowered potassium by about 0.3 mmol/L in health and abolished a 0.58 mmol/L fasting rise in dialysis patients; beta-blockade added about 40% to the exercise potassium rise. The third determinant in the question — acid-base status — is carried in the balance as the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep textbook account (mineral acidosis shifts potassium out of cells; alkalaemia shifts it in), because no primary human acid-infusion record fetched this session reported usable plasma-potassium numbers; no acid-base figure is carded. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (hormonal legs carded; acid-base leg textbook-labelled).
cards.watchOut: Distribution shifts borrow potassium from the intracellular reservoir — they change the plasma number within minutes but not total body potassium, which is why insulin or beta-agonist treatment of hyperkalaemia is always temporary without an excretory or dialytic exit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rosa RM et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1980 (PMID: 6101508); Gastaldelli A et al. American journal of physiology. Regulatory, integrative and comparative physiology. 2000 (PMID: 11080065); Allon M et al. Kidney international. 1993 (PMID: 8433561); Castellino P et al. The American journal of physiology. 1987 (PMID: 3544863). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Vasopressin as the urine-concentration dial: osmotic threshold and sensitivity, water-load excretion, and the graded desmopressin response in humans
shelves.question: In humans, how does vasopressin (ADH) determine urine concentration and free water clearance across states of water balance?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Body Water · Double-Blind Method · Fluoxetine · Humans · Male · Osmolar Concentration · Sodium · Urine · Vasopressins · Water-Electrolyte Balance
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe a steep osmotic control system: plasma vasopressin is essentially off below an osmotic threshold near 280–287 mosmol/kg, rises linearly with osmolality above it (roughly 0.3–0.5 pmol/L per mosmol/kg in the human studies carded here), and at the kidney converts that signal into urine concentration — maximal dilution with free water excretion when vasopressin is absent, maximal concentration when it is high. The carded human studies measure the whole loop. A 20 ml/kg water load suppressed vasopressin to about 0.5 pmol/L and healthy men excreted 95% of the load within 4 hours; hypertonic saline gave a vasopressin sensitivity of 0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg with a threshold of 287 mosmol/kg (Faull 1991). Graded intravenous desmopressin in 72 overhydrated healthy men raised urine osmolality dose-dependently with plasma level, with a modelled pharmacodynamic delay of about 4 hours (Juul 2013). Water loading and hypertonic saline produced the expected reciprocal changes in vasopressin, urine osmolality and free water clearance across the menstrual cycle, with osmotic thresholds shifting 5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal phase (Vokes 1988). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: vasopressin, set by plasma osmolality against a threshold, determines urine concentration and free water clearance across water balance states.

cards.headline: Faull 1991: a 20 ml/kg water load suppressed plasma vasopressin to 0.5 pmol/L and healthy men excreted 95% of the load in 4 hours; hypertonic saline set vasopressin sensitivity at 0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg, threshold 287 mosmol/kg
cards.summary: Faull 1991: a 20 ml/kg water load suppressed plasma vasopressin to 0.5 pmol/L and healthy men excreted 95% of the load in 4 hours; hypertonic saline set vasopressin sensitivity at 0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg, threshold 287 mosmol/kg
cards.type: Human physiology study (water load and hypertonic saline osmoregulation testing, Faull 1991)
cards.people: Normal healthy male volunteers in two placebo-controlled crossover studies of fluoxetine pretreatment (the drug showed no effect, so the placebo arms give clean physiology): Study 1, an oral water load of 20 ml/kg in 9 men; Study 2, intravenous 5% saline (855 mmol/L) at 0.06 ml/kg/min for 120 minutes in 10 men, with serial plasma osmolality, sodium, vasopressin, urine osmolality, urine volume and calculated free water clearance.
cards.result: After the water load, subjects excreted 95% of the load within 4 hours on placebo (99% on fluoxetine, P = 0.407), plasma osmolality fell to a nadir of 285.9 ± 1.4 mosmol/kg, and plasma vasopressin suppressed to a minimum of 0.5 ± 0.1 pmol/L, with maximal urine dilution and positive free water clearance. During hypertonic saline, the sensitivity of vasopressin release to rising plasma osmolality was 0.33 ± 0.06 pmol/L per mosmol/kg (placebo) and the theoretical osmotic threshold for release was 287.0 ± 1.21 mosmol/kg; fluoxetine changed neither (P = 0.347 and P = 0.700).
cards.watchOut: The study was designed to test a serotonin agonist, which proved inert for this system — the carded numbers are the placebo-condition physiology. Groups of 9 and 10 are small, and the threshold/sensitivity figures are regression constructs from serial sampling, standard for this literature.
cards.source: Faull CM et al. The effect of a highly specific serotonin agonist on osmoregulated vasopressin secretion in healthy man. Clinical endocrinology. 1991. PMID: 1814657. cards.headline: Juul 2013: graded desmopressin infusions in 72 overhydrated healthy men raised urine osmolality dose-dependently with plasma desmopressin, with an estimated 4-hour pharmacodynamic delay
cards.summary: Juul 2013: graded desmopressin infusions in 72 overhydrated healthy men raised urine osmolality dose-dependently with plasma desmopressin, with an estimated 4-hour pharmacodynamic delay
cards.type: Randomised controlled dose-response study (intravenous desmopressin, Juul 2013)
cards.people: 72 healthy, overhydrated, nonsmoking men aged 18–55 in an investigator-blind randomised parallel-group study: five dose groups and one placebo group of 12 each, infused intravenously over 2 hours with placebo or 30, 60, 125, 250 or 500 ng desmopressin, with plasma desmopressin and urine osmolality measured serially.
cards.result: Plasma desmopressin and urine osmolality rose by variable amounts during the infusions of 60, 125, 250 and 500 ng desmopressin. Plotting mean urine osmolality against concurrent mean plasma desmopressin showed a temporal delay between the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic responses in all dose groups; indirect-response modelling, assuming a constant desmopressin concentration of 4 ng/ml, estimated that delay at about 4 hours. The study demonstrates the graded vasopressin-to-urine-concentration dose-response in man and quantifies its lag.
cards.watchOut: Desmopressin is a V2-selective synthetic analogue given to overhydrated volunteers — ideal for isolating the renal concentrating response, but the absolute urine osmolality values of an overhydrated starting state should not be quoted as maximal concentrating capacity, which the textbooks place far higher (textbook account, not a carded result).
cards.source: Juul KV et al. Temporal delays and individual variation in antidiuretic response to desmopressin. American journal of physiology. Renal physiology. 2013. PMID: 23136002. cards.headline: Vokes 1988: water loading and hypertonic saline moved vasopressin, urine osmolality and free water clearance reciprocally in healthy women — with osmotic thresholds 5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal phase
cards.summary: Vokes 1988: water loading and hypertonic saline moved vasopressin, urine osmolality and free water clearance reciprocally in healthy women — with osmotic thresholds 5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal phase
cards.type: Human physiology study (osmoregulation across the menstrual cycle, Vokes 1988) — detailed subgroup N = 5
cards.people: 15 healthy women: 10 studied repetitively across two consecutive menstrual cycles for basal osmoregulation, and 5 studied in follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases with water loading and hypertonic saline infusion, measuring thirst, plasma vasopressin, urine osmolality, and osmolal and free water clearance. The detailed-testing subgroup is N = 5 — printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Basal plasma osmolality, sodium and urea fell by 4 mosmol/kg, 2 mEq/L and 0.5 mM respectively from follicular to luteal phase (all P < 0.02), while plasma vasopressin itself did not change. Responses of thirst, plasma vasopressin, urine osmolality and free water clearance to water loading and hypertonic saline were normal and similar across phases, but the plasma osmolality at which vasopressin and urine osmolality were maximally suppressed, and the calculated osmotic thresholds for thirst and vasopressin release, were 5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal than the follicular phase — the set-point itself is a regulated variable.
cards.watchOut: The detailed water-load/saline subgroup is N = 5, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. The study's headline is the threshold shift; the reciprocal vasopressin–urine responses it documents are the standard physiology the other cards quantify.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one hormone, one threshold — vasopressin level reads plasma osmolality and writes urine concentration and free water clearance
cards.summary: Synthesis: one hormone, one threshold — vasopressin level reads plasma osmolality and writes urine concentration and free water clearance
cards.people: The carded evidence: water-load and hypertonic-saline testing in 9–10 healthy men (Faull 1991), a 72-man graded desmopressin dose-response (Juul 2013), and water-balance testing in 15 healthy women with a 5-woman detailed subgroup (Vokes 1988, N on the face).
cards.result: Below a threshold of about 287 mosmol/kg, vasopressin suppresses to ~0.5 pmol/L and a 20 ml/kg water load is 95% excreted in 4 hours as dilute urine with positive free water clearance; above threshold, vasopressin rises at about 0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg, and graded vasopressin-analogue levels produce graded urine osmolality rises (with a ~4-hour effect lag). The set-point itself shifts (5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal phase). That is the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep account measured end-to-end in humans: osmolality determines vasopressin, and vasopressin determines urine concentration and free water clearance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Non-osmotic vasopressin release (severe volume depletion, nausea, pain) can override the osmotic logic — a textbook point; no carded study here quantifies it, and none is claimed to.
cards.source: Synthesis of Faull CM et al. Clinical endocrinology. 1991 (PMID: 1814657); Juul KV et al. American journal of physiology. Renal physiology. 2013 (PMID: 23136002); Vokes TJ et al. The American journal of physiology. 1988 (PMID: 3354712). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Changing the catheter before antibiotics for catheter-associated urinary infection: SPLIT — one small trial favours exchange, the bundled second trial favours retention on recurrence
shelves.question: In adults with an indwelling urinary catheter and urinary infection, does changing the catheter before starting antibiotics improve cure versus leaving it in place?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Infective Agents · Catheters, Indwelling · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Urinary Tract Infections
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised studies point in opposite directions, and the 2024 systematic review of the whole literature says so explicitly. Raz 2000, the small trial guidelines rest on, randomised 54 elderly nursing-home residents with a chronic indwelling catheter and symptomatic urinary infection to catheter replacement before antibiotics or no replacement: clinical status at 72 hours had improved in 25 versus 11 patients (P < 0.001) and symptomatic relapse 28 days after therapy was lower with replacement (3 versus 11, P = 0.015). Darouiche 2014 randomised 61 patients with spinal cord injury and catheter-associated urinary infection to a 5-day antibiotic course after catheter exchange or a 10-day course with the catheter retained: clinical cure was 100% in both groups, but recurrence was higher in the exchange group — a comparison in which the exchange arm also got the shorter antibiotic course, so route and duration are bundled. The systematic review (Westgeest 2024) found only four relevant studies in total (two randomised, two observational): one randomised trial favoured replacement, the other favoured retention on recurrence, and the observational studies were inconclusive; a retrospective VRE urinary-infection cohort (Shah 2018) found cure of 90.5% with catheter exchange or removal versus 87.5% with retention in its catheter subgroup. PROPOSED SPLIT: replacement before antibiotics improved early response and relapse in the one small direct trial, but the only other randomised comparison — confounded by antibiotic duration — favoured retention on recurrence, and the total evidence base is four studies.

cards.headline: Raz 2000 randomised trial: replacing the catheter before antibiotics improved clinical status at 72 hours (25 versus 11 patients) and cut symptomatic relapse (3 versus 11)
cards.summary: Raz 2000 randomised trial: replacing the catheter before antibiotics improved clinical status at 72 hours (25 versus 11 patients) and cut symptomatic relapse (3 versus 11)
cards.people: 54 elderly nursing-home residents (21 male, 33 female; mean age 72.6 years) at two long-term care facilities, each with a chronic indwelling catheter and a clinical diagnosis of symptomatic urinary tract infection, randomised prospectively and open-label to indwelling catheter replacement before initiating antimicrobial therapy or no replacement; urine and blood cultures were taken before therapy began.
cards.result: Catheter replacement was associated with improved clinical status 72 hours after initiation of therapy in 25 versus 11 patients (P < 0.001), a shorter time to becoming afebrile, and a lower rate of symptomatic clinical relapse 28 days after therapy (3 versus 11 patients, P = 0.015). Polymicrobial bacteriuria decreased significantly more with replacement at 3 days after therapy began (24 versus 8 patients, P = 0.002), and at 7 days (18 versus 9, P = 0.01) and 28 days (13 versus 5, P = 0.02) after therapy was discontinued. The authors conclude clinical and bacteriological outcomes are improved when long-term indwelling catheters are replaced before initiating antimicrobial therapy.
cards.watchOut: A single small open-label trial in elderly nursing-home residents with chronic catheters — 54 patients — is the study the guideline recommendation for replacement largely rests on, as the 2024 systematic review on this shelf notes; its population is chronic-catheter residents, not every hospital patient with a catheter.
cards.source: Raz R et al. Chronic indwelling catheter replacement before antimicrobial therapy for symptomatic urinary tract infection. The Journal of urology. 2000. PMID: 10992375. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Darouiche 2014 randomised trial: 5 days of antibiotics after catheter exchange versus 10 days with the catheter retained — clinical cure 100% both ways, but recurrence was higher after exchange
cards.summary: Darouiche 2014 randomised trial: 5 days of antibiotics after catheter exchange versus 10 days with the catheter retained — clinical cure 100% both ways, but recurrence was higher after exchange
cards.people: 61 patients with spinal cord injury who had catheter-associated urinary tract infection, randomised to a 5-day regimen of antibiotics after catheter exchange (experimental group) or a 10-day regimen of antibiotics with catheter retention (control group); 6 patients were excluded because of bacteremia or absence of urinary symptoms. The prespecified non-inferiority margin was 10% and the primary endpoint was clinical cure at end of therapy.
cards.result: All patients (100%) achieved clinical cure at the end of therapy in both groups, meeting the primary non-inferiority criterion. Microbiologic response was 82.1% in the exchange group versus 88.9% in the retention group and resolution of pyuria 89.3% versus 88.9% — non-inferiority criteria were not met for these secondary outcomes. Patients in the exchange (shorter-course) group had higher rates of catheter-associated urinary infection recurrence than the retention group; rates of new infection, diarrhea and Clostridium difficile colitis were similar.
cards.watchOut: Exchange is bundled with antibiotic duration in this trial — exchange came with 5 days, retention with 10 days — so its higher recurrence in the exchange arm may be a duration effect, not a catheter effect; it cannot be read as a clean test of changing the catheter.
cards.source: Darouiche RO et al. Short versus long course of antibiotics for catheter-associated urinary tract infections in patients with spinal cord injury: a randomized controlled noninferiority trial. Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation. 2014. PMID: 24035770. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shah 2018 cohort: in catheterised patients with VRE urinary infection, cure was 90.5% with catheter exchange or removal versus 87.5% with retention — a small, unadjusted subgroup
cards.summary: Shah 2018 cohort: in catheterised patients with VRE urinary infection, cure was 90.5% with catheter exchange or removal versus 87.5% with retention — a small, unadjusted subgroup
cards.people: Retrospective single-centre cohort of 84 hospitalised adults with complicated urinary tract infection caused by ampicillin- and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp treated with ampicillin (2007–2015); the catheter comparison covers the 45 patients with indwelling urinary catheters, of whom 21 had catheter exchange or removal and 24 had catheter retention.
cards.result: Overall clinical cure in the cohort was 88.1% (74 of 84). In patients with indwelling urinary catheters, cure rates were similar with catheter exchange or removal (90.5%, 19 of 21) versus catheter retention (87.5%, 21 of 24). Immunocompromised patients and those with an underlying urinary tract abnormality had significantly lower cure rates; catheter management did not emerge as a predictor of failure.
cards.watchOut: A small retrospective subgroup (45 patients) inside a single-organism, single-drug cohort, with exchange and removal combined and no adjustment; it is supportive context, not a test of the exchange policy.
cards.source: Shah KJ et al. Ampicillin for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections caused by vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp (VRE): a single-center university hospital experience. International journal of antimicrobial agents. 2018. PMID: 28666756. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Westgeest 2024 systematic review: only four studies exist — one randomised trial favoured replacement, the other favoured retention on recurrence, and the observational studies were inconclusive
cards.summary: Westgeest 2024 systematic review: only four studies exist — one randomised trial favoured replacement, the other favoured retention on recurrence, and the observational studies were inconclusive
cards.people: Systematic review (searched to October 2023) of studies investigating the effect of catheter replacement in catheter-associated urinary tract infection on clinical outcomes and recurrence, irrespective of catheter type or setting; of 257 identified studies, four were relevant and included — two randomised controlled trials and two observational studies.
cards.result: One randomised trial showed higher rates of clinical recovery and lower recurrence rates in the replacement group, while the other randomised trial favoured retention, with a lower recurrence rate in the retention group — although that group received longer antimicrobial treatment. The two observational studies were inconclusive. The reviewers conclude that current guidelines rely heavily on recommendations from a single study, that adherence to replacement guidance is low in practice, and that a randomised trial is essential.
cards.watchOut: The review's four included studies are the same small literature carded here (including Raz and Darouiche), so it frames the split rather than adding independent patients; a multicentre non-inferiority trial of retention versus replacement (REPLACE, NCT06936631) is now registered and recruiting, per its 2026 protocol report.
cards.source: Westgeest AC et al. Catheter replacement in catheter-associated urinary tract infection: current state of evidence. European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology. 2024. PMID: 38916643. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — replacement helped in the one small direct trial; the bundled second trial and the review leave the question genuinely open
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — replacement helped in the one small direct trial; the bundled second trial and the review leave the question genuinely open
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small direct randomised trial of replacement before antibiotics (Raz, 54 nursing-home residents), one randomised trial bundling exchange with a shorter antibiotic course (Darouiche, 61 patients with spinal cord injury), one retrospective catheter subgroup (Shah, 45 catheterised patients), and one systematic review of all four existing studies (Westgeest).
cards.result: Replacement before antibiotics was associated with faster clinical improvement (25 versus 11 patients improved at 72 hours) and less symptomatic relapse (3 versus 11) in Raz; clinical cure was 100% in both arms of Darouiche, with higher recurrence in the exchange-plus-shorter-course arm; and cure differed little by catheter management in Shah (90.5% versus 87.5%). PROPOSED SPLIT: changing the catheter before antibiotics may improve early response, as one small trial found, but the total evidence is four studies pointing in different directions — the honest answer is that the benefit is unproven, not established.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two randomised trials into one average: they asked different bundled questions (replacement alone versus replacement plus shorter antibiotics) in different populations, and their disagreement is the finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raz R et al. The Journal of urology. 2000 (PMID: 10992375); Darouiche RO et al. Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation. 2014 (PMID: 24035770); Shah KJ et al. International journal of antimicrobial agents. 2018 (PMID: 28666756); Westgeest AC et al. European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases. 2024 (PMID: 38916643).

shelves.title: Renal functional reserve: a protein meal or amino-acid load raises GFR by roughly a quarter to a third in healthy kidneys — peaking at about 2.5 hours — and the reserve shrinks as nephrons are lost
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much does glomerular filtration rate rise after a protein meal or amino-acid load (renal functional reserve), and for how long?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Dietary Proteins/pharmacology · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Kidney Diseases/diagnosis,metabolism · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Healthy kidneys do not filter at maximum at rest: an oral protein load or intravenous amino-acid infusion raises glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by roughly 20–35% — Bosch's protein-loading test put mean filtration capacity at 157 mL/min against a reserve of 34 mL/min, Castellino's gluconeogenic amino-acid infusion raised GFR 16% within a 3-hour infusion, and Barai's amino-acid-stimulated clearance study measured a mean reserve of 23.4% in healthy volunteers. Bosch's original 1983 description (cited here in prose; its record is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded) found GFR maximal about 2.5 hours after the load. The reserve is a property of remaining nephrons: it falls steadily with chronic kidney disease stage and is blunted or absent when nephron number is reduced. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall (afferent arteriolar dilatation, raised glomerular pressure and renal plasma flow), named as textbook framing, not as evidence. Live shelf #1979 asks a different question — whether protein RESTRICTION slows GFR decline in chronic kidney disease (the MDRD question) — and is cross-pointed, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Bosch 1984 protein-loading test: in normal persons filtration capacity averaged 157 mL/min and renal reserve 34 mL/min
cards.summary: Bosch 1984 protein-loading test: in normal persons filtration capacity averaged 157 mL/min and renal reserve 34 mL/min
cards.type: Human physiological study (oral protein load with pre/post GFR measurement), Am J Med 1984
cards.people: Normal persons and patients with renal disease given an oral protein load, with GFR measured before (baseline) and after (test) loading. The record does not print a participant number for the normal group in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In normal persons, filtration capacity (test GFR after protein loading) averaged 157 ± 13 mL/min and renal reserve (test minus baseline GFR) was 34 mL/min — about a 28% rise over the implied baseline of ~123 mL/min. The test GFR was reproducible and independent of habitual protein intake, whereas baseline GFR was significantly influenced by diet. Patients with renal disease had a reduced reserve and/or a diminished filtration capacity, and the fall in filtration capacity tracked organ damage.
cards.watchOut: Creatinine-based and clearance methods of the era; the abstract does not separate the healthy-volunteer N from the patient N, so no per-group N is claimed. The companion 1983 Bosch description is not carded here (see balance).

cards.headline: Castellino 1990: gluconeogenic amino acids raised GFR 16% and renal plasma flow 28% in 7 healthy volunteers — alanine alone and branched-chain amino acids did not
cards.summary: Castellino 1990: gluconeogenic amino acids raised GFR 16% and renal plasma flow 28% in 7 healthy volunteers — alanine alone and branched-chain amino acids did not
cards.type: Human physiological study (controlled amino-acid infusions with clearance measurement), Am J Physiol 1990
cards.people: Seven healthy young volunteers, each receiving four 3-hour intravenous infusions in separate studies: mixed gluconeogenic amino acids (arginine, glycine, proline, cysteine, methionine, serine), alanine alone, branched-chain amino acids, and saline. N = 7 — a small classic physiology study, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: During gluconeogenic amino-acid infusion, total plasma amino acids rose 40–60% above baseline, GFR rose 16% (from 98 ± 6 to 114 ± 8 mL/min/1.73 m², P < 0.01) and renal plasma flow rose 28% (from 496 ± 47 to 638 ± 70 mL/min/1.73 m², P < 0.01), with plasma glucagon up 30%. Alanine alone and branched-chain amino acids produced only slight, non-significant rises, and saline changed nothing — the reserve response depends on the amino-acid mixture, not on any single amino acid.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 and all male; the 16% rise is smaller than the oral-load reserve in the Bosch card, plausibly because a 3-hour infusion of one amino-acid class is a weaker stimulus than a full protein meal.
cards.source: Castellino P et al. Effect of specific amino acid groups on renal hemodynamics in humans. Am J Physiol. 1990. PMID: 2330990. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: ter Wee 1986: amino-acid infusion raised GFR in 9 healthy volunteers, dopamine added further, and the combination gave the highest filtration — reserve was hardly present once GFR fell below 90
cards.summary: ter Wee 1986: amino-acid infusion raised GFR in 9 healthy volunteers, dopamine added further, and the combination gave the highest filtration — reserve was hardly present once GFR fell below 90
cards.type: Human physiological study (amino-acid and dopamine infusions with clearance measurement), Kidney Int 1986
cards.people: Healthy volunteers (N = 9) and patients with varying degrees of renal insufficiency (N = 36), given low-dose dopamine and/or amino acids intravenously during simultaneous GFR and effective renal plasma flow measurement. The healthy-volunteer N = 9 is printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Dopamine raised GFR and lowered filtration fraction; amino acids raised GFR with filtration fraction unchanged or slightly increased; the combined infusion produced the highest GFR values of all — the two stimuli are additive. A reserve in filtration capacity was not or hardly present in patients with moderate (GFR 30–90 mL/min/1.73 m²) to severe (GFR < 30) renal insufficiency. The authors read dopamine as lowering total renal vascular resistance and amino acids as mainly reducing afferent arteriolar tone.
cards.watchOut: Mixed healthy and renal-insufficiency cohort; the healthy-volunteer leg is small (N = 9). Dopamine co-infusion is a pharmacological amplifier, not part of the normal meal response.
cards.source: ter Wee PM et al. Renal hemodynamics during separate and combined infusion of amino acids and dopamine. Kidney Int. 1986. PMID: 3712970. cards.headline: Barai 2010: amino-acid-stimulated reserve averaged 23.4% in 25 healthy volunteers and fell relentlessly with CKD stage — 19.1%, 15.4%, 8.9% and 6.7% across stages 1–4
cards.summary: Barai 2010: amino-acid-stimulated reserve averaged 23.4% in 25 healthy volunteers and fell relentlessly with CKD stage — 19.1%, 15.4%, 8.9% and 6.7% across stages 1–4
cards.type: Human physiological study (radionuclide clearance, amino-acid stimulation), Nephrology 2010
cards.people: Twenty-five healthy volunteers and 100 patients at various stages of chronic kidney disease; baseline and amino-acid-stimulated GFR measured by plasma clearance of technetium-99m DTPA.
cards.result: Mean renal reserve was 23.4% in healthy controls, then 19.08% in CKD stage 1, 15.4% in stage 2, 8.9% in stage 3 and 6.7% in stage 4. Reserve could be completely exhausted even with a normal or minimally reduced baseline GFR, and some reserve persisted down to a GFR of 15 mL/min — the modern clearance-based confirmation, a generation later, of the Bosch-era reserve estimate of roughly a quarter to a third in health.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre case-control design; stimulated GFR by plasma DTPA clearance is an estimate of true GFR, and reserve percentages are relative to each group's own baseline, which itself falls with CKD stage.
cards.source: Barai S et al. Functional renal reserve capacity in different stages of chronic kidney disease. Nephrology (Carlton). 2010. PMID: 20470306. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the healthy kidney holds roughly a quarter to a third of its filtration in reserve, recruitable within hours by protein — and losing that reserve is an early sign of nephron loss
cards.summary: Synthesis: the healthy kidney holds roughly a quarter to a third of its filtration in reserve, recruitable within hours by protein — and losing that reserve is an early sign of nephron loss
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Bosch 1984; Castellino 1990; ter Wee 1986; Barai 2010), framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall as textbook accounts.
cards.result: Across four decades and three stimulus types (oral protein, mixed amino-acid infusion, amino acids plus dopamine), the healthy response is concordant: GFR rises about 16–34% — 34 mL/min of reserve against a 157 mL/min filtration capacity (Bosch), 23.4% mean reserve in modern clearance testing (Barai) — beginning within the infusion or meal and, in the original 1983 description cited in prose in the balance, maximal at about 2.5 hours after an oral load. The textbook mechanism (Boron & Boulpaep; Guyton & Hall) is afferent arteriolar dilatation with raised renal plasma flow and glomerular pressure, glucagon- and prostaglandin-mediated; Castellino's amino-acid specificity and ter Wee's additivity with dopamine fit that account. The reserve is not a treatment target: it is a diagnostic window — its loss precedes the fall in baseline GFR as nephrons are lost. This shelf is the normal-physiology question; protein restriction as therapy in established kidney disease is live shelf #1979.
cards.watchOut: Stimuli, GFR methods (creatinine clearance, inulin-era clearances, DTPA plasma clearance) and populations differ across cards, so the 16–34% range is a range across methods, not measurement error around one protocol. Two carded studies are small classic physiology cohorts (N = 7 and N = 9 healthy volunteers), labelled on their faces.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bosch JP et al., Am J Med 1984 (PMID: 6496542); Castellino P et al., Am J Physiol 1990 (PMID: 2330990); ter Wee PM et al., Kidney Int 1986 (PMID: 3712970); Barai S et al., Nephrology 2010 (PMID: 20470306). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Excreting a water load (physiology): a standard 20 mL/kg drink is essentially fully excreted by about 2 hours in young healthy adults, with peak free-water clearance around 8–10 mL/min — slower and lower-peaked in healthy elderly men
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how quickly is a standard water load excreted, and what does the free-water clearance time course look like?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/physiology · Arginine Vasopressin/blood · Blood Pressure · *Diuresis · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osmolar Concentration · Sodium/blood · Thirst · Water Deprivation/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): drinking water lowers plasma osmolality, switches vasopressin off, and the kidney answers with a water diuresis — urine flow rises within tens of minutes, peaks, and the load is cleared over a few hours, the textbooks' account, which the carded human studies quantify. In young healthy adults a standard 20 mL/kg oral load was 100.7% excreted by 2 hours, with peak free-water clearance of 8.4 mL/min in water-replete and 9.5 mL/min in water-deprived young men (Crowe 1987). During established water diuresis, urine flow ran at about 12–14 mL/min with free-water clearance of 9.7 mL/min and urine osmolality of 71 mosmol/kg — and even a vasopressin infusion of 1 pg/min/kg, too small to raise plasma levels measurably, cut free-water clearance in half, showing how steeply the time course is gated by vasopressin (Andersen 1990). A 4-hour load-and-replace protocol in 6 men gives the outer time frame, and its indomethacin arm shows prostaglandin inhibition can blunt the diuresis (Vierhapper 1984). Healthy elderly men excreted only 41% by 2 hours with a delayed, lower peak (free-water clearance 5.7 mL/min), a difference that disappeared after adjustment for creatinine clearance (Crowe 1987). FLAG (precedent b): the vasopressin-threshold side of this same physiology — including a 20 mL/kg load study reporting 95% excretion within 4 hours and menstrual-cycle water-loading data — is homed at pack #6079; those reports are gated, are cross-pointed here in prose only, and appear in no card source line. This pack's narrower question is the excretion time course itself, built on three free reports. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Crowe 1987: young men excreted 100.7% of a 20 mL/kg water load by 2 hours (peak free-water clearance 8.4 mL/min); healthy elderly men managed only 41% with a delayed peak of 5.7 mL/min
cards.summary: Crowe 1987: young men excreted 100.7% of a 20 mL/kg water load by 2 hours (peak free-water clearance 8.4 mL/min); healthy elderly men managed only 41% with a delayed peak of 5.7 mL/min
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (standard oral water load, young versus elderly)
cards.people: Water-replete healthy elderly men (n = 6) and two young healthy volunteer control groups (water-replete and water-deprived; group sizes N not documented in the record's abstract), each given a standard oral water load of 20 mL/kg with hourly sampling of urine and plasma vasopressin.
cards.result: After 2 hours the elderly group had excreted 41 ± 2.4% of the load, versus 100.7 ± 8.8% in water-replete young men and 70 ± 3.8% in water-deprived young men (p < 0.01). Peak diuresis and peak free-water clearance were delayed and lower in the elderly (7.01 ± 0.48 mL/kg and 5.7 ± 0.48 mL/min) than in the young groups (peak diuresis 10.86 ± 0.56 and 10.2 ± 0.64 mL/kg; peak free-water clearance 8.4 ± 0.72 and 9.5 ± 0.88 mL/min; p < 0.01), but the differences disappeared after adjustment for reduced creatinine clearance in the elderly. Plasma vasopressin fell similarly in all groups after the load.
cards.watchOut: Very small elderly group (n = 6) and the young groups' sizes are not stated in the record's abstract (printed here as N not documented for those groups); hourly sampling gives the time course at 1-hour resolution, and the elderly slowing is a filtration-rate effect, not a vasopressin effect.
cards.source: Crowe MJ et al. Altered water excretion in healthy elderly men. Age Ageing. 1987. PMID: 3687569. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Andersen 1990: during established water diuresis urine flow ran at 12–14 mL/min with free-water clearance of 9.7 mL/min — and a barely measurable vasopressin infusion halved it
cards.summary: Andersen 1990: during established water diuresis urine flow ran at 12–14 mL/min with free-water clearance of 9.7 mL/min — and a barely measurable vasopressin infusion halved it
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (water diuresis with graded vasopressin infusion)
cards.people: Healthy volunteers undergoing water diuresis induced by an oral water load of 20 mL/kg body weight, given 120-minute infusions of arginine vasopressin at 1, 5 and 25 pg/min/kg; N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Before infusion, urine flow was 12.2 ± 1.7 mL/min with free-water clearance of 9.7 ± 1.5 mL/min and urine osmolality of 71 ± 6 mosmol/kg. Vasopressin at 1 pg/min/kg decreased urine flow to 7.4 ± 1.5 mL/min and free-water clearance to 4.8 ± 1.4 mL/min and raised urine osmolality to 115 ± 15 mosmol/kg; at 5 pg/min/kg urine flow fell to 0.9 ± 0.3 mL/min with maximal urine osmolality of 621 ± 95 mosmol/kg, and at 25 pg/min/kg 869 ± 38 mosmol/kg. Responses developed gradually, stabilised within the second hour, and the two lower infusion rates had no effect for at least 20 minutes. The authors conclude the kidney responds to vasopressin secretion-rate changes of under 1 pg/min/kg, with maximal change after 1–2 hours.
cards.watchOut: An infusion study layered on a water load, carded for what it measures about the diuresis itself — its height (flow ~12–14 mL/min, free-water clearance ~10 mL/min) and its steep vasopressin gating; the volunteer number is not stated in the record's abstract (N not documented).
cards.source: Andersen LJ et al. Antidiuretic effect of subnormal levels of arginine vasopressin in normal humans. Am J Physiol. 1990. PMID: 2375429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vierhapper 1984: a 20 mL/kg load with hourly replacement over 4 hours frames the full excretion window — and indomethacin, unlike aspirin, blunted the diuresis and free-water clearance
cards.summary: Vierhapper 1984: a 20 mL/kg load with hourly replacement over 4 hours frames the full excretion window — and indomethacin, unlike aspirin, blunted the diuresis and free-water clearance
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (water-load diuresis with prostaglandin inhibition)
cards.people: 6 healthy male volunteers studied after overnight deprivation with an oral water load of 20 mL/kg and hourly urine volumes replaced by mouth for 4 hours, after 3 days of aspirin (3 g/day) or indomethacin (150 mg/day); N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Both drugs comparably suppressed prostaglandin E2 excretion (p < 0.05 to < 0.001), but only indomethacin also reduced diuresis, free-water clearance and sodium excretion (p < 0.05); creatinine excretion was unchanged by either drug. The authors conclude a mechanism other than cyclo-oxygenase inhibition is involved in the drugs' differing effects on human diuresis. The protocol itself — load, then hourly replacement for 4 hours — is the classic design for following a water load to complete excretion.
cards.watchOut: Very small study (N = 6) designed around drug effects; its abstract reports the drug contrast rather than hour-by-hour control excretion values, so the hour-by-hour time course on this shelf rests mainly on Crowe 1987 and Andersen 1990.
cards.source: Vierhapper H et al. Effect of acetylsalicylic acid and of indomethacin on diuresis in man: the role of cyclo-oxygenase inhibition. Clin Sci (Lond). 1984. PMID: 6435937. primary human physiology study (water-load diuresis with prostaglandin inhibition) 6 healthy male volunteers studied after overnight deprivation with an oral water load of 20 ml/kg and hourly urine volumes replaced by mouth for 4 hours, after 3 days of aspirin (3 g/day) or indomethacin (150 mg/day); n = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study). both drugs comparably suppressed prostaglandin e2 excretion (p < 0.05 to < 0.001), but only indomethacin also reduced diuresis, free-water clearance and sodium excretion (p < 0.05); creatinine excretion was unchanged by either drug. the authors conclude a mechanism other than cyclo-oxygenase inhibition is involved in the drugs' differing effects on human diuresis. the protocol itself — load, then hourly replacement for 4 hours — is the classic design for following a water load to complete excretion. very small study (n = 6) designed around drug effects; its abstract reports the drug contrast rather than hour-by-hour control excretion values, so the hour-by-hour time course on this shelf rests mainly on crowe 1987 and andersen 1990. vierhapper h et al. effect of acetylsalicylic acid and of indomethacin on diuresis in man: the role of cyclo-oxygenase inhibition. clin sci (lond). 1984. pmid: 6435937. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aspirin/pharmacology · chlorides/urine · *cyclooxygenase inhibitors · depression, chemical · dinoprostone · diuresis/drug effects · humans · indomethacin/pharmacology · male · potassium/urine · prostaglandins e/urine · sodium/urine

cards.headline: Synthesis: a 20 mL/kg load is essentially gone by ~2 hours in young adults (peak free-water clearance ~8–10 mL/min), with the whole course gated steeply by vasopressin and slowed by age-related filtration loss — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 20 mL/kg load is essentially gone by ~2 hours in young adults (peak free-water clearance ~8–10 mL/min), with the whole course gated steeply by vasopressin and slowed by age-related filtration loss — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: young and elderly men after a standard 20 mL/kg load (Crowe 1987), volunteers in established water diuresis (Andersen 1990; N not documented in the record), and 6 men in a 4-hour load-and-replace protocol (Vierhapper 1984).
cards.result: The time course is consistent across the three free reports: vasopressin falls, urine flow climbs to roughly 12–14 mL/min with free-water clearance peaking around 8–10 mL/min, and a standard load is fully excreted by about 2 hours in young water-replete adults (100.7% at 2 hours) — within the 4-hour window of the classic replacement protocols, and concordant with the 95%-in-4-hours figure homed at pack #6079. Age slows and lowers the peak in proportion to lost filtration. This matches the textbook account in Guyton and Hall and in Ganong, which frame this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Healthy-volunteer physiology after a single oral load: it does not describe water handling in heart failure, cirrhosis, SIADH or kidney disease, where the same load is excreted far more slowly or not at all.
cards.source: Synthesis of Crowe MJ et al. Age and ageing. 1987 (PMID: 3687569); Andersen LJ et al. The American journal of physiology. 1990 (PMID: 2375429); Vierhapper H et al. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 1984 (PMID: 6435937). shelves.title: Apixaban versus warfarin in AF on haemodialysis (RENAL-AF): the one randomised trial stopped early at 154 patients - bleeding 32% vs 26% at one year (HR 1.20, wide interval), stroke 3.0% vs 3.3%; underpowered, so the verdict is MAYBE (weak evidence)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation on maintenance haemodialysis, does apixaban, compared with warfarin, reduce bleeding without increasing thromboembolism?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation/diagnosis,drug therapy,complications · Warfarin/adverse effects · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Hemorrhage/epidemiology · Stroke/diagnosis,epidemiology,etiology · Embolism/prevention & control · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications,diagnosis,therapy · Pyrazoles · Pyridones
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). PREMISE VERIFIED with a precedent-(a) call: home #1743 is AXADIA-AFNET 8 (apixaban vs phenprocoumon, a different vitamin K antagonist, in German dialysis practice). The #1743 pack mentions RENAL-AF only as fenced, uncarded context - its own text says no primary journal report of RENAL-AF 'could be pinned in this build, so it is fenced here by name without figures'. Fenced context is not carding (precedent a), and the RENAL-AF primary report (Circulation 2022; NCT02942407) is free in the gate file, so this shelf cards it directly. RENAL-AF randomised 154 patients and stopped early for enrolment failure: one-year major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 32% on apixaban against 26% on warfarin (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.30 - a relative measure whose interval spans halving to doubling), stroke or systemic embolism 3.0% against 3.3%, and death - the commonest major event - 26% against 18%. Warfarin time in therapeutic range was only 44%. The large USRDS observational study (25,523 patients) found no difference in stroke/systemic embolism (HR 0.88) but less major bleeding with apixaban (HR 0.72) - hypothesis-consistent, not decisive. A 2024 review of all six studies (both trials plus four observational) likewise settles nothing. Neither 'apixaban reduces bleeding' nor 'it is equivalent' is earned by this base.

cards.headline: RENAL-AF 2022: in 154 haemodialysis patients with AF, one-year major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 32% on apixaban against 26% on warfarin (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.30) - the trial stopped early and was underpowered
cards.summary: RENAL-AF 2022: in 154 haemodialysis patients with AF, one-year major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 32% on apixaban against 26% on warfarin (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.30) - the trial stopped early and was underpowered
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-outcome (PROBE) trial (RENAL-AF, Circulation 2022) - 154 patients, stopped early
cards.people: 154 patients with atrial fibrillation and end-stage kidney disease on haemodialysis, with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2, randomised 1:1 to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (82 patients; 2.5 mg twice daily if aged at least 80 years, weight at most 60 kg, or both) or dose-adjusted warfarin (72 patients), enrolled January 2017 to January 2019. The trial stopped prematurely because of enrolment challenges; warfarin time in therapeutic range (INR 2.0-3.0) was 44% (interquartile range 23% to 59%).
cards.result: One-year rates of major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (the primary outcome) were 32% on apixaban and 26% on warfarin (hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.30 - a relative measure). One-year stroke or systemic embolism rates were 3.0% and 3.3% respectively. Death was the most common major event: 21 patients (26%) on apixaban and 13 (18%) on warfarin. The authors state there was inadequate power to draw any conclusion on bleeding, and that clinically relevant bleeding was about ten-fold more frequent than stroke or systemic embolism in this anticoagulated population.
cards.watchOut: An underpowered, prematurely stopped trial: the bleeding interval (0.63 to 2.30) is compatible with apixaban halving or doubling bleeding risk, and poor warfarin control (44% time in range) weakens the comparator. The numerically higher death count on apixaban (21 vs 13) is one of many unstable small-number contrasts in this trial and is not a demonstrated harm.
cards.source: Pokorney SD et al. Apixaban for Patients With Atrial Fibrillation on Hemodialysis: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 36335914. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02942407, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: USRDS observational study 2018: in 25,523 dialysis patients with AF, apixaban was associated with less major bleeding than warfarin (HR 0.72; P<0.001) and no difference in stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.88; P=0.29) - relative measures, observational
cards.summary: USRDS observational study 2018: in 25,523 dialysis patients with AF, apixaban was associated with less major bleeding than warfarin (HR 0.72; P<0.001) and no difference in stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.88; P=0.29) - relative measures, observational
cards.type: Retrospective propensity-matched cohort study (USRDS, Circulation 2018) - 25,523 patients (observational evidence, labelled as such)
cards.people: Medicare beneficiaries in the United States Renal Data System (October 2010 to December 2015) with end-stage kidney disease and atrial fibrillation on dialysis who initiated an oral anticoagulant: 25,523 patients (45.7% women; mean age 68.2 years), of whom 2,351 started apixaban and 23,172 warfarin; apixaban and warfarin patients were matched 1:3 on prognostic score. By 2015, 26.6% of new anticoagulant prescriptions in this population were for apixaban.
cards.result: In matched cohorts, there was no difference in stroke or systemic embolism between apixaban and warfarin (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.12; P=0.29 - a relative measure), but apixaban was associated with a significantly lower risk of major bleeding (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.87; P<0.001 - a relative measure). In sensitivity analyses, standard-dose apixaban (5 mg twice daily; n=1,034) was associated with lower risks of stroke/systemic embolism and death than either reduced-dose apixaban (HR 0.61 and 0.64 respectively) or warfarin (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.97; and HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.85).
cards.watchOut: Observational: dialysis patients prescribed apixaban in 2010-2015 differed from warfarin patients in ways matching cannot fully capture (frailty, prior bleeding, clinician judgement), and the standard-dose subgroup findings are especially vulnerable to confounding by indication - sicker patients get reduced doses.
cards.source: Siontis KC et al. Outcomes Associated With Apixaban Use in Patients With End-Stage Kidney Disease and Atrial Fibrillation in the United States. Circulation. 2018. PMID: 29954737. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 2024 systematic review of apixaban versus vitamin K antagonists in dialysis AF (6 studies): the randomised trials were both small and stopped early, and the observational studies disagree on thromboembolism - no settled answer
cards.summary: 2024 systematic review of apixaban versus vitamin K antagonists in dialysis AF (6 studies): the randomised trials were both small and stopped early, and the observational studies disagree on thromboembolism - no settled answer
cards.type: Systematic review (2024) - 6 studies: RENAL-AF, AXADIA-AFNET 8 (homed at #1743; its report is not carded here) and 4 observational studies
cards.people: A systematic review of PubMed and Embase to March 2024 covering six studies of apixaban versus vitamin K antagonists in atrial fibrillation patients on dialysis: the AXADIA-AFNET 8 trial (homed at #1743 against phenprocoumon; not carded on this shelf), the RENAL-AF trial (carded above), and four observational studies including a French nationwide study and two USRDS analyses.
cards.result: The review summarises that the French nationwide observational study found a lower thromboembolic risk on apixaban (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.78 - a relative measure) against vitamin K antagonists, while a two-year retrospective review and both USRDS-based studies found no statistical difference in symptomatic bleeding and stroke between apixaban and warfarin groups (the record's abstract truncates at this point). No pooled estimate is offered; the review's function is to map a small, inconsistent literature.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without a pooled estimate, carded as a map: its included set overlaps this shelf's other cards and the homed AXADIA trial, so it adds structure, not independent patients. The single striking observational hazard ratio (0.49) comes from one nationwide dataset and is not corroborated by the US data.
cards.source: Guo Z et al. Safety and Effectiveness Outcomes between Apixaban Versus Vitamin K Antagonists in Atrial Fibrillation Patients on Dialysis. Reviews in cardiovascular medicine. 2024. PMID: 39355581. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) - RENAL-AF (the apixaban-versus-warfarin trial, fenced but never carded at home #1743) was too small and stopped too early to answer the question; observational data lean toward less bleeding with apixaban and similar thromboembolism
cards.summary: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) - RENAL-AF (the apixaban-versus-warfarin trial, fenced but never carded at home #1743) was too small and stopped too early to answer the question; observational data lean toward less bleeding with apixaban and similar thromboembolism
cards.people: The carded evidence is RENAL-AF (154 randomised patients, stopped early), the USRDS matched observational study (25,523 patients) and a 2024 systematic review of the six-study literature. The distinction from home #1743 was verified this session: #1743 is AXADIA-AFNET 8, apixaban against phenprocoumon; RENAL-AF appears there only as fenced context without figures, which under precedent (a) does not count as carded.
cards.result: Bleeding: RENAL-AF's one-year rates were 32% (apixaban) against 26% (warfarin) with HR 1.20 (95% CI 0.63 to 2.30) - no conclusion possible; the observational USRDS analysis found HR 0.72 for major bleeding favouring apixaban. Thromboembolism: 3.0% against 3.3% at one year in RENAL-AF, and HR 0.88 (0.69 to 1.12) observationally - no demonstrated increase, on very few events. Death dominated both trials' event counts (26% vs 18% in RENAL-AF), reflecting the population's frailty more than drug effects. The question as posed - less bleeding without more thromboembolism - remains unproven in both directions.
cards.watchOut: Weak-evidence stamp is the honest one: a stopped-early 154-patient trial plus confounded observational data cannot carry a stronger verdict. Clinicians choosing between these drugs in dialysis patients are choosing under genuine uncertainty, and this shelf should not be cited as settling it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pokorney SD et al. Circulation. 2022 (PMID: 36335914, NCT02942407); Siontis KC et al. Circulation. 2018 (PMID: 29954737); Guo Z et al. Reviews in cardiovascular medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39355581). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Sodium thiosulfate for calciphylaxis: lesions often improve in uncontrolled series, but the comparative meta-analysis found no difference in healing or survival
shelves.question: In patients with calciphylaxis, does intravenous sodium thiosulfate, compared with standard wound/dialysis care, improve lesion healing or survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Calciphylaxis/drug therapy,mortality · Chelating Agents/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Renal Replacement Therapy · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Statistics, Nonparametric · Survival Rate · Thiosulfates/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only, capped and labelled. Uncontrolled series (Noureddine 2011, n=14; Nigwekar 2013, n=172 treated) report pain and lesion improvement in roughly 70% of patients, with one-year mortality still 35%. The only comparative evidence — a 2023 meta-analysis of 19 retrospective cohorts (422 patients) — found no difference in lesion improvement (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78) or death (risk ratio 0.88, 0.70–1.10) with intravenous thiosulfate, and the apparent benefit shrank in more recent studies. Peritoneal-dialysis evidence is 30 case-literature patients. No RCT exists.

cards.headline: Noureddine 2011: in 14 patients given sodium thiosulfate for calciphylaxis, pain fell in 71% and lesions improved in 70% — yet 71% died, half within 6 months
cards.summary: Noureddine 2011: in 14 patients given sodium thiosulfate for calciphylaxis, pain fell in 71% and lesions improved in 70% — yet 71% died, half within 6 months
cards.people: 14 patients with end-stage renal disease and calciphylaxis who received sodium thiosulfate at four hospitals over 5 years, identified through pharmacy records (so the series is not limited to published case reports); retrospective chart review. N=14 printed plainly. No untreated comparison group.
cards.result: After sodium thiosulfate, pain decreased in 71% of patients and 70% had improvement in their skin lesions. Patients whose lesions did not improve or stabilise tended to have more advanced lesions, longer time on renal replacement therapy, more obesity and a lower total thiosulfate dose. Despite treatment, the mortality rate was 71%, with 50% of patients dying within 6 months. The authors conclude thiosulfate may help pain and lesions when given early and consistently, with little impact on overall mortality compared with historical published cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled: lesion improvement without a comparator cannot separate drug effect from wound care, dialysis changes and natural history — and the authors' own mortality comparison is to historical published cohorts.

cards.headline: Nigwekar 2013: in 172 haemodialysis patients treated with sodium thiosulfate, surveyed physicians reported complete resolution in 26.4% and some improvement in a further 47.2% — but one-year mortality was still 35%
cards.summary: Nigwekar 2013: in 172 haemodialysis patients treated with sodium thiosulfate, surveyed physicians reported complete resolution in 26.4% and some improvement in a further 47.2% — but one-year mortality was still 35%
cards.people: 172 patients on maintenance haemodialysis with calcific uraemic arteriolopathy (calciphylaxis) treated with intravenous sodium thiosulfate at a large dialysis provider between 2006 and 2009; 85% completed therapy (median dose 25 g, median 38 doses). Lesion outcomes come from treating-physician survey responses available for only 53 of the 172 patients. No untreated comparison group.
cards.result: Among the 53 surveyed patients, lesions completely resolved in 26.4%, markedly improved in 18.9%, improved in 28.3%, did not improve in 5.7%, and the response was unknown in 20.8%. One-year mortality in the treated cohort was 35%. Adverse events, laboratory abnormalities and weight changes were mild; serum phosphorus (P=0.02) and parathyroid hormone (P=0.01) fell during treatment in patients who completed therapy. The authors state explicitly that conclusive evidence of efficacy is lacking.
cards.watchOut: The lesion-response percentages rest on 53 of 172 patients (survey responders) — responder bias is likely, and there is no untreated arm, so the 35% one-year mortality cannot be compared with anything inside the study.
cards.source: Single-arm observational cohort (dialysis-provider registry with physician survey) | Nigwekar SU et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2013. PMID: 23520041. cards.headline: Wen 2023 (comparative meta-analysis): across 19 retrospective cohorts and 422 patients, intravenous sodium thiosulfate was NOT associated with better lesion improvement (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78) or survival (risk ratio for death 0.88, 0.70–1.10) versus no thiosulfate
cards.summary: Wen 2023 (comparative meta-analysis): across 19 retrospective cohorts and 422 patients, intravenous sodium thiosulfate was NOT associated with better lesion improvement (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78) or survival (risk ratio for death 0.88, 0.70–1.10) versus no thiosulfate
cards.people: Meta-analysis of the retrospective cohort studies that compared calciphylaxis patients with chronic kidney disease treated with intravenous sodium thiosulfate against patients not so treated: 19 studies, 422 patients (mean age 57 years). Lesion improvement was pooled from 12 studies with 110 patients; death from 15 studies with 158 patients; time-to-event survival from 3 studies with 269 participants. All underlying studies are retrospective — observational evidence only.
cards.result: No difference was observed in skin lesion improvement between thiosulfate and comparator groups (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78 — a relative measure whose confidence interval includes no effect). There was no difference in the risk of death (risk ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.70–1.10) or in overall survival on time-to-event analysis (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.57–1.18). In meta-regression, the apparent lesion benefit of thiosulfate shrank with publication year (coefficient −0.14, P=0.008) — more recent studies are more likely to report a null association. The authors conclude intravenous sodium thiosulfate was not associated with lesion improvement or survival benefit, and that future investigations are warranted.
cards.watchOut: This is the only comparative evidence carded, and it is a pooling of small retrospective cohorts (the lesion analysis totals 110 patients) — confounding by indication (sicker patients may be more, or less, likely to receive thiosulfate) can move the estimate in either direction.

cards.headline: Gossett 2023 (peritoneal dialysis): a systematic review found only 30 reported peritoneal-dialysis patients treated with thiosulfate; 44% of intravenous cases healed, 50% died of calciphylaxis complications, and intraperitoneal administration was stopped for adverse effects in 80%
cards.summary: Gossett 2023 (peritoneal dialysis): a systematic review found only 30 reported peritoneal-dialysis patients treated with thiosulfate; 44% of intravenous cases healed, 50% died of calciphylaxis complications, and intraperitoneal administration was stopped for adverse effects in 80%
cards.people: Systematic review of all reported peritoneal-dialysis patients with calciphylaxis treated with sodium thiosulfate through August 2022: 30 patients across 19 articles (15 case reports, 2 case series, 2 cohort studies). 18 received intravenous, 5 intraperitoneal, 3 switched from intravenous to intraperitoneal, and 2 received oral thiosulfate. Case-report-dominated evidence — the weakest card in this pack, flagged as such.
cards.result: With intravenous administration, 44% of patients achieved successful wound healing, 6% discontinued for adverse effects, 67% transitioned to haemodialysis, and 50% died from calciphylaxis complications. With intraperitoneal administration, 80% achieved wound healing but 80% discontinued because of adverse effects, and 20% died from chemical peritonitis related to intraperitoneal thiosulfate. The authors conclude that successful cases exist but adverse effects were significant, and that larger studies and pharmacokinetic data are needed to establish route, dose and efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients assembled mostly from case reports — publication bias is expected to be extreme (successful cases are written up; failures usually are not), so the healing percentages on this card are upper-bound impressions, not rates.
cards.source: Systematic review of case reports, case series and cohorts | Gossett C et al. Medicina (Kaunas). 2023. PMID: 37512116. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: uncontrolled series say lesions often improve on sodium thiosulfate; the only comparative synthesis says they improve no more often than without it, and survival is unchanged — no randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: uncontrolled series say lesions often improve on sodium thiosulfate; the only comparative synthesis says they improve no more often than without it, and survival is unchanged — no randomised trial exists
cards.people: Synthesis of Noureddine 2011 (n=14, uncontrolled), Nigwekar 2013 (n=172 treated, uncontrolled, lesion outcomes in 53), Wen 2023 (meta-analysis of 19 comparative retrospective cohorts, 422 patients) and Gossett 2023 (30 peritoneal-dialysis cases from the case literature). No calciphylaxis or thiosulfate home exists in the library — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: The uncontrolled experience is superficially encouraging: pain fell in 71% and lesions improved in 70% of the small institutional series, and treating physicians reported resolution or improvement in about three quarters of surveyed patients in the large dialysis cohort — while one-year mortality remained 35%. But when treated patients are compared with untreated patients, the pooled estimate is null for both lesion improvement (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78) and death (risk ratio 0.88, 0.70–1.10), and the apparent benefit fades in more recent studies. The fair reading is that sodium thiosulfate is widely used, reasonably tolerated, and unproven: the treatment made no difference in the comparative data that exist, and the question cannot be settled without a randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: every card is observational and the comparative pool is small; the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence), not a verdict of no effect — the confidence intervals still include a worthwhile benefit, which is precisely why a trial is needed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Noureddine L et al. Clin Nephrol. 2011 (PMID: 21612750); Nigwekar SU et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2013 (PMID: 23520041); Wen W et al. shelves.title: Pressure natriuresis and salt sensitivity: Guyton's renal–body-fluid feedback sets long-term pressure — and humans whose pressure rises on salt loading carry a mortality risk like hypertension itself
shelves.question: How does pressure natriuresis — the renal–body-fluid feedback of Guyton — set long-term arterial pressure, and what human evidence links its impairment to salt-sensitive hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Female · Humans · Hypertension/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Sodium Chloride, Dietary/pharmacology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, framed by Guyton & Hall's renal–body-fluid feedback (Textbook of Medical Physiology, Guyton & Hall): the renal-function curve relates arterial pressure to sodium excretion (pressure natriuresis); at equilibrium, intake must equal output, so long-term arterial pressure settles at the pressure where the curve crosses intake — a steeper/higher-pressure curve (impaired natriuresis) means any given salt intake is excreted only at a higher pressure, which is the textbook account of salt-sensitive hypertension. Those quantitative curve claims are presented as the textbook's account (framing, not an evidence card). The human evidence carded here is concordant with the framework: (1) Weinberger 2002 followed 708 people phenotyped by salt loading/depletion — salt sensitivity, even in normotensive people, carried survival no better than hypertension over up to 28 years; (2) Overlack 1995 showed the phenotype is real and graded under controlled double-blind conditions (46 hypertensive patients cycled between 20 and 300 mmol sodium/day: 23.9% salt-sensitive, 58.7% salt-resistant, 17.4% counter-regulators), with salt-sensitive patients showing lower creatinine clearance and suppressed renin — the human signature of a right-shifted renal-function curve; (3) Weinberger 1988 documents that the blood-pressure response to salt is heritable and continuously distributed, with salt sensitivity more frequent in Black than White Americans — a trait of the feedback system, not a binary disease. Animal mechanism (e.g., Dahl salt-sensitive rats) is mentioned only as labelled textbook background in prose; no animal study is carded.

cards.headline: Weinberger 2002: salt-sensitive normotensive people had survival no better than hypertensive people over up to 28 years (708 phenotyped, 123 deaths)
cards.summary: Weinberger 2002: salt-sensitive normotensive people had survival no better than hypertensive people over up to 28 years (708 phenotyped, 123 deaths)
cards.people: Long-term follow-up cohort: 430 normotensive and 278 hypertensive subjects whose blood-pressure responses to salt and volume expansion and depletion (salt sensitivity) had been characterised by a standardised inpatient protocol as long as 28 years earlier; vital status was then ascertained (123 subjects, 21%, had died).
cards.result: Salt sensitivity was significantly associated with the risk of death, alongside blood pressure itself (systolic, diastolic, mean and pulse), hypertension, age, body mass index and (inversely) baseline renin. Normotensive salt-sensitive subjects had a survival no different from that of hypertensive subjects; only initially normotensive salt-resistant individuals had improved survival. The authors call for work on the mechanisms by which salt sensitivity, even without hypertension, reduces survival — in Guyton's terms, a phenotype whose kidneys require higher pressure to excrete a salt load marks risk even before resting pressure rises.
cards.watchOut: Observational follow-up of a phenotyping cohort assembled over decades — salt sensitivity was measured once, by one protocol; the mortality association is adjusted observational evidence, not a trial of salt restriction.
cards.source: Weinberger MH et al. Salt sensitivity is associated with an increased mortality in both normal and hypertensive humans. J Clin Hypertens (Greenwich). 2002. PMID: 12147930. cards.headline: Overlack 1995: under double-blind controlled intake (20 vs 300 mmol sodium/day), 23.9% of 46 hypertensive patients were salt-sensitive — with lower creatinine clearance and suppressed renin
cards.summary: Overlack 1995: under double-blind controlled intake (20 vs 300 mmol sodium/day), 23.9% of 46 hypertensive patients were salt-sensitive — with lower creatinine clearance and suppressed renin
cards.people: Double-blind randomised crossover dietary study: 46 white non-obese patients with essential hypertension (33 men, 13 women; mean age 45.3 years; range 25–80) each spent 1 week on a low-salt diet (20 mmol sodium/day) and 1 week on a high-salt diet (300 mmol sodium/day). Salt-sensitive was defined as a rise in mean arterial pressure of ≥5 mm Hg on high salt; salt-resistant as a change <5 mm Hg; 'counter-regulators' fell by ≥5 mm Hg.
cards.result: Mean arterial pressure for the whole group rose modestly (101.9 ± 1.4 mm Hg on low salt to 103.7 ± 1.5 on high salt; P<0.05), concealing divergent phenotypes: 11 patients (23.9%) were salt-sensitive, 27 (58.7%) salt-resistant and 8 (17.4%) counter-regulators. Age was the significant determinant of the pressure response (10 of 11 salt-sensitive patients were older than the median 45 years). Compared with salt-resistant patients, salt-sensitive patients had lower creatinine clearance and suppressed plasma renin activity at baseline and on both diets, with higher norepinephrine and atrial natriuretic peptide — the pattern expected if sodium excretion requires a higher perfusion pressure (a right-shifted pressure-natriuresis relationship).
cards.watchOut: One week per diet and 46 patients — a phenotyping experiment, not an outcomes study; the ≥5 mm Hg cut-off is a convention imposed on a continuous response (see card 3).
cards.source: Overlack A et al. Age is a major determinant of the divergent blood pressure responses to varying salt intake in essential hypertension. Am J Hypertens. 1995. PMID: 7576400. cards.headline: Weinberger 1988: blood-pressure responses to salt loading and restriction are normally distributed and heritable — salt sensitivity is a graded trait of the renal feedback system
cards.summary: Weinberger 1988: blood-pressure responses to salt loading and restriction are normally distributed and heritable — salt sensitivity is a graded trait of the renal feedback system
cards.people: Human physiology review-with-primary-data from the Indiana salt-sensitivity programme: series of investigations of blood-pressure responses to acute salt-and-volume loading and to reduced dietary salt intake in normotensive and hypertensive Americans, including twin/family data on genetic variance in blood pressure, humoral regulators and renal sodium handling, and haptoglobin-phenotype analyses.
cards.result: Blood-pressure responses to salt loading and to salt reduction were normally (continuously) distributed rather than bimodal; genetic variance influenced blood pressure, its humoral regulators, renal sodium handling and the pressure change from salt reduction itself. Salt sensitivity occurred significantly more often in Black than in White Americans, and at least half of pharmacologically treated hypertensive patients in the programme's dietary trials appeared salt-sensitive, with medication reducible when intake fell. In the pressure-natriuresis framework, this is the expected picture if each person's renal-function curve sits at a different pressure.
cards.watchOut: A programme synthesis (comparative study) rather than a single protocolised experiment — carded for the heritability/distribution evidence, which the two protocol studies (cards 1–2) do not themselves supply. N per sub-study is not documented in the record; the card therefore prints no single N.
cards.source: Luft FC et al. Heritable aspects of salt sensitivity. Am J Cardiol. 1988. PMID: 3381725. Registry ID: none in the record.
