cards.headline: Synthesis: the human data fit Guyton's frame — natriuretic capacity differs between people, is heritable and age-related, and the salt-sensitive phenotype carries prognostic weight
cards.summary: Synthesis: the human data fit Guyton's frame — natriuretic capacity differs between people, is heritable and age-related, and the salt-sensitive phenotype carries prognostic weight
cards.people: Humans studied: 708 phenotyped and followed in the Weinberger cohort, 46 in the controlled crossover phenotyping study, and the Indiana programme's loading/restriction series (per-study Ns not documented in the record).
cards.result: Guyton & Hall's renal–body-fluid feedback (textbook framing) predicts that long-term pressure is set where sodium output matches intake, so impaired pressure natriuresis must present as salt-sensitive hypertension. The carded human evidence matches each element: the phenotype exists under controlled conditions with a renal signature (lower clearance, suppressed renin); it is graded and heritable; and it predicts mortality even in normotensive people. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED as a framework with concordant human data; the exact quantitative shape of any individual's renal-function curve is a textbook account, not something these studies measured directly.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here licenses a clinical salt-sensitivity test or a treatment claim — dietary sodium trials and hypertension drug shelves live elsewhere in the library; this shelf is the physiology underneath them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weinberger MH et al. J Clin Hypertens (Greenwich). 2002 (PMID: 12147930); Overlack A et al. Am J Hypertens. 1995 (PMID: 7576400); Luft FC et al. Am J Cardiol. 1988 (PMID: 3381725).

shelves.title: Renin release (physiology): three inputs converge on the juxtaglomerular cell — the renal baroreceptor reads perfusion pressure, the macula densa reads distal NaCl, and sympathetic β1 drive reads the circulation at large — and human studies show them integrating within minutes of standing and over days of sodium restriction
shelves.question: What controls renin release at the juxtaglomerular apparatus — renal baroreceptor, macula densa NaCl sensing, and sympathetic β1 input — and how do these integrate in human volume/pressure homeostasis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aldosterone/blood · Angiotensin II/blood · Circadian Rhythm · Corticosterone/blood · Diet · Female · Homeostasis · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Male · Plasma Volume/drug effects · *Posture · Potassium/blood · Renin/blood,physiology · Sodium/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, renin–angiotensin chapter; macula densa signalling as in Vander's Renal Physiology). The textbook's three inputs to the juxtaglomerular (JG) cell: (1) the renal baroreceptor — JG cells themselves sense afferent arteriolar stretch, releasing more renin as perfusion pressure falls; (2) macula densa NaCl sensing — less NaCl delivered to the distal tubule (sensed via Na-K-2Cl cotransport) signals volume depletion and stimulates renin, more NaCl suppresses it; (3) sympathetic β1 input — renal sympathetic nerves and circulating catecholamines stimulate renin directly, the route by which posture and central volume sensing reach the kidney. The carded human studies show the integrated output. Posture: plasma renin activity rose significantly within 5 minutes of standing and was three-fold higher after 2 hours upright (Sassard 1976) — baroreceptor unloading plus sympathetic activation, before any sodium change. Sodium balance: dropping intake from 200 to 10 mEq/day raised renin activity roughly three-fold, diuretic volume depletion abolished the nocturnal fall, and renin was judged the dominant controller of the downstream aldosterone response (Williams 1972). Sympathetic/pressure interplay: sodium depletion stimulated total renin release, while propranolol lowered active renin in every patient and clonidine mimicked it — yet when β-blockade lowered blood pressure, baroreceptor-mediated release pushed back, the three inputs visibly negotiating (Atlas 1977). Downstream of renin sits aldosterone, whose own regulators are homed on pack #6078; this shelf stops at renin release. The later tubuloglomerular-feedback question (slate row 90) shares the macula densa but asks a different, glomerular question. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Williams 1972: cutting sodium intake from 200 to 10 mEq/day tripled plasma renin activity in normal man — and upright posture raised it a further 150–200%
cards.summary: Williams 1972: cutting sodium intake from 200 to 10 mEq/day tripled plasma renin activity in normal man — and upright posture raised it a further 150–200%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (sodium-balance and posture manipulations, Williams programme)
cards.people: Normal human subjects studied supine over consecutive days on a 10 mEq sodium / 100 mEq potassium intake and on a 200 mEq sodium intake, with peripheral plasma aldosterone, plasma renin activity (PRA), potassium, corticosterone, cortisol and in some cases angiotensin II measured through postural changes, acute diuretic-induced volume depletion and dietary sodium alterations. The record does not print the number of subjects (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: On the 10 mEq sodium intake, supine 8 a.m. plasma aldosterone was 55 ± 7 ng/100 ml and PRA 886 ± 121 ng/100 ml per 3 hr; after 3 hours upright both increased by 150–200% (relative increases). Raising sodium intake to 200 mEq reduced plasma aldosterone and PRA to one-third of their previous levels, with the diurnal pattern preserved. Acute diuretic-induced volume depletion abolished the nocturnal fall in aldosterone (11 p.m. value 102 ± 20 ng/100 ml, vs significantly lower pre-diuresis levels). In all studies, changes in aldosterone were invariably associated with parallel changes in PRA and/or angiotensin II, leading the authors to conclude PRA is the dominant factor controlling aldosterone when volume or dietary sodium is altered in normal man — dietary NaCl delivery (the macula densa's signal) setting the system's gain over days.
cards.watchOut: An aldosterone-titled study carded for its renin measurements, which are direct and complete; N not documented in the record. PRA is a downstream readout of renin release (enzyme activity in plasma), the standard human measure — JG-cell secretion itself cannot be sampled in humans, a limitation common to every card on this shelf.
cards.source: Williams GH et al. Studies of the control of plasma aldosterone concentration in normal man. I. Response to posture, acute and chronic volume depletion, and sodium loading. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1972. PMID: 4338121. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sassard 1976: renin rose within 5 minutes of standing and was 3× the recumbent value by 120 minutes in 12 normal subjects — the fast limb of the integration
cards.summary: Sassard 1976: renin rose within 5 minutes of standing and was 3× the recumbent value by 120 minutes in 12 normal subjects — the fast limb of the integration
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (posture kinetics of renin and aldosterone) — N = 12
cards.people: 12 normal human subjects (6 men, 6 women) on an ad lib diet, studied at 8 a.m. through a standardised posture sequence — 1 hour supine, 2 hours upright, 1 hour supine — with cardiovascular parameters, haematocrit, plasma electrolytes, plasma renin activity (PRA) and plasma aldosterone concentration measured serially.
cards.result: On standing, heart rate and systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose immediately and haematocrit rose significantly by the 5th minute in men. PRA rose significantly at the 5th minute and after 120 minutes of orthostatism was 3 times greater than its recumbent value; plasma aldosterone rose significantly at the 15th minute and plateaued at 4.5 times basal values after 90 minutes upright. On returning supine, all parameters except aldosterone fell. During orthostatism, aldosterone correlated more closely with PRA (and PRA plus potassium) than with potassium alone. The speed of the renin response — minutes, with no change in sodium intake — is the signature of the baroreceptor/sympathetic limb acting through the JG apparatus.
cards.watchOut: Posture changes several inputs at once (central volume, arterial pressure, sympathetic tone), so this card demonstrates the integrated fast response rather than isolating the baroreceptor from β1 drive — the pharmacologic dissection is the Atlas card's contribution.
cards.source: Sassard J et al. A kinetic study of plasma renin and aldosterone during changes of posture in man. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1976. PMID: 1249191. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Atlas 1977: sodium depletion stimulated total renin release, while propranolol lowered active renin in all 22 patients — and baroreceptor-mediated release pushed back when pressure fell
cards.summary: Atlas 1977: sodium depletion stimulated total renin release, while propranolol lowered active renin in all 22 patients — and baroreceptor-mediated release pushed back when pressure fell
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (renin/prorenin responses to sodium depletion, β-blockade and pressure change)
cards.people: Patients with essential hypertension studied during sodium deprivation or diuretic therapy (36 patients), during propranolol administration (22 patients), and during clonidine administration (10 patients), with active renin and cryoactivatable 'prorenin' measured separately in plasma.
cards.result: Prorenin increased in parallel with active renin after sodium deprivation or diuretic therapy in the 36 patients, whether or not blood pressure fell — sodium depletion stimulates total renin release. Propranolol lowered active renin in all 22 patients, but increased prorenin by 98% in the 15 in whom systolic pressure fell; in the other 7, pressure did not change and total renin fell. Across all 22, propranolol-induced changes in prorenin correlated inversely with changes in systolic pressure (r = −0.77, P < 0.001), and the active fraction of plasma renin fell from 43% to 18% on propranolol regardless of the pressure response. Clonidine produced similar changes in 10 patients. The authors' interpretation is the integration in miniature: β-blockade suppresses renin release/conversion (the β1 limb), while a fall in pressure recruits baroreceptor-mediated release of total renin (mostly prorenin) that partly offsets it.
cards.watchOut: Hypertensive patients, not healthy volunteers, and prorenin biology (the inactive precursor) is part of the readout: the card is used for the three-input integration the data display — sodium, β-adrenergic and pressure signals visibly interacting — not for prorenin physiology itself.
cards.source: Atlas SA et al. Plasma renin and "prorenin" in essential hypertension during sodium depletion, beta-blockade, and reduced arterial pressure. Lancet (London, England). 1977. PMID: 71600. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fast sympathetic/baroreceptor control in minutes, macula-densa sodium control over days — one cell integrating all three
cards.summary: Synthesis: fast sympathetic/baroreceptor control in minutes, macula-densa sodium control over days — one cell integrating all three
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Vander's Renal Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: The JG cell integrates three signals, and human studies have timed each. Standing raises renin within 5 minutes and three-fold within 2 hours (PMID 1249191) — baroreceptor unloading and sympathetic β1 activation, with no sodium change. Sodium restriction triples the system's baseline over days and volume depletion sustains it (PMID 4338121) — the macula densa reading distal NaCl delivery. β-blockade suppresses active renin in every subject, yet a pressure fall recruits compensatory release (PMID 71600) — proof the inputs are weighed together, not wired in series. Downstream, renin drives angiotensin II and aldosterone; aldosterone's own direct regulators are homed on pack #6078. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: this shelf is renin-release control. Tubuloglomerular feedback — the macula densa's other job, adjusting glomerular filtration — shares the sensor but is a separate question (slate row 90), not answered here; and renin inhibitors as drugs are treatment shelves, not this physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 4338121, 1249191, 71600), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; downstream cross-point: pack #6078 (aldosterone regulation). No additional source.

shelves.title: Felzartamab in transplant antibody-mediated rejection (phase 2 only): biopsy resolution 82% vs 20% in 22 patients — and rejection returned when treatment stopped
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with antibody-mediated rejection, does the anti-CD38 antibody felzartamab resolve rejection activity on biopsy compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,immunology,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Graft Rejection/drug therapy,etiology,immunology · Isoantibodies/blood,immunology · Kidney/drug effects,immunology,pathology · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects · Killer Cells, Natural/immunology · Membrane Glycoproteins · ADP-ribosyl Cyclase 1
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 22. PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY: the whole verdict rests on one phase 2 randomised programme in 22 kidney transplant recipients with late antibody-mediated rejection. At week 24, morphologic rejection had resolved in 9 of 11 patients on felzartamab (82%) vs 2 of 10 on placebo (20%) — a difference of 62 percentage points — but rejection recurred in 3 of the 9 responders by week 52, molecular recurrence was nearly universal after treatment stopped in the biopsy substudy, and an open-label extension retreated 11 patients with recurrent or persistent rejection. No graft-survival or kidney-function outcome has been tested. The N (22) is printed in the stamp line because the total evidence base is under 30 humans.

cards.headline: Mayer 2024 phase 2 trial (n=22): morphologic antibody-mediated rejection resolved in 82% on felzartamab vs 20% on placebo at week 24 — but recurred in 3 of 9 responders by week 52
cards.summary: Mayer 2024 phase 2 trial (n=22): morphologic antibody-mediated rejection resolved in 82% on felzartamab vs 20% on placebo at week 24 — but recurred in 3 of 9 responders by week 52
cards.type: Phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 22 kidney transplant recipients with antibody-mediated rejection occurring at least 180 days after transplantation (median 9 years), randomised double-blind to nine infusions of felzartamab 16 mg/kg (n=11) or placebo (n=11) over 6 months, then observed for 6 months. The trial's primary outcome was safety; biopsy resolution was a key secondary outcome.
cards.result: At week 24, resolution of morphologic antibody-mediated rejection occurred in 9 of 11 felzartamab patients (82%) vs 2 of 10 placebo patients (20%) — a difference of 62 percentage points (95% CI 19 to 100). The median microvascular inflammation score was lower on felzartamab (0 vs 2.5; mean difference −1.95, 95% CI −2.97 to −0.92), as were the molecular rejection-probability score (0.17 vs 0.77) and donor-derived cell-free DNA (0.31% vs 0.82%). At week 52, rejection had recurred in 3 of the 9 felzartamab responders. Mild or moderate infusion reactions occurred in 8 felzartamab patients; serious adverse events occurred in 1 felzartamab and 4 placebo patients, and 1 placebo patient lost the graft.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, n=22, and powered for safety, not for the biopsy outcome — the 62-point difference carries a very wide interval (19 to 100 points). Biopsy and biomarker outcomes, not graft survival. Flagged on the face as phase 2 evidence only.
cards.source: Mayer KA et al. A Randomized Phase 2 Trial of Felzartamab in Antibody-Mediated Rejection. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 38804514. cards.headline: Diebold 2025 molecular substudy (20 of the same 22 patients): felzartamab suppressed molecular rejection activity in all 9 patients with baseline activity — but molecular recurrence was nearly universal by week 52
cards.summary: Diebold 2025 molecular substudy (20 of the same 22 patients): felzartamab suppressed molecular rejection activity in all 9 patients with baseline activity — but molecular recurrence was nearly universal by week 52
cards.type: Molecular secondary analysis of a phase 2 randomised trial, Nature Medicine 2025
cards.people: Biopsies from 20 participants in the Mayer 2024 trial carded above (10 felzartamab, 10 placebo), analysed by genome-wide microarray before treatment, at week 24 and at week 52. This is a secondary analysis of the same trial, not an independent study — the pack's total evidence base remains N = 22.
cards.result: Felzartamab reduced molecular antibody-mediated rejection activity scores in all nine patients who had baseline molecular activity, selectively suppressing interferon-gamma-inducible and natural-killer-cell transcripts, with minimal effect on stage-related endothelial transcripts. Suppression was often incomplete when baseline activity was intense, and molecular recurrence was nearly universal by week 52 after treatment stopped; molecular injury-score trajectories nevertheless appeared slower at week 52 in the felzartamab group.
cards.watchOut: Same patients as the primary card — it deepens the mechanism and the durability warning, it does not add independent evidence or new patients.

cards.headline: Mayer 2026 open-label extension (11 retreated patients from the same trial): 12 more months of felzartamab lowered rejection activity again — microvascular inflammation score 0 in 7 of 11 — with no treatment discontinuations
cards.summary: Mayer 2026 open-label extension (11 retreated patients from the same trial): 12 more months of felzartamab lowered rejection activity again — microvascular inflammation score 0 in 7 of 11 — with no treatment discontinuations
cards.type: Open-label phase 2 extension study, Lancet Regional Health – Europe 2026
cards.people: 11 of the 21 patients who completed the Mayer 2024 trial, selected because antibody-mediated rejection had recurred or persisted after treatment stopped; they received open-label felzartamab 16 mg/kg for a further 12 months (6 months fixed dosing, then 6 months guided by donor-derived cell-free DNA). No control group. These are the same programme's patients — the total evidence base remains N = 22.
cards.result: Median microvascular inflammation score fell from 2 to 0, with 7 of 11 patients (64%) reaching a score of 0 at week 52 of the extension (one developed low-grade intimal arteritis); median molecular rejection probability fell from 0.77 to 0.12, and donor-derived cell-free DNA, natural killer cells and urinary chemokines decreased, while donor-specific antibodies were largely unchanged. Kidney function was described as stable. Treatment was well tolerated, with mild-to-moderate infusion reactions and no discontinuations; the median number of doses in the biomarker-guided phase was two.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, uncontrolled and selected for recurrence or persistence — regression to the mean and selection cannot be excluded. It shows re-treatment can suppress activity again; it cannot show prolonged treatment improves graft outcomes.
cards.source: Mayer KA et al. Prolonged CD38 targeting with felzartamab in antibody-mediated kidney transplant rejection: a biomarker-guided open-label phase 2 extension. The Lancet regional health. cards.headline: Synthesis: felzartamab suppresses late antibody-mediated rejection activity while it is given — one phase 2 programme, N = 22, graded POSSIBLE with the N on the stamp line
cards.summary: Synthesis: felzartamab suppresses late antibody-mediated rejection activity while it is given — one phase 2 programme, N = 22, graded POSSIBLE with the N on the stamp line
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 2 randomised programme — the Mayer 2024 trial (22 randomised patients), its molecular substudy (20 biopsied patients) and its open-label extension (11 retreated patients). Unique humans across the whole pack: 22.
cards.result: On treatment, the effect on rejection activity is large and internally consistent across morphology (82% vs 20% resolution), microvascular inflammation, molecular scores and cell-free DNA. Off treatment, activity returns — 3 of 9 morphologic responders recurred by week 52 and molecular recurrence was nearly universal — and prolonged re-treatment suppressed activity again in the extension. Nothing in this programme tests graft survival, kidney function decline or patient survival, and late antibody-mediated rejection still has no phase 3 evidence here. Phase 2 evidence only, very small N: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 22.
cards.watchOut: Do not sum the cards' patient counts (22 + 20 + 11): all three reports describe the same 22-person programme. A phase 3 trial with graft outcomes is the evidence this question still lacks.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mayer KA et al., N Engl J Med 2024 (PMID: 38804514); Diebold M et al., Nature Medicine 2025 (PMID: 40301559); Mayer KA et al., Lancet Regional Health – Europe 2026 (PMID: 42471965). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors after kidney transplant: one small randomised trial (n=49) shows a modest HbA1c fall and weight loss with no eGFR or drug-level change; observational cohorts and a pooled synthesis agree on glycaemia and stable graft function, with urinary infection the main cost — graft-survival benefit is association only
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with diabetes or post-transplant diabetes, do SGLT2 inhibitors improve glycaemic control and graft outcomes without increasing infection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Benzhydryl Compounds/therapeutic use · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy,epidemiology,etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucosides/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Kidney Transplantation/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/drug therapy,epidemiology · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/epidemiology,surgery · Transplant Recipients/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — evidence mix labelled on the face: one small randomised trial plus observational cohorts and a synthesis of mostly observational studies; observational evidence caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The randomised trial (Halden 2019, n=49 randomised, 44 completing) found empagliflozin lowered HbA1c modestly against placebo (median change −0.2% vs +0.1%, P=0.025) and cut weight (−2.5 kg vs +1.0 kg), with no significant difference in adverse events, immunosuppressive drug levels or eGFR over 24 weeks. The pooled synthesis (Bellos 2024; SGLT2 inhibitor given to 1,003 recipients across 17 observational studies and the one trial) found HbA1c lower by a mean difference of −0.40% and weight by −2.21 kg, no difference in eGFR, and a urinary-tract-infection odds ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.43–1.64) versus control — no infection excess in the pooled estimate, though single-centre cohorts report urinary infection as the commonest adverse event (10 of 39 patients in Lemke 2022 had an adverse event, urinary infection most common; 43% had stopped the drug, mostly for cost or kidney-function decline). The largest single-centre pre/post cohort (Angjeli 2024, n=125) found eGFR essentially unchanged (64.6 before vs 64.3 mL/min/1.73 m² after), no difference in mean HbA1c, urinary infection 13.6% before vs 12% after (the treatment made no difference), and new genital mycotic infection in 4%. Graft outcomes: no carded study is powered for graft survival; the synthesis's reported association with less graft loss and mortality is preliminary observational data and is presented as such, not as a proven graft benefit. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Halden 2019: empagliflozin lowered HbA1c and weight over 24 weeks in post-transplant diabetes — no eGFR, drug-level or adverse-event difference
cards.summary: Halden 2019: empagliflozin lowered HbA1c and weight over 24 weeks in post-transplant diabetes — no eGFR, drug-level or adverse-event difference
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single-centre, double-blind) — N = 49 randomised, 44 completing
cards.people: 49 renal transplant recipients with posttransplant diabetes mellitus, transplanted more than 1 year earlier, with stable renal function (eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m²) and stable immunosuppression, randomised double-blind to empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks; 44 completed (22 per group, 34 men).
cards.result: Median change in HbA1c was −0.2% (−0.6, −0.1) on empagliflozin vs +0.1% (−0.1, +0.4) on placebo (P=0.025); the glucose reduction depended on GFR and baseline HbA1c. Body weight changed by −2.5 kg vs +1.0 kg (P=0.014). There were no significant differences between groups in adverse events, immunosuppressive drug levels, or eGFR (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes).
cards.watchOut: The only randomised trial on this shelf and it is small and short (24 weeks): it can support a glycaemia claim, not a graft-survival claim. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Halden TAS et al. Efficacy and Safety of Empagliflozin in Renal Transplant Recipients With Posttransplant Diabetes Mellitus. Diabetes care. 2019. PMID: 30862658. Registry ID: NCT03157414 (ClinicalTrials.gov, copied from the record). cards.headline: Bellos 2024 synthesis: across 18 studies, SGLT2 inhibitors lowered HbA1c by 0.40% and weight by 2.21 kg with no eGFR difference and no urinary-infection excess (OR 0.84)
cards.summary: Bellos 2024 synthesis: across 18 studies, SGLT2 inhibitors lowered HbA1c by 0.40% and weight by 2.21 kg with no eGFR difference and no urinary-infection excess (OR 0.84)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies in diabetic kidney transplant recipients (17 observational studies and 1 randomised trial); SGLT2 inhibitors were given to 1,003 patients (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, given to 270 patients, are a separate arm of the review and are not this shelf's question).
cards.result: After SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, HbA1c was lower by a mean difference of −0.40% (95% CI −0.57 to −0.23) and body weight by −2.21 kg (95% CI −2.74 to −1.67), with no difference in eGFR or systolic blood pressure and no significant effect on calcineurin inhibitor levels. The risk of urinary tract infection was similar to placebo/control (odds ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.43–1.64). Preliminary data associated SGLT2 inhibitor use with reduced cardiovascular events, graft loss and mortality, and proteinuria evidence was mixed — those outcome associations are observational and preliminary, as the authors present them.
cards.watchOut: MeSH debt: this record carried no MeSH list in the fetched record, so the fallback text is used. 17 of its 18 studies are observational — confounding by indication is the standing risk, and its graft-loss/mortality association must not be read as trial evidence.

cards.headline: Angjeli 2024 (n=125, pre/post cohort): eGFR and HbA1c unchanged after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, urinary infection 13.6% before vs 12% after, genital mycotic infection 4%
cards.summary: Angjeli 2024 (n=125, pre/post cohort): eGFR and HbA1c unchanged after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor, urinary infection 13.6% before vs 12% after, genital mycotic infection 4%
cards.people: 125 adult kidney transplant recipients with type 2 diabetes (73, 58%) or new-onset diabetes after transplantation (52, 42%) at a single centre, studied retrospectively for 24 months before and after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor; mean follow-up 1.8 years.
cards.result: Mean eGFR was stable: 64.6 mL/min/1.73 m² before vs 64.3 after SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and there was no difference in mean HbA1c after initiation (the treatment made no difference on either in this cohort). The slope of urine albumin excretion improved (P=.002). Urinary tract infection occurred in 13.6% before vs 12% after (P=.68; the treatment made no difference), but was higher in patients with a previous urinary infection (23.5% vs 10.2%). New genital mycotic infection risk was 4% (95% CI 1.3%–9.1%). Acute kidney injury was 8% before vs 10.4% after (P=.51).
cards.watchOut: MeSH debt: no MeSH list in the fetched record; fallback text used. A pre/post design has no parallel control group, so stability of eGFR is reassurance about harm, not proof of graft protection.
cards.source: Angjeli A et al. Single Center Experience With Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter-2 Inhibitors (SGLT2i) in Kidney Transplant Recipients With Diabetes. cards.headline: Lemke 2022 (n=39): HbA1c fell from 8.4% to 7.5%, but 25% had an adverse event (urinary infection commonest) and 43% had stopped the drug
cards.summary: Lemke 2022 (n=39): HbA1c fell from 8.4% to 7.5%, but 25% had an adverse event (urinary infection commonest) and 43% had stopped the drug
cards.people: 39 kidney transplant recipients within one health system prescribed an SGLT2 inhibitor after transplantation for diabetes, reviewed retrospectively; 27 remained on therapy for at least 1 year.
cards.result: Median HbA1c fell from 8.4% [7.8–9.2] at initiation to 7.5% [6.8–8.0] at 3 months and 7.5% [6.5–7.9] at 12 months. Ten patients (25%) experienced an adverse event on therapy, urinary tract infections being the most common. Seventeen patients (43%) had discontinued the SGLT2 inhibitor by chart review, most commonly because of cost and kidney function decline. No meaningful change in kidney function or tacrolimus exposure was observed.
cards.watchOut: No comparator group: the HbA1c fall is a before–after change and could reflect concurrent care. Its value on this shelf is the tolerability picture — infection events and high discontinuation — which the trial was too small to characterise.

cards.headline: Synthesis: modest glycaemic benefit and stable graft function, infection cost real but not increased in pooled data — and no trial evidence yet on graft survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: modest glycaemic benefit and stable graft function, infection cost real but not increased in pooled data — and no trial evidence yet on graft survival
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded evidence: one small randomised trial, one predominantly observational synthesis, and two observational cohorts. No new data.
cards.result: The randomised trial and the pooled synthesis agree: HbA1c falls by roughly 0.2–0.4%, weight by about 2–2.5 kg, eGFR and immunosuppressant levels do not change, and pooled urinary-infection risk is not increased (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.43–1.64) even though urinary infection is the commonest adverse event in clinic cohorts and prior urinary infection predicts recurrence. No carded evidence establishes a graft-survival or mortality benefit — the synthesis's favourable associations are preliminary and observational. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a labelled mix of one small trial plus observational evidence.
cards.watchOut: Scope: this shelf is SGLT2 inhibitors started after kidney transplantation for diabetes/PTDM. The large non-transplant kidney and heart-failure trials excluded transplant recipients and are homed on their own shelves; they do not answer this question.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 30862658, 39458136, 39534785, 35593882). No additional source.
cards.search: synthesis: modest glycaemic benefit and stable graft function, infection cost real but not increased in pooled data — and no trial evidence yet on graft survival synthesis: modest glycaemic benefit and stable graft function, infection cost real but not increased in pooled data — and no trial evidence yet on graft survival in kidney transplant recipients with diabetes or post-transplant diabetes, do sglt2 inhibitors improve glycaemic control and graft outcomes without increasing infection? synthesis synthesis of the carded evidence: one small randomised trial, one predominantly observational synthesis, and two observational cohorts. no new data. the randomised trial and the pooled synthesis agree: hba1c falls by roughly 0.2–0.4%, weight by about 2–2.5 kg, egfr and immunosuppressant levels do not change, and pooled urinary-infection risk is not increased (or 0.84, 95% ci 0.43–1.64) even though urinary infection is the commonest adverse event in clinic cohorts and prior urinary infection predicts recurrence. no carded evidence establishes a graft-survival or mortality benefit — the synthesis's favourable associations are preliminary and observational. proposed stamp: possible (benefit), on a labelled mix of one small trial plus observational evidence. scope: this shelf is sglt2 inhibitors started after kidney transplantation for diabetes/ptdm. the large non-transplant kidney and heart-failure trials excluded transplant recipients and are homed on their own shelves; they do not answer this question. synthesis of the cards on this shelf (pmids 30862658, 39458136, 39534785, 35593882). no additional source.

shelves.title: BK nephropathy: immunosuppression reduction is the accepted backbone — pooled graft loss 8 per 100 patient-years — but adding cidofovir or leflunomide showed no graft-survival benefit in the pooled observational record, and the one randomised adjunct test (levofloxacin prophylaxis) was null with more resistance
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients with BK polyomavirus nephropathy, does reducing immunosuppression (with or without adjuncts such as leflunomide, cidofovir or a fluoroquinolone) improve graft survival compared with standard immunosuppression?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · *Antibiotic Prophylaxis · BK Virus/genetics,isolation & purification · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy/adverse effects · *Kidney Transplantation · Levofloxacin/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Polyomavirus Infections/prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Tumor Virus Infections/prevention & control · Urine/virology · Viral Load · Viremia
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled: apart from one randomised prophylaxis trial, every treatment datum on this shelf is observational, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The systematic review of all published treatment (Johnston 2010; 40 studies) found death-censored graft loss of 8 per 100 patient-years with immunosuppression reduction alone, 8 per 100 patient-years when cidofovir was added, and 13 per 100 patient-years when leflunomide was added — no graft-survival benefit from either adjunct, on a poor evidence base the authors themselves flag. The long-term clinicopathological cohort managed with immunosuppression reduction (Drachenberg 2017; 71 patients, mean follow-up 3.09 years after reduction) recorded graft loss of 15.4%, complete viral clearance in 76% (mean 28 weeks), and rejection in 38% of patients overall — reduction works virologically but the rejection it invites is the main predictor of graft loss. A 2024 comparative cohort (Cho; 175 patients with BK viraemia) found tacrolimus dose reduction cleared virus at least as well as converting to an mTOR inhibitor, with less biopsy-proven rejection at lower viral loads and no difference in 12-month renal function. The one randomised adjunct test is null: levofloxacin prophylaxis did not prevent BK viruria (Knoll 2014; hazard ratio 0.91) and increased resistant infections (the prophylaxis made no difference to BK outcomes). PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for immunosuppression reduction as the backbone; adjuncts unproven.

cards.headline: Johnston 2010 systematic review (40 studies): graft loss 8/100 patient-years with immunosuppression reduction alone, 8 with added cidofovir, 13 with added leflunomide — no adjunct benefit
cards.summary: Johnston 2010 systematic review (40 studies): graft loss 8/100 patient-years with immunosuppression reduction alone, 8 with added cidofovir, 13 with added leflunomide — no adjunct benefit
cards.type: Systematic review of observational treatment studies (40 studies)
cards.people: Systematic review of 40 studies in adult kidney transplant recipients with polyomavirus viruria, viraemia or biopsy-proven polyomavirus-associated nephropathy, treated with immunosuppression reduction alone or combined with cidofovir, leflunomide, intravenous immunoglobulin or ciprofloxacin; primary outcome graft failure.
cards.result: Pooled death-censored graft loss was 8 per 100 patient-years for immunosuppression reduction alone, 8 per 100 patient-years for the addition of cidofovir, and 13 per 100 patient-years for the addition of leflunomide. The authors concluded there does not seem to be a graft survival benefit from adding cidofovir or leflunomide to immunosuppression reduction, while emphasising that the evidence base is poor and adequately powered randomised trials are urgently needed.
cards.watchOut: Almost entirely observational, non-comparative series pooled across eras and regimens: the similar graft-loss rates cannot exclude confounding (sicker patients may receive adjuncts). It is carded as the best available summary of the adjunct question, with that limit on its face.
cards.source: Johnston O et al. Treatment of polyomavirus infection in kidney transplant recipients: a systematic review. Transplantation. 2010. PMID: 20090569. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Drachenberg 2017: after immunosuppression reduction, 76% cleared BK virus but graft loss was 15.4% and rejection affected 38% — rejection, not virus, predicted graft loss
cards.summary: Drachenberg 2017: after immunosuppression reduction, 76% cleared BK virus but graft loss was 15.4% and rejection affected 38% — rejection, not virus, predicted graft loss
cards.type: Observational study (long-term clinicopathological cohort) — N = 71 patients
cards.people: 71 kidney transplant patients with BK virus-associated nephropathy (206 biopsies), followed for a mean of 3.09 ± 1.46 years after immunosuppression reduction, with biopsy features, viral load and creatinine correlated over time.
cards.result: Graft loss was 15.4% (0.8–5.3 years after nephropathy diagnosis); 76% of patients achieved complete viral clearance (mean 28 weeks). Acute rejection occurred in 28% at the second biopsy and 50% subsequently, affecting 38% of patients overall (more than half antibody-mediated). The only predictors of graft loss were acute rejection (T cell-mediated rejection P=0.008) and increased tubulitis and interstitial fibrosis scores in the second biopsy. Higher peak viraemia correlated with poorer viral clearance (P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: No untreated comparator (withholding reduction is not an ethical option), so this card shows the course under reduction, not reduction versus standard immunosuppression in a randomised sense. Its key lesson is the trade-off: viral clearance bought at the price of rejection risk.
cards.source: Drachenberg CB et al. Histological Evolution of BK Virus-Associated Nephropathy: Importance of Integrating Clinical and Pathological Findings. American journal of transplantation. 2017. PMID: 28422412. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cho 2024 (n=175): tacrolimus dose reduction cleared BK virus at least as well as converting to sirolimus, with less rejection at lower viral loads and no renal-function difference
cards.summary: Cho 2024 (n=175): tacrolimus dose reduction cleared BK virus at least as well as converting to sirolimus, with less rejection at lower viral loads and no renal-function difference
cards.people: 175 kidney transplant patients with BK viraemia (initial viral load ≥3 log10) at two Korean tertiary hospitals, 2016–2020, managed either by tacrolimus dose reduction (Reduction group) or by stopping tacrolimus and converting to sirolimus (Conversion group), compared within initial-viral-load strata (3–4 and 4–5 log10).
cards.result: In the higher viral-load stratum (4–5), the Reduction group showed potential effectiveness for viral clearance without statistically significant differences. In the lower stratum (3–4), the Reduction group had superior viral clearance and a lower incidence of biopsy-proven acute rejection than the Conversion group. Renal function over 12 months after BK diagnosis showed no statistically significant difference between the approaches (the conversion strategy made no difference to renal function). The authors concluded dose reduction is the more appropriate approach for viral clearance.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: clinicians chose the strategy, so group differences may reflect patient selection. Graft survival itself was not the reported endpoint — viral clearance, rejection and 12-month renal function were.
cards.source: Cho A et al. A comparative analysis of clinical outcomes between conversion to mTOR inhibitor and calcineurin inhibitor reduction in managing BK viremia among kidney transplant patients. Scientific reports. 2024. PMID: 38834615. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Knoll 2014 randomised trial (n=154): 3 months of levofloxacin did not prevent BK viruria (29% vs 33.3%; HR 0.91) and increased resistant infections (the prophylaxis made no difference)
cards.summary: Knoll 2014 randomised trial (n=154): 3 months of levofloxacin did not prevent BK viruria (29% vs 33.3%; HR 0.91) and increased resistant infections (the prophylaxis made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (multicentre, double-blind, prophylaxis) — N = 154
cards.people: 154 kidney-only transplant recipients at 7 Canadian centres, randomised double-blind within 5 days of transplantation to levofloxacin 500 mg daily (n=76) or placebo (n=78) for 3 months; primary outcome time to BK viruria within the first year; mean follow-up about 46 weeks; the trial stopped early for lack of funding.
cards.result: BK viruria occurred in 22 patients (29%) on levofloxacin and 26 (33.3%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.51–1.63, P=.58) — levofloxacin made no difference to BK viruria, nor to any secondary endpoint (BK viraemia, peak viral load, rejection, patient and graft survival). Resistant infection among isolates usually sensitive to quinolones was more frequent on levofloxacin (14/24 [58.3%] vs 15/45 [33.3%]; risk ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.01–2.98), with a non-significant excess of suspected tendinitis (7.9% vs 1.3%). The authors concluded these findings do not support levofloxacin to prevent posttransplant BK virus infection.
cards.watchOut: This is a prophylaxis trial, not a treatment trial for established nephropathy — it is carded because it is the only randomised test of a fluoroquinolone adjunct in the BK pathway, and its null result plus resistance harm close off that adjunct. Stopped early for funding, so confidence intervals are wide.
cards.source: Knoll GA et al. Levofloxacin for BK virus prophylaxis following kidney transplantation: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25399012. Registry ID: NCT01353339 (ClinicalTrials.gov, copied from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: reduction is the backbone and clears virus in about three-quarters, adjuncts add nothing proven, and rejection after reduction is what costs grafts
cards.summary: Synthesis: reduction is the backbone and clears virus in about three-quarters, adjuncts add nothing proven, and rejection after reduction is what costs grafts
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded evidence: one systematic review of observational treatment studies, two observational cohorts, and one null randomised prophylaxis trial. No new data.
cards.result: Immunosuppression reduction is the only strategy with a consistent record: pooled graft loss 8 per 100 patient-years (PMID 20090569), viral clearance in 76% of a closely followed cohort (PMID 28422412), and simple tacrolimus dose reduction performing at least as well as mTOR-inhibitor conversion (PMID 38834615). Adding cidofovir or leflunomide showed no graft-survival benefit in the pooled record, and levofloxacin prophylaxis was null with more resistance (PMID 25399012; the prophylaxis made no difference). The dominant risk after reduction is rejection, which predicted graft loss in the long-term cohort. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, with the one randomised adjunct test null.
cards.watchOut: Scope: established BK nephropathy/viraemia management after kidney transplant. BK screening schedules and donor/recipient risk prediction are different questions, not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 20090569, 28422412, 38834615, 25399012). No additional source.

shelves.title: Tubuloglomerular feedback: the macula densa reads distal NaCl and, through adenosine-mediated afferent constriction, trims single-nephron GFR — but in humans the loop has never been measured at the nephron; the human evidence is three indirect drug-perturbation studies, so this shelf is stamped EMERGING and says so plainly
shelves.question: How does tubuloglomerular feedback work — what does the macula densa sense, and how does it adjust afferent arteriolar tone and renin release?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzhydryl Compounds/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood,drug therapy,physiopathology · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects,physiology · Glucose Clamp Technique/methods · Glucosides/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Hemodynamics/drug effects,physiology · Humans · Kidney/drug effects,physiology · Male · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2/physiology · *Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — thin-human-evidence flag, stated plainly as the slate required: tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) as a mechanism rests on animal micropuncture; in humans it has never been measured at the single nephron, and every human datum on this shelf is an indirect inference from a drug perturbation. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the macula densa cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus sense NaCl concentration in the tubular fluid leaving the loop of Henle (via Na-K-2Cl cotransport); rising NaCl delivery signals that filtration is more than sufficient, and — through adenosine acting on the afferent arteriole — constricts it, lowering single-nephron GFR, while falling NaCl delivery dilates the arteriole and releases renin. The human studies are consistent with that loop but cannot isolate it. Blocking proximal sodium-glucose reabsorption with empagliflozin increased distal delivery and attenuated hyperfiltration by 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in type 1 diabetes, an effect the authors attribute to TGF mechanisms, accompanied by a rise in renal vascular resistance (Cherney 2014). Blocking proximal salt reabsorption with acetazolamide in obese hyperfiltering men cut GFR by 21% while equipotent furosemide — which blocks the macula densa's own cotransporter — did not, the cleanest human pharmacological dissociation available (Zingerman 2015; N=12). Blocking the proposed mediator tells a weaker story: the adenosine antagonist theophylline did not preserve GFR beyond hydration in contrast studies, though it blunted a tubular-injury marker (Erley 1999) — a null glomerular result, printed as such. Renin-release control at the same apparatus — the baroreceptor, sympathetic and macula-densa inputs to the juxtaglomerular cell — is homed on pack #6305 and cross-pointed, not re-carded here; this shelf is only the feedback's glomerular arm. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, because the human base is indirect inference, however concordant.

cards.headline: Cherney 2014: empagliflozin attenuated hyperfiltration by 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in type 1 diabetes — interpreted by the authors as a tubuloglomerular-feedback effect of increased distal sodium delivery
cards.summary: Cherney 2014: empagliflozin attenuated hyperfiltration by 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in type 1 diabetes — interpreted by the authors as a tubuloglomerular-feedback effect of increased distal sodium delivery
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (mechanistic SGLT2-inhibition trial) — N = 40 (27 hyperfilterers, 13 normal GFR)
cards.people: 40 subjects with type 1 diabetes in an open-label mechanistic trial, stratified by baseline GFR into hyperfilterers (GFR ≥135 mL/min/1.73 m², n=27) and normal-GFR subjects (90–134, n=13), given empagliflozin 25 mg daily for 8 weeks; inulin and para-aminohippurate clearances and renin–angiotensin mediators measured under clamped euglycaemia (4–6 mmol/L, 72–108 mg/dL) and hyperglycaemia (9–11 mmol/L, 162–198 mg/dL).
cards.result: During clamped euglycaemia, hyperfiltration was attenuated by −33 mL/min/1.73 m² in the hyperfilterers (GFR 172 ± 23 → 139 ± 25 mL/min/1.73 m², P<0.01), accompanied by declines in plasma nitric oxide and effective renal plasma flow and an increase in renal vascular resistance (all P<0.01); similar effects occurred during hyperglycaemia. In normal-GFR subjects, GFR and renal parameters were not altered. HbA1c fell in both groups despite lower insulin doses. The authors' conclusion: short-term SGLT2 inhibition attenuated renal hyperfiltration in type 1 diabetes, likely by affecting tubular-glomerular feedback mechanisms — more distal sodium delivery, sensed at the macula densa, constricting the afferent arteriole.
cards.watchOut: Indirect by design: whole-kidney GFR and vascular resistance were measured, not macula-densa NaCl or single-nephron GFR, and the TGF attribution is the authors' mechanistic interpretation. Open-label, no placebo arm. This is the strongest human card available for TGF and its limits are the reason for this shelf's EMERGING stamp.
cards.source: Cherney DZ et al. Renal hemodynamic effect of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Circulation. 2014. PMID: 24334175. Registry ID: NCT01392560 (ClinicalTrials.gov, copied from the record). cards.headline: Zingerman 2015 randomised crossover (n=12): acetazolamide — which raises distal salt delivery — cut GFR by 21%, while equipotent furosemide — which blocks the macula-densa sensor — did not
cards.summary: Zingerman 2015 randomised crossover (n=12): acetazolamide — which raises distal salt delivery — cut GFR by 21%, while equipotent furosemide — which blocks the macula-densa sensor — did not
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (double-blind crossover, mechanistic) — N = 12
cards.people: 12 obese non-diabetic men with glomerular hyperfiltration in a randomised double-blind crossover study, receiving intravenous acetazolamide or furosemide at equipotent natriuretic doses, then the other drug two weeks later; inulin clearance (GFR), para-aminohippurate clearance and fractional lithium excretion measured before and after each drug.
cards.result: GFR decreased by 21% following acetazolamide and did not decrease following furosemide. Renal vascular resistance increased by 12% after acetazolamide and was unchanged after furosemide, while natriuresis and sodium balance were similar with both drugs. The authors' reading is the TGF logic in pharmacological form: acetazolamide inhibits proximal salt reabsorption, increasing salt delivery to the macula densa and activating tubuloglomerular feedback, whereas furosemide acts at the macula densa's own Na-K-2Cl cotransporter and so cannot trigger the same signal — hence the dissociation at equal natriuresis.
cards.watchOut: Small and indirect: 12 men, whole-kidney GFR, and a mechanistic interpretation that depends on the drugs' sites of action being as selective as the textbook describes. It is the most specific human TGF test available — a dissociation design — and still an inference, which is precisely the EMERGING point.
cards.source: Zingerman B et al. Effect of Acetazolamide on Obesity-Induced Glomerular Hyperfiltration: A Randomized Controlled Trial. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 26367377. Registry ID: NCT01146288 (ClinicalTrials.gov, copied from the record). cards.headline: Erley 1999 randomised trial (n=80): the adenosine antagonist theophylline added nothing to hydration for GFR preservation (the treatment made no difference) — the mediator limb is unproven in humans
cards.summary: Erley 1999 randomised trial (n=80): the adenosine antagonist theophylline added nothing to hydration for GFR preservation (the treatment made no difference) — the mediator limb is unproven in humans
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (adenosine antagonism, contrast nephropathy prevention) — N = 80 randomised, 64 completing
cards.people: 80 patients with pre-existing chronic renal insufficiency (creatinine >1.5 mg/dL) receiving more than 100 mL of the contrast medium iopromide, all hydrated from at least 24 hours before to 24 hours after, randomised double-blind to theophylline 810 mg daily (an adenosine receptor antagonist) or placebo; 64 completed the protocol (35 theophylline, 29 placebo).
cards.result: Serum creatinine and creatinine clearance did not change significantly in either group; acute renal failure (creatinine rise of at least 0.5 mg/dL) occurred in 2 theophylline patients (5.7%) and 1 placebo patient (3.4%) — theophylline made no difference to glomerular outcomes. The urinary NAG (tubular injury enzyme) rise reached significance in the placebo group on days 2–3 but not with theophylline. The authors concluded the results indicate a role for adenosine in contrast-induced tubulotoxicity, but that GFR is preserved by hydration alone in these patients and theophylline brought no additional benefit.
cards.watchOut: A null glomerular result for blocking the textbook's proposed TGF mediator, in a contrast-injury setting rather than a feedback experiment — carded honestly as the human mediator evidence being weak/indirect. It does not disprove adenosine's role in TGF; it shows the human test has not confirmed it.
cards.source: Erley CM et al. Prevention of radiocontrast-media-induced nephropathy in patients with pre-existing renal insufficiency by hydration in combination with the adenosine antagonist theophylline. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation. 1999. PMID: 10344353. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a textbook-solid loop with a human evidence base made entirely of drug-perturbation shadows — hence EMERGING, and renin control lives on #6305
cards.summary: Synthesis: a textbook-solid loop with a human evidence base made entirely of drug-perturbation shadows — hence EMERGING, and renin control lives on #6305
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No new data.
cards.result: The macula-densa loop (textbook account) is coherent and, in animals, directly measured. In humans the evidence is three shadows of it: raise distal delivery proximally and GFR falls, whether the tool is an SGLT2 inhibitor (PMID 24334175) or acetazolamide — but not when the sensor itself is blocked by furosemide (PMID 26367377); block the proposed mediator, adenosine, and no glomerular effect is demonstrable (PMID 10344353). That pattern is consistent with TGF operating in humans, and it is not a direct measurement of it — no carded study senses NaCl at a human macula densa or measures a human single-nephron response. The renin-release arm of the same apparatus is a separate, better-evidenced human question, homed on pack #6305 and cross-pointed here without re-carding its studies. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Scope and honesty flag: this shelf answers the glomerular-feedback question only, and stamps it EMERGING because the human base is indirect — if a reader needs the settled human physiology of the same anatomical apparatus, it is renin-release control on pack #6305. SGLT2 inhibitors as diabetes/kidney therapy are treatment shelves, not this physiology.

shelves.title: Countercurrent multiplication: the loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient, urea recycling sustains it, medullary blood flow can wash it out — and the human ceiling is about 1,000 mOsm/kg, falling with age
shelves.question: How does countercurrent multiplication build the medullary osmotic gradient, what washes it out (medullary blood flow, urea recycling), and what is the concentrating ceiling — the maximum urine osmolality a healthy human kidney can reach?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Child · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin · Dietary Proteins/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Kidney Concentrating Ability/physiology · Male · Osmolar Concentration · Regional Blood Flow · Urea/metabolism
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle — NaCl extruded in the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, diluted tubular fluid leaving the loop, and single effects stacked along the corticomedullary axis — builds a medullary interstitial gradient that the vasa recta preserve by countercurrent exchange; urea recycling from the inner medullary collecting duct contributes roughly half the inner medullary osmolality in the textbook's account, and vasopressin-regulated water reabsorption lets final urine approach medullary osmolality. The textbook ceiling of about 1,200 mOsm/kg is the textbook's account: no record fetched this session confirms it directly, and the largest human series carded here measured a mean ceiling near 982 mOsm/kg in 20-year-olds after desmopressin, falling to 823 mOsm/kg by age 80. The human studies carded confirm the three load-bearing pieces in people: the ceiling and its age decline (Tryding, n=212), washout — concentrating capacity fell when medullary blood flow rose in acute pyelonephritis and recovered as flow normalised (Berg, n=14 children) — and the protein/urea dependence of concentrating activity (Hadj-Aïssa, n=10: free-water reabsorption rose 70% after a protein meal under low hydration and tracked urine urea). Animal micropuncture mechanism is textbook prose only, never a card, on this shelf.

cards.headline: Tryding 1988: in 212 healthy adults the desmopressin concentrating ceiling averaged 982 mOsm/kg at age 20 and fell to 823 mOsm/kg by age 80
cards.summary: Tryding 1988: in 212 healthy adults the desmopressin concentrating ceiling averaged 982 mOsm/kg at age 20 and fell to 823 mOsm/kg by age 80
cards.type: Human physiological study (desmopressin concentrating test with age reference intervals), Scand J Urol Nephrol 1988
cards.people: 212 healthy adults aged 20 to 80 years given a single subcutaneous injection of 4 micrograms desmopressin (DDAVP), with maximal urinary osmolality measured as the reference standard for renal concentration capacity; a preliminary arm tested whether strict fluid restriction changed the result.
cards.result: Maximal urinary osmolality after DDAVP did not significantly differ whether strict fluid restriction was kept or not (headache was commoner after fluid deprivation). The ceiling fell steadily with age: mean maximum values ranged from 982 mOsm/kg at 20 years to 823 mOsm/kg at 80 years. This is the human concentrating ceiling as measured — near, but below, the round textbook figure — and it is age-dependent, so a 'normal' maximum in an older adult is lower than in a young adult.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacological (DDAVP) ceiling in healthy volunteers, not a water-deprivation maximum in disease: it defines what the gradient can deliver when vasopressin action is saturated, and says nothing about concentrating ability when the medulla itself is diseased.
cards.source: Tryding N et al. DDAVP test for renal concentration capacity. Age-related reference intervals. Scandinavian journal of urology and nephrology. 1988. PMID: 3206218. cards.headline: Berg 1981: in 14 children with acute pyelonephritis, maximal urine osmolality fell during infection and recovered afterwards — attributed to medullary washout from increased medullary blood flow
cards.summary: Berg 1981: in 14 children with acute pyelonephritis, maximal urine osmolality fell during infection and recovered afterwards — attributed to medullary washout from increased medullary blood flow
cards.type: Human physiological study (clearance studies during and after infection), Kidney Int 1981
cards.people: 14 children aged 5 to 16 years with acute febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis), studied during infection and again within 10 months after it, with inulin and PAH clearances, free-water clearance, urinary sodium excretion and maximal urine osmolality after 18 hours of thirst.
cards.result: Glomerular filtration rate and renal plasma flow were increased during infection and normalised afterwards; urinary sodium excretion, distal sodium delivery and maximal urine osmolality were decreased during infection and increased afterwards, and kidney size was increased during infection. The author postulated that the reduced concentrating capacity is due to a washout effect mediated by an increased medullary blood flow, together with low distal tubular sodium delivery — the human demonstration that raising medullary perfusion dissipates the gradient the countercurrent multiplier builds.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=14) and in infected children: the washout mechanism is the author's postulate from concordant flow and osmolality changes, not a direct medullary osmolality measurement — no human study can sample papillary tissue the way animal micropuncture does.
cards.source: Berg U. Renal function in acute febrile urinary tract infection in children: pathophysiologic aspects on the reduced concentrating capacity. Kidney international. 1981. PMID: 7334747. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hadj-Aïssa 1992: in 10 healthy volunteers a protein meal raised free-water reabsorption 70% under low hydration, and concentrating activity tracked urea — the protein/urea limb of the gradient in humans
cards.summary: Hadj-Aïssa 1992: in 10 healthy volunteers a protein meal raised free-water reabsorption 70% under low hydration, and concentrating activity tracked urea — the protein/urea limb of the gradient in humans
cards.type: Human physiological study (controlled protein meal under two hydration states), Kidney Int 1992
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers studied twice, 2–3 weeks apart, under constant low hydration and constant high hydration, with clearance studies before and for 3 hours after a protein meal of 1.5 g/kg body weight as cooked meat.
cards.result: Baseline urine osmolality was 501 ± 42 mOsm/kg under low hydration versus 99 ± 3 mOsm/kg under high hydration. After the meal, solute-free water reabsorption (TcH2O) increased progressively by 70% under low hydration, while free-water clearance fell 40% under high hydration; plasma vasopressin rose under low hydration only (1.10 to 1.98 pg/mL by hour 3), GFR rose at hour 2 under low hydration only, and excretion rates of sodium, chloride, potassium and urea all increased. GFR correlated positively with TcH2O, urine osmolality and the urine-to-plasma urea ratio under low hydration — the authors concluded the protein effect depends, directly or indirectly, on the urine concentrating activity, i.e. on the urea-supplied medullary gradient.
cards.watchOut: n=10 and a 3-hour window: it shows the concentrating mechanism responding to a urea-generating load, not the steady-state contribution of urea recycling to papillary osmolality, which in humans remains a textbook (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) account rather than a measured quantity.
cards.source: Hadj-Aïssa A et al. Influence of the level of hydration on the renal response to a protein meal. Kidney international. 1992. PMID: 1453605. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: multiplication builds the gradient, exchange preserves it, urea feeds it, flow washes it out — and the measured human ceiling sits near 1,000 mOsm/kg and falls with age
cards.summary: Synthesis: multiplication builds the gradient, exchange preserves it, urea feeds it, flow washes it out — and the measured human ceiling sits near 1,000 mOsm/kg and falls with age
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies (Tryding 1988; Berg 1981; Hadj-Aïssa 1992), framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook accounts.
cards.result: The mechanism itself — the single effect of the thick ascending limb multiplied along the loop, vasa-recta countercurrent exchange limiting dissipation, and urea recycling sustaining the inner medulla — is established physiology whose direct evidence is animal micropuncture; it is presented here as the textbook account, not as human data. What the human record confirms is the mechanism's three testable consequences: a ceiling near 982 mOsm/kg in young adults declining to 823 mOsm/kg by age 80 (Tryding), loss of concentrating capacity when medullary blood flow rises and recovery when it normalises (Berg), and concentrating activity that rises and falls with urea delivery from a protein load (Hadj-Aïssa). The often-quoted 1,200 mOsm/kg maximum is the textbook's round figure; the measured human mean ceiling is lower and age-graded, and any shelf or clinician quoting a ceiling should quote the age alongside it.
cards.watchOut: No carded human study measures medullary interstitial osmolality directly; the gradient's internal composition (NaCl versus urea shares) in humans is inferred, and the synthesis keeps that inference labelled as textbook framing rather than measurement.

shelves.title: Renal acid excretion: titratable acid is capped by phosphate supply, ammonium is the adaptable limb — and in CKD each surviving nephron makes more ammonia even as total ammonium excretion falls
shelves.question: How does the kidney excrete acid — titratable acid versus ammonium — and how does ammonium excretion adapt as chronic kidney disease progresses?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/etiology · Adult · Aged · Ammonia/urine · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Glutamine/blood,metabolism,pharmacology · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications,metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/blood,physiopathology,urine
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: net acid excretion equals titratable acid plus ammonium minus bicarbonate; titratable acid is limited by the supply of urinary buffers, chiefly phosphate, and cannot rise much, whereas ammonium — made from glutamine in the proximal tubule — is the adaptable limb that rises severalfold under a sustained acid load. The carded human studies show both limbs and the CKD twist. In healthy people, glutamine delivery is rate-limiting for ammonium excretion, including after acid-loading adaptation (Welbourne 1972); in renal disease it is not — surviving mass and enzyme activity limit instead. In advanced chronic renal failure, total ammonium excretion was roughly a third of normal (11 vs 32 mEq/day) and titratable acid also fell (18 vs 28 mEq/day), yet expressed per 100 mL of GFR both were markedly increased (Ray 1990): per-nephron adaptation is real but cannot offset nephron loss, which is why acidosis supervenes as CKD advances. The CRIC analysis (Khairallah 2017, n=980) shows the titratable-acid limb being pushed in CKD — higher net acid excretion tracked higher urinary phosphate excretion, the adaptation that supplies more buffer. Healthy acid-load adaptation as a standalone question is a separate later slate row; this pack stays on mechanism plus CKD progression.

cards.headline: Welbourne 1972: in healthy humans, glutamine delivery limits ammonium excretion — an oral glutamine load raised ammonium output in health and in acidosis, but not in renal disease
cards.summary: Welbourne 1972: in healthy humans, glutamine delivery limits ammonium excretion — an oral glutamine load raised ammonium output in health and in acidosis, but not in renal disease
cards.type: Human physiological study (glutamine loading under three acid–base states), J Clin Invest 1972
cards.people: Healthy subjects and patients with intrinsic renal disease (glomerulonephritis, nephrosclerosis), each studied under three acid–base conditions: unaltered balance, ammonium-chloride-induced acidosis, and bicarbonate-induced alkalosis, with a single oral dose of 260 mmol anhydrous L-glutamine in each state. The record does not print the number of participants, so N is not documented on this card.
cards.result: Endogenous plasma glutamine fell during acidosis and rose during alkalosis in both groups. In healthy subjects, oral glutamine raised plasma glutamine markedly over 2–3 hours and increased urinary ammonium excretion under normal conditions and during metabolic acidosis — but not during alkalosis, despite an equal rise in plasma glutamine. In patients with renal disease, glutamine loading failed to increase ammonium excretion significantly in any state even though plasma glutamine rose as high as in healthy subjects. The authors concluded glutamine delivery is rate-limiting for ammonium excretion in healthy subjects, before and after the cellular enzyme adaptation induced by metabolic acidosis, whereas in renal disease surviving renal mass and intracellular enzyme activity are the limits.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, and a single acute glutamine dose tests delivery limitation, not the full multi-day adaptation of ammoniagenesis; the alkalosis arm shows delivery is not the only gate — tubular handling still decides whether ammonia reaches the urine.
cards.source: Welbourne T et al. The effect of glutamine administration on urinary ammonium excretion in normal subjects and patients with renal disease. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1972. PMID: 4555786. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ray 1990: in 19 patients with advanced chronic renal failure, total ammonium excretion was 11 vs 32 mEq/day in normals and titratable acid 18 vs 28 — but per 100 mL of GFR, both were markedly increased
cards.summary: Ray 1990: in 19 patients with advanced chronic renal failure, total ammonium excretion was 11 vs 32 mEq/day in normals and titratable acid 18 vs 28 — but per 100 mL of GFR, both were markedly increased
cards.type: Human physiological study (controlled acid-excretion measurement in advanced CKD), Miner Electrolyte Metab 1990
cards.people: 19 patients with severe but stable chronic renal failure studied under controlled conditions (12 with hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, 3 with elevated-anion-gap acidosis, 4 with mild acidosis), with acid excretion compared against normal subjects.
cards.result: Ammonium excretion was markedly reduced in the renal-failure patients (11 ± 1 vs 32 ± 2 mEq/day in normal subjects, P < 0.005), and urinary titratable acid was likewise diminished (18 ± 2 vs 28 ± 3 mEq/day, P < 0.005). Yet when expressed per 100 mL of GFR, ammonium and titratable acid excretion were markedly increased in all patient groups compared with normal subjects, and the bicarbonate reabsorptive maximum was essentially preserved (22.5 ± 3.7 mEq/L overall). The authors concluded the hyperchloraemic acidosis of advanced renal failure is due to diminished excretion of ammonium and titratable acid in absolute terms — the per-nephron adaptation is genuine but arithmetically overwhelmed by nephron loss.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional and small (n=19), in severe disease only: it fixes the end-stage arithmetic (per-nephron up, total down) but does not map the GFR at which total ammonium excretion first fails to match the daily acid load.
cards.source: Ray S et al. Acid excretion and serum electrolyte patterns in patients with advanced chronic renal failure. Mineral and electrolyte metabolism. 1990. PMID: 2128531. cards.headline: Khairallah 2017 (CRIC, n=980): in CKD, higher net acid excretion tracked higher urinary phosphate excretion — the titratable-acid buffer supply being recruited as ammonium capacity shrinks
cards.summary: Khairallah 2017 (CRIC, n=980): in CKD, higher net acid excretion tracked higher urinary phosphate excretion — the titratable-acid buffer supply being recruited as ammonium capacity shrinks
cards.type: Cross-sectional cohort analysis (CRIC), Am J Kidney Dis 2017
cards.people: 980 participants with chronic kidney disease in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) Study, cross-sectional: net acid excretion measured in 24-hour urine, potential renal acid load estimated from food-frequency questionnaires, and serum bicarbonate, related to 24-hour urinary phosphorus and calcium excretion and serum phosphorus, FGF-23 and parathyroid hormone.
cards.result: Twenty-four-hour urine phosphorus excretion was higher at higher net acid excretion, higher potential renal acid load, and lower serum bicarbonate (each P < 0.05); serum phosphorus was also higher with higher net acid excretion and lower bicarbonate (each P = 0.001), and only higher net acid excretion associated with higher urinary calcium excretion (P < 0.001). Parathyroid hormone was 26% (95% CI 13% to 40%) higher in participants with serum bicarbonate below 22 mEq/L than at or above it (P < 0.001), without consistent FGF-23 or PTH association with net acid excretion itself. The authors' interpretation: in CKD, higher acid load and acidosis associate with augmented phosphaturia — an adaptation that increases titratable acid excretion and thus helps maintain acid–base homeostasis as ammonium excretion fails.
cards.watchOut: Observational and cross-sectional: phosphaturia rising with acid load is consistent with buffer recruitment but cannot prove the kidney raises phosphate excretion in order to carry acid; urine phosphorus also enters the titratable-acid calculation itself, a circularity the authors flag.
cards.source: Khairallah P et al. Acid Load and Phosphorus Homeostasis in CKD. American journal of kidney diseases. 2017. PMID: 28645705. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: titratable acid is the capped limb, ammonium the adaptable one — CKD acidosis is what adaptation looks like when nephron number, not per-nephron effort, becomes the binding constraint
cards.summary: Synthesis: titratable acid is the capped limb, ammonium the adaptable one — CKD acidosis is what adaptation looks like when nephron number, not per-nephron effort, becomes the binding constraint
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies (Welbourne 1972; Ray 1990; Khairallah 2017), framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook accounts.
cards.result: The division of labour is consistent across five decades of human measurement: titratable acid rides on phosphate and cannot expand far, so adaptation to an acid load is ammonium adaptation — glutamine delivery and proximal ammoniagenesis in health (Welbourne). In chronic kidney disease the same adaptation runs per surviving nephron — ammonium and titratable acid excretion per unit GFR are markedly increased (Ray) and phosphate excretion is recruited to feed the titratable limb (Khairallah) — but total ammonium excretion still falls to about a third of normal in advanced failure (11 vs 32 mEq/day), and metabolic acidosis is the residue. The clinical corollary the physiology dictates: a normal serum bicarbonate in mid-stage CKD does not mean acid excretion is unstrained; it means the per-nephron adaptation is still winning.
cards.watchOut: The per-nephron figures rest on GFR-indexed excretion in small classic studies; modern measured-GFR confirmation across CKD stages is thinner than the textbook confidence suggests, and the synthesis does not upgrade it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Welbourne T et al., J Clin Invest 1972 (PMID: 4555786); Ray S et al., Miner Electrolyte Metab 1990 (PMID: 2128531); Khairallah P et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2017 (PMID: 28645705). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
