shelves.title: Blunted thirst in older adults: after 24 hours without water, older men were less thirsty and drank less despite higher plasma osmolality — while their vasopressin response was fully preserved (N = 7 per group in each classic study)
shelves.question: After 24 hours of water deprivation, do healthy older adults report less thirst and drink less than young adults despite equal or greater rises in plasma osmolality — and is vasopressin release preserved while thirst is blunted?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Humans · Male · Osmolar Concentration · Plasma · Sodium/blood · Thirst/physiology · Urine · Vasopressins/metabolism · Water Deprivation/physiology · Water-Electrolyte Balance
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED as a directional finding, on a frankly small base: three classic human experiments, each with 7 older and 7 young men (total N = 42, printed here and on the stamp line per the small-N labelling rule). The answer to both halves of the question is yes. Phillips 1984: after 24 hours of water deprivation, older men (67–75 years) had greater rises in plasma osmolality, sodium and vasopressin than young men (20–31 years) at matched weight loss — yet they were less thirsty, drank less when water returned, and did not dilute their plasma and urine back to pre-deprivation levels; vasopressin osmoreceptor responsiveness was maintained or even increased, and the older men's lower urinary osmolality reflected the known renal concentrating deficit, not lack of hormone. Phillips 1991 isolated the osmotic limb: with hypertonic saline infusion (no volume depletion), older men were less thirsty and drank about a third as much (3.9 vs 11.1 mL/kg), mainly through lower thirst sensitivity to hypertonicity, while plasma vasopressin rises were the same as the young group's. McAloon Dyke 1997 confirmed the functional consequence: with free access to water during a hypertonic challenge, older volunteers' serum osmolality still climbed 17 mosmol/kg (vs 7 in the young) because they drank about half as much. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence cards): thirst and vasopressin are normally driven by the same osmoreceptor input; the ageing dissociation — hormone arm preserved, thirst arm blunted — is the physiological point, and it is why older patients cannot be relied on to drink their way out of hypertonicity.

cards.headline: Phillips 1984: after 24 hours of water deprivation, 7 older men had greater rises in osmolality, sodium and vasopressin than 7 young men — yet were less thirsty, drank less, and did not restore their pre-deprivation levels (N = 7 per group)
cards.summary: Phillips 1984: after 24 hours of water deprivation, 7 older men had greater rises in osmolality, sodium and vasopressin than 7 young men — yet were less thirsty, drank less, and did not restore their pre-deprivation levels (N = 7 per group)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (small, N = 7 per group), New England Journal of Medicine 1984
cards.people: Seven healthy active elderly men (67–75 years) and seven healthy young men (20–31 years), matched for weight loss during 24 hours of water deprivation; thirst, fluid and electrolyte responses and hormonal responses were measured before and after deprivation and during rehydration. Small classic study — N = 7 per group, printed on the face.
cards.result: After deprivation, the older men had greater increases in plasma osmolality, sodium concentration and vasopressin levels than the young men, but their urinary osmolality was lower and they were less thirsty and drank less after deprivation, so their plasma and urine were not diluted back to pre-deprivation levels. Regression analysis indicated increased sensitivity of vasopressin osmoreceptors in the older group, though this difference was not statistically significant. The authors concluded there is a deficit in thirst and water intake in healthy elderly men after water deprivation, while vasopressin osmoreceptor responsiveness is maintained or even increased — and that the age-related urinary concentrating deficit is renal, not a lack of circulating vasopressin.
cards.watchOut: Seven men per group, all healthy and active: the effect direction is clear and was replicated by the later cards, but magnitudes from samples this size are imprecise, and nothing here covers women, the frail elderly, or patients with illness — the groups in whom the clinical risk is highest.
cards.source: Phillips PA et al. Reduced thirst after water deprivation in healthy elderly men. The New England journal of medicine. 1984. PMID: 6472364. cards.headline: Phillips 1991: with pure hypertonicity (hypertonic saline, no volume loss), 7 older men drank 3.9 ± 0.6 mL/kg vs 11.1 ± 1.2 in 7 young men (P <0.001) — lower thirst sensitivity, with identical vasopressin rises (N = 7 per group)
cards.summary: Phillips 1991: with pure hypertonicity (hypertonic saline, no volume loss), 7 older men drank 3.9 ± 0.6 mL/kg vs 11.1 ± 1.2 in 7 young men (P <0.001) — lower thirst sensitivity, with identical vasopressin rises (N = 7 per group)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (small, N = 7 per group; double-blind crossover infusions), American Journal of Physiology 1991
cards.people: Seven healthy community-dwelling non-smoking old men (65–78 years) and seven young men (20–32 years), each receiving 120-minute infusions of hypertonic (0.855 M) and isotonic (0.154 M) saline (0.06 mL/min/kg) in double-blind randomised order at least two weeks apart, after an overnight fast. Small classic study — N = 7 per group, printed on the face.
cards.result: Both groups increased thirst (P <0.001) and water intake (P <0.05) after hypertonic versus isotonic saline. But despite similar plasma sodium increases — and less plasma-volume expansion — the old group was less thirsty (P <0.01) and drank far less room-temperature tap water (old 3.9 ± 0.6 mL/kg vs young 11.1 ± 1.2 mL/kg; P <0.001). The reduced thirst was mainly due to lower thirst sensitivity to hypertonicity (P <0.05), with a tendency toward a higher thirst threshold. Plasma arginine vasopressin increases were similar in old and young groups with hypertonic saline, and did not change significantly with isotonic saline in either group.
cards.watchOut: This is the cleanest dissociation experiment of the three — osmotic stimulus isolated from volume depletion — and still only 14 men. 'Lower sensitivity' (a shallower thirst-versus-osmolality slope) plus a possible threshold shift is the precise claim; a total absence of thirst is not claimed by any card.

cards.search: phillips 1991: with pure hypertonicity (hypertonic saline, no volume loss), 7 older men drank 3.9 ± 0.6 ml/kg vs 11.1 ± 1.2 in 7 young men (p <0.001) — lower thirst sensitivity, with identical vasopressin rises (n = 7 per group) phillips 1991: with pure hypertonicity (hypertonic saline, no volume loss), 7 older men drank 3.9 ± 0.6 ml/kg vs 11.1 ± 1.2 in 7 young men (p <0.001) — lower thirst sensitivity, with identical vasopressin rises (n = 7 per group) after 24 hours of water deprivation, do healthy older adults report less thirst and drink less than young adults despite equal or greater rises in plasma osmolality — and is vasopressin release preserved while thirst is blunted? primary human physiology study (small, n = 7 per group; double-blind crossover infusions), american journal of physiology 1991 seven healthy community-dwelling non-smoking old men (65–78 years) and seven young men (20–32 years), each receiving 120-minute infusions of hypertonic (0.855 m) and isotonic (0.154 m) saline (0.06 ml/min/kg) in double-blind randomised order at least two weeks apart, after an overnight fast. small classic study — n = 7 per group, printed on the face. both groups increased thirst (p <0.001) and water intake (p <0.05) after hypertonic versus isotonic saline. but despite similar plasma sodium increases — and less plasma-volume expansion — the old group was less thirsty (p <0.01) and drank far less room-temperature tap water (old 3.9 ± 0.6 ml/kg vs young 11.1 ± 1.2 ml/kg; p <0.001). the reduced thirst was mainly due to lower thirst sensitivity to hypertonicity (p <0.05), with a tendency toward a higher thirst threshold. plasma arginine vasopressin increases were similar in old and young groups with hypertonic saline, and did not change significantly with isotonic saline in either group. this is the cleanest dissociation experiment of the three — osmotic stimulus isolated from volume depletion — and still only 14 men. 'lower sensitivity' (a shallower thirst-versus-osmolality slope) plus a possible threshold shift is the precise claim; a total absence of thirst is not claimed by any card. phillips pa et al. reduced osmotic thirst in healthy elderly men. the american journal of physiology. 1991. pmid: 1858944. registry id: none in the record (pre-registration era). mesh: adult · aged · aging/blood,physiology · arginine vasopressin/blood · humans · male · osmolar concentration · osmosis · sodium/blood · thirst/physiology

cards.headline: McAloon Dyke 1997: with free access to water during hypertonic saline infusion, 7 older volunteers' serum osmolality still rose 17 mosmol/kg vs 7 in 7 young volunteers — they drank about half as much (N = 7 per group)
cards.summary: McAloon Dyke 1997: with free access to water during hypertonic saline infusion, 7 older volunteers' serum osmolality still rose 17 mosmol/kg vs 7 in 7 young volunteers — they drank about half as much (N = 7 per group)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (small, N = 7 per group), Geriatric Nephrology and Urology 1997
cards.people: Seven healthy young volunteers (20–28 years) and seven healthy old volunteers (72–89 years), given free access to water during and after a two-hour intravenous infusion of 5% hypertonic saline at 0.06 mL/kg/min; cumulative water intake and serum osmolality were compared between groups. Small classic study — N = 7 per group, printed on the face.
cards.result: Serum osmolality and water intake differed markedly between groups. In the old group, serum osmolality increased by 17 mosmol/kg above baseline despite free access to water; in the young group it rose only 7 mosmol/kg and did not rise further, because by ingesting water the young defended against additional increase. The young drank approximately twice as much as the old during the infusion period. The authors concluded that healthy older individuals drink less than the young despite significantly increased serum osmolality — a hypodipsia that increases susceptibility to hypertonicity.
cards.watchOut: The oldest group here (72–89 years) extends the age range of the Phillips studies, but the design is again 14 healthy volunteers under an artificial infusion challenge; it demonstrates failure to defend osmolality when drinking is voluntary, which is the clinically relevant behaviour, in miniature.
cards.source: McAloon Dyke M et al. Effects of hypertonicity on water intake in the elderly: an age-related failure. Geriatric nephrology and urology. 1997. PMID: 9422434. cards.headline: Synthesis: thirst blunts with age while vasopressin does not — three small concordant experiments, total N = 42 — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (small-N base, printed)
cards.summary: Synthesis: thirst blunts with age while vasopressin does not — three small concordant experiments, total N = 42 — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (small-N base, printed)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above, framed by Guyton & Hall, Ganong's Review and Boron & Boulpaep as named in the balance.
cards.result: Across water deprivation (Phillips 1984), isolated hypertonicity (Phillips 1991) and free-drinking defence of osmolality (McAloon Dyke 1997), the pattern is identical: older men sense less thirst per unit of osmotic stimulus, drink roughly a third to a half as much, and fail to correct the rise in osmolality — while vasopressin release to the same stimulus is preserved or increased. The dissociation localises the ageing defect to the thirst arm of osmoregulation (sensitivity, and possibly threshold), not to osmoreception as a whole and not to the hormone. The stamp reads ESTABLISHED for direction because three independent small experiments agree and no fetched record contradicts them; the total base of 42 participants is printed on the stamp line and on every card, as the small-N rule requires.
cards.watchOut: All 42 participants across the three studies were healthy men; extrapolation to older women and to sick or frail inpatients is physiological reasoning, not fetched evidence, and this shelf presents it as such.
cards.source: Synthesis of Phillips PA et al. N Engl J Med. 1984 (PMID: 6472364); Phillips PA et al. Am J Physiol. 1991 (PMID: 1858944); McAloon Dyke M et al. Geriatr Nephrol Urol. 1997 (PMID: 9422434). Registry IDs: none in the records. MeSH: as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Renal adaptation to an acid load: ammonium excretion climbs over days to ~200 mmol/day (ceiling 200–300), and net acid excretion rises to match the load
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does the kidney adapt to a sustained acid load over days — how much do ammonium excretion and net acid excretion rise, and over what time course?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis, Renal Tubular · Adult · Ammonia · Bicarbonates · Female · Growth Hormone · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Kidney · Male · Natriuresis · Sodium Chloride, Dietary · Urine
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account of the time course: titratable acid can rise only modestly because it is capped by urinary phosphate, so the adaptable limb is ammonium — made from glutamine in the proximal tubule — which climbs over roughly 3–5 days of sustained loading as ammoniagenic enzymes are induced, from a baseline of a few tens of mmol/day to a plateau at which net acid excretion (titratable acid + ammonium − bicarbonate) equals the daily acid load and plasma bicarbonate stabilises at a new, lower steady state; that shape and the baseline figure are the textbook account. The carded human studies quantify the adapted state the textbook describes: under NH4Cl at 4.2 mmol/kg/day for 7 days, healthy subjects excreted 202 ± 17 mmol/day of ammonium (Jehle 2000); in chronic metabolic acidosis urinary ammonia excretion was 186% higher and total ammonia production 110% higher than in non-acidemic controls, with 82% (versus 65%) of produced ammonia partitioned into urine (Garibotto 2004); and the quantified ceiling is an ammonium excretion of 200–300 mmol/day, with loaded fasted controls excreting 176 ± 26 mmol/day of net acid (Kamel 1990). The acute phase is separately testable within hours by a single 50 mEq NH4Cl load (Bobulescu 2013). Refused anchor, reported plainly: the Pitts programme's 1949 balance studies (e.g. PMID 18127528) carry no abstract in their PubMed records, so no numbers could be verified from the record and they are not carded. Adjacency: renal acid excretion in CKD — per-nephron adaptation as total ammonium falls — is Pack #6358; its references (PMIDs 4555786, 2128531, 28645705) are deliberately not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Jehle 2000: under sustained ammonium-chloride loading (4.2 mmol/kg/day for 7 days), healthy subjects excreted ~200 mmol of ammonium a day — the adapted state in which net acid excretion matches the load
cards.summary: Jehle 2000: under sustained ammonium-chloride loading (4.2 mmol/kg/day for 7 days), healthy subjects excreted ~200 mmol of ammonium a day — the adapted state in which net acid excretion matches the load
cards.type: Human physiology study (sustained NH4Cl acid loading, Jehle, Hulter & Krapf 2000)
cards.people: 4 normal subjects on a sodium-restricted intake (0.3 mmol/kg/day) studied through three phases: chronic metabolic acidosis from NH4Cl 4.2 mmol/kg/day for 7 days, then acidosis plus growth hormone for 5 days, then plus dietary NaCl for 6 days, with daily urine net acid excretion, ammonium, pH and plasma bicarbonate. N = 4 for this protocol arm — very small, labelled plainly; the study's comparisons rest on the group's previously reported salt-replete NH4Cl-fed subjects.
cards.result: During chronic acidosis, urinary ammonium excretion was 202 ± 17 mmol/24 h, essentially unchanged by growth hormone (211 ± 19 mmol/24 h) while sodium was restricted, and plasma bicarbonate sat at 14.2 ± 0.8 mmol/L (rising only to 15.0 ± 1.1 with growth hormone). When dietary NaCl was added, a large increment in net acid excretion accumulated (233 ± 20 mmol over the phase) and plasma bicarbonate rose to 18.7 ± 1.3 mmol/L — ammonia production had risen with adaptation, but obligating it into net acid excretion required distal sodium-dependent acidification.
cards.watchOut: N = 4 and a deliberately sodium-restricted design testing a growth-hormone question — the carded ammonium level (~200 mmol/day under load) is the adapted-state value; the day-by-day rise is the textbook account in the balance, not a curve measured in this small protocol.
cards.source: Jehle S et al. On the mechanism of growth hormone-induced stimulation of renal acidification in humans: effect of dietary NaCl. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 2000. PMID: 10887057. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garibotto 2004: in chronic metabolic acidosis, urinary ammonia excretion was 186% higher and total ammonia production 110% higher than in non-acidemic controls, with 82% of produced ammonia partitioned into urine
cards.summary: Garibotto 2004: in chronic metabolic acidosis, urinary ammonia excretion was 186% higher and total ammonia production 110% higher than in non-acidemic controls, with 82% of produced ammonia partitioned into urine
cards.type: Human physiology study (renal ammoniagenesis in chronic acidosis, Garibotto 2004)
cards.people: 11 subjects with normal renal function undergoing venous catheterisation, 5 studied in metabolic acidosis and 6 in normal acid–base balance, with renal mass-balance and [14C]leucine isotope techniques measuring kidney protein dynamics, ammonia production and urinary ammonia excretion.
cards.result: Urinary ammonia excretion and total ammonia production were 186% and 110% higher, respectively, in acidemic subjects than controls, and more of the ammonia produced was shifted into urine (82% versus 65%). Kidney protein degradation fell to match synthesis in acidosis (significantly lower than in controls, P < 0.05), and across all studies protein degradation and net balance were inversely related to urinary ammonia excretion and its urinary partition.
cards.watchOut: Subjects were patients undergoing venous catheterisation for clinical reasons, with normal renal function — not screened healthy volunteers; the acidosis was chronic metabolic acidosis, not a standardised NH4Cl protocol. Percentages are relative to the study's own control group.
cards.source: Garibotto G et al. Kidney protein dynamics and ammoniagenesis in humans with chronic metabolic acidosis. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2004. PMID: 15153572. cards.headline: Kamel 1990: a large inorganic acid load is eliminated because ammonium excretion can rise to 200–300 mmol/day; fasted controls excreted 176 ± 26 mmol/day of net acid on the load
cards.summary: Kamel 1990: a large inorganic acid load is eliminated because ammonium excretion can rise to 200–300 mmol/day; fasted controls excreted 176 ± 26 mmol/day of net acid on the load
cards.type: Human physiology study (inorganic acid load disposal, Kamel 1990)
cards.people: Subjects with ketoacidosis of chronic fasting and fasted control subjects, each consuming a large inorganic acid load, with net acid excretion (conventional and expanded definitions), blood bicarbonate and ketoacid anions measured in steady state.
cards.result: The record's framing measurement: when a large inorganic acid load is ingested by normals, the proton load is eliminated because the rate of ammonium excretion can rise to 200 to 300 mmol/day. Fasted controls on the load excreted 176 ± 26 mmol/day of net acid by the conventional definition, versus 136 ± 6 mmol/day in the chronic-fasting ketoacidotic subjects — whose blood bicarbonate was nonetheless only slightly lower (13 ± 0.6 versus 15 ± 0.5 mmol/L), because they reabsorbed ketoacid anions ('potential bicarbonate') at a much higher fractional rate (97% versus 77%).
cards.watchOut: A fasting/ketoacidosis model, not fed healthy volunteers on NH4Cl — carded for the quantified ceiling of ammonium excretion (200–300 mmol/day) and the control net-acid value, both stated in the record. Subject numbers are not documented in the fetched record ('N not documented').
cards.source: Kamel KS et al. Removal of an inorganic acid load in subjects with ketoacidosis of chronic fasting. Kidney international. 1990. PMID: 2232494. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bobulescu 2013: a single 50 mEq ammonium-chloride load in 8 healthy controls produced an hourly ammonium excretory response over 4 hours that uric-acid stone formers could not match
cards.summary: Bobulescu 2013: a single 50 mEq ammonium-chloride load in 8 healthy controls produced an hourly ammonium excretory response over 4 hours that uric-acid stone formers could not match
cards.type: Human physiology study (acute acid load test, Bobulescu 2013)
cards.people: 14 patients with idiopathic uric acid nephrolithiasis, 13 patients with type 2 diabetes and 8 healthy control subjects of similar BMI, equilibrated on a fixed diet for 5 days, then given a single oral acid load of 50 mEq ammonium chloride with hourly urine collections for 4 hours.
cards.result: Uric acid stone formers had a lower ammonium excretory response to acute acid loading than diabetic and non-diabetic non-stone formers — an ammonium excretory defect unmasked by the challenge. The healthy controls define the normal acute response against which the defect was shown; the fetched record reports the group contrast without printing the controls' hourly ammonium values, so none are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: Acute (hours), not sustained (days) loading — this card anchors the early phase and the clinical acid-load test; the sustained adaptation is carried by the Jehle and Garibotto cards. The study's purpose was a disease contrast, with healthy controls as the reference arm (n = 8).
cards.source: Bobulescu IA et al. Renal ammonium excretion after an acute acid load: blunted response in uric acid stone formers but not in patients with type 2 diabetes. American journal of physiology. Renal physiology. 2013. PMID: 24026180. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 4 + 11 + 8 healthy or normal-renal-function subjects in the quantified arms, plus fasted controls (N not documented) in Kamel 1990.
cards.result: The kidney meets a sustained acid load mainly by making and excreting ammonium: from a normal output of a few tens of mmol/day (textbook account) ammonium excretion rises over days to ~200 mmol/day and can reach 200–300 mmol/day, urinary ammonia excretion runs ~186% above non-acidemic controls with a greater share of produced ammonia partitioned into urine, and net acid excretion rises to match the load (~176 mmol/day measured in loaded controls). An acute 50 mEq load tests the early response within hours. Cross-point: how this system fails as nephrons are lost in CKD is Shelf/Pack #6358, whose references are not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The classic Pitts-programme balance studies (1949) were refused as evidence cards because their PubMed records carry no abstract to verify numbers from; the time-course shape in the balance is labelled textbook account. Carded Ns are small, as throughout this classic literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jehle S et al., Clinical science (London, England : 1979) 2000 (PMID: 10887057); Garibotto G et al., Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN 2004 (PMID: 15153572); Kamel KS et al., Kidney international 1990 (PMID: 2232494); Bobulescu IA et al., American journal of physiology. shelves.question: In adults with primary FSGS, does sparsentan, compared with irbesartan, slow eGFR decline and reduce proteinuria?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent; Adult; Aged; Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers; Child; Creatinine; Dose-Response Relationship, Drug; Double-Blind Method; Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists; Female; Glomerulosclerosis, Focal Segmental; Humans; Irbesartan; Male; Middle Aged; Proteinuria; Spiro Compounds; Sulfonamides; Young Adult
shelves.balance: ⚠ PARTIAL — READ FIRST: the adult DUPLEX phase 3 trial (Rheault et al., N Engl J Med 2023, PMID: 37921461) is already carded inside pack #1742 (the paediatric-subgroup shelf, where the parent trial is its first card) and that PMID is on the gated carded list, so DUPLEX is NOT re-carded here; #1742 is the home to consult for DUPLEX, whose own result — proteinuria lower on sparsentan but the eGFR-slope primary endpoint not met — bounds everything below. This pack builds only the uncovered remainder of the adult question from ≥3 free reports, all from the earlier DUET programme. In DUET's 8-week double-blind phase (109 randomised, 96 analysed; ages 8-75, so a mixed adult-paediatric phase 2 population), sparsentan reduced urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 45% versus 19% on irbesartan (p=0.006), with the FSGS partial remission endpoint reached by 28% versus 9% (p=0.04). In the open-label extension (108 patients receiving sparsentan, follow-up to 4.6 years, no comparator), proteinuria reductions were sustained, 52.8% achieved partial remission within 9 months, and achieving remission was associated with slower eGFR decline (-2.70 vs -6.56 mL/min per 1.73 m² per year; p=0.03) — an association inside uncontrolled follow-up, not a randomised effect. A DUET post-hoc analysis likewise linked complete proteinuria remission (43% at least once over a median 47 months) with slower eGFR decline. Hypotension and oedema were the characteristic adverse effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, proteinuria only) — the eGFR half of the question is not answered affirmatively by any evidence carded here, and DUPLEX (in #1742) answered it negatively on its primary endpoint.

cards.headline: DUET double-blind phase (96 analysed): sparsentan cut proteinuria 45% versus 19% on irbesartan at 8 weeks (p=0.006); partial remission 28% vs 9% (p=0.04)
cards.summary: DUET double-blind phase (96 analysed): sparsentan cut proteinuria 45% versus 19% on irbesartan at 8 weeks (p=0.006); partial remission 28% vs 9% (p=0.04)
cards.people: 109 patients aged 8-75 years with biopsy-proven primary FSGS, eGFR >30 mL/min per 1.73 m² and urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio ≥1.0 g/g, randomised to sparsentan 200, 400 or 800 mg/day or irbesartan 300 mg/day for 8 weeks (96 received study drug with baseline and week-8 measurements), followed by open-label sparsentan. A mixed adult and paediatric phase 2 population — the adult-only randomised evidence is the gated DUPLEX trial homed in pack #1742.
cards.result: Urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell more with sparsentan than irbesartan when all doses were pooled (45% vs 19% reduction; p=0.006) and at the 400/800 mg doses (47% vs 19%; p=0.01). The FSGS partial remission endpoint (ratio ≤1.5 g/g and >40% reduction) was achieved by 28% on sparsentan versus 9% on irbesartan (p=0.04). Blood pressure fell with sparsentan but not irbesartan; eGFR was stable in both groups over 8 weeks. Adverse events were similar overall; hypotension and oedema were more common on sparsentan but caused no withdrawals.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks, proteinuria surrogate only, and not adults-only (ages 8-75): this card cannot answer the eGFR half of the question, and it must not be presented as the adult phase 3 result — that is DUPLEX, homed in pack #1742.

cards.headline: DUET open-label extension (108 patients, up to 4.6 years, no comparator): proteinuria falls were sustained; achieving partial remission within 9 months (52.8%) was associated with slower eGFR decline (-2.70 vs -6.56; p=0.03)
cards.summary: DUET open-label extension (108 patients, up to 4.6 years, no comparator): proteinuria falls were sustained; achieving partial remission within 9 months (52.8%) was associated with slower eGFR decline (-2.70 vs -6.56; p=0.03)
cards.people: 109 patients enrolled in DUET; 108 received at least one sparsentan dose and 103 entered the open-label extension (68 previously on sparsentan, 35 previously on irbesartan), followed from first sparsentan dose through 4.6 years with urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio, eGFR and blood pressure roughly every 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean percent proteinuria reduction from baseline was sustained through follow-up, and sparsentan was still being taken by 45 of 108 patients (41.7%) at analysis (median time to discontinuation 3.9 years). Patients achieving the partial remission endpoint within 9 months (52.8%) had a significantly slower eGFR decline over the whole period than those who did not (-2.70 vs -6.56 mL/min per 1.73 m² per year; p=0.03). Commonest treatment-emergent events (>9 per 100 patient-years) were headache, peripheral oedema, upper respiratory infection, hyperkalaemia and hypotension; oedema and hypotension fell to ≤4% after year 1. No heart-failure cases and no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: No comparison group: the remission-versus-eGFR association is observational within a treated cohort (patients destined to remit may have milder disease), and 58% had stopped sparsentan by analysis, so long-term figures describe a selected continuing population.

cards.headline: DUET post-hoc remission analysis (108 patients): complete proteinuria remission at least once (43% over a median 47 months) was associated with significantly slower eGFR decline
cards.summary: DUET post-hoc remission analysis (108 patients): complete proteinuria remission at least once (43% over a median 47 months) was associated with significantly slower eGFR decline
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a phase 2 trial and its extension (DUET)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of all 108 DUET participants who received at least one sparsentan dose (double-blind period plus open-label extension), with complete remission defined as urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio ≤0.3 g/g in a first morning sample; median follow-up 47.0 months.
cards.result: Forty-six patients (43%) achieved complete remission at least once, 61% of them within 12 months of starting sparsentan; higher dose and baseline subnephrotic-range proteinuria made remission more likely. Achieving complete remission was associated with a significantly slower rate of eGFR decline versus non-remitters (p<0.05). Immunosuppressant use was more frequent among remitters, though sparsentan's antiproteinuric effect appeared additive to it. No unanticipated adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and associational: remission may be a marker of treatment-responsive, lower-risk disease rather than the mechanism of slower decline, and concomitant immunosuppression confounds the comparison.
cards.source: Trachtman H et al. Implications of Complete Proteinuria Remission at any Time in Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis: Sparsentan DUET Trial. Kidney international reports. 2023. PMID: 37850006. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Desmopressin in uraemia: bleeding time shortened in every patient in the 1983 crossover trial — a 28-patient evidence base built on a surrogate
shelves.question: In patients with kidney failure and uraemic platelet dysfunction, does desmopressin, compared with placebo or no treatment, shorten the bleeding time and reduce bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antigens · Arginine Vasopressin · Bleeding Time · Clinical Trials as Topic · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin · Double-Blind Method · Factor VIII · Female · Fibrinogen · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Function Tests · Random Allocation · Uremia · von Willebrand Factor
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 28 randomised patients, and on a surrogate outcome. In the anchor randomised double-blind crossover trial (Mannucci et al., PMID: 6401193), all 12 uraemic patients with haemorrhagic tendencies and prolonged bleeding times had a shortened bleeding time after desmopressin infusion, lasting at least four hours in most, with rises in factor VIII coagulant activity and larger von Willebrand-factor multimers; a second double-blind crossover study (Malyszko et al., PMID: 1697836) found bleeding time fell from 21.3 ± 8 to 11.5 ± 6 minutes (p < 0.001) in 16 uraemic haemodialysis patients, with no change on placebo. What has never been shown in a randomised trial is fewer clinical bleeding events: the only systematic review of desmopressin before kidney biopsy (Lim et al., PMID: 32040251; 2 studies, 738 biopsies) rated the evidence low quality and insufficient to support routine use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for temporary correction of the bleeding time; clinical bleeding prevention is unproven.

cards.headline: Mannucci 1983: desmopressin shortened the bleeding time in all 12 uraemic patients in a randomised double-blind crossover trial
cards.summary: Mannucci 1983: desmopressin shortened the bleeding time in all 12 uraemic patients in a randomised double-blind crossover trial
cards.people: 12 patients with uraemia, haemorrhagic tendencies and prolonged bleeding times received either desmopressin (1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin) or placebo in a randomised double-blind crossover design. Nine additional patients with acute or chronic renal failure and prolonged bleeding times were given the compound openly before major surgery or renal biopsy.
cards.result: After desmopressin infusion, all 12 trial patients had shortened bleeding times, with the effect lasting at least four hours in most cases. Platelet count, platelet cyclic AMP, platelet retention on glass beads, plasma fibronectin, serum thromboxane B2, residual prothrombin, haematocrit and plasma osmolarity were unchanged; factor VIII coagulant activity rose consistently, with smaller rises in factor VIII-related antigen and ristocetin cofactor, and larger von Willebrand-factor multimers appeared in plasma. In the nine openly treated patients, shortening of the bleeding time was associated with normal haemostasis at surgery or biopsy.
cards.watchOut: Twelve patients, 1983, and the endpoint is the bleeding time — a laboratory surrogate that predicts clinical bleeding imperfectly. The surgical series (9 patients) was uncontrolled. Print the N: this is a very small base.
cards.source: Mannucci PM et al. Deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin shortens the bleeding time in uremia. N Engl J Med. 1983. PMID: 6401193. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Malyszko 1990: bleeding time fell from 21.3 to 11.5 minutes on desmopressin in 16 uraemic haemodialysis patients — no change on placebo
cards.summary: Malyszko 1990: bleeding time fell from 21.3 to 11.5 minutes on desmopressin in 16 uraemic haemodialysis patients — no change on placebo
cards.people: 16 uraemic patients maintained on chronic haemodialysis received intravenous desmopressin 0.4 micrograms/kg or placebo in a double-blind crossover study; bleeding time, platelet serotonin and haemostasis parameters were measured.
cards.result: Bleeding time shortened significantly after desmopressin, from 21.3 ± 8 minutes to 11.5 ± 6 minutes (p < 0.001). Factor VIII antigen rose from 239.1 ± 94% to 473 ± 293% (p < 0.01), euglobulin lysis time shortened from 238 ± 101 to 148 ± 84 minutes (p < 0.005), and platelet serotonin fell from 532 ± 141 to 366 ± 88 ng/10(9) platelets (p < 0.02). Haematocrit, platelet count, factor VIII coagulant activity and blood serotonin did not change, and there were no changes in the placebo periods.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic crossover study in 16 patients from a low-circulation journal; it confirms the bleeding-time effect and its time course, not protection against real bleeding.

cards.headline: Lim 2021 systematic review: prospective evidence for desmopressin before kidney biopsy is low quality and insufficient — 2 studies, 738 biopsies
cards.summary: Lim 2021 systematic review: prospective evidence for desmopressin before kidney biopsy is low quality and insufficient — 2 studies, 738 biopsies
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials, quasi-randomised trials and prospective cohorts comparing desmopressin with placebo or no intervention before percutaneous native or transplant kidney biopsy (search to May 2019). Two studies — one RCT and one prospective cohort, together 738 native kidney biopsies — met the inclusion criteria; desmopressin was a single subcutaneous dose of 0.3 micrograms/kg in both.
cards.result: Data were not pooled because of clinical heterogeneity. GRADE quality of evidence was low for desmopressin preventing any bleeding complication after native kidney biopsy, and low-quality evidence suggested adverse effects were not increased. No prospective studies evaluated desmopressin in transplant kidney biopsies. The authors conclude the available prospective data are insufficient to support routine use of desmopressin before percutaneous kidney biopsy and that high-quality trials are required.
cards.watchOut: This is the clinical-outcome slice of the question and it is nearly empty: one of the two studies enrolled patients with serum creatinine ≤1.5 mg/dL (132 micromol/L) and/or eGFR ≥60 — barely uraemic at all.
cards.source: Lim CC et al. Desmopressin acetate to prevent bleeding in percutaneous kidney biopsy: a systematic review. Intern Med J. 2021. PMID: 32040251. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Biopsy · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin · Hemorrhage · Hemostatics · Humans · Kidney

cards.result: Two small double-blind crossover trials from 1983 and 1990, totalling 28 uraemic patients, agree that a single dose of desmopressin shortens the prolonged uraemic bleeding time for at least four hours, alongside rises in factor VIII and von Willebrand factor. No randomised trial has tested clinical bleeding, transfusion or procedural outcomes, and the biopsy systematic review found the prospective evidence low quality and insufficient. The honest verdict is a short-lived laboratory correction in a very small, old evidence base.
cards.watchOut: Desmopressin in kidney failure also carries hyponatraemia and fluid-retention risks that these small trials were not sized to measure; the stamp covers the bleeding-time effect only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mannucci PM et al. N Engl J Med. 1983 (PMID: 6401193); Malyszko J et al. Folia Haematol Int Mag Klin Morphol Blutforsch. 1990 (PMID: 1697836); Lim CC et al. Intern Med J. 2021 (PMID: 32040251). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Pre-dialysis midodrine for intradialytic hypotension: nadir systolic pressure up roughly 10–18 mm Hg in four small crossover-era studies — no placebo-controlled trial of size
shelves.question: In patients on haemodialysis with intradialytic hypotension, does pre-dialysis midodrine, compared with placebo or no treatment, reduce hypotensive episodes and improve dialysis tolerance?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic alpha-Agonists · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Pressure · Diastole · Dizziness · Fatigue · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypotension · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Midodrine · Prospective Studies · Pulse · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — every study is small, old and from the crossover era, but they point the same way on blood pressure. In the first prospective series (Cruz et al., PMID: 9398120), 10 haemodialysis patients with persistent intradialytic hypotension had a lowest intradialytic systolic pressure of 114.7 mm Hg on pre-dialysis midodrine versus 96.6 mm Hg off it (P < 0.001), with uniform subjective improvement in cramps, fatigue, dizziness and weakness. A crossover comparison (Cruz et al., PMID: 10213650; 11 patients) found the lowest intradialytic systolic pressure was 103.9 mm Hg with midodrine and 102.6 mm Hg with cool dialysate versus 90.6 mm Hg in the control phase, with fewer nursing interventions and less saline infused; the one double-blind placebo-controlled crossover (Cotera et al., PMID: 12434648; 10 patients) found smaller falls in systolic pressure on midodrine (19.3 ± 28 mm Hg) than on placebo (23.4 ± 28 mm Hg), without statistical testing of the difference in the record. No trial was powered for symptoms, hospitalisation or death, and the only systematic review of this literature is already carded elsewhere in the library and so is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): midodrine raises the intradialytic pressure nadir; how much that helps patients feel or fare better is untested at scale.

cards.headline: Cruz 1997: lowest intradialytic systolic pressure 114.7 vs 96.6 mm Hg on pre-dialysis midodrine in 10 patients — symptoms improved in all
cards.summary: Cruz 1997: lowest intradialytic systolic pressure 114.7 vs 96.6 mm Hg on pre-dialysis midodrine in 10 patients — symptoms improved in all
cards.people: 10 haemodialysis patients with persistent intradialytic hypotension received midodrine (mean dose 5.5 mg, range 5–10 mg) 30 minutes before each session; blood pressure, pulse, weight and symptoms were compared over 10 consecutive dialysis sessions off and on midodrine.
cards.result: Lowest intradialytic systolic blood pressure improved from 96.6 to 114.7 mm Hg (P < 0.001), lowest diastolic from 53.2 to 59.0 mm Hg (P = 0.002) and lowest mean arterial pressure from 67.7 to 77.6 mm Hg (P < 0.001); post-haemodialysis systolic pressure rose from 116.5 to 127.1 mm Hg (P < 0.001). Pre-dialysis pressures did not change. Improvements were accompanied by uniform subjective improvement in cramps, fatigue, dizziness and weakness; the only adverse effect was scalp paraesthesia in one patient.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, no placebo and no blinding — expectation and regression to the mean can produce exactly this pattern in symptomatic hypotension. N printed on the face deliberately.
cards.source: Cruz DN et al. Intradialytic hypotension: is midodrine beneficial in symptomatic hemodialysis patients? Am J Kidney Dis. 1997. PMID: 9398120. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic alpha-Agonists · Blood Pressure · Hypotension · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Midodrine · Renal Dialysis

cards.headline: Cruz 1999 crossover: midodrine and cool dialysate each raised the pressure nadir by about 13 mm Hg over control in 11 patients; combining them added nothing
cards.summary: Cruz 1999 crossover: midodrine and cool dialysate each raised the pressure nadir by about 13 mm Hg over control in 11 patients; combining them added nothing
cards.people: 11 patients (6 men, 5 women; mean age 67.5 years) with known symptomatic intradialytic hypotension passed through a control phase and three 9-treatment phases: midodrine 10 mg orally pre-dialysis, cool dialysate (35.5 °C), and the combination. Blood pressures, weights, laboratory values and interventions for hypotension were recorded.
cards.result: Lowest intradialytic systolic pressure was 103.9 ± 4.1 mm Hg with midodrine and 102.6 ± 2.9 mm Hg with cool dialysate versus 90.6 ± 2.5 mm Hg in the control phase (P < 0.001 for both); post-dialysis systolic pressures were likewise higher (116.9 and 118.2 vs 109.0 mm Hg; P < 0.01). The combination phase (103.7 mm Hg) was no better than either treatment alone. Nursing interventions and saline volume for hypotension fell significantly with both treatments, symptoms trended better, and Kt/V did not change.
cards.watchOut: Eleven patients, unblinded, and the comparison that matters clinically — midodrine versus the free alternative of cool dialysate — showed the two to be equivalent, not additive.
cards.source: Cruz DN et al. Midodrine and cool dialysate are effective therapies for symptomatic intradialytic hypotension. Am J Kidney Dis. 1999. PMID: 10213650. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Blood Pressure · Cold Temperature · Cross-Over Studies · Hemodialysis Solutions · Hypotension · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Midodrine · Renal Dialysis

cards.headline: Cotera 2002: the one double-blind placebo-controlled crossover — pressure fell less on midodrine (systolic fall 19.3 vs 23.4 mm Hg) in 10 patients
cards.summary: Cotera 2002: the one double-blind placebo-controlled crossover — pressure fell less on midodrine (systolic fall 19.3 vs 23.4 mm Hg) in 10 patients
cards.people: 10 patients on chronic haemodialysis with a history of hypotension during the procedure received midodrine 10 mg orally or placebo for 5 dialysis procedures each in a double-blind crossover design; blood pressure before and during dialysis was compared between periods.
cards.result: Pre-dialysis blood pressures were similar in the two periods. During dialysis, systolic blood pressure fell 19.3 ± 28 mm Hg with midodrine and 23.4 ± 28 mm Hg with placebo; diastolic pressure fell 7.3 ± 11.5 mm Hg versus 11.1 ± 12 mm Hg, and the reduction in mean arterial pressure was also less pronounced with midodrine. The authors conclude midodrine lessens the fall in arterial pressure during haemodialysis in patients with symptomatic hypotension.
cards.watchOut: The standard deviations (±28 mm Hg) are larger than the difference between treatments, and the abstract reports no significance test for the between-period difference — the most rigorous design here is also the least decisive.
cards.source: Cotera A et al. [Effects of midodrine on symptomatic hypotension during hemodialysis]. Rev Med Chil. 2002. PMID: 12434648. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Hypotension · Midodrine · Renal Dialysis

cards.headline: Alappan 2001: adding high dialysate calcium to midodrine and/or cool dialysate improved pressures further in 23 patients with severe hypotension — but caused hypercalcaemia in 22%
cards.summary: Alappan 2001: adding high dialysate calcium to midodrine and/or cool dialysate improved pressures further in 23 patients with severe hypotension — but caused hypercalcaemia in 22%
cards.people: 28 patients with severe intradialytic hypotension entered a prospective crossover study of high dialysate calcium concentration (3.5 mEq/L) added to midodrine and/or cool dialysate versus low dialysate calcium; 23 completed the study and 5 dropped out because of hypercalcaemia.
cards.result: Adding high dialysate calcium significantly improved post-haemodialysis mean arterial pressure (95.6 ± 12.7 versus 90.8 ± 12.5 mm Hg; P = 0.002) and reduced the falls in mean arterial pressure from pre-dialysis to the intradialytic nadir (16.3 ± 8.2 versus 20.6 ± 10.0 mm Hg; P = 0.009) and to post-dialysis (2.0 ± 8.5 versus 8.15 ± 10.8 mm Hg; P = 0.002). There were no significant improvements in symptoms of, or interventions for, intradialytic hypotension, and hypercalcaemia complicated therapy in 22% of patients.
cards.watchOut: This card tests the calcium add-on, not midodrine itself — it is included because its midodrine-treated population shows the ceiling of the combined approach: pressures improve, symptoms and interventions do not, and a fifth of patients became hypercalcaemic.
cards.source: Alappan R et al. Treatment of Severe Intradialytic Hypotension With the Addition of High Dialysate Calcium Concentration to Midodrine and/or Cool Dialysate. Am J Kidney Dis. 2001. cards.headline: Synthesis: the pressure nadir rises about 10–18 mm Hg across four small studies; patient-important benefit is unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pressure nadir rises about 10–18 mm Hg across four small studies; patient-important benefit is unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of Cruz DN et al. Am J Kidney Dis. 1997 (PMID: 9398120); Cruz DN et al. Am J Kidney Dis. 1999 (PMID: 10213650); Cotera A et al. Rev Med Chil. 2002 (PMID: 12434648); Alappan R et al. Am J Kidney Dis. 2001 (PMID: 11157369).
cards.result: Four small studies (10–23 patients each, 1997–2002, largely one research group) consistently show pre-dialysis midodrine raising the lowest intradialytic blood pressure, roughly matching cool dialysate and adding nothing to it. The single double-blind placebo-controlled trial is the weakest numerically. No study measured hospitalisation, mortality or dialysis adequacy at scale, so the verdict rests on a haemodynamic surrogate in a few dozen patients.
cards.watchOut: Studies of 10–11 patients cannot detect uncommon harms such as supine hypertension or ischaemic events; the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, for exactly that reason.

shelves.title: Fosinopril in haemodialysis (FOSIDIAL): the primary endpoint was not met — relative risk 0.93 in 397 patients, and the class meta-analysis agrees
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with cardiovascular disease, does the ACE inhibitor fosinopril, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Female · Forecasting · Fosinopril · Humans · Hypertension · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Placebos · Renal Dialysis · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). In FOSIDIAL (Zannad et al., PMID: 16871247), 397 haemodialysis patients with left ventricular hypertrophy were randomised to fosinopril 5 mg titrated to 20 mg daily (n = 196) or placebo (n = 201) for 24 months; the intention-to-treat analysis found no significant benefit on the composite of fatal and nonfatal major cardiovascular events (adjusted relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.68–1.26, P = 0.35). A per-protocol secondary analysis (n = 380) showed only a trend (adjusted relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.59–1.1, P = 0.099). The wider randomised record agrees: a meta-analysis of five ACE-inhibitor/ARB trials in 1,582 dialysis patients (Georgianos et al., PMID: 36069890) found no significant reduction in cardiovascular events (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11), cardiovascular mortality or all-cause mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the confidence intervals still admit a moderate benefit, so this is 'not shown to work' rather than proof of no effect.

cards.headline: FOSIDIAL 2006: fosinopril did not significantly reduce cardiovascular events in 397 haemodialysis patients — adjusted RR 0.93 (0.68–1.26)
cards.summary: FOSIDIAL 2006: fosinopril did not significantly reduce cardiovascular events in 397 haemodialysis patients — adjusted RR 0.93 (0.68–1.26)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial — FOSIDIAL main results (Zannad 2006)
cards.people: 397 patients with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis and left ventricular hypertrophy were randomised to fosinopril 5 mg titrated to 20 mg daily (n = 196) or placebo (n = 201), plus conventional therapy, for 24 months. The primary endpoint was the combined fatal and nonfatal first major cardiovascular event: cardiovascular death, resuscitated death, nonfatal stroke, heart failure, myocardial infarction or revascularisation.
cards.result: No significant benefit for fosinopril was observed in the intention-to-treat analysis (n = 397) after adjusting for independent predictors of cardiovascular events (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.68–1.26, P = 0.35) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint. The per-protocol secondary supportive analysis (n = 380) found a trend towards benefit (adjusted relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.59–1.1, P = 0.099). In patients hypertensive at baseline, systolic and diastolic pressures fell significantly more on fosinopril than on placebo. The authors note the trends might have become significant with a larger sample and warrant further study.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered optimistically for a population with very high event rates; the 95% CI (0.68–1.26) cannot exclude a 32% relative benefit. A null this wide is 'unproven', and the per-protocol trend is hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Zannad F et al. Prevention of cardiovascular events in end-stage renal disease: results of a randomized trial of fosinopril and implications for future studies. Kidney Int. 2006. PMID: 16871247. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FOSIDIAL predictors analysis 2007: prior cardiovascular disease, CRP, LV mass, diabetes and age — not treatment — drove events in the same 397 patients
cards.summary: FOSIDIAL predictors analysis 2007: prior cardiovascular disease, CRP, LV mass, diabetes and age — not treatment — drove events in the same 397 patients
cards.people: The same 397 FOSIDIAL participants with end-stage renal disease and left ventricular hypertrophy, followed for 2 years with adjudicated cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, revascularisation, heart failure hospitalisation, resuscitated cardiac arrest). A forward-selection risk model and a structural equation model were built from baseline variables.
cards.result: A history of cardiovascular disease was the most important prognostic factor for events, followed by C-reactive protein, left ventricular mass index, diabetes and age; smoking, low HDL, female sex and Kt/V were indirectly associated. The authors conclude that prior cardiovascular disease, elevated CRP, left ventricular hypertrophy, diabetes or advanced age identifies the patients at highest risk, and that effective approaches to reduce events in this population still need to be found.
cards.watchOut: This is a prognostic analysis of the trial cohort, not a second treatment comparison — it is carded to show what actually predicted events in FOSIDIAL's population, and it must not be counted as independent evidence about fosinopril.
cards.source: Kessler M et al. Predictors of cardiovascular events in patients with end-stage renal disease: an analysis from the Fosinopril in dialysis study. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2007. cards.headline: Georgianos 2023 meta-analysis: five ACE-inhibitor/ARB trials in 1,582 dialysis patients — no significant reduction in cardiovascular events (RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11)
cards.summary: Georgianos 2023 meta-analysis: five ACE-inhibitor/ARB trials in 1,582 dialysis patients — no significant reduction in cardiovascular events (RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Georgianos 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials comparing ACE inhibitors or ARBs with placebo or no add-on treatment in patients receiving dialysis, requiring fatal or nonfatal cardiovascular events as a primary efficacy endpoint (search to February 2022). Five trials involving 1,582 dialysis patients were included, FOSIDIAL among them.
cards.result: ACE-inhibitor/ARB use was not associated with a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular events (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11), cardiovascular mortality (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.59–1.14) or all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.64–1.15). Results were consistent across subgroups by hypertension, ethnicity, sample size, follow-up duration and quality. The authors conclude these agents are not associated with significantly lower cardiovascular event or mortality risk in dialysis patients.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate mixes ACE inhibitors and ARBs and only five trials; the confidence interval still includes a 43% relative reduction in events, so the class verdict is 'not demonstrated', not 'disproven'.
cards.source: Georgianos PI et al. Effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers on cardiovascular outcomes in dialysis patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2023. PMID: 36069890. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one dedicated trial and the class meta-analysis both miss significance — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one dedicated trial and the class meta-analysis both miss significance — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of Zannad F et al. Kidney Int. 2006 (PMID: 16871247); Kessler M et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2007 (PMID: 17611249); Georgianos PI et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2023 (PMID: 36069890).
cards.result: FOSIDIAL, the only placebo-controlled trial of fosinopril in haemodialysis, found a relative risk of 0.93 (0.68–1.26) for major cardiovascular events over 24 months, and the five-trial ACE-inhibitor/ARB meta-analysis in dialysis found 0.79 (0.57–1.11) — both point estimates favour treatment, neither reaches significance, and no dialysis trial since has settled the question. Blood pressure does fall on fosinopril in hypertensive dialysis patients; event prevention is unproven.
cards.watchOut: Do not import the non-dialysis ACE-inhibitor evidence into this population: FOSIDIAL exists precisely because extrapolation failed, and its population (all with left ventricular hypertrophy) is narrower than 'haemodialysis patients' generally.

shelves.title: Carvedilol in dialysis cardiomyopathy (Cice): two-year mortality 51.7% vs 73.2% in one 114-patient single-centre trial — capped at POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In haemodialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy or reduced ejection fraction, does carvedilol, compared with placebo, improve survival and ventricular function?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Aged · Carbazoles · Cardiomyopathy, Dilated · Carvedilol · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kidney Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Propanolamines · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small trial, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE however large the effect looks. In the Cice trial (PMID: 12742278), 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy were randomised to carvedilol or placebo on top of standard therapy: at two years 51.7% of the carvedilol group had died versus 73.2% on placebo (p < 0.01) — a 21.5-percentage-point absolute difference — with fewer cardiovascular deaths (29.3% vs 67.9%) and hospital admissions (34.5% vs 58.9%). The one-year report (PMID: 11216954) showed ejection fraction rising from 26.3% to 34.8% on carvedilol with reduced ventricular volumes. A meta-analysis of beta-blockers in dialysis (Jin et al., PMID: 31039562) found the randomised pool — only 363 patients across 3 trials, this trial dominant — gave a relative risk of 0.73 (95% CI 0.54–0.97) for all-cause mortality, while its observational pool showed no significant cardiovascular mortality difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent and the mechanism plausible, but one single-centre trial of 114 patients from 2003 has never been replicated in this population.

cards.headline: Cice 2001 (one-year report): ejection fraction rose from 26.3% to 34.8% on carvedilol in 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.summary: Cice 2001 (one-year report): ejection fraction rose from 26.3% to 34.8% on carvedilol in 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.people: 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and symptomatic heart failure (NYHA class II or III) were randomised to carvedilol or placebo added to conventional therapy for 12 months in a double-blind trial, with echocardiography at baseline and 1, 6 and 12 months and NYHA class assessed at 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: In the carvedilol group, left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 26.3% to 34.8% (p < 0.05 versus baseline and placebo), left ventricular end-diastolic volume fell from 100 to 94 mL/m2 and end-systolic volume from 74 to 62 mL/m2, all significant by six months and maintained at one year. NYHA functional class improved during treatment, and at the end of the trial no carvedilol patient was in NYHA class IV, compared with 5.9% of the placebo arm.
cards.watchOut: This is the first-year report of the same 114 patients as the survival paper — one trial, not two. Echocardiographic endpoints in a single centre, with the survival claim resting on the follow-up report.
cards.source: Cice G et al. Dilated cardiomyopathy in dialysis patients--beneficial effects of carvedilol: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2001. PMID: 11216954. cards.headline: Cice 2003 (two-year report): mortality 51.7% on carvedilol vs 73.2% on placebo — cardiovascular deaths 29.3% vs 67.9%
cards.summary: Cice 2003 (two-year report): mortality 51.7% on carvedilol vs 73.2% on placebo — cardiovascular deaths 29.3% vs 67.9%
cards.people: The same 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy randomised to carvedilol or placebo in addition to standard therapy, analysed at one year and followed for a further 12 months, with two-year echocardiography, mortality, cardiovascular death and hospital admission outcomes.
cards.result: At two years, 51.7% of patients in the carvedilol group had died, compared with 73.2% in the placebo group (p < 0.01) — an absolute difference of 21.5 percentage points. Cardiovascular deaths (29.3% vs 67.9%) and hospital admissions (34.5% vs 58.9%) were significantly fewer on carvedilol (p < 0.00001 for both comparisons as reported). Two-year echocardiography showed attenuated remodelling, with smaller cavity diameters and higher ejection fractions on carvedilol. Fatal myocardial infarctions, fatal strokes and admissions for worsening heart failure were also lower; reductions in sudden and pump-failure deaths did not reach significance.
cards.watchOut: A 21.5-point absolute mortality difference from 114 patients at one centre is implausibly large as a stable estimate — small trials overestimate. Two-year mortality above 50% in both arms also marks how selected and sick this population was.
cards.source: Cice G et al. Carvedilol increases two-year survival in dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy: a prospective, placebo-controlled trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2003. PMID: 12742278. cards.headline: Jin 2019 meta-analysis: beta-blocker randomised pool in dialysis is only 363 patients — all-cause mortality RR 0.73 (0.54–0.97); observational cardiovascular mortality null
cards.summary: Jin 2019 meta-analysis: beta-blocker randomised pool in dialysis is only 363 patients — all-cause mortality RR 0.73 (0.54–0.97); observational cardiovascular mortality null
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials and observational studies of beta-blockers in adult dialysis patients (search to May 2018): 3 RCTs and 9 observational studies met the criteria, with outcomes of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, cardiovascular events and hospitalisations.
cards.result: The RCTs showed beta-blockers associated with reduced all-cause mortality (n = 363; relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.54–0.97), cardiovascular mortality (n = 314; relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.29–0.68), cardiovascular events (n = 363; relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.31–0.88) and hospitalisations (n = 314; relative risk 0.61, 95% CI 0.48–0.78). The observational studies (n = 35,233) showed lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.80–0.92) but no significant difference in cardiovascular mortality (n = 19,413; hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11) or cardiovascular events. The authors caution that heterogeneity and the small randomised pool limit the strength of the findings.
cards.watchOut: The randomised pool is three small trials of which Cice is the largest — the meta-analysis largely repackages the single trial rather than independently confirming it.
cards.source: Jin J et al. Effects of Beta-Blockers on Cardiovascular Events and Mortality in Dialysis Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Blood Purif. 2019. PMID: 31039562. cards.headline: Synthesis: one unreplicated 114-patient trial carries the whole claim — POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the single-trial rule
cards.summary: Synthesis: one unreplicated 114-patient trial carries the whole claim — POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the single-trial rule
cards.people: Synthesis of Cice G et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2001 (PMID: 11216954); Cice G et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2003 (PMID: 12742278); Jin J et al. Blood Purif. 2019 (PMID: 31039562).
cards.result: Carvedilol improved ejection fraction within a year and was associated with substantially lower two-year mortality in the only randomised trial ever run in dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. The non-dialysis heart-failure beta-blocker evidence cannot be imported directly — dialysis patients were excluded from those trials — and no second dialysis trial exists. The effect size should be read as an upper bound from a small, single-centre, pre-registration-era trial.
cards.watchOut: The trial predates trial registration and modern dialysis-era background therapy; carvedilol is also dialysable to a degree that later dialysability comparisons have questioned. None of that negates the trial — it bounds how far it travels.

shelves.title: Early erythropoietin to prevent AKI: EARLYARF was null, and the 2024 Cochrane review of 5,348 patients agrees — the treatment made no difference
shelves.question: In patients at risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery or in critical illness, does early erythropoietin, compared with placebo, prevent AKI or reduce dialysis or death?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase · Biomarkers · Creatinine · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Erythropoietin · Female · Hematinics · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Kidney Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Placebo Effect · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Treatment Outcome · Triage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The anchor trial, EARLYARF (Endre et al., PMID: 20164823), randomised 162 biomarker-positive intensive-care patients (of 529 screened) to two doses of erythropoietin or placebo within hours of a urinary biomarker rise: there was no difference in the primary outcome (relative average plasma creatinine increase over 4–7 days) or in erythropoietin-specific adverse events. Note the population honestly: EARLYARF enrolled general ICU patients triaged by urinary gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase × alkaline phosphatase, not cardiac-surgery patients specifically. The cardiac-surgery slice agrees: a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs in 423 patients (Tie et al., PMID: 25312524) found no significant reduction in cardiac-surgery AKI overall (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.35–1.16). The definitive synthesis is the 2024 Cochrane review (Nishiwaki et al., PMID: 39301879): 20 studies, 5,348 participants — erythropoiesis-stimulating agents probably make little or no difference to AKI (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85–1.10; moderate-certainty) or death (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06), and may make little or no difference to starting dialysis (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.90–1.51). One smaller meta-analysis (Shin et al., PMID: 35244046) reports a benefit confined to pre-operative dosing — a subgroup signal the Cochrane analysis, testing timing and dose explicitly, did not confirm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: EARLYARF 2010: biomarker-triggered early erythropoietin did not change creatinine outcome in 162 randomised ICU patients — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: EARLYARF 2010: biomarker-triggered early erythropoietin did not change creatinine outcome in 162 randomised ICU patients — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: 529 patients in two general intensive care units were screened with urinary gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase; 162 whose biomarker concentration product rose above 46.3 were randomised within an average of 3.5 hours of the positive sample to two doses of erythropoietin or placebo. The primary outcome was the relative average plasma creatinine increase from baseline over 4 to 7 days.
cards.result: There was no difference in the primary outcome between the placebo and erythropoietin groups, and no difference in the incidence of erythropoietin-specific adverse events — the treatment made no difference. The triggering biomarkers did select patients with more severe illness and greater risk of AKI, dialysis or death, but the marker elevations were transient, which the authors note compromised effective triage; they conclude the biomarker composite was insufficient for risk stratification in a population with heterogeneous onset of injury. Early high-dose erythropoietin was safe but did not alter outcome.
cards.watchOut: EARLYARF is an ICU trial, not a cardiac-surgery trial — the slate question's cardiac-surgery framing is carried by the meta-analysis cards, and this card's population is stated plainly so the two are not conflated.
cards.source: Endre ZH et al. Early intervention with erythropoietin does not affect the outcome of acute kidney injury (the EARLYARF trial). Kidney Int. 2010. PMID: 20164823. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Acute Disease · Alkaline Phosphatase · Biomarkers · Creatinine · Double-Blind Method · Erythropoietin · Intensive Care Units · Kidney Diseases · Treatment Outcome · Triage

cards.headline: Tie 2015 meta-analysis (cardiac surgery): 5 RCTs, 423 patients — AKI relative risk 0.64 (0.35–1.16), not significant
cards.summary: Tie 2015 meta-analysis (cardiac surgery): 5 RCTs, 423 patients — AKI relative risk 0.64 (0.35–1.16), not significant
cards.type: Meta-analysis of RCTs in cardiac surgery (Tie 2015)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials of erythropoietin for prevention of cardiac surgery-associated AKI in adults: 5 RCTs involving 423 patients, with subgroup analysis by AKI risk factors.
cards.result: Overall, erythropoietin was not associated with a reduced incidence of cardiac surgery-associated AKI (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.35–1.16), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 67.4%). In the subgroup without high risk factors for AKI, erythropoietin did significantly reduce AKI (relative risk 0.38, 95% CI 0.24–0.61) and shortened ICU and hospital stay; the authors attribute the heterogeneity to high-risk-factor status and caution that the finding rests on few studies and needs high-quality RCTs.
cards.watchOut: The 'low-risk patients benefit' subgroup is counter-intuitive (protection where injury is least likely) and is exactly the kind of split that small heterogeneous meta-analyses generate by chance; the Cochrane review below found no such pattern by background disease.
cards.source: Tie HT et al. Erythropoietin administration for prevention of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Shin 2022 meta-analysis: pre-operative erythropoietin subgroup showed less AKI (OR 0.60) across 8 cardiac-surgery RCTs, 610 patients — a timing subgroup, not the overall verdict
cards.summary: Shin 2022 meta-analysis: pre-operative erythropoietin subgroup showed less AKI (OR 0.60) across 8 cardiac-surgery RCTs, 610 patients — a timing subgroup, not the overall verdict
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of perioperative erythropoietin in cardiac surgery: 8 RCTs with 610 patients, primary outcome incidence of cardiac surgery-associated AKI, with subgroup analysis by timing of administration (pre-, intra- or post-operative).
cards.result: Erythropoietin significantly decreased the incidence of AKI (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43–0.85, P = 0.004; I2 = 52%), intra-operative red-cell transfusion and hospital stay (mean difference −1.54 days, 95% CI −2.70 to −0.39). Subgroup analysis showed the AKI reduction was confined to pre-operative administration; erythropoietin given intra- or post-operatively did not reduce AKI. The authors conclude pre-operative treatment can be considered to improve postoperative outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Carded because it is the strongest contrary signal — but it is a timing subgroup across 610 patients, and the larger Cochrane synthesis, which tested route, dose and duration explicitly, found no difference in any subgroup. Read the two together.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2024: 20 studies, 5,348 participants — ESAs probably make little or no difference to AKI (RR 0.97, 0.85–1.10) or death
cards.summary: Cochrane 2024: 20 studies, 5,348 participants — ESAs probably make little or no difference to AKI (RR 0.97, 0.85–1.10) or death
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials comparing erythropoiesis-stimulating agents with placebo or standard care in people at risk of AKI in any setting (search to 30 August 2024): 20 studies, 5,348 participants, study sizes 10 to 1,302, mostly single-centre.
cards.result: ESAs probably make little or no difference to the risk of AKI (18 studies, 5,314 participants: relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.10; moderate-certainty evidence) or death (18 studies, 5,263 participants: relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06; moderate-certainty), and may make little or no difference to initiation of dialysis (14 studies, 2,059 participants: relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51; low-certainty). No differences emerged by route of administration, background disease (cardiac surgery, children or neonates, other at-risk adults), dose or duration; thrombosis risk was also similar (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.24). The authors conclude ESAs probably do not reduce AKI or death and advise caution in using them to prevent AKI.
cards.watchOut: Two ongoing studies were unpublished at the review date; the authors note it is unclear whether they will change the results. Moderate certainty is not high certainty — but it is the strongest verdict this question has.
cards.source: Nishiwaki H et al. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents for preventing acute kidney injury. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024. PMID: 39301879. cards.summary: Synthesis: a null anchor trial, a null cardiac-surgery pool and a moderate-certainty Cochrane null — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

cards.result: The animal rationale for erythropoietin as a kidney protectant did not survive human testing: EARLYARF's early, biomarker-triggered dosing was null, the cardiac-surgery trial pool is null overall, and the 5,348-patient Cochrane synthesis finds no reduction in AKI, dialysis or death in any subgroup it tested. The residual pre-operative-timing signal from one smaller meta-analysis is a hypothesis, not a practice basis.
cards.watchOut: Safety was reassuring throughout (no excess thrombosis signal in the Cochrane pool) — this is a verdict of no benefit, not of harm.

shelves.title: Parathyroidectomy vs medical therapy in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: every comparison is observational — surgery carries a 3.1% 30-day mortality, then lower long-term mortality in matched cohorts
shelves.question: In dialysis patients with severe secondary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy, compared with medical therapy (calcimimetics or vitamin D analogues), improve survival, fractures and symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Case-Control Studies · Cohort Studies · Databases, Factual · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroidectomy · Renal Dialysis · Risk · Survival Analysis · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OBSERVATIONAL EVIDENCE ONLY: no randomised trial of parathyroidectomy versus medical therapy in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism exists, and every number on this shelf comes from cohorts in which sicker or more refractory patients are selected for surgery. The largest matched cohort (Kestenbaum et al., PMID: 15496173; 4,558 parathyroidectomy patients matched to 4,558 USRDS controls) found a 3.1% 30-day postoperative mortality, survival curves that crossed at 587 days, and long-term relative risks of death 10–15% lower after surgery (median survival 53.4 vs 46.8 months). Against cinacalcet specifically, a Japanese propensity-matched cohort (Komaba et al., PMID: 35277957; 894 surgery vs 2,682 cinacalcet) found a mortality hazard ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.67–0.91), and a USRDS matched analysis (Alvarado et al., PMID: 35022799) found hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.70–0.85) but a higher rate of pathologic fractures after surgery (27.8% vs 24.9%). A meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies (Song et al., PMID: 38583772; 24,398 patients) pooled an all-cause mortality hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.61) — yet in its subgroup where the medical group all received cinacalcet, the difference vanished (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.49–2.11). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), labelled observational: surgery plausibly helps the most severe, refractory cases live longer, at a real upfront operative risk, and confounding by indication could manufacture much of the apparent benefit.

cards.headline: Kestenbaum 2004: 4,558 matched pairs — 3.1% died within 30 days of parathyroidectomy, then long-term mortality ran 10–15% lower; median survival 53.4 vs 46.8 months
cards.summary: Kestenbaum 2004: 4,558 matched pairs — 3.1% died within 30 days of parathyroidectomy, then long-term mortality ran 10–15% lower; median survival 53.4 vs 46.8 months
cards.people: 4,558 US dialysis patients undergoing a first parathyroidectomy while on haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, individually matched by age, race, sex, cause of end-stage renal disease, dialysis duration, prior transplantation status and modality to 4,558 control patients who did not undergo parathyroidectomy, followed from the date of surgery until death or loss to follow-up.
cards.result: The 30-day postoperative mortality rate following parathyroidectomy was 3.1%. Long-term relative risks of death among patients undergoing parathyroidectomy were estimated to be 10% to 15% lower than in matched controls, but the survival curves crossed 587 days after surgery — surgery cost lives early and was associated with fewer deaths later. Median survival was 53.4 months (95% CI 51.2–56.4) in the parathyroidectomy group and 46.8 months (95% CI 44.7–48.9) in the control group.
cards.watchOut: Observational: matching cannot remove confounding by indication — patients referred for surgery differ from those managed medically in severity, frailty and clinician expectation, in directions that can favour either arm. The crossing curves are the honest picture: harm first, association with benefit later.
cards.source: Kestenbaum B et al. Survival following parathyroidectomy among United States dialysis patients. Kidney Int. 2004. PMID: 15496173. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Cohort Studies · Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Parathyroidectomy · Renal Dialysis · Survival Analysis · United States
