cards.headline: Komaba 2022: parathyroidectomy vs cinacalcet in Japan — mortality HR 0.78 (0.67–0.91) over 6 years in propensity-matched cohorts (894 vs 2,682)
cards.summary: Komaba 2022: parathyroidectomy vs cinacalcet in Japan — mortality HR 0.78 (0.67–0.91) over 6 years in propensity-matched cohorts (894 vs 2,682)
cards.people: Patients in the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy Renal Data Registry with intact PTH ≥300 pg/mL in late 2007 who underwent parathyroidectomy or started cinacalcet in 2008–2009, matched 1:3 by propensity score: 894 parathyroidectomy patients and 2,682 cinacalcet patients, median baseline intact PTH 588 and 566 pg/mL respectively, followed for all-cause mortality within 6 years.
cards.result: Parathyroidectomy produced greater reductions in intact PTH, calcium and phosphorus than cinacalcet. During 6 years, 201 patients (22.5%) in the parathyroidectomy group and 736 (27.4%) in the cinacalcet group died; parathyroidectomy was associated with a lower mortality risk (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.91; P = 0.002). The association was more pronounced at intact PTH ≥500 pg/mL and serum calcium ≥10.0 mg/dL (both P for interaction < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Observational and propensity-matched, not randomised: patients whose PTH was highest before treatment (the surgery group in US data) are exactly those with most to gain biochemically, and unmeasured frailty decides who is offered an operation.
cards.source: Komaba H et al. Parathyroidectomy vs Cinacalcet Among Patients Undergoing Hemodialysis. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2022. PMID: 35277957. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Alvarado 2022 (USRDS): surgery vs cinacalcet — 5-year survival 65.6% vs 57.8% (HR 0.77), but more pathologic fractures after surgery (27.8% vs 24.9%)
cards.summary: Alvarado 2022 (USRDS): surgery vs cinacalcet — 5-year survival 65.6% vs 57.8% (HR 0.77), but more pathologic fractures after surgery (27.8% vs 24.9%)
cards.people: Adult haemodialysis patients in the United States Renal Data System treated with cinacalcet or parathyroidectomy for secondary hyperparathyroidism; the surgery group (n = 2,023) was compared with a cinacalcet cohort after 1:1 propensity score matching, with Cox regression for overall mortality and follow-up of coronary, cerebrovascular and fracture outcomes.
cards.result: The surgery group had a higher mean peak PTH before therapy (2066.8 vs 1425.4, P < 0.001). New-onset coronary artery disease (7.7% vs 7.9%, P = 0.8) and cerebrovascular disease (7% vs 6.7%, P = 0.8) did not differ, but surgical patients had a higher rate of pathologic fractures (27.8% vs 24.9%, P = 0.04). Five-year survival was 65.6% after surgery versus 57.8% on cinacalcet, and surgical patients were less likely to die during the study period (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.70–0.85, P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: The fracture excess runs against the survival finding and may reflect the surgery group's much higher pre-treatment PTH (more severe bone disease to begin with) — a visible residue of confounding by indication inside a matched analysis.
cards.source: Alvarado L et al. Parathyroidectomy Versus Cinacalcet for the Treatment of Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in Hemodialysis Patients. World J Surg. 2022. PMID: 35022799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Song 2024 meta-analysis: 23 cohort studies, 24,398 patients — pooled mortality HR 0.47, but HR 1.02 in the subgroup where medical therapy was cinacalcet for all
cards.summary: Song 2024 meta-analysis: 23 cohort studies, 24,398 patients — pooled mortality HR 0.47, but HR 1.02 in the subgroup where medical therapy was cinacalcet for all
cards.people: Meta-analysis of cohort studies or RCTs comparing parathyroidectomy with medical treatment in dialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism (search to August 2023; transplant recipients excluded): 23 studies involving 24,398 patients, analysed with hazard ratios for mortality and weighted mean differences for laboratory parameters.
cards.result: Parathyroidectomy was associated with lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.35–0.61) and cardiovascular mortality (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.40–0.84), with a greater mortality reduction at PTH over 585 pg/mL (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.24–0.58). However, no mortality difference was found when all patients in the medical group received cinacalcet alongside standard therapy (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.49–2.11). Parathyroidectomy also lowered PTH (weighted mean difference 1078 pg/mL), calcium (0.86 mg/dL) and phosphate (0.74 mg/dL) more than medical therapy.
cards.watchOut: Pooling observational cohorts pools their biases: the headline 0.47 is far stronger than either large matched cohort (0.77–0.78), and the cinacalcet-for-all subgroup — the fairest modern comparison — is null. Weight the matched cohorts over the pooled figure.
cards.source: Song Z et al. The Effects of Parathyroidectomy vs Medical Treatments for Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in Patients Undergoing Dialysis: A Meta-Analysis. Endocr Pract. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: no RCT exists; matched cohorts agree on lower long-term mortality after surgery, paid for upfront — POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only
cards.summary: Synthesis: no RCT exists; matched cohorts agree on lower long-term mortality after surgery, paid for upfront — POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only
cards.people: Synthesis of Kestenbaum B et al. Kidney Int. 2004 (PMID: 15496173); Komaba H et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2022 (PMID: 35277957); Alvarado L et al. World J Surg. 2022 (PMID: 35022799); Song Z et al. Endocr Pract. 2024 (PMID: 38583772).
cards.result: Across US and Japanese registry cohorts, dialysis patients who underwent parathyroidectomy for severe secondary hyperparathyroidism had lower long-term mortality than matched medically treated or cinacalcet-treated patients (hazard ratios 0.77–0.78 in the two best-matched analyses), after an early postoperative mortality of about 3%. Biochemical control is unambiguously better after surgery. Symptom outcomes were not comparatively measured in any carded study, and the one fracture comparison favoured cinacalcet.

shelves.title: NephroCheck ([TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7]) accuracy for AKI: at the 0.3 cut-off it catches ~9 of 10 imminent stage 2–3 injuries but half of positives are false alarms; at 2.0 it rarely cries wolf
shelves.question: In hospitalised and perioperative patients, how accurately does urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] (the NephroCheck test) predict moderate-to-severe AKI within 12 hours, and what changes between the 0.3 and 2.0 cut-offs?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Aged · Biomarkers · Cell Cycle Checkpoints · Cohort Studies · Female · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Proteins · Male · Middle Aged · Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinase-2
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (test accuracy) — this shelf answers the accuracy question only. The test's use as the triage tool for the biomarker-guided KDIGO care bundle is homed at live shelf #2083 (PrevAKI) and is not re-carded here; the homed trial records are deliberately left out of this pack's card sources. On accuracy: in the Sapphire validation cohort (Kashani et al., PMID: 23388612; 728 critically ill patients, 14% developing KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours), urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] achieved an AUC of 0.80, superior to all previously described AKI markers (none above 0.72). The cut-off study (Hoste et al., PMID: 25237065) replicated across Sapphire and the Opal cohort (154 patients): at 0.3, sensitivity was 89% in both studies with specificity only 50–53%; at 2.0, sensitivity fell to 42–44% while specificity rose to 90–95%. The Topaz validation with blinded expert adjudication (Bihorac et al., PMID: 24559465; 420 patients) found sensitivity 92% at 0.3, a negative likelihood ratio of 0.18, and sevenfold risk above the cut-off. A cut-off meta-analysis (Zhang et al., PMID: 31261582; 1,619 patients) pooled sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.48 at 0.3 and sensitivity 0.45 / specificity 0.93 at 2.0. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test accuracy): a rule-out test at 0.3 and a rule-in test at 2.0, with a wide grey zone between — not a stand-alone diagnosis.

cards.headline: Sapphire 2013 (Kashani): [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] AUC 0.80 for stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours in 728 critically ill patients — better than every older marker (all ≤0.72)
cards.summary: Sapphire 2013 (Kashani): [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] AUC 0.80 for stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours in 728 critically ill patients — better than every older marker (all ≤0.72)
cards.people: Two multicentre observational studies in critically ill adults at risk of AKI: a discovery phase enrolling 522 adults across sepsis, shock, major surgery and trauma cohorts screening over 300 candidate markers, and the Sapphire validation study enrolling 744 adults without AKI at enrolment (final analysis cohort 728). The primary endpoint was moderate-to-severe AKI (KDIGO stage 2–3) within 12 hours of sampling; 14% of Sapphire subjects reached it.
cards.result: The two top discovery markers — urinary IGFBP7 and TIMP-2, both inducers of G1 cell-cycle arrest — validated as a product: [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] gave an AUC of 0.80 (0.76 and 0.79 for the markers alone) and was significantly superior to all previously described AKI markers (P < 0.002), none of which achieved an AUC above 0.72. The test also significantly improved risk stratification when added to a nine-variable clinical model by Cox modelling, integrated discrimination improvement and net reclassification improvement, and remained superior in sensitivity analyses using different reference creatinine methods.
cards.watchOut: Industry-era validation in a mixed ICU population with a 14% event rate: predictive values will fall in lower-risk ward or perioperative populations, and AUC 0.80 is good-not-excellent discrimination. The endpoint is AKI within 12 hours — a prediction, not a diagnosis of established injury.
cards.source: Kashani K et al. Discovery and validation of cell cycle arrest biomarkers in human acute kidney injury. Crit Care. 2013. PMID: 23388612. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01209169, from the record. cards.headline: Hoste 2014 (Sapphire + Opal): at 0.3, sensitivity 89% and specificity ~50%; at 2.0, sensitivity ~43% and specificity 90–95% — replicated in both cohorts
cards.summary: Hoste 2014 (Sapphire + Opal): at 0.3, sensitivity 89% and specificity ~50%; at 2.0, sensitivity ~43% and specificity 90–95% — replicated in both cohorts
cards.people: Cut-offs were derived from the Sapphire cohort for prediction of KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours, then verified in the new Opal study enrolling 154 critically ill adults at six US sites. One hundred subjects (14%) in Sapphire and 27 (18%) in Opal met the primary endpoint.
cards.result: Opal replicated Sapphire. For the 0.3 cut-off, sensitivity was 89% in both studies and specificity 50% and 53%. For the 2.0 cut-off, sensitivity was 42% and 44% and specificity 95% and 90%. Relative risk for subjects testing ≤0.3 versus the >0.3–2.0 band was 4.7 (95% CI 1.5–16) and 4.4 (2.5–8.7) in the two studies, and ≤0.3 versus >2.0 was 12 (4.2–40) and 18 (10–37). The authors conclude values ≥0.3 identify patients at high risk and values >2 those at highest risk.
cards.watchOut: At the headline 0.3 cut-off, roughly half of all positive results occur in patients who do not develop stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours — the test stratifies risk bands; it does not diagnose. Opal's 27 endpoint events make its percentages fragile.
cards.source: Hoste EA et al. Derivation and validation of cutoffs for clinical use of cell cycle arrest biomarkers. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2014. PMID: 25237065. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01209169 and NCT01846884, from the record. cards.headline: Topaz 2014 (Bihorac): with blinded expert adjudication, sensitivity 92% at 0.3, negative likelihood ratio 0.18, sevenfold risk above the cut-off (420 patients)
cards.summary: Topaz 2014 (Bihorac): with blinded expert adjudication, sensitivity 92% at 0.3, negative likelihood ratio 0.18, sevenfold risk above the cut-off (420 patients)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre validation with clinical adjudication — Topaz (Bihorac 2014)
cards.people: 420 critically ill patients in a prospective multicentre study; the primary analysis tested a single urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] measurement at the prespecified high-sensitivity cut-off of >0.3 (ng/mL)2/1,000 for predicting moderate-to-severe AKI within 12 hours, with AKI adjudicated by three independent expert nephrologists masked to the test result. The primary endpoint was reached in 17% of patients.
cards.result: Sensitivity at the 0.3 cut-off was 92% (95% CI 85–98%) with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.18 (95% CI 0.06–0.33). Patients with a result >0.3 had seven times the risk of AKI (95% CI 4–22) compared with those below the cut-off. In a multivariable model, adding the test to clinical variables raised the AUC from 0.70 (95% CI 0.63–0.76) to 0.86 (95% CI 0.80–0.90), and the test remained a strong independent predictor.
cards.watchOut: Adjudication strengthens the reference standard, but this remains the manufacturer's validation ecosystem (same assay platform, overlapping investigators with Sapphire) — independent, non-ICU validations show weaker performance, which the meta-analysis card reflects.
cards.source: Bihorac A et al. Validation of cell-cycle arrest biomarkers for acute kidney injury using clinical adjudication. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2014. PMID: 24559465. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01573962, from the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2019 cut-off meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.48 at 0.3 versus 0.45 / 0.93 at 2.0 across 1,619 critically ill patients
cards.summary: Zhang 2019 cut-off meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.48 at 0.3 versus 0.45 / 0.93 at 2.0 across 1,619 critically ill patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cut-offs (Zhang 2019)
cards.people: PRISMA-compliant systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis of urinary TIMP-2 and IGFBP7 cut-offs for predicting AKI in critically ill patients (search to June 2018): 5 studies with 1,619 patients at the 0.3 cut-off and 4 studies with 891 patients at the 2.0 cut-off.
cards.result: At the 0.3 (ng/mL)/1000 cut-off, pooled sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93), specificity 0.48 (95% CI 0.45–0.51), diagnostic odds ratio 8.33 (95% CI 5.55–12.52) and summary AUC 0.748. At the 2.0 cut-off, sensitivity was 0.45 (95% CI 0.37–0.53), specificity 0.93 (95% CI 0.91–0.95), diagnostic odds ratio 11.43 (95% CI 7.43–17.57) and summary AUC 0.844. The authors conclude the 2.0 cut-off has the highest overall accuracy, while 0.3 serves as the high-sensitivity threshold.
cards.watchOut: Five studies is a thin pool and the component studies overlap the Sapphire/Opal/Topaz populations — the meta-analysis summarises the same validation ecosystem rather than adding independent patients.
cards.source: Zhang D et al. Comparison of urinary TIMP-2 and IGFBP7 cut-offs to predict acute kidney injury in critically ill patients: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine (Baltimore). 2019. PMID: 31261582. Registry ID: none in the record (the review's PROSPERO registration, CRD42018084457, is stated in its abstract). cards.headline: Synthesis: one test, two jobs — 0.3 rules out, 2.0 rules in, and the middle band is a grey zone — POSSIBLE (test accuracy)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one test, two jobs — 0.3 rules out, 2.0 rules in, and the middle band is a grey zone — POSSIBLE (test accuracy)
cards.people: Synthesis of Kashani K et al. Crit Care. 2013 (PMID: 23388612); Hoste EA et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2014 (PMID: 25237065); Bihorac A et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2014 (PMID: 24559465); Zhang D et al. Medicine (Baltimore). 2019 (PMID: 31261582). Cross-point: the care-bundle strategy that uses this test as its triage tool is homed at live shelf #2083 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Across the Sapphire, Opal and Topaz validations and the cut-off meta-analysis, urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] discriminates imminent stage 2–3 AKI with an AUC around 0.80. At 0.3 it is a sensitive rule-out (sensitivity ~89–92%, negative likelihood ratio 0.18 in Topaz) bought with ~50% specificity; at 2.0 it becomes a specific rule-in (specificity ~90–95%) that misses over half of cases. Accuracy is best characterised as risk stratification into three bands, validated mainly in critically ill patients within a 12-hour horizon.
cards.watchOut: Whether acting on a positive result improves outcomes is a different question — answered (split) at home #2083, not here. Do not cite this shelf's accuracy figures as evidence that testing helps patients.

shelves.title: dd-cfDNA for kidney transplant rejection: a good antibody-mediated-rejection test (AUC ~0.87–0.89), a moderate any-rejection test — and one small RCT that guided biopsies found rejection ~12 months sooner
shelves.question: In kidney transplant recipients, how accurately does donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) detect active rejection compared with biopsy, and does dd-cfDNA-guided monitoring change management or outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Allografts · DNA · Female · Graft Rejection · Humans · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (test accuracy). In the DART validation (Bloom et al., PMID: 28280140; 102 recipients, 107 biopsies), dd-cfDNA discriminated any rejection from no rejection with an AUC of 0.74 (95% CI 0.61–0.86) and antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) with an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.75–0.97); at a 1.0% cut-off, positive and negative predictive values were 61% and 84% for active rejection and 44% and 96% for ABMR. The diagnostic meta-analysis (Xiao et al., PMID: 32890130; 9 studies) pooled sensitivity 0.70 / specificity 0.78 / AUC 0.81 for main rejection episodes and sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.80 / AUC 0.89 for ABMR. The largest validation (Aubert et al., PMID: 38824959; 2,882 recipients enrolled, 1,134 in the primary analysis) found dd-cfDNA independently associated with rejection (odds ratio 2.275, 95% CI 1.902–2.739) and improved a standard-of-care model's AUC from 0.777 to 0.821. For the management limb, the only randomised test (Akifova et al., PMID: 39673311; 40 recipients with de novo donor-specific antibodies) found dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy diagnosed ABMR at a median 2.8 months versus 14.5 months with clinician-guided biopsy (P = 0.003), with 77% positive and 85% negative predictive value for ABMR. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test accuracy): a useful adjunct that is strongest against ABMR and weakest for low-grade T-cell-mediated rejection; it does not replace biopsy, and outcome benefit from monitoring is unproven beyond earlier diagnosis in one 40-patient trial.

cards.headline: Bloom 2017 (DART): dd-cfDNA AUC 0.74 for any rejection, 0.87 for antibody-mediated rejection — at 1.0%, NPV 84% and 96% respectively (102 recipients, 107 biopsies)
cards.summary: Bloom 2017 (DART): dd-cfDNA AUC 0.74 for any rejection, 0.87 for antibody-mediated rejection — at 1.0%, NPV 84% and 96% respectively (102 recipients, 107 biopsies)
cards.people: 102 kidney transplant recipients with blood specimens collected at scheduled intervals and at clinically indicated biopsies; plasma dd-cfDNA was correlated with allograft rejection status on 107 biopsy specimens, with rejection comprising T-cell-mediated rejection or antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) versus histologically negative controls.
cards.result: dd-cfDNA discriminated any rejection from controls (P < 0.001; AUC 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.86). At a 1.0% cut-off, positive and negative predictive values for active rejection were 61% and 84%. For ABMR the AUC was 0.87 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.97), with positive and negative predictive values of 44% and 96% at the same cut-off. Median dd-cfDNA was 2.9% in ABMR, 1.2% in T-cell-mediated rejection types ≥IB, 0.2% in type IA and 0.3% in controls. The authors conclude levels <1% reflect absence of active rejection (≥IB or ABMR) and levels >1% indicate a probability of active rejection.
cards.watchOut: Predictive values were measured in a biopsy-enriched population with high rejection prevalence — the 44% positive predictive value for ABMR will fall further in stable surveillance populations, and type IA T-cell-mediated rejection was essentially invisible to the test (median 0.2%, same as controls).

prospective diagnostic validation — dart cohort (bloom 2017) 102 kidney transplant recipients with blood specimens collected at scheduled intervals and at clinically indicated biopsies; plasma dd-cfdna was correlated with allograft rejection status on 107 biopsy specimens, with rejection comprising t-cell-mediated rejection or antibody-mediated rejection (abmr) versus histologically negative controls. dd-cfdna discriminated any rejection from controls (p < 0.001; auc 0.74, 95% ci 0.61 to 0.86). at a 1.0% cut-off, positive and negative predictive values for active rejection were 61% and 84%. for abmr the auc was 0.87 (95% ci 0.75 to 0.97), with positive and negative predictive values of 44% and 96% at the same cut-off. median dd-cfdna was 2.9% in abmr, 1.2% in t-cell-mediated rejection types ≥ib, 0.2% in type ia and 0.3% in controls. the authors conclude levels <1% reflect absence of active rejection (≥ib or abmr) and levels >1% indicate a probability of active rejection. predictive values were measured in a biopsy-enriched population with high rejection prevalence — the 44% positive predictive value for abmr will fall further in stable surveillance populations, and type ia t-cell-mediated rejection was essentially invisible to the test (median 0.2%, same as controls). bloom rd et al. cell-free dna and active rejection in kidney allografts. j am soc nephrol. 2017. pmid: 28280140. registry id: none in the record. mesh: allografts · dna · female · graft rejection · humans · kidney transplantation · male · middle aged · postoperative complications

cards.headline: Xiao 2021 meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.70 / specificity 0.78 for main rejection episodes; 0.84 / 0.80 for antibody-mediated rejection (9 studies)
cards.summary: Xiao 2021 meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.70 / specificity 0.78 for main rejection episodes; 0.84 / 0.80 for antibody-mediated rejection (9 studies)
cards.type: Diagnostic accuracy systematic review and meta-analysis (Xiao 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of dd-cfDNA diagnostic accuracy in renal-allograft rejection: 9 studies included, 6 reporting accuracy for main rejection episodes (MRE) and 5 data sets for antibody-mediated rejection (AMR).
cards.result: For main rejection episodes, pooled sensitivity was 0.70 (95% CI 0.57–0.81), specificity 0.78 (0.70–0.84), AUC 0.81 (0.77–0.84), diagnostic odds ratio 8.18 (5.11–13.09), positive likelihood ratio 3.15 (2.47–4.02) and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (0.27–0.55). For AMR, pooled sensitivity was 0.84 (0.75–0.90), specificity 0.80 (0.74–0.84), AUC 0.89 (0.86–0.91) and diagnostic odds ratio 20.48 (10.76–38.99). The authors conclude dd-cfDNA is a helpful marker for diagnosing AMR in recipients with suspected dysfunction, while accuracy for main rejection episodes remains uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The component studies use different assays, cut-offs and biopsy indications; the pooled 'any rejection' figure averages over the test's known blind spot (low-grade T-cell-mediated rejection).
cards.source: Xiao H et al. Diagnostic Accuracy of Donor-derived Cell-free DNA in Renal-allograft Rejection: A Meta-analysis. Transplantation. 2021. PMID: 32890130. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aubert 2024: in 1,134 analysed recipients, dd-cfDNA was independently associated with rejection (OR 2.28) and lifted a standard-of-care model's AUC from 0.777 to 0.821
cards.summary: Aubert 2024: in 1,134 analysed recipients, dd-cfDNA was independently associated with rejection (OR 2.28) and lifted a standard-of-care model's AUC from 0.777 to 0.821
cards.people: 2,882 kidney allograft recipients enrolled from 14 transplantation centres in Europe and the United States in an observational population-based study; the primary analysis included 1,134 patients, with external validation cohorts totalling 1,748 patients including a cohort of 439 African American patients. dd-cfDNA was tested against biopsy-proven rejection and against a standard-of-care monitoring model.
cards.result: dd-cfDNA levels strongly correlated with allograft rejection, including antibody-mediated, T-cell-mediated and mixed rejection (all P < 0.0001). In multivariable analysis, circulating dd-cfDNA was significantly associated with rejection (odds ratio 2.275, 95% CI 1.902–2.739; P < 0.0001) independently of standard-of-care monitoring parameters. Adding dd-cfDNA to the standard-of-care prediction model improved discrimination (AUC 0.777, 95% CI 0.741–0.811, to 0.821, 95% CI 0.784–0.852; P = 0.0011) and calibration, results confirmed in the external validation cohorts; dd-cfDNA also showed high predictive value for subclinical rejection in stable patients.
cards.watchOut: An AUC gain of 0.044 over standard monitoring is real but modest — this is an adjunct that sharpens existing surveillance, not a stand-alone replacement for biopsy, and the study is observational: it shows association and discrimination, not that acting on results improves graft outcomes.
cards.source: Aubert O et al. Cell-free DNA for the detection of kidney allograft rejection. Nat Med. 2024. PMID: 38824959. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05995379, from the record. cards.headline: Akifova 2025 RCT: dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy diagnosed antibody-mediated rejection at 2.8 vs 14.5 months in 40 recipients with donor-specific antibodies
cards.summary: Akifova 2025 RCT: dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy diagnosed antibody-mediated rejection at 2.8 vs 14.5 months in 40 recipients with donor-specific antibodies
cards.people: 40 kidney transplant recipients with prevalent de novo donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies, eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m2 and no previous biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection, randomised at a single centre to dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy (biopsy if dd-cfDNA >50 copies/mL) or clinician-guided biopsy over 12 months; dd-cfDNA was measured in both groups at inclusion and 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months, with a protocol biopsy at 12 months for those not yet biopsied. The primary endpoint was time to diagnosis of active or chronic active AMR.
cards.result: Thirty-nine of 40 patients had functioning grafts at completion and 26 underwent biopsy (13 per group). AMR was diagnosed earlier in the intervention group (median 2.8 months, IQR 1.7–5.3) than in the control group (median 14.5 months, IQR 13.3–16.7; P = 0.003). Longitudinal dd-cfDNA monitoring had 77% positive predictive value and 85% negative predictive value for AMR. The authors conclude dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy can reduce time to AMR diagnosis and expedite therapy initiation.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, one centre, open-label, and the endpoint is time to diagnosis — earlier detection only helps if earlier treatment changes outcomes, which this trial was not sized to test. The control arm's 14.5-month median is inflated by the 12-month protocol biopsy design.
cards.source: Akifova A et al. Donor-derived cell-free DNA monitoring for early diagnosis of antibody-mediated rejection after kidney transplantation: a randomized trial. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2025. PMID: 39673311. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04897438, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: strongest against antibody-mediated rejection, blind to low-grade cellular rejection; monitoring buys earlier diagnosis in one small trial — POSSIBLE (test accuracy)
cards.summary: Synthesis: strongest against antibody-mediated rejection, blind to low-grade cellular rejection; monitoring buys earlier diagnosis in one small trial — POSSIBLE (test accuracy)
cards.people: Synthesis of Bloom RD et al. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017 (PMID: 28280140); Xiao H et al. Transplantation. 2021 (PMID: 32890130); Aubert O et al. Nat Med. 2024 (PMID: 38824959); Akifova A et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2025 (PMID: 39673311).
cards.result: The accuracy record is consistent across a 102-patient validation, a 9-study meta-analysis and a 2,882-patient multinational cohort: dd-cfDNA detects antibody-mediated rejection well (AUC ~0.87–0.89, negative predictive value 96% at 1.0% in DART) and any rejection only moderately (AUC ~0.74–0.81), with low-grade T-cell-mediated rejection its blind spot. Added to standard monitoring it improves discrimination modestly. The single randomised monitoring trial shows substantially earlier AMR diagnosis with guided biopsy; graft-survival benefit is untested.
cards.watchOut: Assay, units and cut-offs differ between studies (fraction % versus copies/mL) — figures from one platform do not transfer automatically to another, and predictive values move with rejection prevalence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bloom RD et al. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017 (PMID: 28280140); Xiao H et al. Transplantation. 2021 (PMID: 32890130); Aubert O et al. Nat Med. 2024 (PMID: 38824959); Akifova A et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2025 (PMID: 39673311).

shelves.title: Kidney Failure Risk Equation: discrimination holds worldwide (C 0.88–0.90 in 721,357 patients) but calibration drifts outside North America — and a 30% fall in albuminuria carries its own prognostic information
shelves.question: In adults with CKD, how accurately does the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (Tangri) predict 2- and 5-year kidney failure, does adding more variables improve on the 4-variable version, and does change in albuminuria add prognostic information?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Albuminuria · Biomarkers · Calcium · Calibration · Cohort Studies · Disease Progression · Female · Forecasting · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Models, Theoretical · Renal Insufficiency · Risk · Risk Assessment · Serum Albumin · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (prognostic accuracy) for discrimination, with a calibration caveat. In the original development and validation (Tangri et al., PMID: 21482743; development cohort 3,449 patients with 386 kidney-failure events, validation cohort 4,942 with 1,177), the full 8-variable model reached a C statistic of 0.917 in development and 0.841 in validation — and, importantly for the 'added value' limb, it beat the simpler 4-variable model (age, sex, eGFR, albuminuria) only modestly: integrated discrimination improvement 3.2% (95% CI 2.4%–4.2%), with better calibration and small net reclassification gains. The multinational meta-validation (Tangri et al., PMID: 26757465; 31 cohorts, 721,357 participants, 23,829 kidney-failure cases) found the original equations discriminated excellently everywhere (overall C statistic 0.90, 95% CI 0.89–0.92, at 2 years; 0.88, 95% CI 0.86–0.90, at 5 years) and pooled equations did not improve on them — but calibration was adequate in North American cohorts while risk was overestimated in some non-North American cohorts, fixed in most by a calibration factor lowering baseline risk by 32.9% at 2 years and 16.5% at 5 years. For albuminuria change (Coresh et al., PMID: 30635225; 675,904 individuals, 7,461 end-stage kidney disease events — observational consortium data), a 30% decrease in albumin-to-creatinine ratio over a 2-year baseline period carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.74–0.94) for subsequent end-stage kidney disease, 0.78 (0.66–0.92) after regression-dilution adjustment. PROPOSED LIKELY (prognostic accuracy): quote the risk with the regional calibration caveat, prefer the 4-variable equation for simplicity unless the extra variables are already in hand, and treat a sustained albuminuria fall as genuinely better prognosis — an association, not proof that lowering albuminuria causes the benefit.

cards.headline: Tangri 2011: the 8-variable equation reached C 0.917 (development) and 0.841 (validation); the extra four variables improved on the 4-variable version only modestly (IDI 3.2%)
cards.summary: Tangri 2011: the 8-variable equation reached C 0.917 (development) and 0.841 (validation); the extra four variables improved on the 4-variable version only modestly (IDI 3.2%)
cards.people: Two independent Canadian cohorts of nephrologist-referred patients with CKD stages 3–5 (eGFR 10–59 mL/min/1.73 m2), enrolled 2001–2008: a development cohort of 3,449 patients (386 kidney-failure events, 11%) and a validation cohort of 4,942 patients (1,177 events, 24%). Kidney failure was need for dialysis or preemptive transplantation; models were Cox models assessed by C statistic, calibration, integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) and net reclassification improvement (NRI).
cards.result: The most accurate model included age, sex, eGFR, albuminuria, serum calcium, phosphate, bicarbonate and albumin (C statistic 0.917, 95% CI 0.901–0.933, in development and 0.841, 95% CI 0.825–0.857, in validation). In the validation cohort it was more accurate than the simpler 4-variable model (age, sex, eGFR, albuminuria): IDI 3.2% (95% CI 2.4%–4.2%), better calibration (Nam–D'Agostino chi-squared 19 vs 32), and NRI of 8.0% (95% CI 2.1%–13.9%) in CKD stage 3 and 4.1% (95% CI −0.5% to 8.8%) in stage 4. The authors conclude routinely obtained laboratory tests can accurately predict progression to kidney failure in CKD stages 3–5.
cards.watchOut: Both cohorts were nephrology-referred Canadians with high event rates (11% and 24%) — discrimination this high partly reflects a wide case mix, and calibration in unreferred or non-Canadian populations is exactly what the 2016 paper then tested.
cards.source: Tangri N et al. A predictive model for progression of chronic kidney disease to kidney failure. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21482743. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tangri 2016 multinational validation: 721,357 participants — C 0.90 at 2 years and 0.88 at 5 years everywhere, but risk was overestimated outside North America until a calibration factor was applied
cards.summary: Tangri 2016 multinational validation: 721,357 participants — C 0.90 at 2 years and 0.88 at 5 years everywhere, but risk was overestimated outside North America until a calibration factor was applied
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis — multinational validation (Tangri 2016)
cards.people: 31 cohorts in the CKD Prognosis Consortium, 721,357 participants with CKD stages 3–5 in more than 30 countries across 4 continents (data 1982–2014), with 23,829 kidney-failure cases over a median follow-up of 4 years. Original versus pooled risk equations were compared for discrimination and calibration, overall and by region.
cards.result: The original risk equations achieved excellent discrimination across all cohorts (overall C statistic 0.90, 95% CI 0.89–0.92, at 2 years; 0.88, 95% CI 0.86–0.90, at 5 years), similar in subgroups by age, race and diabetes status, and the pooled equations did not improve on them. Calibration was adequate in North American cohorts, but the original equations overestimated risk in some non-North American cohorts; adding a calibration factor that lowered baseline risk by 32.9% at 2 years and 16.5% at 5 years improved calibration in 12 of 15 and 10 of 13 non-North American cohorts respectively (P = 0.04 and P = 0.02).
cards.watchOut: Discrimination is not calibration: a C statistic of 0.90 can coexist with systematically overstated absolute risks in a new region, and it is the absolute 2- and 5-year percentages — the numbers quoted to patients — that the calibration factor changes.
cards.source: Tangri N et al. Multinational Assessment of Accuracy of Equations for Predicting Risk of Kidney Failure: A Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 26757465. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Coresh 2019: a 30% fall in albuminuria over 2 years carried an adjusted HR of 0.83 for later end-stage kidney disease across 675,904 people (observational)
cards.summary: Coresh 2019: a 30% fall in albuminuria over 2 years carried an adjusted HR of 0.83 for later end-stage kidney disease across 675,904 people (observational)
cards.type: Individual participant-level consortium meta-analysis of observational studies (Coresh 2019)
cards.people: 28 cohorts of the CKD Prognosis Consortium with repeated albuminuria measures over baseline periods of 1, 2 and 3 years: 693,816 individuals (80% with diabetes), with data for 675,904 individuals and 7,461 end-stage kidney disease events in the primary (2-year baseline) analysis; end-stage kidney disease was initiation of kidney replacement therapy. Parallel analyses used 14 clinical-trial populations.
cards.result: Change in albumin-to-creatinine ratio was consistently associated with subsequent end-stage kidney disease risk. The adjusted hazard ratio after a 30% decrease in ACR during a 2-year baseline period was 0.83 (95% CI 0.74–0.94), strengthening to 0.78 (0.66–0.92) after adjustment for regression dilution. Associations were fairly consistent across cohorts and subgroups (eGFR, diabetes, sex) but stronger at higher baseline ACR (P for interaction < 0.0001); at baseline ACR ≥300 mg/g, a 30% decrease over 2 years was estimated to confer a more than 1% absolute reduction in 10-year end-stage kidney disease risk. Results were similar for protein-to-creatinine ratio change and in trial populations.
cards.watchOut: Observational: albuminuria change tracks risk, and the authors frame it as support for a surrogate endpoint — it does not prove that a treatment-induced albuminuria fall causes the lower risk, and single ACR measurements are noisy enough that the consortium needed regression-dilution correction.
cards.source: Coresh J et al. Change in albuminuria and subsequent risk of end-stage kidney disease: an individual participant-level consortium meta-analysis of observational studies. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019. PMID: 30635225. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.search: coresh 2019: a 30% fall in albuminuria over 2 years carried an adjusted hr of 0.83 for later end-stage kidney disease across 675,904 people (observational) coresh 2019: a 30% fall in albuminuria over 2 years carried an adjusted hr of 0.83 for later end-stage kidney disease across 675,904 people (observational) in adults with ckd, how accurately does the kidney failure risk equation (tangri) predict 2- and 5-year kidney failure, does adding more variables improve on the 4-variable version, and does change in albuminuria add prognostic information? individual participant-level consortium meta-analysis of observational studies (coresh 2019) 28 cohorts of the ckd prognosis consortium with repeated albuminuria measures over baseline periods of 1, 2 and 3 years: 693,816 individuals (80% with diabetes), with data for 675,904 individuals and 7,461 end-stage kidney disease events in the primary (2-year baseline) analysis; end-stage kidney disease was initiation of kidney replacement therapy. parallel analyses used 14 clinical-trial populations. change in albumin-to-creatinine ratio was consistently associated with subsequent end-stage kidney disease risk. the adjusted hazard ratio after a 30% decrease in acr during a 2-year baseline period was 0.83 (95% ci 0.74–0.94), strengthening to 0.78 (0.66–0.92) after adjustment for regression dilution. associations were fairly consistent across cohorts and subgroups (egfr, diabetes, sex) but stronger at higher baseline acr (p for interaction < 0.0001); at baseline acr ≥300 mg/g, a 30% decrease over 2 years was estimated to confer a more than 1% absolute reduction in 10-year end-stage kidney disease risk. results were similar for protein-to-creatinine ratio change and in trial populations. observational: albuminuria change tracks risk, and the authors frame it as support for a surrogate endpoint — it does not prove that a treatment-induced albuminuria fall causes the lower risk, and single acr measurements are noisy enough that the consortium needed regression-dilution correction. coresh j et al. change in albuminuria and subsequent risk of end-stage kidney disease: an individual participant-level consortium meta-analysis of observational studies. lancet diabetes endocrinol. 2019. pmid: 30635225. registry id: none in the record. mesh: albuminuria · disease progression · glomerular filtration rate · humans · kidney failure, chronic · kidney function tests · observational studies as topic · prognosis · risk factors

cards.result: The Kidney Failure Risk Equation is among the best-validated prognostic tools in nephrology: discrimination of 0.88–0.90 held across 31 cohorts and 721,357 patients, the 8-variable version adds only a small increment over the 4-variable version (IDI 3.2%), and absolute risks need a downward calibration factor in many non-North American settings. Separately, change in albuminuria over about two years carries prognostic information beyond a single measurement — a 30% fall corresponds to roughly a 17–22% lower subsequent hazard of kidney failure in observational consortium data.
cards.watchOut: All three cards are cohort/prognosis evidence by design — there is no randomised test of KFRE-guided care on this shelf, and the stamp grades prediction accuracy, not proof that acting on the prediction improves outcomes.

shelves.title: The renal glucose threshold: a splayed titration curve — diabetes raises its ceiling, pregnancy halves it, SGLT2 blockade collapses it
shelves.question: In humans, what determines the renal threshold for glucose — how much filtered glucose do SGLT2 and SGLT1 reabsorb, where does glycosuria begin on the glucose titration curve, and how does this change in diabetes and pregnancy?
shelves.mesh: Glucose · Glycosuria · Kidney · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Glucose Clamp Technique · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human titration-curve evidence is direct: stepped hyperglycaemic clamps (plasma glucose raised stepwise, e.g. 5.5–30.5 mmol/L, about 99–549 mg/dL) let investigators draw each person's glucose titration curve and read off its three features — the threshold at which glucose first spills, the splay (the rounded shoulder, reflecting nephron-to-nephron variation), and the tubular maximum for glucose (TmG). In type 2 diabetes all three are shifted up (DeFronzo 2013, n = 12 + 12; Al-Jobori 2017: baseline TmG 459 ± 53 vs 337 ± 25 mg/min in diabetes vs controls), which is one reason hyperglycaemia sustains itself; SGLT2 blockade cuts TmG by roughly half within 48 hours and drags the threshold below 40 mg/dL. The genetic and pregnancy experiments of nature point the same way: familial renal glycosuria pedigrees separate a low-TmG form (type A) from a pure increased-splay form (type B), and pregnancy roughly halves TmG. Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing assigns most reabsorption to SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule with SGLT1 completing uptake downstream — presented here as the textbook's account; the carded human studies measure the whole-kidney curve, not the transporter split directly. Classic small groups are labelled on the face (titration studies of 8–15 per group).

cards.headline: DeFronzo 2013: stepped-clamp titration curves in type 2 diabetes show a raised TmG, a wider splay and a higher threshold than in matched controls — and dapagliflozin lowers all three
cards.summary: DeFronzo 2013: stepped-clamp titration curves in type 2 diabetes show a raised TmG, a wider splay and a higher threshold than in matched controls — and dapagliflozin lowers all three
cards.type: Human physiological study (stepped hyperglycaemic clamp with glucose titration curves), Diabetes Care 2013
cards.people: Twelve subjects with type 2 diabetes and 12 matched healthy subjects; each underwent a pancreatic/stepped hyperglycaemic clamp (plasma glucose raised across 5.5–30.5 mmol/L, about 99–549 mg/dL) at baseline and after 7 days of dapagliflozin, with a pharmacodynamic model fitted to each individual glucose titration curve.
cards.result: At baseline the diabetic subjects had elevated maximum renal glucose reabsorptive capacity (TmG), increased splay and a raised threshold for glucose excretion compared with controls. Dapagliflozin reduced TmG and splay in both groups, but its most significant effect was to reduce the renal threshold for glucose excretion in both diabetic and control subjects — the titration-curve demonstration that blocking SGLT2 moves the whole curve, not just its ceiling.
cards.watchOut: Small clamp study (12 per group) and the intervention limb uses a drug to probe physiology; the baseline diabetes-vs-control curve difference is the physiology finding. The record reports the direction of the TmG/splay/threshold differences rather than a single threshold number in mg/dL, so none is printed here.
cards.source: DeFronzo RA, Hompesch M, Kasichayanula S, Liu X, et al. Characterization of renal glucose reabsorption in response to dapagliflozin in healthy subjects and subjects with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23735727. cards.headline: Al-Jobori 2017: baseline TmG was 459 vs 337 mg/min in type 2 diabetes vs controls; empagliflozin cut TmG by about half in 48 hours and dropped the spillage threshold below 40 mg/dL
cards.summary: Al-Jobori 2017: baseline TmG was 459 vs 337 mg/min in type 2 diabetes vs controls; empagliflozin cut TmG by about half in 48 hours and dropped the spillage threshold below 40 mg/dL
cards.type: Human physiological study (stepped hyperglycaemic clamp, before/after SGLT2 inhibition), Diabetes 2017
cards.people: Fifteen subjects with type 2 diabetes and 15 without diabetes; renal glucose reabsorption measured with the stepped hyperglycaemic clamp after 2 days and after 14 days of empagliflozin.
cards.result: At baseline, maximal renal glucose transport (TmG) was significantly greater in type 2 diabetes than in controls (459 ± 53 vs 337 ± 25 mg/min; P < 0.05). Empagliflozin for 48 hours reduced TmG by 44 ± 7% in diabetes and 53 ± 6% in controls (both P < 0.001), and by day 14 by 65 ± 5% and 75 ± 3% respectively. The plasma glucose threshold for spillage into urine fell similarly in both groups to <40 mg/dL — well below the normal fasting glucose — quantifying how far pharmacological SGLT2 blockade moves the threshold that, untreated, sits near the top of the physiological range.
cards.watchOut: A drug-probe study: the untreated baseline comparison (TmG 459 vs 337 mg/min) is the disease-physiology finding; the on-treatment values show transporter capacity, not the natural threshold.
cards.source: Al-Jobori H, Daniele G, Cersosimo E, Triplitt C, et al. Empagliflozin and Kinetics of Renal Glucose Transport in Healthy Individuals and Individuals With Type 2 Diabetes. Diabetes. 2017. PMID: 28428225. Registry ID: NCT01867307. cards.headline: Elsas & Rosenberg 1969: titration studies in familial renal glycosuria pedigrees separate type A (low threshold AND low TmG) from type B (low threshold, exaggerated splay, normal TmG)
cards.summary: Elsas & Rosenberg 1969: titration studies in familial renal glycosuria pedigrees separate type A (low threshold AND low TmG) from type B (low threshold, exaggerated splay, normal TmG)
cards.type: Human physiological study (renal glucose titration in pedigrees), J Clin Invest 1969
cards.people: Ten members of two pedigrees with familial renal glycosuria underwent renal glucose titration studies; intestinal hexose transport was also tested in controls and in the three brothers with the most severe renal glycosuria. Small classic pedigree study — N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: In one family a brother and sister each had a moderately reduced threshold and tubular maximum for glucose (type A) while both parents reabsorbed normally. In the second family, two brothers had severe type A glycosuria, their mother and a brother a mild type A defect, and another brother showed a reduced threshold with an exaggerated splay and a normal tubular maximum — type B. Jejunal glucose transport was normal in the patients, showing the defect is renal, not intestinal. The pedigrees demonstrate in humans that 'threshold' and 'TmG' are separable properties of the titration curve: glycosuria can begin early either because the ceiling is low or because the splay is wide.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 across two families, 1969 methods; carded as the classic human demonstration that threshold, splay and TmG dissociate — the genetic lesion (now known to involve the SGLT2 gene in most families) is textbook framing, not a finding of this record.
cards.source: Elsas LJ, Rosenberg LE. Familial renal glycosuria: a genetic reappraisal of hexose transport by kidney and intestine. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1969. PMID: 5822589. cards.headline: Drexel & Sailer 1980: in pregnancy with renal glucosuria the tubular maximum for glucose fell to about half — the threshold can be lowered physiologically, with familial type-A-like kinetics
cards.summary: Drexel & Sailer 1980: in pregnancy with renal glucosuria the tubular maximum for glucose fell to about half — the threshold can be lowered physiologically, with familial type-A-like kinetics
cards.type: Human physiological study (renal glucose titration in pregnancy), Klin Wochenschr 1980
cards.people: Eight pregnant women with renal glucosuria and six female control subjects underwent renal glucose titration studies. Small classic study — groups of 8 and 6 printed on the face.
cards.result: The kinetics of renal glucosuria in pregnancy were very similar to familial renal glycosuria of type A: the tubular maximum of glucose reabsorption was lowered in the pregnant women to about half. The authors concluded that the renal threshold for glucose can be lowered significantly in humans by a still-unknown endogenous factor — i.e. glycosuria in pregnancy reflects a real fall in reabsorptive capacity, not simply a rise in filtered load.
cards.watchOut: Very small groups (8 and 6) and an older titration method; the halving of TmG is the record's own figure and is printed as such. The mechanism of the pregnancy effect was unknown to the authors and remains presented here as unresolved.
cards.source: Drexel H, Sailer S. Kinetics of glucose handling in renal glucosuria during pregnancy. Klinische Wochenschrift. 1980. PMID: 7464008. cards.headline: Synthesis: glycosuria begins where the titration curve's splay meets the threshold — a whole-kidney property that diabetes raises, pregnancy halves, and SGLT2 blockade collapses
cards.summary: Synthesis: glycosuria begins where the titration curve's splay meets the threshold — a whole-kidney property that diabetes raises, pregnancy halves, and SGLT2 blockade collapses
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (DeFronzo 2013; Al-Jobori 2017; Elsas & Rosenberg 1969; Drexel & Sailer 1980), framed by the Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall account of proximal-tubule glucose transport as textbook framing.
cards.result: Filtered glucose is reabsorbed until transport saturates: the titration curve rises with filtered load, rounds off through the splay (nephrons saturate at different loads), and plateaus at TmG. Glycosuria therefore begins gradually, at the foot of the splay — the clinical 'threshold' — well below the load at which TmG is reached. The carded human data show each element moving independently: diabetes raises TmG (459 vs 337 mg/min) and threshold together; familial glycosuria lowers TmG (type A) or widens splay alone (type B); pregnancy halves TmG; and SGLT2 inhibition cuts TmG by ~44–53% within 48 hours and pulls the threshold below 40 mg/dL. The textbook framing (Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall) assigns the bulk of reabsorption to SGLT2 early in the proximal tubule and the remainder to SGLT1 downstream; that transporter split is the textbook's account — the human records carded here measure the integrated whole-kidney curve and the effects of blocking SGLT2, not transporter-by-transporter fluxes.
cards.watchOut: The often-quoted single 'normal threshold' figure is a population shorthand for the foot of a splayed curve; individual thresholds vary, which is exactly what the titration studies show. No animal titration data are carded.

shelves.title: Nephron urate handling: filtered, almost all reabsorbed, secreted, then mostly reabsorbed again — the four-component model the drug-probe tests actually proved
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is urate handled along the nephron — the classic four-component model of filtration, reabsorption, secretion and post-secretory reabsorption — and what did the probenecid and pyrazinamide suppression tests actually show?
shelves.mesh: Absorption · Adult · Aged · Aspirin · Benzbromarone · Biological Transport, Active · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney · Kidney Tubules · Male · Middle Aged · Probenecid · Pyrazinamide · Sulfinpyrazone · Uric Acid
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account — the classic four-component model built by Gutman & Yü and by Steele & Rieselbach from drug-probe studies in humans: urate is freely filtered at the glomerulus; most of the filtered load is reabsorbed before the secretory site (presecretory reabsorption); urate is then secreted into the tubule; and a large share of that secreted urate is reabsorbed again downstream (post-secretory reabsorption), leaving fractional excretion of roughly a tenth of the filtered load. The fetched probe records show what the tests actually demonstrated. Pyrazinamide, used to suppress secretion, cut urate excretion during probenecid-induced uricosuria from 463 to 135 µg/min, and from 2,528 to 574 µg/min at a larger probenecid dose — decrements two- to fourfold larger than total control-period excretion, proving secretion greatly exceeds final excretion and that much secreted urate is reabsorbed post-secretorily; the pyrazinamide test therefore underestimates secretion (Diamond & Paolino 1973). Combining pyrazinamide with probenecid pretreatment (blocking post-secretory reabsorption) unmasked abnormal tests that pyrazinamide alone called normal in tubular urate wasting — the non-suppressible fraction was 19.6 ± 12.7% of filtered urate in urate-wasting patients versus 3.4 ± 3.4% in controls (Colussi 1987; 8 controls, 9 low-excretory hyperuricaemics, 7 urate-wasting patients). Solving the four-component equations from benzbromarone and pyrazinamide states in 4 healthy volunteers put presecretory reabsorption at 93–98%, secretion at 30–44% and post-secretory reabsorption at 79–92% (Moriwaki 1990, N = 4 — printed on the face). Steele & Rieselbach's own 1975 summary states the model with its gaps honestly: extensive reabsorption after filtration, then secretion, then reabsorption of an unknown amount of secreted urate, with regulation most likely via secretion, post-secretory reabsorption, or both. The named classic anchors whose records carry no abstract (Gutman & Yü's programme papers; Steele's 1973 pyrazinamide paper) were refused as cards — see the build summary — and the model is presented as the textbook account anchored by the probe studies that do carry verifiable records.

cards.headline: The post-secretory site proven: pyrazinamide cut probenecid-driven urate excretion from 463 to 135 µg/min — and from 2,528 to 574 µg/min at higher uricosuria — so secretion must far exceed excretion (Diamond & Paolino 1973)
cards.summary: The post-secretory site proven: pyrazinamide cut probenecid-driven urate excretion from 463 to 135 µg/min — and from 2,528 to 574 µg/min at higher uricosuria — so secretion must far exceed excretion (Diamond & Paolino 1973)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (drug-probe clearance study: probenecid/sulfinpyrazone ± pyrazinamide)
cards.people: Humans given drug combinations — pyrazinamide 3 g orally during probenecid uricosuria (500 mg every 6 h, or a single 2 g dose), sulfinpyrazone 800 mg as the alternative uricosuric, and low-dose aspirin as an alternative secretory inhibitor — with timed urinary urate excretion measured in µg/min. The fetched abstract does not state the number of subjects — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Pyrazinamide during probenecid uricosuria decreased urate excretion from 463 µg/min (probenecid alone) to 135 µg/min (P < 0.01); with the greater uricosuria from 2 g probenecid, the fall was from 2,528 to 574 µg/min; with sulfinpyrazone, from 1,885 to 475 µg/min. cards.headline: Stress-testing the suppression test: adding probenecid pretreatment unmasked urate wasting that pyrazinamide alone called normal — non-suppressible excretion 19.6% of filtered urate vs 3.4% in controls
cards.summary: Stress-testing the suppression test: adding probenecid pretreatment unmasked urate wasting that pyrazinamide alone called normal — non-suppressible excretion 19.6% of filtered urate vs 3.4% in controls
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (combined pyrazinamide/probenecid probe test)
cards.people: 8 controls, 9 patients with 'low-excretory' hyperuricaemia, and 7 patients with tubular urate wasting; each underwent the pyrazinamide test alone and again after probenecid pretreatment intended to block post-secretory reabsorption. Small classic study — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Pyrazinamide-non-suppressible urate excretion after probenecid pretreatment barely differed from pyrazinamide alone in hyperuricaemic patients (mean difference 1.33 ± 2.3% of filtered urate; NS), was slightly higher in controls (3.4 ± 3.4%; P < 0.05), but was much higher in tubular urate wasting (19.6 ± 12.7%; P < 0.005). The pyrazinamide test alone was normal in three urate-wasting patients but abnormal in all of them after probenecid pretreatment — consistent with urate escaping presecretory reabsorption being recaptured at postsecretory sites during pyrazinamide alone, so the single test overestimates presecretory reabsorption.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (8/9/7) and an indirect pharmacological dissection: the percentages are fractions of filtered urate inferred from drug responses, not micropuncture measurements — in humans the components are solved from probe states, exactly the limitation the four-component model carries.

cards.headline: The four components quantified in health: presecretory reabsorption 93–98%, secretion 30–44%, post-secretory reabsorption 79–92% of the relevant loads (N = 4)
cards.summary: The four components quantified in health: presecretory reabsorption 93–98%, secretion 30–44%, post-secretory reabsorption 79–92% of the relevant loads (N = 4)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (four-state probe quantification in healthy volunteers) — N = 4
cards.people: 4 healthy male volunteers undergoing the benzbromarone loading test alone and the pyrazinamide suppression test combined with benzbromarone loading, with fractional uric-acid clearance measured in four states (control, benzbromarone, pyrazinamide, both). Very small classic study — N = 4 printed here on the face.
cards.result: Solving the four-component equations across the four drug states, presecretory reabsorption, tubular secretion and post-secretory reabsorption of uric acid were calculated to be about 93–98%, 30–44% and 79–92% respectively. Benzbromarone was calculated to inhibit post-secretory reabsorption selectively, which the authors argue makes its loading test reflect urate transport more precisely than probenecid-based tests. These are the proportions the textbook four-component model quotes for healthy humans: near-complete early reabsorption, a secretory flux of roughly a third to a half of the filtered load, and recapture of most of what is secreted.
cards.watchOut: N = 4: the ranges are the model's arithmetic on four volunteers under drug states, presented because they are the only direct human quantification the fetched records contain — they should be read as the classic model's estimates, not as population norms.

cards.headline: The model's own summary, with its gaps stated: filtration, extensive reabsorption, secretion, then reabsorption of an unknown amount of secreted urate (Steele & Rieselbach 1975)
cards.summary: The model's own summary, with its gaps stated: filtration, extensive reabsorption, secretion, then reabsorption of an unknown amount of secreted urate (Steele & Rieselbach 1975)
cards.type: Investigator synthesis of the human probe literature (labelled — not a primary trial)
cards.people: Summary by the programme's own investigators of the development of knowledge of intrarenal urate handling in normal man, drawing on the human clearance and drug-probe literature available to 1975 (labelled synthesis — not a primary trial).
cards.result: Current evidence favours extensive tubular reabsorption of urate following glomerular filtration; subsequently, tubular secretion of urate and reabsorption of an unknown amount of the secreted urate probably take place. The authors state plainly that there are many gaps in knowledge and that different interpretations may be given to the available data, and judge it most likely that regulation and control of urate excretion are accomplished through modulations in tubular secretion, post-secretory reabsorption, or both.
cards.watchOut: The earlier primary papers of this programme (and Gutman & Yü's) carry no abstracts in their PubMed records and were refused as cards under the verifiability rule; this synthesis is carded because its record does carry an abstract, and it is deliberately quoted with its uncertainty intact.

cards.headline: Synthesis: filtered, ~95% reabsorbed, secreted, mostly reabsorbed again — a model solved from drug probes, not seen directly
cards.summary: Synthesis: filtered, ~95% reabsorbed, secreted, mostly reabsorbed again — a model solved from drug probes, not seen directly
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human probe studies and the investigator synthesis above.
cards.result: Human nephron urate handling, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) present the four-component model and the fetched records support, is: free filtration; presecretory reabsorption of about 93–98% of the filtered load; tubular secretion of about 30–44%; and post-secretory reabsorption of about 79–92% of the secreted amount (Moriwaki 1990, N = 4). The probenecid test showed uricosurics act at least partly by blocking post-secretory reabsorption, and the pyrazinamide suppression test showed secretion must exceed final excretion two- to fourfold — while itself underestimating secretion and, used alone, missing reabsorptive defects that the combined probenecid-plus-pyrazinamide test exposes (Diamond & Paolino 1973; Colussi 1987). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED as the classic human model, with its probe-derived, small-N basis stated on the face.
cards.watchOut: Every component percentage is inferred from whole-kidney clearance under drug probes in small samples — no human micropuncture exists — and modern transporter biology (URAT1/GLUT9/ABCG2 era) has since re-assigned molecular identities to these components without changing the four-component flux picture this shelf describes.

shelves.title: Distal potassium secretion: delivery and voltage proven by human drug probes, adaptation by balance studies — the segment mechanism itself is animal work, and this shelf says so
shelves.question: In humans, what controls distal potassium secretion — how do distal sodium delivery/flow, aldosterone and plasma potassium itself each change urinary potassium excretion, and how does the kidney adapt excretion after potassium loading or depletion?
shelves.mesh: Acetazolamide · Adaptation, Biological · Aldosterone · Amiloride · Blood Pressure · Citric Acid · Furosemide · Homeostasis · Humans · Kidney Tubules · Kidney Tubules, Collecting · Kidney Tubules, Distal · Male · Natriuresis · Potassium · Potassium, Dietary · Renin · Sodium · Sodium Chloride, Dietary · Spironolactone
shelves.balance: THIN-HUMAN-EVIDENCE FLAG, stated plainly: the segment-level account in the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) — principal-cell sodium entry through ENaC making the lumen negative and driving potassium out through ROMK channels, flow washing secreted potassium away and sustaining the gradient — rests largely on animal micropuncture and isolated-tubule work, extrapolated to humans. What humans have directly is whole-kidney balance and drug-probe evidence, and this shelf grades itself EMERGING for that reason: each control is supported by a human probe, but no human study observes the segment itself. The human probes do converge. Raising distal sodium delivery with furosemide increased potassium excretion in 10 normal subjects, and amiloride — which blocks distal sodium reabsorption and collapses the lumen-negative voltage — obliterated that increase (Batlle 1986): the delivery/voltage limb, in humans. Adapting to a 300 mEq/day potassium diet for 18 days raised urinary potassium excretion from 50 ± 12 to 233 ± 45 mEq/day with only modest rises in serum potassium and aldosterone and no change in the distal tubule's handling of an acetazolamide delivery challenge or its sensitivity to infused aldosterone — the authors locate adaptation in a shift of sodium reabsorption toward the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron rather than in a rebuilt tubule (Hené 1986, N = 6). Plasma potassium itself is not the whole story: oral potassium citrate produced a kaliuresis peaking 60–80 minutes after intake with no change in plasma potassium and no preceding aldosterone rise, pointing to a feedforward gut/portal signal (Calò 1995). And dietary sodium intake across 3–15 g/day of salt did not change 24-hour potassium excretion in 16 healthy men, while thiazide increased and amiloride decreased kaliuresis similarly on every diet (Pechère-Bertschi 2022) — distal delivery manipulations move potassium; background salt intake, within this range, did not. Neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere and not duplicated: potassium distribution between cells and blood is pack #6075, and what drives aldosterone secretion is pack #6078; this shelf asks only how the nephron secretes potassium. The build-or-fold determination: BUILD (not fold into #6078) — because furosemide/amiloride, thiazide/amiloride and loading-balance probes in humans test distal secretion directly at whole-kidney level; the fold would only be required if no direct human probe existed. Sebastian's human potassium-depletion balance paper was refused as a card because its PubMed record carries no abstract (see summary).

cards.headline: Distal delivery drives secretion in humans: furosemide raised K+ excretion in 10 normal subjects — and amiloride, collapsing the lumen-negative voltage, obliterated it
cards.summary: Distal delivery drives secretion in humans: furosemide raised K+ excretion in 10 normal subjects — and amiloride, collapsing the lumen-negative voltage, obliterated it
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (furosemide/amiloride probe of collecting-tubule function) — N = 10 normal subjects
cards.people: 10 normal subjects (with 13 patients with distal renal tubular acidosis studied for contrast) given furosemide 80 mg orally to enhance sodium delivery and transport in the cortical collecting tubule, with and without amiloride; urine pH, net acid and potassium excretion measured.
cards.result: In the ten normal subjects, furosemide resulted in a fall in urine pH below 5.5 and an increase in net acid and K+ excretion. These effects were obliterated by amiloride, a drug which decreases transtubular epithelial voltage (lumen-negative) in the cortical collecting tubule by blocking Na reabsorption. The human inference: potassium secretion in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron rises when distal sodium delivery and its voltage-generating reabsorption rise, and falls when that sodium entry is blocked — the delivery/flow limb of distal potassium control, demonstrated at whole-kidney level in humans.
cards.watchOut: Whole-kidney probe inference, not segment observation: furosemide changes delivery, flow and volume status together, and the study's primary purpose was acidification phenotyping in tubular acidosis — the potassium result is the normal-subject control arm, which is exactly why it is carded here as physiology.

cards.headline: Adaptation to loading: 18 days at 300 mEq/day raised urinary potassium from 50 to 233 mEq/day — without the distal tubule changing its delivery handling or aldosterone sensitivity (N = 6)
cards.summary: Adaptation to loading: 18 days at 300 mEq/day raised urinary potassium from 50 to 233 mEq/day — without the distal tubule changing its delivery handling or aldosterone sensitivity (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (potassium loading/depletion balance and probe study) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy males studied on a normal (80 mEq/day) and a high (300 mEq/day) potassium diet, with balance measurements, an intravenous acetazolamide distal-delivery challenge, a high-dose aldosterone infusion test, and aldosterone-antagonist probes (canrenoate, then spironolactone 200 mg/day for 5 days). Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: After 18 days of the potassium-rich diet, urinary potassium excretion had increased from 50 ± 12 to 233 ± 45 mEq/day; plasma renin activity and body weight were unchanged, serum potassium and plasma aldosterone somewhat increased, and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio consistently elevated. Acetazolamide increased sodium and potassium excretion equally on the two diets (a sudden rise in distal solute delivery was not handled differently after loading), and the response to infused aldosterone was comparable (no altered aldosterone sensitivity). Canrenoate raised NaCl excretion without changing potassium excretion on the high-potassium diet, and 5 days of spironolactone produced no fall in renal potassium excretion while mean serum potassium rose 0.3–0.4 mEq/L. The authors conclude adaptation does not involve intrinsic changes of the distal tubule, but a shift of sodium reabsorption from proximal to distal (aldosterone-sensitive) nephron levels.
cards.watchOut: Six subjects, and the headline mechanism (a proximal-to-distal shift of sodium reabsorption) is the authors' inference from probe responses, not a measured segment flux — the honest human-level statement is that excretion quadruples with only small plasma-potassium and aldosterone changes and no detectable change in distal sensitivity.
cards.source: Hené RJ et al. Adaptation to chronic potassium loading in normal man. Mineral and electrolyte metabolism. 1986. PMID: 3523191. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Plasma potassium is not required: oral potassium citrate triggered a kaliuresis peaking at 60–80 minutes with no rise in plasma potassium and no preceding aldosterone rise
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oral potassium load with timed excretion and hormone sampling)
cards.people: Normal healthy adults undergoing water diuresis who ingested potassium citrate or sodium citrate (0.5 mmol/kg body weight) or continued as a time-control group, with urine collected in 20-minute periods and mid-interval venous sampling (Calò, Borsatti, Favaro & Rabinowitz 1995). The fetched abstract does not state the total number of subjects — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Potassium citrate intake led to a significant increase in potassium excretion beginning in the first post-ingestion collection and peaking 60–80 min after intake, with a maximal increase above baseline of 1.60 µmol/min/kg. The kaliuresis occurred without changes in plasma potassium concentration, creatinine or calcium excretion, or urine hypo-osmolality; plasma aldosterone was only insignificantly elevated and its initial increase did not occur until 40–60 min — after the kaliuresis had begun. Sodium citrate produced no kaliuresis. The authors propose a reflex initiated at potassium sensors in gut, portal vein or liver — a feedforward signal that raises excretion before plasma potassium or aldosterone can explain it.
cards.watchOut: The feedforward reflex is a proposed mechanism from a negative result (no plasma-K or aldosterone explanation), with supporting evidence in the wider literature partly from animal work (the senior author's sheep/rat programme) — carded here for the human observation itself: kaliuresis without a plasma-potassium rise.
cards.source: Calò L et al. Kaliuresis in normal subjects following oral potassium citrate intake without increased plasma potassium concentration. Nephron. 1995. PMID: 7753258. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Administration, Oral · Adult · Citrates · Citric Acid · Diuresis · Female · Homeostasis · Humans · Male · Potassium · Water

cards.headline: Background salt intake does not set potassium excretion: across 3–15 g/day of salt, 24-hour K+ excretion was unchanged — while thiazide raised and amiloride lowered kaliuresis on every diet (N = 16)
cards.summary: Background salt intake does not set potassium excretion: across 3–15 g/day of salt, 24-hour K+ excretion was unchanged — while thiazide raised and amiloride lowered kaliuresis on every diet (N = 16)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled sodium-intake crossover with thiazide/amiloride probes) — N = 16
cards.people: 16 healthy young males studied over three 7-day periods on low (3 g NaCl/day), normal (6 g/day) and high (15 g/day) salt diets at constant potassium intake, with steady-state probe responses to hydrochlorothiazide 100 mg and added amiloride 10 mg.
cards.result: Diurnal blood pressure rose slightly from low to high salt (119.30 ± 7.95 to 123.00 ± 7.50 mmHg; P = 0.02) and estimated GFR rose (133.20 ± 34.68 to 187.00 ± 49.10 mL/min; P = 0.005), but 24-h potassium excretion remained stable on all sodium intakes (66.28 ± 19.12 mmol/24 h low; 55.91 ± 21.17 normal; 66.81 ± 20.72 high; P = 0.9). Hydrochlorothiazide increased kaliuresis and amiloride decreased kaliuresis similarly on all three diets: neither spontaneous nor diuretic-induced potassium excretion was influenced by sodium intake, although the relative contributions of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to sodium handling did depend on intake.
cards.watchOut: Young healthy men over 7-day diet periods: the null is for background dietary sodium at constant potassium intake — it does not contradict the acute delivery effect in Reference 1, where a diuretic suddenly raises distal delivery within hours.
cards.source: Pechère-Bertschi A et al. Dietary sodium intake does not alter renal potassium handling and blood pressure in healthy young males. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association. 2022. PMID: 33492394. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: delivery and voltage are human-proven, adaptation is real but re-allocative, plasma K is partly feedforward — and the segment picture itself is animal-derived
cards.summary: Synthesis: delivery and voltage are human-proven, adaptation is real but re-allocative, plasma K is partly feedforward — and the segment picture itself is animal-derived
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human probe/balance studies above.
cards.result: What humans show directly: distal potassium secretion rises when distal sodium delivery and its reabsorptive voltage rise (furosemide) and falls when distal sodium entry is blocked (amiloride) (Batlle 1986); excretion adapts from 50 to 233 mEq/day over 18 days of loading with only small plasma-potassium and aldosterone rises and no change in distal sensitivity — adaptation by re-allocation of sodium reabsorption, per the authors (Hené 1986, N = 6); an oral load can raise excretion before plasma potassium or aldosterone move (Calò 1995); and background salt intake does not set daily excretion (Pechère-Bertschi 2022, N = 16). What humans do not show directly is the segment mechanism — principal-cell ENaC/ROMK flux, flow-dependence at the single-nephron level — which the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) present from animal micropuncture and isolated-tubule experiments. This shelf is therefore graded EMERGING: the controls are human-verified, the cellular picture is an extrapolation, and it says so on its face. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Deliberately not folded into pack #6078 (aldosterone secretion): the secretion question has its own direct human probes, carded here; but any reader should treat single-nephron numbers in textbook accounts of this topic as animal numbers until a human method measures them.

Nephron. 1995 (PMID: 7753258); Pechère-Bertschi A et al. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation. 2022 (PMID: 33492394). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.
