shelves.title: Telitacicept in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria −58.9% vs −8.8% on placebo in the phase 3 interim (NEJM 2026) — China programme, interim data
shelves.question: In adults with IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL inhibitor telitacicept, compared with placebo on supportive care, reduce proteinuria?
mesh: Tumor Necrosis Factor Ligand Superfamily Member 13
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Telitacicept is a single-source product (RemeGen; ex-China rights Vor Biopharma), named under the clarification exception. Publication status, re-verified at build from the fetched record: the phase 3 primary report IS published — a prespecified interim analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine (2026), not merely a supplement or sponsor statement. In that trial (TELIGAN, n=318), the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell 58.9% on telitacicept 240 mg weekly versus 8.8% on placebo at 39 weeks — a relative difference of −55.0% in favour of the drug — while eGFR changed −1.0% versus −7.7%. The earlier phase 2 (n=44) agrees in direction (proteinuria −49% at 240 mg vs placebo, P=0.013). A small real-world observational study (n=38) is concordant on eGFR but its proteinuria difference was not significant (P=0.081) — it is labelled observational and adds no weight beyond consistency. Cautions: the phase 3 is an interim analysis, the programme is single-country (China), adverse events were commoner on drug (89.3% vs 78.6%) though serious events were fewer (2.5% vs 8.2%), and the 2-year results are conference-only and are fenced, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: TELIGAN phase 3 interim (N Engl J Med 2026): 24-h UPCR −58.9% vs −8.8% on placebo at 39 weeks (relative difference −55.0%); eGFR −1.0% vs −7.7%
cards.summary: TELIGAN phase 3 interim (N Engl J Med 2026): 24-h UPCR −58.9% vs −8.8% on placebo at 39 weeks (relative difference −55.0%); eGFR −1.0% vs −7.7%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (TELIGAN, prespecified interim analysis)
cards.people: 318 adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy and persistent proteinuria (≥1.0 g/day) despite appropriate supportive care, randomised 1:1 to once-weekly subcutaneous telitacicept 240 mg (n=159) or placebo (n=159); prespecified interim analysis of the phase 3 trial.
cards.result: Percentage change in 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 39 was −58.9% on telitacicept versus −8.8% on placebo, a relative difference of −55.0% (95% CI −61.3 to −47.6; P<0.001) in favour of telitacicept (relative measure, labelled as reported). eGFR changed −1.0% (95% CI −3.2 to 1.2) versus −7.7% (95% CI −9.9 to −5.4). Adverse events occurred in 89.3% versus 78.6%, but serious adverse events were less common on telitacicept (2.5% vs 8.2%); no unexpected safety findings.
cards.watchOut: Interim, not final, analysis — the trial continues and later readouts could shift the picture. Single-country (China) phase 3 programme. Publication status verified from this fetched record at build: the NEJM primary publication is real (the slate-stage flag asked for this re-verification). Tested product: telitacicept, RemeGen.
cards.source: TELIGAN phase 3 trial of telitacicept in IgA nephropathy — prespecified interim analysis, The New England Journal of Medicine 2026. PMID: 42127391. NCT05799287. cards.headline: Phase 2 (Kidney Int Rep 2023): proteinuria −49% on 240 mg vs placebo at 24 weeks (P=0.013); −25% on 160 mg, not significant
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Kidney Int Rep 2023): proteinuria −49% on 240 mg vs placebo at 24 weeks (P=0.013); −25% on 160 mg, not significant
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 trial (telitacicept in IgA nephropathy)
cards.people: 44 adults with IgA nephropathy (eGFR >35 mL/min/1.73 m², proteinuria ≥0.75 g/day despite optimal supportive therapy) randomised 1:1:1 to weekly subcutaneous telitacicept 160 mg (n=16), 240 mg (n=14) or placebo (n=14) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean proteinuria fell 49% from baseline on telitacicept 240 mg (change vs placebo −0.88 g/day as reported, 95% CI −1.57 to −0.20; P=0.013) and 25% on 160 mg (−0.29; 95% CI −0.95 to 0.37; P=0.389, not significant). Serum IgA, IgG and IgM fell continuously on drug; eGFR remained stable. Treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate, with no severe events.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=44) and short (24 weeks) — a dose-finding precursor whose 240 mg result the phase 3 later confirmed in direction. Tested product: telitacicept, RemeGen.

cards.headline: Real-world observational study (Clin Kidney J 2026) — observational: low-dose telitacicept, UPCR −51.5% vs −33.3% in controls (P=0.081, not significant); eGFR +1.77 vs −4.06 (P=0.008)
cards.summary: Real-world observational study (Clin Kidney J 2026) — observational: low-dose telitacicept, UPCR −51.5% vs −33.3% in controls (P=0.081, not significant); eGFR +1.77 vs −4.06 (P=0.008)
cards.people: 38 adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy in a single-centre real-world comparison: 19 treated with weekly telitacicept 80 mg (a lower dose than the trials) and 19 contemporaneous patients not receiving telitacicept, followed for 12 months. Observational — treatment was not randomised.
cards.result: Over 12 months, UPCR fell 51.52% in the telitacicept group versus 33.31% in controls — a difference that was a trend only (P=0.081, not significant) — while eGFR change favoured telitacicept (+1.77 vs −4.06 mL/min/1.73 m²; P=0.008). No severe adverse events occurred on telitacicept versus one in controls. The authors call for larger prospective studies.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence caps at POSSIBLE and is labelled as such: confounding by treatment choice is expected, the proteinuria endpoint itself was not significant, and the 80 mg dose is below the trialled 160–240 mg range.
cards.source: Real-world observational study of low-dose telitacicept in IgA nephropathy, Clinical Kidney Journal 2026. PMID: 42899115. No registry ID appears in the fetched record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

shelves.title: Povetacicept in IgA nephropathy: UPCR −52.0% vs −4.3% on placebo in the RAINIER phase 3 interim (NEJM 2026); earlier single-arm data in IgAN and membranous nephropathy
shelves.question: In adults with IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL TACI-Fc povetacicept, compared with placebo, reduce proteinuria — and what did the earlier single-arm study show in IgA nephropathy and primary membranous nephropathy?
mesh: Tumor Necrosis Factor Ligand Superfamily Member 13
Transmembrane Activator and CAML Interactor Protein
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Premise correction, flagged for the coordinator: at slate stage this row was framed on single-arm evidence alone because the randomised trial was still ongoing — the RAINIER phase 3 prespecified interim analysis has since been published (New England Journal of Medicine 2026), so the question and the balance are built on it. In RAINIER's interim efficacy set (the first 199 randomised participants), 24-hour UPCR fell 52.0% on povetacicept 80 mg every 4 weeks versus 4.3% on placebo at week 36 (adjusted difference −49.8 percentage points), galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 77.4% versus a 9.1% rise, and haematuria resolved in 85% versus 23% of those with baseline haematuria; adverse and serious adverse events were similar between groups (75% vs 78%; 3% vs 4%). The earlier RUBY-3 single-arm study (IgAN n=54, primary membranous nephropathy n=10 — Ns printed on the face) showed a 64% mean UPCR fall in the IgAN 80 mg cohort and 82% in pMN at week 48 against baseline only, with no comparator. Povetacicept is a single-source product of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, named under the clarification exception. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): strong interim randomised data, one programme, trial ongoing.

cards.headline: RAINIER phase 3 interim (N Engl J Med 2026): UPCR −52.0% vs −4.3% on placebo at week 36; haematuria resolution 85% vs 23%
cards.summary: RAINIER phase 3 interim (N Engl J Med 2026): UPCR −52.0% vs −4.3% on placebo at week 36; haematuria resolution 85% vs 23%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (RAINIER, prespecified interim analysis)
cards.people: 557 participants with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy on stable background therapy received povetacicept 80 mg (n=372) or placebo (n=185) subcutaneously every 4 weeks (2:1 randomisation) in the ongoing phase 3 trial; this prespecified interim efficacy analysis covers the first 199 randomised participants (131 povetacicept, 68 placebo).
cards.result: At week 36, 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell 52.0% on povetacicept versus 4.3% on placebo (adjusted difference −49.8 percentage points, 95% CI −58.6 to −39.2; P<0.001). Galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 77.4% versus a 9.1% rise (adjusted difference −79.3 points). Among participants with baseline haematuria, resolution occurred in 85% versus 23% (adjusted difference 62 points, 95% CI 45–78). Adverse events: 75% versus 78%; serious adverse events 3% versus 4%.
cards.watchOut: Interim analysis of an ongoing trial, on the first 199 of 557 dosed participants — effect sizes can move as the full cohort matures. Single sponsor programme (Vertex Pharmaceuticals). Tested product: povetacicept, Vertex Pharmaceuticals.

cards.headline: RUBY-3 phase 1/2, single-arm (Kidney Int Rep 2026): IgAN (n=54) UPCR −64% on 80 mg at week 48 vs baseline; primary membranous nephropathy (n=10) −82% — no comparator
cards.summary: RUBY-3 phase 1/2, single-arm (Kidney Int Rep 2026): IgAN (n=54) UPCR −64% on 80 mg at week 48 vs baseline; primary membranous nephropathy (n=10) −82% — no comparator
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1/2 study (RUBY-3, open-label, no comparator)
cards.people: 54 adults with IgA nephropathy (21 on povetacicept 80 mg, 33 on 240 mg, every 4 weeks) and 10 adults with primary membranous nephropathy (all 80 mg), eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m², in an open-label single-arm phase 1/2 study — Ns printed here on the face, as required for small single-arm evidence.
cards.result: In the IgAN 80 mg cohort, mean 24-hour UPCR fell 64% from baseline (1.3 to 0.5 g/g) at week 48 with stable eGFR; 65% reached UPCR <0.5 g/g, about 90% achieved haematuria resolution and 53% clinical remission; galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 77% by week 48. Results at 240 mg were similar. In primary membranous nephropathy (n=10), UPCR fell 82% (3.8 to 0.7 g/g) with stable eGFR, anti-PLA2R fell 83%, and all participants achieved at least partial remission (40% complete). Povetacicept was generally safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and open-label: every percentage here is change from baseline with no control group, so regression to the mean and background care are unmeasured. The membranous cohort is n=10 — at the reference floor; treat its figures as hypothesis-generating only.

cards.result: Povetacicept was well tolerated at single doses up to 960 mg, with dose-dependent pharmacokinetics. shelves.title: Isatuximab desensitisation in highly sensitised kidney-transplant candidates (single-arm, N = 23): composite response 83%/82% by cohort, but only 39% reached the cPRA target
shelves.question: In highly sensitised adults awaiting kidney transplantation (cPRA ≥80%), does isatuximab monotherapy, compared with baseline (single-arm), reduce anti-HLA antibodies enough to reach desensitisation targets?
shelves.balance: One open-label, single-arm phase 1/2 trial (N = 23; NCT04294459) is the whole efficacy evidence base, carded here as its two enrolled cohorts plus a mechanistic second report of the same trial. The predefined composite desensitisation response was 83.3% in the cPRA ≥99.90% cohort and 81.8% in the cPRA 80.00% to <99.90% cohort — but cPRA values were minimally affected overall, and only 9 of 23 patients (39%) reached the cPRA target, which is printed as plainly as the composite figure. Anti-HLA antibody decreases were maintained for 26 weeks after the last dose in most responders; by a median follow-up of 68 weeks, six patients had received transplant offers and four had accepted. Isatuximab was well tolerated, with exposure similar to multiple-myeloma trials. A mechanistic report on 16 of the trial's patients found that pretreatment memory B-cell phenotypes predicted serologic response (AUC 0.958), validated in a separate 10-patient daratumumab cohort — a different CD38 antibody, printed as such. There is no randomised or comparative evidence, and no standardised desensitisation regimen exists to compare against. The imlifidase desensitisation question is homed on pack #3199 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Cohort A of the phase 1/2 trial (cPRA ≥99.90%, n = 12): composite desensitisation response 83.3% on isatuximab
cards.summary: Cohort A of the phase 1/2 trial (cPRA ≥99.90%, n = 12): composite desensitisation response 83.3% on isatuximab
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 1/2 trial, cohort A (NCT04294459), J Am Soc Nephrol 2024
cards.people: Cohort A of an open-label, single-arm phase 1/2 study (NCT04294459): 12 kidney-transplant candidates with calculated panel reactive antibody (cPRA) ≥99.90%, given isatuximab 10 mg/kg weekly for 4 weeks then every 2 weeks for 8 weeks. This card and the next are the two explicitly labelled cohorts of the one trial report (PMID: 38147137); together they total 23 patients, not 46.
cards.result: The overall response rate on the predefined composite desensitisation end point was 83.3% in cohort A. Isatuximab decreased CD38+ plasmablasts, plasma cells and NK cells and significantly reduced HLA-specific IgG-producing memory B cells; in responders, anti-HLA antibody decreases were maintained for 26 weeks after the last dose. The drug was well tolerated, with pharmacokinetic exposure similar to multiple-myeloma trials.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: a composite response rate against baseline cannot separate drug effect from assay variation or natural antibody fluctuation, and the composite end point is a surrogate for actually receiving a compatible transplant.

cards.headline: Cohort B of the phase 1/2 trial (cPRA 80.00% to <99.90%, n = 11): composite response 81.8% — but across both cohorts only 9/23 (39%) reached the cPRA target
cards.summary: Cohort B of the phase 1/2 trial (cPRA 80.00% to <99.90%, n = 11): composite response 81.8% — but across both cohorts only 9/23 (39%) reached the cPRA target
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 1/2 trial, cohort B (NCT04294459), J Am Soc Nephrol 2024
cards.people: Cohort B of the same open-label, single-arm phase 1/2 study (NCT04294459): 11 kidney-transplant candidates with cPRA 80.00% to <99.90%, given the same isatuximab regimen (10 mg/kg weekly for 4 weeks, then every 2 weeks for 8 weeks). Second labelled cohort card of the one trial report (PMID: 38147137).
cards.result: The composite desensitisation response was 81.8% in cohort B. Across both cohorts, however, cPRA values were minimally affected: only 9 of 23 patients (39%) had cPRA decreases to target levels. By the study cutoff (median follow-up 68 weeks), six patients had received transplant offers, of which four were accepted.
cards.watchOut: The gap between the 83%/82% composite response and the 39% cPRA-target rate is the central fact of this trial: most of the composite response did not translate into the allocation-relevant cPRA change.

cards.headline: Mechanistic second report of the same trial: pretreatment memory B-cell phenotypes predicted serologic response (AUC 0.958) in 16 isatuximab patients
cards.summary: Mechanistic second report of the same trial: pretreatment memory B-cell phenotypes predicted serologic response (AUC 0.958) in 16 isatuximab patients
cards.type: Mechanistic substudy of NCT04294459 with external validation cohort, Am J Transplant 2025
cards.people: Second, explicitly labelled report of NCT04294459: spectral flow cytometry and HLA-specific memory B-cell (mBC) assessment in 16 of the trial's isatuximab-treated patients with paired samples, with an external validation cohort of 10 highly sensitised candidates treated with daratumumab (NCT04204980) — a different CD38 antibody, not isatuximab.
cards.result: Isatuximab depleted bone marrow plasma cells, peripheral CD38-expressing plasmablasts, plasma cells, transitional B cells and class-switched mBCs, reducing HLA-specific IgG-producing mBC frequencies. Pretreatment abundance of circulating mBC phenotypes — especially CD38-negative class-switched mBCs — distinguished high serologic responders from low/non-responders (AUC 0.958, 95% CI 0.860 to 1.000; P = .009), and the signature was validated in the daratumumab cohort.
cards.watchOut: This report adds no new isatuximab patients beyond the 23 in the parent trial (16 with paired samples), and its validation cohort received daratumumab, not isatuximab — it explains response variability; it is not independent efficacy evidence.

shelves.title: Urinary CCL14 for persistent severe AKI (observational): AUC 0.83 in RUBY and 0.81 on external validation, but 0.70 in the adjudicated Diamond validation — cut-offs 1.3 and 13 ng/mL
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with stage 2–3 acute kidney injury, how accurately does urinary CCL14 predict persistent severe AKI (stage 3 lasting ≥72 h, or death/dialysis), and at which cut-offs?
shelves.balance: This is a prognosis/test-accuracy question and the evidence is observational by design, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. In the RUBY discovery cohort (331 patients analysed), urinary C-C motif chemokine ligand 14 (CCL14) predicted persistent severe AKI with an AUC of 0.83, better than urinary KIM-1, plasma cystatin C or urinary NGAL (none above 0.75). The standardised clinical assay — named in the publications as the NEPHROCLEAR uCCL14 Test on the Astute 140 Meter (Astute Medical) — uses two cut-offs: 1.3 ng/mL (sensitivity 91%, negative predictive value 92%) and 13 ng/mL (specificity 93%, positive predictive value 72%). External validation in SAPPHIRE gave an AUC of 0.81, and serial measurements added information (a falling category: odds ratio 0.20; a rising category: 4.04 — relative measures). The largest, clinically adjudicated validation (Diamond, 476 patients) was weaker: AUC 0.70, and at 1.3 ng/mL sensitivity 78.1% with specificity only 49.8%, though values above 13 ng/mL still carried a hazard ratio of 5.70 for kidney replacement therapy. CCL14 stratifies risk; it does not by itself direct a proven treatment. The neighbouring [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] imminent-AKI question is a different question, homed elsewhere, and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: RUBY 2020: urinary CCL14 predicted persistent stage 3 AKI with AUC 0.83 — better than KIM-1, cystatin C or NGAL (all ≤0.75)
cards.summary: RUBY 2020: urinary CCL14 predicted persistent stage 3 AKI with AUC 0.83 — better than KIM-1, cystatin C or NGAL (all ≤0.75)
cards.type: Prospective observational biomarker study (RUBY), Intensive Care Med 2020
cards.people: Multicentre international prospective observational study (RUBY, NCT01868724): 364 critically ill patients enrolled in intensive care with KDIGO stage 2 or 3 AKI, 331 (91%) available for the primary analysis; 110 (33%) developed persistent stage 3 AKI (≥72 h).
cards.result: Of the biomarkers tested, urinary CCL14 was the most predictive of persistent stage 3 AKI, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.83 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.87) — significantly greater than urinary KIM-1, plasma cystatin C and urinary NGAL, none of which achieved an AUC above 0.75.
cards.watchOut: Observational prognostic accuracy in one (large, heterogeneous) cohort: an AUC of 0.83 ranks risk but does not show that acting on the result improves outcomes.

cards.type: Standardised-assay cut-off report of the RUBY study, Kidney360 2022
cards.people: Second, explicitly labelled report of the RUBY study (NCT01868724), establishing two cut-offs for the standardised clinical assay for prediction of persistent severe AKI (KDIGO stage 3 for at least 72 consecutive hours; patients receiving renal replacement therapy or dying before 72 h in stage 3 also counted as reaching the end point). cards.result: A urinary CCL14 cut-off of 1.3 ng/mL achieved sensitivity 91% (95% CI 84% to 96%) with a negative predictive value of 92%; a cut-off of 13 ng/mL achieved specificity 93% (89% to 96%) with a positive predictive value of 72% (negative predictive value 75%). cards.watchOut: Cut-offs derived and assessed within the RUBY programme; predictive values depend on the 33% event prevalence in this cohort and will shift in lower-risk populations.

cards.headline: SAPPHIRE external validation 2021: AUC 0.81 for persistent severe AKI in an independent cohort (n = 195, 28 events)
cards.summary: SAPPHIRE external validation 2021: AUC 0.81 for persistent severe AKI in an independent cohort (n = 195, 28 events)
cards.type: External validation, secondary analysis of SAPPHIRE, Crit Care 2021
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the prospective multicentre SAPPHIRE study: 195 critically ill patients with cardiac and/or respiratory dysfunction who developed KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI within one week of enrolment; urinary CCL14 was measured at onset of stage 2–3 AKI; 28 patients (14%) developed persistent severe AKI (≥72 h of stage 3, or death or renal replacement therapy before 72 h).
cards.result: The AUC for urinary CCL14 to predict persistent severe AKI was 0.81 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.89). Risk of persistent severe AKI rose with higher CCL14 values, and renal replacement therapy and/or death at 90 days increased across CCL14 tertiles.
cards.watchOut: Only 28 outcome events, so the confidence interval is wide (0.72 to 0.89); a secondary analysis of a cohort assembled for a different biomarker programme.

cards.headline: Serial CCL14 (RUBY + SAPPHIRE, n = 417): a falling risk category carried odds ratio 0.20 and a rising category 4.04 for persistent severe AKI
cards.summary: Serial CCL14 (RUBY + SAPPHIRE, n = 417): a falling risk category carried odds ratio 0.20 and a rising category 4.04 for persistent severe AKI
cards.type: Retrospective observational serial-measurement analysis, Crit Care Explor 2023
cards.people: Retrospective observational analysis of two multinational ICU studies (RUBY and SAPPHIRE): 417 critically ill patients with early stage 2–3 AKI and three consecutive urinary CCL14 measurements at 12-hour intervals, measured with the NEPHROCLEAR uCCL14 Test on the Astute 140 Meter (Astute Medical, San Diego, CA) — the assay named in the publication; 75 patients developed persistent severe AKI.
cards.result: The initial CCL14 category (low ≤1.3, medium >1.3 to ≤13, high >13 ng/mL) strongly correlated with the primary end point and was unchanged over the first 24 hours in 66% of patients. Compared with no change and accounting for baseline category, a decrease in category was associated with lower odds of persistent severe AKI (odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.45; P < 0.001) and an increase with higher odds (odds ratio 4.04, 1.75 to 9.46; P = 0.001) — relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Overlaps the RUBY and SAPPHIRE populations carded above rather than adding an independent cohort; category changes may partly track the clinical course they are meant to predict.
cards.source: Prowle JR et al. Serial Urinary C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 14 and Risk of Persistent Severe Acute Kidney Injury. Critical care explorations. 2023. PMID: 36875557. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Diamond validation 2026 (adjudicated, n = 476): weaker discrimination — AUC 0.70; at 1.3 ng/mL sensitivity 78.1% but specificity only 49.8%
cards.summary: Diamond validation 2026 (adjudicated, n = 476): weaker discrimination — AUC 0.70; at 1.3 ng/mL sensitivity 78.1% but specificity only 49.8%
cards.type: Prospective observational validation with clinical adjudication (Diamond), CJASN 2026
cards.people: Multicentre prospective observational study (Diamond, NCT04785391): 476 ICU patients with KDIGO stage 2 or 3 AKI within the previous 36 hours, with the primary end point (persistent severe AKI: stage 3 lasting ≥72 h) determined by a clinical adjudication committee of three nephrologists; 151 patients (32%) were adjudicated to have persistent severe AKI, 95 (20%) received kidney replacement therapy and 98 (21%) died.
cards.result: The AUC for CCL14 prediction of persistent severe AKI was 0.70 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.76). At the 1.3 ng/mL cut-off, sensitivity was 78.1% (70.9% to 84.0%) and specificity 49.8% (44.4% to 55.3%); at 13 ng/mL, sensitivity was 24.5% and specificity 93.5%. For every 1 ng/mL increase in CCL14 there was a 6% higher rate of kidney replacement therapy initiation (a relative measure), and values above 13 ng/mL carried a hazard ratio of 5.70 (3.22 to 10.11) for kidney replacement therapy and 3.50 (2.19 to 5.60) for kidney replacement therapy or death versus ≤1.3 ng/mL. There was no increased risk of death per ng/mL.
cards.watchOut: The most rigorous validation is also the weakest result: at the sensitive cut-off, about half of patients who will not develop persistent severe AKI still test positive, so a positive low-cut-off result is a weak rule-in.
cards.source: Kampf JP et al. Validation of Urinary C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 14 for Persistent Severe Acute Kidney Injury Using Clinical Adjudication. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2026. PMID: 42747895. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04785391, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: CCL14 stratifies persistence risk (AUC 0.70–0.83 across cohorts); the 13 ng/mL cut-off rules in, the 1.3 ng/mL cut-off only partly rules out
cards.summary: Synthesis: CCL14 stratifies persistence risk (AUC 0.70–0.83 across cohorts); the 13 ng/mL cut-off rules in, the 1.3 ng/mL cut-off only partly rules out
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf: RUBY (331 analysed), its standardised-assay report, SAPPHIRE external validation (195), a serial-measurement analysis (417, overlapping), and the Diamond adjudicated validation (476).
cards.result: Urinary CCL14 predicted persistent severe AKI with AUC 0.83 (RUBY), 0.81 (SAPPHIRE) and 0.70 (Diamond, adjudicated). The standardised cut-offs are 1.3 ng/mL (sensitive: 91% in RUBY, 78.1% in Diamond, with Diamond specificity only 49.8%) and 13 ng/mL (specific: 93–93.5% in both). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — observational prognostic accuracy); no carded study shows that CCL14-guided management improves patient outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This is a synthesis card, not a separate study; it adds no patients to the evidence base.

shelves.title: Proactive desmopressin clamp in severe hyponatraemia (SPLIT): the large cohort found less overcorrection (6.8% vs 27.1%), the one small randomised trial found no significant difference
shelves.question: In adults with severe hyponatraemia (sodium ≤120–125 mmol/L) treated with hypertonic saline, does a proactive desmopressin “clamp” strategy, compared with reactive/rescue desmopressin or none, reduce overcorrection without causing harm?
shelves.balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: live shelf #126 covers bolus-versus-infusion delivery and correction ceilings, and pack #5655 covers correction RATE versus osmotic demyelination risk; neither poses the proactive-clamp STRATEGY question, and no PMID from either home is re-carded here. The strategy evidence splits. The largest cohort (184 admissions, sodium ≤120 mEq/L, four hospitals) found overcorrection by >8 mEq/L in 24 hours in 6.8% with proactive desmopressin versus 27.1% without, despite the proactive group starting lower (110.2 vs 115.2 mEq/L) — but sodium was also checked more often in the proactive group, and the design is retrospective. The only randomised trial (n = 49, sodium <125 mmol/L ≈ <125 mEq/L) found overcorrection in 16.7% proactive versus 28% reactive (P = 0.54) — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome in this small trial). An earlier ICU cohort likewise found no significant difference in goal correction or overcorrection, with longer hypertonic-saline duration when desmopressin was used. No osmotic demyelination cases occurred in the large cohort, and mortality did not differ in any carded report. Sodium values are given in mmol/L, numerically equal to mEq/L as used in US practice.

cards.headline: Multicentre cohort 2025 (n = 184): proactive desmopressin — overcorrection >8 mEq/L in 6.8% vs 27.1% without a proactive strategy
cards.summary: Multicentre cohort 2025 (n = 184): proactive desmopressin — overcorrection >8 mEq/L in 6.8% vs 27.1% without a proactive strategy
cards.people: Retrospective cohort at four University of Pittsburgh Medical Center hospitals (2018–2023): 184 adult admissions with plasma sodium ≤120 mEq/L (≤120 mmol/L) treated with 3% hypertonic saline; 57.6% female, mean age 60.6 years; hyponatraemia was chronic in 93.5%, with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis the leading cause (51.6%); 44 admissions received proactive desmopressin and 140 did not (reactive/rescue or none).
cards.result: Despite a lower baseline sodium in the proactive group (110.2 ± 6.3 vs 115.2 ± 7.2 mEq/L; P < 0.001), correction by >8 mEq/L within 24 hours occurred in 6.8% versus 27.1% (P = 0.009) and by >10 mEq/L in 0% versus 15% (P = 0.014). Hospital mortality (6.8% vs 6.4%), length of stay, fluid overload (9.1% vs 9.5%) and worsening hyponatraemia (2.3% vs 1.5%) were similar; no osmotic demyelination and no cerebral-oedema deaths were identified. Plasma sodium was checked significantly more often in the proactive group (20.9 vs 17.4 checks; P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by indication and by monitoring intensity: clinicians who clamp also check sodium more often, and the proactive group differed at baseline — the association cannot be read as the clamp's causal effect.
cards.source: AlShanableh Z et al. Plasma Sodium Correction Rates in Patients with Severe Hyponatremia Treated with Hypertonic Saline with and without Proactive Desmopressin. Kidney360. 2025. PMID: 40272897. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Randomised trial 2024 (n = 49): proactive vs reactive desmopressin — overcorrection 16.7% vs 28%, P = 0.54 (no significant difference)
cards.summary: Randomised trial 2024 (n = 49): proactive vs reactive desmopressin — overcorrection 16.7% vs 28%, P = 0.54 (no significant difference)
cards.people: Single randomised controlled trial (June 2022 to February 2023): 49 patients with severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (serum sodium below 125 mmol/L, numerically 125 mEq/L) assigned to proactive desmopressin (given immediately on diagnosis) or reactive desmopressin (given only if sodium tended to overcorrect). Primary outcome: incidence of overcorrection.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in overcorrection incidence between proactive (16.7%) and reactive (28%) groups (P = 0.54) — on its primary outcome, the proactive strategy made no difference that this trial could detect. Sodium change did not differ at 1, 6, 12 or 24 hours; at 48 hours the proactive group's change was higher but still within safe limits (10.3 ± 3.6 vs 7.7 ± 3.6 mmol/L; P = 0.013). Time to symptom improvement, fluid volume, desmopressin dose, urine volume, hospital stay, osmotic demyelination incidence and 28-day mortality did not differ significantly. The authors state that larger studies are needed.
cards.watchOut: Only 49 patients: the trial cannot exclude a clinically important benefit or harm — its confidence around the 11-percentage-point observed gap is wide, and 'no significant difference' here is absence of evidence as much as evidence of absence.
cards.source: Pakchotanon K et al. Safety and efficacy of proactive versus reactive administration of desmopressin in severe symptomatic hyponatremia: a randomized controlled trial. Scientific reports. 2024. PMID: 38553491. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Retrospective single-centre study of critically ill patients with hyponatraemia (serum sodium ≤125 mEq/L) receiving 3% hypertonic saline (2015–2019), divided into hypertonic saline alone versus saline plus proactive or reactive desmopressin (rescue desmopressin possible in either group). The record does not document the number of patients — N not documented.
cards.result: Goal sodium correction of 5–10 mEq/L at 24 hours was achieved in 52.5% on saline alone versus 65.6% with desmopressin added (P = 0.21) — not significantly different. Overcorrection during any 24- or 48-hour period was not statistically different between groups, and ICU length of stay, free-water intake, urine output and sodium rises at 12 and 24 hours did not differ; the desmopressin group had a significantly longer duration of hypertonic saline infusion (P = 0.0022) and a larger total amount.
cards.watchOut: Proactive and reactive desmopressin are pooled in one group, so this cohort cannot isolate the proactive clamp; it is also retrospective, and its patient number is not documented in the record.
cards.source: Tran LK et al. Evaluation of Desmopressin in Critically Ill Patients with Hyponatremia Requiring 3% Hypertonic Saline. The American journal of the medical sciences. 2021. PMID: 33812910. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the cohort signal for less overcorrection is not confirmed by the only randomised trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the cohort signal for less overcorrection is not confirmed by the only randomised trial
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf: one multicentre retrospective cohort (184 admissions), one small randomised trial (49 patients), and one ICU retrospective cohort (N not documented).
cards.result: Proactive desmopressin was associated with less >8 mEq/L overcorrection in the large cohort (6.8% vs 27.1%), while the randomised trial found 16.7% versus 28% (P = 0.54, no significant difference) and the ICU cohort found no significant difference in goal correction or overcorrection, with longer saline exposure when desmopressin was used. No carded report showed a mortality or demyelination difference. Proposed stamp: SPLIT — observational-dominant evidence; the strategy remains unproven by randomised data. Cross-points: delivery/ceilings home live #126; correction-rate/demyelination home pack #5655 — neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: This is a synthesis card, not a separate study; it adds no patients to the evidence base.

shelves.title: Evocalcet and upacicalcet in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: evocalcet non-inferior to cinacalcet with fewer gut effects; upacicalcet beat placebo in three placebo-controlled programmes — iPTH surrogates only
shelves.question: In patients on haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, do the newer calcimimetics evocalcet (oral) and upacicalcet (intravenous), compared with cinacalcet or placebo, achieve parathyroid-hormone targets with fewer gastrointestinal effects?
shelves.balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: home live #1197 cards etelcalcetide only, and no evocalcet or upacicalcet record appears there; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. Evocalcet (oral): in the Japanese phase 3 head-to-head (n = 634), 72.7% on evocalcet versus 76.7% on cinacalcet reached the intact PTH target of 60–240 pg/mL (difference −4.0 percentage points, within the −15% non-inferiority margin), with gastrointestinal adverse events in 18.6% versus 32.8%; a 52-week East Asian trial (n = 403) confirmed non-inferiority (mean iPTH change −34.7% vs −30.2%) with fewer gastrointestinal events (33.5% vs 50.5%). Upacicalcet (intravenous, given after each dialysis session): in the Japanese phase 3 (n = 153), 67% versus 8% on placebo reached the iPTH target; in the twin PATH-1/PATH-2 phase 3 trials (n = 768), a ≥30% iPTH reduction occurred in 42.1%/43.5% versus 16.8%/17.4% on placebo, with gastrointestinal rates similar to placebo but more asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL in 31%/45% vs 12%/19%) and more dose interruptions; symptomatic hypocalcaemia was infrequent (0.8% and 2%). Regulatory status, stated on the face: the evocalcet evidence is Japan-only (the second trial is East Asian), and upacicalcet is approved in Japan and investigational in the US. Every end point here is a biochemical surrogate (iPTH) — no carded trial measured fractures, cardiovascular events or death.

cards.headline: Evocalcet head-to-head 2018 (n = 634): non-inferior to cinacalcet for iPTH target (72.7% vs 76.7%), with gastrointestinal events 18.6% vs 32.8%
cards.summary: Evocalcet head-to-head 2018 (n = 634): non-inferior to cinacalcet for iPTH target (72.7% vs 76.7%), with gastrointestinal events 18.6% vs 32.8%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind head-to-head phase 3 trial, Kidney Int 2018
cards.people: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial in Japanese patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism on haemodialysis, randomised to oral evocalcet or cinacalcet (317 patients each) for 30 weeks. Primary end point: non-inferiority in the proportion achieving mean intact PTH 60–240 pg/mL at weeks 28–30 (non-inferiority margin −15%, per-protocol analyses).
cards.result: Target intact PTH was achieved by 72.7% on evocalcet and 76.7% on cinacalcet (between-group difference −4.0 percentage points, 95% CI −11.4% to 3.5%) — non-inferiority demonstrated. Gastrointestinal-related adverse events occurred in 18.6% versus 32.8% (difference −14.2 points, −20.9% to −7.5%), significant for superiority on that safety outcome.
cards.watchOut: Japan-only population and a biochemical (iPTH) end point; the −15% non-inferiority margin is wide, so 'non-inferior' tolerates a modest true deficit, though the observed difference was small.
cards.source: Fukagawa M et al. Head-to-head comparison of the new calcimimetic agent evocalcet with cinacalcet in Japanese hemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Kidney international. 2018. PMID: 30049473. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Evocalcet East Asian trial 2023 (n = 403, 52 weeks): mean iPTH change −34.7% vs −30.2% on cinacalcet (non-inferior); gastrointestinal events 33.5% vs 50.5%
cards.summary: Evocalcet East Asian trial 2023 (n = 403, 52 weeks): mean iPTH change −34.7% vs −30.2% on cinacalcet (non-inferior); gastrointestinal events 33.5% vs 50.5%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial, Kidney Int Rep 2023
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group international multicentre trial in East Asian haemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism: 203 randomised to evocalcet and 200 to cinacalcet for 52 weeks; 70.1% had baseline intact PTH ≥500 pg/mL, with no between-group difference.
cards.result: Mean percentage change in intact PTH at 52 weeks was −34.7% on evocalcet and −30.2% on cinacalcet (between-group difference −4.4%, 95% CI −13.1% to 4.3%, below the predefined 15% non-inferiority margin). A ≥30% iPTH decrease was achieved by 67.3% versus 58.7% (difference 8.6 points, −1.8% to 19.1%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were significantly less frequent with evocalcet (33.5% vs 50.5%; P = 0.001); hypocalcaemia incidence did not differ, and no major safety concerns were observed.
cards.watchOut: East Asian population only, and again a surrogate end point; the gastrointestinal advantage is consistent across both evocalcet trials but absolute event rates differ between the two reports' definitions and durations.
cards.source: Ni Z et al. Comparison of the Oral Calcimimetics Evocalcet and Cinacalcet in East Asian Patients on Hemodialysis with Secondary Hyperparathyroidism. Kidney international reports. 2023. PMID: 38025238. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Upacicalcet Japanese phase 3 (n = 153): iPTH target reached by 67% vs 8% on placebo; upper gastrointestinal events similar to placebo
cards.summary: Upacicalcet Japanese phase 3 (n = 153): iPTH target reached by 67% vs 8% on placebo; upper gastrointestinal events similar to placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, CJASN 2023
cards.people: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03801980) in Japanese haemodialysis patients with serum intact PTH >240 pg/mL and corrected calcium ≥8.4 mg/dL: 103 received intravenous upacicalcet and 50 placebo, after each dialysis session for 24 weeks. Primary outcome: percentage achieving mean iPTH 60–240 pg/mL at weeks 22–24.
cards.result: The iPTH target was achieved by 67% (69/103) on upacicalcet versus 8% (4/50) on placebo (difference 59 percentage points, 95% CI 48% to 71%). Upacicalcet also lowered fibroblast growth factor-23 and bone-turnover markers. Adverse events occurred in 85% versus 72%; upper gastrointestinal events such as nausea and vomiting were similar between groups, and corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL occurred in 2% on upacicalcet and no placebo patients.
cards.watchOut: Japan-only, 24 weeks, surrogate end point; the placebo target rate (8%) is very low because spontaneous iPTH control to 60–240 pg/mL without a calcimimetic is uncommon at these entry levels.
cards.source: Shigematsu T et al. Efficacy and Safety of Upacicalcet in Hemodialysis Patients with Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2023. PMID: 37696667. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03801980, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: PATH-1 and PATH-2 2026 (twin trials, n = 768): ≥30% iPTH reduction 42.1%/43.5% on upacicalcet vs 16.8%/17.4% on placebo — with more asymptomatic hypocalcaemia
cards.summary: PATH-1 and PATH-2 2026 (twin trials, n = 768): ≥30% iPTH reduction 42.1%/43.5% on upacicalcet vs 16.8%/17.4% on placebo — with more asymptomatic hypocalcaemia
cards.type: Twin randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (PATH-1/PATH-2), J Am Soc Nephrol 2026
cards.people: Two identical, parallel, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (PATH-1, NCT05832931; PATH-2, NCT05836220) in 768 haemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism and iPTH ≥400 to ≤1500 pg/mL: 510 received intravenous upacicalcet and 258 placebo after haemodialysis for 27 weeks, titrated by iPTH and corrected calcium. Primary outcome: ≥30% decrease in mean iPTH during weeks 22–27.
cards.result: The primary outcome was achieved in PATH-1 by 42.1% on upacicalcet versus 16.8% on placebo (difference 25.3 points, 95% CI 16.2 to 34.5; P < 0.001) and in PATH-2 by 43.5% versus 17.4% (difference 26.1 points, 17.4 to 34.8; P < 0.001). Gastrointestinal symptoms and serious adverse events were similar between groups. Corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL occurred in 31% versus 12% (PATH-1) and 45% versus 19% (PATH-2), and dose interruptions in 44% versus 24% and 52% versus 27%; investigator-attributed symptomatic hypocalcaemia occurred in 0.8% and 2% of upacicalcet patients and no placebo patients.
cards.watchOut: The twin trials are one programme run in parallel, not two independent confirmations in different settings; hypocalcaemia (mostly asymptomatic) and dose interruptions were substantially more frequent on upacicalcet, and the end point remains the iPTH surrogate.
cards.source: Kendrick J et al. Efficacy and Safety of Upacicalcet in Hemodialysis Patients with Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: Two Randomized Clinical Trials. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2026. PMID: 42914959. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05832931 and NCT05836220, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: both newer calcimimetics control iPTH; evocalcet's edge is gastrointestinal tolerability, upacicalcet's cost is hypocalcaemia — all on surrogate evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: both newer calcimimetics control iPTH; evocalcet's edge is gastrointestinal tolerability, upacicalcet's cost is hypocalcaemia — all on surrogate evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf: evocalcet head-to-head trials (634 and 403 patients) and upacicalcet placebo-controlled trials (153 and 768 patients), all in haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
cards.result: Evocalcet was non-inferior to cinacalcet for iPTH control in two trials, with gastrointestinal events lower by 14–17 percentage points. Upacicalcet beat placebo for iPTH targets/reductions in the Japanese phase 3 (67% vs 8% at target) and in PATH-1/PATH-2 (≥30% reduction 42–44% vs 17%), with gastrointestinal rates similar to placebo but corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL in 31–45% versus 12–19%. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit — for intact PTH control, a biochemical surrogate). Regulatory status: evocalcet evidence is Japan/East Asia only; upacicalcet is approved in Japan and investigational in the US. Etelcalcetide is homed on live shelf #1197 and EVOLVE on #296; neither is re-carded here.

shelves.title: Phosphate handling in health: the TmP/GFR threshold, its fall with rising PTH, and adaptation to a phosphate load
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is phosphate handled — what is the tubular maximum for phosphate corrected for GFR (TmP/GFR), how do PTH and dietary phosphate loading change fractional excretion within hours to days, and what did the classic phosphate-infusion and deprivation studies show about adaptation?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). The kidney defends plasma phosphate at a tubular threshold, TmP/GFR: Walton & Bijvoet's method (PMID 923101) made that threshold measurable from single paired samples. In health the threshold is not fixed — it falls as PTH rises with ageing (Endres, PMID 2821053) and the system adapts to a sustained load by excreting it, with an early FGF23 rise that normalises by 8 weeks and no change in fasting plasma phosphate (Trautvetter, PMID 26786148). The textbook's normative TmP/GFR range (about 0.80–1.35 mmol/L, about 2.5–4.2 mg/dL) is the textbook's account: no carded record prints it. Adjacent pack #6306 covers the calcium-sensing set-point — a different question; this pack does not duplicate its calcium content.

cards.headline: Walton & Bijvoet 1977: renal phosphate handling is best expressed as TmP/GFR — the tubular maximum reabsorption rate divided by GFR — derivable from single paired plasma and urine samples
cards.summary: Walton & Bijvoet 1977: renal phosphate handling is best expressed as TmP/GFR — the tubular maximum reabsorption rate divided by GFR — derivable from single paired plasma and urine samples
cards.people: Methods paper applying the Bijvoet programme's existing human data; no new cohort is described in the record, so N is not documented in the fetched record.
cards.result: The record states that the activity of renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate in man is best expressed as the ratio of the maximum rate of reabsorption to the glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR), and describes a slide-rule method to derive TmP/GFR from phosphate and creatinine concentrations in single samples of plasma and urine — suitable for research and clinical use. TmP/GFR is therefore a threshold expressed in plasma-concentration units: below it, filtered phosphate is essentially fully reabsorbed; above it, the excess is excreted. The record itself prints no normative range, so the normal range quoted in teaching (the textbook's account, roughly 0.80–1.35 mmol/L, about 2.5–4.2 mg/dL) is presented in this pack's balance as the textbook's account, not as a carded measurement.
cards.watchOut: A derivation/methods paper, not a cohort study: it standardises how TmP/GFR is obtained but its abstract reports no subjects and no normative values — do not cite it for a normal range.
cards.source: Primary human physiology methods study | Walton RJ, Bijvoet OL et al. A simple slide-rule method for the assessment of renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate in man. Clin Chim Acta. 1977. PMID: 923101. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Endres 1987: in healthy ageing, immunoreactive PTH rises and TmP/GFR falls — the phosphate threshold is PTH-sensitive across adult life
cards.summary: Endres 1987: in healthy ageing, immunoreactive PTH rises and TmP/GFR falls — the phosphate threshold is PTH-sensitive across adult life
cards.people: Healthy free-living young and elderly men and women residing in the Southwest (United States), studied with two characterised PTH radioimmunoassays plus urinary cAMP and calcium/phosphate measures. N not documented in the fetched record's abstract.
cards.result: Serum immunoreactive PTH was significantly increased in the elderly by both an amino-terminal and a midregion assay; total urinary cAMP and serum alkaline phosphatase also rose with age, while the tubular reabsorptive maximum for phosphate (TmP/GFR) decreased with age. TmP/GFR declined with age in men but not women, and serum phosphate was significantly lower in elderly men than in elderly women; neither total nor ionised calcium fell with age. The authors read the pattern as increased parathyroid function with ageing — the expected direction, since PTH lowers TmP/GFR and raises fractional phosphate excretion.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional age comparison, not a PTH-infusion experiment: the PTH–TmP/GFR link here is concordant association in health, and the sex difference in the TmP/GFR decline is unexplained in the record.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Endres DB et al. Age-related changes in serum immunoreactive parathyroid hormone and its biological action in healthy men and women. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1987. PMID: 2821053. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Trautvetter 2016: eight weeks of 1 g/day extra phosphorus in 62 healthy adults — fasting plasma phosphate did not move, urinary excretion rose, and FGF23 rose at 4 weeks then normalised
cards.summary: Trautvetter 2016: eight weeks of 1 g/day extra phosphorus in 62 healthy adults — fasting plasma phosphate did not move, urinary excretion rose, and FGF23 rose at 4 weeks then normalised
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised controlled feeding intervention)
cards.people: 62 healthy adults who completed a double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel study: 2 weeks of placebo sherbet, then 8 weeks of monosodium phosphate providing 1 g/day phosphorus, with 0, 0.5 or 1.0 g/day calcium carbonate, with diet records, fasting bloods, urine and faecal collections.
cards.result: Fasting plasma phosphate concentrations did not change after any intervention. Renal and faecal phosphorus excretion increased significantly after 8 weeks in all phosphorus groups — the kidney excreted the load rather than letting plasma phosphate rise. Plasma FGF23 was significantly higher after 4 weeks than after 8 weeks of all interventions: an early phosphaturic-hormone response that normalised with continued intake, i.e. adaptation over weeks. With phosphorus but no added calcium, renal calcium and magnesium excretion fell significantly versus placebo — the calcium-dependence of the adaptation. The trial is registered as NCT02095392 (registry ID as printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: Supplemental phosphorus on top of habitual diet in healthy adults, not a deprivation study: it shows loading adaptation (excretion + transient FGF23), and the record reports no TmP/GFR or fractional-excretion time course in the first hours to days.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Trautvetter U et al. Consequences of a high phosphorus intake on mineral metabolism and bone remodeling in dependence of calcium intake in healthy subjects — a randomized placebo-controlled human intervention study. Nutr J. 2016. PMID: 26786148. Registry ID: NCT02095392 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: Phosphate handling in health: the TmP/GFR threshold, its fall with rising PTH, and adaptation to a phosphate load
cards.summary: Synthesis: Phosphate handling in health: the TmP/GFR threshold, its fall with rising PTH, and adaptation to a phosphate load
cards.people: Synthesis of Walton & Bijvoet 1977, Endres 1987 and Trautvetter 2016, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence cards). Adjacent pack #6306 (calcium-sensing set-point) is cross-pointed, not duplicated.
cards.result: Plasma phosphate in health is set renally. Filtered phosphate is reabsorbed up to a tubular maximum; expressed per unit GFR (TmP/GFR) that maximum behaves as a plasma threshold, measurable from single plasma and urine samples by the Walton–Bijvoet method. PTH lowers the threshold: in healthy ageing, rising immunoreactive PTH is accompanied by a falling TmP/GFR (in men) and lower serum phosphate. Dietary loading is handled by excretion, not by a higher plasma level: 1 g/day of extra phosphorus for 8 weeks left fasting plasma phosphate unchanged, raised urinary and faecal phosphorus excretion, and produced only a transient FGF23 rise (higher at 4 weeks, normalised at 8 weeks) — adaptation over days to weeks, with the calcium intake modifying the calcium/magnesium cost. The often-quoted normal TmP/GFR range is the textbook's account; the carded records establish the method, the PTH direction and the loading adaptation, not the range itself.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: hour-scale fractional-excretion responses to a single phosphate load or PTH infusion are described in the older balance literature but were not carded here because no verifiable primary record with those time-course figures was fetched this session; the carded adaptation evidence is at the days-to-weeks scale.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID: 923101; PMID: 2821053; PMID: 26786148. Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies), except Trautvetter 2016 (PMID: 26786148), which reports NCT02095392.

shelves.title: Balcinrenone added to dapagliflozin in heart failure and chronic kidney disease (MIRACLE) and in CKD with albuminuria (MIRO-CKD)
shelves.question: In adults with heart failure (EF <60%) and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–60) already taking dapagliflozin, does adding the selective mineralocorticoid-receptor modulator balcinrenone, compared with dapagliflozin alone, reduce albuminuria — and at what potassium and eGFR cost?
shelves.balance: The two phase 2b trials of the same combination answer differently in different populations, and the shelf is that split. In the population this question asks about — symptomatic heart failure with ejection fraction <60% and eGFR 30–60 — MIRACLE (n=133) did NOT meet its primary endpoint: relative reductions in urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) at 12 weeks were not significantly different between balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin and dapagliflozin plus placebo (the treatment made no difference), with no clear dose-response; MIRACLE was also under-enrolled (133 randomised of about 500 planned; enrolment stopped early for slow recruitment), so the null is an underpowered null. In CKD with albuminuria without a heart-failure entry requirement, MIRO-CKD (n=324) was positive: UACR differences versus dapagliflozin alone of −22.8% and −32.8% relative at 15 mg and 40 mg. The cost side: in MIRACLE there were possible dose-dependent increases in serum potassium, a reduced eGFR in the highest-dose group, and two hyperkalaemia discontinuations on the combination versus none on dapagliflozin alone; in MIRO-CKD investigator-reported hyperkalaemia was 6–7% on the combination versus 5% on dapagliflozin alone. An earlier phase 1b study (n=68) found balcinrenone's potassium rise over 28 days was similar to spironolactone's. UACR is a surrogate endpoint in both trials; there are no heart-failure hospitalisation, kidney-progression or mortality data. The DapaBalci-Leap mechanistic study is conference-abstract only and is not carded.

cards.headline: MIRACLE phase 2b in HF + CKD (2024): primary UACR endpoint NOT met — balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin made no difference versus dapagliflozin alone, n = 133 (enrolment stopped early)
cards.summary: MIRACLE phase 2b in HF + CKD (2024): primary UACR endpoint NOT met — balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin made no difference versus dapagliflozin alone, n = 133 (enrolment stopped early)
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, European Journal of Heart Failure 2024
cards.people: 133 adults with symptomatic heart failure, ejection fraction <60%, eGFR ≥30 to ≤60 mL/min/1.73 m² and UACR ≥30 to <3000 mg/g, randomised to balcinrenone 15, 50 or 150 mg/day plus dapagliflozin 10 mg/day, or dapagliflozin 10 mg/day plus placebo, for 12 weeks. Enrolment was stopped early because of slow recruitment, well short of the planned sample.
cards.result: Relative reductions in UACR from baseline to week 12 (the primary endpoint) were not significantly different between the balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin groups and dapagliflozin plus placebo (the treatment made no difference), and there was no clear balcinrenone dose-response relationship. There were possible dose-dependent increases in serum potassium, a reduced eGFR in the highest-dose group, and non-significant trends towards reduced NT-proBNP. Hyperkalaemia adverse events led to discontinuation in two participants on balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin and none on dapagliflozin plus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Under-enrolled and stopped early (133 of about 500 planned): the null result is compatible with a missed modest effect as well as with no effect. Twelve weeks, surrogate endpoint (UACR) only.
cards.source: Lam CSP, Køber L, Kuwahara K, et al. Balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin in patients with heart failure and chronic kidney disease: Results from the phase 2b MIRACLE trial. Eur J Heart Fail. 2024;26(8):1727-1735. PMID: 38783712. Registry ID: NCT04595370. cards.headline: MIRO-CKD phase 2b in CKD with albuminuria (2025): balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin beat dapagliflozin alone on UACR by 22.8% and 32.8% relative at week 12, n = 324
cards.summary: MIRO-CKD phase 2b in CKD with albuminuria (2025): balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin beat dapagliflozin alone on UACR by 22.8% and 32.8% relative at week 12, n = 324
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind active-controlled trial (MIRO-CKD), The Lancet 2025
cards.people: 324 adults with CKD (eGFR 25 to <60 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR >100 to ≤5000 mg/g, serum potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L [≈14–20 mg/dL]) at 106 sites in 15 countries (mean age 64.6 years; 34% female; mean eGFR 42.2 mL/min/1.73 m²; median UACR 365 mg/g), randomised to balcinrenone 15 mg plus dapagliflozin 10 mg (n=108), balcinrenone 40 mg plus dapagliflozin 10 mg (n=110), or dapagliflozin 10 mg plus placebo (n=106), once daily for 12 weeks as adjunct to renin-angiotensin system inhibitors.
cards.result: At week 12 the UACR difference versus dapagliflozin plus placebo was −22.8% (90% CI −33.3 to −10.7; p=0.0038) for balcinrenone 15 mg and −32.8% (−42.0 to −22.1; p<0.0001) for balcinrenone 40 mg — relative reductions. Investigator-reported hyperkalaemia occurred in 6% (7/108) and 7% (8/110) of the combination groups versus 5% (5/106) on dapagliflozin alone; hypotension and renal adverse events were few and balanced, none serious. Two deaths occurred, both more than 28 days after the last dose.
cards.watchOut: Different population from MIRACLE: MIRO-CKD required albuminuric CKD, not heart failure, so its positive result does not answer the heart-failure question. Twelve weeks of treatment plus an 8-week wash-out; UACR is a surrogate, and 56% were already taking an SGLT2 inhibitor at entry.
cards.source: Heerspink HJL, Cardona JF, Jolly S, et al. Balcinrenone in combination with dapagliflozin compared with dapagliflozin alone in patients with chronic kidney disease and albuminuria: a randomised, active-controlled double-blind, phase 2b clinical trial. Lancet. 2025;406(10518):2449-2460. PMID: 41218621. Registry ID: NCT06350123. cards.headline: Phase 1b (2022): over 28 days, balcinrenone (AZD9977) raised serum potassium about as much as spironolactone in HF with renal impairment, n = 68
cards.summary: Phase 1b (2022): over 28 days, balcinrenone (AZD9977) raised serum potassium about as much as spironolactone in HF with renal impairment, n = 68
cards.type: Phase 1b randomised active-comparator trial, Clinical and Translational Science 2022
cards.people: 68 patients with heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction (EF ≥40%) and renal impairment (eGFR 40–70 mL/min/1.73 m²; mean age 73.0 years; 51.5% men), randomised to once-daily balcinrenone (AZD9977) 100 mg up-titrated to 200 mg (n=33) or spironolactone 25 mg up-titrated to 50 mg (n=35) for 28 days.
cards.result: Mean serum potassium change from baseline to day 28 was +5.7% on balcinrenone and +4.2% on spironolactone; the relative change for balcinrenone versus spironolactone was −0.3% (95% CI −5.3% to 4.4%) at day 28. No discontinuations due to hyperkalaemia occurred with either treatment, and balcinrenone was well tolerated, with evidence of mineralocorticoid-receptor target engagement (median plasma aldosterone increase 89.8 pmol/L versus 67.4 pmol/L on spironolactone).

cards.headline: Synthesis: the combination lowers albuminuria in albuminuric CKD, but the heart-failure trial asked for here was null and under-enrolled
cards.summary: Synthesis: the combination lowers albuminuria in albuminuric CKD, but the heart-failure trial asked for here was null and under-enrolled
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MIRACLE (133 patients with heart failure and CKD), MIRO-CKD (324 patients with CKD and albuminuria) and the phase 1b potassium study (68 patients).
cards.result: Split verdict. For the question as asked — heart failure with CKD on dapagliflozin — the only direct trial, MIRACLE, found the treatment made no difference on albuminuria, in a sample stopped early at about a quarter of its planned size. The positive MIRO-CKD result belongs to albuminuric CKD without a heart-failure requirement and cannot be carried across. The potassium and eGFR costs are real but modest at the doses carried forward (hyperkalaemia 6–7% versus 5% in MIRO-CKD; dose-dependent potassium rise and eGFR fall at the highest MIRACLE dose).
cards.watchOut: Both phase 2b trials ran only 12 weeks and used a surrogate endpoint; neither can speak to kidney progression, heart-failure hospitalisation or death.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above (PMIDs 38783712, 41218621, 35971596). No additional source.

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Volume kinetics of infused crystalloid: Ringer's expands a ~5.9 L central space in volunteers and is eliminated with a half-life of 24 minutes in women and 38 minutes in men; elimination slows in proportion to falling arterial pressure, and under general anaesthesia distribution doubles in speed while the half-life stretches from 1.8 to 16.6 hours
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is an infused crystalloid distributed between plasma and interstitium and eliminated over time — what are the volumes of distribution and elimination half-lives, and how do sex, arterial pressure and general anaesthesia change them?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. The textbook framing (Guyton & Hall's body-fluid compartments: infused isotonic crystalloid distributes across the extracellular space, plasma plus interstitium, and is cleared by the kidneys) is given quantitative, time-resolved form by the volume-kinetic literature: serial haemoglobin dilution is fitted to a two-volume model (a central space, Vc, approximating plasma volume, exchanging with a peripheral interstitial space) to yield distribution and elimination rate constants. The stamp is EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED for a reason printed here, not hidden: this evidence base is dominated by one research group (Hahn and co-workers), the quantities are model-derived rather than directly measured, and the framework is not yet textbook-settled in Guyton & Hall or Ganong. Within that frame the human data are concordant: the founding volunteer study (Svensén & Hahn 1997; N=8, labelled on its card as a sub-10 physiology classic) estimated the space expanded by Ringer's at 5.9 L with an elimination rate constant of 94 mL/min, far faster than dextran 70 (12 mL/min). Population analyses then quantified the modifiers: elimination half-life 24 min in female vs 38 min in male volunteers (111 infusions); elimination rate falling in proportion to mean arterial pressure (78 subjects); and, in 262 infusions, distribution twice as fast under general anaesthesia with the elimination half-life stretching from 1.8 to 16.6 hours and 88% more fluid residing extravascularly in the first hour. Values no fetched record confirms are presented as the model's account, not as measurements.

cards.headline: Founding study 1997 (physiology classic, N=8 — sub-10, labelled): Ringer's expanded a 5.9 L space and was eliminated at 94 mL/min, versus 2.6 L and 12 mL/min for dextran 70 (8 male volunteers)
cards.summary: Founding study 1997 (physiology classic, N=8 — sub-10, labelled): Ringer's expanded a 5.9 L space and was eliminated at 94 mL/min, versus 2.6 L and 12 mL/min for dextran 70 (8 male volunteers)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (volunteer kinetic study, N=8 — labelled classic)
cards.people: 8 male volunteers aged 25–36 years (mean 31) — N printed plainly: this study is below the library's usual 10-human floor and is carded only as a labelled physiology classic alongside the larger pooled analyses, per the physiology carve-out. Each volunteer received, over 30 minutes, 25 mL/kg of Ringer's acetate, 5 mL/kg of 6% dextran 70 in saline, and 3 mL/kg of 7.5% saline, with serial total haemoglobin, serum albumin and blood-water measurements fitted to one- and two-volume kinetic models.
cards.result: By blood-water dilution, the mean size of the expandable volume (V) was 5.9 L (±0.8, SEM) for Ringer's solution, 2.6 L (±0.3) for dextran 70 and 1.2 L (±0.1) for hypertonic saline. The corresponding elimination rate constants (kr) were 94 (±42) mL/min for Ringer's, 12 (±6) mL/min for dextran and 30 (±4) mL/min for hypertonic saline. Haemoglobin indicated a dilution similar to blood water; albumin indicated a more pronounced dilution (a larger apparent volume with greater curve-fitting error), which the authors attribute to loss of intravascular albumin into the tissues along with the infused fluid.
cards.watchOut: Eight volunteers, and every number is a model parameter fitted to a dilution curve, not a direct measurement — the marker chosen (blood water, haemoglobin or albumin) changes the answer, as the paper itself shows. Carded as the field's founding classic, with its N on the face.
cards.source: Svensén C, Hahn RG. Volume kinetics of Ringer solution, dextran 70, and hypertonic saline in male volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1997. PMID: 9286883. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Population analysis 2016: the elimination half-life of Ringer's acetate was 24 minutes in female vs 38 minutes in male volunteers (111 infusions)
cards.summary: Population analysis 2016: the elimination half-life of Ringer's acetate was 24 minutes in female vs 38 minutes in male volunteers (111 infusions)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population kinetic analysis of volunteer infusions)
cards.people: Retrospective population kinetic analysis of seven series of experiments in healthy volunteers: 111 intravenous infusions of Ringer's acetate (44 in female volunteers, 67 in male volunteers), with frequent blood haemoglobin measurements and urinary excretion fitted to a two-volume model with micro-constants and covariates using nonlinear mixed-effects software. The fetched record gives infusion counts by sex; it does not state the total number of individual volunteers, so none is printed.
cards.result: The elimination half-life of the infused fluid was 24 minutes (95% CI 21–27) in females and 38 minutes (33–42) in males — 60% longer in males. Urinary excretion over the 3–4 hour experiments differed somewhat less than the half-lives suggest, because plasma volume became less expanded in females: fluid distributed to the interstitium returned slightly more slowly to the central (plasma) space in females. Sex was not a statistically significant covariate for the other rate constants in the model.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective re-analysis of experiments from the same research programme that founded the field — internally consistent, but not independent replication. Half-life here is a model-derived quantity (urine excreted divided by modelled plasma-volume expansion), not a directly timed disappearance.
cards.source: Hahn RG. The elimination half-life of crystalloid fluid is shorter in female than in male volunteers: a retrospective population kinetic analysis. Biology of sex differences. 2016. PMID: 27761234. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Arterial pressure analysis 2017: crystalloid elimination rate fell in direct proportion to mean arterial pressure, independent of consciousness or anaesthetic type (30 volunteers and 48 anaesthetised patients)
cards.summary: Arterial pressure analysis 2017: crystalloid elimination rate fell in direct proportion to mean arterial pressure, independent of consciousness or anaesthetic type (30 volunteers and 48 anaesthetised patients)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (pooled kinetic analysis, volunteers and surgical patients)
cards.people: Kinetic re-analysis of four separately published studies in which 30 volunteers and 48 anaesthetised patients received buffered Ringer's solution at 0.833 mL/kg/min (one series 0.667) over 30 minutes, with frequent haemoglobin measurements and mean urinary excretion (2,108 data points) fitted to a two-volume model with covariates. Mean arterial pressure across the data was 81.3 mmHg and mean age 40 years.
cards.result: The rate of elimination of crystalloid fluid decreased with mean arterial pressure (MAP) and with patient age, but was unaffected by consciousness and by inhalational versus intravenous anaesthesia. The central fluid space expanded by the infusion (Vc, plasma volume) increased with body weight and decreased with general anaesthesia and with reductions in MAP. Simulations showed a more than 10-fold difference in excreted fluid volume after a theoretical 30-minute infusion depending on whether MAP was 50 or 100 mmHg.
cards.watchOut: The MAP relationship is a covariate fitted inside the same group's model across its own prior studies; the 10-fold excretion contrast is a simulation from that model, presented here as the model's account. Hypotension in real patients usually travels with illness and vasopressors, which this volunteer/anaesthesia dataset does not capture.
cards.source: Hahn RG. Arterial Pressure and the Rate of Elimination of Crystalloid Fluid. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2017. PMID: 28452823. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Anaesthesia analysis 2025: under general anaesthesia, crystalloid distribution to the interstitium ran twice as fast and elimination half-life stretched from 1.8 to 16.6 hours (262 infusions)
cards.summary: Anaesthesia analysis 2025: under general anaesthesia, crystalloid distribution to the interstitium ran twice as fast and elimination half-life stretched from 1.8 to 16.6 hours (262 infusions)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (secondary population kinetic analysis)
cards.people: Secondary population volume-kinetic analysis of 262 infusions of crystalloid fluid (mean 1,647 ± 461 mL over 30 minutes) in adults, conscious and under general anaesthesia, using haemodilution and urine output measured during and after infusion, fitted with population pharmacokinetic modelling.
cards.result: Distribution of fluid from plasma to the interstitial space occurred twice as fast during general anaesthesia as in the conscious state. This increased capillary filtration was coupled with a still greater reduction in urinary output and accumulation of fluid in both a fast-exchange interstitial space and a remote 'third fluid space' acting as an overflow reservoir: during the first hour, 88% more fluid resided extravascularly under general anaesthesia than in the awake state. General anaesthesia increased the elimination half-life from 1.8 to 16.6 hours.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis pooling experiments run over many years by the same programme; the 'third fluid space' is a model compartment inferred from curve shape, not an anatomical space anyone has sampled. The 16.6-hour half-life describes the model's slow phase under anaesthesia, not a claim that a litre of Ringer's needs 16 hours to leave the body in ordinary recovery.
cards.source: Hahn RG. Capillary Filtration of Plasma Is Accelerated During General Anesthesia: A Secondary Population Volume Kinetic Analysis. Journal of clinical pharmacology. 2025. PMID: 39775740. cards.headline: Synthesis: crystalloid handling is fast when awake and pressurised, slow when anaesthetised and hypotensive — EMERGING, because one research group and one model carry the numbers
cards.summary: Synthesis: crystalloid handling is fast when awake and pressurised, slow when anaesthetised and hypotensive — EMERGING, because one research group and one model carry the numbers
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Svensén & Hahn 1997 (8 volunteers), Hahn 2016 (111 volunteer infusions), Hahn 2017 (78 volunteers/patients) and Hahn 2025 (262 infusions). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (body-fluid compartments and extracellular fluid distribution).
cards.result: The qualitative picture is stable across three decades of the programme's data and matches the textbook compartment account: isotonic crystalloid expands a central space of roughly plasma-plus-fast-interstitial size (~5.9 L for Ringer's in the founding study), distributes to the interstitium within minutes, and is eliminated by the kidneys with a half-life measured in tens of minutes in awake volunteers (24 min in women, 38 min in men). The modifiers are the clinically useful part: elimination slows in proportion to mean arterial pressure, and general anaesthesia simultaneously speeds capillary filtration (distribution twice as fast; 88% more extravascular fluid in the first hour) and cripples elimination (modelled half-life 1.8 → 16.6 hours) — the kinetic explanation for why intraoperative crystalloid lingers. The stamp is PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED: essentially all carded data come from Hahn and co-workers, the quantities are parameters of their two-volume model, and independent groups have not yet reproduced the modifier estimates. Where a number appears on this shelf it is tied to a fetched record; anything beyond those records is the model's account and is labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: Single-group dominance is the shelf's main limitation and is stated in the stamp choice itself. Do not use these half-lives as dosing rules for sick, bleeding or vasopressor-dependent patients — the underlying experiments are volunteers and elective anaesthesia.
cards.source: Synthesis of Svensén C, Hahn RG. Anesthesiology. 1997 (PMID: 9286883), Hahn RG. Biol Sex Differ. 2016 (PMID: 27761234), Hahn RG. Anesth Analg. 2017 (PMID: 28452823) and Hahn RG. J Clin Pharmacol. 2025 (PMID: 39775740). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Measured GFR in humans: iohexol and ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearances agree with inulin within a few mL/min — but iohexol and iothalamate differ from each other by ~15%, and PAH plasma flow is an approximation
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how well do measured-GFR methods agree — inulin, iohexol, iothalamate and 51Cr-EDTA clearances against each other — and what are normal effective renal plasma flow (PAH clearance) and filtration fraction?
shelves.mesh: Glomerular Filtration Rate · Inulin · Iohexol · Edetic Acid · Iothalamic Acid · Aminohippuric Acids · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for measured-GFR method agreement and PAH plasma flow, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep. Agreement with the inulin reference is close and quantified: iohexol plasma clearance correlates highly across GFR 6–169 with four calculation formulas equivalent (best median bias −0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at high GFR, N = 144), and two-sample ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance biases ~2.8 mL/min against inulin (N = 44 + 22). The discordance limb is equally firm: iohexol urinary clearance runs at 0.85 (relative) of iothalamate across the range (N = 150) — surrogates that each agree with inulin are not interchangeable with each other. Flow: in healthy men, PAH clearance fell 52 mL/min/decade after age 50 against iohexol's 12, so filtration fraction rises with age, and a total-versus-renal PAH discrepancy shows renal PAH metabolism — extraction is incomplete even in health (the row's caveat, on the face). REFUSAL: the 1969 Bröchner-Mortensen-era inulin-versus-EDTA anchor was refused as a card — its fetched record has no abstract (reported on the Synthesis card). Textbook normal values are carried as the textbook's account. The companion pack #6959 covers creatinine secretion — the endogenous-marker error, a different quantity.

cards.headline: Gaspari 1995: plasma clearance of non-radioactive iohexol tracked renal inulin clearance across a GFR range of 6–160 mL/min/1.73 m² — including with the simplified Bröchner-Mortensen-corrected one-compartment method (41 patients)
cards.summary: Gaspari 1995: plasma clearance of non-radioactive iohexol tracked renal inulin clearance across a GFR range of 6–160 mL/min/1.73 m² — including with the simplified Bröchner-Mortensen-corrected one-compartment method (41 patients)
cards.type: Human method-comparison study (iohexol plasma clearance versus inulin), J Am Soc Nephrol 1995
cards.people: 41 patients with creatinine clearance from 6 to 160 mL/min per 1.73 m² undergoing simultaneous renal clearance of inulin and plasma clearance of iohexol (single intravenous dose of unlabelled iohexol, blood samples to 600 minutes, HPLC assay, two-compartment open model; a simplified one-compartment analysis corrected with the Bröchner-Mortensen formula was also tested).
cards.result: A highly significant correlation between plasma clearance of iohexol and renal clearance of inulin was found over the wide GFR range, and the simplified one-compartment method with the Bröchner-Mortensen correction also correlated excellently with inulin clearance; in the subgroup with moderate to severe renal failure the correlation remained significant. Iohexol plasma clearance thereby earned its place as the practical, non-radioactive stand-in for the inulin reference — with the correction formula, not the raw one-compartment slope, doing the work at the extremes.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract is truncated at 250 words and reports correlations rather than bias limits — the Dubourg card supplies the formula-by-formula accuracy numbers.
