cards.headline: Medeiros 2009: plasma ⁵¹Cr-EDTA clearance agreed with renal inulin clearance with a bias of only ~2.8 mL/min using two samples (4 and 8 hours) — in 44 transplant recipients, with repeatability checked in 22 kidney donors
cards.summary: Medeiros 2009: plasma ⁵¹Cr-EDTA clearance agreed with renal inulin clearance with a bias of only ~2.8 mL/min using two samples (4 and 8 hours) — in 44 transplant recipients, with repeatability checked in 22 kidney donors
cards.type: Human method-comparison study (⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance versus inulin), Transpl Int 2009
cards.people: 44 adult renal transplant recipients and 22 kidney donors; simultaneous ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance (single 3.7 MBq dose, plasma disappearance from samples at 2, 4, 6 and 8 hours, all sampling combinations tested by Bland–Altman analysis) and renal inulin clearance.
cards.result: Mean inulin clearance was 44.5 ± 17.9 mL/min/1.73 m². All ⁵¹Cr-EDTA sampling schemes correlated positively with inulin clearance; the two-sample schemes (4 and 8 hours, or 4 and 6 hours) gave the narrowest limits of agreement, with a difference (bias) of 2.8 and 2.7 mL/min respectively. Two plasma samples therefore suffice for a ⁵¹Cr-EDTA GFR that sits within ~3 mL/min of the inulin reference on average — the modern, quantified version of the classic EDTA–inulin comparison (whose original report could not be carded; see the Synthesis card).
cards.watchOut: A transplant-recipient GFR range (mean ~45 mL/min/1.73 m²); agreement at normal and high GFR is addressed by the Dubourg card's range (to 169), not by this one.
cards.source: Medeiros FS, Sapienza MT, Prado ES, Agena F, Shimizu MH, Lemos FB, et al. Validation of plasma clearance of 51Cr-EDTA in adult renal transplant recipients: comparison with inulin renal clearance. Transplant International. 2009. PMID: 19055616. cards.headline: Dubourg 2021: against inulin urinary clearance in 144 people (GFR 15–169), all four iohexol plasma-clearance formulas were equivalent in precision and accuracy — the Ng-Schwartz-Munoz formula edged ahead above GFR 90 (median bias −0.5)
cards.summary: Dubourg 2021: against inulin urinary clearance in 144 people (GFR 15–169), all four iohexol plasma-clearance formulas were equivalent in precision and accuracy — the Ng-Schwartz-Munoz formula edged ahead above GFR 90 (median bias −0.5)
cards.type: Human method-comparison study (iohexol formulas versus inulin urinary clearance), Clin Chem Lab Med 2021
cards.people: 144 participants aged 10–84 years with inulin GFR from 15 to 169 mL/min/1.73 m², in a retrospective cross-sectional comparison of four published one-compartment iohexol plasma-clearance formulas (Bröchner-Mortensen; Fleming et al.; Jødal-Bröchner-Mortensen; Ng-Schwartz-Munoz) against simultaneous renal inulin clearance, scored by bias, precision, accuracy within 5/10/15%, root mean square error and concordance correlation.
cards.result: There was no difference between the four formulas in root mean square error or in accuracy at the 5%, 10% or 15% levels, and all four concordance correlation coefficients against inulin GFR were high and not significantly different. At inulin GFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m², the Ng-Schwartz-Munoz formula performed slightly better (median bias −0.5 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI −3.0 to 2.0; accuracy within 15% of 95.0%). The choice among established iohexol formulas is therefore a second-order decision — the method family agrees with inulin; the formula matters mainly at high GFR.
cards.watchOut: Includes children and adolescents (age from 10) and is retrospective; the equivalence claim is among these four formulas, not among all published GFR methods.
cards.source: Dubourg L, Lemoine S, Joannard B, Chardon L, de Souza V, Cochat P. Comparison of iohexol plasma clearance formulas vs. inulin urinary clearance for measuring glomerular filtration rate. Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33068376. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Seegmiller 2016: iohexol and iothalamate urinary clearances do NOT agree — iohexol ran at 0.85 (relative) of iothalamate across the GFR range, so studies using the two markers are not directly interchangeable (150 participants)
cards.summary: Seegmiller 2016: iohexol and iothalamate urinary clearances do NOT agree — iohexol ran at 0.85 (relative) of iothalamate across the GFR range, so studies using the two markers are not directly interchangeable (150 participants)
cards.type: Human method-comparison study (iohexol versus iothalamate urinary clearance), Am J Kidney Dis 2016
cards.people: 150 participants with a wide range of GFRs studied in an outpatient clinical laboratory, with simultaneous urinary clearances of iothalamate, iohexol and creatinine, all assayed concurrently by a single liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry method.
cards.result: Mean clearances were 52 ± 28 (iohexol), 60 ± 34 (iothalamate) and 74 ± 40 (creatinine) mL/min/1.73 m². The proportional bias of iohexol to iothalamate urinary clearance was 0.85 (95% CI 0.83–0.88) — a relative difference, consistent across the GFR range — while iothalamate clearance stood at 1.09 (95% CI 1.03–1.15) relative to creatinine clearance and iohexol at 1.27 (95% CI 1.20–1.34) on the record's presentation. Two markers that have both 'supplanted inulin' thus differ from each other by about 15% (relative): a measured GFR is a marker-specific number, and comparing an iohexol GFR with an iothalamate GFR without accounting for this bias manufactures a difference that is in the assay, not the kidney. (The companion creatinine-secretion pack, #6959, explains the creatinine column of this same table.)
cards.watchOut: No inulin reference in this study (the record states this as its limitation) — it establishes iohexol–iothalamate discordance, not which of the two sits closer to inulin.
cards.source: Seegmiller JC, Burns BE, Schinstock CA, Lieske JC, Larson TS. Discordance Between Iothalamate and Iohexol Urinary Clearances. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2016. PMID: 26454686. cards.headline: Bäck 1989: in healthy men, PAH clearance (renal plasma flow) fell by 52 mL/min per decade after age 50 while iohexol GFR fell by 12 — so filtration fraction rises with age; and total PAH clearance exceeded renal PAH clearance, showing renal PAH metabolism
cards.summary: Bäck 1989: in healthy men, PAH clearance (renal plasma flow) fell by 52 mL/min per decade after age 50 while iohexol GFR fell by 12 — so filtration fraction rises with age; and total PAH clearance exceeded renal PAH clearance, showing renal PAH metabolism
cards.type: Human clearance study (iohexol GFR and PAH renal plasma flow across age, in health), Scand J Clin Lab Invest 1989
cards.people: Healthy male volunteers aged 21–77 years given single-injection iohexol clearance for GFR and continuous-infusion p-aminohippuric acid (PAH) total clearance for renal plasma flow, with renal (urinary) PAH clearance also measured. The record does not print the volunteer number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In subjects older than 50, both clearances fell with age — PAH clearance by 52 mL/min per decade and iohexol clearance by 12 mL/min per decade — while no age dependence was found in younger subjects; the two clearances correlated at 0.81. Because plasma flow fell faster than filtration, the filtration fraction (iohexol/PAH clearance ratio) was higher in the elderly. A consistent discrepancy between total and renal PAH clearance indicated significant renal metabolism of PAH — the extraction caveat on this shelf's face: PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow on the assumption of near-complete extraction, and this record shows in healthy men that the assumption is an approximation, before any question of the extraction failure seen in disease. Renal creatinine clearance, for comparison, correlated poorly with iohexol clearance and showed no age relationship.
cards.watchOut: Healthy men only, N not documented in the record; absolute young-adult PAH and filtration-fraction values are not printed in the record's abstract, so the textbook's normal figures are carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card, not as this study's results.
cards.source: Bäck SE, Ljungberg B, Nilsson-Ehle I, Borgå O, Nilsson-Ehle P. Age dependence of renal function: clearance of iohexol and p-amino hippurate in healthy males. cards.headline: Synthesis: inulin is the reference, iohexol and ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearances agree with it within a few mL/min — but iohexol and iothalamate differ from each other by ~15%, and PAH flow is an extraction-limited approximation
cards.summary: Synthesis: inulin is the reference, iohexol and ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearances agree with it within a few mL/min — but iohexol and iothalamate differ from each other by ~15%, and PAH flow is an extraction-limited approximation
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human records above (the Gaspari and Dubourg iohexol programmes, the Medeiros ⁵¹Cr-EDTA validation, the Seegmiller marker-discordance study and the Bäck PAH ageing study), framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on GFR and renal plasma flow measurement. REFUSAL, reported as required: the classic Bröchner-Mortensen-era report 'Renal inulin clearance versus total plasma clearance of 51Cr-EDTA' (1969), the anchor comparison named for this row, was refused as a card because its PubMed record fetched this session carries no abstract, so its agreement figures could not be verified from the record — it is named here, not carded, and the modern Medeiros validation carries the EDTA limb instead.
cards.result: The agreement structure, from the carded records: iohexol plasma clearance correlates highly with inulin across GFR 6–169, with four established calculation formulas equivalent in accuracy (median bias −0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² for the best at high GFR); ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance with two samples sits within ~2.8 mL/min bias of inulin; but iohexol and iothalamate urinary clearances differ proportionally by 0.85 (relative) across the range — agreement with the reference does not make two surrogate markers interchangeable with each other. On the flow side: effective renal plasma flow by PAH clearance falls with age after 50 about four times faster per decade than GFR (52 vs 12 mL/min per decade), so filtration fraction rises with age in health; and total-versus-renal PAH clearance discrepancy in healthy men shows renal PAH metabolism, i.e. extraction is incomplete even before disease — the health-only framing and extraction caveat this row requires. The textbook's standard normal values (GFR ~125 mL/min/1.73 m², effective renal plasma flow ~650 mL/min, filtration fraction ~0.2, as Guyton & Hall present them) are the textbook's account: consistent with the carded records' ranges and ratios, but not numbers any single fetched record on this shelf printed, and the shelf does not present them as measured here. The estimating-equation and CKD shelves ask what to do clinically with a GFR; this shelf asks how the measured quantity itself behaves.
cards.watchOut: Method agreement is range-dependent: several carded cohorts are patient populations spanning wide GFR ranges rather than healthy-only samples, and each card prints its population — healthy-only normative precision is thinner than the agreement literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 7579093, 19055616, 33068376, 26454686, 2609107), with Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Tubular creatinine secretion: creatinine clearance overestimates GFR by a share that grows as GFR falls — and cimetidine blockade brings the ratio to 1.01–1.02 against inulin
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much creatinine is secreted — by how much does creatinine clearance overestimate true GFR, and what do cimetidine-blocked creatinine-clearance studies show about the secreted fraction across GFR levels?
shelves.mesh: Creatinine · Cimetidine · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Inulin · Kidney Tubules · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for tubular creatinine secretion as measured against true filtration markers, framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall (tubular secretion). The size of the error: creatinine's fractional clearance against inulin averaged 1.64 ± 0.05 in 171 glomerulopathic patients (Shemesh) — an average ~64% relative overestimation — with individual baseline creatinine/inulin ratios of 1.14–2.27 in the van Acker cohort, and the secreted fraction varying inversely with GFR, so the overestimation grows as filtration falls and blunts creatinine-based monitoring. The blockade proof is concordant across three studies: after adequate oral cimetidine (which does not change true GFR), creatinine clearance matched ⁵¹Cr-EDTA (ratio 1.02 ± 0.13) and inulin (1.01 ± 0.13) across renal-function ranges (Hilbrands, 10 healthy men + 29 patients), reached unity in lupus nephritis under double-blind conditions (DTPA ratio 1.33 on placebo → 1.07 on cimetidine, N = 13), and failed at 1.33 in half of one cohort until the cimetidine dose was raised — dose adequacy is part of the method. The healthy-GFR overestimation figure (~10–20% relative) is carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card. Cross-point (prose only): pack #6958, exogenous-marker agreement — a different quantity, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Shemesh 1985: creatinine's fractional clearance averaged 1.64 ± 0.05 against inulin — creatinine is progressively hypersecreted as GFR falls, so creatinine clearance grossly and unpredictably overestimates GFR (171 patients)
cards.summary: Shemesh 1985: creatinine's fractional clearance averaged 1.64 ± 0.05 against inulin — creatinine is progressively hypersecreted as GFR falls, so creatinine clearance grossly and unpredictably overestimates GFR (171 patients)
cards.type: Human clearance study (creatinine secretion fraction against inulin), Kidney Int 1985
cards.people: 171 patients with various glomerular diseases in whom simultaneous clearances of creatinine and three true filtration markers of graded size were compared — inulin (radius 15 Å) as reference, ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA (4 Å) and a 19 Å dextran — with acute intravenous cimetidine blockade used to test the secretion mechanism, and longitudinal substudies in 28 patients with deteriorating and 26 with remitting disease.
cards.result: The fractional clearance (relative to inulin) of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA was 1.02 ± 0.14 and of the 19 Å dextran 0.98 ± 0.13 — neither different from unity, so true markers are unrestricted even in glomerular disease. Creatinine's fractional clearance, by contrast, averaged 1.64 ± 0.05 (P < 0.001) — creatinine clearance overestimated inulin GFR by roughly two-thirds on average — and could be lowered towards unity by acute blockade of tubular creatinine secretion with intravenous cimetidine, proving the secretory origin. Cross-sectionally and longitudinally, fractional creatinine secretion varied inversely with GFR: the worse the filtration, the larger the secreted share, which blunted or even erased creatinine-based changes when true GFR moved. The overestimation is therefore not a fixed percentage to correct for — it grows as GFR falls.
cards.watchOut: A glomerulopathic population — the 1.64 figure is that population's average, and the inverse relation with GFR means no single overestimation factor exists; in normal-GFR health the secreted fraction is smaller (see the Hilbrands card's healthy limb).
cards.source: Shemesh O, Golbetz H, Kriss JP, Myers BD. Limitations of creatinine as a filtration marker in glomerulopathic patients. Kidney International. 1985. PMID: 2418254. cards.headline: Hilbrands 1991: after 3–6 days of oral cimetidine, creatinine clearance matched the true filtration markers almost exactly — ratios 1.02 ± 0.13 against ⁵¹Cr-EDTA and 1.01 ± 0.13 against inulin, across the whole range of renal function (10 healthy men, 29 patients)
cards.summary: Hilbrands 1991: after 3–6 days of oral cimetidine, creatinine clearance matched the true filtration markers almost exactly — ratios 1.02 ± 0.13 against ⁵¹Cr-EDTA and 1.01 ± 0.13 against inulin, across the whole range of renal function (10 healthy men, 29 patients)
cards.type: Human clearance study (cimetidine-blocked creatinine clearance versus inulin/EDTA), Kidney Int 1991
cards.people: 10 healthy men and 29 patients with varying degrees of renal dysfunction, in whom creatinine clearance was compared with clearances of ⁵¹Cr-EDTA and inulin after oral cimetidine taken for three to six days; in a subgroup of 14, the filtration markers were measured before as well as after cimetidine to confirm the drug did not itself change GFR.
cards.result: Serum creatinine rose in all participants on cimetidine (secretion blocked, filtration unchanged — ⁵¹Cr-EDTA and inulin clearances remained stable in the subgroup measured twice), and the cimetidine-aided creatinine clearance then matched the true markers: mean (± SD) ratios of creatinine clearance to ⁵¹Cr-EDTA clearance (N = 39) and to inulin clearance (N = 19) were 1.02 ± 0.13 and 1.01 ± 0.13, not significantly different from unity, with that accuracy present over the entire range of renal function studied. Precision also improved, to a variability not significantly different from that of the filtration markers themselves. Blocking the secreted component converts creatinine clearance from a biased estimate into a measurement.
cards.watchOut: Cimetidine was given for days before measurement in this protocol; the result validates the blocked measurement, not a single-dose shortcut, and serum creatinine on cimetidine must not be fed into unblocked estimating equations.
cards.source: Hilbrands LB, Artz MA, Wetzels JF, Koene RA. Cimetidine improves the reliability of creatinine as a marker of glomerular filtration. Kidney International. 1991. PMID: 1762320. cards.headline: van Acker 1992: baseline creatinine/inulin clearance ratios ran 1.14–2.27; with cimetidine, half the patients reached unity (1.02 ± 0.03) and half did not (1.33 ± 0.14) — until the dose was raised, when secretion was completely inhibited and creatinine clearance equalled GFR (16 + 6 patients)
cards.summary: van Acker 1992: baseline creatinine/inulin clearance ratios ran 1.14–2.27; with cimetidine, half the patients reached unity (1.02 ± 0.03) and half did not (1.33 ± 0.14) — until the dose was raised, when secretion was completely inhibited and creatinine clearance equalled GFR (16 + 6 patients)
cards.type: Human clearance study (dose-dependence of cimetidine blockade of creatinine secretion), Lancet 1992
cards.people: 16 patients with renal disease with simultaneous inulin and endogenous creatinine clearances measured before cimetidine and during 8 successive 3-hour clearance periods on cimetidine (400 mg priming dose, then 200 mg every 3 hours); a further 6 patients, previously incompletely inhibited, were restudied at an increased cimetidine dose.
cards.result: At baseline the creatinine-to-inulin clearance ratio ranged from 1.14 to 2.27 — creatinine clearance overestimated true GFR by 14% to 127% (relative) across individuals. With the standard cimetidine regimen the ratio approached unity in 8 patients (mean 1.02, SD 0.03) but still considerably exceeded unity in 8 others (1.33, SD 0.14); the incomplete group had a smaller plasma cimetidine/creatinine ratio because their renal cimetidine clearance was higher (333 [136] versus 165 [89] mL/min, P = 0.01). At the increased dose, tubular creatinine secretion was completely inhibited from the third to the sixth hour and creatinine clearance equalled GFR. The record's practical conclusion: provided an adequate dose is given, creatinine clearance during cimetidine measures GFR accurately — but because of the advised maximum daily dose, short (3-hour) clearance periods are recommended.
cards.watchOut: Renal-disease patients and short clearance periods; the dose-dependence is the finding — a 'cimetidine creatinine clearance' done at an inadequate dose silently retains part of the secretion error.
cards.source: van Acker BA, Koomen GC, Koopman MG, de Waart DR, Arisz L. Creatinine clearance during cimetidine administration for measurement of glomerular filtration rate. The Lancet. 1992. PMID: 1360044. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Roubenoff 1990: in lupus nephritis, cimetidine moved the DTPA-to-creatinine-clearance ratio from 1.33 on placebo to 1.07 — and made creatinine clearance the most precise of the standard estimators (13 patients, double-blind crossover)
cards.summary: Roubenoff 1990: in lupus nephritis, cimetidine moved the DTPA-to-creatinine-clearance ratio from 1.33 on placebo to 1.07 — and made creatinine clearance the most precise of the standard estimators (13 patients, double-blind crossover)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover study (cimetidine-aided creatinine clearance in lupus nephritis), Ann Intern Med 1990
cards.people: 13 patients with lupus nephritis and mild renal insufficiency (mean serum creatinine 230 µmol/L [2.6 mg/dL]; median 106 µmol/L [1.2 mg/dL]) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of oral cimetidine 400 mg four times daily for 2 days, with ambulatory 24-hour urine collection and simultaneous 4-hour ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA and creatinine clearances after each arm.
cards.result: Cimetidine improved the accuracy of creatinine clearance, as measured by the DTPA-to-creatinine-clearance ratio (1.07 on cimetidine compared with 1.33 on placebo, P < 0.05), and also improved its precision (P < 0.05); the cimetidine-aided clearance explained more of the variation in GFR (R² = 0.78) than any other standard clinical estimator (R² = 0.52 to 0.63), under both simultaneous and outpatient conditions, with no side effects from cimetidine. In a disease where injured tubules secrete creatinine, pharmacological blockade recovered a measurement that the unblocked test could not give.
cards.watchOut: N = 13, one disease, mild renal insufficiency — a confirmation of the blockade principle under blinded conditions, not a general-population validation.
cards.source: Roubenoff R, Drew H, Moyer M, Petri M, Whiting-O'Keefe Q, Hellmann DB. Oral cimetidine improves the accuracy and precision of creatinine clearance in lupus nephritis. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1990. PMID: 2393206. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: creatinine is filtered and secreted — the secreted share is what creatinine clearance adds to GFR, it grows as GFR falls, and cimetidine blockade removes it almost exactly
cards.summary: Synthesis: creatinine is filtered and secreted — the secreted share is what creatinine clearance adds to GFR, it grows as GFR falls, and cimetidine blockade removes it almost exactly
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (the Shemesh secretion-fraction programme and the three cimetidine-blockade studies), framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall on tubular secretion. Cross-point, in prose only: the companion pack #6958 covers exogenous-marker agreement (inulin, iohexol, iothalamate, ⁵¹Cr-EDTA) — this pack is the endogenous-secretion error, a different quantity, and the two are not duplicated.
cards.result: The mechanism and its size: creatinine reaches urine by filtration plus proximal tubular secretion, so creatinine clearance = GFR + secreted clearance. Against inulin, creatinine's fractional clearance averaged 1.64 in glomerulopathic patients — an average ~64% (relative) overestimation — with individual baseline ratios elsewhere running 1.14–2.27, and the secreted fraction rising as GFR falls, which is why creatinine-based monitoring blunts real change. The blockade experiments are the proof and the remedy in one: adequate cimetidine (an inhibitor of tubular creatinine secretion that does not change true GFR) brings the creatinine/inulin ratio to 1.01–1.02 across renal-function ranges and diseases — provided the dose is adequate, since half of one cohort remained at 1.33 on a standard regimen until the dose was raised and secretion was completely inhibited. In health, where GFR is normal, the secreted fraction is at its smallest — the textbook's account (Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall) puts the usual creatinine-clearance overestimation at roughly 10–20% (relative) at normal GFR — presented as the textbook's account: the carded records quantify the fraction chiefly in kidney-disease populations and in the healthy limb of the Hilbrands study the blocked ratio, not a separate healthy unblocked percentage, is what was printed. The clinical moral the physiology dictates: serum creatinine and unblocked creatinine clearance are secretion-contaminated estimates whose error is largest exactly where accuracy matters most.
cards.watchOut: Secretion fractions are population- and GFR-dependent; no single correction factor converts creatinine clearance to GFR, and cimetidine-aided values must never be entered into equations calibrated on unblocked creatinine.

shelves.title: Body water compartments by dilution: total water ~0.61 L/kg in men and 0.54 L/kg in women, split about 39% extracellular / 61% intracellular in young men
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large are the body water compartments — total body water by deuterium dilution, extracellular water by bromide dilution, and the derived intracellular volume — as fractions of body weight by sex, age and adiposity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Water · Deuterium Oxide · Electric Impedance · Extracellular Space · Humans · Intracellular Fluid · Linear Models · Male · Models, Biological · Radioisotope Dilution Technique · Reproducibility of Results · Body Water/metabolism · Breath Tests · Deuterium Oxide/pharmacokinetics · Ethanol/blood/pharmacokinetics · Female · Kinetics · Middle Aged · Osmolar Concentration · Reference Values · Time Factors · Aged · Extracellular Space/metabolism · Growth Hormone/therapeutic use · Human Growth Hormone/deficiency/therapeutic use · Indicator Dilution Techniques · Absorptiometry, Photon · Body Composition/drug effects · Caffeine/pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, body-fluid compartments chapter; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): in a healthy young man total body water is about 60% of body weight, split roughly one-third extracellular and two-thirds intracellular, with the extracellular share falling as adiposity rises because fat tissue is water-poor. The dilution measurements fetched this session land on that account. In 13 healthy young men (mean body mass 80.6 kg), deuterium dilution gave total body water 51.00 L — about 63% of body mass — and bromide dilution gave extracellular water 19.88 L, leaving intracellular water (by subtraction) 31.12 L: about 39% extracellular and 61% intracellular (Armstrong 1997). Measured per kilogram by deuterium dilution, Norberg 2001 found 0.61 L/kg in men and 0.54 L/kg in women (44.1 vs 37.4 L) — the sex difference the textbook attributes to women's higher average fat fraction. Janssen 1997 used the same deuterium/bromide pair in 28 healthy controls as the comparator for growth-hormone-deficient patients, who had lower total and extracellular water and a lower extracellular-to-total ratio. Silva 2013 (N = 30 healthy young men; NCT01477294) confirms the derived intracellular volume is a subtraction (total minus extracellular), not a direct measurement. A standing caution runs through these records and is stated on the cards: impedance estimates are NOT dilution measurements — multifrequency impedance overestimated both compartments in Janssen 1997 and differed significantly from dilution for extracellular and intracellular volumes in Armstrong 1997, so impedance numbers must never be quoted as dilution values. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Dilution values in 13 healthy young men: total body water 51.0 L (~63% of body mass), extracellular 19.9 L, intracellular 31.1 L (Armstrong 1997)
cards.summary: Dilution values in 13 healthy young men: total body water 51.0 L (~63% of body mass), extracellular 19.9 L, intracellular 31.1 L (Armstrong 1997)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (deuterium and bromide dilution with impedance comparison) — N = 13
cards.people: 13 healthy males (mean age 23 years, SD 3; mean body mass 80.6 kg, SD 14.7) who ingested dilution tracers (7.27 g deuterium oxide for total body water; 1.70 g sodium bromide for extracellular volume), with blood sampled at 0 and 4 hours; intracellular volume calculated as total minus extracellular. Small classic study — N = 13 printed here on the face.
cards.result: Dilution measures were: total body water 51.00 L (SD 9.30), extracellular volume 19.88 L (SD 3.14) and intracellular volume 31.12 L (SD 6.80) — total water about 63% of the group's mean body mass, split about 39% extracellular and 61% intracellular. Bioimpedance spectroscopy estimates (50.03, 20.95 and 29.04 L respectively) differed significantly from dilution for extracellular (P < 0.01) and intracellular (P < 0.05) volumes, though correlations were high (r = 0.93 to 0.96). The authors conclude impedance spectroscopy is valid for between-subject comparisons but individual differences from dilution can be large.
cards.watchOut: Young lean men only: the ~63% figure is the top of the human range, not a universal constant — women and people with more adipose tissue sit lower (see the per-kilogram sex data on the next card).
cards.source: Armstrong LE et al. Medicine and science in sports and exercise. 1997. PMID: 9432101. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Primary human physiology study (deuterium dilution in healthy volunteers)
cards.people: 16 healthy volunteers (men and women) given intravenous deuterium oxide with serum measurement by isotope-ratio mass spectrometry, as the reference arm of an ethanol distribution study; total body water determined by deuterium dilution.
cards.result: Mean total body water by deuterium dilution was 44.1 L (SD 3.9) for men, corresponding to 0.61 L/kg, and 37.4 L (SD 3.2) for women, or 0.54 L/kg. (The study's ethanol finding — ethanol's distribution volume was only about 85-95% of total body water depending on the kinetic model — is why these dilution values were measured; the water values themselves are the physiology content of this card.)
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not split the 16 volunteers by sex on the face of the record, and the cohort is a pharmacokinetic study sample, not a population sample — the per-kilogram sex contrast (0.61 vs 0.54 L/kg) is the durable content, matching the textbook's adiposity explanation.
cards.source: Norberg A et al. Alcoholism, clinical and experimental research. 2001. PMID: 11696661. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The healthy-control arm (N = 28): deuterium/bromide dilution sets the normal extracellular-to-total ratio that growth hormone deficiency falls below (Janssen 1997)
cards.summary: The healthy-control arm (N = 28): deuterium/bromide dilution sets the normal extracellular-to-total ratio that growth hormone deficiency falls below (Janssen 1997)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dilution techniques in healthy controls and patients)
cards.people: 28 healthy controls compared with 14 adults with adult-onset growth hormone deficiency; total body water by deuterium dilution and extracellular water by bromide dilution in all subjects, with multifrequency bioelectrical impedance measured in parallel (the patient treatment limb is not this shelf's content).
cards.result: Patients with growth hormone deficiency had significantly lower extracellular water and total body water than healthy controls, and their extracellular-to-total body water ratio was significantly lower. Correlations between dilution-measured and impedance-estimated compartments were high (r > 0.91), but multifrequency impedance overestimated both extracellular and total body water in the deficient adults, and the authors conclude impedance does not give valid estimates of body water compartments in follow-up. The fetched abstract reports the healthy controls as the reference standard without printing their absolute litre values — no healthy-control litres are claimed on this card beyond that comparative role.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its method and its healthy-control comparison, honestly labelled: the absolute compartment sizes on this shelf come from the Armstrong and Norberg dilution cohorts, not from this record.
cards.source: Janssen YJ et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1997. PMID: 9329367. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Compartments are stable quantities in healthy young men (N = 30): total, extracellular and intracellular water unchanged over 4 days and unrelated to fat-free mass, water intake or activity in this trial (Silva 2013)
cards.summary: Compartments are stable quantities in healthy young men (N = 30): total, extracellular and intracellular water unchanged over 4 days and unrelated to fat-free mass, water intake or activity in this trial (Silva 2013)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dilution-measured compartments, randomised crossover design)
cards.people: 30 healthy active men aged 20-39 years (non-smokers, low caffeine users) in a double-blind randomised crossover trial; total body water by deuterium oxide dilution, extracellular water by sodium bromide dilution, intracellular water calculated as total minus extracellular; body composition by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry.
cards.result: No changes in total body water, extracellular water or intracellular water were observed over the 4-day study conditions, and no interaction with treatment order or time (P > 0.05); the compartments were also unrelated to fat-free mass, water ingestion and physical activity in this sample (P > 0.05). The trial's intervention question (a moderate caffeine dose, about 5 espresso cups daily) did not alter the compartments — the physiology content is the demonstrated short-term stability of the dilution-measured compartments and the explicit derivation of intracellular water by subtraction. The fetched abstract does not print the absolute litre values, and none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Stability over 4 days in young active men does not imply stability across illness, ageing or major weight change — and, as on every card here, intracellular water is arithmetic (total minus extracellular), inheriting the errors of both dilution spaces.
cards.source: Silva AM et al. Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme. 2013. PMID: 23724879. Registry ID: NCT01477294. cards.headline: Synthesis: about 60% of body weight is water in healthy young men (0.61 L/kg; 0.54 L/kg in women), split about one-third extracellular / two-thirds intracellular — measured by dilution, not impedance
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 60% of body weight is water in healthy young men (0.61 L/kg; 0.54 L/kg in women), split about one-third extracellular / two-thirds intracellular — measured by dilution, not impedance
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human dilution studies above.
cards.result: The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) and the fetched dilution records agree: total body water is 51.0 L in young men averaging 80.6 kg (about 63% of mass; Armstrong 1997) and 0.61 L/kg in men versus 0.54 L/kg in women per kilogram (Norberg 2001) — the sex gap the textbook assigns to adiposity, since fat is water-poor and the water fraction of any individual falls as fat fraction rises. The split is about 39% extracellular (19.88 L by bromide) to 61% intracellular (31.12 L, always by subtraction) in young men. Healthy controls anchor the normal extracellular-to-total ratio in Janssen 1997, and the compartments are stable over days in health (Silva 2013). Impedance-derived numbers are a different measurement and overestimate against dilution in these records — they are never presented here as dilution values. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The classic mid-century dilution cohorts behind the textbook's age tables were not re-verified from fetched records in this build and are presented only as the textbook's account; every litre value on the cards above comes from a record fetched this session.

shelves.title: Molidustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to darbepoetin on haemoglobin in three Japanese phase 3 trials (differences −0.38 to +0.13 g/dL) — a single-region HIF-PHI programme
shelves.question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (dialysis and non-dialysis), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor molidustat, compared with placebo or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, control haemoglobin (MIYABI / DIALOGUE programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anemia · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles
shelves.balance: Across the Japanese MIYABI phase 3 programme, oral molidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin control in every population tested: ESA-naive non-dialysis patients (evaluation-period mean Hb 11.28 vs 11.70 g/dL; difference −0.38 g/dL against a 1.0 g/dL margin), ESA-treated non-dialysis patients (11.67 vs 11.53 g/dL; difference +0.13 g/dL), and haemodialysis patients (10.63 vs 10.77 g/dL; difference −0.13 g/dL), with the DIALOGUE long-term extensions showing similar Hb maintenance and adverse-event proportions for up to 36 months against darbepoetin or epoetin. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and treatment-emergent adverse events were near-universal in both arms (~93–96%) in these sick populations, with small numbers of deaths in both arms of the phase 3 trials. This is a single-region programme (Japan; approved there, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question, including cardiovascular-safety experience across the class, is homed at live #731 and pack #5753 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: MIYABI ND-C phase 3 RCT (Yamamoto 2021): molidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin for Hb correction in ESA-naive non-dialysis CKD (mean Hb 11.28 vs 11.70 g/dL; difference −0.38 g/dL)
cards.summary: MIYABI ND-C phase 3 RCT (Yamamoto 2021): molidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin for Hb correction in ESA-naive non-dialysis CKD (mean Hb 11.28 vs 11.70 g/dL; difference −0.38 g/dL)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label active-controlled trial (MIYABI ND-C), molidustat vs darbepoetin alfa
cards.people: 162 Japanese patients with renal anaemia due to CKD stages 3–5, not on dialysis and not receiving ESA treatment, randomised 1:1 to molidustat (n=82, starting 25 mg once daily) or darbepoetin alfa (n=80, 30 μg every 2 weeks) for 52 weeks, doses titrated to keep Hb ≥11.0 and <13.0 g/dL; baseline mean Hb was 9.84 (SD 0.64) g/dL on molidustat and 10.00 (SD 0.61) g/dL on darbepoetin.
cards.result: Mean Hb during the evaluation period (weeks 30–36) was 11.28 g/dL (95% CI 11.07 to 11.50) on molidustat and 11.70 g/dL (95% CI 11.50 to 11.90) on darbepoetin, both within target. The least-squares mean difference in Hb change was −0.38 g/dL (95% CI −0.67 to −0.08), meeting the 1.0 g/dL noninferiority margin. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 93.9% (molidustat) and 93.7% (darbepoetin); there were 3 deaths in the molidustat group and 1 in the darbepoetin group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, Japanese patients only, and noninferiority on a haemoglobin surrogate — the trial does not test cardiovascular outcomes, and the small death imbalance (3 vs 1) is a count too small to interpret either way.
cards.source: Yamamoto H et al. Efficacy and Safety of Molidustat for Anemia in ESA-Naive Nondialysis Patients: A Randomized, Phase 3 Trial. American journal of nephrology. 2021. PMID: 34569489. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anemia · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles

cards.headline: MIYABI phase 3 RCT in ESA-treated non-dialysis patients (Yamamoto 2021): switching to molidustat maintained Hb noninferiorly to continuing darbepoetin (11.67 vs 11.53 g/dL; difference +0.13 g/dL)
cards.summary: MIYABI phase 3 RCT in ESA-treated non-dialysis patients (Yamamoto 2021): switching to molidustat maintained Hb noninferiorly to continuing darbepoetin (11.67 vs 11.53 g/dL; difference +0.13 g/dL)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label active-controlled trial (MIYABI), molidustat vs darbepoetin alfa
cards.people: 164 Japanese patients with anaemia due to CKD stages 3–5, not on dialysis and previously treated with ESAs, randomised 1:1 to molidustat (n=82, starting 25 or 50 mg once daily according to previous ESA dose) or darbepoetin alfa (n=82) for 52 weeks, titrated to keep Hb 11.0–13.0 g/dL; baseline mean Hb was 11.31 (SD 0.68) and 11.27 (SD 0.64) g/dL.
cards.result: Mean Hb during the evaluation period (weeks 30–36) was 11.67 g/dL (95% CI 11.48 to 11.85) on molidustat and 11.53 g/dL (95% CI 11.31 to 11.74) on darbepoetin, both within target; the least-squares mean difference was +0.13 g/dL (95% CI −0.15 to 0.40), meeting the 1.0 g/dL noninferiority margin. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 92.7% (molidustat) and 96.3% (darbepoetin); adverse events leading to death were reported in 2 patients (2.4%) on molidustat and none on darbepoetin, and serious adverse events in 32.9% and 26.8% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Open-label switch design in Japanese patients; haemoglobin maintenance is a surrogate, and the trial was not powered for the death or serious-event differences it reports.

cards.headline: MIYABI haemodialysis phase 3 RCT (Akizawa 2021): molidustat maintained Hb noninferiorly to darbepoetin in dialysis patients (10.63 vs 10.77 g/dL; difference −0.13 g/dL)
cards.summary: MIYABI haemodialysis phase 3 RCT (Akizawa 2021): molidustat maintained Hb noninferiorly to darbepoetin in dialysis patients (10.63 vs 10.77 g/dL; difference −0.13 g/dL)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind double-dummy trial (MIYABI haemodialysis-maintenance), molidustat vs darbepoetin
cards.people: 229 Japanese patients receiving haemodialysis and ESA treatment, randomised to molidustat (n=153, starting dose 75 mg/day) or darbepoetin (n=76) in a 52-week double-blind, double-dummy study, both titrated to keep Hb ≥10.0 and <12.0 g/dL; mean baseline Hb was 10.8 g/dL.
cards.result: Mean Hb during the evaluation period (weeks 33–36) was 10.63 g/dL (95% CI 10.42 to 10.84) on molidustat and 10.77 g/dL (95% CI 10.59 to 10.95) on darbepoetin, both within target. The least-squares mean difference in Hb change was −0.13 g/dL (95% CI −0.46 to 0.19), meeting the 1.0 g/dL noninferiority margin. Most participants in both groups had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, as the authors note is expected in this population.
cards.watchOut: The one double-blind trial of the three — but still Japanese patients only, a haemoglobin surrogate, and the record carries no MeSH terms, so none are printed.

cards.headline: DIALOGUE long-term extensions (Akizawa 2019): molidustat maintained Hb similarly to darbepoetin (non-dialysis) and epoetin (dialysis) for up to 36 months, with similar adverse-event proportions
cards.summary: DIALOGUE long-term extensions (Akizawa 2019): molidustat maintained Hb similarly to darbepoetin (non-dialysis) and epoetin (dialysis) for up to 36 months, with similar adverse-event proportions
cards.type: Two open-label long-term extension studies (DIALOGUE) with ESA active controls
cards.people: Two open-label long-term extension studies of the phase 2b programme, of up to 36 months: patients with anaemia due to CKD not receiving dialysis (n=164) and patients receiving haemodialysis (n=88), each with an ESA active control (darbepoetin and epoetin respectively).
cards.result: In non-dialysis patients, mean overall study Hb was 11.10 (SD 0.508) g/dL on molidustat versus 10.98 (SD 0.571) g/dL on darbepoetin, with at least one adverse event in 85.6% and 85.7%. In dialysis patients, mean study Hb was 10.37 (SD 0.56) g/dL on molidustat versus 10.52 (SD 0.47) g/dL on epoetin, with at least one adverse event in 91.2% and 93.3%. The authors concluded molidustat was well tolerated for up to 36 months and appears an effective alternative to ESAs for long-term management.
cards.watchOut: Open-label extensions of earlier phase 2b trials — patients who entered extensions are a selected, tolerating population, so long-term adverse-event proportions here flatter both arms and cannot be compared with the phase 3 trials' rates.
cards.source: Akizawa T et al. Long-Term Efficacy and Safety of Molidustat for Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease: DIALOGUE Extension Studies. American journal of nephrology. 2019. PMID: 30852574. cards.headline: Synthesis: molidustat matched darbepoetin on haemoglobin in ESA-naive, ESA-treated and dialysis populations across three Japanese phase 3 trials, with long-term extension support — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region noninferiority base
cards.summary: Synthesis: molidustat matched darbepoetin on haemoglobin in ESA-naive, ESA-treated and dialysis populations across three Japanese phase 3 trials, with long-term extension support — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region noninferiority base
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Evaluation-period mean Hb differences (molidustat minus darbepoetin) were −0.38, +0.13 and −0.13 g/dL in the three phase 3 trials, each inside the 1.0 g/dL noninferiority margin and each with mean Hb inside its target range; DIALOGUE extensions showed similar maintenance to 36 months. No card here reports a cardiovascular or mortality outcome as its primary result, and every phase 3 trial was conducted in Japan.

shelves.title: Enarodustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to darbepoetin and to erythropoietin on haemoglobin, +1.60 g/dL versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD — a Japan/China HIF-PHI programme
shelves.question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis and non-dialysis), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor enarodustat, compared with placebo, recombinant human erythropoietin or standard ESA therapy, control haemoglobin (SYMPHONY / ENARODIAL programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anemia · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors · Female · Ferritins · Hemoglobins · Hepcidins · Humans · Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-Proline Dioxygenases · Male · Middle Aged · N-substituted Glycines · Pyridines · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Triazoles
shelves.balance: Enarodustat controlled haemoglobin wherever it was tested in this programme: a dose-related Hb rise versus placebo over 6 weeks in the phase 2b haemodialysis trial; noninferiority to darbepoetin alfa in SYMPHONY HD (mean Hb 10.73 vs 10.85 g/dL; difference −0.12 g/dL); noninferiority to recombinant human erythropoietin in ENARODIAL (mean Hb 106.81 g/L [10.68 g/dL] vs 99.68 g/L [9.97 g/dL] over weeks 20–24); a clear placebo-controlled Hb rise in Chinese non-dialysis patients (+15.99 g/L [+1.60 g/dL] vs −0.14 g/L over weeks 7–9); and target-range maintenance in the small single-arm peritoneal dialysis study ENAROPERA (mean Hb 110.50 g/L [11.05 g/dL], n=37). Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, several records do not report their randomised N in the abstract, and this is a single-region programme (Japan/China; approved in Japan, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question is homed at live #731 and pack #5753, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Phase 2b RCT + long-term extension (Akizawa 2019): enarodustat raised Hb dose-dependently versus placebo over 6 weeks in haemodialysis patients, and 65.1% maintained target Hb in the 24-week open phase
cards.summary: Phase 2b RCT + long-term extension (Akizawa 2019): enarodustat raised Hb dose-dependently versus placebo over 6 weeks in haemodialysis patients, and 65.1% maintained target Hb in the 24-week open phase
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with open-label extension, enarodustat vs placebo then enarodustat maintenance
cards.people: Japanese patients with haemodialysis-dependent CKD receiving a stable ESA dose, randomised double-blind to once-daily enarodustat 2, 4 or 6 mg or placebo for 6 weeks (Period 1), followed by 24 weeks of open enarodustat (2–8 mg) titrated to keep Hb 10.0–12.0 g/dL (Period 2). The record does not state the total randomised N in its abstract, so none is printed here.
cards.result: Change in Hb from baseline in Period 1 increased with enarodustat dose. In Period 2, 65.1% of subjects maintained Hb within the target range at the end of treatment, and about 80% required two or fewer dose adjustments to do so. Enarodustat decreased hepcidin and ferritin, increased total iron-binding capacity, and was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase lasted only 6 weeks and the record's abstract gives no arm sizes or numeric Hb changes — it establishes dose response and maintenance feasibility, while the efficacy weight of this shelf rests on the phase 3 trials.
cards.source: Akizawa T et al. Enarodustat, Conversion and Maintenance Therapy for Anemia in Hemodialysis Patients: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Phase 2b Trial Followed by Long-Term Trial. cards.headline: SYMPHONY HD phase 3 RCT (Akizawa 2021): enarodustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa in Japanese haemodialysis patients (mean Hb 10.73 vs 10.85 g/dL; difference −0.12 g/dL)
cards.summary: SYMPHONY HD phase 3 RCT (Akizawa 2021): enarodustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa in Japanese haemodialysis patients (mean Hb 10.73 vs 10.85 g/dL; difference −0.12 g/dL)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (SYMPHONY HD), enarodustat vs darbepoetin alfa
cards.people: Japanese patients with CKD anaemia receiving maintenance haemodialysis, randomised 1:1 to oral enarodustat once daily or intravenous darbepoetin alfa weekly for 24 weeks, with dose adjustment every 4 weeks to keep Hb ≥10.0 to <12.0 g/dL; intravenous iron was prohibited during screening and weeks 0–4. The record does not state the total randomised N in its abstract, so none is printed here.
cards.result: Mean Hb during the evaluation period (weeks 20–24) was 10.73 g/dL (95% CI 10.56 to 10.91) on enarodustat and 10.85 g/dL (95% CI 10.72 to 10.98) on darbepoetin; the difference was −0.12 g/dL (95% CI −0.33 to 0.10), confirming noninferiority against the −1.0 g/dL margin, and mean Hb stayed within target throughout. Increased total iron-binding capacity and serum iron and decreased hepcidin were seen by week 4 on enarodustat. No apparent safety concerns versus darbepoetin were observed.
cards.watchOut: Haemoglobin surrogate over 24 weeks in a Japanese haemodialysis population; the record carries no MeSH terms and no abstract N, so neither is printed.
cards.source: Akizawa T et al. A Phase 3 Study of Enarodustat (JTZ-951) in Japanese Hemodialysis Patients for Treatment of Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease: SYMPHONY HD Study. Kidney diseases (Basel, Switzerland). 2021. PMID: 34901195. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: ENARODIAL phase 3 RCT (Wu 2026): enarodustat was noninferior to recombinant human erythropoietin in haemodialysis-dependent CKD (mean Hb 106.81 vs 99.68 g/L over weeks 20–24; n=100)
cards.summary: ENARODIAL phase 3 RCT (Wu 2026): enarodustat was noninferior to recombinant human erythropoietin in haemodialysis-dependent CKD (mean Hb 106.81 vs 99.68 g/L over weeks 20–24; n=100)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised open-label active-comparator trial (ENARODIAL), enarodustat vs recombinant human erythropoietin
cards.people: 100 ESA-treated patients with haemodialysis-dependent CKD, randomised 1:1 to enarodustat (50 patients) or recombinant human erythropoietin (50 patients) for 24 weeks, doses adjusted every 4 weeks to keep Hb within 100–120 g/L (10.0–12.0 g/dL); 93 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Mean Hb over the evaluation period (weeks 20–24) was 106.81 g/L (10.68 g/dL) on enarodustat and 99.68 g/L (9.97 g/dL) on erythropoietin; the least-squares mean difference was 7.47 g/L (0.75 g/dL; 95% CI 4.17 to 10.78; p<0.001), meeting noninferiority against the −10 g/L (−1.0 g/dL) margin. Target-range maintenance during weeks 20–24 was 79.6% on enarodustat versus 51.0% on erythropoietin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 90.0% of both groups, with no additional safety concerns for enarodustat.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and modest in size (100 patients, 24 weeks); the erythropoietin arm's mean Hb sat just below the target range, which flatters the between-group difference — the safe reading is noninferiority, not superiority.
cards.source: Wu H et al. cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT in Chinese non-dialysis CKD (Liang 2025): enarodustat raised Hb by 15.99 g/L (1.60 g/dL) versus −0.14 g/L on placebo over weeks 7–9 (n=156)
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT in Chinese non-dialysis CKD (Liang 2025): enarodustat raised Hb by 15.99 g/L (1.60 g/dL) versus −0.14 g/L on placebo over weeks 7–9 (n=156)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (8 weeks) with open-label extension, enarodustat vs placebo
cards.people: 156 patients with non-dialysis CKD anaemia at 48 centres in China, randomised 2:1 to enarodustat or placebo for an 8-week double-blind period, followed by a 16-week open-label period in which all patients received enarodustat; the primary endpoint was mean change in Hb from baseline to the average of weeks 7–9.
cards.result: Mean Hb change to weeks 7–9 was +15.99 (SD 9.46) g/L (+1.60 g/dL) on enarodustat versus −0.14 (SD 8.08) g/L on placebo — a mean difference of 16.00 g/L (1.60 g/dL; p<0.001). During weeks 7–9, 85.3% of enarodustat patients achieved Hb ≥100 g/L (≥10.0 g/dL), and hepcidin fell by 42.94 ng/mL on enarodustat versus a rise of 4.58 ng/mL on placebo by week 9. Adverse events were comparable to placebo and the safety profile was reported as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase is short (8 weeks) in ESA-naive-style correction; longer-term data in this report are open-label, and the record carries no MeSH terms, so none are printed.

cards.headline: ENAROPERA phase 3 single-arm study (Liu 2026): enarodustat maintained target Hb in peritoneal dialysis patients (mean 110.50 g/L [11.05 g/dL]; 83.8% in target) — n=37, no comparator
cards.summary: ENAROPERA phase 3 single-arm study (Liu 2026): enarodustat maintained target Hb in peritoneal dialysis patients (mean 110.50 g/L [11.05 g/dL]; 83.8% in target) — n=37, no comparator
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label single-arm study (ENAROPERA), enarodustat in peritoneal dialysis — no comparator
cards.people: 37 Chinese patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis with anaemia, treated open-label with enarodustat starting at 2 mg once daily for 4 weeks, then dose-adjusted every 4 weeks toward a target Hb of 100–120 g/L (10.0–12.0 g/dL); mean adherence was 99.21%.
cards.result: Mean Hb during the evaluation period (weeks 20–24 or end of treatment) was 110.50 g/L (11.05 g/dL; 95% CI 107.72 to 113.28), and 31 of 37 patients (83.8%) achieved the target range. Hb change at week 4 was −3.1 g/L. Drug-related adverse events occurred in 21.6% (8/37), with no grade 3 or higher drug-related events; serious adverse events occurred in 21.6% (8/37), none judged related to enarodustat.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and small (N=37, printed on the face): it shows target maintenance is achievable in peritoneal dialysis patients, but with no comparator it cannot show enarodustat is better than, or equal to, ESA therapy in this population.

shelves.title: Desidustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to epoetin alfa and to darbepoetin on haemoglobin in the Indian DREAM-D and DREAM-ND phase 3 trials, with more responders
shelves.question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis-dependent), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor desidustat, compared with epoetin alfa, control haemoglobin (DREAM programme)?
shelves.mesh: Anemia · Epoetin Alfa · Erythropoietin · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Quinolones · Recombinant Proteins · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic
shelves.balance: In the Indian DREAM programme, oral desidustat (thrice weekly) was noninferior to injectable ESAs on haemoglobin in both settings: versus epoetin alfa in dialysis-dependent CKD (Hb change to weeks 16–24 of 0.95 vs 0.80 g/dL; difference 0.14 g/dL, inside the prespecified margin, with more haemoglobin responders on desidustat, 59.22% vs 48.37%) and versus darbepoetin in non-dialysis CKD (Hb change 1.95 vs 1.83 g/dL; difference 0.11 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin, responders 77.78% vs 68.48%). The phase 2 dose-ranging trial showed the expected dose-related Hb rise versus placebo over 6 weeks (1.57, 2.22 and 2.92 g/dL at 100, 150 and 200 mg). Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, both phase 3 trials were open-label and 24 weeks, and this is a single-region programme (India; approved there, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question is homed at live #731 and pack #5753, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: DREAM-D phase 3 RCT (Gang 2022): desidustat was noninferior to epoetin alfa in dialysis-dependent CKD (Hb change 0.95 vs 0.80 g/dL), with more responders (59.22% vs 48.37%)
cards.summary: DREAM-D phase 3 RCT (Gang 2022): desidustat was noninferior to epoetin alfa in dialysis-dependent CKD (Hb change 0.95 vs 0.80 g/dL), with more responders (59.22% vs 48.37%)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label randomised active-controlled trial (DREAM-D), desidustat vs epoetin alfa
cards.people: 392 patients with anaemia due to dialysis-dependent CKD (ESA-naive or prior ESA users; baseline Hb 8.0–11.0 g/dL) at 38 centres in India, randomised 1:1 to desidustat oral tablets thrice a week or epoetin alfa subcutaneous injection for 24 weeks, targeting Hb 10–12 g/dL; the primary endpoint was change in Hb from baseline to the evaluation period, weeks 16–24.
cards.result: Least-squares mean Hb change to weeks 16–24 was 0.95 (SE 0.09) g/dL on desidustat and 0.80 (SE 0.09) g/dL on epoetin alfa (difference 0.14 [SE 0.14] g/dL; 95% CI −0.1304 to 0.4202), meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin. Haemoglobin responders were significantly more frequent on desidustat (106 patients, 59.22%) than on epoetin alfa (89 patients, 48.37%) (p=0.0382). The safety profile was comparable, with no new or increased risks identified for desidustat.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 24 weeks, Indian centres only, and a haemoglobin surrogate: noninferiority here is about Hb control, not about cardiovascular outcomes or mortality.
cards.source: Gang S et al. Desidustat in Anemia due to Dialysis-Dependent Chronic Kidney Disease: A Phase 3 Study (DREAM-D). American journal of nephrology. 2022. PMID: 35462369. cards.headline: DREAM-ND phase 3 RCT (Agrawal 2022): desidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin in non-dialysis CKD (Hb change 1.95 vs 1.83 g/dL), with more responders (77.78% vs 68.48%)
cards.summary: DREAM-ND phase 3 RCT (Agrawal 2022): desidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin in non-dialysis CKD (Hb change 1.95 vs 1.83 g/dL), with more responders (77.78% vs 68.48%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised active-controlled trial (DREAM-ND), desidustat vs biosimilar darbepoetin
cards.people: 588 patients with anaemia due to non-dialysis-dependent CKD (baseline Hb 7.0–10.0 g/dL), randomised 1:1 to desidustat 100 mg oral tablets thrice a week or biosimilar darbepoetin subcutaneous injection 0.75 μg/kg once every 2 weeks, for 24 weeks; the primary outcome was change in Hb from baseline to the evaluation period, weeks 16–24.
cards.result: Hb change to weeks 16–24 was 1.95 g/dL on desidustat and 1.83 g/dL on darbepoetin (difference 0.11 g/dL; 95% CI −0.12 to 0.34), meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin of −0.75 g/dL. Haemoglobin responders were significantly more frequent on desidustat (196 patients, 77.78%) than darbepoetin (176 patients, 68.48%) (p=0.0181). Hepcidin change differed significantly between groups at weeks 12 and 24, as did LDL change at week 24; VEGF change did not differ significantly. Desidustat was reported as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was a biosimilar darbepoetin at a fixed starting dose, the trial ran 24 weeks in a single region (India), and the endpoint is again haemoglobin, a surrogate.

cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging RCT (Parmar 2019): desidustat raised Hb dose-dependently over 6 weeks in non-dialysis CKD (1.57, 2.22 and 2.92 g/dL at 100, 150 and 200 mg; n=117)
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging RCT (Parmar 2019): desidustat raised Hb dose-dependently over 6 weeks in non-dialysis CKD (1.57, 2.22 and 2.92 g/dL at 100, 150 and 200 mg; n=117)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, desidustat vs placebo
cards.people: 117 adults with anaemia and CKD not on dialysis, randomised to desidustat 100, 150 or 200 mg or placebo, given every alternate day for 6 weeks in fasting conditions; the primary endpoint was change in Hb from baseline to week 6 (modified intention-to-treat population).
cards.result: Mean Hb increased by 1.57, 2.22 and 2.92 g/dL in the 100, 150 and 200 mg arms respectively at 6 weeks, with responder rates (≥1 g/dL increase) of 66%, 75% and 83%, in a dose-related pattern versus placebo in both modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations. Eighteen patients had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event and five had a drug-related mild event; no death or serious adverse event was reported during the trial.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks and 117 patients across four arms: a dose-finding study whose role here is to show the pharmacology behaves as expected; the clinical weight rests on the two DREAM phase 3 trials.

shelves.title: Leflunomide in lupus nephritis: comparable to azathioprine for maintenance and to cyclophosphamide for induction in Chinese trials — never superior, with teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity leading the harm side
shelves.question: In adults with lupus nephritis, does leflunomide, compared with cyclophosphamide for induction or azathioprine for maintenance (each with glucocorticoids), achieve and sustain renal remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Azathioprine · Creatinine · Cyclophosphamide · Drug Therapy, Combination · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Leflunomide · Lupus Nephritis · Mycophenolic Acid · Prednisone · Prospective Studies · Serum Albumin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence, all from China and all with glucocorticoids in both arms, shows leflunomide performing comparably to the standard it was tested against — not better. As maintenance after cyclophosphamide induction, kidney flares occurred in 15.7% on leflunomide versus 17.8% on azathioprine over 36 months (time to flare 16 vs 14 months, p=0.676), with similar adverse-event incidence (56.5% vs 58.9%). As induction in proliferative lupus nephritis, complete remission at 24 weeks was 23% on leflunomide versus 27% on cyclophosphamide and partial remission 56% versus 42% — neither difference significant. A small prospective study in refractory disease (n=20, no comparator) and a 2005 multicentre controlled trial (n=51) point the same general way without adding comparative weight. The harm side must lead with leflunomide's class warnings — teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity — which these trials are too small and short to quantify. The CIST combined-immunosuppression trial (PMID 30488367) is NOT counted here: its oral agent was mycophenolate, azathioprine or leflunomide at clinician choice, so it is not a leflunomide report. Lupus nephritis homes for other agents (obinutuzumab live #1819, anifrolumab pack #6975) are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Maintenance RCT (Fu 2022): leflunomide matched azathioprine after cyclophosphamide induction — kidney flares 15.7% vs 17.8% over 36 months, time to flare not significantly different
cards.summary: Maintenance RCT (Fu 2022): leflunomide matched azathioprine after cyclophosphamide induction — kidney flares 15.7% vs 17.8% over 36 months, time to flare not significantly different
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised trial, leflunomide vs azathioprine maintenance (after cyclophosphamide induction), with long-term follow-up
cards.people: 270 adults with biopsy-confirmed active lupus nephritis at 7 Chinese rheumatology centres, all given induction with 6–9 months of intravenous cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids; the 215 who achieved complete or partial response were randomised to prednisone plus leflunomide (n=108) or prednisone plus azathioprine (n=107) as maintenance for 36 months. Primary endpoint: time to kidney flare.
cards.result: Kidney flares occurred in 17 leflunomide patients (15.7%) and 19 azathioprine patients (17.8%); time to kidney flare did not differ significantly (16 months vs 14 months, p=0.676). Proteinuria, serum creatinine, albumin, C3 and C4 improved similarly in both groups; extrarenal flare occurred in one leflunomide and two azathioprine patients. Adverse-event incidence was similar (leflunomide 56.5%, azathioprine 58.9%). The authors concluded leflunomide's efficacy and safety profile are non-inferior to azathioprine for maintenance therapy of lupus nephritis.
cards.watchOut: Only induction responders were randomised (215 of 270 enrolled), the population is Chinese, and 'non-inferior' here is the authors' conclusion from a non-significant difference — the record reports no prespecified noninferiority margin, so read it as 'no detected difference' in a modest sample.
cards.source: Fu Q et al. Leflunomide versus azathioprine for maintenance therapy of lupus nephritis: a prospective, multicentre, randomised trial and long-term follow-up. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2022. PMID: 35788493. Registry ID: NCT01172002. cards.headline: Induction RCT (Zhang 2019): low-dose leflunomide + prednisone matched intravenous cyclophosphamide + prednisone at 24 weeks (complete remission 23% vs 27%; partial remission 56% vs 42% — neither significant)
cards.summary: Induction RCT (Zhang 2019): low-dose leflunomide + prednisone matched intravenous cyclophosphamide + prednisone at 24 weeks (complete remission 23% vs 27%; partial remission 56% vs 42% — neither significant)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised controlled trial, leflunomide vs cyclophosphamide induction (each with prednisone)
cards.people: 100 Chinese patients with biopsy-proven proliferative lupus nephritis, randomised to leflunomide (48 patients; loading dose 40 mg/day for 3 days, then 20 mg/day) or intravenous cyclophosphamide (52 patients; 0.8–1.0 g monthly), each with prednisone, for 24 weeks. Primary outcome: complete and partial remission rates at week 24.
cards.result: Complete remission at week 24 was 23% on leflunomide versus 27% on cyclophosphamide (P=0.64) and partial remission 56% versus 42% (P=0.16) — no statistically significant differences. SLEDAI, serum albumin, complement 3, anti-dsDNA antibody and urinary protein excretion improved significantly in both groups, with no significant between-group differences in the changes and no significant difference in side effects.
cards.watchOut: 100 patients and 24 weeks is small and short for an induction question in proliferative lupus nephritis, and a non-significant difference at this size is compatible with clinically important differences in either direction.

cards.headline: Prospective study in refractory lupus nephritis (Zhang 2023): leflunomide 20–40 mg/day gave objective responses in 30–40% over follow-up — N=20, single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: Prospective study in refractory lupus nephritis (Zhang 2023): leflunomide 20–40 mg/day gave objective responses in 30–40% over follow-up — N=20, single-arm, no comparator
cards.type: Prospective single-arm interventional study in refractory lupus nephritis (no comparator; N=20)
cards.people: 20 patients with refractory lupus nephritis (N=20, printed on the face), given oral leflunomide 20–40 mg/day while other immunosuppressives were withdrawn and corticosteroids gradually tapered, with follow-up at 3, 6 and 12 months and some patients observed to 24 months; 18 patients (90%) completed the study.
cards.result: At 3 months, 80% (16/20) had more than a 25% decrease in 24-hour urine protein. At 6 months, 15% (3 patients) achieved partial response and 25% (5 patients) complete response; by 12 and 24 months the complete response rate was 15% and 20% respectively. Objective response rates were 30% (6/20), 40% (8/20), 40% (8/20) and 30% (6/20) at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months. Two patients withdrew after developing cytopenia and leucopenia.
cards.watchOut: Sub-floor-adjacent by design: N=20 with no control group, in patients whose other immunosuppressives were withdrawn — response rates here cannot be attributed to leflunomide alone and this card is never load-bearing for the stamp; it is carded, with its N on the face, as the only refractory-disease report.
cards.source: Zhang S et al. Treatment of refractory lupus nephritis using leflunomide: A prospective study. Frontiers in immunology. 2023. PMID: 37006280. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Leflunomide · Lupus Nephritis · Cyclophosphamide · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Multicentre controlled trial (Cui 2005): leflunomide + steroid matched intravenous cyclophosphamide in newly treated proliferative lupus nephritis (total response 80% vs 75%; complete remission 40% vs 25%, not significantly different) — n=51
cards.summary: Multicentre controlled trial (Cui 2005): leflunomide + steroid matched intravenous cyclophosphamide in newly treated proliferative lupus nephritis (total response 80% vs 75%; complete remission 40% vs 25%, not significantly different) — n=51
cards.type: Prospective multicentre controlled clinical trial, leflunomide + steroid vs intravenous cyclophosphamide (2005, Chinese-language journal with English abstract)
cards.people: 51 patients with biopsy-confirmed proliferative lupus nephritis in a prospective multicentre controlled clinical trial (Chinese-language journal, English abstract): newly treated patients received oral leflunomide (group A) or intravenous cyclophosphamide (group B), and 14 relapsed patients who had received immunosuppressive therapy 3 months before received leflunomide (group C); efficacy and safety were evaluated at 6 months, and 4 patients withdrew due to adverse events.
cards.result: In newly treated patients, total response was 80% in group A and 75% in group B, and complete remission 40% and 25% respectively — not statistically different; proteinuria, serum albumin, serum creatinine and SLEDAI improved similarly. In the 14 relapsed patients on leflunomide, total response was 60% and complete remission 6.7%. Major adverse events on leflunomide were infection and alopecia; herpes zoster was the most frequent infection, and one case of severe lung infection was reported.
cards.watchOut: The oldest and smallest comparative report (n=51, mixed newly treated and relapsed groups, 6 months), verified from its English abstract only — supportive historical evidence, not a pillar of the shelf.
cards.source: Cui TG et al. [Treatment of proliferative lupus nephritis with leflunomide and steroid: a prospective multi-center controlled clinical trial]. Zhonghua nei ke za zhi. 2005. PMID: 16202258. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: leflunomide performed comparably to azathioprine (maintenance) and to cyclophosphamide (induction) in Chinese randomised trials, with only small uncontrolled support in refractory disease — comparable, not superior, on a single-region base
cards.summary: Synthesis: leflunomide performed comparably to azathioprine (maintenance) and to cyclophosphamide (induction) in Chinese randomised trials, with only small uncontrolled support in refractory disease — comparable, not superior, on a single-region base
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Maintenance: kidney flares 15.7% (leflunomide) versus 17.8% (azathioprine), n=215 randomised after induction response. Induction: complete remission 23% versus 27% and partial remission 56% versus 42% against cyclophosphamide, n=100, neither significant; the 2005 controlled trial (n=51) was concordant. The refractory-disease report is single-arm with N=20 and adds no comparative weight. No trial showed leflunomide superior to its comparator, all comparative evidence is from China with open-label-style designs, and the trials cannot quantify leflunomide's teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity risks, which lead the harm side of any clinical use.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Mizoribine in lupus nephritis: one phase 3 trial (n=250) found it noninferior to IV cyclophosphamide (remission 66.1% vs 76.8%); older Japanese reports are small and uncontrolled
shelves.question: In adults with lupus nephritis, does the oral purine-synthesis inhibitor mizoribine, compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide (and in earlier Japanese reports, as pulse or long-term therapy), induce and maintain renal remission?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cyclophosphamide · Lupus Nephritis · Female · Ribonucleosides · Adult · Male · Middle Aged · Immunosuppressive Agents · Administration, Oral · Young Adult · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Adolescent · Aged · China
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), as a noninferior alternative to intravenous cyclophosphamide — not as a superior treatment. The entire comparative base is one modern open-label phase 3 randomised trial from China (n=250 randomised): at 52 weeks total remission was 66.1% on oral mizoribine versus 76.8% on intravenous cyclophosphamide (relative risk ratio 0.861, 95% CI 0.729 to 1.016), which met the prespecified noninferiority margin of 0.726, with similar rates of treatment-related adverse events (80.5% vs 78.7%). The supporting Japanese reports are small and uncontrolled: weekly pulse therapy in refractory disease (n=17), long-term maintenance (n=10, exactly at the reference floor), and one sub-floor pilot (N=6, printed on its card and never load-bearing). Single-region programme (China/Japan; mizoribine is not FDA/EMA-approved for lupus nephritis) — flagged on the face. The mizoribine/tacrolimus multitarget cohort is a combination study and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT (Dong 2025): oral mizoribine was NONINFERIOR to intravenous cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis induction — total remission 66.1% vs 76.8% at 52 weeks (relative risk ratio 0.861)
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT (Dong 2025): oral mizoribine was NONINFERIOR to intravenous cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis induction — total remission 66.1% vs 76.8% at 52 weeks (relative risk ratio 0.861)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label parallel-group randomised noninferiority trial, oral mizoribine vs intravenous cyclophosphamide, both with glucocorticoid
cards.people: 250 patients with class III, III+V, IV, IV+V, or V lupus nephritis (aged 18–70 years, 24-hour urinary protein ≥1.0 g, SLEDAI ≥8) were randomised at 40 centres in China; 243 were treated (123 mizoribine, 120 cyclophosphamide; mean age 34.6 years, 87.7% women). Mizoribine was 50 mg orally three times daily; cyclophosphamide was 6 intravenous doses of 0.5–1.0 g/m2; both groups also received oral glucocorticoid for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Total remission (complete plus partial) at 52 weeks was 66.1% (76 of 115) on mizoribine versus 76.8% (86 of 112) on cyclophosphamide; the relative risk ratio was 0.861 (95% CI 0.729 to 1.016) and the lower confidence limit exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of 0.726, so mizoribine was noninferior — remission was nonetheless numerically lower on mizoribine. Changes in immune parameters and kidney function were generally similar. Any treatment-related treatment-emergent adverse events: 80.5% (99 of 123) versus 78.7% (96 of 122); the most frequent event in both groups was upper respiratory tract infection (33.3% vs 30.3%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country (China) and a noninferiority design: it shows mizoribine is an acceptable alternative to cyclophosphamide, not that it works better — the point estimate for remission favoured cyclophosphamide.
cards.source: Dong Z et al. Mizoribine or Cyclophosphamide for Lupus Nephritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2025. PMID: 40085084. Registry ID: NCT02256150. cards.headline: Weekly mizoribine pulse therapy in refractory lupus nephritis (Nishi 2013): urinary protein fell and steroids could be tapered in an uncontrolled series of 17 patients — 10 of 17 were responders by the authors' definition
cards.summary: Weekly mizoribine pulse therapy in refractory lupus nephritis (Nishi 2013): urinary protein fell and steroids could be tapered in an uncontrolled series of 17 patients — 10 of 17 were responders by the authors' definition
cards.type: Uncontrolled prospective series — weekly high-dose mizoribine pulse therapy in refractory lupus nephritis (no comparator group)
cards.people: 17 patients with lupus nephritis resistant to corticosteroid and immunosuppressant therapy received weekly mizoribine pulse therapy: 350 mg three times at 12-hour intervals over 2 consecutive days (700 mg day 1, 350 mg day 2), then a washout from day 3 to day 7, designed to push peak blood levels above 3 μg/mL.
cards.result: Peak levels above 3 μg/mL were achieved in most patients. SLEDAI, anti-ds-DNA antibody titre, CH-50 and serum albumin did not significantly improve, but urinary protein levels decreased and concomitant steroid doses could be tapered. By the authors' definition of clinical response, 10 of the 17 patients were responders and 4 were nonresponders; responders' average peak serum mizoribine concentration was 3.5 μg/mL. Elevated liver enzymes occurred in 1 patient and hyperuricaemia in 4, none serious.
cards.watchOut: No control group and only 17 patients with treatment-resistant disease — a different, harder population than the induction trial above; proteinuria change without a comparator cannot be attributed to mizoribine alone.
cards.source: Nishi E et al. Efficacy of weekly mizoribine pulse therapy in refractory lupus nephritis. Modern Rheumatology. 2013. PMID: 22526831. Registry ID: none in the record.
