cards.headline: Long-term mizoribine maintenance (Yumura 2005): proteinuria fell significantly by 2 years and steroids were spared by 3 years in 10 patients followed for a mean of about 90 months — N=10, exactly at the reference floor
cards.summary: Long-term mizoribine maintenance (Yumura 2005): proteinuria fell significantly by 2 years and steroids were spared by 3 years in 10 patients followed for a mean of about 90 months — N=10, exactly at the reference floor
cards.type: Uncontrolled long-term observational series — mizoribine plus prednisolone maintenance in severe proliferative lupus nephritis (no comparator group)
cards.people: 10 patients (all women, mean age 43.0 years) with biopsy-proven proliferative lupus nephritis and proteinuria ≥0.5 g despite plasma exchange and/or pulse methylprednisolone received maintenance mizoribine (average dose 140 mg, given two to three times daily) plus prednisolone for an average of 89.7 months (range 70–126).
cards.result: Proteinuria decreased significantly two years after starting the combination (P=0.0016). Five patients experienced lupus nephritis relapse; patients who did not relapse had started mizoribine earlier (P=0.037). Serum creatinine remained unchanged in all patients, C3 and CH50 normalised as proteinuria fell, a significant steroid-sparing effect was seen at three years (P=0.0025), and no patient developed serious side effects.
cards.watchOut: N=10 sits exactly at the reference floor and there is no comparator: half the patients still relapsed over the long follow-up. Supportive background only; the randomised trial above carries the shelf.
cards.source: Yumura W et al. Effects of long-term treatment with mizoribine in patients with proliferative lupus nephritis. Clinical Nephrology. 2005. PMID: 16047642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SUB-FLOOR pilot (Tanaka 2003) — N=6, printed on the face and never load-bearing: mizoribine oral pulse therapy for lupus nephritis flare — proteinuria 1.9 to 0.2 g/day in six uncontrolled patients
cards.summary: SUB-FLOOR pilot (Tanaka 2003) — N=6, printed on the face and never load-bearing: mizoribine oral pulse therapy for lupus nephritis flare — proteinuria 1.9 to 0.2 g/day in six uncontrolled patients
cards.type: SUB-FLOOR uncontrolled prospective pilot study (phase 2), N=6 — labelled sub-floor on the face, never load-bearing
cards.people: 6 Japanese patients with biopsy-proven lupus nephritis experiencing disease flare (4 had refused a corticosteroid dose increase; 2 had opportunistic infection) received oral mizoribine pulse therapy, 5–10 mg/kg per day (up to 500 mg) in 1–2 divided doses, twice a week for 3 months.
cards.result: Urine protein excretion fell from 1.9 ± 0.6 to 0.2 ± 0.1 g/day and serum anti-dsDNA antibody from 164.8 ± 184.0 to 29.7 ± 23.4 IU/ml (both P<0.05), while serum CH50 recovered from 15.7 ± 5.8 to 35.1 ± 10.4 U/ml (P<0.05). Peak serum mizoribine levels of 3.0–6.0 μg/ml were achieved in all patients and no serious adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: N=6 is below the ~10-human reference floor. It is carded, labelled, only to complete the older Japanese pulse-therapy record; with no control subjects it carries no weight in the balance.
cards.source: Tanaka H et al. Mizoribine oral pulse therapy for patients with disease flare of lupus nephritis. Clinical Nephrology. 2003. PMID: 14690255. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one modern randomised trial (n=250) found oral mizoribine noninferior to intravenous cyclophosphamide for induction; the older Japanese reports (n=17, n=10 and a sub-floor N=6) are uncontrolled and supportive only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one modern randomised trial (n=250) found oral mizoribine noninferior to intravenous cyclophosphamide for induction; the older Japanese reports (n=17, n=10 and a sub-floor N=6) are uncontrolled and supportive only
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The claim this shelf can support is narrow: in Chinese patients with active lupus nephritis, oral mizoribine plus glucocorticoid was noninferior to intravenous cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoid for total remission at 52 weeks (66.1% vs 76.8%; relative risk ratio 0.861, with the confidence interval excluding the noninferiority margin), at similar overall adverse-event rates. Nothing here shows mizoribine superior to cyclophosphamide, and the pulse-therapy and maintenance reports are small, uncontrolled, single-region series — one of them sub-floor at N=6. Lupus nephritis questions for other agents are homed elsewhere (for example obinutuzumab and anifrolumab shelves) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Bixalomer for hyperphosphataemia in CKD: lowered phosphate versus placebo (−0.98 mg/dL in predialysis CKD) and non-inferior to sevelamer on dialysis — Japan-only programme, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In patients with hyperphosphataemia due to chronic kidney disease (on haemodialysis, and not on dialysis), does the non-calcium, non-metal phosphate binder bixalomer, compared with placebo or sevelamer hydrochloride, control serum phosphate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chelating Agents · Female · Humans · Hyperphosphatemia · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphates · Polyamines · Renal Dialysis · Sevelamer · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the surrogate only. Bixalomer lowered serum phosphate dose-dependently versus placebo over 4 weeks in haemodialysis patients (−1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day versus +0.24 mg/dL), was non-inferior to sevelamer hydrochloride at 12 weeks (5.87 versus 5.55 mg/dL; difference 0.31 mg/dL, upper 95% CI below the 1.0 mg/dL margin), and beat placebo in CKD patients not on dialysis (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL, P<0.001). Two open-label 48-week programme reports support durability, with constipation the commonest drug reaction (21.0% in the haemodialysis report). Two limits lead the balance: this is a single-region programme (Japan; bixalomer — Astellas, Kiklin — is approved there and is not FDA/EMA-approved), and serum phosphate is a surrogate endpoint throughout the binder class — no bixalomer trial exists for mortality, cardiovascular events or fractures.

cards.headline: Dose-finding RCT (Akizawa 2014): bixalomer lowered serum phosphorus dose-dependently versus placebo over 4 weeks in haemodialysis patients (adjusted mean change −1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day versus +0.24 mg/dL on placebo)
cards.summary: Dose-finding RCT (Akizawa 2014): bixalomer lowered serum phosphorus dose-dependently versus placebo over 4 weeks in haemodialysis patients (adjusted mean change −1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day versus +0.24 mg/dL on placebo)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled dose-finding trial (with open-label sevelamer reference arm), haemodialysis
cards.people: Patients with CKD on haemodialysis with hyperphosphataemia: 32 randomised to placebo and 31 to each bixalomer dose group (1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 g/day); sevelamer hydrochloride was an open-label reference arm without statistical comparison. Baseline serum phosphorus was 7.95 to 8.25 mg/dL.
cards.result: Adjusted mean change in serum phosphorus from baseline to week 4 (or discontinuation) was +0.24 mg/dL on placebo, −0.75 mg/dL at bixalomer 1.5 g/day, −1.32 mg/dL at 3.0 g/day and −1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day — a significant, dose-dependent decrease at all doses versus placebo. The open-label sevelamer reference arm (mean dose 4.8 g/day) changed by −2.32 mg/dL. Major adverse events included constipation, hard faeces and vomiting; none were serious or severe.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 weeks of treatment and about 31 patients per dose group; the sevelamer arm was a non-randomised-comparison reference, so no bixalomer-versus-sevelamer conclusion can be drawn from this study. Serum phosphate is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: RCT versus sevelamer (Akizawa 2014): bixalomer was non-inferior to sevelamer hydrochloride for serum phosphate at 12 weeks in haemodialysis patients (5.87 versus 5.55 mg/dL; difference 0.31 mg/dL, upper 95% CI below the 1.0 mg/dL margin)
cards.summary: RCT versus sevelamer (Akizawa 2014): bixalomer was non-inferior to sevelamer hydrochloride for serum phosphate at 12 weeks in haemodialysis patients (5.87 versus 5.55 mg/dL; difference 0.31 mg/dL, upper 95% CI below the 1.0 mg/dL margin)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised open-label non-inferiority trial, bixalomer vs sevelamer hydrochloride, haemodialysis
cards.people: 110 haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia randomised — 55 to bixalomer (started 1.5 g/day, titrated to a maximum 7.5 g/day) and 55 to sevelamer hydrochloride (started 3.0 or 6.0 g/day, maximum 9.0 g/day) for 12 weeks (multicentre, open-label, non-inferiority design).
cards.result: Baseline-adjusted mean serum phosphate on completion was 5.87 mg/dL with bixalomer versus 5.55 mg/dL with sevelamer (difference 0.31 mg/dL, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.76); the upper confidence limit was below the pre-set 1.0 mg/dL non-inferiority margin, confirming non-inferiority. The incidence of adverse events was lower in the bixalomer group, and bixalomer did not promote acidosis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and small (55 per group); non-inferiority on a surrogate (serum phosphate) over 12 weeks says nothing about mortality, cardiovascular events or fractures, for which no bixalomer trial exists.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT in CKD not on dialysis (Akizawa 2016): bixalomer beat placebo — adjusted mean change in serum phosphorus −0.78 versus +0.20 mg/dL (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL, P<0.001)
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT in CKD not on dialysis (Akizawa 2016): bixalomer beat placebo — adjusted mean change in serum phosphorus −0.78 versus +0.20 mg/dL (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL, P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, CKD not on dialysis
cards.people: 163 Japanese predialysis patients with CKD and hyperphosphataemia randomised 1:1 (bixalomer 81, placebo 82) for 12 weeks; bixalomer started at 1500 mg/day and was titrated to a maximum 7500 mg/day by serum phosphorus.
cards.result: The adjusted mean change in serum phosphorus from baseline to end of treatment was −0.78 mg/dL (95% CI −0.98 to −0.57) with bixalomer versus +0.20 mg/dL (95% CI −0.00 to 0.41) with placebo (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL, 95% CI −1.27 to −0.69; P<0.001). At end of treatment 57.5% of bixalomer-treated patients had achieved target serum phosphorus; intact parathyroid hormone and fibroblast growth factor-23 fell, corrected calcium did not change significantly, and bicarbonate rose significantly versus placebo (P=0.003). Safety and tolerability were similar to placebo; gastrointestinal events were the most common drug-related events (>24% per group).
cards.watchOut: A 12-week surrogate-endpoint trial in Japanese predialysis patients only; no trial in this population tests dialysis initiation, cardiovascular events or death.

cards.headline: Programme support — long-term open-label haemodialysis report (Akizawa 2013): serum phosphate held around 5.5 mg/dL over 48 weeks in 248 patients; constipation was the commonest drug reaction (21.0%)
cards.summary: Programme support — long-term open-label haemodialysis report (Akizawa 2013): serum phosphate held around 5.5 mg/dL over 48 weeks in 248 patients; constipation was the commonest drug reaction (21.0%)
cards.type: Programme support: multicentre open-label 48-week long-term study (no comparator), haemodialysis — not independent comparative evidence
cards.people: 248 Japanese haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia started open-label bixalomer (1.5 g/day, titrated to a maximum 7.5 g/day) for 48 weeks; 179 completed the study.
cards.result: Mean serum phosphate fell over time and remained around 5.5 mg/dL from weeks 16 to 48; the target range (3.5–6.0 mg/dL) was reached in over 50% by week 7 and maintained in 65.2% to 75.9% until week 48. Adverse events occurred in 94.4% and adverse drug reactions in 29.4%; four serious events were potentially drug-related (ischaemic colitis, haemorrhagic intestinal diverticulum, oesophageal ulcer, acute cholecystitis — one patient each). Constipation was the most common drug reaction (21.0%). Bixalomer did not lower bicarbonate or promote metabolic acidosis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no comparator and 69 of 248 patients not completing: it can describe durability and tolerability only, and cannot confirm efficacy. Carded, labelled as programme support, to complete the record.
cards.source: Akizawa T et al. Long-term treatment of hyperphosphatemia with bixalomer in Japanese hemodialysis patients. cards.type: Programme support: multicentre open-label phase 3 48-week long-term study (no comparator), CKD not on dialysis — not independent comparative evidence
cards.people: 105 Japanese predialysis patients with CKD and hyperphosphataemia received open-label bixalomer (initial 1500 mg/day, titrated to a maximum 7500 mg/day) for 48 weeks; 39 completed, the commonest reason for discontinuation being initiation of dialysis.
cards.result: Mean serum phosphorus fell from 5.15 mg/dL at baseline to 4.67 mg/dL at week 12 and was 4.58 mg/dL at week 48; the proportion achieving the target concentration (≥2.5 to <4.6 mg/dL) peaked at 66.2% at week 20 and was 51.3% at week 48. Most adverse events occurred in the first 12 weeks and incidence did not rise with long-term treatment; common events were nasopharyngitis (29.5%), constipation (19%) and upper respiratory tract inflammation (12.4%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, no comparator, and only 39 of 105 patients completed (many started dialysis, as expected in this population): descriptive only. Carded, labelled as programme support, to complete the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bixalomer lowers serum phosphate versus placebo and was non-inferior to sevelamer in haemodialysis patients — a single-region (Japan) programme, on a surrogate endpoint, with no outcomes trial

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The comparative record is three randomised trials from one Japanese development programme: a 4-week dose-finding trial showing dose-dependent phosphate lowering versus placebo (to −1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day versus +0.24 mg/dL on placebo), a 12-week open-label trial showing non-inferiority to sevelamer hydrochloride (difference 0.31 mg/dL, upper 95% CI below the 1.0 mg/dL margin), and a 12-week phase 3 trial in CKD patients not on dialysis showing superiority to placebo (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL). Two open-label 48-week programme reports (248 haemodialysis and 105 predialysis patients) describe durability and a mainly gastrointestinal tolerability profile, constipation foremost. Serum phosphate is a surrogate endpoint throughout the phosphate-binder class: no bixalomer trial tests mortality, cardiovascular events or fractures. Bixalomer is a single-source product (Astellas; Kiklin) approved in Japan and not FDA/EMA-approved.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Peginesatide in CKD anaemia — WITHDRAWN 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis: non-inferior for haemoglobin in EMERALD and PEARL, with a cardiovascular-safety signal in non-dialysis patients (HR 1.32)
shelves.question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (undergoing haemodialysis, not receiving dialysis, or on peritoneal dialysis), does the erythropoiesis-stimulating agent peginesatide, compared with epoetin/darbepoetin or placebo, control haemoglobin (EMERALD / PEARL programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anemia · Antibodies · Disease-Free Survival · Drug Administration Schedule · Erythropoietin · Female · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Peptides · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the product is WITHDRAWN. Peginesatide (Omontys) was withdrawn from the market in 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis reactions, including first-dose reactions in the post-marketing setting — that history leads this shelf; the drug cannot be prescribed. On the trials: once-monthly peginesatide was non-inferior to epoetin for haemoglobin in haemodialysis patients (EMERALD 1 and 2 — two trials in one paper) and non-inferior to darbepoetin in CKD patients not on dialysis (PEARL 1 and 2 — two trials in one paper). The split is safety by population: pooled composite cardiovascular hazard ratio 1.06 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.26), but 1.32 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.81) in PEARL, with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia in non-dialysis patients. A 59-patient open-label peritoneal-dialysis conversion report is programme support only. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint; ESA-class cardiovascular-safety evidence is cross-pointed to the ESA class shelves, not re-carded here.

cards.summary: EMERALD 1 and EMERALD 2 (Fishbane 2013 — one paper reporting TWO trials, labelled as such): once-monthly peginesatide was non-inferior to epoetin for haemoglobin in haemodialysis patients; pooled composite cardiovascular-safety hazard ratio 1.06
cards.type: Two randomised open-label non-inferiority trials reported in one paper (EMERALD 1 and EMERALD 2 — two trials, one publication), peginesatide vs epoetin, haemodialysis
cards.people: Patients with anaemia undergoing haemodialysis in two randomised, controlled, open-label studies — EMERALD 1 (693 patients analysed) and EMERALD 2 (725 patients analysed); 1608 patients in total received peginesatide once monthly or continued epoetin one to three times weekly, doses adjusted to maintain haemoglobin 10.0–12.0 g/dL for 52 weeks or more.
cards.result: Peginesatide was non-inferior to epoetin in maintaining haemoglobin: mean between-group difference −0.15 g/dL (95% CI −0.30 to −0.01) in EMERALD 1 and +0.10 g/dL (95% CI −0.05 to 0.26) in EMERALD 2 (non-inferiority required the lower confidence limit to be −1.0 g/dL or higher). For the adjudicated composite safety endpoint (death, stroke, myocardial infarction, or serious congestive heart failure, unstable angina or arrhythmia), the hazard ratio was 1.06 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.26) in the pooled four-study cohort of 2591 patients and 0.95 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.17) in the EMERALD studies alone. Adverse and serious adverse event proportions were similar between groups in EMERALD.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trials of a surrogate endpoint (haemoglobin). The pooled safety analysis mixes the dialysis (EMERALD) and non-dialysis (PEARL) populations — the PEARL safety picture was worse (next card), so the pooled hazard ratio must not be read as the whole story. Peginesatide was withdrawn from the market in 2013 (see balance).
cards.source: Fishbane S et al. Peginesatide in patients with anemia undergoing hemodialysis. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23343061. Registry ID: NCT00597753 (EMERALD 1) and NCT00597584 (EMERALD 2), as named in the record. cards.headline: PEARL 1 and PEARL 2 (Macdougall 2013 — one paper reporting TWO trials, labelled as such): peginesatide was non-inferior to darbepoetin for haemoglobin in CKD patients not on dialysis, but the cardiovascular-safety hazard ratio was 1.32, with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia
cards.summary: PEARL 1 and PEARL 2 (Macdougall 2013 — one paper reporting TWO trials, labelled as such): peginesatide was non-inferior to darbepoetin for haemoglobin in CKD patients not on dialysis, but the cardiovascular-safety hazard ratio was 1.32, with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia
cards.type: Two randomised open-label non-inferiority trials reported in one paper (PEARL 1 and PEARL 2 — two trials, one publication), peginesatide vs darbepoetin, CKD not on dialysis
cards.people: 983 patients with anaemia of CKD not undergoing dialysis in two randomised, controlled, open-label studies (PEARL 1 and PEARL 2), receiving peginesatide once monthly (starting dose 0.025 or 0.04 mg/kg) or darbepoetin once every 2 weeks (starting dose 0.75 μg/kg), doses adjusted to maintain haemoglobin 11.0–12.0 g/dL for 52 weeks or more.
cards.result: Peginesatide was non-inferior to darbepoetin for haemoglobin at both starting doses in both studies (mean differences 0.03 and 0.26 g/dL in PEARL 1; 0.14 and 0.31 g/dL in PEARL 2; non-inferiority margin −1.0 g/dL on the 97.5% confidence interval). The hazard ratio for the adjudicated cardiovascular safety endpoint was 1.32 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.81) for peginesatide relative to darbepoetin, with higher incidences of death, unstable angina and arrhythmia with peginesatide. The authors concluded efficacy was similar but cardiovascular events and mortality were increased in patients not undergoing dialysis.
cards.watchOut: The safety hazard ratio of 1.32 is a relative measure: the confidence interval (0.97 to 1.81) crosses 1, but the point estimate and the pattern of more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia are the signal the authors themselves drew attention to — neither dismiss it as 'non-significant' nor overstate it as proven harm. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Macdougall IC et al. Peginesatide for anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease not receiving dialysis. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23343062. Registry ID: NCT00598273 (PEARL 1) and NCT00598442 (PEARL 2), as named in the record. cards.headline: Phase 2 peritoneal-dialysis report (Zabaneh 2015): once-monthly peginesatide maintained haemoglobin after conversion from epoetin in 59 peritoneal-dialysis patients (mean change +0.10 g/dL) — an open-label, uncontrolled programme report
cards.summary: Phase 2 peritoneal-dialysis report (Zabaneh 2015): once-monthly peginesatide maintained haemoglobin after conversion from epoetin in 59 peritoneal-dialysis patients (mean change +0.10 g/dL) — an open-label, uncontrolled programme report
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label single-arm conversion study (programme report), peritoneal dialysis — no comparator
cards.people: 59 patients with CKD on peritoneal dialysis, previously on epoetin (alfa or beta), converted to once-monthly peginesatide with doses titrated to maintain haemoglobin 10–12 g/dL over 25 weeks (median starting dose 0.047 mg/kg; median prior weekly epoetin dose 96.0 U/kg).
cards.result: Mean haemoglobin during the evaluation period (weeks 20–25) was 11.3 ± 1.07 g/dL, a mean change from baseline of +0.10 ± 1.15 g/dL (95% confidence limits −0.24 to 0.44); 63.0% maintained haemoglobin between 10 and 12 g/dL during evaluation. Forty-three patients (72.9%) completed the study; 6 (10.2%) received red-cell transfusions. The commonest adverse event was peritonitis (20.3%), a recognised peritoneal-dialysis complication; four deaths occurred (two septic shock, one myocardial ischaemia, one myasthenia gravis).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and small (59 patients): it shows haemoglobin could be maintained after conversion, nothing more — it is not comparative evidence and must not be counted alongside EMERALD/PEARL as a third trial.
cards.source: Zabaneh R et al. Peginesatide to Manage Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease Patients on Peritoneal Dialysis. Peritoneal dialysis international : journal of the International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis. 2015. PMID: 24584613. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: peginesatide matched epoetin/darbepoetin for haemoglobin in four randomised trials (EMERALD 1/2, PEARL 1/2), with a cardiovascular-safety signal in non-dialysis patients — and the product was withdrawn in 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis
cards.summary: Synthesis: peginesatide matched epoetin/darbepoetin for haemoglobin in four randomised trials (EMERALD 1/2, PEARL 1/2), with a cardiovascular-safety signal in non-dialysis patients — and the product was withdrawn in 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: WITHDRAWN PRODUCT: peginesatide (Omontys) was withdrawn from the market in 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis reactions, including first-dose reactions in the post-marketing setting — it cannot be prescribed, and this shelf is the record of its evidence base. On efficacy, once-monthly peginesatide was non-inferior to epoetin in haemodialysis patients (EMERALD 1 and 2, two trials reported in one paper) and non-inferior to darbepoetin in CKD patients not on dialysis (PEARL 1 and 2, two trials reported in one paper). On safety the programme split by population: the pooled composite cardiovascular hazard ratio was 1.06 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.26), but within PEARL (non-dialysis) it was 1.32 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.81) with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia. The peritoneal-dialysis report (59 patients) is an uncontrolled conversion study, labelled as such. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint; the cardiovascular-safety questions belong to the ESA class shelves, cross-pointed here, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Cystatin C reference intervals: 0.61–1.01 mg/L on ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable methods (n=304) vs 0.54–1.21 mg/L pre-standardisation (n=270); age moves the upper limit, sex barely does
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for serum / plasma cystatin C — the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by age and sex — and how much do assay calibration (ERM-DA471/IFCC traceability), population and age move the limits that feed cystatin-C eGFR?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Creatinine/blood · Cystatin C · Cystatins/blood · Female · Humans · Immunoassay · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Reproducibility of Results · Clinical Laboratory Techniques/standards · Predictive Value of Tests · Reference Standards · Biomarkers · East Asian People · Obesity/epidemiology · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, renal physiology / glomerular filtration, and Guyton & Hall, kidney chapters — framing only; the row rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four datasets, three of them healthy blood-donor series from the same Danish group across two calibrator generations, tell one coherent story with a calibration lesson at its centre: pre-standardisation (1998, DAKO PET kit) the common adult interval was 0.54–1.21 mg/L; with the Gentian method traceable to the international calibrator ERM-DA471/IFCC (2018) the common interval narrowed and fell to 0.61–1.01 mg/L. The independent UK donor series (2000) gave 0.51–0.98 mg/L overall, with the upper limit rising after age 50 (0.53–0.92 mg/L under 50; 0.58–1.02 mg/L over 50). The large Chinese health-examination cohort (10,640 healthy adults) centres lower (median 0.73 mg/L; men 0.79, women 0.67) and confirms age, male sex and BMI push values up. Sex differences for cystatin C are small or absent in the donor series — unlike creatinine, whose intervals are sex-split on every card. Pre- and post-standardisation values are NOT interchangeable, and the assay generation is printed beside every interval. This shelf reports the analyte interval only; cystatin-C eGFR prediction is homed at pack #6070 and the CKD shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Pre-standardisation interval (Erlandsen 1998): 270 healthy blood donors — serum cystatin C 0.54–1.21 mg/L common interval (women 0.62–1.15, men 0.51–1.25; median 0.85), no sex difference (P=0.48), DAKO PET immunoassay
cards.summary: Pre-standardisation interval (Erlandsen 1998): 270 healthy blood donors — serum cystatin C 0.54–1.21 mg/L common interval (women 0.62–1.15, men 0.51–1.25; median 0.85), no sex difference (P=0.48), DAKO PET immunoassay
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cystatin C and creatinine reference intervals, healthy blood donors, pre-standardisation assay)
cards.people: 270 healthy adult blood donors (135 men and 135 women aged 20–65 years, 15 of each sex per five-year band); serum cystatin C measured by automated particle-enhanced immunoassay (DAKO Cystatin C PET kit) on a Cobas Mira S analyser; serum creatinine by an enzymatic Vitros method.
cards.result: Reference intervals for serum cystatin C were 0.62–1.15 mg/L in women (median 0.84) and 0.51–1.25 mg/L in men (median 0.87), with no gender-related difference (P=0.48), giving a common interval of 0.54–1.21 mg/L (median 0.85; full range 0.42–1.39). Creatinine, by contrast, was sex-split: 57–95 µmol/L (≈0.64–1.07 mg/dL) in women and 69–111 µmol/L (≈0.78–1.26 mg/dL) in men.
cards.watchOut: A 1998 pre-standardisation assay generation: its upper limit (1.21 mg/L) is about 0.2 mg/L higher than the ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable interval on the next card — the two must never be interchanged for the same patient result.
cards.source: Erlandsen EJ et al. Reference intervals for serum cystatin C and serum creatinine in adults. Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 1998. PMID: 9711428. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Post-standardisation interval (Erlandsen 2018): 304 healthy donors, Gentian method traceable to ERM-DA471/IFCC — plasma cystatin C 0.61–1.01 mg/L common interval (women 0.58–1.00, men 0.62–1.04; median 0.79), no sex difference (P=.21)
cards.summary: Post-standardisation interval (Erlandsen 2018): 304 healthy donors, Gentian method traceable to ERM-DA471/IFCC — plasma cystatin C 0.61–1.01 mg/L common interval (women 0.58–1.00, men 0.62–1.04; median 0.79), no sex difference (P=.21)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cystatin C and creatinine reference intervals, ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable methods)
cards.people: 304 healthy blood donors (152 men and 152 women aged 17–66 years, 30–31 of each sex per ten-year band); plasma cystatin C by the Gentian Cystatin C assay (traceable to the international calibrator ERM-DA471/IFCC) on a Roche cobas c702; plasma creatinine by an IDMS-traceable assay. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Nonparametric reference intervals for plasma cystatin C were 0.58–1.00 mg/L in women (median 0.78) and 0.62–1.04 mg/L in men (median 0.79), with no gender-related difference (P=.21), giving a common interval of 0.61–1.01 mg/L (median 0.79). Plasma creatinine remained sex-split: 52–89 µmol/L (≈0.59–1.01 mg/dL) in women versus 61–108 µmol/L (≈0.69–1.22 mg/dL) in men (P<.0001).
cards.watchOut: Serum (1998 card) versus plasma (this card) and a different calibrator generation both contribute to the shift in limits; the traceability statement, not the fluid alone, is what makes this the current-generation interval.

cards.headline: Independent UK donor series (Finney 2000): 309 healthy donors — cystatin C 95% interval 0.51–0.98 mg/L overall; under 50 years 0.53–0.92 mg/L, over 50 years 0.58–1.02 mg/L, so a single range serves all adults under 50
cards.summary: Independent UK donor series (Finney 2000): 309 healthy donors — cystatin C 95% interval 0.51–0.98 mg/L overall; under 50 years 0.53–0.92 mg/L, over 50 years 0.58–1.02 mg/L, so a single range serves all adults under 50
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cystatin C, creatinine and predicted clearance reference ranges, healthy blood donors)
cards.people: 309 healthy blood donors; serum creatinine and cystatin C measured by commercially available automated methods, with Cockcroft–Gault predicted creatinine clearance also calculated; intervals reported overall, by sex and by age split at 50 years.
cards.result: The 95% reference interval for cystatin C was 0.51–0.98 mg/L in all donors (women 0.49–0.94; men 0.56–0.98). By age, the interval was 0.53–0.92 mg/L under 50 years and 0.58–1.02 mg/L over 50 years — the upper limit rises with age while sex differences stay small, so the authors proposed a single cystatin C range for all adults under 50. Companion intervals: creatinine 68–118 µmol/L (≈0.77–1.33 mg/dL) overall and predicted creatinine clearance 58–120 ml/min/1.73 m2.
cards.watchOut: A 2000 commercial-assay generation, pre-dating ERM-DA471 standardisation: its overall upper limit (0.98 mg/L) happens to sit close to the 2018 standardised interval, but the age split — not the headline interval — is this card's durable content.

cards.headline: Large Chinese cohort (Ji 2023): 10,640 healthy adults — median cystatin C 0.73 mg/L (men 0.79, women 0.67); elevated values (>1.03 mg/L) independently associated with male sex (OR 1.94), older age (OR 1.04 per year) and higher BMI (OR 1.70)
cards.summary: Large Chinese cohort (Ji 2023): 10,640 healthy adults — median cystatin C 0.73 mg/L (men 0.79, women 0.67); elevated values (>1.03 mg/L) independently associated with male sex (OR 1.94), older age (OR 1.04 per year) and higher BMI (OR 1.70)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cystatin C distribution and influencing factors, healthy Chinese adults)
cards.people: Prospective health-examination cohort at a Chinese hospital health management centre: 10,640 healthy adults aged 18 years and over (mean age 40 ± 12 years, 52% men) after exclusion of hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease and obesity (BMI ≥28 kg/m2); cystatin C distribution and factors associated with elevation above 1.03 mg/L analysed.
cards.result: Median serum cystatin C was 0.73 mg/L overall (spread printed as 95% CI 0.52–1.03), 0.79 mg/L in men (0.59–1.07) and 0.67 mg/L in women (0.49–0.95) — a clearer sex gap than the European donor series found. In multivariable analysis, elevated cystatin C (>1.03 mg/L) was independently associated with male sex (odds ratio 1.94, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.52), older age (odds ratio 1.04 per year, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.06), higher BMI (odds ratio 1.70, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.83), uric acid and β2-microglobulin.
cards.watchOut: A health-examination cohort with disease exclusions rather than a formal CLSI reference-interval study, and its spread is printed as a confidence interval around the median rather than 2.5th–97.5th percentiles — compare its centre with the donor cards, not its tails.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the current-generation (ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable) adult cystatin C interval is about 0.61–1.01 mg/L with no useful sex split; pre-standardisation intervals ran about 0.2 mg/L higher at the top, and age — not sex — is the variable that moves the upper limit
cards.summary: Synthesis: the current-generation (ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable) adult cystatin C interval is about 0.61–1.01 mg/L with no useful sex split; pre-standardisation intervals ran about 0.2 mg/L higher at the top, and age — not sex — is the variable that moves the upper limit
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above (270, 304 and 309 healthy donors; 10,640 healthy Chinese adults).
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (glomerular filtration) and Guyton & Hall (kidney chapters); the shelf rests on the primary reference-interval literature. Three donor series and one large cohort agree: cystatin C in healthy adults centres near 0.73–0.85 mg/L; the 97.5th percentile sits near 1.0 mg/L on standardised methods (0.61–1.01 mg/L, Erlandsen 2018; 0.51–0.98 mg/L, Finney 2000) but reached 1.21 mg/L on the 1998 pre-standardisation kit; the upper limit rises after age 50 (to 1.02 mg/L in Finney); and sex differences are small in European donors though the Chinese cohort centres lower in women (median 0.67 vs 0.79 mg/L). Creatinine intervals beside them are always sex-split — the contrast is the teaching point for why cystatin C was adopted. eGFR equation performance is a different question, homed at pack #6070. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: four concordant datasets including a standardised-method interval and a 10,640-person cohort.
cards.watchOut: Always read a cystatin C result against the interval belonging to its own assay generation: applying the 1998 upper limit (1.21 mg/L) to a standardised-method result would misclassify genuinely raised values as normal.

shelves.title: Conivaptan in euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia: sodium rose about 6–9 mEq/L vs about 1–3 mEq/L on placebo in three programme trials — a biochemical benefit, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia, does the vasopressin V1A/V2-receptor antagonist conivaptan (intravenous or oral), compared with placebo, raise serum sodium?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Arginine Vasopressin · Benzazepines · Cytochrome P-450 CYP3A · Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme Inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyponatremia · Male · Sodium
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the biochemical endpoint — serum sodium — on three randomised placebo-controlled trials from one development programme (two oral, one intravenous). Least-squares mean sodium change from baseline to end of treatment: 6.4 and 8.2 mEq/L at oral 40 and 80 mg/day vs 3.4 mEq/L on placebo (74 patients); 6.3 and 9.4 mEq/L on intravenous 40 and 80 mg/day vs 0.8 mEq/L on placebo (84 patients); and 6.8 and 8.8 mEq/L on oral 40 and 80 mg/day vs 1.2 mEq/L on placebo (83 patients). Serum sodium is a biochemical endpoint: no trial here measured mortality, falls or cognition. The oral formulation was investigational; the intravenous product (Vaprisol) was FDA-approved in 2005. Overly rapid correction is the class harm; infusion-site reactions led to withdrawal in 3% and 15% at the two intravenous doses. The tolvaptan question is homed separately (live #744) and is cross-pointed only.

cards.headline: Oral conivaptan RCT (Ghali 2006): least-squares mean sodium change 6.4 mEq/L at 40 mg/day and 8.2 mEq/L at 80 mg/day vs 3.4 mEq/L on placebo (P = 0.002)
cards.summary: Oral conivaptan RCT (Ghali 2006): least-squares mean sodium change 6.4 mEq/L at 40 mg/day and 8.2 mEq/L at 80 mg/day vs 3.4 mEq/L on placebo (P = 0.002)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, oral conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day vs placebo for 5 days
cards.people: 74 hospitalised patients with euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (average baseline serum sodium 115 to <130 mEq/L), in a 5-day placebo-controlled randomised double-blind study of oral conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day in two divided doses, or placebo.
cards.result: The least-squares mean change from baseline in the serum sodium area under the curve was 2.0-fold (P = 0.03) and 2.5-fold (P < 0.001) greater on conivaptan 40 and 80 mg/day than on placebo. Median time to a confirmed increase of at least 4 mEq/L was 71.7 hours on placebo, 27.5 hours on 40 mg/day (P = 0.044) and 12.1 hours on 80 mg/day (P = 0.002). A confirmed normal serum sodium (at least 135 mEq/L) or an increase of at least 6 mEq/L was observed in 48% of patients on placebo, 71% on 40 mg/day and 82% on 80 mg/day (P = 0.014). Headache, hypotension, nausea, constipation and postural hypotension were the most common adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 5-day biochemical-endpoint trial of the investigational oral formulation, from the same development programme as the other two cards; it measured serum sodium, not mortality, falls or cognition.
cards.source: Ghali JK et al. Efficacy and safety of oral conivaptan: a V1A/V2 vasopressin receptor antagonist, assessed in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in patients with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2006. PMID: 16522696. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Intravenous conivaptan RCT (Zeltser 2007): least-squares mean sodium increase 6.3 mEq/L at 40 mg/day and 9.4 mEq/L at 80 mg/day vs 0.8 mEq/L on placebo; infusion-site reactions led to withdrawal in 3% and 15%
cards.summary: Intravenous conivaptan RCT (Zeltser 2007): least-squares mean sodium increase 6.3 mEq/L at 40 mg/day and 9.4 mEq/L at 80 mg/day vs 0.8 mEq/L on placebo; infusion-site reactions led to withdrawal in 3% and 15%
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial, intravenous conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day vs placebo over 4 days
cards.people: 84 hospitalised patients with euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (serum sodium 115 to <130 mEq/L), randomly assigned to intravenous placebo or conivaptan as a 30-minute 20 mg loading dose followed by a 96-hour infusion of 40 or 80 mg/day.
cards.result: Both conivaptan doses increased the baseline-adjusted area under the sodium-time curve during the 4-day treatment (P < 0.0001 vs placebo), and all secondary efficacy measures improved significantly (P < 0.001, both doses). From baseline to end of treatment, the least-squares mean sodium increase was 0.8 mEq/L on placebo, 6.3 mEq/L on conivaptan 40 mg/day and 9.4 mEq/L on 80 mg/day. Conivaptan was generally well tolerated, although infusion-site reactions led to the withdrawal of 1 patient (3%) on 40 mg/day and 4 patients (15%) on 80 mg/day.
cards.watchOut: The intravenous formulation is the marketed route (Vaprisol, FDA-approved in 2005); the dose-related infusion-site reaction rate — withdrawals in 3% and 15% — is this route's distinctive harm, alongside the class risk of overly rapid sodium correction.
cards.source: Zeltser D et al. Assessment of the efficacy and safety of intravenous conivaptan in euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia. American journal of nephrology. 2007. PMID: 17664863. cards.headline: Second oral conivaptan RCT (Annane 2009): sodium change 6.8 and 8.8 mEq/L at 40 and 80 mg/day vs 1.2 mEq/L on placebo (P = 0.0001); a rise of at least 6 mEq/L or normal sodium in 67% and 88% vs 20%
cards.summary: Second oral conivaptan RCT (Annane 2009): sodium change 6.8 and 8.8 mEq/L at 40 and 80 mg/day vs 1.2 mEq/L on placebo (P = 0.0001); a rise of at least 6 mEq/L or normal sodium in 67% and 88% vs 20%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, oral conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day vs placebo for 5 days
cards.people: 83 patients with euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (serum sodium less than 130 mEq/L), stratified by volume status and randomly assigned to placebo or oral conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day for 5 days. Placebo-controlled randomised double-blind multicentre study.
cards.result: Conivaptan increased the baseline-adjusted area under the serum sodium-time curve significantly more than placebo (P = 0.0001); patients on either dose reached a sodium at least 4 mEq/L above baseline significantly faster (P < 0.001) and maintained it for a greater total time (P = 0.0001). The least-squares mean change in serum sodium from baseline to end of treatment was 6.8 mEq/L (40 mg/day) and 8.8 mEq/L (80 mg/day) vs 1.2 mEq/L on placebo (P = 0.0001). The most frequent adverse events were urinary tract infection, anaemia, pyrexia, cardiac failure, hypotension and hypokalaemia.
cards.watchOut: A distinct report from the first oral trial (different N, setting and placebo-arm change) but from the same development programme — the programme lineage is printed here, not hidden. Again a 5-day biochemical endpoint with the investigational oral formulation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three programme trials agree that conivaptan raises serum sodium by roughly 6 to 9 mEq/L against roughly 1 to 3 mEq/L on placebo over 4 to 5 days — a biochemical benefit with no outcomes trial behind it
cards.summary: Synthesis: three programme trials agree that conivaptan raises serum sodium by roughly 6 to 9 mEq/L against roughly 1 to 3 mEq/L on placebo over 4 to 5 days — a biochemical benefit with no outcomes trial behind it
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: All three randomised trials (74 oral, 84 intravenous, 83 oral patients) found significantly greater sodium rises on conivaptan 40 or 80 mg/day than on placebo, with responder rates (a rise of at least 6 mEq/L or normal sodium) of 67–88% on conivaptan vs 20–48% on placebo. The two oral trials are distinct reports from one development programme, labelled as such on their cards. Serum sodium is a biochemical endpoint: no trial in this base randomised patients and measured mortality, falls or cognition. The oral formulation was investigational; the intravenous product (Vaprisol) was FDA-approved in 2005. The tolvaptan trials (SALT-1/SALT-2) are homed at live #744 and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Doxercalciferol in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: PTH fell 55% and target was reached in 83% in the one efficacy trial (withdrawal design); conversion factor 0.57 vs paricalcitol; paediatric anchor printed as paediatric
shelves.question: In patients on dialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the vitamin D analogue doxercalciferol (1α-hydroxyvitamin D2), compared with placebo, paricalcitol or calcitriol, suppress parathyroid hormone — and at what cost in calcium and phosphate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase · Calcium · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Ergocalciferols · Female · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone · Phosphorus
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the surrogate endpoint of parathyroid hormone suppression, resting on one efficacy trial: in 138 haemodialysis patients, intact PTH fell 55% by week 16 of open-label doxercalciferol, reached the 150–300 pg/mL target in 83% of patients, and in the randomised double-blind withdrawal phase PTH returned to baseline on placebo while remaining suppressed on doxercalciferol — at the cost of more hypercalcaemia measurements above 11.2 mg/dL (3.26% vs 0.46% of measurements, P < 0.01). The second anchor (n=27) answers a dose-conversion question, not efficacy: doxercalciferol at about 0.57 of the paricalcitol dose gave equivalent suppression. The third anchor is a PAEDIATRIC peritoneal-dialysis population (60 children), printed as such and not presented as adult evidence: PTH fell 35% in all groups and bone formation rates fell into the normal range in 72%, with FGF-23 rising over fourfold on both vitamin D agents. PTH is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists for this agent.

cards.headline: Modified double-blind controlled trial (Frazão 2000): intact PTH fell 55% by week 16 and reached target in 83% of patients; in the randomised withdrawal phase PTH returned to baseline on placebo but remained suppressed on doxercalciferol
cards.summary: Modified double-blind controlled trial (Frazão 2000): intact PTH fell 55% by week 16 and reached target in 83% of patients; in the randomised withdrawal phase PTH returned to baseline on placebo but remained suppressed on doxercalciferol
cards.type: Multicentre modified double-blind controlled trial: open-label doxercalciferol run-in followed by a randomised double-blind withdrawal/continuation phase vs placebo
cards.people: 138 haemodialysis patients with moderate to severe secondary hyperparathyroidism enrolled (99 completed), in a trial of washout (8 weeks), open-label doxercalciferol treatment (16 weeks) and then randomised double-blind treatment with doxercalciferol or placebo (8 weeks); oral doxercalciferol was given at each haemodialysis session, titrated to a target intact PTH of 150 to 300 pg/mL. The randomised phase is a withdrawal/continuation design after an open-label run-in — labelled as such.
cards.result: Baseline intact PTH (897 ± 52 pg/mL) decreased by 20% by week 1 (P < 0.001) and by 55% at week 16; in 80% of patients intact PTH decreased by 70%, reaching the target level in 83% of patients. During the double-blind phase, intact PTH returned to baseline on placebo while remaining suppressed on doxercalciferol. During open-label treatment, serum calcium rose from 9.2 to 9.7 mg/dL and phosphorus from 5.4 to 5.9 mg/dL. During double-blind treatment, 3.26% of serum calcium measurements on doxercalciferol exceeded 11.2 mg/dL vs 0.46% on placebo (P < 0.01), with a median level of 11.6 mg/dL during hypercalcaemia; phosphorus levels did not differ between groups in that phase.
cards.watchOut: The randomised evidence is a withdrawal design in run-in survivors (138 enrolled, 99 completing): it shows suppression is maintained on drug and lost on placebo, which is a weaker efficacy design than a parallel-group trial in untreated patients. This is the shelf's one efficacy anchor.

cards.headline: Dose-equivalency study (Zisman 2005) — a conversion question, not an efficacy question: doxercalciferol at a conversion factor of 0.57 of the paricalcitol dose gave equivalent PTH suppression, with similar calcium and phosphate
cards.summary: Dose-equivalency study (Zisman 2005) — a conversion question, not an efficacy question: doxercalciferol at a conversion factor of 0.57 of the paricalcitol dose gave equivalent PTH suppression, with similar calcium and phosphate
cards.type: Randomised dose-equivalency study, doxercalciferol at three fractions of the prior paricalcitol dose — a conversion report, labelled as such
cards.people: 27 chronic haemodialysis patients on a stable dose of paricalcitol for at least 3 months, randomised to receive doxercalciferol at 35%, 50% or 65% of their paricalcitol dose for 6 weeks, with intact PTH, calcium, phosphorus and albumin measured at baseline and every 2 weeks.
cards.result: Initial intact PTH, adjusted serum calcium, serum phosphorus and calcium–phosphate product were similar among the groups. Linear regression analysis of percent change in intact PTH by dose group gave a conversion factor of 0.57 for the dose of doxercalciferol relative to paricalcitol resulting in equivalent suppression of intact PTH; the authors conclude that dosing doxercalciferol at 55–60% of the paricalcitol dose results in comparable inhibition of PTH. Corrected serum calcium, phosphorus, calcium–phosphate product, and the incidence of hypercalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and calcium–phosphate product above 50 were similar for all groups.
cards.watchOut: This report answers 'how much doxercalciferol replaces a given paricalcitol dose', not 'does doxercalciferol work': patients were already suppressed on paricalcitol at entry. It is never load-bearing for efficacy on this shelf.
cards.source: Zisman AL et al. Inhibition of parathyroid hormone: a dose equivalency study of paricalcitol and doxercalciferol. American journal of nephrology. 2005. PMID: 16282676. cards.headline: Paediatric peritoneal-dialysis trial (Wesseling-Perry 2011) — POPULATION: 60 CHILDREN on peritoneal dialysis: calcitriol and doxercalciferol were equivalent, PTH fell 35% in all groups, bone formation rates normalised in 72%, and FGF-23 rose over fourfold on both agents
cards.summary: Paediatric peritoneal-dialysis trial (Wesseling-Perry 2011) — POPULATION: 60 CHILDREN on peritoneal dialysis: calcitriol and doxercalciferol were equivalent, PTH fell 35% in all groups, bone formation rates normalised in 72%, and FGF-23 rose over fourfold on both agents
cards.type: Randomised equivalence trial, calcitriol vs doxercalciferol in factorial combination with phosphate binder — in children on peritoneal dialysis
cards.people: 60 paediatric patients treated with peritoneal dialysis — a PAEDIATRIC PERITONEAL-DIALYSIS population, printed exactly and not adult haemodialysis evidence — randomised to 8 months of oral calcitriol or doxercalciferol, combined in factorial design with either calcium carbonate or sevelamer as phosphate binder.
cards.result: Serum parathyroid hormone levels decreased by 35% in all groups. Bone formation rates decreased during therapy, with final values within the normal range in 72% of patients; a greater improvement in eroded surface was found with doxercalciferol than with calcitriol, while an initial mineralisation defect in the majority of patients did not normalise with therapy. Serum phosphate was controlled equally well by both binders, but serum calcium increased during treatment with calcium carbonate. Baseline plasma FGF-23 was significantly elevated and rose over fourfold with both calcitriol and doxercalciferol, irrespective of phosphate binder.
cards.watchOut: Population discipline: these are children on peritoneal dialysis, and the bone-biopsy findings are paediatric bone data — they must not be presented as adult haemodialysis evidence. The fourfold FGF-23 rise on both agents is printed on the face; its implications, per the authors, remain to be established.
cards.source: Wesseling-Perry K et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: doxercalciferol suppresses PTH in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism on one withdrawal-design efficacy trial (n=138), with a dose-conversion report (n=27) and a paediatric peritoneal-dialysis equivalence trial (n=60 children) completing — not strengthening — the base
cards.summary: Synthesis: doxercalciferol suppresses PTH in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism on one withdrawal-design efficacy trial (n=138), with a dose-conversion report (n=27) and a paediatric peritoneal-dialysis equivalence trial (n=60 children) completing — not strengthening — the base
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The efficacy claim rests on the 138-patient haemodialysis trial: intact PTH fell 55% on open-label doxercalciferol, reached target in 83%, and stayed suppressed on drug while returning to baseline on placebo in the randomised withdrawal phase, with more hypercalcaemia measurements on drug (3.26% vs 0.46% above 11.2 mg/dL). The 27-patient report is a dose-equivalency study (conversion factor 0.57 vs paricalcitol), labelled as a conversion question, not efficacy. The 60-patient report is in children on peritoneal dialysis and found doxercalciferol equivalent to calcitriol on PTH and bone formation, with FGF-23 rising over fourfold on both agents. Parathyroid hormone is a surrogate endpoint; no trial of this agent measured fractures, cardiovascular events or mortality. The paricalcitol shelves (live #1740, #2047) are different agent questions and are cross-pointed only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Maxacalcitol in haemodialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: no significant PTH difference vs calcitriol or paricalcitol in three Japanese trials (dose ratio 5.5:1 vs calcitriol) — single-region, surrogate endpoint
shelves.question: In patients on haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the vitamin D analogue maxacalcitol (22-oxacalcitriol), compared with calcitriol or paricalcitol, suppress parathyroid hormone with comparable calcium control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calcitriol · Calcium · Double-Blind Method · Ergocalciferols · Female · Humans · Hypercalcemia · Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone · Receptors, Calcitriol · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — single-region evidence (Japan; an intravenous agent, not FDA/EMA-approved), flagged on the face. Against calcitriol over 12 months (91 patients) there were no significant differences in intact PTH, phosphate, calcium–phosphate product or bone alkaline phosphatase, with serum calcium significantly higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only; in the crossover dose-equivalence study (31 patients) intact PTH was 267 pg/mL on maxacalcitol vs 343 pg/mL on calcitriol (P = 0.11) at a dose ratio of 5.5:1. Against paricalcitol in the phase 3 trial (255 Japanese haemodialysis patients), target intact PTH without hypercalcaemia was achieved by 30.5% on maxacalcitol vs 27.7% on paricalcitol; that trial's primary non-inferiority test concerned paricalcitol against maxacalcitol and was not met, and both agents reduced intact PTH with similar safety. Parathyroid hormone is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists for this agent. This shelf and the doxercalciferol shelf are different agents in the same condition — their anchors are never pooled.

cards.headline: Randomised multicentre trial vs calcitriol (Hayashi 2004): no significant differences between maxacalcitol and calcitriol in intact PTH, phosphate, calcium–phosphate product or bone alkaline phosphatase over 12 months; serum calcium was significantly higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only
cards.summary: Randomised multicentre trial vs calcitriol (Hayashi 2004): no significant differences between maxacalcitol and calcitriol in intact PTH, phosphate, calcium–phosphate product or bone alkaline phosphatase over 12 months; serum calcium was significantly higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only
cards.type: Randomised prospective multicentre trial, maxacalcitol vs calcitriol over 12 months
cards.people: 91 patients on chronic haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism (intact PTH at least 150 pg/mL), randomly assigned to calcitriol (47 patients) or maxacalcitol (44 patients) therapy for 12 months after a 1-month control period, in a randomised prospective multicentre study.
cards.result: Treatment was discontinued for various reasons in nine patients in each group, with no serious side effects in either group. The numbers reaching the first endpoint (serum intact PTH below 150 pg/mL) were not significantly different between the groups. Serum calcium concentration was significantly higher in the maxacalcitol than the calcitriol group during early treatment, but not at the end of treatment. Throughout the treatment period there were no significant differences between the groups in serum intact PTH, inorganic phosphate, the calcium–phosphate product, bone alkaline phosphatase, or the ratio of whole PTH to total PTH minus whole PTH — including in patients with moderate to severe hyperparathyroidism (basal intact PTH at least 500 pg/mL). The authors conclude the two are equally effective on PTH and bone metabolism.
cards.watchOut: A no-significant-difference result in 91 patients is not a formal equivalence demonstration; the early-treatment calcium excess on maxacalcitol is printed on the face, not buried.
cards.source: Hayashi M et al. Comparison of the effects of calcitriol and maxacalcitol on secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients on chronic haemodialysis: a randomized prospective multicentre trial. cards.headline: Randomised crossover dose-equivalence study (Mochizuki 2007): no significant differences in calcium, phosphate or intact PTH after 12 weeks on each agent (intact PTH 267 vs 343 pg/mL, P = 0.11), at a maxacalcitol:calcitriol dose ratio of 5.5:1
cards.summary: Randomised crossover dose-equivalence study (Mochizuki 2007): no significant differences in calcium, phosphate or intact PTH after 12 weeks on each agent (intact PTH 267 vs 343 pg/mL, P = 0.11), at a maxacalcitol:calcitriol dose ratio of 5.5:1
cards.type: Multicentre randomised crossover dose-equivalence study, maxacalcitol vs calcitriol, 12 weeks on each agent
cards.people: 31 patients on chronic haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism who had not received maxacalcitol or calcitriol in the previous 3 months, randomly divided into two groups and given maxacalcitol or calcitriol in a crossover design for 12 weeks each, doses adjusted on serum calcium and intact PTH, in a multicentre randomised crossover study.
cards.result: After the 12-week administrations there were no significant differences in serum calcium (maxacalcitol 2.40 mmol/L (9.6 mg/dL), calcitriol 2.42 mmol/L (9.7 mg/dL), P = 0.71), phosphate (maxacalcitol 1.97 mmol/L (6.1 mg/dL), calcitriol 2.00 mmol/L (6.2 mg/dL), P = 0.64), intact parathyroid hormone (maxacalcitol 267 pg/mL, calcitriol 343 pg/mL, P = 0.11) or other bone-metabolic parameters. The doses were 49.3 µg/month of maxacalcitol and 9.0 µg/month of calcitriol — a dose ratio of 5.5:1. No severe adverse reactions were seen with either agent.
cards.watchOut: A 31-patient crossover equivalence study: its product is the 5.5:1 dose ratio as much as the comparison itself, and its no-difference findings carry the precision limits of its size.

multicentre randomised crossover dose-equivalence study, maxacalcitol vs calcitriol, 12 weeks on each agent 31 patients on chronic haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism who had not received maxacalcitol or calcitriol in the previous 3 months, randomly divided into two groups and given maxacalcitol or calcitriol in a crossover design for 12 weeks each, doses adjusted on serum calcium and intact pth, in a multicentre randomised crossover study. after the 12-week administrations there were no significant differences in serum calcium (maxacalcitol 2.40 mmol/l (9.6 mg/dl), calcitriol 2.42 mmol/l (9.7 mg/dl), p = 0.71), phosphate (maxacalcitol 1.97 mmol/l (6.1 mg/dl), calcitriol 2.00 mmol/l (6.2 mg/dl), p = 0.64), intact parathyroid hormone (maxacalcitol 267 pg/ml, calcitriol 343 pg/ml, p = 0.11) or other bone-metabolic parameters. the doses were 49.3 µg/month of maxacalcitol and 9.0 µg/month of calcitriol — a dose ratio of 5.5:1. no severe adverse reactions were seen with either agent. a 31-patient crossover equivalence study: its product is the 5.5:1 dose ratio as much as the comparison itself, and its no-difference findings carry the precision limits of its size. mochizuki t et al. prospective comparison of the effects of maxacalcitol and calcitriol in chronic hemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism: a multicenter, randomized crossover study. clinical nephrology. 2007. pmid: 17269594. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · calcitriol · calcium · cross-over studies · dose-response relationship, drug · female · humans · hyperparathyroidism, secondary · male · middle aged · parathyroid hormone · renal dialysis · vitamin d

cards.headline: Phase 3 double-blind trial vs paricalcitol (Akizawa 2015): target intact PTH without hypercalcaemia achieved by 30.5% on maxacalcitol vs 27.7% on paricalcitol; the trial's primary non-inferiority test (paricalcitol vs maxacalcitol) was not met, and both agents reduced intact PTH with similar safety
cards.summary: Phase 3 double-blind trial vs paricalcitol (Akizawa 2015): target intact PTH without hypercalcaemia achieved by 30.5% on maxacalcitol vs 27.7% on paricalcitol; the trial's primary non-inferiority test (paricalcitol vs maxacalcitol) was not met, and both agents reduced intact PTH with similar safety
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind double-dummy parallel-group trial, intravenous paricalcitol vs intravenous maxacalcitol
cards.people: 255 Japanese haemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism, randomised 1:1 to intravenous paricalcitol (n=127) or intravenous maxacalcitol (n=128) injections for 12 weeks, in a double-blind double-dummy parallel-group phase 3 study, with dynamic allocation by screening intact PTH (below 500 vs at least 500 pg/mL).
cards.result: The primary efficacy analysis found that 27.7% of the paricalcitol group vs 30.5% of the maxacalcitol group achieved target intact PTH in the last 3 weeks without hypercalcaemia during treatment (95% CI −14.34% to 8.79%, P = 0.353), failing to achieve the prespecified non-inferiority margin of −5% for paricalcitol against maxacalcitol. Both intravenous paricalcitol and maxacalcitol were effective in reducing intact PTH and provided similar safety profiles; however, non-inferiority for paricalcitol vs maxacalcitol was not demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Direction matters: the failed non-inferiority test was paricalcitol's against maxacalcitol, not the reverse — maxacalcitol's own target-achievement rate (30.5%) was numerically the higher of the two. Absolute target rates were low in both groups (about 3 in 10 patients).

cards.headline: Synthesis: across three Japanese trials (91, 31 and 255 patients) maxacalcitol suppressed PTH comparably to calcitriol and paricalcitol, with an early calcium excess vs calcitriol and a 5.5:1 dose ratio against calcitriol — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region base with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three Japanese trials (91, 31 and 255 patients) maxacalcitol suppressed PTH comparably to calcitriol and paricalcitol, with an early calcium excess vs calcitriol and a 5.5:1 dose ratio against calcitriol — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region base with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No comparison in this base found a significant difference in intact PTH between maxacalcitol and its comparator: not vs calcitriol over 12 months (with serum calcium significantly higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only), not in the 12-week crossover (intact PTH 267 vs 343 pg/mL, P = 0.11; dose ratio 5.5:1), and not vs paricalcitol on target achievement (30.5% vs 27.7%), in a trial whose own non-inferiority question ran in the paricalcitol direction and was not met. The evidence is single-region (Japan), the agent is intravenous and not FDA/EMA-approved, and parathyroid hormone is a surrogate endpoint — no trial measured fractures, cardiovascular events or mortality. This shelf's anchors are never pooled with the doxercalciferol shelf's: different agents, separate programme shelves.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Measured-GFR reference values: 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m² (percentiles 76–137) in healthy adults by iohexol; ≈100 until age 35 in 2,974 donors, then declining 6.6–7.7 per decade; 67.7 ± 10.8 at ages 70–110
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR) — mean, spread and 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by age and sex, and the size of the decline after age 40 — measured by exogenous-marker clearance (iohexol, iothalamate), and how far do donor-cohort ranges sit from general-population ranges?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Africa, Western/epidemiology · Aged · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Healthy Volunteers · Humans · Kidney Function Tests/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/epidemiology,physiopathology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, renal physiology chapters; Boron & Boulpaep, glomerular filtration sections — framing only; this shelf rests on four primary measured-GFR datasets in healthy adults, carded per marker and per cohort. PARTIAL slice, stated plainly: home pack #6958 asks how measured-GFR METHODS AGREE (inulin vs iohexol vs iothalamate vs 51Cr-EDTA, plus renal plasma flow and filtration fraction) and cards none of these datasets; this shelf cards only the reference-VALUES slice — what the values are, by age and sex — and cross-points #6958 rather than re-carding it (its gated iohexol age-dependence dataset, PMID 2609107, stays solely at #6958 under the one-home rule). The values: a general healthy-adult West African cohort (n=237, iohexol) gives mean mGFR 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m² with 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 76–137 and a decline after age 40, with no sex difference. Three of the four datasets are donor or donor-adjacent cohorts — screened, healthier than the general population — and that selection is stated on the face, never merged with the general-population dataset: 2,974 UK prospective living donors (mean ≈100 mL/min/1.73 m² until age 35, then a linear decline, faster in women, 7.7 vs 6.6 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade; 10.5% of donors over 60 had mGFR <60); 365 US potential donors by iothalamate (normalised mean 111 mL/min/1.73 m² at age 20, declining 4.9 per decade); and 52 healthy elderly people aged 70–110 by iohexol (mean 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m²; decline ≈1.05 mL/min per year; the elderly dataset's N of 52 is printed on its card). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: General healthy-adult reference values (Yayo 2018, West Africa, n=237, iohexol plasma clearance): mean measured GFR 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m², 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 76–137, no sex difference, decline after age 40
cards.summary: General healthy-adult reference values (Yayo 2018, West Africa, n=237, iohexol plasma clearance): mean measured GFR 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m², 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 76–137, no sex difference, decline after age 40
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (measured-GFR reference values, iohexol plasma clearance, general healthy adults)
cards.people: 237 healthy adult subjects (103 women, 134 men; mean age 34 ± 10 years) in West Africa, with GFR measured by iohexol plasma clearance. This is the one general healthy-adult (non-donor) dataset on this shelf.
cards.result: Mean measured GFR was 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m² and the median was 103 mL/min/1.73 m², with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 76 and 137 mL/min/1.73 m². There was no significant difference in mGFR below 40 years of age, whereas a significant decline was observed after 40 years. There was no significant difference between men and women. The authors note the same age-associated decline after 40, and the same absence of a sex difference, as reported in Caucasian populations.
cards.watchOut: A young cohort (mean age 34) from one region: its 76–137 percentile range describes healthy West African adults measured by iohexol plasma clearance, and the over-40 decline is characterised within a cohort with few older participants — the older-age values on this shelf come from the donor and elderly datasets, which are different populations.
cards.source: Yayo E et al. Measured (and estimated) glomerular filtration rate: reference values in West Africa. Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association. 2018. PMID: 28992086. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Donor-cohort reference ranges (Fenton 2018, 18 UK centres, n=2,974 prospective living kidney donors): mean mGFR ≈100 mL/min/1.73 m² until age 35, then a linear decline — faster in women (7.7 vs 6.6 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade); 10.5% of donors over 60 had mGFR <60
cards.summary: Donor-cohort reference ranges (Fenton 2018, 18 UK centres, n=2,974 prospective living kidney donors): mean mGFR ≈100 mL/min/1.73 m² until age 35, then a linear decline — faster in women (7.7 vs 6.6 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade); 10.5% of donors over 60 had mGFR <60
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (measured-GFR age- and sex-specific reference ranges, multicentre prospective living-donor cohort)
cards.people: Individual-level pre-donation measured-GFR data from 2,974 prospective living kidney donors at 18 UK renal centres (2003–2015), amalgamated to derive age- and sex-specific reference ranges (means ± two standard deviations, by segmented multiple linear regression) and advisory GFR thresholds for living kidney donation. A donor cohort: screened and healthier than the general population, stated on the face.
cards.result: Men had a higher GFR than women (92.0 vs 88.1 mL/min/1.73 m², P<0.0001). Mean mGFR was 100 mL/min/1.73 m² until 35 years of age, after which there was a linear decline that was faster in women than in men (7.7 vs 6.6 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade, P=0.013). Among individuals aged over 60 years, 10.5% had a GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² — which the authors note may have implications for the definition of chronic kidney disease. The ranges were used, with other published evidence, to set advisory age- and sex-specific GFR thresholds for living kidney donation.
cards.watchOut: Donor selection is the caveat: prospective donors are screened to be healthy, so these ranges sit above unscreened general-population values at the same age — which is precisely the donor-versus-population gap the shelf's question asks about. The abstract does not name the exogenous marker per centre, and this card claims none.
cards.source: Fenton A et al. Glomerular filtration rate: new age- and gender- specific reference ranges and thresholds for living kidney donation. BMC nephrology. 2018. PMID: 30466393. cards.headline: Donor-cohort normal range by iothalamate (Rule 2004, n=365 potential kidney donors): normalised mean GFR 111 mL/min/1.73 m² at age 20, declining 4.9 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade; creatinine-based estimates correlated only weakly with measured GFR (r = 0.26–0.35)
cards.summary: Donor-cohort normal range by iothalamate (Rule 2004, n=365 potential kidney donors): normalised mean GFR 111 mL/min/1.73 m² at age 20, declining 4.9 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade; creatinine-based estimates correlated only weakly with measured GFR (r = 0.26–0.35)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (measured-GFR normal range, nonradiolabelled iothalamate clearance, potential kidney donors)
cards.people: 365 healthy potential kidney donors whose medical records were reviewed; GFR was measured by clearance of nonradiolabelled iothalamate, and age- and sex-specific normal values were derived by linear regression. A donor cohort: screened and healthier than the general population, stated on the face.
cards.result: GFR declined significantly with increasing age (P<0.001) and was lower in women than men in unnormalised terms (P<0.001): men at age 20 had an estimated mean GFR of 129 mL/min, declining by 4.6 mL/min per decade; women at age 20 had a mean of 123 mL/min, declining by 7.1 mL/min per decade. For body-surface-area-normalised GFR, age was significant (P<0.001) but sex was not (P=0.826): a 20-year-old had a mean normalised GFR of 111 mL/min/1.73 m², declining by 4.9 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade. Correlation between measured normalised GFR and creatinine-estimated GFR was weak (r = 0.26 for the abbreviated MDRD equation; r = 0.35 for Cockcroft-Gault), and the authors concluded GFR cannot be estimated accurately from creatinine in healthy individuals.
cards.watchOut: Marker-specific: these are iothalamate-clearance values, and home pack #6958 shows iohexol and iothalamate clearances differ from each other by ~15% — the two markers' reference values on this shelf are not interchangeable. The age-20 means are regression estimates, not measurements in 20-year-olds alone.

cards.headline: Elderly reference values (Fehrman-Ekholm 2004, N = 52 healthy elderly aged 70–110, iohexol clearance): mean measured GFR 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m², declining ≈1.05 mL/min per year; Cockcroft-Gault underestimated measured GFR (46.2 vs 67.7)
cards.summary: Elderly reference values (Fehrman-Ekholm 2004, N = 52 healthy elderly aged 70–110, iohexol clearance): mean measured GFR 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m², declining ≈1.05 mL/min per year; Cockcroft-Gault underestimated measured GFR (46.2 vs 67.7)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (measured-GFR values in healthy elderly, iohexol clearance; N = 52)
cards.people: 52 elderly 'healthy' persons aged 70–110 years with two kidneys, in whom renal function was determined by the iohexol injection technique alongside blood tests; estimated clearances were computed with the Cockcroft-Gault, Walser and Levey equations. The N of 52 is small and is printed on the face of this card, as the commissioning row directs.
cards.result: Measured GFR correlated strongly with age (P=0.0002), with an annual decline of 1.05 mL/min. The measured mean GFR was 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m²; the Cockcroft-Gault formula underestimated it (mean 46.2 ± 11.3 mL/min/1.73 m²), while the Levey equation correlated best with the measurements. Serum creatinine did not correlate with age (P=0.3997), whereas serum urea rose with age (P=0.0019). Of the 52 subjects, 21 (reported as 30% in the record) had a GFR above 70 mL/min/1.73 m², and none of those was aged over 90 years.

cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (renal physiology) and Boron & Boulpaep (glomerular filtration). The general healthy-adult dataset (West Africa, iohexol, n=237) gives mean 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m², percentiles 76–137, decline after 40 and no sex difference (Yayo 2018). The donor datasets — screened, healthier populations — give mean ≈100 mL/min/1.73 m² until age 35 then a linear decline, faster in women (Fenton 2018, n=2,974), and a normalised mean of 111 mL/min/1.73 m² at age 20 declining 4.9 per decade by iothalamate (Rule 2004, n=365). At the old-age end, healthy 70–110-year-olds averaged 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m² by iohexol (Fehrman-Ekholm 2004, N = 52). Marker matters: iohexol and iothalamate values are carded per dataset and are not merged, because the method-agreement home, pack #6958, shows the two clearances differ by ~15%; #6958's own datasets (including its iohexol age-dependence study) are cross-points only and are not re-carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: four independent cohorts spanning young adults to age 110 agree on the level and on an age decline beginning around 35–40, with the donor-selection offset stated rather than hidden.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a single 'normal GFR' without its age band, marker and cohort: a screened donor's 100 mL/min/1.73 m² at 35 and a healthy 85-year-old's 68 mL/min/1.73 m² are both inside this shelf's reference data.
