shelves.title: Verinurad + xanthine-oxidase inhibitor for albuminuria: exactly 2 reports — a 60-patient positive phase 2 against the 861-patient negative SAPPHIRE trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic kidney disease (with type 2 diabetes, or with CKD and hyperuricaemia), does intensive urate lowering with the URAT1 inhibitor verinurad combined with a xanthine-oxidase inhibitor (febuxostat or allopurinol), compared with placebo or the xanthine-oxidase inhibitor alone, reduce albuminuria?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Allopurinol/therapeutic use,/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/drug therapy,/complications
shelves.balance: SPLIT — on exactly 2 results reports, and the split is the answer. A 60-patient phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes with hyperuricaemia and albuminuria found urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) lower on verinurad 9 mg + febuxostat 80 mg than on placebo by −39.4% relative at week 12 and −49.3% relative at week 24, with serum urate about 60% lower relative — but its own abstract states the sample size and duration were insufficient for definitive albuminuria or filtration conclusions. The much larger SAPPHIRE phase 2b trial (861 randomised with CKD and hyperuricaemia) found the geometric mean percentage change in UACR at week 34 did not differ among placebo, allopurinol alone and three verinurad + allopurinol dose arms — the primary endpoint was not met — while serum urate fell dose-dependently. The larger, later trial carries the greater weight: intensive urate lowering lowered urate but did not lower albuminuria where it was properly tested. UACR is a surrogate endpoint; neither trial tested kidney progression, and verinurad was never marketed. A third card below is the SAPPHIRE design paper — a programme report of the same trial, not a third results report; the report count of this shelf is exactly 2.

cards.headline: Phase 2 trial (Stack 2021): in 60 patients with type 2 diabetes, hyperuricaemia and albuminuria, verinurad + febuxostat lowered UACR by −39.4% relative at week 12 and −49.3% relative at week 24 versus placebo
cards.summary: Phase 2 trial (Stack 2021): in 60 patients with type 2 diabetes, hyperuricaemia and albuminuria, verinurad + febuxostat lowered UACR by −39.4% relative at week 12 and −49.3% relative at week 24 versus placebo
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, verinurad 9 mg + febuxostat 80 mg vs placebo, 24 weeks
cards.people: 60 patients aged 18 or older with type 2 diabetes, hyperuricaemia and albuminuria, randomised 1:1 to verinurad 9 mg plus febuxostat 80 mg (32 patients) or matched placebo (28 patients) once daily for 24 weeks, in a multicentre phase 2 double-blind trial supported by AstraZeneca; patients with stage 4 or 5 CKD were excluded.
cards.result: UACR on verinurad plus febuxostat was lower than on placebo by −38.6% relative (90% CI −60.9 to −3.6) at week 1, −39.4% relative (90% CI −61.8 to −3.8) at week 12 (the primary endpoint) and −49.3% relative (90% CI −68.2 to −19.0) at week 24 — all percent changes are relative measures. Serum urate was 59.6% and 63.7% lower relative than placebo at 12 and 24 weeks. No clinically meaningful changes were seen in estimated glomerular filtration rate, serum creatinine or serum cystatin C, and the combination was well tolerated. The authors state plainly that the sample size and study duration were insufficient to evaluate definitive effects on UACR and glomerular filtration.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient, 24-week trial with a surrogate endpoint whose own abstract disclaims definitive conclusions: this is the positive limb of a two-report split, and it must not be read as kidney protection — the 861-patient SAPPHIRE trial (next card) tested the same idea properly and found nothing.

cards.headline: SAPPHIRE phase 2b (Heerspink 2024): in 861 patients with CKD, verinurad + allopurinol did NOT reduce albuminuria versus allopurinol alone or placebo at week 34 — the primary endpoint was not met
cards.summary: SAPPHIRE phase 2b (Heerspink 2024): in 861 patients with CKD, verinurad + allopurinol did NOT reduce albuminuria versus allopurinol alone or placebo at week 34 — the primary endpoint was not met
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised placebo- and active-controlled trial (SAPPHIRE), verinurad 3/7.5/12 mg + allopurinol vs allopurinol alone vs placebo, primary endpoint at week 34
cards.people: 861 adults with CKD and hyperuricaemia (mean age 65 years, 33.0% female, mean eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m², median UACR 217 mg/g; entry serum urate ≥6.0 mg/dL, eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR 30–5000 mg/g), randomised 1:1:1:1:1 to placebo, allopurinol 300 mg/day alone, or verinurad 3, 7.5 or 12 mg plus allopurinol 300 mg/day, enrolled August 2019 to November 2021.
cards.result: At week 34 the geometric mean percentage change in UACR from baseline did not differ among treatment groups: +16.7% (95% CI −0.6 to 37.1) in the verinurad 3 mg group, +15.0% (95% CI −1.85 to 34.6) in the 7.5 mg group and +14.0% (95% CI −3.4 to 34.4) in the 12 mg group, versus +9.9% (95% CI −6.6 to 29.4) on allopurinol alone and +37.3% (95% CI 16.6 to 61.8) on placebo — the primary endpoint was not met. UACR and eGFR change did not differ among groups after 60 weeks either. Verinurad/allopurinol dose-dependently reduced serum urate concentrations compared with placebo, and adverse and serious adverse event proportions were balanced among groups. The drug lowered urate; it did not lower albuminuria.
cards.watchOut: The definitive report of this two-report shelf: fourteen times the size of the positive phase 2 trial, with both a placebo and an active-comparator arm, and null on its primary endpoint at every verinurad dose. Any summary that averages this trial with the 60-patient trial into a benefit claim misstates the record.

cards.people: The SAPPHIRE programme as designed: adults with CKD, eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR 30–5000 mg/g and serum urate ≥6.0 mg/dL, to be randomised 1:1:1:1:1 to verinurad 12, 7.5 or 3 mg plus allopurinol, allopurinol alone, or placebo, with an 8-week dose-titration period and 12-month treatment; approximately 725 patients were planned (861 were ultimately enrolled in the results report carded above).
cards.result: The design paper sets out the rationale — that URAT1 inhibition might reduce albuminuria beyond standard care — and the prespecified primary efficacy endpoint, change from baseline in UACR at 6 months in the design as published (the results report's primary read was at week 34). It also records the phase 2a finding that motivated SAPPHIRE: verinurad + febuxostat lowered UACR at 12 weeks by 39% relative (90% CI 4 to 62) in the 60-patient diabetes trial carded above. It contains no SAPPHIRE results.
cards.watchOut: A protocol/design paper carded, labelled as a programme report, only to complete the record of this exactly-two-results-report programme: it carries no efficacy results and must never be counted as a third report. The verinurad gout/hyperuricaemia urate-lowering studies and the dapagliflozin add-on (QUARTZ) study ask urate questions, not the albuminuria question, and are not carded or counted here.

cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Exactly 2 results reports exist for this question, and they disagree in proportion to their size. The 60-patient phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes (verinurad + febuxostat) found UACR −39.4% relative at week 12 and −49.3% relative at week 24 versus placebo, while disclaiming definitive conclusions in its own abstract. The 861-patient SAPPHIRE phase 2b trial in CKD (verinurad + allopurinol, three doses, against allopurinol alone and placebo) met neither its week-34 primary endpoint nor any week-60 UACR or eGFR difference, despite dose-dependent serum urate lowering. The honest balance is that intensive urate lowering with verinurad lowered urate without lowering albuminuria in the trial large enough to test it. UACR is a surrogate; no trial tested kidney progression, and verinurad was never marketed.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 reports. Both are phase 3 trials from one sponsor's programme in euvolaemic hyponatraemia only, and both met their day-7 serum-sodium primary endpoint: in hospitalised patients sodium rose 6.7 mmol/L (approx. 15.4 mg/dL) on lixivaptan versus 4.5 mmol/L (approx. 10.4 mg/dL) on placebo (P=0.034), and in outpatients 3.2 mmol/L (approx. 7.4 mg/dL) versus 0.8 mmol/L (approx. 1.8 mg/dL), with normal sodium by day 7 in 39.4% versus 12.2%. Serum sodium is a surrogate endpoint: neither trial tested mortality or length of stay, the effect reversed within 7 days of stopping in the inpatient trial, no hypervolaemic results report was located, and lixivaptan was never marketed for this indication in the US. The homed vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan, satavaptan) are different agents and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Inpatient phase 3 RCT (Abraham 2012): lixivaptan raised serum sodium by 6.7 mmol/L (approx. 15.4 mg/dL) versus 4.5 mmol/L (approx. 10.4 mg/dL) on placebo at day 7 (P=0.034) in euvolaemic hyponatraemia

cards.type: Phase 3 multinational double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, lixivaptan vs placebo, initially hospitalised euvolaemic hyponatraemia
cards.people: 106 initially hospitalised patients with euvolaemic hyponatraemia (serum sodium <130 mmol/L (approx. 299 mg/dL)); 54 received lixivaptan 50 mg once daily titrated to 25-100 mg and 52 received placebo, for 30 days in total, with fluid restriction at the investigator's discretion.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in serum sodium from baseline to day 7 — was 6.7 mmol/L (approx. 15.4 mg/dL) on lixivaptan versus 4.5 mmol/L (approx. 10.4 mg/dL) on placebo (P=0.034). Sodium normalised more rapidly on lixivaptan (P=0.004), and the drug was well tolerated. After discontinuation, serum sodium fell back to near-baseline levels within 7 days.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base: this is one of exactly two lixivaptan sodium reports in existence. Serum sodium is a surrogate endpoint; the trial did not test mortality or length of stay, and the correction reversed within a week of stopping.

PMID: 22932119. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Normal intrarenal resistive index in healthy adults: age-defined values 0.59 / 0.61 / 0.63 at ages 25 / 45 / 65 across 4 datasets — and a single reading exceeds 0.70 in health 6% of the time (PHYS)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal values for the intrarenal (renal) resistive index on Doppler ultrasound — the central range at the renal, interlobar and cortical arteries — how steeply does the index rise with age (and does it differ by sex or by arterial level), and how much measurement variability sits inside a single reported value?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame renal haemodynamics briefly, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature, as stated on its face. Four independent healthy-adult datasets (78, 80, 58 and 90 subjects; 1996–2018) agree that the intrarenal resistive index (RI) is age-defined, not a single normal number: Kaiser 2007 gives 0.59 at age 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65 (RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age), with no significant effect of sex, region or side; the Nigerian dataset (Ismail 2018) likewise found a significant RI–age correlation and no gender correlation; Keogan 1996 found region, territory and side without consistent effect but age significant — and quantified single-reading variability (a healthy 45-year-old's single reading exceeds 0.70 with probability 6%, falling to 3% averaged over three readings); Rivolta 2000 found interlobar and cortical RI rising selectively with age as renal blood flow fell, RI higher in women, and cortical RI lower than interlobar and renal RI. Levels are never merged, and the sex disagreement between datasets prints unresolved.

cards.headline: Age-defined normal values (Kaiser 2007): in 78 healthy subjects, intrarenal RI rose with age at every measuring point (P<0.01) — normal RI 0.59 at age 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65, summarised as RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age; sex, kidney region and side had no significant effect
cards.summary: Age-defined normal values (Kaiser 2007): in 78 healthy subjects, intrarenal RI rose with age at every measuring point (P<0.01) — normal RI 0.59 at age 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65, summarised as RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age; sex, kidney region and side had no significant effect
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative intrarenal resistive index, age regression) — dataset 1 of 4 on this shelf
cards.people: 78 healthy subjects (46 men, 32 women) — with a comparison group of 35 patients with fatty liver disease not counted in this shelf's healthy base. Intrarenal RI was measured in three distinct interlobar and cortical arteries in both kidneys after conventional abdominal ultrasound; age and sex effects were evaluated by linear regression.
cards.result: In the healthy group, sex, kidney region and right-versus-left kidney had no significant effect on intrarenal RI (P>0.05), while age showed a significant positive correlation at all four defined measuring points (P<0.01; correlation coefficients r = 0.26, left kidney central, to r = 0.37, right kidney cortical). Normal RI values could therefore be defined by age: 0.59 at 25 years, 0.61 at 45 years and 0.63 at 65 years, expressed as RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age. Patients with fatty liver disease showed the same age dependency. The authors concluded the age of the examined person must be considered to interpret RI values correctly.
cards.watchOut: A regression line through a modest correlation (r = 0.26 to 0.37): the age-defined values are central expectations, not tight individual limits — individual healthy values scatter around them, as the variability card below quantifies.
cards.source: Kaiser C et al. Age dependency of intrarenal resistance index (RI) in healthy adults and patients with fatty liver disease. European journal of medical research. 2007. PMID: 17513189. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nigerian healthy-adult dataset (Ismail 2018): in 80 healthy adults, the mean resistive index showed a statistically significant correlation with age (and with the systolic–diastolic ratio), while gender showed no significant correlation with these indices
cards.summary: Nigerian healthy-adult dataset (Ismail 2018): in 80 healthy adults, the mean resistive index showed a statistically significant correlation with age (and with the systolic–diastolic ratio), while gender showed no significant correlation with these indices
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (renal arterial Doppler velocimetric indices in healthy adults) — dataset 2 of 4 on this shelf
cards.people: 80 healthy adults in north-west Nigeria (36 men, 44 women), scanned with a 3.5 MHz transducer; after parenchymal assessment the renal arteries were identified by colour mapping and velocimetric indices measured on spectral Doppler tracings on each side. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Mean peak systolic velocity was highest on the left side in men (65.75 ± 28.41 cm/sec, vs 60.7 ± 24.20 cm/sec on the right) and in women measured 61.83 ± 22.50 cm/sec on the right and 60.04 ± 24.67 cm/sec on the left. Mean end-diastolic velocity was higher on the right in both sexes (men 23.59 ± 11.45 cm/sec right vs 22.50 ± 8.37 left; women 25.19 ± 10.72 right vs 22.33 ± 8.47 left). There was age-related dependency of the mean resistive index: RI and the systolic–diastolic ratio correlated significantly with age, while gender did not correlate significantly with these indices. The fetched record prints no single mean RI value, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A velocimetry dataset whose printed content is the age correlation and the velocity values, not a tabulated RI reference interval — it corroborates the age gradient in a West African population and must not be quoted for a numeric RI limit it does not print.
cards.source: Ismail A et al. RENAL ARTERIAL DOPPLER VELOCIMETRIC INDICES AMONG HEALTHY SUBJCTS IN NORTH WEST NIGERIA. Journal of the West African College of Surgeons. 2018. PMID: 30899703. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Measurement-variability dataset (Keogan 1996): in 118 kidneys of 58 healthy subjects aged 24–70, region, vascular territory and side had no consistent effect but age did — and a single RI reading in a healthy 45-year-old exceeds 0.70 with probability 6%, falling to 3% when three readings are averaged
cards.summary: Measurement-variability dataset (Keogan 1996): in 118 kidneys of 58 healthy subjects aged 24–70, region, vascular territory and side had no consistent effect but age did — and a single RI reading in a healthy 45-year-old exceeds 0.70 with probability 6%, falling to 3% when three readings are averaged
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (resistive-index variability in a healthy population) — dataset 3 of 4 on this shelf
cards.people: 58 healthy subjects (35 women, 23 men; aged 24 to 70 years) who subsequently underwent angiography; Doppler ultrasound RI measurements in the upper, middle and lower regions of 118 kidneys, assessing the effects of parenchymal region, vascular territory and kidney side, and the correlation of readings within a subject and within a kidney.
cards.result: Kidney region, vascular territory and right-versus-left kidney had no consistently significant effect on RI; age had a statistically significant effect. RI readings were highly correlated with each other both within a subject and within a kidney. The probability that a single RI value would exceed 0.70 in a healthy 45-year-old subject was 6%; this decreased to 3% when three readings were averaged. The authors concluded that, given the variability of RI measurements within a kidney, a number of RI readings should be averaged before a single representative value is reported.
cards.watchOut: The threshold lesson of this shelf: even in health, a single reading crosses the conventional 0.70 line about 1 time in 17 at age 45 — a single RI value is a sample, not a verdict, and averaging three readings halves that false-crossing probability.
cards.source: Keogan MT et al. Renal resistive indexes: variability in Doppler US measurement in a healthy population. Radiology. 1996. PMID: 8633141. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arterial-level dataset (Rivolta 2000): in 90 healthy adults aged 20–65, interlobar and cortical RI rose selectively with age (P<0.0001) while renal blood flow fell; RI were higher in women, and cortical RI was lower than interlobar and renal RI
cards.summary: Arterial-level dataset (Rivolta 2000): in 90 healthy adults aged 20–65, interlobar and cortical RI rose selectively with age (P<0.0001) while renal blood flow fell; RI were higher in women, and cortical RI was lower than interlobar and renal RI
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (renal echo-Doppler variability in healthy adults, by arterial level) — dataset 4 of 4 on this shelf
cards.people: 90 healthy subjects stratified by sex and age (range 20 to 65 years), with additional small groups with a congenital solitary kidney (8) and after surgical nephrectomy (15) not counted in this shelf's healthy base. Kidney diameters and volume, renal blood flow (RBF) and resistive index were measured at the renal, interlobar and cortical arteries.
cards.result: Renal blood flow showed an age-dependent reduction (P<0.0001), while interlobar and cortical RI showed a selective age-dependent increase (both P<0.0001). RI were higher in females, while diameters, volume and RBF — after correction for body surface area — did not differ between the sexes. Cortical RI was lower than the interlobar and renal RI (P<0.0001). The left kidney was longer than the right (P<0.01) and the right wider (P<0.02), with no volume difference between sides. The authors concluded the integrated use of these measurements offers precision and repeatability for evaluating diffuse or localised abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: Levels must never be merged: cortical RI runs lower than interlobar and renal RI in the same healthy kidneys, so an RI value is uninterpretable without its arterial level — and this dataset disagrees with the Kaiser dataset on a sex effect (higher RI in women here; no significant sex effect there), which prints as a genuine between-dataset difference.
cards.source: Rivolta R et al. Variability of renal echo-Doppler measurements in healthy adults. Journal of nephrology. 2000. PMID: 10858972. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Kidney/abnormalities/diagnostic imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Reproducibility of Results · Ultrasonography, Doppler, Color

cards.headline: Synthesis: across four independent healthy-adult datasets (58–90 subjects each, 1996–2018), the intrarenal resistive index is an age-defined value — about 0.59 at 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65 — not a single normal number; it differs by arterial level (cortical < interlobar / renal), and a single reading in a healthy 45-year-old exceeds 0.70 about 6% of the time (3% averaged over three readings)
cards.summary: Synthesis: across four independent healthy-adult datasets (58–90 subjects each, 1996–2018), the intrarenal resistive index is an age-defined value — about 0.59 at 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65 — not a single normal number; it differs by arterial level (cortical < interlobar / renal), and a single reading in a healthy 45-year-old exceeds 0.70 about 6% of the time (3% averaged over three readings)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above (78, 80, 58 and 90 healthy subjects; 306 in total).
cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame renal haemodynamics and renal blood flow, but that framing is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature, and says so. Age gradient: significant in all four datasets (Kaiser 2007: RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age, giving 0.59 / 0.61 / 0.63 at ages 25 / 45 / 65; Ismail 2018: significant RI–age correlation; Keogan 1996: significant age effect; Rivolta 2000: interlobar and cortical RI up with age, P<0.0001, as renal blood flow fell). Level: cortical RI lower than interlobar and renal RI (Rivolta). Variability: a single reading exceeds 0.70 in a healthy 45-year-old with probability 6%, 3% when three readings are averaged (Keogan). Sex: no significant effect in two datasets (Kaiser; Ismail), higher RI in women in one (Rivolta) — printed as a disagreement, not resolved. An unbanded 'normal RI < 0.70' is exactly the error these datasets document, since a healthy older adult's expected value approaches that line. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: four independent datasets spanning two decades agree on the age gradient and the level ordering.
cards.watchOut: Never apply one dataset's values to another arterial level or a single reading to a threshold decision: age band, level and averaging are part of the measurement.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Sulodexide in diabetic kidney disease (PARTIAL vs live #1598): Di.N.A.S. positive on albuminuria (n = 223), but SUN-micro (n = 1,056) and SUN-MACRO (n = 1,248) both null
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic kidney disease, does oral sulodexide, compared with placebo on top of renin-angiotensin blockade, reduce albuminuria or slow kidney progression (the Di.N.A.S. / SUN programme)? PARTIAL beside live #1598, which homes sulodexide for recurrent venous thromboembolism — that question is not re-asked here.
shelves.mesh: Albuminuria · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycosaminoglycans · Humans · Kidney Diseases · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) for kidney protection, on a PARTIAL slice beside live #1598. This shelf cards only the diabetic-kidney-disease question; the venous-thromboembolism question (SURVET) is homed at live #1598 and is not re-carded here. The programme arc runs small-and-positive to large-and-null twice, and the two SUN trials carry the weight: Di.N.A.S. (223 randomised, 4 months, albuminuria surrogate) found dose-linear relative reductions in albumin excretion versus placebo of 30%, 49% and 74% at 50/100/200 mg/day; SUN-microalbuminuria (1,056 randomised on maximal ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy) then MISSED its own albuminuria primary endpoint (achieved in 16.5% on sulodexide vs 18.4% on placebo); and SUN-MACRO (1,248 enrolled of 2,240 planned, terminated early) found no difference on a hard kidney composite (doubling of creatinine, ESRD, or creatinine at least 6.0 mg/dL: 26 events on sulodexide vs 30 on placebo over 1,029 person-years). Albuminuria is a surrogate; the one trial that measured kidney outcomes found nothing, and the larger trial that measured the surrogate itself also found nothing.

cards.headline: Di.N.A.S. dose-ranging RCT (Gambaro 2002): sulodexide reduced albumin excretion dose-linearly versus placebo — relative reductions of 30%, 49% and 74% at 50/100/200 mg/day over 4 months
cards.summary: Di.N.A.S. dose-ranging RCT (Gambaro 2002): sulodexide reduced albumin excretion dose-linearly versus placebo — relative reductions of 30%, 49% and 74% at 50/100/200 mg/day over 4 months
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (Di.N.A.S.), sulodexide 50/100/200 mg/day vs placebo
cards.people: 223 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and micro- or macroalbuminuria, serum creatinine at most 150 µmol/L (≈ 1.7 mg/dL), with stable blood pressure and metabolic control, randomised to sulodexide 50, 100 or 200 mg/day or placebo for 4 months, with 4 further months off-drug follow-up.
cards.result: Albumin excretion rate (AER) percent reductions versus placebo at 4 months were 30% relative (95% confidence limits 4 to 49%, P = 0.03) at 50 mg/day, 49% relative (30 to 63%, P = 0.0001) at 100 mg/day and 74% relative (64 to 81%, P = 0.0001) at 200 mg/day — all relative measures, printed beside the trial's design as a short albuminuria-surrogate study. At 200 mg/day, log AER fell from 5.25 (SE 0.18) at baseline to 3.98 (SE 0.11) at 4 months, and the effect was maintained 4 months after stopping (62% relative reduction vs placebo, P = 0.0001). Findings were similar across diabetes type, albuminuria stratum and concomitant ACE-inhibitor use; very few adverse events were reported and none were serious.
cards.watchOut: A small (n = 223), short (4-month) trial of a surrogate endpoint from 2002, run before the modern background-therapy era; its dose-linear relative reductions were not confirmed by either of the two much larger SUN trials carded below.
cards.source: Gambaro G et al. Oral sulodexide reduces albuminuria in microalbuminuric and macroalbuminuric type 1 and type 2 diabetic patients: the Di.N.A.S. randomized trial. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2002. PMID: 12039991. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SUN-microalbuminuria RCT (Lewis 2011): the primary endpoint was NOT met — achieved in 16.5% on sulodexide versus 18.4% on placebo in 1,056 patients on maximal ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy
cards.summary: SUN-microalbuminuria RCT (Lewis 2011): the primary endpoint was NOT met — achieved in 16.5% on sulodexide versus 18.4% on placebo in 1,056 patients on maximal ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SUN-microalbuminuria), sulodexide vs placebo on maximal renin-angiotensin blockade
cards.people: 1,056 randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria (urine albumin-creatinine ratio 35–200 mg/g in men, 45–200 mg/g in women; mean baseline ACR 107.8 (SD 83.7) mg/g; serum creatinine below 1.5 mg/dL), all on a maximum approved dose of an ACE inhibitor or ARB for at least 4 months, given sulodexide 200 mg/day or placebo.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (normoalbuminuria — ACR below 20 mg/g with a decrease over 25% — or a 50% decrease in baseline ACR) was achieved in 16.5% on sulodexide versus 18.4% on placebo; normoalbuminuria occurred in 7.9% versus 6.1% and a 50% albuminuria decrease in 15.4% versus 17.6%. The relative probability of any given change in albuminuria was identical in both groups, and the investigators could not determine whether the administered sulodexide was absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. The abstract concludes that sulodexide failed to decrease urine albumin excretion in this population.
cards.watchOut: This trial measured the same albuminuria surrogate that Di.N.A.S. had won on, in nearly five times as many patients on modern background therapy — and found nothing; the unverified gastrointestinal absorption of the study drug is a stated caveat of the trial itself.
cards.source: Lewis EJ et al. Sulodexide for kidney protection in type 2 diabetes patients with microalbuminuria: a randomized controlled trial. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2011. PMID: 21872376. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SUN-MACRO RCT (Packham 2012): no renoprotective benefit on hard kidney outcomes — primary composite in 26 patients on sulodexide versus 30 on placebo; the trial was terminated after enrolling 1,248 of 2,240 planned
cards.summary: SUN-MACRO RCT (Packham 2012): no renoprotective benefit on hard kidney outcomes — primary composite in 26 patients on sulodexide versus 30 on placebo; the trial was terminated after enrolling 1,248 of 2,240 planned
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SUN-MACRO), sulodexide vs placebo on maximal ARB therapy — terminated early
cards.people: 1,248 enrolled patients (2,240 planned) with type 2 diabetes, renal impairment and proteinuria over 900 mg/day, already receiving maximal angiotensin-receptor-blocker therapy, randomised to sulodexide or placebo; follow-up totalled 1,029 person-years before early termination.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint — doubling of baseline serum creatinine, development of end-stage renal disease, or serum creatinine at least 6.0 mg/dL — occurred in 26 patients on sulodexide and 30 on placebo, with no significant difference between groups. Side-effect profiles were similar. The abstract concludes that the data do not suggest a renoprotective benefit of sulodexide in type 2 diabetes with renal impairment and macroalbuminuria.
cards.watchOut: Terminated at just over half its planned enrolment, so it is underpowered for small effects — but its point result is null on the only hard kidney-outcome composite in the programme, and it aligns with the larger albuminuria trial's null.
cards.source: Packham DK et al. Sulodexide fails to demonstrate renoprotection in overt type 2 diabetic nephropathy. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2012. PMID: 22034636. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Di.N.A.S. showed dose-dependent relative reductions in albumin excretion over 4 months. SUN-microalbuminuria, testing the same surrogate in 1,056 patients on maximal renin-angiotensin blockade, found the primary endpoint achieved slightly less often on sulodexide than on placebo (16.5% vs 18.4%). SUN-MACRO, testing hard kidney outcomes in 1,248 patients, found 26 versus 30 primary composite events and was stopped early. Weighted by size and by outcome hardness, the programme's answer for diabetic kidney disease is no demonstrated benefit. A small biomarker RCT and a 1997 trial are further programme reports — support only, not carded or counted. The venous-thromboembolism question for this drug stays homed at live #1598 under the one-home rule and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Serum anion gap reference interval: 3–11 mmol/L on ion-selective-electrode analysers, 5–10 / 9–14 / 8–13 mmol/L across three 1997 analysers, and 10–18 mmol/L in a contemporary screening population — the interval is analyser property, not a biological constant (5 datasets)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for the serum anion gap — the central range by analyser / method — how far apart do the published intervals sit (3–11 mmol/L on ion-selective-electrode analysers against 10–18 mmol/L in a contemporary screening population), how much of that spread is instrument and derivation method rather than biology, and how often does an outdated interval misclassify healthy people as having a high gap?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, as an instrument property. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep, acid–base sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Five datasets: three direct healthy-volunteer derivations (Roberts 1997: 5–10, 9–14 and 8–13 mmol/L on three analysers in the same volunteers; Lolekha 2001: 3–11 mmol/L on four ion-selective-electrode analysers in 124 volunteers, against 8–16 or 9–18 mmol/L on the older continuous-flow methods; Chionh 2022: 10–18 mmol/L in 284 screening volunteers) and two indirect derivations from patient populations with healthy or normal-electrolyte subgroups (Ayala-Lopez 2020: 7–18 mmol/L, median 13, in a 17,137-patient derivation, with 5% of healthy adults misclassified as high by the previous 6–16 mmol/L interval; Pratumvinit 2020: all-patient intervals 9–19, 5–15 and 5–15 mmol/L across three hospitals, with albumin shifting the gap). The 3–11 and 10–18 mmol/L intervals may never be merged: the spread is method, not biology. Values print in mmol/L, numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity. The potassium-inclusive gap (AGK, 14.6–22.5 mmol/L) is a different calculated quantity and is carded separately on its own card line.

cards.headline: Three-analyser volunteer study (Roberts 1997): the same healthy volunteers (aged 20–60) gave parametric intervals of 5–10 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) (Beckman Synchron CX3), 9–14 (Hitachi 717) and 8–13 (Vitros 950) — volunteer N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Three-analyser volunteer study (Roberts 1997): the same healthy volunteers (aged 20–60) gave parametric intervals of 5–10 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) (Beckman Synchron CX3), 9–14 (Hitachi 717) and 8–13 (Vitros 950) — volunteer N not documented in the record
cards.type: Direct healthy-volunteer reference-interval derivation on three analysers (N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Healthy volunteers aged 20–60 recruited from within a clinical laboratory, with serum sodium, chloride and total carbon dioxide measured on aliquoted specimens across three clinical laboratories of one university medical centre; the volunteer N is not documented in the abstract and this card prints 'N not documented' per the standing reference-floor labelling rule.
cards.result: Mean and standard deviations were calculated per method and parametric reference intervals (±2 SD) were 5 to 10 mmol/L for the Beckman Synchron CX3 analyser, 9 to 14 mmol/L for the Boehringer Mannheim Hitachi 717 analyser and 8 to 13 mmol/L for the Johnson & Johnson Vitros 950 analyser. The authors conclude that lowering the interval to 5–10 mmol/L may suit some analysers while 9–14 mmol/L suits others, and that laboratories must establish or verify the interval for their own instrumentation.
cards.watchOut: Same volunteers, three intervals spanning 5–14 mmol/L: the cleanest demonstration on this shelf that the interval belongs to the analyser. N not documented — the card is a method comparison, never a population norm on its own.

cards.headline: Ion-selective-electrode derivation (Lolekha 2001): 124 healthy volunteers on four analysers — anion gap reference range 3–11 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity), against 8–16 or 9–18 on the older continuous-flow analysers; the outdated range misinterprets values
cards.summary: Ion-selective-electrode derivation (Lolekha 2001): 124 healthy volunteers on four analysers — anion gap reference range 3–11 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity), against 8–16 or 9–18 on the older continuous-flow analysers; the outdated range misinterprets values
cards.type: Direct healthy-volunteer reference-interval derivation on four ion-selective-electrode analysers (124 volunteers)
cards.people: 124 healthy volunteers; clotted and lithium-heparinised blood measured on the Beckman E4A and Beckman Synchron CX5 (serum), the Nova CRT (serum and plasma) and the Nova Stat Profile Ultra; anion gap calculated as [Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−)]; reference ranges set by non-parametric percentile estimation.
cards.result: Electrolyte reference values were similar across analysers, with Nova bicarbonate ranges higher than Beckman values. For the anion gap, the reference ranges were low but similar to other ion-selective-electrode studies (3–11 mmol/L), and lower than the previous continuous-flow ranges (8–16 or 9–18 mmol/L) obtained with flame photometry and colorimetry. The authors warn that the widespread use of ion-selective electrodes has lowered the anion gap range and that using the outdated 8–16 mmol/L range leads to misinterpretation — an analyser-specific range must be used.
cards.watchOut: The 3–11 mmol/L interval is the low anchor of this shelf and belongs to ion-selective-electrode measurement; printing it beside a modern screening interval (10–18) without the method note would manufacture a contradiction that is really a method change.
cards.source: Lolekha PH et al. Reference ranges of electrolyte and anion gap on the Beckman E4A, Beckman Synchron CX5, Nova CRT, and Nova Stat Profile Ultra. cards.headline: Large indirect derivation (Ayala-Lopez 2020): 17,137 adult and paediatric patients at Yale–New Haven — healthy-adult interval 7–18 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity), median 13, and 5% of healthy adults misclassified as high by the previous 6–16 interval
cards.summary: Large indirect derivation (Ayala-Lopez 2020): 17,137 adult and paediatric patients at Yale–New Haven — healthy-adult interval 7–18 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity), median 13, and 5% of healthy adults misclassified as high by the previous 6–16 interval
cards.type: Indirect (retrospective patient-population) reference-interval derivation, 17,137 patients with a healthy-adult interval
cards.people: Retrospective derivation from 17,137 adult and paediatric patients presenting to Yale–New Haven Hospital outpatient clinics, emergency department or intensive care units, 2012–2017; the healthy-adult interval was derived within that population, with workup patterns, repeat-testing variation and a subgroup with annual testing also examined. Derivation kind: indirect (patient-population derivation with a healthy-adult interval), stated here per the shelf's derivation rule.
cards.result: The new reference interval was 7 to 18 mmol/L with a median of 13 mmol/L in healthy adults, with no significant differences by sex or age partitioning. Against the previous interval of 6 to 16 mmol/L, 5% of healthy adults, 23% of emergency-department adults and 18% of intensive-care adults were misclassified as having high values. Most increased gaps that were repeated normalised by 12 hours, and in the annual-testing subgroup the median within-person change from 2015 to 2016 was about 13%. The authors argue for an appropriate interval and note a moderate degree of individuality.
cards.watchOut: An indirect derivation: the 'healthy adult' interval is extracted from a hospital population, not measured in recruited volunteers — derivation kind prints with the interval. The 5% misclassification figure is the practical cost of an outdated interval.
cards.source: Ayala-Lopez N et al. Interpreting Anion Gap Values in Adult and Pediatric Patients: Examining the Reference Interval. The journal of applied laboratory medicine. 2020. PMID: 32445342. cards.headline: Three-hospital instrument study (Pratumvinit 2020): all-patient intervals 9–19, 5–15 and 5–15 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) on two platforms; normal-electrolyte subgroup intervals 10–17, 6–14 and 5–12; hypoalbuminaemia lowered and hyperalbuminaemia raised the gap
cards.summary: Three-hospital instrument study (Pratumvinit 2020): all-patient intervals 9–19, 5–15 and 5–15 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) on two platforms; normal-electrolyte subgroup intervals 10–17, 6–14 and 5–12; hypoalbuminaemia lowered and hyperalbuminaemia raised the gap
cards.type: Indirect multi-hospital instrument-comparison derivation (consecutive adults, three hospitals, two platforms)
cards.people: Consecutive adults (≥18 years) with samples sent for electrolytes and creatinine at three Southeast Asian hospitals — one using the cobas 8000 and two the Architect c16000; intervals derived for all patients and for the subgroup with normal electrolytes, and compared by albumin group. Derivation kind: indirect (consecutive patient samples), stated per the shelf's rule.
cards.result: Anion gap means differed significantly (P < 0.001) between the three hospitals in all patients and in the normal-electrolyte subgroup. Reference intervals from all patients were 9–19, 5–15 and 5–15 mmol/L, and for the normal-electrolyte subgroup 10–17, 6–14 and 5–12 mmol/L respectively. Compared with the normal-albumin group, hypoalbuminaemia patients showed lower anion gaps in two hospitals (P < 0.001, P = 0.03), while hyperalbuminaemia patients showed higher gaps in all three (P < 0.001). The authors conclude different instruments produce different gaps, with a weak correlation between albumin and the gap.
cards.watchOut: Two hospitals on the same platform (Architect c16000) still produced different subgroup intervals — population and derivation sit alongside instrument as sources of spread. Albumin shifts the gap, so an interval derived in low-albumin patients does not transfer to healthy adults.
cards.source: Pratumvinit B et al. Anion gap reference intervals show instrument dependence and weak correlation with albumin levels. cards.headline: Contemporary screening derivation (Chionh 2022): 284 health-screening volunteers — verified interval 10–18 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) (median 13), unchanged in the 156-person no-suboptimal-indicators subcohort; the potassium-inclusive AGK interval was 14.6–22.5
cards.summary: Contemporary screening derivation (Chionh 2022): 284 health-screening volunteers — verified interval 10–18 mmol/L (numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity) (median 13), unchanged in the 156-person no-suboptimal-indicators subcohort; the potassium-inclusive AGK interval was 14.6–22.5
cards.type: Direct health-screening-volunteer reference-interval derivation (284 volunteers; 156-person subcohort)
cards.people: 284 health-screening participants with no major illnesses who volunteered surplus blood, tested in an internationally accredited laboratory (median age 35 years, BMI 23.4 kg/m2, GFR 106 mL/min/1.73 m2); anion gap calculated as [Na+] − [Cl−] − [HCO3−] and AGK as [Na+] + [K+] − [Cl−] − [HCO3−]; intervals at the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles, with a subcohort of 156 individuals with no suboptimal health indicators.
cards.result: Median anion gap was 13 mmol/L and the reference interval 10–18 mmol/L at a 99% level of confidence; the interval was the same in the 156-person subcohort. Statistically significant differences by sex, race, obesity and serum albumin amounted to 1 mmol/L between subgroups. Median AGK was 17.7 mmol/L with a reference interval of 14.6–22.5 mmol/L. The authors conclude the 10–18 mmol/L interval is valid for laboratories with similar electrolyte intervals, and that the lower values expected with current techniques were not observed.
cards.watchOut: AGK (potassium-inclusive) is a different calculated quantity from the standard gap — its 14.6–22.5 mmol/L interval must never be quoted as an anion-gap interval. This contemporary direct derivation (10–18) sitting above the 2001 ion-selective derivation (3–11) is the shelf's central caution against merging intervals.
cards.source: Chionh CY et al. Serum anion gap revisited: a verified reference interval for contemporary use. Internal medicine journal. 2022. PMID: 34028972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: five datasets, one lesson — the anion gap interval belongs to the analyser and the derivation (3–11 mmol/L by ion-selective electrode in 2001; 10–18 mmol/L in 2022 screening volunteers; 7–18 indirect), and an outdated interval misclassifies 5% of healthy adults as high
cards.summary: Synthesis: five datasets, one lesson — the anion gap interval belongs to the analyser and the derivation (3–11 mmol/L by ion-selective electrode in 2001; 10–18 mmol/L in 2022 screening volunteers; 7–18 indirect), and an outdated interval misclassifies 5% of healthy adults as high
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: three direct healthy-volunteer derivations (Roberts 1997, N not documented; Lolekha 2001, 124 volunteers; Chionh 2022, 284 volunteers) and two indirect patient-population derivations (Ayala-Lopez 2020, 17,137 patients; Pratumvinit 2020, three hospitals). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame acid–base physiology briefly; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so.
cards.result: No single 'normal anion gap' exists on this evidence. Within one 1997 study the same volunteers spanned 5–14 mmol/L across three analysers; across two decades the direct derivations span 3–18 mmol/L. Print every interval with its analyser, its derivation kind (direct volunteer vs indirect patient-population) and its population — and keep AGK (14.6–22.5 mmol/L) separate from the standard gap. Values are in mmol/L, numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Normal kidney size on ultrasound by population: European volunteer medians 11.2 cm (left) and 10.9 cm (right) against Jamaican means of 9.7 and 10.0 cm and a Saudi right-kidney mean of 9.79 cm — no length is a universal normal (5 populations)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal kidney dimensions on ultrasound — renal length, width, thickness, cortical thickness and volume — by side, sex and body size, how much smaller are the Saudi, Kuwaiti and Jamaican population means than the classic European volunteer medians, and does renal length actually fall with age once body size is accounted for?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Body Constitution · Female · Humans · Kidney/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Ultrasonography · Adolescent · Aged, 80 and over · Body Height · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Kuwait · Organ Size · Young Adult · Saudi Arabia · Kidney/diagnostic imaging,anatomy & histology · Prospective Studies · Ultrasonography/methods · Cross-Sectional Studies · Jamaica · Random Allocation · Turkey · Spleen/diagnostic imaging,anatomy & histology · Liver/diagnostic imaging,anatomy & histology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, population by population. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, kidney sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The population gradient is the content: the classic European random-sample medians (Emamian 1993; 665 volunteers: length 11.2 cm left, 10.9 cm right; volumes 146 cm³ left, 134 cm³ right) sit about 1.5 cm above the Jamaican means (Barton 2000; 49 adults: 9.7 ± 0.7 cm right, 10.0 ± 0.7 cm left) and the Saudi right-kidney mean (Alyami 2024; 95 adults: 9.79 cm right, 10.1 cm left), with Kuwaiti means between (El-Reshaid 2014; 252 adults: 10.68 ± 1.4 cm right, 10.71 ± 1.0 cm left; minimum cortical thickness 0.6 cm). Left exceeds right in every dataset. The age question is genuinely unsettled: size fell with age, almost entirely through parenchymal reduction, in the European sample, while the Kuwaiti dataset found no significant age variation in length or cortical thickness — printed as a disagreement, not a consensus. The Turkish cohort (Tiryaki 2024; 1,918 adults) is shared with the spleen shelf #7721 for its spleen limb and is carded here for its kidney limb only, with its abstract-level findings stated as such. Each card carries its population; no length prints as a universal normal.

cards.headline: European random sample (Emamian 1993): 665 volunteers — median renal length 11.2 cm left and 10.9 cm right, median volumes 146 cm³ left and 134 cm³ right; size fell with age almost entirely through parenchymal reduction, and volume correlated best with total body area
cards.summary: European random sample (Emamian 1993): 665 volunteers — median renal length 11.2 cm left and 10.9 cm right, median volumes 146 cm³ left and 134 cm³ right; size fell with age almost entirely through parenchymal reduction, and volume correlated best with total body area
cards.type: Population sonographic reference study, age- and sex-stratified random sample (665 adult volunteers) — European population
cards.people: Age- and sex-stratified random sample of 665 adult volunteers aged 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 years; length, width and thickness of the kidney and its central echogenic area and upper-pole parenchymal thickness measured prone (94 subjects also measured supine, with no significant difference), and kidney, central-area and parenchymal volumes calculated.
cards.result: Median renal lengths were 11.2 cm on the left side and 10.9 cm on the right side. Median renal volumes were 146 cm3 in the left kidney and 134 cm3 in the right kidney. Renal size decreased with age, almost entirely because of parenchymal reduction. Renal volume correlated best with total body area; renal length correlated best with body height. The authors conclude renal volume is the most exact measure of renal size, while length is the most practical clinical measurement.
cards.watchOut: These are the classic textbook-adjacent numbers, and they are the LARGEST on this shelf: quoting 11.2 cm as 'normal' mislabels the healthy Jamaican and Saudi means below as small. Medians, not means — do not average them with the mean-based datasets.

cards.headline: Kuwaiti screened adults (El-Reshaid 2014): 252 healthy adults — mean length 10.68 ± 1.4 cm right and 10.71 ± 1.0 cm left, minimum cortical thickness 0.6 cm; length correlated with weight and BMI but not height, and did NOT vary significantly with age
cards.summary: Kuwaiti screened adults (El-Reshaid 2014): 252 healthy adults — mean length 10.68 ± 1.4 cm right and 10.71 ± 1.0 cm left, minimum cortical thickness 0.6 cm; length correlated with weight and BMI but not height, and did NOT vary significantly with age
cards.type: Population sonographic reference study in screened healthy Kuwaiti adults (252 adults)
cards.people: 252 healthy individuals self-referred to a renal clinic in Kuwait (January 2006 to December 2011), screened for absence of renal abnormalities; sonographic renal length and cortical thickness measured, with weight, height, BMI and body surface area recorded and reference graphs generated across five age groups (18–30 to 61–80 years).
cards.result: Mean renal lengths were 10.68 ± 1.4 cm (right) and 10.71 ± 1.0 cm (left) (P = 0.56), without a significant change with age. Minimum cortical thickness was 0.6 cm. Renal length correlated with weight (P < 0.01) and BMI (P < 0.01) but not with height. There was no difference in renal size or cortical thickness in patients older than 60 years despite an age-related decline in glomerular filtration rate (P < 0.001). The authors conclude renal length and cortical thickness did not vary significantly with age.
cards.watchOut: This dataset contradicts the European age gradient on the same measurement — the disagreement prints, it is not averaged away. Self-referred clinic attenders screened healthy are not a random population sample, and the card says so.
cards.source: El-Reshaid W et al. Sonographic assessment of renal size in healthy adults. Medical principles and practice : international journal of the Kuwait University, Health Science Centre. 2014. PMID: 25060323. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Saudi prospective study (Alyami 2024): 95 healthy adults — right kidney length 9.79 cm, width 5.09 cm, thickness 4.10 cm; left length 10.1 cm; men's kidneys larger than women's
cards.summary: Saudi prospective study (Alyami 2024): 95 healthy adults — right kidney length 9.79 cm, width 5.09 cm, thickness 4.10 cm; left length 10.1 cm; men's kidneys larger than women's
cards.type: Prospective population sonographic reference study in healthy Saudi adults (95 adults)
cards.people: Prospective single-centre study in Jazan City, Saudi Arabia (February to August 2022): 95 healthy adult participants underwent abdominal ultrasonography with renal length, width and thickness measured and sex, age, height and weight documented.
cards.result: Right-kidney mean dimensions were length 9.79 cm, width 5.09 cm and thickness 4.10 cm; the left kidney measured 10.1 cm (length), 5.09 cm (width) and 4.10 cm (thickness). The left kidney was larger than the right, and male participants had larger kidney measurements than female participants. A positive correlation was observed between left-kidney thickness and sex, while no significant correlations were found with age, weight or height overall. The study provides population reference tables.
cards.watchOut: A small (N = 95), single-city dataset: its means describe Jazan adults, not a regional norm. Identical width and thickness values for the two sides are as published and are not corrected here.
cards.source: Alyami AS et al. Normal sonographic measurements for kidney dimensions in Saudi adult population: A cross-sectional prospective study. Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38875368. cards.headline: Jamaican random sample (Barton 2000): 49 healthy adults — mean length 9.7 ± 0.7 cm right and 10.0 ± 0.7 cm left, the smallest means on this shelf; lengths were not associated with height in either sex

cards.type: Population sonographic reference study in randomly selected healthy Jamaican adults (49 adults)
cards.people: 49 randomly selected healthy adult Jamaicans; sonographic renal length and width measured, with renal surface area and renal index (renal length relative to parenchymal assessment) calculated by sex and side.
cards.result: Mean length of the right kidney was 9.7 ± 0.7 cm and of the left 10 ± 0.7 cm; the left kidney was longer than the right overall and in males. There was no difference in width between sides overall or within either gender. Weight was associated with kidney width in males (not females) and with left-kidney length in females only. Lengths and widths were not associated with height in either gender, and renal surface area was similar between genders and sides. Renal index was 20.92 (right) and 22.86 (left) in males and 23.76 (right) and 25.54 (left) in females, as published.
cards.watchOut: The smallest dataset on the shelf (N = 49 — above the ~10-human floor, with its N printed here on the face): it establishes that a healthy population mean can sit 1.5 cm below the European median, and nothing finer than that.

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: European random sample (665 volunteers), Kuwaiti screened adults (252), Saudi prospective adults (95), Jamaican random sample (49) and the Turkish community cohort (1,918; shared with shelf #7721 for its spleen limb, counted once per measurement). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall frame kidney structure and function briefly; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Cross-point: intrarenal Doppler resistive index (a flow index, not a dimension) is a different shelf.
cards.result: Print every length with its population, side and summary statistic (median vs mean). The consistent findings are asymmetry (left > right everywhere) and body-size correlation (volume best with total body area; length with height in the European sample, with weight/BMI in the Kuwaiti sample, with neither in the Jamaican sample — the correlates themselves vary by population). The age question stays open on this evidence and prints as a disagreement.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Urinary albumin excretion reference values in healthy adults (PHYS, 3 datasets, all 1988–1993 RIA/turbidimetric era — era on the face): excretion rate 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day), daytime higher than overnight, high within-person variability; third dataset mixed ages 6–39, flagged
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for urinary albumin excretion — the distribution and upper reference range for overnight albumin excretion rate, the albumin/creatinine ratio and first-morning urine albumin concentration — how much higher is excretion in daytime ambulant than overnight recumbent samples, how large is within-person variability on repeat measurement, and how do the reference values shift across age and sex in the years around puberty? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, glomerular filtration / tubular handling sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded. Datasets: 3 independent populations, all 1988–1993 radioimmunoassay / turbidimetric era — the era prints on the face.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Albuminuria/urine · Child · Creatinine/urine · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Three independent datasets, all 1988–1993 radioimmunoassay / turbidimetric era — the era prints on the face, because all three predate modern immunoturbidimetric/HPLC albumin assays and creatinine standardisation, and no figure may be printed as a current-assay reference interval without the assay era beside it. Watts 1988 (127 healthy normotensive adults) derived reference values for concentration, albumin/creatinine ratio (mg/mmol) and excretion rate (µg/min): distributions positively skewed, Gaussian after log transformation, excretion significantly higher in daytime ambulant than overnight recumbent samples (P < 0.001), and within-person variability on repeat measurement high and comparable across all three expressions. Giampietro 1988 (122 healthy subjects; the paper's 145 diabetic patients are not counted) gives the healthy excretion-rate range 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day). Yokoyama 1993 (2,990 healthy individuals aged 6–39 — a mixed child–adult dataset, flagged on the face; only its 17–39 bands are adult data) gives first-morning concentration by age and sex: 1.3–2.2 mg/dL at ages 6–11, rising through puberty with significant sex differences at 12–14, then falling after 17 to 3.3 mg/dL (females) and 2.9 mg/dL (males); its one internally inconsistent abstract figure is omitted at build, per the row. The three expressions are never merged into one range. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall) is framing only; the shelf rests on these datasets.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 3 (Watts 1988, Clinica Chimica Acta — 127 healthy normotensive adult volunteers, 59 men and 68 women, mean age 33.3 years, radioimmunoassay): reference values derived for urine albumin concentration, albumin/creatinine ratio (mg/mmol) and albumin excretion rate (µg/min) in overnight recumbent and daytime ambulant samples; distributions positively skewed and Gaussian after log transformation; excretion significantly higher in daytime ambulant than overnight recumbent samples (P < 0.001), and within-person variability on repeat measurement was high and comparable across all three expressions

cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — urinary albumin reference values, overnight vs daytime, radioimmunoassay (1988)
cards.people: 127 healthy, normotensive volunteers (mean age 33.3 years, SD 12.4; 59 males, 68 females) measured by a conventional radioimmunoassay in overnight recumbent and daytime ambulant samples, with two repeated measurements for variability. A 1988 radioimmunoassay-era dataset — the era prints on the face of this shelf.
cards.result: Reference values were obtained for urine albumin concentration (mg/l), albumin/creatinine ratio (mg/mmol) and albumin excretion rate (µg/min). The frequency distributions of all three were positively skewed but became Gaussian on logarithmic transformation. Albumin excretion was significantly higher in daytime, ambulant samples than in overnight, recumbent samples (P < 0.001). Surface area was not correlated with urine albumin concentration but was negatively correlated with albumin/creatinine ratio (P < 0.05), due to the association between surface area and creatinine excretion. Urine albumin concentration was negatively correlated with age, due to a higher urine flow rate in older subjects; there was no significant association with sex or with mean arterial blood pressure in the normal range. Variability on repeat measurement was high and comparable for all three expressions, and not significantly less in overnight recumbent than in daytime ambulant samples.
cards.watchOut: 1988 radioimmunoassay-era values: no figure from this dataset may be printed as a current-assay reference interval without the assay era beside it. The abstract reports that reference values were derived for the three expressions without printing the numeric intervals for each — none are reconstructed here; the numeric range on this shelf comes from dataset 2.
cards.source: Watts GF et al. Urinary albumin excretion in healthy adult subjects: reference values and some factors affecting their interpretation. Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry. 1988. PMID: 3370833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 3 (Giampietro 1988, Clinical Biochemistry — radioimmunoassay developed and applied to 122 healthy subjects; the 145 diabetic patients in the same paper are not counted): healthy albumin excretion rate range 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day), with 20% of the diabetic cohort exceeding the previously chosen 15 µg/min microalbuminuria threshold
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 3 (Giampietro 1988, Clinical Biochemistry — radioimmunoassay developed and applied to 122 healthy subjects; the 145 diabetic patients in the same paper are not counted): healthy albumin excretion rate range 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day), with 20% of the diabetic cohort exceeding the previously chosen 15 µg/min microalbuminuria threshold
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — urinary albumin excretion rate by radioimmunoassay, healthy subjects (1988)
cards.people: 122 healthy subjects in whom albumin excretion rate (µg/min) was measured by the authors' newly developed radioimmunoassay (sensitivity 0.39 ± 0.08 mg/L, coefficient of variation 5–8%, reliable on previously frozen samples), alongside 145 diabetic patients (115 type 1, 30 type 2) who are part of the paper's clinical limb and are NOT counted in this dataset. A 1988 radioimmunoassay-era dataset — the era prints on the face.
cards.result: The distribution of albumin excretion rate values in healthy subjects and diabetic patients was not normal, and was normalised by log or square-root transformation. Seventy-three percent of diabetic patients lay within the normal (healthy) range of 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day, converting at 1 µg/min = 1.44 mg/day). Twenty percent of diabetic patients could be considered at risk of overt diabetic nephropathy because their albuminuria exceeded a threshold of 15 µg/min chosen previously as the cut-off for microalbuminuria. There was no correlation between albumin excretion rate and glycated haemoglobin, and only a weak correlation with diabetes duration in type 1 diabetic patients.
cards.watchOut: The healthy range (0.6–10.6 µg/min) is this shelf's adult excretion-rate anchor, and it is a 1988 RIA range — it predates modern immunoturbidimetric/HPLC albumin assays and creatinine standardisation. The diabetic cohort's figures describe that cohort against the healthy range; they are not reference data and are never counted toward the dataset's N.

cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 3 (Yokoyama 1993, Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice — first-morning urine albumin concentration in 2,990 healthy individuals aged 6–39 years, 1,713 male and 1,277 female, by turbidimetric immunoassay — a MIXED child–adult dataset, flagged on the face: only its 17–39-year bands are adult data): age- and sex-specific 95% reference values, 1.3–2.2 mg/dL in children aged 6–11, rising through puberty (with significant sex differences at ages 12–14) and falling after age 17 to 3.3 mg/dL in females and 2.9 mg/dL in males

cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — first-morning urine albumin concentration by age and sex, mixed ages 6–39 (1993)
cards.people: 2,990 healthy individuals aged 6 to 39 years (1,713 males, 1,277 females) whose first-morning urine albumin concentration was measured by turbidimetric immunoassay; reference values for each age group were obtained from the 95% confidence limits of the simulated distribution. Composition prints on every card: this dataset spans childhood, puberty and young adulthood — it is not an adult-only dataset. A 1993 turbidimetric-era dataset.
cards.result: Reference values were 1.3–2.2 mg/dL in children aged 6–11 years. Values rose through puberty — females reaching 3.9 mg/dL at age 12 years (P < 0.0001 for the rise) and males rising gradually to 3.9 mg/dL at age 16 years — with significant differences between males and females at ages 12 (P < 0.0001), 13 (P < 0.0001) and 14 (P < 0.0007). After 17 years, values decreased from 3.9 mg/dL to 3.3 mg/dL in females and to 2.9 mg/dL in males. The authors conclude reference values change with age and sex and should be taken into account in assessing diabetic nephropathy in insulin-dependent diabetes. (One internally inconsistent figure in this record's abstract — a female age-11 value printed as '22 mg/dl' against 2.2 mg/dL in its own children's range — is omitted at build per the row's flag, never printed as fetched.)
cards.watchOut: Mixed child–adult composition (ages 6–39) prints wherever this dataset's figures are used: its childhood and pubertal bands are not adult reference data. Its expression (mg/dL first-morning concentration) differs from datasets 1–2 (µg/min timed excretion; mg/mmol ratio) and is never merged with them into one range.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 independent populations, all 1988–1993 radioimmunoassay / turbidimetric era (the era prints on the face) — healthy adult albumin excretion rate 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day), daytime ambulant excretion higher than overnight recumbent with high within-person variability on repeat measurement, and first-morning concentration varying by age and sex through puberty before settling at 3.3 mg/dL (females) and 2.9 mg/dL (males) after age 17 in the mixed-age dataset

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: Watts 1988 (127 healthy adults, overnight vs daytime), Giampietro 1988 (122 healthy subjects, excretion-rate range) and Yokoyama 1993 (2,990 healthy individuals aged 6–39 — mixed child–adult, flagged). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, glomerular filtration / tubular handling sections — framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Cross-point: the built albuminuria shelves ask treatment questions in diabetes/CKD populations and supply no healthy-population reference distribution; nothing here sets a treatment target in disease.
cards.result: The three datasets express excretion differently (µg/min timed excretion, mg/mmol ratio, mg/dL first-morning concentration) and are never merged into one range. The adult overnight excretion-rate range is the established limb; any age-curve claim rests on the single mixed-age dataset and is emerging, as the stamp states.

shelves.title: Colestilan (colestimide; MCI-196) for hyperphosphataemia in CKD stage 5 on dialysis
shelves.question: In adults with chronic kidney disease stage 5 on dialysis and hyperphosphataemia, does colestilan (colestimide; MCI-196), compared with placebo or sevelamer, lower serum phosphorus?
shelves.mesh: Bile Acids and Salts/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Dyslipidemias/drug therapy/etiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hyperphosphatemia/drug therapy/etiology · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Renal Dialysis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications · Risk Factors · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers/blood · Calcium/blood · Cholesterol/blood · Phosphorus/blood · Polyamines/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/therapy · Sevelamer · Young Adult · Bile Acids and Salts/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Endpoint Determination · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Lipids/blood · Treatment Outcome · Bile Acids and Salts/administration & dosage · Hyperphosphatemia/blood/drug therapy · Kidney Diseases/blood/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit on serum phosphorus, a surrogate endpoint) — a phosphorus-surrogate base: every report's primary outcome is serum phosphorus (with LDL cholesterol as a genuine second action of the drug), and no report is powered for death, cardiovascular events or fractures; the binder-mortality question is homed separately at live #295 and is not borrowed here. Four reports: a 642-patient fixed-dose trial (significant phosphorus lowering only at 9 g/day and pooled 12/15 g/day), a 1-year placebo-withdrawal/sevelamer study whose abstract prints no total enrolment N (labelled N not documented for that figure), a 245-patient North American withdrawal trial (169 randomised), and a 120-patient 3-week dose trial. Two of the four reports are withdrawal designs in pre-stabilised populations. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common in every report. Colestilan, colestimide and MCI-196 are the same compound's European/North American, Japanese and development names, printed as the publications give them (clarification, not promotion).

cards.headline: Locatelli 2013: colestilan lowered phosphorus vs placebo only at 9 g/day (−0.28 mmol/L, ≈ −0.9 mg/dL) and pooled 12/15 g/day (−0.34 mmol/L, ≈ −1.1 mg/dL); LDL cholesterol fell at every dose
cards.summary: Locatelli 2013: colestilan lowered phosphorus vs placebo only at 9 g/day (−0.28 mmol/L, ≈ −0.9 mg/dL) and pooled 12/15 g/day (−0.34 mmol/L, ≈ −1.1 mg/dL); LDL cholesterol fell at every dose
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multiple fixed-dose trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 642 patients with CKD stage 5 on dialysis with hyperphosphataemia and dyslipidaemia, randomised to colestilan 3, 6, 9, 12 or 15 g/day or placebo.
cards.result: The mean phosphorus reduction vs placebo was significantly greater at 9 g/day (−0.28 mmol/L, ≈ −0.9 mg/dL) and pooled 12/15 g/day (−0.34 mmol/L, ≈ −1.1 mg/dL). The per cent LDL-cholesterol reduction was significantly greater than placebo at every dose from 3 g/day up (15.9% to 27.6% relative reduction, dose-dependent). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate-endpoint trial: phosphorus and LDL cholesterol, not clinical outcomes. The lower doses (3 and 6 g/day) did not significantly lower phosphorus vs placebo.
cards.source: Locatelli F et al. Evaluation of colestilan in chronic kidney disease dialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia and dyslipidaemia: a randomized, placebo-controlled, multiple fixed-dose trial. Nephrol Dial Transplant. 2013. PMID: 23610100. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Locatelli 2014: phosphorus 0.43 mmol/L (1.32 mg/dL) lower on colestilan than placebo at week 16 (P < 0.001); 1-year target attainment similar to sevelamer — enrolment N not documented in the abstract
cards.summary: Locatelli 2014: phosphorus 0.43 mmol/L (1.32 mg/dL) lower on colestilan than placebo at week 16 (P < 0.001); 1-year target attainment similar to sevelamer — enrolment N not documented in the abstract
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised study: 16-week flexible-dose period with a 4-week placebo-controlled withdrawal, then a 40-week extension vs sevelamer (1 year total)
cards.people: Patients with CKD 5D and hyperphosphataemia. N not documented: the fetched abstract prints no total enrolment figure for this report, so none is carded.
cards.result: At week 16 serum phosphorus was 0.43 mmol/L (1.32 mg/dL) lower with colestilan than placebo (P < 0.001, primary end point). Over 1 year the proportions reaching phosphorus ≤1.78 mmol/L (5.5 mg/dL) were similar (65.3% colestilan, 66.9% sevelamer).
cards.watchOut: The placebo contrast is a 4-week withdrawal period inside a longer open comparison, and the abstract's missing enrolment N means this report's size cannot be verified from the record — it is supporting, never the sole basis for the stamp.

cards.headline: Hertel 2015: continuing colestilan vs switching to placebo differed by −1.01 mg/dL (−0.33 mmol/L) in phosphorus change over 4 weeks (p < 0.001)
cards.summary: Hertel 2015: continuing colestilan vs switching to placebo differed by −1.01 mg/dL (−0.33 mmol/L) in phosphorus change over 4 weeks (p < 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled withdrawal study after open-label titration (North America)
cards.people: 245 patients titrated on colestilan 6–15 g/day; 169 randomised (85 continue colestilan, 84 placebo) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: The mean change in serum phosphorus differed by −1.01 mg/dL (−0.33 mmol/L) favouring colestilan (p < 0.001). cards.headline: Synthesis: colestilan lowers serum phosphorus in dialysis patients — POSSIBLE on a surrogate base of 4 reports
cards.summary: Synthesis: colestilan lowers serum phosphorus in dialysis patients — POSSIBLE on a surrogate base of 4 reports
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional population.
cards.result: Across four randomised reports colestilan lowered serum phosphorus vs placebo by roughly 0.26–0.43 mmol/L (≈ 0.8–1.3 mg/dL) at effective doses, with 1-year target attainment similar to sevelamer, and lowered LDL cholesterol at every dose. No report measures death, cardiovascular events or fractures. One report's enrolment N is not documented in its abstract and is labelled as such; two reports are withdrawal designs.
cards.watchOut: Do not borrow the binder-mortality question from live #295, and do not present phosphorus lowering as a clinical-outcome benefit. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common harm throughout.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PARTIAL beside live #1747: #1747 asks only whether ferric citrate improves haemoglobin and iron indices in NON-dialysis CKD with iron deficiency; this pack cards only the dialysis phosphate-binder slice (different population, different primary outcome) and pools nothing with #1747. The placebo contrast is a 4-week withdrawal tail: the large phase 3 trial's placebo comparison rests on its final 4-week placebo-control period in completers after a 52-week active-control period, not on a 52-week placebo arm. In that tail ferric citrate controlled phosphorus vs placebo (difference −2.2 ± 0.2 mg/dL, P < 0.001). A 28-day open-label dose-response trial and a 12-week head-to-head vs sevelamer (non-inferior) complete the base. The iron/ESA-sparing findings are prespecified secondaries of the same sponsor programme — real, but one programme's. JTT-751 is ferric citrate's development name as the publication gives it (clarification, not promotion).

cards.headline: Lewis 2015: ferric citrate controlled phosphorus vs placebo in the 4-week placebo-control tail (difference −2.2 ± 0.2 mg/dL, P < 0.001) after a 52-week active-control period
cards.summary: Lewis 2015: ferric citrate controlled phosphorus vs placebo in the 4-week placebo-control tail (difference −2.2 ± 0.2 mg/dL, P < 0.001) after a 52-week active-control period
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised sequential trial: 52-week active-control period, then a 4-week placebo-control period in ferric-citrate completers re-randomised to ferric citrate or placebo
cards.people: 441 subjects on dialysis randomised to ferric citrate or active control for 52 weeks; completers on ferric citrate were then re-randomised for the 4-week placebo-control period.
cards.result: Ferric citrate controlled phosphorus vs placebo with a mean treatment difference of −2.2 ± 0.2 mg/dL (P < 0.001) in the placebo-control period. Phosphorus during the 52-week active-control period was similar between ferric citrate and active control.
cards.watchOut: The placebo figure comes from a 4-week withdrawal tail in completers — the design leads. It is not a 52-week placebo-controlled result.
cards.source: Lewis JB et al. Ferric citrate controls phosphorus and delivers iron in patients on dialysis. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2015. PMID: 25060056. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lewis 2015 (labelled secondary slice of the same trial, never a second report): iron indices higher on ferric citrate, with less IV iron and less ESA use
cards.summary: Lewis 2015 (labelled secondary slice of the same trial, never a second report): iron indices higher on ferric citrate, with less IV iron and less ESA use
cards.type: Labelled slice — prespecified secondary outcomes of the phase 3 trial carded above (52-week active-control period)
cards.people: The same 441-subject dialysis trial carded above; this slice reports its prespecified iron and ESA-use secondaries only.
cards.result: Iron parameters were higher on ferric citrate (ferritin 899 ± 488 vs 628 ± 367 ng/mL; transferrin saturation 39% ± 17% vs 30% ± 12%; P < 0.001 for both). Ferric-citrate subjects received less intravenous elemental iron (median 12.95 vs 26.88 mg/week; P < 0.001) and less ESA (median 5,306 vs 6,951 epoetin-equivalent units/week; P = 0.04). Haemoglobin was statistically higher on ferric citrate (no magnitude printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: Secondaries from one sponsor programme. The haemoglobin/iron question in non-dialysis CKD stays homed at live #1747 — cross-point only, never pooled with this dialysis slice.
